# Volume III: Manuscript Binding

->**Description of the External Binding**<-

This historical volume is encased in a **dark brown leather binding**. The surface is decorated with extensive **blind-stamped** <term>blind-stamped: a decorative technique where patterns are pressed into the leather using heated metal tools without the use of gold or color</term> ornamentation. The design is composed of several concentric rectangular borders framing a central panel. This central area is filled with vertical bands of **foliate and floral motifs** <note>scrolling patterns of leaves and flowers</note>, a style that is repeated in the outer borders of the cover.

The leather shows significant signs of age and historical use. There are numerous scratches and scuffs across the surface, with a notable area where the leather has peeled away at the bottom left corner. 

On the right edge of the front board, two **brass clasps** <note>metal fasteners used to keep the heavy parchment or paper pages flat and protect them from humidity</note> remain attached. The spine of the book features **raised bands** <note>horizontal ridges created by the cords used to sew the book's sections together</note>. Though the gold-tooled decoration on the spine has faded, the Roman numeral **III** <note>original: "III"; signifies this is the third volume</note> is still partially legible.

<summary>This page provides a detailed description of the manuscript's physical exterior, a dark brown leather cover featuring traditional blind-stamped floral patterns and brass clasps. The spine identifies the work as the third volume of a collection.</summary>

<keywords>bookbinding, leather, blind-stamping, foliate motifs, brass clasps, raised bands, Volume III</keywords>

Positioned below this oval is a shield displaying **four red roses** arranged in the shape of a cross, a motif often associated with Rosicrucianism.*

# Behold, most kind reader. Macrobius: <note>Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius (fl. c. 400 AD) was a Roman provincial intellectual whose works on Neoplatonic philosophy and classical lore were essential to Medieval and Renaissance scholars.</note> he who previously was circulated as crippled, mutilated, and mangled; now for the first time complete, polished, and restored to his original luster, in which the dignity of the Greek majesty <note>Macrobius frequently quoted Greek authors, and earlier Renaissance editions often struggled to typeset or correctly transmit these Greek passages.</note>—as far as was possible—is found surviving.

<insert>
House of the Professed Society of Jesus <note>The Jesuits</note> at St. Nicholas in Prague
</insert>

<meta>This page follows the title page, serving as the formal dedication of the volume. Joannes Rivius, the editor introduced on the previous page, addresses his patron and mentor, Raphael Regius.</meta>

### Giovanni Rivio of Venice sends greetings to Raphael Regius, <note>Raphael Regius (c. 1440–1520) was a renowned Venetian humanist and professor of rhetoric, famous for his commentaries on Quintilian and Ovid.</note> a most venerable and learned man.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing a profile portrait of a man with a beard and a soft cap, possibly representing a classical author or a contemporary scholar. The letter is surrounded by floral and foliate motifs within a square border.</image-desc> Recently, as if returning to my studies after a long absence—and encouraged by certain friends, so that I might not seem the only one left idle in the schools—I have revised the writings of Macrobius Aurelius Theodosius regarding *The Dream of Scipio*. <note>original: "Somnium Scipionis." This was a famous section of Cicero's "Republic" for which Macrobius wrote a massive, influential commentary on the nature of the soul and the cosmos.</note> This work was, as they say, scattered with much "poppy and marjoram" <note>original: "papavere ac sansucco." A proverbial expression likely meaning the text was cluttered with errors or confusing additions that needed weeding out.</note>; I have also, to the best of my ability, corrected his *Banquets* <note>original: "Convivia," referring to the "Saturnalia," Macrobius's most famous work, which takes the form of a dinner-party conversation about history, myth, and grammar.</note>—those "bitter Attic olives," I might call them. This is a work, by Hercules, clearer, purer, and more brilliant than any gold. Without it, scholars can no more understand the "Venetian Maro" <note>Rivio refers here to the poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro). Macrobius’s "Saturnalia" is largely a deep-dive into Virgil’s hidden meanings; without it, Virgil's complexity remains hidden.</note>—that most eminent of all poets—than those who spend all day in a kitchen can hope to smell sweet. 

Therefore, it seemed to me that it would not be out of place to dedicate this work, whatever its worth, to you: a most venerable and eloquent man, who alone among all has perfectly mastered and long practiced both Greek and Latin. I have done this all the more gladly because I saw no one more honorable to whom I might dedicate these efforts of ours. For I am accustomed to take delight in your learning, most excellent Raphael, no less than in that of any other scholar, past or present. 

And lest anyone think I say this out of mere personal affection, I would have them know this: just as Praxiteles was made famous by his *Cnidian Venus*, Phidias by his *Olympian Jove*, and Mentor by his *Ephesian Diana*, <note>Rivio lists three of the most famous artists of Greek antiquity to create a comparison with the intellectual "artistry" of his recipient.</note> you are made famous by your "pictures." <note>original: "picturis." Rivio is likely playing on his recipient's name, Raphael, who shared a name with the great painter Raphael Sanzio, while also suggesting that Regius’s scholarly writings are as vivid and masterful as fine art.</note> You, therefore, in your characteristic modesty, will kindly and humanely recognize how much clarity we have added to this work. 

Furthermore, because I know that a few envious little people will immediately rise up against us and make a noise with their foot-stomping, <note>original: "supplosione." A classical reference to the Roman oratorical practice of stamping the feet in disapproval.</note> let me feel the protection of your patronage. For through your authority, a certain authority will be granted to this labor of ours. Farewell.

June 22, 1513. <note>original: "Decimo Calendas Iulii, M.D.XIII." The date follows the Roman calendar, counting ten days back from the first of July.</note>

<summary>This dedication letter from the editor Giovanni Rivio to the scholar Raphael Regius justifies the new edition of Macrobius by arguing that his works are essential for understanding Virgil. Rivio compares his editorial work to the fine arts and asks for Regius's protection against academic critics.</summary>
<keywords>Giovanni Rivio, Raphael Regius, Macrobius, Virgil, humanism, patronage, Renaissance scholarship, Venice, 1513</keywords>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the actual text of the Dream of Scipio, following the alphabetical index of Macrobius’s commentary. While the previous pages were reference tools, we now move into the narrative of Scipio Aemilianus as preserved by Cicero and annotated by Macrobius.</meta>

->THE DREAM OF SCIPIO<-

# THE DREAM OF SCIPIO, EXCERPTED FROM CICERO'S BOOK ON THE REPUBLIC.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting three scholars or astronomers using scientific instruments. On the left, a man observes a stone building crumbling, labeled "EARTHQUAKE" <note>original: "TERRE MOTVS"</note> above it, while using a quadrant. In the center, a man uses a large astronomical instrument on a pedestal. On the right, a man looks through a long sighting tube toward the sun, stars, and a crescent moon in the sky.</image-desc>

WHEN I HAD COME TO AFRICA: being a military tribune <term>tribunus militum</term> <note>A high-ranking officer in a Roman legion, often from the noble class.</note> of the fourth legion under the consul Manilius (as you know): nothing was more important to me than to meet King Massinissa, a man who, for good reasons, was a very close friend to our family. When I came to him, the old man embraced me and wept for some time; afterward, he looked up toward heaven and said, "I give thanks to you, supreme Sun, and to you, the rest of the heavenly beings, that before I depart from this life, I behold within my kingdom and under this roof Publius Cornelius Scipio, by whose very name I am refreshed; so never has the memory of that most excellent and unconquerable man <note>Referring to Scipio Africanus the Elder, the hero of the Second Punic War.</note> left my mind." Then I questioned him about his kingdom, and he questioned me about our republic. 

<margin>Back and forth</margin>When many words had been exchanged back and forth <note>original: "Vltro citroque"</note>, that day was finished for us. Later, after being received with royal hospitality, we prolonged our conversation late into the night, while the old man spoke of nothing except Africanus <note>Scipio Africanus the Elder.</note> and remembered all his deeds as well as his sayings. Then, when we departed to sleep, a deeper sleep than usual embraced me, both from the journey and because I had stayed awake until late at night. Here, then (I believe, indeed, because of what we had been talking about; for it often happens that our thoughts and conversations give birth in sleep to something like that which Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius, an early Roman poet often called the "father of Roman poetry."</note> writes about Homer, of whom he was clearly accustomed to think and speak very often while awake), Africanus showed himself to me in that form which was better known to me from his ancestral bust <note>original: "imagine"; Roman families kept wax or marble masks of their ancestors.</note> than from the man himself. When I recognized him, I truly shuddered. But he said, "Be present in mind, and cast away fear, Scipio, and commit what I shall say to your memory. 

"Do you see that city, which, although forced by me to obey the republic, renews its former wars and cannot remain at peace?" (He was pointing out Carthage from a high place, full of stars, bright and clear.) "To attack this city, you now come almost as a mere soldier. Within these two years, you, as consul, shall overthrow it; and that surname <note>Africanus.</note> which you have until now held as an inheritance from us, shall be won by you through your own deeds. When, moreover, you have destroyed Carthage, celebrated a triumph, and been censor..."

<sig>A</sig>

<summary>This page begins the famous "Dream of Scipio," where Scipio Aemilianus recounts meeting King Massinissa and subsequently dreaming of his grandfather, Scipio Africanus, who predicts his future military success against Carthage.</summary>
<keywords>Scipio Aemilianus, Scipio Africanus, Massinissa, Carthage, prophecy, Roman Republic, Cicero, dream theory</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the narrative of Scipio Aemilianus’s dream. After meeting King Massinissa on the previous page, Scipio has fallen asleep and is now being addressed by his grandfather by adoption, Scipio Africanus the Elder, who provides a prophecy of his future and begins a lecture on the nature of the soul and the cosmos.</meta>

<header>THE DREAM</header>
<sig>A</sig>

...[you will have] traveled as an envoy to Egypt, Syria, Asia, and Greece; you will be chosen consul again in your absence; you will finish a very great war; you will destroy Numantia <note>A city in Spain destroyed by Scipio in 133 BCE.</note>. But when you have been carried in your chariot to the Capitol <note>Referring to a Roman Triumph, the highest honor for a general.</note>, you will find the Republic <note>original: "repub."</note> thrown into confusion by the counsels of my grandson <note>Scipio Africanus the Elder is referring to Tiberius Gracchus, his grandson through his daughter Cornelia, whose radical land reforms led to political chaos.</note>. At this point, Africanus, it will be necessary for you to show to your fatherland the light of your character, talent, and wisdom. But I see at that time a fork, as it were, in the path of the fates.

<margin>Cycles</margin>
For when your age has completed eight times seven circuits and returns of the Sun; and when these two numbers [7 and 8], each of which is considered "full" for a different reason in the natural circuit, have completed your fatal sum: the whole state will turn itself to you alone and to your name. The senate, all good men, the allies, and the Latins will look to you. You will be the one on whom the safety of the state depends. In short: you must establish the Republic as dictator, if you escape the impious hands of your kinsmen <note>A veiled prophecy of Scipio’s death; he died suddenly in 129 BCE, and many suspected he was murdered by his political rivals, including his own relatives.</note>. When Laelius <note>Gaius Laelius, a close friend of Scipio present in the dialogue.</note> cried out at this, and the others groaned loudly, Scipio said, smiling gently: "I beg you, do not wake me from my sleep, and let there be peace. Hear the rest." But so that you may be more eager, Africanus, to protect the Republic, know this: for all those who have preserved, aided, or enlarged their fatherland, a certain place is defined in heaven where the blessed enjoy eternal life. For nothing is more pleasing to that supreme God who rules the whole world than the councils and assemblies of men joined by law, which are
<margin>What states are</margin>
called states. The rulers and preservers of these states set out from here and return here. At this point I (though I was terrified, not so much by the fear of death as by the plots of my own people) asked whether he himself and my father [Aemilius] Paullus were living, and others whom we thought were dead. "On the contrary," he said, "those people are alive who have flown out of the bonds of the body as if from a prison. Indeed, what you call life is death. But look, there is your father Paullus coming toward you." When I saw him, I broke into a flood of tears; but he, embracing and kissing me, forbade me to weep. And as soon as I had suppressed my tears and was able to speak, I said, "I beg you, most holy and excellent father, since this is life, as I hear Africanus say, why do I linger on earth? Why do I not hasten to come here to you?" "It is not so," he replied. "Unless that God, whose temple is everything you see here, has freed you from those prison-guards of the body, the way here cannot be open to you. For humans were created under this law: to tend that globe which you see in the middle of this temple, which is called Earth; and a soul was given to them from those eternal fires which you call stars and planets <note>original: "sydera & stellas"</note>, which, being round and spherical and animated by minds, complete their circles and orbits with wonderful speed. Therefore, Publius, you and all pious men must keep your soul in the custody of the body, nor must you depart from human life without the command of him who gave it to us, lest you seem to have shirked the human duty assigned by God. But Scipio, like your grandfather here and like me who fathered you, cherish justice and piety; which, while great toward parents and kin, is greatest toward the fatherland. That life is the way to heaven and to this assembly of those who have already lived, and being released from the body, inhabit that place you see." (Now, this was a circle shining with the most brilliant whiteness among the flames)
<margin>The Milky Circle</margin>
which you call the Milky Way <note>original: "orbē lacteū"</note>, as you have learned from the Greeks. From there, as I looked out, everything else appeared glorious and wonderful. There were stars which we have never seen from Earth, and they were of such magnitudes as we never suspected existed.
<margin>The Moon nearest the Earth</margin>
Of these, the smallest was the one furthest from heaven and nearest the Earth, shining with a borrowed light <note>The Moon, which reflects the sun's light.</note>. Moreover, the globes of the stars easily surpassed the size of the Earth. Indeed, the Earth itself then seemed so small to me that I was ashamed of our empire, with which we touch only a mere point of it. As I gazed at it more closely, Africanus said:
<margin>

</margin>
"I ask you, how long will your mind be fixed upon the ground? Do you not see into what temples you have come? All things are connected by nine circles, or rather spheres, one of which is the outermost celestial sphere, which embraces all the others: the supreme God himself, confining and containing the rest, in which are fixed those eternal courses of the stars as they revolve. Below this are seven spheres which revolve backwards with a motion contrary to that of the heaven. Of these, one globe is held by that which on Earth is named Saturn. Next is that brilliance, prosperous and healthy for the human race, which is called Jupiter; then the reddish one, dreaded by the Earth, which you call Mars. Then, below the middle region, the Sun holds its place: the leader, chief, and governor of the other lights, the mind and regulator of the world, of such great size that [it illuminates] all things...

# THE DREAM OF SCIPIO, PART II
## SCIPIONIS II
### A ii

<margin>Of Venus, Mercury, and the Moon</margin>
[The Sun] fills and illuminates all things with his light. Two courses follow him as companions: one is the path of Venus, the other of Mercury. In the lowest sphere, the Moon revolves, kindled by the rays of the Sun. Below the Moon, however, there is nothing that is not mortal and fleeting—except for the souls given to the human race by the gift of the gods. 
<margin>Or by motion</margin>
Above the Moon, all things are eternal. For the Earth, which is the ninth and occupies the middle, does not move; it is the lowest point, and toward it all heavy weights are carried by their own gravity. As I gazed at these things in a stupor, I eventually recovered myself and asked: "What is this great and so sweet a sound that fills my ears?"

<margin>The harmony of the heavens</margin>
"This is the sound," he replied, "which is produced by the impulse and motion of the spheres themselves. It is joined by unequal intervals, yet intervals which are nonetheless distinguished by a proportional logic. By tempering high notes with low, it creates various balanced harmonies. Such great motions cannot be stirred in silence, and nature dictates that the extremes sound low on one side and high on the other. For this reason, that highest starry sphere of heaven, whose revolution is more rapid, moves with a high and sharp sound, while this lunar and lowest sphere moves with the deepest sound. For the Earth, the ninth sphere, remains motionless in its fixed seat, 
<margin>Seven sounds</margin>
clinging always to the central place of the universe. However, those eight moving spheres, in which two have the same power <note>Referring to Mercury and Venus, which move at similar speeds relative to the Sun.</note>, produce seven distinct sounds with different intervals. This number [seven] is the knot of almost all things. Learned men, by imitating this with strings and songs, have opened for themselves a path back to this celestial place, just as others have done who, with outstanding genius, cultivated divine studies during their human lives. The ears of men, filled with this sound, have grown deaf. Indeed, you have no 
<margin>The Cataracts</margin>
duller sense than your hearing. It is just like where the Nile plunges from the highest mountains at the place called the Cataracts <note>original: "catadupa"</note>; the tribe that inhabits that place lacks the sense of hearing because of the magnitude of the noise. But this sound of the whole world’s rapid revolution is so great that human ears cannot capture it, just as you cannot look directly at the Sun; your eyesight and senses are overwhelmed by its rays." While I marveled at these things, I nevertheless kept turning my eyes back to the Earth.

Then Africanus said: "I perceive that you are even now contemplating the seat and home of men. If it seems small to you—as it truly is—then look always upon these celestial things and despise those human ones. For what fame can you achieve from the speech of men, or what glory that is worth seeking? You see that the Earth is inhabited in scattered and narrow places, and that between those 'spots' where people live, vast wildernesses are spread. Those who inhabit the Earth are not only so separated that nothing can flow between them from one to another, but they stand partly oblique, partly transverse, and partly even directly opposite to you <note>Referring to the 'Antipodes' or people living on the opposite side of the globe.</note>. From these people, you certainly can expect no glory. You perceive, moreover, that the same Earth is, as it were, girded and 
<margin>Zones of the heavens</margin>
surrounded by belts. You see that two of these, which are most distant from each other and rest upon the very poles of the heavens on both sides, are stiff with frost. The middle and largest zone, however, is scorched by the heat of the Sun. Two zones are habitable. Of these, the southern one (in which those who dwell there plant their footsteps opposite to yours) has nothing to do with your race. But this other one, situated to the North, see how small a part of it touches you! For all the land which you inhabit, narrowed at the poles and wider at the sides, is a small island, surrounded by that sea which you call the 'Atlantic,' the 'Great Sea,' or the 'Ocean' on Earth. Yet you see how small it is despite such a great name! From these very lands that are cultivated and known, has either your name or that of any of us ever been able to cross this Caucasus mountains which you see, or swim across that Ganges? Who in the remaining parts of the East, or the furthest West, or the North or South, will ever hear your name? With these removed, you surely see in what narrow limits your glory wishes to spread itself. And as for those who do speak of us—how long will they speak? Even if the generations of future men should desire to pass down the praises of each of us, received from their fathers, to their descendants: nevertheless, because of the floods and fires of the earth, which must happen at certain times, we are unable to achieve a glory that is even long-lasting, let alone eternal. What does it matter that those born after you will talk about you, when there was no mention of you by those born before—who were no fewer in number and certainly better men? Especially since among them..."

<summary>Scipio Africanus the Elder explains the "Harmony of the Spheres" created by the celestial orbits and describes the Earth's geography to demonstrate the insignificance of human fame.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the celestial revelation given to Scipio Aemilianus by his grandfather, Scipio Africanus the Elder. Following the description of the celestial harmonies, Africanus now explains the "Great Year" and the true nature of the human soul as a divine, self-moving entity that must be cultivated through service to the state.</meta>

# THE DREAM
## SOMNIVM
### II

<margin>The turning year</margin>
...even those by whom our name can be heard: no one can achieve the memory of even a single year. For men usually measure the year only by the return of the sun—that is, of a single star. But in reality, when all the stars have returned to the same point from which they once set out, and have restored the same configuration of the whole sky after long intervals, then that can truly be called a "turning year" <note>original: "annus uertens." This refers to the 'Great Year' or 'Platonic Year,' a cycle of roughly 25,800 years when all celestial bodies return to their original positions.</note>. In this cycle, I hardly dare to say how many generations of men are contained. For just as the sun once seemed to fail and be extinguished for men when the soul of Romulus <note>The legendary founder of Rome, who was said to have been taken up to heaven during a solar eclipse.</note> entered these very shrines, so when the sun fails again in the same part of the sky and at the same time, then—with all the constellations and stars recalled to their beginning—consider a year to have been completed. Know that not even a twentieth part of this year has yet revolved. Therefore, if you despair of a return to this place, where all things exist for great and eminent men, how small then is that human glory which can scarcely pertain to a tiny part of a single year? Therefore, if you wish to look on high and behold this seat and eternal home, do not give yourself over to the talk of the common crowd, nor place the hope of your affairs in human rewards. 
<margin>Virtue draws one to true glory</margin>
It is necessary that Virtue <note>original: "uirtus"</note> itself, by its own charms, should draw you toward true glory. Let others see to what they say about you—but they will speak regardless. For all such talk is confined within the narrow regions which you see. It has never been everlasting for anyone; it is buried by the death of men and extinguished by the forgetfulness of posterity.

When he had said these things, I replied: "Truly, Africanus, if indeed a path to the entrance of heaven lies open to those who have served their country well—though from my boyhood, following in my father’s footsteps and yours, I have not failed your honor—now, however, with such a great reward set before me, I shall strive much more vigilantly."

And he said: "Strive indeed, and hold this truth: it is not you who are mortal, but this body. For you are not what that physical form declares you to be; rather, the mind of each man is who he is, not that shape which can be pointed to with a finger. 
<margin>Man can be called a god</margin>
Know therefore that you are a god <note>original: "Deum te igitur scito esse." A central Stoic idea that the rational soul is a fragment of the divine.</note>, if indeed he is a god who flourishes, who feels, who remembers, who foresees, and who so rules, moderates, and moves that body over which he is placed, just as that lead god rules this world. And as the eternal god moves the world, which is in some part mortal, so the everlasting soul moves the fragile body. For that which is always in motion is eternal. But that which brings motion to something else, and which is itself moved from elsewhere, must necessarily have an end to its living when it has an end to its motion. Only that which moves itself, because it is never deserted by itself, never indeed ceases to move; furthermore, for all other things that are moved, this is the fountain, this is the beginning <note>original: "principium"</note> of motion. 
<margin>The Beginning</margin>
But there is no origin for a beginning; for all things arise from a beginning, but the beginning itself cannot be born from any other thing. For it would not be a beginning if it were generated from elsewhere. And if it never rises, it certainly never sets. For if a beginning were extinguished, it could neither be reborn from another nor create another from itself, since all things must necessarily arise from a beginning. Thus it happens that the beginning of motion comes from that which is moved by itself. This, moreover, can neither be born nor die. Otherwise, the whole heaven and all of nature would necessarily collapse and stand still, and would not find any force by which they might be moved from a primary impulse.

Since it is clear, therefore, that what is moved by itself is eternal, who is there who would deny that this nature has been granted to souls? For everything that is agitated by an external pulse is inanimate. But that which is an animal <note>original: "anima" / "animal." In Latin, "animal" refers to anything possessing a soul or 'anima' (breath/life).</note> 
<margin>The nature and power of the soul</margin>
is stirred by an internal and its own motion. For this is the proper nature and power of the soul. If the soul is the only thing among all others that moves itself, then it was certainly not born, and it is eternal. Exercise this soul in the best matters! The best concerns are those regarding the safety of the fatherland. The soul, stirred and exercised by these, will fly more swiftly to this seat and its own home. And it will do this more quickly if, even then when it is shut up in the body, it stands out abroad and, contemplating those things which are outside, withdraws itself as much as possible from the body. For the souls of those who have surrendered themselves to the pleasures of the body, and have offered themselves as if they were servants to them, and who—by the impulse of lusts obedient to pleasures—have violated the laws of gods and men, wander around the earth itself after they have slipped out of their bodies. Nor do they return to this place until they have been tossed about for many ages."

He departed; I was released from sleep.

BOOK THE FIRST ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO
A iii

# THE FIRST BOOK OF THE MOST ELEGANT EXPOSITION BY MACROBIUS AVRELIVS THEODOSIVS, A MAN OF CONSULAR AND ILLUSTRIOUS RANK, ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO.

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut illustration on the left and a large historiated initial 'I' on the right. The woodcut depicts a figure labeled 'SCIPIVS' lying in a bed with a detailed canopy and patterned coverlet, eyes closed in sleep. The historiated initial 'I' is highly decorative, featuring intertwined foliage, flowers, and symmetrical scrollwork within a square border.</image-desc>

**I**NTER <note>The text begins with a large decorative 'I'.</note> the books of Plato and Cicero—both of whom, it is well known, established works concerning the republic—I have observed at the very outset, Eustathius <note>Macrobius addresses the work to his son, Eustathius.</note>, my sweetness and my pride in life, this primary difference: the former [Plato] organized a republic, while the latter [Cicero] reported on one. The one discussed what a republic *ought* to be; the other discussed what kind of republic had been established by our ancestors. Nevertheless, in this one aspect especially, Cicero’s imitation preserved a similarity to the work of Plato: for just as Plato, at the conclusion of his volume <note>Referencing the "Myth of Er" at the end of Plato's *Republic*.</note>, causes it to be revealed by a certain man who returned to life (which he seemed to have left behind) what the state of souls is once they have been stripped of their bodies—adding to this a significant description of the spheres and stars—a nearly identical face of things is narrated by Cicero’s Scipio <note>Scipio Aemilianus, the protagonist of Cicero's *Dream*.</note> as having been presented to him during his sleep. But why there was a need for such a device as that myth, or for such a dream in these particular books (in which they were speaking of the state of republics), and what relevance it had to describe circles, orbits, and spheres, or to treat the measurement of stars and the turning of the heavens amidst the established rules for governing cities—this seemed to me, and perhaps may seem to others, a matter worthy of investigation. We must not suspect that men of such excelling wisdom, who were accustomed to think only divinely in the pursuit of truth, would have added anything superfluous to a refined work.

<margin>The love of Justice</margin>
Concerning this, therefore, a few things must first be said, so that the purpose of the work we are discussing may become clearly known. Plato, looking deeply into the nature of all things and actions, noticed in every discourse proposed concerning the institution of a republic that a love of justice must be infused into minds. Without justice, not only a republic, but not even a tiny gathering of men, nor indeed a small household, will hold together. Furthermore, to instill this affection for justice in human hearts, he saw that nothing would be as effective as showing that the fruits of justice do not seem to end with the life of a man. But how could it be shown that these fruits endure and survive after a man's death, unless it were first established that the soul is immortal? Once the belief in the perpetuity of souls was established, he noticed it followed that certain places—once the bonds of the body are released—are assigned to them, according to the consideration of their good or evil merits. Thus in the *Phaedo* <note>original: "Phedone." Plato’s dialogue on the soul’s immortality.</note>, after the soul is raised to the true dignity of its own immortality by the light of unassailable reasons, there follows a distinction of the places which are owed to those leaving this life by that law which each man has enacted for himself by his way of living. So too in the *Gorgias* <note>Another Platonic dialogue that ends with a myth of judgment in the afterlife.</note>, after a debate conducted on behalf of justice, we are reminded of the condition of souls after the body with the moral gravity of Socratic sweetness. Therefore, Cicero followed the same pattern observantly in those volumes especially where he undertook to shape the state of a republic. For after he gave primacy to justice and taught that the soul does not perish after the living being dies, he finally asserted at the end of the work—through that "fable" (for so some call it)—where the soul goes after the body, or from whence it comes to the body. He did this to teach that a reward is reserved for the cultivation of justice, or a punishment for its neglect, for souls that are indeed immortal and destined to undergo judgment. Cicero is found to have preserved this order with no less judgment than the genius with which it was invented. After he gave the palm to justice in every leisure and business of the republic, in the sacred...

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Macrobius's commentary. Having established that Cicero modeled his "Republic" on Plato's, the author now addresses the specific literary device used at the end of both works: a supernatural revelation. He defends the use of "fables" (fictional narratives) in philosophical writing against critics like the Epicureans who argued that philosophers should only use literal, plain speech.</meta>

III
-># ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO<-

<margin>Er, who returned to life after death</margin>
...the dwelling of such souls and the secrets of the celestial regions at the very pinnacle of the completed work. He indicates where those who have managed the republic with prudence, justice, fortitude, and moderation must arrive, or rather, to where they must return. But that Platonic narrator of secrets was a man named Er, a Pamphylian <note>A region in southern Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey.</note> by nation and a soldier by profession. Having received wounds in battle, he appeared to have poured out his life; yet on the twelfth day, when he was finally to be honored by the funeral pyre along with others killed at the same time, he suddenly either recovered his soul or had retained it. He announced to the human race what he had done or seen during the days spent between both lives, as if making a public declaration. Although Cicero laments that this fable was mocked by the unlearned (as if he himself were conscious of the truth), he avoided the example of such foolish criticism. He preferred for his narrator to be awakened <note>original: "excitari narraturū," referring to Scipio waking from a dream.</note> rather than to return to life <note>original: "reuiuiscere," referring to Er's resurrection.</note>. And before we join together the words of the dream, we must explain which kind of men Tullius <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> mentions as having mocked Plato's fable, or why he himself does not fear the same happening to him. For by these words he does not mean the ignorant common folk, but a class of men ignorant of the truth under a pretense of expertise—people who had certainly read such things but were intent on criticizing them. We shall therefore say whom he refers to as having exercised a certain levity of judgment against such a great philosopher, for whom he also left a written accusation, and finally, what response should be given to these objections regarding the part necessary for this work. Once these are weakened (which is easy to do), then whatever bite of envy has ever been—or perhaps will be—hurled against Cicero's opinion or Scipio’s dream will be dissolved. The whole faction of the Epicureans <note>A school of philosophy that generally rejected the idea of an afterlife or divine intervention in human affairs.</note>, always wandering from the truth by a consistent error and thinking those things which they do not know are to be laughed at, mocked this sacred volume and the most venerable mysteries <note>original: "Augustissima... seria"</note> of nature.

<margin>Colotes the Epicurean</margin>
Indeed, Colotes, more notable for talkativeness among the followers of Epicurus, even recorded in a book those things about which he had bitterly joked. But other matters which he marked with insult—since they do not pertain to the dream discussed here—must be omitted by us in this place. Let us pursue that specific slander which, unless it is overturned, will remain a charge common to both Cicero and Plato. For he says that a fable ought not to have been invented by a philosopher, since no kind of fiction is suitable for those who profess the truth. "For why," he says, "if you wished to demonstrate the concept of celestial things or the condition of souls, was this not handled with a simple and absolute presentation? Instead, a persona was sought, and a sequence of events, and a novelty devised, and a stage of fiction composed, polluting the very gateway of seeking truth with a lie." These things, while they are thrown about regarding the Platonic Er, also attack the rest of our dreaming Africanus <note>Scipio Africanus the Younger, the protagonist of Cicero's dream.</note>. (For in both cases, the persona was chosen under an appropriate theme to be suitable for making the announcement). Let us resist this pressure, and let the slander, arguing in vain, be refuted; so that by dissolving one, the deeds of both may retain their uninjured dignity (as is right). Philosophy does not reject all fables, nor does it accept all of them. So that it may be easily discerned which it rejects and excludes as profane from the very threshold of sacred dispute, and which it even frequently and gladly admits, this must be explained through the levels of classification.

<margin>Why fables were invented</margin>
Fables—the very name of which indicates a profession of falsehood—were invented either solely for the sake of pleasing the ears, or for the sake of encouragement toward good character. They soothe the listener, such as the comedies which Menander <note>A famous Greek playwright of the "New Comedy."</note> or his imitators gave to be performed, or plots filled with the fictional misfortunes of lovers, in which the Arbiter <note>Petronius Arbiter, author of the *Satyricon*.</note> busied himself much, or in which we are sometimes surprised that Apuleius <note>Author of *The Golden Ass*, an early Roman novel.</note> toyed.

<margin>The genres of fables</margin>
This whole category of fables, which professes only the delights of the ears, the treatise of wisdom banishes from its sanctuary to the cradles of nurses. However, of those which encourage the reader's understanding toward some appearance of virtue, a second distinction is made. In some, the plot is based on fiction and the order of the narrative itself is woven through lies, such as those Aesopic fables famous for the elegance of their invention. But in others, the plot is indeed grounded in the solidness of truth, but this very truth is [presented] through certain composed and fictional...

<summary>Macrobius defends Cicero’s use of a dream narrative by comparing it to Plato’s "Myth of Er" and refuting Epicurean critics like Colotes. He begins a systematic classification of fables, distinguishing between those used for mere entertainment and those used by philosophers to convey moral and cosmic truths.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Macrobius’s defense of using "mythical narratives" in philosophy. Having introduced the "Dream of Scipio," he now classifies different types of fables, distinguishing between those that are mere entertainment and those that use allegory to protect sacred truths from the uninitiated.</meta>

IV
->### BOOK ONE ###<-

is brought forward. And this is now called a mythical narrative <note>original: "narratio fabulosa"</note>, not a mere fable: such are the sacred ceremonies of Hesiod and Orpheus <note>Hesiod and Orpheus were legendary Greek figures associated with the origins of the gods and mystical poetry.</note>, which are told as active accounts of the ancestry of the gods, just as the mystical meanings of the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, known for their secrecy and use of mathematical symbolism.</note> relate. Therefore, from this second division which we have mentioned, the first species—that which is conceived of falsehood for the sake of falsehood—is foreign to the books of philosophy. The following species is divided again into another distinction. For when truth underlies the argument, and it is a purely mythical narrative, more than one way of relating the truth through fiction is found. For either the context of the narrative is composed of base and unworthy things, shameful to the divine powers and resembling monsters—such as the adulteries of the gods, or Saturn cutting off the genitals of his father Caelus <note>Uranus/Heaven; Macrobius is referring to the violent Greek creation myths.</note>, and he himself in turn being cast into the waves by his son who seized the kingdom—a whole genre which philosophers prefer not to know; or, the understanding of sacred matters is expressed under a pious veil of fictions, hidden by honorable things and clothed in names. And this is the only kind of fiction that the song <note>or "treatise"</note> of a philosopher concerning divine matters admits. Since, therefore, neither the character Er nor the dreaming Africanus <note>Scipio Africanus the Younger, the narrator of the Dream of Scipio.</note> causes any injury to the discussion, but rather the expression of sacred things is hidden under these names while its dignity remains intact, let the accuser at last be taught to distinguish mythical narratives from mere fables, and hold his peace.

It must be known, however, that philosophers do not admit mythical narratives, even the permissible ones, into every discussion; they are accustomed to use them only when they speak of the soul, or of the powers of the air or the heavens, or of the other gods. Otherwise, when the treatise dares to raise itself to the highest and supreme God of all—who is called by the Greeks "The Good" and "The First of All" <note>original Greek: τ’ἀγαθόν πρωτοπαντόν</note>—or to the Mind, which the Greeks call *Nous* <note>original Greek: νοῦν</note>, which contains the original forms of things called "Ideas" <note>original Greek: ἰδέας</note> born from the supreme and perfect God; when, I say, they speak of these, of God and the Mind, they touch upon nothing mythical at all. But if they attempt to assign anything regarding these matters—which surpass not only speech but human thought itself—they fly to similes and examples. Thus Plato, when he had attempted to speak concerning "The Good" <note>original Greek: περὶ τ’ἀγαθόν</note>, 

<margin>What God is cannot be explained</margin>

did not dare to say what it *is*, knowing only this about it: that it is not possible for a human to know what its nature is. Indeed, he found the sun to be the only thing most similar to it among visible things, and through its likeness he opened a path for his discourse to raise itself to incomprehensible things. Therefore, antiquity fashioned no image for Him to be set up with the other gods, because the supreme God and the Mind born from Him are above nature, just as they are beyond the soul, where it is not lawful for fables to reach. Concerning the other gods, however (as I have said), and concerning the soul, they turn to mythical narratives not in vain nor merely to delight, but because they know that an open and naked exposition of herself is an enemy to Nature. Just as she has withdrawn the understanding of herself from the common senses of men by a varied covering and protection of things, so she willed that her secrets be treated by the wise through mythical narratives. Thus, the mysteries themselves are covered in the tunnels of figures, lest she offer her naked nature even to those who have attained such things; but let the highest men alone, who are conscious of the true secret with wisdom as their interpreter, be content, while the rest are kept by these protective figures from a cheapening of the secret, leading them instead to veneration.

<margin>Numenius and the Eleusinian Mysteries</margin>

Finally, the dreams of Numenius <note>A 2nd-century Neopythagorean philosopher.</note>—a man more curious than others about hidden things—betrayed that he had offended the divine powers because he had publicized the Eleusinian Mysteries by interpreting them. He saw in a dream the goddesses of Eleusis themselves standing before an open brothel in the habit of harlots; and when he wondered at this foulness, so unbecoming of the gods, they answered him in anger that they had been dragged by force by him from the sanctuary of their modesty and prostituted to every passerby. For the divine powers willed themselves to be known and worshipped in the way that antiquity itself spoke of them in myths—which assigned images and statues to those entirely foreign to such forms, and ages of both growth and decay to those who know them not, and various garments and ornaments to those who have no bodies. Following these, Pythagoras himself and Empedocles, Parmenides also and Heraclitus, spoke of the gods in myths; nor did Timaeus do otherwise when he followed the genealogy of the gods as it had been handed down. Having tasted these things <note>i.e., having provided this introduction</note> before we treat the words of the dream itself, and before the observation of the modes of dreaming is grasped, let us use the liberty of figures which...

<meta>This page transitions from Macrobius’s general discussion of philosophical fables to a specific scientific classification of dreams. He seeks to categorize Scipio’s dream to determine if it carries prophetic weight or is merely a trick of the mind.</meta>

-># ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO #<-

<margin>Types of dreams</margin>
...are thrust upon those at rest: antiquity placed them under definition and rule. Let us distinguish them, so that it may become known to which of these categories the dream we are dealing with should be applied. Of all the things that people seem to see while sleeping, there are five principal diversities and names. It is either an **oneiros** <note>original: "ὄνειρος"</note> according to the Greeks, which the Latins call a *somnium* (dream); or an **orama** <note>original: "ὄραμα"</note>, which is rightly called a *visio* (vision); or a **chrematismos** <note>original: "χρηματισμός"</note>, which is named an *oraculum* (oracle); or an **enypnion** <note>original: "ἐνύπνιον"</note>, which is called an *insomnium* (nightmare/non-prophetic dream); or a **phantasma** <note>original: "φάντασμα"</note>, which Cicero, whenever he had need of this name, called a *visum* (apparition). The last two of these—the *enypnion* and the *phantasma*—are considered unworthy of the care of interpretation, because they bring no power of divination. The **enypnion** <note>original: "ἐνύπνion"</note> occurs whenever a mental, physical, or external distress, of the sort that tired a person while awake, thrusts itself upon them while sleeping. In the mind: such as if a lover sees himself either enjoying or lacking his delights; or if one fearing a person threatening him with snares or power seems, from the image of his own thoughts, to have either encountered or escaped that person. In the body: if one gorged with wine or distended with food thinks he is either being suffocated by the abundance or relieved by heavy purging; or conversely, if one who is hungry seems to seek food, or one thirsty for drink seeks water, or even seems to have found it. In external fortune: when one thinks himself either increased in power or office according to his desire, or stripped of them according to his fear. Because these and similar things have disturbed the rest of the sleeper just as they preceded it from the state of his mind, they fly in along with sleep and vanish equally with it. Hence the name *insomnium* (non-prophetic dream): not because it is seen through sleep (for this is common to this type and all others), but because it is believed to exist only during the sleep itself while it is seen; after sleep, it leaves no usefulness or significance. That these nightmares are false, Maro <note>The poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro).</note> did not remain silent: *“But the spirits of the dead send false dreams <note>original: "insomnia"</note> to the sky,”* calling “the sky” here
<margin>The Sky</margin>
the region of the living, because just as the gods are above us, so we are held to be the "upper ones" to the dead. Describing love as well—whose cares nightmares always follow—he says: *“His features and words remain fixed in her heart, nor does care allow calm rest to her limbs.”* And after this: *“Sister Anna, what dreams <note>original: "insomnia"</note> terrify me in my suspense?”*

The **phantasma** <note>original: "φάντασμα"</note>, or "apparition," is this: when between wakefulness and deep rest, in a certain (as they say) cloud of the dawn of sleep, one who thinks himself still awake—having barely begun to sleep—seems to behold forms rushing toward him or wandering about, differing in nature, size, or appearance, and various disturbances of things, either joyful or turbulent. In this category is the **epialtes** <note>original: "ἐπιάλτης"; a Greek term for the "incubus" or "night-hag" effect, where a sleeper feels a heavy weight on their chest.</note>, whom popular belief
<margin>Apparition</margin>
imagines invades those resting and burdens them, pressed down by his weight while they are conscious. Since these two modes are received for no help in knowing the future, we are instructed in the art of divination by the three remaining types. An **oracle** <note>original: "oraculum"</note> is when, in sleep, a parent or another holy and grave person, or a priest, or even a god, openly announces what will or will not happen, what
<margin>Oracle</margin>
should be done or avoided. A **vision** <note>original: "visio"</note> is when someone sees something which happens in the same way it appeared: for instance, one seems
<margin>Vision</margin>
to see a friend living abroad (whom he was not thinking of) returning, and as he walks out, he meets the one he had seen and they embrace. Or one receives a deposit in the quiet of sleep, and in the morning a petitioner meets him, entrusting money to his protection and the custody of his faith to be hidden. A **dream** properly so-called <note>original: "Somnium proprie"</note> is that which covers its meaning with figures
<margin>Dream</margin>
and veils it in ambiguities, such that the significance of the thing being shown cannot be understood without interpretation. What kind of thing this is need not be explained by us, since everyone recognizes what it is from experience. Of this type, there are five species: it is either personal, alien, common, public, or general. It is "personal" when someone dreams of himself doing or suffering something; "alien" when he dreams of another; "common" when he dreams of himself together with another; it is "public" when he thinks something sad or joyful has happened to the city, the forum, the theater, or any public walls or acts; it is "general" when someone dreams that something has changed regarding the sun's orb, the lunar globe, the other stars, or the whole sky and all the lands. This, however, which...

<meta>This page continues the classification of dreams from the previous section. Having established the five general types of dreams (oracle, vision, dream, nightmare, and apparition), Macrobius now applies these categories specifically to the "Dream of Scipio" to prove its philosophical and prophetic validity.</meta>

# BOOK ONE #

Scipio reported what he had seen: his dream embraces those three types which alone are considered reliable <note>original: "probabilia," meaning those that carry prophetic weight</note> and touches upon every species of the dream itself. It is an **oracle** <note>original: "oraculum"</note> because both Paulus and Africanus—his two fathers, both holy and grave men, and neither of them strangers to the priesthood—announced to him what would happen. It is a **vision** <note>original: "visio"</note> because he beheld the very places in which he was to be after leaving the body, and what he himself would be like. It is a **dream** <note>original: "somnium"</note> because the height of the things told to him, covered by a depth of wisdom, cannot be opened to us except through the science of interpretation. 

It also refers to all the sub-species of the dream itself. It is **personal** <note>original: "proprium"</note> because he himself was led to the heights and learned of his own future. It is **alien** <note>original: "alienum"</note> because he discovered what state the souls of others have obtained. It is **common** <note>original: "commune"</note> because he learned that the same places were prepared for himself as for others of the same merit. It is **public** <note>original: "publicum"</note> because he recognized the victory of his fatherland, the destruction of Carthage, the triumphal procession to the Capitol, and the anxiety over future civil strife. It is **general** <note>original: "generale"</note> because, while still a living man, he grasped the heaven, the circles of the sky, and the harmony of their rotation—things new and unknown to him—as well as the movements of the stars and lights, and the situation of the whole earth, by looking both up and down upon them. 

Nor can it be said that the dream was unsuited to Scipio's person, even though it was "general" and "public," on the grounds that he had not yet attained the highest magistracy—indeed, as he says himself, he was still considered almost a common soldier. For they say that boys should not have dreams about the state of the city, unless they are seen by its ruler or magistrate, or unless many of the common people, rather than just one, have dreamed similar things. Therefore, in Homer, when Agamemnon published in the council of the Greeks the dream he had seen concerning the marshaling of the battle, Nestor—who aided the army no less by his wisdom than the youth did by their strength—conciliated their faith in the report by saying: "regarding the public state, we must believe a king's dream; if another had seen it, we would reject it as futile." <note>Homer, Iliad, Book 2. Nestor argues that the leader's dream carries the weight of the whole community.</note> But it was not out of place for Scipio to dream of the destruction of Carthage, even if he had not yet attained the consulship nor was the leader of the army; for he was to be the author of its fall. He heard of the victory to be made public by his own service, and as a man excelling no less in philosophy than in valor, he saw the secrets of nature.

<margin>
The gates
of sleep
</margin>
Having asserted these things—and because we previously mentioned Virgil as a witness to the falsehood of certain "nightmares" <note>original: "insomniorū"</note> and his verse describing the twin gates of sleep—if anyone should perchance wish to ask why the **gate of ivory** is assigned to false things and the **gate of horn** to true ones, he may be instructed by the authority of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on Homer and Virgil.</note>. Porphyry, in his commentaries, says that these same things were described by Homer under the same division. He says: "All truth lies hidden; yet sometimes the soul, when it is a little free from the duties of the body during sleep, beholds it. Occasionally it stretches its gaze, yet does not reach it; and when it does behold it, it sees not with a free and direct light, but through an intervening veil, which the bond of darkening nature draws over it." Virgil asserts that this is also in nature, saying: *"Look now: for I shall tear away every cloud which, drawn over your sight, dulls your mortal vision and spreads a damp fog around you."* <note>Virgil, Aeneid, Book 2. Venus speaks to Aeneas to reveal the gods destroying Troy.</note> When this veil admits the gaze of the one looking inward toward the truth without restlessness, it is believed to be made of **horn**, the nature of which is such that when thinned, it is transparent to the sight. But when it dulls and repels the gaze from the truth, it is thought to be **ivory**, the body of which is by nature so dense that, no matter how extreme its thinness, it remains opaque, and no vision can penetrate through it to what lies beyond.

The types and modes to which Scipio's dream refers having been treated, let us now attempt to open the mind and the very purpose—which the Greeks call the **aim** <note>original: "σκόπον" (skopos)</note>—of this dream before the words themselves are inspected. I assert that the purpose of the present work pertains to this: just as we established at the beginning of this discourse, it teaches us that the souls of those who have served the republic well are restored to heaven after leaving their bodies, and there enjoy a perpetuity of happiness.

<margin>

of good deeds
is the 
reward 
of virtue
</margin>

When Laelius complained that no statues had been placed in public for Nasica as a reward for killing the tyrant, Scipio replied, after other things, with these words: "But although for wise men the **conscience itself of excellent deeds** is the greatest reward of virtue, nevertheless, that divine virtue does not...

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO #

...statues fixed in lead, nor triumphs with wilting laurels; rather, he desires certain more stable and more enduring <note>original: *viridiora*, literally "greener" or more flourishing</note> kinds of rewards. "What then are these rewards?" asked Laelius. "Permit me," Scipio replied, "since we have now been on holiday for three days," and he proceeded with the rest, leading to the narration of the dream itself. He teaches that those more stable and enduring kinds of rewards are those he himself had seen in heaven, preserved for the good rulers of commonwealths, just as is shown in these words of his: "But so that you, Africanus, may be more eager to protect the commonwealth, know this: for all who have preserved, aided, or increased their fatherland, there is a certain and defined place in heaven where the blessed enjoy eternal life." And a little later, designating what this certain place is, he says: "But Scipio, just like this grandfather of yours and I who fathered you, cultivate justice and piety; while this is great toward parents and kin, it is greatest toward the fatherland. That life is the path to heaven and to this assembly of those who have already lived and, released from the body, inhabit the place you see," 

<margin>The Galaxy</margin>

signifying the Galaxy. For it must be understood that the place in which Scipio seems to be during his rest is the Milky Circle, which is called the Galaxy <note>the Milky Way</note>. Indeed, he uses these words at the beginning: "He showed Carthage from a high place, full of stars, bright and clear." and a little later he says more openly: "It was a circle shining with the most brilliant whiteness among the flames, which you (as you have received from the Greeks) call the Milky Circle. Looking out from it, all things seemed to me magnificent and wonderful." We shall discuss this Galaxy more fully when we speak of the celestial circles. 

But now, since we have expressed the difference and similarity between the books on the Commonwealth written by Cicero and those written earlier by Plato—and why either Plato chose the Judgment of Er <note>A soldier in Plato's Republic who returned from the dead to describe the afterlife</note> or Cicero chose the Dream of Scipio for his work—and what the Epicureans objected to in Plato, or how that weak slander may be refuted—and in which treatises philosophers admit fables or from which they exclude them entirely—we shall hereafter necessarily add the types of all images that appear, both false and true, in dreams. We have distinguished the species of dreams to which it is agreed Africanus’s dream refers, and why it was fitting for Scipio to dream such things. Regarding the twin gates of sleep <note>The gates of Horn (true dreams) and Ivory (false dreams)</note>, we have marked the opinion expressed by the ancients on all these matters, as well as the mind and purpose of the dream itself of which we speak; and we have clearly shown the part of heaven in which Scipio seemed to himself to have seen or heard these things which he reported during his rest. 

Now we must discuss the words of the dream itself—not all of them, but those that seem worthy of inquiry. The first part that presents itself to be treated is that regarding numbers, in which he says: "For when your age has completed eight times seven <note>7 x 8 = 56 years, the age Scipio Aemilianus died</note> circuits and returns of the sun, and these two numbers—each of which is considered 'full' for its own reason—have completed your fatal sum through their natural circuit, the whole state will turn to you alone and to your name. The senate, all good men, the allies, and the Latins will look to you; you will be the one on whom the safety of the state rests; in short, it will be necessary for you as dictator to restore the commonwealth, if you escape the impious hands of your kinsmen." 

<margin>The fullness of numbers</margin>

He does not assign "fullness" to these numbers here in vain; for fullness, properly speaking, does not belong to anything except divine and celestial things. You would not properly call a body "full," for while it is unable to contain itself by flowing out, it is greedy for external things by drinking them in. Even if this does not happen to metallic bodies, they should nonetheless be called "vast" rather than "full." This, then, is the common fullness of all numbers: that the first perfection of incorporeality in numbers occurs to our thought as it travels toward the heavens. Among them, however, they are properly called "full" according to these modes which are necessary for the present treatise: those which either obtain the power of links, or again create bodies, or create a body. But this "body" is something you grasp by understanding, not by sensing; the whole of this must be unfolded, guided by light, by repeating it from a slightly deeper level so that the offense of obscurity may be driven away. All bodies are bounded by a surface, and that surface is terminated by its own outermost part...

<meta>This page continues the technical and philosophical commentary on Cicero’s "Dream of Scipio." Having discussed the Galaxy (Milky Way), the author now moves into a Pythagorean analysis of geometry and numerology to explain the nature of the physical and incorporeal worlds.</meta>

# BOOK ONE #

These boundaries, however—since they are always found around the bodies they define—are nevertheless understood to be incorporeal <note>non-physical or spiritual in nature</note>. For as long as something is said to be a "body," its boundary is not yet understood on its own; once the mind conceives of the boundary, it has left the body behind. Therefore, the first transition from physical bodies to incorporeal things is found at the boundaries of bodies. This is the first nature of "bodily things" after the body itself, yet it is not purely or entirely free from the body. For although its nature exists outside the body, it only appears around the body. Finally, when you name a "whole body," the surface is included in that term. From these bodies, the intellect separates the surface, even if it is not a separate thing in reality. Just as this surface is the boundary of bodies, so it is bounded by lines, 

<margin>Lines</margin>

which Greece called *grammai* <note>original: *grammas*</note> in its own language. Lines are finished by points; and these are the "mathematical bodies," as they are called, about which the diligent industry of geometry disputes. Therefore, when this surface is conceived 

<margin>The division of a body</margin>

apart from the rest of the body, it takes on a number of lines according to the shape of the underlying body. Whether it has three lines, like a triangle <note>original: *trigonum*</note>, or four, like a square, or more angles, its flat area is enclosed by as many lines touching each other at their ends. At this point we must be reminded that every body consists of dimensions of length, width, and height <note>or depth</note>. Out of these three, in the drawing of a line, there is only one dimension: length; for it is without width. 

<margin>The Flat Surface</margin>

But the flat surface, which they call an *epiphania* <note>original: *epiphaniam*, meaning "appearance" or surface</note>, is stretched out in length and width, but lacks height. We have already expressed by how many lines this surface is contained. However, the "solidity" of bodies consists of these two dimensions with height added to them; for a solid body is made when three dimensions are filled. This they call a *stereon* <note>original: *streon*, a Greek term for a solid</note>, such as a die, which is called a cube. But if you wish to conceive of the surface not of one part, but of the whole body—let us propose it is a square, to discuss one example that will suffice—now not four but eight angles are gathered. You notice this if you mentally envision another square, like the one we first mentioned, placed high above the first, so that the height which the flat surface lacked is added. Thus, with three dimensions filled, it becomes a solid body which they call a *stereon*, in imitation of a 

<margin>Die, Cube, Drawing</margin>

gaming die <note>original: *tessera*</note>, which is called a cube. From this, it appears that the number eight both is and is considered a "solid body." Indeed, among geometers, one <note>the number 1</note> occupies the place of a point. Two make the drawing of a line, which is confined by two points (as we said above). Four points, placed in two rows of two across from each other, express the appearance of a square when a line is cast from each point to the point opposite it. These four, when doubled as we said, become eight and describe two similar squares. When these are placed one above the other and height is added, they create the form of a cube, which is a solid body. From this, it is clear that number is "older" <note>logically prior</note> than the surface and the lines from which we mentioned the surface consists, and older than all shapes. For one ascends from lines to number as if to something prior; thus it is understood that geometric shapes are described from various numbers of lines. We said the surface itself, with its lines, is the first incorporeal nature after bodies, yet it is not to be separated from them because of its perpetual association with bodies. Therefore, that which recedes upward from this is now purely incorporeal. The preceding discourse has revealed the numbers that are higher than this. Therefore, the first perfection of incorporeality is in numbers; and this is (as we said) the fullness of all numbers. Separately, however, (as we said above) that is the fullness of those things which either create a body or are created by one, or hold the power of bonds—though I do not doubt there are other causes by which full numbers are created. How the number eight 

<margin>The number eight</margin>

creates a solid body has been proven previously. Therefore, it will also be rightly called "singularly full" because of the effect of bodily solidity. But there is no doubt that this number is also more suited to the very harmony of heaven—that is, its containment—since the spheres themselves which move are eight, about which the following discourse will proceed. All the parts of which this number consists are such that fullness is born from their joining. For it is either from those which neither ge <note>catchword: *neque ge...* [neither beget/produce]</note>

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic and Pythagorean commentary on Cicero's "Dream of Scipio" by Macrobius. Having previously discussed the geometric foundations of the physical world (points, lines, and surfaces), the author now shifts to the mystical and mathematical properties of numbers, specifically focusing on the number four, seven, and the "Monad" (the number one), explaining how these numerical ratios form the "World Soul."</meta>

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO #

...are neither generated nor do they generate from the Monad <note>original: *monade*; the number one, viewed as the source of all but not a "number" in the same sense</note> and seven: the nature of which will be explained more fully in its proper place. Or they come from that doubled number which both is generated and generates: that is, the number four. For this number, four, is born from two and generates eight. It is also composed of three and five; of these, the first [three] appeared as the first of all odd numbers. The following treatise will touch upon the power of the number five. Indeed, the Pythagoreans <note>followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who believed the universe was built on numerical ratios</note> called this number [four] "Justice" because it is the first of all numbers to be resolved into "evenly even" numbers <note>original: *pariter pares*; a technical term for numbers that can be divided by two all the way down to one, like 4, 8, or 16</note>—that is, into two fours—in such a way that the division itself is resolved into numbers equally "evenly even," namely two twos. It is woven together with the same quality: that is, two times two, twice <note>referring to the cube of 2, which is 8</note>. Since, therefore, its weaving proceeds with equal balance and its resolution returns equally all the way to the Monad—which does not admit division by arithmetic reasoning—it rightly received the name of Justice because of this equal division. And because it appears from all the aforementioned factors how much it relies on both the fullness of its parts and its own separate fullness, it is rightly called "full."

<margin>The number seven is full</margin>

It remains for reason, placed in our midst, to persuade us that the number seven <note>original: *septenarius*</note> should also rightly be called "full." And first, we cannot pass over this without wonder: that two numbers which, when multiplied together, would encompass the vital life span of a brave man [7 x 8 = 56], are constituted from the even and the odd. For that which is generated from the mixing of these numbers is truly perfect.

<margin>Odd number</margin>

For the odd number is called male, and the even is called female. Likewise, arithmeticians revere the odd by the name of "father" and the even by the name of "mother."

<margin>Even number</margin>

Hence, too, in Plato's *Timaeus* <note>a famous dialogue regarding the creation of the universe</note>, the God who is the maker of the World Soul recorded that he interwove its parts from even and odd—that is, from the double and triple series—so that the alternation of exchange stood from the double series up to eight, and from the triple series up to twenty-seven. For these first cubes are born on both sides: if indeed from the even numbers, "two times two" (which are four) make a surface, and "two times two twice" (which are eight) form a solid body. From the odd number, however, "three times three" (which are nine) return a surface, and "three times three thrice"—that is, three nines, which are twenty-seven—complete the first equal cube of the other side. From this, it is given to be understood that these two numbers—eight and seven, I say—which come together for the multiplication of the years of a perfect man in the State, were judged to be the only ones fit for creating the World Soul, because nothing after the Creator can be more perfect. This must also be noted: while we asserted above the common dignity of all numbers, showing them to be older than the surface and all its lines which we see in bodies, the proceeding treatise finds that numbers existed even before the World Soul, with which the most venerable reasoning of the *Timaeus*, as a witness aware of nature itself, expressed that the soul was woven. Hence it is that the wise have not hesitated to pronounce: "The soul is a self-moving number."

<margin>Of what the number seven consists</margin>

Now let us see why the number seven is held to be "full" by its own separate merit. To know its fullness more closely, let us first investigate the merits of the parts of which it consists, and finally what it can do itself. The number seven consists either of one and six, or of two and five, or of three and four. Let us treat the members of each combination; from these, we shall admit that no other number is so fertile with such varied majesty. The first combination is composed of one and six.

<margin>The Monad, that is, unity</margin>

One, however—which is called the Monad, that is, Unity—is both male and female; it is both even and odd, not a number itself but the source and origin of numbers. This Monad is the beginning and end of all things, yet itself knowing neither beginning nor end; it is referred to the Supreme God and separates His intellect from the number of things and powers that follow. Nor would you look for it in vain in the lower rank after God. This is that Mind <note>original: *mens*; the Neoplatonic 'Nous' or Divine Intellect</note> born from the Supreme God, which, knowing no changes of time, consists always in the one present age. And since, as it is one, it is not countable, it nevertheless both creates from itself and contains within itself innumerable species of kinds. Turning the sharp edge of thought a little from there, you will find this Monad refers also to the soul.
