For the soul, being foreign to the contagion of wild matter <note>original: "siluestris materiae"; in Neoplatonic thought, "matter" is often described as a dark, chaotic "forest"</note>, and owing itself only to its creator and to itself, possesses a simple nature. When it pours itself into the immense vastness of the universe to give it life, it nevertheless suffers no divorce from its own unity. You see how this Monad <note>original: "monas"; the number one, representing the ultimate source of all existence</note>, arising as the first cause of things, maintains its continuity of power all the way to the soul, everywhere whole and always indivisible. These things concerning the Monad are said more concisely than the abundance of the subject suggested; nor should it trouble you that, while it seems to preside over every number, it is especially praised in its connection with the Septenary <note>original: "septenarii"; the number seven</note>. For the incorruptible Monad is joined to nothing more fittingly than to a virgin. Indeed, the reputation for virginity has so grown around this number—that is, the seven—that it is even called Pallas <note>another name for the goddess Athena/Minerva, who was famously a virgin</note>.

<margin>
Pallas
<image-desc>A small circle diagram.</image-desc>
</margin>
For it is believed to be a virgin because it produces no number from itself when doubled that stays within the Decad <note>original: "denarium"; the number ten</note>, which is well known to be the first limit of numbers. It is called Pallas because it proceeded solely from the birth and multiplication of the Monad, just as Minerva <note>the Roman name for Pallas</note> is said to have been born from only one parent <note>referring to the myth that she sprang fully formed from the head of Zeus</note>.

<margin>
The Senary number
<image-desc>A small square diagram.</image-desc>
</margin>
The Senary <note>original: "Senarius"; the number six</note>, however, which when joined with one makes the Septenary, is of varied and manifold religious significance and power. First, it is the only number among all those below ten that is composed of its own parts: for it has a half, a third part, and a sixth part. The half is three, the third part is two, and the sixth part is one; all of which together make six. It has other signs of its veneration as well, but lest a longer discourse cause weariness, we shall follow only one of its functions, which we have preferred because, once mentioned, it will establish the dignity not only of the Senary but also of the Septenary. Nature has established the more frequent use of nine months for human birth through a certain rhythm of numbers; but reason, proceeding through the multiplication of the adopted Senary number, has also compelled seven months to be used.

We expressed briefly and absolutely above that there are two primary cubes of all numbers: that is, eight from the even and twenty-seven from the odd; and that the odd is male and the even is female. If each of these is multiplied by the Senary number, they produce the number of days that are completed in seven months. For let the numbers join: that male which was mentioned and the female—namely eight and twenty-seven; they give birth from themselves to thirty-five. These, when multiplied six times, create two hundred and ten; this number of days concludes the seventh month. This number is so fertile by nature, therefore, that it completes the first perfection of human birth as a kind of judge of maturity.

The distinction of a future birth (as Hippocrates <note>the famous Greek physician, often called the "Father of Medicine"</note> reports) is recognized in the womb thus: the conception moves either on the seventieth or the ninetieth day. Therefore, whatever day of movement it was, when multiplied three times, it explains either the seventh or the ninth month. Let these be the first tastes of the first coupling of the Septenary.

The second coupling is of two and five. 
<margin>Dyad</margin>
Of these, the Dyad <note>original: "Dyas"; the number two</note> is the first number because it comes after the Monad. This first line flowed down from that solitary, incorporeal, and intelligible omnipotence. Therefore, it is also referred to the spheres of the wandering stars and lights; for these too were cut into a number from that which is called Aplanes <note>original: "Aplanes"; the sphere of the fixed stars which does not "wander"</note> and were twisted back into the opposition of varied motion. This number [two], therefore, is most aptly joined with the Quinary <note>the number five</note>, while the former refers to the wandering stars (as we said) and the latter to the zones of heaven. But the former by reason of division; the latter by number. Truly, that property of power, eminent beyond the others, falls to the Quinary number because it alone has embraced all things that are, and all things that seem to be. Now, we say that "intelligible" things "are," and all "corporeal" things "seem to be," whether they have a divine body or a perishable one. This number, therefore, designates all things together, both the higher and the lower. For either it is the most high God; or the Mind born from Him, in which the forms of things are contained; or the Soul of the World, which is the fountain of all souls; or things are celestial down to us; or it is terrestrial nature. And thus the Quinary number of all things is filled. Let these things said of the second conjunction of the Septenary number suffice for the sake of necessary brevity.

The third is of three and four; let us revolve how much power this has. The first surface of a geometric body from an odd number consists of three lines, for by these a triangular form is enclosed. From an even number, however, the first is found in four. Likewise, we know according to Plato...

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO #

...are neither generated nor do they generate, such as the monad <note>original: "monade"; the number one</note> and the number seven: the nature of which will be more fully explained in its proper place. Or we might speak of that doubled number which is both generated and generates: that is, the number **four**. For this number four is born from two, and it generates eight. It is also composed of three and five—the former being the first of all the odd numbers. The power of the number five will be touched upon in the following treatise.

The Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed that numbers were the fundamental reality of the universe</note> called this number **justice**, because it is the first of all numbers to be resolved into "even-even" parts <note>original: "pariter pares"; numbers that can be divided by two all the way down to one</note>. That is, it can be divided into two fours <note>referring here to the resolution of eight, which 4 generates</note>, and furthermore, the division itself is resolved into "equally even-even" numbers, namely two twos. It is woven together by this same quality: that is, twice two, twice. Since its composition proceeds with such equal balance, and its resolution returns equally all the way to the monad—which by arithmetic logic does not admit division—it deservedly received the name of **justice** because of this equal division. And because it is clear from all the points mentioned above how much it relies on the fullness of its parts and its own completeness, it is rightly called "full."

<margin>The number seven is full</margin>
It remains for us to use reason to persuade the reader that the number **seven** <note>original: "septenarium"</note> also deserves to be called "full." First, we cannot pass over this without wonder: that the two numbers which, when multiplied together, encompass the life span of a mature man <note>Macrobius refers to 7 x 8 = 56 years, considered the "prime" or "perfect" age of a man in antiquity</note>, are constituted from an even and an odd number. This is truly perfect, as it is generated from the mixing of these numbers.

<margin>Odd number:</margin>
For the **odd** number is called male, and the **even** is called female.
<margin>Even number</margin>
Likewise, mathematicians honor the odd number with the name "father" and the even with the name "mother." Hence, Plato’s *Timaeus* records that God, the fabricator of the world soul, interwove its parts from the even and the odd—that is, from the "doubling" and "tripling" numbers. He did this so that the alternating exchange would stand from the doubling sequence up to eight <note>The sequence 2, 4, 8</note> and from the tripling sequence up to twenty-seven <note>The sequence 3, 9, 27</note>. For these are the first **cubes** born on either side: if you take the even numbers, twice two makes four (a surface), and twice two, twice (which is eight) creates a solid body. From the odd numbers, three times three gives nine (a surface), and three times three, three times (that is, thrice nine, which is twenty-seven) produces the first equal cube of the other side.

From this, we are given to understand that these two numbers—I mean eight and seven—which meet in the multiplication of the years of a man perfected in the republic, were judged the only ones fit for creating the world soul. Nothing after the Creator himself can be more perfect. It must also be noted that, while we previously asserted the common dignity of all numbers as being older than surfaces and lines, the present treatise finds that numbers existed even before the world soul. The most venerable logic of the *Timaeus*, acting as a witness conscious of nature itself, expressed that the soul was woven from these numbers. This is why the wise have not hesitated to pronounce that **the soul is a self-moving number.**

Now let us see why the number seven is considered full in its own right. To understand its fullness more precisely, let us first investigate the merits of the parts of which it consists, and then finally what the number itself can do.

<margin>Of what parts the number seven consists.</margin>
The number seven consists of either one and six, or two and five, or three and four. Let us examine the members of these individual combinations; we shall confess that no other number is fertile with such varied majesty.

From **one** and **six**, the first combination is composed.
<margin>Monad, that is, unity</margin>
**One**, however, which is called the **Monad** (that is, unity), is both male and female; it is both even and odd, yet it is not a number itself but the source and origin of numbers. This Monad is the beginning and end of all things, yet it knows neither beginning nor end itself. It is referred to the **Supreme God**, and it separates His intellect from the number of following things and powers; you would not seek it in any lower grade after God. This is that **Mind** <note>original: "mens"; the Divine Mind or Nous in Neoplatonism</note> born from the Supreme God which, knowing no change of time, always consists in the "one" which is the present age. Since it is one, it cannot be numbered; nevertheless, it creates from itself and contains within itself innumerable species of kinds. From there, inclining the sharp edge of thought just a little, you will find that this Monad is also referred to the **Soul**.

<margin>The number six</margin>
The **Senary** <note>The number six</note>, however, which when joined with one makes the Septenary, is of varied and manifold religious significance and power. It has other signs of its veneration, but lest a long speech cause weariness, we will follow just one of its duties. We expressed above, briefly and absolutely, that there are two primary **cubes** of all numbers: that is, **eight** from the even and **twenty-seven** from the odd. The second joining is of two and five. 
<margin>The Dyad</margin>
Of these, the **Dyad** <note>original: "Dyas"; the number two</note> is the first number because it comes after the Monad. This number flowed down from that solitary omnipotence as the first line of the intelligible, incorporeal world. For this reason, it is also referred to the spheres of the wandering stars and lights, 
<margin>Aplanes</margin>
because these too were split into a number from that sphere which is called the **Aplanes** <note>original: "A planes"; the "non-wandering" or Fixed Sphere of the stars</note> and were twisted back into the opposition of varied motion. This number, therefore, is most fittingly joined with the **Quinary** <note>original: "quinario"; the number five</note>. While the former is referred to the wandering stars, the latter is referred to the zones of heaven. But the former is by reason of its splitting, and the latter by its number. 

Indeed, a certain property of power, eminent beyond all others, belongs to the number five: for it alone has embraced all things that are, and all things that seem to be. We say that "to be" refers to intelligible things, and "to seem to be" refers to all corporeal things, whether they have a divine body or a perishing one. This number, then, designates all things—both the higher and the lower—at the same time. For there is either the **Supreme God**; or the **Mind** <note>original: "mens"; the Neoplatonic *Nous* or Divine Intellect</note> born from Him, in which the forms of things are contained; or the **Soul of the World**, which is the source of all souls; or there are the **Celestial things** down to us; or there is **Terrestrial nature**. And thus the Quinary number of all things is fulfilled. Let these things said about the second joining of the number seven suffice for the sake of necessary brevity.

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO #

...the secret of truth itself: that those things are bound together by a strong link: in which an intervening middle term <note>original: "medietas"; in Pythagorean mathematics, a "mean" or middle number that links two extremes in a proportion</note> provides the firmness of the bond. But when that middle term itself is doubled: those things which are at the edges are bound not only tenaciously, but even indissolubly. Therefore, it first happened with the **ternary** <note>The number three</note> number that it received a middle between two extremes by which it might be bound. The **quaternary** <note>The number four</note>, however, was the first of all to obtain two middle terms; the God who is the artisan and founder of the world's massive structure borrowed these from this number to bind the elements together with an unbreakable link, just as is asserted in Plato’s *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue regarding the creation of the physical world</note>. Nor could things so contrary, so repugnant to one another, and by nature refusing to commune—I speak of **Earth** and **Fire**—be mixed or allied through such a joining harmony, unless they were bound by two middle terms: the links of **Air** and **Water**.

<image-desc>A line drawing of an equilateral triangle.</image-desc>
<image-desc>A line drawing of a square.</image-desc>

<margin>
The
quaternary
number.
The

</margin>

For in this way, God the Creator connected the most diverse elements through the suitability of order so that they might be easily joined. For since there were two qualities in each, He gave to each one of the two qualities in such a way that it would find a quality related and similar to itself in the element to which it adhered. **Earth** is dry and cold; **Water**, however, is cold and moist. Although these two elements are contrary to each other through the "dry" and the "moist," they join through the "cold" which they have in common. **Air** is moist and hot; and although it is the contrary of cold water because of its heat, it is nonetheless joined as an ally through the reconciliation of "moisture." Above this, **Fire**, since it is hot and dry, rejects the moisture of the air through its dryness, but connects through the partnership of "heat." And so it happens that each individual element embraces the two neighbors on either side of it with single qualities, as if with certain arms. Water binds Earth to itself by cold, and Air to itself by moisture. Air associates with Water through a similar moisture, and with Fire through heat. Fire mixes with Air as something hot, so that it may be joined to Earth through dryness. Earth allows Fire through dryness, and does not reject Water because of cold. 

Yet this variety of bonds, if there were only two elements, would have no firmness between them; if there were three, they would be tied by a link that was somewhat stronger, yet still not fully powerful. But between four elements there is an indissoluble binding, since two extremes are bound by two intervening terms. This will be manifest if you place in the middle the very substance of the meaning taken from Plato’s *Timaeus*: "The reason of Divine beauty," he says, "demanded that the world be made such that it would be open to both sight and touch." <note>original: "visum... et tactum"</note> It was established, however, that nothing can be seen without the benefit of fire, nor touched without being solid; and nothing is solid without earth. Whence the Creator, beginning to fashion the whole body of the world out of fire and earth, saw that two things cannot fit together without a middle term binding them. And that this is the best bond: that which binds itself and the things to be bound together equally. 

A single intervening term can suffice only when a surface without depth is to be bound; but where a deep dimension is to be tightened with bonds, the knot is not tied except by a double intervention. Therefore, He wove Air and Water between Fire and Earth; and so, through all things, a single and self-consistent joining harmony ran, cleansing the diversity of the elements by the very equality of their differences. For just as much as there is a difference between Water and Air in the cause of density and weight, there is exactly as much between Air and Fire. And again, what exists between Air and Water by reason of lightness and rarity, this same exists between Earth and Water. Likewise, what exists between Earth and Water by reason of density and weight, this same exists between Water and Air. And what is between Water and Air, this is between Air and Fire. And conversely, what is between Fire and Air because of thinness and lightness, this is between Air and Water; and what is between Air and Water, this is understood to be between Water and Earth. Nor are only neighboring and coherent things compared, but the same equality is preserved even when skipping every other step. For what Earth is to Air, Water is to Fire; and as often as you turn it, you will find the same joining harmony; thus they associate out of the very fact that they are equally different from one another. 

These things were said so that it might be established by clear reason: that neither a plane surface can be bound without three, nor a solid society without four. Therefore, the **septenary number** <note>The number seven</note> obtains a double power of binding, because both its parts have obtained their own unique bonds: the ternary [3] with one middle term, and the quaternary [4] with two. Hence, in another place in this same *Dream*, Cicero says of the septenary: "which number is the knot of almost all things." <note>original: "qui numerus rerum omnium fere nodus est"</note> Likewise, all bodies are either mathematical...

</margin>
The number three indeed marks the soul as complete in its three parts: the first of which is Reason, which they call **rational** <note>Greek: λογικόν; logikon</note>. The second is high-spiritedness, which they call **spirited** <note>Greek: θυμικόν; thymikon</note>: The third is desire, which is named **appetitive** <note>Greek: ἐπιθυμητικόν; epithymetikon</note>. Likewise, none of the wise have doubted that the soul also consists of musical harmonies. Among these, the one called the **diapason** <note>an octave</note> is of no small power. This consists of two others: that is, the **diatessaron** <note>a perfect fourth</note> and the **diapente** <note>a perfect fifth</note>. Now, the diapente comes from the **hemiolic** <note>original: "hemiolio"; a 3:2 ratio</note> and the diatessaron comes from the **epitrite** <note>original: "epitrito"; a 4:3 ratio</note>. And the 
<margin>

Diatessaron
</margin>
first hemiolic is three: and the first epitrite is four. We shall follow this up more fully in its proper place. Therefore, from these two numbers consist the diatessaron and the diapente: from which the diapason harmony is generated. Whence Virgil: lacking no discipline: wishing to describe those who were fully and in all ways blessed, said: 
> "O three and four times blessed." <note>Latin: "O terque quaterque beati"; from Aeneid I.94</note>
We have said these things as summaries following the parts of the number seven: we shall say a few things about the number itself. This number is now called the 
<margin>
Heptad
</margin>
**Heptad** <note>Greek: heptas</note>, the use of the first letter having become obsolete: For among the ancients it was called the **Septad**, which testified to the veneration due to the number by its Greek name <note>The author suggests the Greek "hepta" (seven) was originally "septa," derived from "sebas" meaning "veneration"</note>. For first of all, the World Soul was generated by this number: just as Plato's *Timaeus* taught. For with the **Monad** <note>The number one</note> located at the peak: three numbers flowed from it on each side. From this side the even: from that side the odd. That is, after the monad, on one side two: then four: then eight: on the other side truly three: then nine: and then twenty-seven. The mixture made from these numbers effects the generation of the soul by the command of the Creator. Not a small power of this number is shown from this: because the origin of the World Soul is contained within seven limits: also seven...

### VIII
## ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

<margin>The course of the moon through the zodiac</margin>
The providence of the divine Architect has placed the order of the wandering spheres <note>The "wandering spheres" refers to the planets, which appear to move against the backdrop of the "fixed" stars.</note> beneath that star-bearing sphere <note>The "stellifera," or the highest heaven of the fixed stars.</note> so that they might both counter the rapid motions of the upper heaven and govern all things below. The Moon also, which is numbered as the seventh among them, is moved by the number seven <note>original: "septenarius"; the number seven was considered sacred and fundamental to the structure of the universe in Pythagorean thought.</note>, and this number itself dispenses her course. Although this may be proven in many ways, let it first be shown by this: the Moon completes the circuit of the entire zodiac in nearly twenty-eight days. For even if she returns to the Sun from which she departed in thirty days, she spends only about twenty-eight days in the actual circuit of the zodiac; in the remaining days, she catches up to the Sun, which had moved away from the place where she left it. For the Sun measures out one of the twelve signs in an entire month. Let us suppose, therefore, that the Moon has emerged from the Sun's orb (as it were)—which we call being "born"—while the Sun is positioned in the first part of Aries. After twenty-eight days and about seven hours, she returns to the first part of Aries, but she does not find the Sun there. In the meantime, the Sun has also moved further along by the law of its own progression. Therefore, she is not yet thought to have returned to the place from which she started, because our eyes perceive her to have proceeded not from the first part of Aries, but from the Sun. Thus, in the remaining days—that is, two, more or less—she follows him, and then, coming under his orb once more and proceeding from there, she is said to be "born" again. From this, it happens that she is almost never born in the same sign twice in a row, except in Gemini, where this occasionally occurs because the Sun consumes thirty-two days lingering in the height of that sign; this is very rare in others unless she proceeds from the Sun near the very first part of the sign. Of this number of twenty-eight days, therefore, the number seven is the origin. For if you proceed from one up to seven, adding each number to the sum of those preceding it <note>This refers to a triangular number: 1+2+3+4+5+6+7 = 28.</note>, you will find that twenty-eight is born from seven.

<margin>The ecliptic place</margin>
The Moon also consumes this number—which is fortunately divided into four times seven—to measure and re-measure the entire width of the zodiac. For in seven days, traveling obliquely through the width from the extremity of the northern edge, she reaches the middle of the latitude, which place is called the **ecliptic**. In the following seven days, she glides from the middle to the lowest southern point; in another seven days, turning obliquely, she ascends back to the middle; and in the final seven days, she is restored to the northern summit. Thus, in those same four-times-seven days, she runs through and around the entire length and width of the zodiac. By similar dispensations of weeks, she arranges the changes of her light by an eternal law.

<margin>The dichotomy of the moon</margin>
In the first seven days, she grows until she appears as a halved orb, and she is then called **Dichotomos** <note>original: "Διχότομος"; meaning "cut in half," referring to the first quarter moon.</note>. In the second seven days, gathering her burgeoning fire, she now completes the whole orb and is then called **Full**. In the third seven, she becomes **Dichotomos** again, as she is contracted by decreasing to a half. In the fourth seven, she is thinned by the final diminishing of her light.

<margin>The gibbous moon</margin>
Throughout the entire month, she is also distinguished by seven permutations which the Greeks call **phases** <note>original: "fasis" / "φάσεις".</note>: when she is born; when she becomes **dichotomos**; when she becomes **amphicyrtos** <note>original: "ἀμφίκυρτος"; meaning "curved on both sides" or gibbous.</note>; when she is full; and again **amphicyrtos**; then **dichotomos** once more; and when she is deprived of the entirety of her light to us. She is **amphicyrtos** either when she is beyond the diameter of the half-moon before she is encircled by the closure of the full orb, or when she is already diminishing from the full orb between the full and the half, showing a curved prominence in the middle of her light. The Sun himself, from whom all things borrow life, also varies his turns in the seventh sign. For from the winter solstice to the summer solstice, he arrives at the seventh sign; and from the spring tropic <note>The Spring Equinox.</note> to the autumnal tropic, he is led through the completion of the seventh sign.

<margin>Conversions of light</margin>
Three conversions of celestial light also consist of this number. The first is the greatest; the second is the middle; and the third is the smallest. The greatest is the conversion of the **year** according to the sun; the middle is the **month** according to the moon; the smallest is the **day** according to the rising and setting. Truly, every single conversion is four-parted; and thus the number seven consists of three kinds of conversions and the four modes by which each one is converted. These are the four modes: first it becomes **humid**, then **hot**, then **dry**, and finally **cold**. And the greatest conversion—that is, the year—is humid in the spring time, hot in the summer, dry in the autumn, and cold through the winter. The middle conversion of the month through the moon happens thus: the first week is humid, because the new moon usually stirs up moisture; the second is hot, as the light in her is now maturing from the sight of the sun; the third is dry, being further removed from her "birth"; the fourth is cold, as her light is now failing.

<margin>The smallest conversion of the day</margin>
The third conversion, which is that of the day according to the rising and sett...

<page-num>IX</page-num>
<header>BOOK ONE</header>

...disposes it thus: so that it is humid until the first of the four parts of the day; hot until the second; dry until the third; and cold in the fourth. <margin>The increase of the Ocean</margin> The Ocean also maintains this number in its increase. For on the first day of the rising moon, it is fuller than usual; it decreases a little on the second; and the third sees it smaller than the second; and thus decreasing, it reaches the seventh day. Again, the eighth day remains equal to the seventh; and the ninth becomes like the sixth; the tenth like the fifth; and the eleventh becomes equal to the fourth; the twelfth like the third; and the thirteenth becomes similar to the second; the fourteenth to the first. Indeed, the third week <note>original: "hebdomas"; a period of seven days.</note> does the same as the first, and the fourth the same as the second. Finally, this is the number which causes a human to be conceived, formed, brought forth, to live, be nourished, and to be passed through all the stages of age to senility, and entirely to consist. For, to say nothing of the fact that nature has established by this number of days that which is occupied by no force in women—namely, the monthly purification as if by a decree for discharging a tax from the woman as the month returns—yet this must not be passed over: that the seed which, after its casting, has not fallen back in effusion within seven hours, is pronounced to have adhered for life.

<margin>The Mint. The formation of Man in the womb. The Follicle.</margin> But once the seed is placed within the "mint" <term>moneta</term> <note>Macrobius uses the word "moneta" or mint to describe the womb as a place where the human form is "stamped" or "coined" into existence by nature.</note> of forming a human, nature the artisan first strives for this: that on the seventh day she surrounds the generative moisture with a follicle <note>original: "folliculus"; a small sac or membrane.</note> made of a membrane as thin as that which is enclosed by the outer shell in an egg, and it encloses the liquid within itself. Since this was discovered by physicists, Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician of the 5th century BC, often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> himself—who knows as little how to deceive as to be deceived—asserted it, being certain of the experiment, reporting in the book inscribed *On the Nature of the Child* <note>original: "De natura pueri".</note>: that such a receptacle of seed was ejected from the womb as he had understood on the seventh day after conception. For he had ordered a woman—who was praying not to remain pregnant since the seed had not been effused—to be spurred by jumping; and on the seventh day, it was ejected by jumping with such a follicle as we mentioned above, sufficing for the conception.

This was Hippocrates; but Strato the Peripatetic <note>Strato of Lampsacus, a Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle.</note> and Diocles of Carystus <note>A celebrated 4th-century BC Greek physician.</note> distribute the construction of the conceived body through seven-day periods: so that they believe in the second week drops of blood appear on the surface of the follicle we mentioned; in the third, they sink inward toward the moisture of the conception itself; in the fourth, the moisture itself coagulates so that a certain liquid solidity, as if between flesh and blood, comes together; in the fifth, however, the human figure is formed in the substance of the moisture, the size of a bee, but so that in that briefness all the limbs and the designated outlines of the whole body consist. <margin>Formation of the body</margin> Therefore, it is established that as often as this designation of limbs is formed in the fifth week, the birth matures in the seventh month. But when the completion is to be in the ninth month, if a female is being fashioned, the limbs are divided in the sixth week; if a male, in the seventh. <margin>Birth</margin> After birth, whether that which has been poured forth will live, or whether it was dead in the womb and born only breathing, is discerned at the seventh hour. For beyond this number of hours, those born dead cannot bear the nourishment of the air; whoever has sustained it beyond seven hours is understood to be created for life, unless some other accident should snatch away what is perfect. <margin>The Navel</margin> Likewise, after seven days, the remains of the umbilical cord fall away; after twice seven days [14], the sight begins to move toward light; and after seven times seven [49], it freely turns both its pupils and the whole face toward individual movements of things to be seen. <margin>When teeth arise in children. The Jaw.</margin> After seven months, the teeth begin to emerge from the jaws; after twice seven [14 months], the child sits without fear of falling; after thrice seven [21 months], his sound breaks forth into words; and after four times seven [28 months], he not only stands firmly but also walks. After five times seven [35 months], he begins to loathe the nurse's milk, unless perhaps it is prolonged by continued habit; after seven years, the teeth that first emerged give way to others more suitable for solid food; and in that same year, the seventh, the integrity of speaking is fully completed. <margin>Seven vowels. The growth of Man through the septenary number.</margin> Whence also seven vocal letters <note>Macrobius refers to the seven vowels of the Greek alphabet (α, ε, η, ι, ο, υ, ω).</note> are said to be discovered by nature, although Latinity has preferred to hold five instead of seven by pronouncing the same ones now long, now short. Among the Romans, however, if you count the sounds of the vowels and not the shapes [of the letters], there are similarly seven. After twice seven years [14], he reaches puberty by the necessity of age itself. For then the power of generation begins to move in males and the purification in females.

# XI
<header>ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO</header>

For this reason, guardianship for boys is ended just as their manly strength matures; however, females are released from these laws two years earlier because of the haste of their marriage vows <note>In Roman law, girls reached legal maturity at 12, boys at 14.</note>. After three times seven years [21], youth clothes the cheeks with down; this same year also marks the limit of growing tall. The fourth week of years being completed [28] prevents any further growth in width as well. The fifth week [35] <margin>The custom of boxers</margin> completes the full increase of all the strength that can be in any individual. In no way can anyone become stronger than this; they should hope for no further increase in their strength. Those who have remained without this glory until that time <margin>The seventh week</margin> will begin to descend from their peak. For six times seven years [42], the strength gathered before is preserved; no <margin>Ancient custom</margin> diminution occurs except by accident. But from the sixth to the seventh week [49], a decline does indeed occur, though it is hidden and does not reveal its loss through a sudden failure. Therefore, it is the custom of some republics that no one is forced into military service after the sixth week [age 42]. In most, a just release is granted after the seventh [age 49]. It should be noted that when the number seven multiplies itself [7 x 7 = 49], it creates the age which is properly considered and called "perfect." A man of that age, having reached perfection and not yet passed it, is considered fit for counsel and not yet a stranger to the exercise of strength. When the decade, which is itself a most perfect number, is joined with the perfect number seven—so that either ten times seven or seven times ten years are calculated—this is believed by natural philosophers <note>original: "physicis"</note> <margin>The limit of living</margin> to be the limit of living <term>meta vivendi</term> <note>literally "the goal-post of life"</note>. This marks the full span of human life. Whoever exceeds this is free from all duty and is free for the exercise of wisdom alone; he is useful only for giving counsel and is venerable because of his exemption from other duties. From the seventh to the tenth week, <margin>The human members arranged by the septenary number</margin> duties vary according to the capacity of the strength that still persists in each.

This same number arranges the members of the entire body. For there are seven within a human which are called the "black members" <note>original: "nigra membra"; a term for the major internal organs or viscera</note> by the Greeks: the tongue, the heart, the lung, the liver, the spleen, and two kidneys. And there are seven other parts for vessels and passages, which are adjacent to the individual organs for receiving and returning food and breath: the throat, the stomach, the belly, the bladder, and the three principal intestines. One of these is called the "divider" <note>original: "dissipium"</note> <margin>The divider</margin> which separates the belly from the other intestines. The second is the middle, which the Greeks call the mesentery <margin>Mesentery</margin> <note>original: "messenteron"</note>. The third, which the ancients called the lower gut <margin>Hira</margin> <note>original: "hira"</note>, contains the beginning of all the intestines and carries away the waste of food. <margin>Waste</margin> Regarding the breath and food, for the receiving and returning of which the members we have mentioned are used (following the passages adjacent to them), this is observed: that life does not last beyond seven hours without the drawing of breath, nor beyond as many days without food.

There are also seven levels in the body which complete the dimension of depth from the bottom to the surface: <margin>Seven parts of the body</margin> marrow, bone, nerve, vein, artery, flesh, and skin. These are the internal parts. In the visible body, there are also seven parts: the head, chest, hands, feet, and the genitals. Likewise, the parts that are divided are joined by no more than seven joints: in the hands, there is the shoulder, upper arm, elbow, palm, <margin>Seven parts of the hand</margin> and the three joints of the fingers. In the feet, there is the thigh, knee, shin, the foot itself, under which is the sole, and similarly the three joints of the toes. <margin>Seven parts of the foot</margin> And because nature has placed the senses and their mysteries in the head as if in a citadel, the functions of the senses are performed through seven openings: <margin>Seven openings of the head</margin> the mouth, and then two each for the eyes, nostrils, and ears. Hence, not without reason is this number considered the dispenser and master of the entire structure, announcing danger or health to sick bodies. Indeed, the entire body is moved by seven motions: either forward <note>original: "accessio"</note> or backward <note>original: "recessio"</note>, <margin>The seven motions of the body</margin> or turning to the left or right, or moving up or down, or rotating in a circle.

The number seven, distinguished by so many virtues—which it either borrows from its parts or exercises as a whole—is rightly called and considered "full." It is now established by absolute reason why, for various causes, eight and seven are called full. This is the meaning: when your age has completed fifty-six years [7 x 8], which sum will be fatal to you, the hope of public safety will look to you; and for the common remedies of all good men, the state will owe a dictatorship to your virtues—but only if you can overcome the snares of your kinsmen (for through the seven...

<meta>This page continues Macrobius’s commentary on the "Dream of Scipio," moving from the mathematical properties of the number seven to its application in prophecy and the lifespan of Scipio Africanus the Younger. It explains why divine predictions are often shrouded in riddles.</meta>

# BOOK ONE

Eight circuits of the sun signify fifty-six years <note>Macrobius calculates this as 7 x 8 = 56, a crucial "fatal" number in Scipio's life</note>. He calls this the "winding path and return of the sun": the "winding path" because of the circuit of the Zodiac, and the "return" because the sun measures out the same signs every year by a fixed law. Here, some wonder what this uncertainty means: "if you escape," as if a divine soul, already returned to heaven and possessing the greatest knowledge of the future, could be ignorant of whether his grandson could escape his fate or not. But they fail to notice that all signs and dreams have this law: they announce, threaten, or warn of adversity through indirect means. Therefore, we avoid some things by taking care; others are avoided through prayer and sacrifice <note>The original term "litando" refers to a sacrifice that yields favorable omens</note>. There are other things that are inescapable, which are turned aside by no art and no cleverness. For where there is a warning, it is escaped by the vigilance of caution; what a threat brings, the sacrifice of propitiation turns away; but those things that are truly "announced" <note>In the sense of a final, divine decree</note> never vanish into nothing. Here you might ask: how do we discern these things, so it can be understood whether we should take care, or pray, or simply endure? It is the purpose of the present work to show what kind of intentional confusion usually exists in divinations, so that you may stop wondering at this apparent uncertainty. Otherwise, it is the task of the practitioner in his own art to seek the signs by which to discern these things, provided divine power does not prevent it. For as the poet says: "the Fates forbid us to know the rest" <note>original: "prohibent nam cetera parcae scire," a quote from Virgil's Aeneid</note>. This sentiment of Virgil's <note>referred to here as "Maro," his family name</note> comes from the deepest depths of hidden knowledge. We are also taught by famous examples that future events, when predicted, are always so locked away in doubt that a diligent seeker—unless divine power (as we said) blocks them—will find the traces of truth to be grasped beneath the surface.

<margin>Virgil</margin>

Take, for example, the Homeric dream sent by Jove (as it is told) to join battle with the enemy on the following day. With an open promise of victory, it animated the king's hope. Following that divine oracle, as it were, he began the battle, lost many of his men, and with great difficulty and pain retreated to his camp. Must we say that God commanded a lie? It is not so. But because the Fates had decreed that disaster for the Greeks, the truth lay hidden in the words of the dream, which, if noticed, could have instructed him either how to truly win or at least how to be cautious. For the instruction was that the "entire army" should be led out. But the king, content with the mere exhortation to fight, did not see what was commanded regarding the "entirety" to be led forth. By leaving out Achilles—who at that time, stung by a recent injury, was staying away from arms with his own soldiers—the king went forward into battle and received the disaster that was owed. Thus, he cleared the dream of the suspicion of lying by not following everything that was commanded. Virgil, an imitator of Homeric perfection in all things, maintained a similar diligence in such matters. For in his work, Aeneas—who had been sufficiently and abundantly instructed by the oracle at Delos regarding the region to be chosen by fate for establishing his kingdom—nevertheless fell into error through the neglect of a single word. It was not that the name of the place he should seek had been inserted; rather, when it was said that he should follow his "ancient mother" <note>The oracle told Aeneas to "seek your ancient mother" (Antiquam exquirite matrem)</note>, there were clues in the words that pointed more toward Italy than Crete (both of which had produced the founders of that race). The oracle "pointed its finger," as they say, at Italy. For while Teucer was from Crete, Dardanus was from Italy; the sacred voice, by addressing them as "Hardy sons of Dardanus," <note>original: "Dardanidae duri"</note> pointed toward Italy to those who consulted it aptly, for that was where Dardanus had come from. By calling them by the name of that ancestor, the oracle indicated whose origin was the correct one to choose. 

And here, certainly, is a clear announcement concerning the end of Scipio. But for the sake of creating a graceful obscurity, a doubt was inserted; yet it is resolved by what is contained in the evidence of the dream. For when it is said that he will have completed his fatal sum through a natural circuit, it announces that this end cannot be avoided. As for why he recounted the other acts of Scipio's life in order without any doubt, but seemed to hesitate regarding his death alone, the reason is this: either out of mercy for human grief or fear, or because it is most useful for this to remain hidden, the ends of lives are expressed by oracles more obscurely than other events. 

Having treated these matters in part, let us proceed to the rest. "But so that you may be more eager, Africanus, to protect the republic, hold this truth: for all those who have preserved, aided, or enlarged their fatherland, there is a certain and defined place in heaven where the blessed enjoy eternal life. For nothing is more acceptable to that principal God who rules the entire world—at least of what happens on earth—than the councils and assemblies of men united by law, which are called ci..." <note>The text cuts off mid-word "civitates" (cities/states)</note>

<sig>B ii</sig>

<summary>Macrobius explains that prophetic dreams are often intentionally ambiguous to test the recipient or fulfill fate, citing examples from Homer and Virgil. He concludes by affirming that a divine reward in heaven awaits those who serve their country.</summary>
<keywords>Scipio, prophecy, Homer, Virgil, Aeneas, Agamemnon, fate, solar cycle, divination, civic virtue, heaven</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Macrobius’s commentary on the "Dream of Scipio." Having established the fatal timeline of Scipio's life, the text now transitions into the rewards of the soul and a philosophical classification of the four types of virtue based on the teachings of Plotinus and Plato.</meta>

->### ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO<-

...are called states <note>The original Latin "civitates" refers to organized political communities</note>: their rulers and preservers, having set out from here, return hither. Well and opportunely, after he spoke of death, he immediately added the rewards to be hoped for by the good after their passing; by these, the thoughts of the living man were so raised from the fear of the aforementioned death that he was inspired of his own will to a desire for dying, moved by the majesty of the promised blessedness and the celestial dwelling. But concerning the blessedness <margin>Blessedness which is given to the preservers of the fatherland</margin> owed to the preservers of the fatherland, a few things must be said, so that afterwards we may resolve the entire topic we have undertaken to treat here. Virtues alone make one blessed; by no other way does anyone attain this name. Hence, those who believe that none but philosophers possess virtues declare that none but philosophers are blessed. For, calling the knowledge of divine things "wisdom," they say that only those are wise who seek it with the sharp edge of the mind and, with the sagacious diligence of searching, comprehend it—imitating the clarity of divine life as much as possible. And they say the exercise of the virtues <margin>The exercise of the virtues</margin> exists in this alone. They distribute the duties of these virtues as follows:

It is the part of **Prudence** to despise this world and all things in it through the contemplation of the divine, and to direct every thought of the soul toward the divine alone. It is the part of **Temperance** to abandon everything, as far as nature allows, that the use of the body requires. It is the part of **Fortitude** that the soul not be terrified as it withdraws from the body, led in a certain way by philosophy, nor to shrink from the height of the perfect ascent to the heavens. It is the part of **Justice** to consent to this single path of purpose, following the service of each individual virtue. Thus it happens that, according to the abruptness of such a rigid definition, the rulers of states cannot be blessed. 

But Plotinus, the prince among the professors of philosophy along with Plato, in his book *On the Virtues*, arranges their levels in order, composed by a true and natural method of division. "There are," he says, "four types of the fourfold virtues. Of these, the first are called **Political**; the second, **Purgatorial** <note>Also known as "cleansing" virtues</note>; the third, **Virtues of the Purified Mind**; the fourth, **Exemplary Virtues**." <margin>Political virtues</margin> And the political virtues belong to man because he is a social animal. By these, good men provide for the republic and protect their cities; by these, they venerate their parents, love their children, and cherish their neighbors; by these, they govern the safety of the citizens; by these, they protect their allies with circumspect providence and bind them with just liberality; and by these, they make others mindful of them through their merit. 

It is the part of political **Prudence** to direct all things according to the norm of reason—whatever one thinks or does—and to do nothing except what is right or praiseworthy, providing for human acts as if before divine judges. <margin>Prudence, Fortitude</margin> Within Prudence are: reason, intellect, circumspection, providence, teachability, and caution. It is the part of **Fortitude** to drive the mind above the fear of danger, to fear nothing except what is base, and to bravely endure either adversity or prosperity. Fortitude provides magnanimity, confidence, security, magnificence, constancy, tolerance, and firmness. It is the part of **Temperance** to desire nothing that leads to regret, to exceed the law of moderation in nothing, and to tame desire under the yoke of reason. Temperance is followed by modesty, reverence, abstinence, chastity, honesty, moderation, thrift, sobriety, and purity. It is the part of **Justice** to preserve for each person what is their own. From Justice come innocence, friendship, concord, piety, religion, affection, and humanity. <margin>A good man</margin> By these virtues, a good man is first made the ruler of himself and then of the republic, governing human affairs justly and providently, without abandoning them.

The second type, which they call **Purgatorial**, belong to the man who is capable of the divine; they set free the soul of him alone who has decided to cleanse himself from the contagion of the body and, by a certain flight from human affairs, to join himself to the divine alone. These belong to those at leisure <note>The "leisure" of the scholar or monk, away from public business</note> who sequester themselves from the acts of the republic. What each of these virtues intends, we expressed above when we spoke of the virtues of those practicing philosophy, <margin>Virtues of the purified mind</margin> which some believed were the only virtues. 

The third are the virtues of the mind already **purified** and cleansed, wiped clean and pure from every speck of this world. There, the part of Prudence is not to prefer divine things as if by choice, but to know them alone, and to look upon them as if nothing else exists. The part of Temperance is not to repress tender desires, but to forget them entirely. The part of Fortitude is to be ignorant of passions, not to conquer them—so that the soul does not know how to be angry and desires nothing. The part of Justice is to be so associated with the celestial and divine Mind <note>original: νοῦ (Nous)</note> that it preserves a perpetual covenant with it by imitation. 

The fourth are those which consist in the divine Mind itself, which we said is called *Nous* <note>The Greek term for the "Divine Intellect"</note>, from whose example all the rest flow down in order. For if other things, then much more the virtues...

ii ii

<summary>Macrobius outlines a hierarchy of virtues based on Neoplatonist thought, categorizing them into four levels: Political, Purgatorial, Purified, and Exemplary. This framework justifies how both active statesmen and contemplative philosophers can achieve celestial rewards.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Macrobius’s philosophical exploration of the "Dream of Scipio." On the previous page, the author began defining the four cardinal virtues. Here, he moves from the "political" virtues practiced in civic life to the higher forms of these virtues that exist in the divine mind and assist the soul's return to the heavens.</meta>

### BOOK ONE

...one must believe that the archetypes <note>The text uses "ideas," referring to the Platonic forms or perfect patterns</note> exist in the mind. Therein is Prudence: the divine mind itself. **Temperance** is found there because it is turned toward itself with perpetual focus. **Fortitude** is that which is always the same and never changes. **Justice** is that which, through eternal law, does not deviate from the everlasting continuity of its own work. These are the four types of the four virtues which, among other things, have their greatest distinction in how they relate to the passions.
<margin>Passions of the soul</margin>
Passions, however (as we know), are named for what men fear and desire, or what they grieve and rejoice in. The first level of virtues [Political] softens these passions; the second [Purifying] removes them; the third [Purified] forgets them; in the fourth [Exemplary], it is a sin even for them to be named.

If this is the duty and effect of the virtues, it is well established that even political virtues make one blessed; therefore, men are made blessed by political acts as well. Rightly, then, did Tullius <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> say concerning the rulers of republics: "where the blessed may enjoy eternal life." In order to show that some are made blessed by virtues of leisure <note>contemplative life</note> and others by virtues of business <note>active political life</note>, he did not say absolutely that nothing is more acceptable to that primary God than states, but added "at least among those things that happen on earth." He did this to distinguish those who begin their journey from the celestial realms themselves from the rulers of cities, for whom a path to heaven is prepared through earthly deeds. 

Moreover, what could be more precise or more cautious than his definition of the name of "cities"? He calls them "councils and gatherings of men associated by law." For once even a band of slaves or gladiators were "gatherings and councils of men," but they were not "associated by law." That multitude alone is just whose entire body consents to the obedience of the laws. 

As for his statement, "The rulers and preservers of these cities set out from here and return hither," it must be understood in this way: that the origin of souls flows from heaven is an undisputed opinion among those who philosophize correctly. While the soul uses the body, this is perfect wisdom: that it should recognize where it arose and from what source it came. 
<margin>Perfect wisdom</margin>
Hence, that saying was seriously adopted by a certain man <note>attributed to various philosophers or the Delphic Oracle</note> among other festive or biting remarks: "Know Thyself" <note>original: "γνῶθι σαυτόν"</note> descended from heaven. For this is said to be the voice of the Delphic oracle to one consulting it on how to reach blessedness. "If you know yourself," it says; indeed, this sentence was inscribed on the front of the temple itself. For a man, there is only one way to recognize himself: if he looks back to the principles and first beginnings of his origin and birth, and does not seek himself outside of himself. Thus the soul clothes itself in the virtues through the consciousness of its own nobility; by these virtues, it is carried back, after leaving the body, to the place from which it descended. For a soul that is nourished by the pure and light fuel of the virtues does not become filthy or weighed down by the dregs of the body, nor does it ever seem to have truly left heaven, which it still possessed through its gaze and thoughts. 

Conversely, the soul that creates for itself a prison through the use of the body—and has in a sense deformed itself from a human into a beast—dreads the release from the body. When it must leave, it does not flee except with a groan, indignant, into the shadows. Even after death, it does not easily leave the body, because the bodily plagues do not fundamentally depart; instead, it either wanders around its own corpse or seeks the dwelling of a new body—not only human, but also choosing a type of beast consistent with the habits it freely practiced as a human. It prefers to suffer anything rather than escape to the heaven which it abandoned through ignorance, indifference, or rather, by losing it. 

The rulers of cities and other wise men, however, dwell in heaven by their gaze even while they are still held by the body; thus, after the body, they easily reclaim the celestial seat which they had almost never left. Indeed, it was not out of nothing or through vain flattery that antiquity consecrated certain founders of cities or famous men of the republic into the number of the gods.
<margin>Founders of cities counted among the gods</margin>
Even Hesiod <note>An early Greek poet</note>, a claimant of divine lineage, numbers ancient kings among the other gods; here, by the example of ancient power, he assigns them the duty of ruling human affairs even in heaven. And lest it be tedious to anyone, if we repeat the verses themselves as the Greek poet produced them, we shall report them as they have been translated from his words into Latin words:

> These are the ancestral gods <note>original: "Indigetes divi"</note> by the fate of supreme Jove.
> Once they were men; now with the dwellers above they watch over human affairs,
> Generous and munificent, having now also obtained the right of kings.

Virgil, too, is not ignorant of this. Although, serving his own plot, he bound his heroes in the underworld, he nonetheless does not lead them away from heaven; rather, he assigns to them a more generous atmosphere, and professes that they know their own sun and their own stars, so that he might provide observations of a dual doctrine...

He supports this by citing the Delphic oracle and the works of Cicero, Hesiod, and Virgil to show that virtuous rulers earn a place among the stars.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Macrobius’s commentary on the "Dream of Scipio." Having previously discussed the four cardinal virtues, the author now explains how these virtues manifest in Scipio’s dream and begins a philosophical interpretation of the soul's journey from the heavens into the physical body, which he characterizes as a "prison" or "underworld."</meta>

### ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

...both the fiction of poetry and the truth of philosophy. And if, according to him <note>The author refers here to the poet Virgil</note>, even the lighter matters which they practiced while alive are still practiced after leaving the body:
"The same pride in chariots and arms that they had while living, the same care in feeding sleek horses, follows them when they are laid in the earth." <note>original: "quæ gratia currum / Armorumq; fuit uiuis: quæ cura nitentis / Pascere equos: eadem sequitur tellure repostos." — Virgil, Aeneid 6.653-655</note>

<margin>
The Fixed Sphere [Aplanes] is the dwelling of souls
</margin>
Much more so do the former rulers of cities, once received into heaven, not abandon the care of ruling men. These souls are believed to be received into the furthest sphere, which is called the *Aplanes* <term>Aplanes: A Greek term meaning 'not wandering,' referring to the outermost sphere of the universe containing the fixed stars</term>. Nor is this name used without reason, since they set out from there. For to souls not yet entangled by the desire for a body, the starry part of the world provides a dwelling, and from there they slide down into bodies. Therefore, return to that place is for those who deserve it. Most rightly, then, was it said—since this discourse proceeds to the Milky Way <note>original: "galaxian"</note> which the Fixed Sphere contains—"having set out from here, they return here." Let us pass to what follows. "Here, therefore, although I was terrified, not so much by the fear of death as by the plots of my own people, I nevertheless asked whether he himself was living, and my father Paulus, and others whom we thought were extinct." Even by chance and among stories, the seeds of ingrained virtues shine forth; you may see them now as they emerge from the breast of Scipio even while dreaming. For in this one matter, he exercises the duty of the political virtues. That his mind does not fail though terrified by the prediction of death is **fortitude**. That he is terrified by the plots of his own people, and dreads another's crime more than his own destruction, proceeds from **piety** <note>In the Roman sense of 'pietas,' meaning duty to family, country, and gods</note> and excessive love for his kin. We have said these things refer to **justice**, which preserves for each what is his own. That he does not take as certain those things he used to believe, but, having discarded the opinion that grows in less cautious minds as if it were truth, seeks to speak more certain things, is undoubted **prudence**. When perfect happiness and a heavenly dwelling are promised to human nature—in which he knew himself to be—yet he bridles, tempers, and sets aside the desire to hear such things so that he may ask about the life of his grandfather and father; what is this but **temperance**? Thus it became clear that Africanus was led through quietude to those places which were owed to him.

<margin>
Immortality of the soul
</margin>
In this questioning, the immortality of the soul is treated. For here is the sense of the consultation itself: "We," he says, "thought that the soul was extinguished with the end of the dying man, and was no more after the man." For he said, "those whom we thought were extinct." That which is extinguished, however, ceases to be. "Therefore," he says, "I would wish you to say if both my father Paulus and others are still with you." To this question—which he framed both concerning parents, as a pious son, and concerning others, as a wise man investigating nature itself—the other replied: "On the contrary," he said, "those are alive who have flown out from the bonds of the body as if from a prison. But your life, as it is called, is death."

<margin>
Who the inhabitants of the underworld are. The River Lethe
</margin>
If one must travel to the underworld, if it has been established what place must be held for the inhabitants of the underworld—so that while the soul is thrust into this [the body], it is believed to die, but when it is far from it, it enjoys life and truly survives. And because you will find the whole treatise which the wisdom of the ancients conducted regarding the investigation of this question hidden in this small number of words, we have excerpted from all of them a few things which will suffice to remind us of the resolution of the matter we seek, for the sake of brevity. Before the study of philosophy grew to such vigor regarding the inquiry into nature, the authors among various nations who established sacred ceremonies denied that the underworld <note>original: "inferos," literally "the ones below"</note> was anything other than the bodies themselves, in which the enclosed souls suffer a prison foul with darkness and horrid with filth and blood. This they called the sepulcher of the soul; this the "Cave of Dis" <note>Dis was the Roman name for Pluto, god of the underworld</note>; this they called the underworld. And everything which fabulous persuasion believed to be there, they attempted to assign to ourselves and to these human bodies. They asserted that the River of Oblivion <note>Lethe</note> is nothing else than the error of the soul forgetting the majesty of its prior life, which it possessed before it was thrust into the body, and thinking that the only life is in the body.

<margin>
Phlegethon, Acheron, Coccytus, Styx
</margin>
By a similar interpretation, they thought **Phlegethon** was the fire of anger and desires; **Acheron**, whatever we regret having done or said, following the custom of human variability, leading even to sadness; **Coccytus**, whatever compels men to mourning and tears; **Styx**, whatever [exists] among

<summary>Macrobius interprets Scipio’s dream-dialogue as proof of the soul’s immortality and provides an allegorical reading of the underworld, suggesting that the physical body itself is the "hell" where souls suffer forgetfulness and unruly passions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Macrobius’s philosophical interpretation of Scipio's dream. Having established that the soul descends from the heavens, the author now uses classical myths of the underworld (Tityus, Sisyphus, Tantalus) as allegories for the psychological and physical suffering of the soul while it is imprisoned in the living human body.</meta>

<page-num>XII</page-num>
<header>BOOK ONE</header>

<margin>
The vulture tearing at the liver of Tityus
</margin>
...drowns human souls in a whirlpool of hatred. Indeed, the ancients believed that the very description of the punishments in the underworld was drawn from the experience of human life itself. They intended the vulture plucking at the immortal liver <note>In myth, the giant Tityus was punished in Hades by a vulture eating his regenerating liver</note> to be understood as nothing other than the torments of a conscience guilty of a crime. This conscience searches the inner vitals and tears at the very heart with a tireless reminder of the sin committed. Whenever the soul tries to rest, the conscience stirs up these cares again, clinging to them as if they were regenerating fibers, sparing itself no mercy. By this law, no guilty person is acquitted when they are their own judge, nor can they escape their own sentence. Furthermore, those who are tortured by hunger and waste away from starvation with feasts placed before their eyes <note>An allusion to the myth of Tantalus</note> represent those whom the desire for acquiring more and more forces to ignore their present abundance; even in the midst of plenty, they suffer the evils of poverty and want, not knowing how to look back at what they have gained because they are so preoccupied with what they still lack. Those who hang stretched upon wheels <note>An allusion to Ixion</note> are those who, providing nothing by counsel, moderating nothing by reason, and achieving nothing by virtue, surrender themselves and all their actions to fortune; they are forever tossed about by accidents and chance. Those who roll a huge stone <note>An allusion to Sisyphus</note> wear away their lives in ineffective and most laborious efforts. A dark flint stone, always about to slip and seemingly falling, hangs over the heads of those <note>An allusion to the Sword of Damocles</note> who pursue high positions of power and unlucky tyranny, destined to live never without fear. By forcing the common people they rule to hate them while fearing them, they always seem to see their own deserved destruction hanging over them.

<margin>
Dionysius the Sicilian
</margin>
Nor did the theologians suspect this without cause. For Dionysius of the Sicilian court <note>Dionysius I or II, the famously paranoid tyrants of Syracuse</note>, a most harsh usurper, once wished to show a member of his inner circle who thought the life of a tyrant was uniquely blessed just how wretched that life is due to perpetual fear and how full of impending dangers. He ordered a sword, drawn from its scabbard and hanging by a thin thread from its hilt with the point facing down, to hang over that man’s head during a banquet. When the man began to despise both the Sicilian riches and the tyrant's wealth because of the immediate danger of death, Dionysius said: "Such is the life you thought was blessed; thus we always see death looming over us." Consider, then, how anyone can be happy if they never cease to feel fear. According to these things asserted by the theologians, if we truly "suffer our own ghosts" <note>original: "quisque suos patimur manes" — a quote from Virgil, Aeneid 6.743</note> and believe the underworld is within these bodies, what else is to be understood but that the soul dies when it sinks into the infernal regions of the body, but lives when it escapes to the heights after leaving the body?

<margin>
Two deaths
</margin>
We must now state what further truths the more diligent study of philosophy has added to these ideas. For first Pythagoras, and later those who followed Plato, declared that there are two deaths: one of the soul, and another of the living creature. They say the "creature" dies when the soul departs from the body, but the soul itself "dies" when it is dissipated from the simple and indivisible source of nature into the limbs of the body. And because one of these deaths is manifest and known to all, while the other is only grasped by the wise (with others believing it to be "life"), most people are ignorant as to why we call the god of death sometimes "Rich" <term>Ditem: The Latin name for Pluto/Hades, etymologically linked to 'dives' or riches</term> and sometimes "Mild." Through the first death—that is, the death of the living creature—the soul is released and sent back to the true riches of nature and its own freedom, which the favorable name indicates. But through the other death, which is commonly thought to be "life," we testify with a name of horror that the soul is driven from the light of its immortality into certain shadows of death.

<margin>
The Body as a Tomb
</margin>
For a living creature to exist, the soul must be bound in a body. Therefore, the body is called a *Bond* <note>original: Δέμασ (Demas)</note>, and *Soma* <note>original: σῶμα</note>, as if it were a *Sema* <note>original: σῆμα</note>, that is, the "sepulcher" or tomb of the soul. Hence Cicero, signifying both at once—that the body is a bond and the body is a tomb—says that it is a "prison of the buried." Those who have flown out from the bonds of bodies as if from a prison [are the truly living].

<margin>
The Platonic opinion of the Underworld
</margin>
The Platonists, however, said that the underworld is not *in* the bodies—that is, it does not begin with the bodies—but they called a certain part of this world the "Seat of Dis" <note>The Underworld</note>. Concerning the boundaries of this place, they published conflicting views among themselves, and their opinion is divided into three sects. 

<margin>
The World divided in two. The life and death of the soul.
</margin>
Some divided the world into two parts: one that acts, and one that is acted upon. They said that which "acts" is that which, being immutable itself, imposes the cause and necessity of change upon the other. That which is "acted upon" is that which varies through changes. They said the immutable part of the world extends from the sphere called the *Aplanes* <term>Aplanes: The fixed, non-wandering sphere of the stars</term> down to the beginning of the lunar globe. The mutable part, they said, extends from the moon down to the earth. And they said that souls live while they are in the immutable...

<meta>catchword: immutable</meta>

<summary>Macrobius interprets underworld myths as allegories for the soul's suffering while trapped in the physical body, which he calls a "prison" and "tomb." He explains the Neoplatonic concept of "two deaths": the physical death of the body and the spiritual "death" the soul undergoes when it enters the material world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Macrobius’s commentary on the "Dream of Scipio." While the previous page used mythological allegories to describe the soul’s suffering within the body, Macrobius now turns to cosmology and the physical journey the soul takes from the heavens down to Earth, specifically focusing on the role of the Moon and the celestial spheres.</meta>

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

...consist in that part; however, they are said to die when they fall into the part capable of change. And for this reason, the space between the moon and the earth is called the place of death and of the <term>inferi</term> <note>original: "inferorum"; referring to the underworld or lower regions</note>. The moon itself is the boundary of life and death. Souls flowing from there down to the earth are said to die; those passing from there back to the upper regions are said to return to life. 

<margin>Lunar peoples</margin>
This has been judged not without merit. For from the moon downward, the nature of perishable things begins. From this point, souls begin to fall under the count of days. Finally, the <term>physici</term> <note>Natural philosophers or scientists of the ancient world</note> called that region the "ethereal earth," and they named its inhabitants the "lunar peoples." Many have taught that this is so by various arguments which would be long to enumerate here. Nor is there any doubt that the moon is the author and creator of mortal bodies, to such an extent that some bodies suffer increase as her light waxes and are diminished as she wanes. But lest a long-winded assertion create boredom regarding a manifest matter, let us pass on to what others define concerning the place of the underworld.

<margin>Division of the world</margin>
For others have preferred to divide the world into groups of four elements. In the first order are counted: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire (which is the more liquid part of the air neighboring the moon). Above this, there are again the same number of elements but of a purer nature: so that the Moon stands for Earth (which we said was called the "ethereal earth" by the natural philosophers); Water is the sphere of Mercury; Air is the sphere of Venus; and Fire is in the Sun. 

Yet a third order of elements is turned toward us in such a way that it makes Earth the last, and with the others reduced into the middle, it ends in the Earth as the lowest and highest extremity. 

<margin>Elysian fields</margin>
Therefore, let the sphere of Mars hold Fire; Jupiter, Air; Saturn, Water; and the <term>aplanes</term> <note>original: "aplanes"; the sphere of the fixed stars that does not wander</note> hold Earth. In this sphere, antiquity has left us to understand that the "Elysian fields" are located, designated for pure souls. When a soul is sent from these fields into a body, it descends through these three orders of elements toward the body by a "triple death." 

<margin>Third division of the world</margin>
This is the second opinion among the Platonists concerning the death of the soul when it is thrust into the body. However, others (for we noted before that there are three different opinions among them) also divide it into two parts just as the first group does, but they do not divide the world at these same boundaries. For here, they want the heaven—which is called the unmoving sphere <note>the "aplanes"</note>—to be one part, while the seven spheres which are called "wandering" <note>the planets</note>, together with what is between them and the earth, and the earth itself, to be the other part. 

According to these thinkers—whose sect possesses a more friendly reasoning—blessed souls, free from all contagion of any body whatsoever, possess the heaven. But those souls which, looking down from that highest watchtower and perpetual light with a desire for the body and for this which we call "life" on earth, have meditated with a hidden longing, gradually slide down into the lower regions by the very weight of that earthly thought. 

The soul does not suddenly put on the "clay body" from a state of perfect incorporeality, but gradually, through silent losses and a longer withdrawal from simple and absolute purity, it swells with the increases of a certain "starry body." For in each of the spheres that lie below the heaven, it is clothed in an ethereal envelope so that, through these stages, it may be reconciled to the company of this "earthen garment." Therefore, it arrives at what is called "life" on earth after passing through as many motions as there are spheres.

<margin>Order of the soul descending into the body</margin>
The order of its descent, by which the soul slides from heaven into the depths of this life, is arranged thus: it embraces the Zodiac where it meets the Milky Way in an oblique curve, intersecting it at the two tropical signs, Capricorn and Cancer. 

<margin>Gates of the Sun</margin>
The natural philosophers called these the "Gates of the Sun," because at each solstice, the further progress of the sun is inhibited, and a return is made for it to the path of its zone, whose boundaries it never leaves. 

<margin>The Gate of Cancer is for humans</margin>
They believe that souls travel from heaven to earth and return from earth to heaven through these gates. Therefore, one is called the Gate of Men and the other the Gate of Gods. Cancer is the Gate of Men because the descent into the lower parts is through it. 

<margin>The Gate of Capricorn is for the gods</margin>
Capricorn is the Gate of the Gods because through it, souls return to the seat of their proper immortality and into the number of the gods. And this is what the divine wisdom of Homer signifies in his description of the Cave of Ithaca. 

<margin>The Empire of Dis</margin>
Here Pythagoras also thinks that the "Empire of Dis" <note>The underworld realm of Pluto</note> begins downward from the Milky Way, because souls falling from there seem already to have withdrawn from the upper world. 

<margin>Milk is the first nourishment</margin>
For this reason, he says that the first nourishment of milk is offered to the newborn, because their first movement begins from the Milky Way as they slide into earthly bodies. Thus, after the Milky Way was shown to Scipio regarding the souls of the blessed, it was said to him: "From here they set out, and to here they return." Therefore, while those about to descend are still in Cancer, because they are placed there and have not yet left the Milky Way, they are still in the number of the gods. But when, by sliding, they have reached Leo, they begin the prelude of their future condition. And because in Leo they are in the first stages...
