<meta>This page continues Macrobius’s Neo-Platonic exposition on the soul's journey. Having established the Moon as the boundary between the eternal and the perishable, Macrobius now details the specific mechanics of the soul's "descent" from the Milky Way through the planetary spheres, where it acquires various human faculties before becoming imprisoned in a physical body.</meta>

# BOOK ONE

<margin>Aquarius is contrary to human life</margin>
...of being born: and certain initiations of human nature. However, Aquarius is opposite to Leo; and as Leo rises, Aquarius soon sets. Therefore, when the sun holds Aquarius, offerings are made to the spirits of the dead <note>original: "parentatur"; referring to Parentalia, a Roman festival honoring deceased ancestors</note>, as it is in a sign that is considered contrary or adverse to human life. From there, therefore—that is, from the boundary where the zodiac and the Milky Way touch—the soul begins its descent. From its perfectly round shape, which is the only divine form, it is drawn out and flows down into a cone <note>Macrobius uses the geometric transition from a point to a cone to symbolize the soul's loss of simplicity as it enters the material world</note>; just as a line is born from a point and proceeds from the indivisible into length. There, from its own point, which is the **monad** <note>the unit or "one"</note>, it comes into the **dyad** <note>duality</note>, which is the first falling away from unity. 

<margin>The time of offerings for the dead</margin>
And this is the essence which Plato, in the *Timaeus*, expressed as being both indivisible and divisible when he spoke of the construction of the world-soul. For the souls of the world and of an individual man are found to be at one moment ignorant of division—if the simplicity of divine nature is considered—and at another moment capable of it, when they are diffused through the members of the world or of a man. 

<margin>The descent of the soul</margin>
Therefore, when the soul is drawn toward the body, in this first extension of itself, it begins to experience a "wood-like" or chaotic tumult—that is, <term>hyle</term> <note>the Greek term for raw matter or "stuff"</note> flowing into it. And this is what Plato noted in the *Phaedo*: that the soul is drawn into the body trembling with a new drunkenness, meaning the new drink of material flooding, by which it is soaked and weighed down as it is led downward. 

<margin>The Bowl of Father Liber</margin>
A sign of this mystery is also that starry **Bowl of Father Liber** <note>The constellation Crater; Father Liber is the Roman equivalent of Bacchus or Dionysus</note> located in the region between Cancer and Leo, signifying that drunkenness first occurs there for souls about to descend, as matter flows in. From this, forgetfulness, the companion of drunkenness, begins to creep secretly upon the souls there. 

<margin>The forgetfulness of souls</margin>
For if souls carried the memory of divine things—of which they were conscious in heaven—all the way to their bodies, there would be no disagreement among men concerning divinity. But indeed, all drink of forgetfulness while descending, some more, others less. And therefore on earth, although the truth is not clear to everyone, everyone nevertheless has opinions, because the origin of opinion is a defect of memory. However, those find the truth more easily who have drunk less of forgetfulness, because they easily remember what they knew there before. This is why what the Latins call "reading" <note>original: "lectio"</note> is called "repeated knowledge" <note>original Greek: "anamnesis"; the Platonic theory that learning is actually a process of remembering</note> by the Greeks; because when we learn true things, we recognize those things which we naturally knew before the material influx made the souls drunk as they came into the body. 

<margin>Matter (Hyle)</margin>
This is <term>hyle</term>, which formed every body of the world we see anywhere, having been impressed with "Ideas." But its highest and purest part, by which the divine is either sustained or consists, is called **nectar**, and is believed to be the drink of the gods. 

<margin>Nectar</margin>
The lower and more turbulent part is the drink of souls. And this is what the ancients called the **River Lethe** <note>The mythological river of forgetfulness in the underworld</note>. 

<margin>River Lethe</margin>
Moreover, the Orphics <note>Followers of the mystical Orphic religion</note> suspect that **Father Liber** himself is understood as the "material mind" <note>original Greek: "noūs hylikos"</note>, because, born from that indivisible Mind, he himself is divided into individuals. 

<margin>Father Liber</margin>
Therefore, in their sacred rites, it is handed down that he was torn into limbs by a Titanic fury and, with the pieces buried, he emerged again as one and whole; because Mind—which we said is called <term>mens</term>—by offering itself to be divided from the indivisible, and returning from the divided to the indivisible, both fulfills the duties of the world and does not desert the secrets of its own nature. 

Therefore, having slipped down from the zodiac and the Milky Way with this first weight toward the underlying spheres, while the soul glides through them, it is not only clothed (as we have said) in the approach of a luminous body, but it also produces each of the motions which it is to have in practice:

<margin>The soul receives: From Saturn, From Jupiter, From Mars, From the Sun, From Venus, From Mercury, From the Moon</margin>
*   In **Saturn**: reasoning and intelligence (which they call "logical and theoretical" <note>original Greek: "logistikon theoretikon"</note>).
*   In **Jupiter**: the power of acting (which is called "practical" <note>original Greek: "praktikon"</note>).
*   In **Mars**: the heat of spiritedness (which is named "spirited" <note>original Greek: "thymikon"</note>).
*   In **the Sun**: the nature of sensing and imagining (which they call "sensory" <note>original Greek: "aisthetikon"</note> and "imaginative" <note>original Greek: "phantastikon"</note>).
*   In **Venus**: the motion of desire (which is called "appetitive" <note>original Greek: "epithymetikon"</note>).
*   In **Mercury**: the power of pronouncing and interpreting what it feels (which is called "interpretive" <note>original Greek: "hermeneutikon"</note>).
*   In the **Moon**: it exercises the "vegetative" <note>original Greek: "phytikon"</note> power—that is, the nature of planting and growing bodies. 

This last power is the furthest from divine things and the first in our earthly spheres. For this human body is just as the dregs of divine things, so it is the first substance of the animal soul. And this is the difference between earthly bodies and the celestial ones—I mean the heavens, the stars, and the other elements: those indeed were summoned upward to the seat of the soul, and earned immortality from the very nature of the region and by imitation of the height. But to these earthly bodies, the soul itself leads down; and therefore it is believed to die when it is enclosed in a decaying region and in the seat of mortality.

<summary>Macrobius explains the Neoplatonic descent of the soul, describing how it passes from the Milky Way through the seven planetary spheres, acquiring a specific mental or physical faculty from each planet before entering a mortal body. He uses the myth of Father Liber (Dionysus) and the concept of "Hyle" (matter) to explain how the soul becomes "drunk" with forgetfulness and divided among individuals.</summary>
<keywords>soul's descent, planetary spheres, celestial faculties, Hyle, Dionysus, Lethe, Macrobius, Neoplatonism, anamnesis, forgetfulness, monad, dyad</keywords>

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

<margin>What the death of the soul is</margin>
Do not let it disturb you that we so often use the name "death" regarding the soul, which we claim is immortal. For the soul is not extinguished by its own death, but is overwhelmed for a time. Nor is the benefit of its perpetuity removed by this temporary submergence. When the soul has earned the right to be purged—having the contagion of its vices thoroughly washed away—it is restored to the light of the "parent life" <note>original: "parentis uitae lucem"; refers to the divine source or the Father from which the soul originated</note> and returns to its original wholeness. I believe the definition of the life and death of the soul is now fully clear; it is a doctrine drawn from the inner shrines of philosophy by the teaching of Cicero. But Scipio, encouraged by the promise of immortality and his place in heaven—which is granted as a reward to the blessed—strengthened this glorious and renowned hope more and more upon seeing his father. Though he seemed to doubt whether his father was still living, he asked him directly. He then began to prefer death so that he might truly live. Not content with weeping at the sight of the parent he had believed was dead, as soon as he was able to speak, he first wanted to prove that he desired nothing more than to remain with him now. Yet, he did not decide to do what he desired on his own initiative until he had consulted his elders; the first of these actions is an assertion of prudence, the second of piety. Now, let us examine the words of the one seeking advice and the one giving it. "I beg you," he said, "most holy and best father, since this is truly life (as I hear Africanus <note>Scipio Africanus the Elder, the grandfather of the narrator, who appears in the dream</note> say), why do I linger on earth? Why do I not hasten to come here to you?"

"It is not so," his father replied. "For unless the god whose temple this is—and everything you see—has freed you from these physical guards <note>original: "corporis custodijs"; a common Platonic metaphor for the body as a prison or a guard-post</note> of the body, the path here cannot lie open for you. For humans were brought into being under this law: to tend to that globe which you see in the middle of this temple, which is called Earth. To them, a soul was given from those eternal fires which you call constellations and stars;

<margin>Death is to be sought, but not inflicted on oneself</margin>
these, being spherical and round and animated by divine minds, complete their circles and orbits with wonderful speed. Therefore, Publius, you and all pious men must keep the soul in the custody of the body. You must not depart from human life without the command of him by whom the soul was given to you, lest you seem to have fled the task assigned by God." This is the sect and precept of Plato, who defines in the *Phaedo* <note>One of Plato's most famous dialogues, set on the day of Socrates' execution, dealing with the immortality of the soul</note> that a human being must not die of his own accord. Yet, in that same dialogue, he also says that death is to be sought by those practicing philosophy, and that philosophy itself is a "meditation on dying."

<margin>The two deaths of man</margin>
These statements seem to contradict one another, but it is not so. For Plato recognizes two deaths of man. I am not now repeating what was said above—that there are two deaths, one of the soul and another of the living creature—but he asserts there are two deaths even for the living man himself. One of these is granted by nature, the other by the virtues.

<margin>The death of the wise man</margin>
For a man "dies" when the soul leaves the body, released by the law of nature. But he is also said to "die" when the soul, while still situated in the body, scorns bodily allurements through the teachings of philosophy and strips away the sweet snares of desires and all other remaining passions. This is what we noted earlier regarding the second order of virtues <note>Macrobius refers to the "purifying virtues" (purgatoriae), which separate the mind from the body's influence</note>, which belong only to those practicing philosophy. This, then, is the death that Plato says is to be sought by the wise. But that other death, which nature has established for everyone, he forbids to be forced, or self-inflicted, or summoned; he teaches that nature must be waited for. And he reveals the causes of this decree, which are borrowed from the common experiences of daily life. He says that those who are thrust into prison by the command of a governing power ought not to flee from there until the power that shut them in permits them to leave. For the punishment is not avoided by a stealthy escape; rather, it increases. He also adds that we are under the ownership of the gods, by whose guardianship and providence we are governed.

<margin>Those who bring death upon themselves</margin>
Furthermore, nothing should be taken away from the place where a master has stationed it without the master's consent. Just as one who wrests a slave's life away from another owner will not be free of crime, so too he who seeks an end for himself while the Master has not yet ordered it does not achieve absolution, but guilt. Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) whose works Macrobius frequently uses</note> follows these seeds of the Platonic school more deeply. He says it is necessary for the soul to be found free from bodily passions after a man’s death, but he who violently thrusts the soul out of the body does not allow it to be free. For whoever prepares his own death does so either because he is pressed by necessity, or out of fear, or out of hatred—all of which are regarded as passions. Therefore, even if the soul was pure of these stains before, it becomes stained by the very fact that its exit was forced. Furthermore, death ought to be the soul's release from the body, not a new binding. But by a forced exit, the soul is bound to the body more and more.

<summary>Macrobius explains the Platonic view on death, distinguishing between natural physical death and the "philosophical death" (detachment from passions). He argues that suicide is a violation of divine law and prevents the soul from achieving true purity.</summary>
<keywords>Macrobius, Somnium Scipionis, Plato, Phaedo, Plotinus, immortality of the soul, suicide, philosophical death, virtue, divine law</keywords>

# BOOK ONE

And indeed, for this reason, souls that are violently torn away linger for a long time around the body, its burial, or the place where the hand was laid upon them <note>original: "eiusue sepulturam uel locum : ī quo iniecta manus est"; referring to the belief that victims of violence or suicide haunt the site of their death</note>. In contrast, those souls that, in this life, dissolve themselves from the bonds of the body through "philosophical death" <note>original: "philosophiæ morte"; a state of meditative detachment where the mind lives independently of bodily desires</note> are joined to the heavens and the stars even while the body still exists. Therefore, he indicates that this is the only praiseworthy form of voluntary death: one achieved through the reason of philosophy (as we have said), not by the sword; through prudence, not by poison.

<margin>Natural death</margin>
He also adds that natural death is the only kind where the body leaves the soul, not the soul leaving the body. For it is established that a certain and fixed ratio of numbers <note>Pythagorean and Platonic philosophy held that mathematical proportions bound the soul to the physical world; when these "harmonies" expired, life ended</note> associates souls with bodies. As long as these numbers remain, the body continues to be animated; but when they fail, that secret force which held the partnership together is quickly dissolved.

<margin>Fate and the fated times of life</margin>
And this is what we call fate and the "fated times" of life. The soul itself, therefore, does not fail—since it is immortal and eternal—but when the numbers are fulfilled, the body grows weary. The soul does not tire of animating, but the body abandons its duty when it can no longer be given life. From this comes the saying of the most learned poet <note>Virgil, in the Aeneid, Book VI</note>:

<margin>"I will complete the number" in Aeneid, Book VI</margin>
> "I will fulfill the number and be returned to the shadows." <note>original: "Explebo numerum: reddarq̃ tenebris"</note>

This, then, is truly natural death: when the failure of its own numbers alone brings an end to the body, and not when life is extorted from a body still fit to continue bearing it. There is no small difference between dissolving life by nature or by one's own will. For the soul, when it is abandoned by the body, can retain nothing corporeal within itself if it has kept itself pure while in this life. But when it is violently pushed out of the body—because it exits through a broken rather than an untied bond—the very necessity of the event becomes an occasion for passion; and while the bond is being broken, it becomes stained by those evil ties. He adds this further reason for not perishing by one's own hand: since it is established, he says, that the reward for souls must be granted there according to the measure of perfection each reached in this life, the end of life must not be hurried while there is still a possibility of increasing that perfection. Nor was this said in vain: for in the secret discussions concerning the return of the soul, it is said that those who stumble in this life are like those who fall on level ground; they are able to rise again without difficulty. But souls departing this life with the filth of their transgressions are to be compared to those who have fallen from a high and steep precipice, from which there is never a chance to rise again. Therefore, one must use the granted spans of life so that there may be a greater opportunity for perfect purification.

Someone might then ask: "Should he who is already perfectly purified lay hands upon himself, since there is no reason to remain and he requires no further perfection once he has reached the higher realms?" But by the very act of summoning a swift end for himself in the hope of enjoying blessedness, he is caught in the snare of passion—for hope, like fear, is a passion <note>In Stoic and Neoplatonic thought, "passions" are emotional disturbances that soil the soul's purity</note>. Moreover, he incurs the other risks mentioned in the previous reasoning. This is why Plotinus <note>A foundational Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD)</note> prohibits and pushes away his "son" <note>This refers to Porphyry, Plotinus's student, whom he famously talked out of suicide</note> when he hastens to come to him in hope of the beyond; he did so lest the hurried desire for release and ascent should bind and retard him even more through this very passion. He does not say that you will not be able to die unless natural death arrives, but that you will not be able to *reach that place*. For unless God has freed you from these "guards of the body" <note>original: "corporis custodiis"; often translated as the "prison" or "stronghold" of the body</note>, he says, the entrance cannot lie open for you; for he knows that once received into heaven, the entrance is not open except to those of perfect purity. With equal constancy, death is neither to be feared when it comes by nature, nor forced against the order of nature. From these things which we have related that Plato and Plotinus pronounced regarding voluntary death, nothing will remain obscure in the words of Cicero by which he forbids it. But let us repeat those words that were inserted besides this: "For men were created under this law: that they should guard that globe which you see in the middle of this temple, which is called Earth. And to them, a soul was given from those eternal fires which you call stars and constellations, which, being spherical and round, complete their circles and orbits with marvelous speed, animated by divine minds." We shall discuss more fully why the Earth is called a globe positioned in the middle of the world when we speak of the nine spheres.

<margin>The world is called the Temple of God</margin>
It is fitting that the entire universe is called the "temple of God," for the sake of those who think there is nothing else to God but the sky itself and these celestial things we see. Therefore, to show that the power of the most high God can hardly be understood and never seen, he called everything subject to human sight His "temple," for He is conceived by the mind alone. Thus, whoever venerates this world as a temple should owe the greatest worship to the Creator; and whoever is brought into the service of this temple should know that he must live according to the ritual of a priest. From this, he testifies to the human race, as if by a public proclamation, that such great divinity dwells within them, so that—

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the soul's nature, moving from the mechanics of its descent to the specific hierarchy of the mind and the distinction between the divine "Mind" and the animating "Soul."</meta>

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

<margin>The Soul</margin>
All are noble by the kinship of their soul to the stars. It should be noted that in this passage, he uses the term "soul" <note>original: "animum"; here referring to the rational spirit</note> both in its proper sense and in a looser sense. Properly speaking, "soul" <note>animus</note> is the Mind <note>mens</note>, which no one has ever doubted is the more divine part of the soul <note>anima</note>. But we often use these terms interchangeably. Therefore, when he says, *To these, a soul was given from those everlasting fires,* he intends for "Mind" to be understood, which is specifically what we have in common with the heavens and the stars. However, when he says, *The soul must be kept in the custody of the body,* he is naming the "animating soul" <note>anima</note> itself, which is bound by the prison of the body and to which the divine Mind is not subject. Now, let us discuss according to the theologians how the soul—that is, the Mind—is shared with the stars.

<margin>
God the first cause
The Mind
The origin of the Soul and its parts.
</margin>
God, who both is and is called the First Cause, is the one Beginning and Origin of all things that are, and that seem to be. Out of the overflowing fertility of His majesty, He created Mind <note>Mens</note> from Himself. This Mind, which is called *Nous* <note>Greek: ΝΟΥΣ; the divine intellect</note> in Greek, maintains a perfect likeness to its Author as it gazes upon its Father. However, it creates the Soul <note>Anima</note> from itself while looking toward what follows it. In turn, the Soul takes on the nature of the part it gazes upon; and as its gaze gradually recedes toward the creation of bodies, the Soul itself, though incorporeal, begins to degenerate into the material world.

<margin>
Reason
The Rational
That is, the sensitive
The Vegetative
That is, the generative.
</margin>
The soul therefore possesses the purest Reason <note>ratio</note> from the Mind from which it was born; this is called the *Logikon* <note>Greek: λογικόν; the rational faculty</note>. From its own nature, it also receives the seeds for providing sensation and providing growth; one of these is called the *Aisthetikon* <note>Greek: αἰσθητικόν; the faculty of sense perception</note>, and the other the *Phytikon* <note>Greek: φυτικόν; the vegetative or growing faculty</note>. But of these, the first—that is, the *Logikon*—which it took as something innate from the Mind, is truly divine and suited only for divine beings. The remaining two—the sensitive and the vegetative—as they move further away from divine things, are fitting for perishable things. Thus, the Soul, creating and building bodies for itself (for nature begins from the Soul, which the wise name *Nous* from God and the Mind), animated those divine bodies above—I mean the heavens and the stars—which it was first building, using that pure and most perfect fountain of Mind which it had drawn from the abundance of its origin at its birth. And divine Minds were infused into all bodies that are formed into a rounded shape—that is, in the manner of a sphere. And this is what he meant when, speaking of the stars, he said: *which [are endowed] with divine souls and minds.* But as it degenerated into lower and earthly things, it discovered that the fragility of perishable bodies could not sustain the pure divinity of the Mind. Indeed, barely a portion of it is suited only to human bodies, because they alone appear upright as if receding from the depths toward the heights, and they alone easily look up to heaven as if always standing erect; and in man alone, particularly in the head, is there the likeness of a sphere, which we have said is the only form capable of containing the Mind.

<margin>The seat of the Mind</margin>
Therefore, into man alone did He pour Reason—that is, the power of the Mind—the seat of which is in the head. But He also inserted that twin nature of growing and sensing because the body is perishable. And this is why man possesses reason, and senses, and grows. He deserves to excel over other animals by reason alone; for they, because they are always prone <note>leaning toward the ground</note> and have receded from higher things due to the very difficulty of receiving them, have not deserved any likeness to divine bodies in any of their parts; they have received nothing from the Mind, and therefore they lacked reason. They attained only two faculties: sensing and growing. For if anything in them seems to imitate reason, it is not reason but memory—and not a memory mixed with reason, but that which accompanies the dullness of the five senses. We shall omit saying more about this now, as it does not pertain to the present work. The third order of earthly bodies is in trees and herbs, which lack both reason and sensation. And because only the function of growing is active in them, they are said to live by this part alone.

<margin>In the beginning, the heaven... in Aeneid Book 6.</margin>
Virgil also expressed this order of things. For he gave a soul to the world, and to attest to its purity, he called it "Mind." For he says: *In the beginning, a spirit within nourishes the heaven, the lands, the seas, and the stars* <note>Aeneid 6.724</note>—that is, a soul. Just as elsewhere he uses "breath" to mean soul: *As much as fires and souls are strong.* And to assert the dignity of that world-soul, he testified that it is a Mind: *Mind moves the mass* <note>Aeneid 6.727</note>. Furthermore, to show that all living things consist of and are animated by this very soul, he added: *From this comes the race of men and cattle,* and so on. And to assert that the same vigor of spirit is in the soul, but its use grows dull in animals because of the density of the body, he added: *Insofar as harmful bodies do not slow them down,* and the rest. According to these things, therefore, since from the highest God comes the Mind, and from the Mind the Soul, and the Soul in turn builds and fills all following things with life, one single glow illuminates all things and appears in all, like a single face reflected in many mirrors placed in order. And since all things follow one another in continuous successions...

It details the three faculties of the soul—rational, sensitive, and vegetative—and uses Virgil’s poetry to illustrate how a single divine Mind animates the entire cosmos.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the general nature of the soul's descent to a specific philosophical and linguistic distinction between the "Mind" and the "Soul." It explores the Neoplatonic hierarchy of being—from God to Mind to Soul—and explains how these divine elements manifest differently in celestial bodies, humans, animals, and plants, using Virgil’s poetry as supporting evidence.</meta>

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

<margin>
The Mind
</margin>
...all are noble by their kinship to the starry mind. It must be noted that in this passage, he uses the word "mind" <note>original: "animum"</note> both in its proper sense and in an informal sense. Properly speaking, the "mind" <note>original: "animus"</note> is the intellect <note>original: "mens"</note>, which no one doubts is more divine than the "soul" <note>original: "anima"</note>. Yet, we sometimes use the terms interchangeably. Therefore, when he says, "To these, a mind was given from those eternal fires," he intends for "intellect" to be understood, which is properly shared between us and the heavens and stars. However, when he says, "The mind must be kept in the custody of the body," he is then naming the "soul" itself, which is bound by bodily custody—the divine intellect is not subject to such things. Now, let us discuss, according to the theologians, how our mind (that is, the intellect) is shared with the stars.

<margin>
God as the first cause
Mind
The origin of the Soul and its parts.
Reason
Rational <note>Greek: λογικόν</note>
That is, sensitive
Vegetative <note>Greek: φυτικόν</note>
That is, generative.
</margin>
God, who both is and is called the First Cause, is the one ruler and origin of all things that are or seem to be. From the overflowing fertility of His majesty, He created Mind <note>original: "mentem"</note> from Himself. This Mind, which is called *Nous* <note>Greek: νοῦς; the divine intellect or "Reason" of the universe</note>, maintains a full likeness to its author as it gazes upon its Father; however, it creates the Soul <note>original: "Animam"</note> from itself while looking toward the things that follow. In turn, the Soul puts on the likeness of that part which it gazes upon, but as its gaze gradually turns back toward the construction of bodies, the soul itself—though incorporeal—degenerates into the physical realm. Therefore, it possesses a most pure reason from the Mind from which it was born, which is called *logikon* <note>Greek: λογικόν; the rational faculty</note>. From its own nature, it also receives the seeds of providing sensation and providing growth, of which one is called *aisthetikon* <note>Greek: αἰσθητικόν; the perceptive or sensitive faculty</note> and the other *phytikon* <note>Greek: φυτικόν; the vegetative or growth faculty</note>. But of these, the first—the rational—having taken what was innate to it from the Mind, is truly divine and suited only to divine beings. The remaining two, the sensitive and the vegetative, as they recede from the divine, are suited to perishable things. Therefore, the Soul, creating and building bodies for itself (for nature begins from the Soul, which the wise call *Nous* <note>Note: Here Macrobius suggests a continuity between Mind and the creative aspect of Soul</note> from God and Mind), animated those divine bodies above—I mean the heavens and the stars—which it built first, drawing from that pure and most clear fountain of the Mind which it had drunk from in the abundance of its origin. These divine intellects were infused into all bodies that are formed into a rounded shape—that is, into the form of a sphere. And this is what he meant when speaking of the stars: "which [are endowed] with the divine minds of souls." But as it degenerates into lower and earthly things, it discovers that the fragility of perishable bodies cannot sustain the pure divinity of the Mind; indeed, a portion of it is barely suitable even for human bodies alone. This is because humans alone are seen to stand erect, as if receding from the lowest depths toward the heights, and they alone easily look up to heaven, and in their head alone is the likeness of a sphere—the form we said was the only one capable of containing the Mind.

<margin>
The seat of the Mind
</margin>
Therefore, into man alone has He infused reason (that is, the power of the Mind), the seat of which is in the head. But He also inserted that twin nature of growth and sensation because the body is perishable. And this is why man possesses reason, senses things, and grows; and by reason alone, he has earned the right to stand above all other animals. Because other animals are always prone <note>meaning face-down or horizontal</note>, and by the very difficulty of looking upward have receded from higher things, they have not earned any likeness to divine bodies in any part of themselves; they have received nothing from the Mind, and therefore they lack reason. They have obtained only two things: the ability to sense and to grow. For if anything in them seems to imitate reason, it is not reason but memory—and not a memory mixed with reason, but one that accompanies the dullness of the five senses. We shall omit saying more on this for now, as it does not pertain to the present work. The third order of earthly bodies is in trees and plants, which lack both reason and sensation. And because only the function of growth flourishes in them, they are said to live by this part alone.

<margin>
"In the beginning the heaven" in [Book] 6 of the Aeneid.
</margin>
Virgil also expressed this order of things. For he gave a soul to the world, and to attest to its purity, he called it "Mind." For he says: "The heaven, the lands, the watery plains, and the stars, an internal spirit nourishes" <note>original: "Cælu. n. ait & terras & maria & ſydera ſpiritus itus alit"; quoting Virgil, Aeneid 6.724-6.726</note>—that is, a soul. Just as elsewhere he calls the soul a "breath." "As much as the fires and the souls are strong." And so that he might assert the dignity of that world-soul, he testified that it is a Mind: "Mind moves the mass" <note>original: "Mens agitat molē"; a famous phrase describing the divine intelligence permeating the universe</note>. Furthermore, to show that all living things consist of and are animated by that soul, he added: "Thence the race of men and beasts, and the rest." And to assert that the same vigor is in the soul, but its use grows dull in animals due to the density of the body, he added: "Insofar as harmful bodies do not slow them down" <note>original: "Quantum nō noxia corpa tardant"</note>, and so forth. According to these things, therefore, since from the highest God comes the Mind, and from the Mind the Soul, and the Soul creates and fills with life all things that follow—since this one radiance illuminates all and appears in everyone, like a single face in many mirrors placed in order—and since all things follow one another in continuous successions...

As things degenerate in order of their descent to the lowest level, one will find, by observing from the highest God down to the very dregs of things, a connection—binding itself together with mutual links—that is never interrupted. And this is **Homer’s golden chain**,
<margin>Homer’s golden chain</margin>
which he recalls God ordered to hang from heaven to earth. Therefore, after these things are said, it is certain that of all earthly things, only man has a fellowship of mind—that is, of soul—in common with heaven and the stars. And this is what he <note>Cicero, in the Dream of Scipio</note> says: *To these, a soul was given from those everlasting fires which you call constellations and stars.* However, he does not say we are animated by those celestial and everlasting fires themselves. For that fire, though divine, is still a body. Nor could we be animated by a body, even a divine one; rather, we are animated from that source whence those very bodies—which are and appear divine—are animated: that is, from that part of the World Soul which we said consists of pure Mind. And therefore, after he said: *To these, a soul was given from those everlasting fires which you call constellations and stars,* he immediately added: *which are animated by divine minds.* Thus, by "everlasting fires," the body of the stars is meant, and by "divine minds," their souls are signified in a clear description; this shows that the power of the mind comes into our souls from them. It is not out of place for this discussion on the soul to contain, at its end, the opinions of everyone who is seen to have pronounced a judgment on the soul.
<margin>What the soul is according to various opinions of the philosophers</margin>
**Plato** said the soul is a self-moving essence. **Xenocrates** called it a self-moving number. **Aristotle** called it an *entelechy* <note>Greek: ἐντελέχειαν; a state of completion or the "actualization" of a body</note>. **Pythagoras** and **Philolaus** called it harmony. **Posidonius** called it an idea. **Asclepiades** called it the harmonious exercise of the five senses. **Hippocrates** called it a thin spirit dispersed through the whole body. **Heraclitus of Pontus** called it light. **Heraclitus the Physicist** called it a spark of stellar essence. **Zeno** called it a spirit joined to the body. **Democritus** called it a spirit inserted into atoms, with such ease of movement that the whole body is permeable to it. **Critolaus the Peripatetic** said it consists of the fifth essence <note>the quintessence, or a non-earthly element</note>. **Hipparchus** called it fire; **Anaximenes**, air; **Empedocles** and **Critias**, blood; **Parmenides**, a mixture of earth and fire; **Xenophantes**, earth and water; **Boetos**, air and fire; **Epicurus**, a species mixed from fire, air, and spirit. Nevertheless, the opinion regarding its incorporeality has prevailed no less than that of its immortality. Now let us see what these two names are, which he mentions together when he says: *which you call constellations and stars.* For he does not show one thing by two names here,

as one might say "sword" and "blade." Rather, **stars** <note>original: stellæ</note> are individual ones, such as the five wandering planets and others which are carried alone, not mixed with others. **Constellations** <note>original: sydera</note>, however, are those formed into some sign by the composition of many stars: such as Aries, Taurus, Andromeda, Perseus, or the Crown, and whatever types of various forms are believed to be received into heaven. So also among the Greeks, *astēr* and *astron*
<margin>Astēr and Astron</margin>
signify different things. For an *astēr* <note>Greek: ἀστὴρ</note> is a single star, and an *astron* <note>Greek: ἄστρον</note> is a sign gathered from stars, which we call a constellation. When he calls the stars "globose and round," he is expressing the appearance not only of individual ones, but also of those that come together to form signs. For all stars, even if they differ somewhat in size, have no difference in their species. By these two names, the sphere is soundly described;
<margin>Sphere</margin>
for a sphere is not made from a globe if roundness is lacking, nor from roundness if a globe is lacking, since one refers to the form and the other to the solidity of the body. Here we call the bodies of the stars themselves "spheres," as all are formed in this appearance. Furthermore, they are called spheres: the "fixed" sphere <note>Greek: ἀπλανὴς; the outermost shell of the universe</note> which is the greatest, and the seven beneath it, through which the two lights [the Sun and Moon] and the five wandering stars [planets] run. "Circles" and "orbs," however, are two names for two different things. And indeed, these names are used differently elsewhere. For he has used "orb" for a circle (as in "the milky orb") and "orb" for a sphere (as in "with nine orbs, or rather globes, for you"). Rather, an **orb** in this place is one complete and finished revolution of a star;
<margin>Orb</margin>

<margin>Circle</margin>

# BOOK ONE

<margin>Homer’s Golden Chain</margin>
If one follows the descending order from the highest God down to the very last series of things, they will find a connection, binding itself with mutual links and never interrupted. And this is Homer’s Golden Chain, which he records that God commanded to hang from heaven to earth. It is established, then, that man alone of all earthly creatures shares a common fellowship of mind—that is, of soul—with the heavens and the stars. And this is what he means when he says: *To these, a soul was given from those everlasting fires which you call constellations and stars.* Yet he does not say we are animated by those celestial and everlasting fires themselves. For that fire, though divine, is a body. We could not be animated by a body, however divine; but rather from that source by which those bodies, which are and appear divine, are themselves animated: that is, from that part of the world-soul which we said consists of pure Mind. Therefore, after he said, *To these, a soul was given from those everlasting fires which you call constellations and stars,* he immediately added: *which are animated by divine minds.* This clear description signifies the body of the stars by "everlasting fires," and their souls by "divine minds," showing that the power of the mind comes from them into our souls.

<margin>What the soul is according to the various opinions of philosophers</margin>
It is not out of place for this discussion on the soul to conclude with the opinions of all those who seem to have pronounced upon the soul. Plato said the soul is a self-moving essence. Xenocrates, a self-moving number. Aristotle called it *entelechy* <note>original Greek: εντελεχειαν; a term meaning a state of completed realization or the "vital principle" that makes a body live</note>. Pythagoras and Philolaus called it a harmony. Posidonius, an Idea. Asclepiades, whatever exercise of the senses is harmonious to itself. Hippocrates, a thin spirit dispersed through the whole body. Heraclides of Pontus, light. Heraclitus the physicist, a spark of stellar essence. Zeno, a spirit joined to the body. Democritus, a spirit inserted among atoms with such ease of movement that every body is permeable to it. Critolaus the Peripatetic, that it consists of a "fifth essence" <note>the quintessence, or a non-earthly element</note>. Hipparchus, fire. Anaximenes, air. Empedocles and Critias, blood. Parmenides, from earth and fire. Xenophanes, from earth and water. Boethus, from air and fire. Epicurus, a form mixed from fire, air, and spirit. Nevertheless, the opinion regarding its incorporeality <note>being without a physical body</note> prevailed no less than that of its immortality.

<margin>What are Constellations and what are Stars</margin>
Now let us see what these two names are, both of which he mentions when he says: *which you call constellations and stars.* For here, one thing is not shown by two names, like "blade" and "sword." Rather, stars <note>original: stellae</note> are individual, such as the five "wandering ones" [planets] and others that are carried alone without being mixed with others. Constellations <note>original: sydera</note>, however, are those which are formed into some sign by the composition of several stars, such as Aries, Taurus, Andromeda, Perseus, or the Crown, and whatever types of various forms are believed to have been received into heaven.

<margin>Aster: Astron</margin>
So also among the Greeks, *aster* <note>Greek: αϛηρ</note> and *astron* <note>Greek: αϛρον</note> signify different things. For an *aster* is a single star, and an *astron* is a sign formed of stars, which we call a constellation. When he calls stars "globular and round," he is speaking not only of the appearance of individual ones, but also of those which come together to form signs. For all stars, though they differ somewhat in size, have no difference in their appearance.

<margin>The Sphere</margin>
Through these two names, a solid sphere is described, which is produced neither from a globe if roundness is lacking, nor from roundness if a globe is lacking, since the one provides the form and the other the solidity of the body. Here we call "spheres" the bodies of the stars themselves, which are all formed with this appearance. Furthermore, spheres are called "the fixed" <note>original: aplanes; referring to the outer shell of the universe</note>, which is the greatest, and the seven subject to it, through which the two lights [Sun and Moon] and the five wanderers [planets] run. Now, "circles" and "orbs" are two names for two different things. He has used these names differently elsewhere. For he used "orb" for "circle," as in the "milky orb" [Milky Way], and "orb" for "sphere," as in "for you, nine orbs, or rather globes." But they also call "circles" those things which gird the greatest sphere, as the following treatise will show, one of which is the Milky Way, of which he says: *a circle shining out among the flames.*

<margin>The Orb</margin>
But here, he intended neither "circle" nor "orb" to be understood by these names. Instead, an *orb* in this place is a single whole star and its completed revolution—that is, the return to the same place after traversing the circuit of the sphere through which it moves.

<margin>The Circus</margin>
The *circus* <note>meaning a track or circle</note>, however, is here the line surrounding the sphere, making a sort of path through which both lights [Sun and Moon] run, and within which the lawful wandering of the erratic stars is confined.

<margin>Wandering Stars</margin>
These the ancients called "wandering" <note>original: errantes; from which we get the word "planet"</note> because they are carried by their own course, and move with a contrary motion toward the east against the force of the greatest sphere, which is the heaven itself...

### ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

...all are made noble by their kinship with the starry mind.

<margin>The Mind</margin> It should be noted that in this passage he <note>Cicero</note> has used "mind" <note>original: *animum*</note> both in its proper sense and in a looser sense. For the "Mind" <note>original: *Animus*</note> is properly the Intellect <note>original: *mens*</note>, which no one doubts is more divine than the "Soul" <note>original: *anima*</note>. But sometimes we use the word loosely, calling the soul by that name as well. Therefore, when he says: *To these, a mind was given from those everlasting fires,* he intends for "Intellect" to be understood, which is properly what we have in common with the heavens and the stars. But when he says: *The mind must be kept in the custody of the body,* he is then naming the Soul itself, which is bound by the imprisonment of the body—something the divine Intellect is not subject to. Now, let us discuss how the mind—that is, the intellect—is common to us and the stars, according to the theologians.

<margin>God the first cause, the Mind, the origin of the Soul and its parts.</margin> God, who is and is called the First Cause, is the one ruler and origin of all things that are and that seem to be. He, from the overflowing fertility of his majesty, created the Mind <note>original: *mentem*</note> from himself. This Mind, which is called *Nous* <note>original: νοῦν</note>, maintains a full likeness to its Author as it looks toward its Father; however, it creates the Soul <note>original: *Animam*</note> from itself while looking toward the things that follow. In turn, the Soul puts on the character of that part which it gazes upon: as it looks back, it is clothed in the Intellect, but as its gaze gradually turns back toward the fashioning of bodies, the Soul—though incorporeal itself—degenerates.

<margin>Reason: *Logikon*. That is, the sensitive: *Aisthetikon*. That is, the generative: *Phytikon*.</margin> Therefore, from the Mind from which it was born, the Soul possesses a most pure Reason, which is called *Logikon* <note>original: λογικόν</note>. From its own nature, it also receives the seeds of providing sensation and providing growth; the first of these is called *Aisthetikon* <note>original: αἰσθητικόν</note> and the other *Phytikon* <note>original: φυτικόν</note>. But of these, the first—the *Logikon*—which it took as something innate from the Mind, is truly divine and suited only for divine beings. The remaining two—the sensitive and the generative—as they recede from the divine, are suited to perishable things. Therefore, the Soul, creating and building bodies for itself—for this is why Nature begins from the Soul, which the wise call *Nous* <note>original: νοῦν</note> after God and Mind—animated those divine bodies above (I mean the heavens and the stars) which it first established from that pure and most clear fountain of the Mind, which it had drawn from the abundance of its origin at its birth. Divine minds were infused into all bodies that are formed into a rounded shape—that is, in the manner of a sphere. And this is what he <note>Cicero</note> meant when speaking of the stars: *which are animated by divine minds.* But as the Soul degenerated toward lower and earthly things, it discovered that the fragility of perishable bodies could not sustain the pure divinity of the Mind; indeed, it found that a part of it could scarcely fit even human bodies. This is because humans alone appear upright, as if they have moved away from the lowest depths toward the heights, and they alone easily look up at the heaven as they are always erect; in them alone, specifically in the head, is there the likeness of a sphere, which we have said is the only form capable of containing the Mind.

<margin>The seat of the Mind</margin> Therefore, into man alone has he infused Reason—that is, the power of the Mind—which has its seat in the head. But he also inserted that twin nature of growth and sensation because the body is perishable. And this is why man both possesses reason and perceives and grows; through reason alone, he deserves to stand above the other animals. Because animals are always prone <note>leaning toward the ground</note>, and by the very difficulty of looking upward have receded from higher things, they have not deserved any likeness to divine bodies in any part of themselves; they have received nothing from the Mind, and therefore they lack reason. They have obtained only two things: to perceive and to grow. For if anything in them mimics the likeness of reason, it is not reason but memory—and not a memory mixed with reason, but that which accompanies the dullness of the five senses. We shall omit saying more about this now, as it does not pertain to the present work. The third order of earthly bodies is in trees and plants, which lack both reason and sensation. And because only the function of growth flourishes in them, they are said to live by this part alone.

<margin>In the beginning, the heaven... in the 6th book of the Aeneid.</margin> Virgil also expressed this order of things. For he gave a soul to the world, and to attest to its purity, he called it "Mind." For he says: *The spirit within nourishes the heaven and the earth and the seas and the stars*—that is, the Soul. Just as elsewhere he uses "breath" to mean the soul: *As much as fires and souls are strong.* And so that he might assert the dignity of that World Soul, he testified that it is a Mind: **Mind moves the mass.** Furthermore, to show that all things that live consist of and are animated by that same soul, he added: **From this comes the race of men and beasts, and the rest.** And to assert that the same vigor is in the soul, but its use grows dull in animals because of the density of the body, he added: **So much as harmful bodies do not hinder, etc.** According to these things, therefore, since from the highest God comes Mind, and from Mind comes Soul, and the Soul establishes and fills with life all things that follow—and since this one glow illuminates everything and appears in all things—it is like a single face reflected in many mirrors placed in order. And since all things follow one another in continuous successions...

# BOOK ONE

<margin>Homer’s Golden Chain</margin>
...degenerating by degrees as they move toward the lowest point, one will find—if they look closely—an unbroken connection, binding everything together in mutual links from the High God down to the very dregs of the last things. This is **Homer’s Golden Chain**, which he records God commanded to hang from heaven to the earth. Given these facts, it is clear that of all earthly things, only man shares a common bond of mind—that is, of soul—with the heavens and the stars. And this is what he <note>Cicero</note> means when he says: *To these, a mind was given from those everlasting fires, which you call constellations and stars.* However, he does not mean we are animated by those celestial and everlasting fires themselves. For that fire, though divine, is still a body. We could not be animated by a body, even a divine one; rather, we are animated from that same source as those bodies—which are and appear divine—are themselves animated: namely, from that part of the World-Soul which we have said consists of pure Mind. Therefore, after he said, *To these, a mind was given from those everlasting fires, which you call constellations and stars,* he immediately added: *which are animated by divine minds.* This clear description signifies the bodies of the stars through the "everlasting fires," and their souls through the "divine minds," showing that the power of Mind comes into our souls from them.

<margin>What the soul is according to various opinions of philosophers</margin>
It is not out of place for this discussion on the soul to conclude with the opinions of all those who are seen to have pronounced on the matter. **Plato** said the soul is a self-moving essence. **Xenocrates** called it a self-moving number <note>In Pythagorean thought, numbers were considered the fundamental building blocks of reality</note>. **Aristotle** called it *entelecheia* <note>original: ἐντελέχειαν; meaning "actualized completion" or the state of a thing having reached its purpose</note>. **Pythagoras** and **Philolaus** called it harmony. **Posidonius** called it an idea. **Asclepiades** called it the exercise of the senses in unison. **Hippocrates** called it a thin spirit dispersed through the whole body. **Heraclitus of Pontus** called it light. **Heraclitus the Physician** called it a spark of stellar essence. **Zeno** called it a spirit joined to the body. **Democritus** called it a spirit inserted among atoms, with such ease of movement that every body is permeable to it. **Critolaus the Peripatetic** said it consists of a fifth essence <note>original: *quinta essentia*; the "quintessence" or ether, distinct from earth, air, fire, and water</note>. **Hipparchus** called it fire; **Anaximenes**, air; **Empedocles** and **Critias**, blood. **Parmenides** said it was made of earth and fire; **Xenophanes**, of earth and water; **Boethus**, of air and fire. **Epicurus** believed it was a mixture of fire, air, and spirit. Nevertheless, the opinion regarding its incorporeality has prevailed no less than that of its immortality.

<margin>What constellations and stars are</margin>
Now let us see what these two names are, both of which he mentions when he says: *which you call constellations and stars.* For here, a single thing is not being shown by two names, as with "blade" and "sword." Rather, "stars" <note>original: *stellae*</note> are individual, such as the five wandering stars <note>the planets</note> and others which are carried alone without being mixed with others. But "constellations" <note>original: *sydera*</note> are those which are formed into some sign by a grouping of many stars, such as Aries, Taurus, Andromeda, Perseus, or the Crown, and whatever other types of various forms are believed to have been received into the heavens.

<margin>Star: Constellation</margin>
So too among the Greeks, *aster* <note>original: ἀστηρ</note> and *astron* <note>original: ἀστρον</note> signify different things. For an *aster* is a single star, and an *astron* is a sign forced together from stars, which we call a constellation. When he calls the stars "globular and round," he is not just describing the appearance of individual stars, but also those which come together to form signs. For all stars, even if they differ in size, have no difference in their basic appearance.

<margin>The Sphere</margin>
By these two terms, the sphere <note>original: *sphaera*</note> is solidly described. It is not made from a globe if roundness is lacking, nor from roundness if the globe is lacking, since one refers to the form and the other to the solidity of the body. Here we call the bodies of the stars themselves "spheres," for they are all formed in this shape. Furthermore, they call that greatest one the "fixed" sphere <note>original: *aplanes*; the outermost heaven of the fixed stars</note>, and there are seven beneath it, through which the two lights <note>the Sun and Moon</note> and the five wanderers <note>Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> run their courses.

<margin>The Orbit</margin>
"Circuits" <note>original: *circi*</note> and "orbits" <note>original: *orbes*</note> are two names for two different things. These names are used differently elsewhere. For he has used "orbit" for a circle, such as the "milky orbit" <note>the Milky Way</note>, and "orbit" for a sphere, as in "nine orbits, or rather globes." They are also called "circuits" when they surround the greatest sphere, as the following treatise will show—one of which is the Milky Way, of which he says: *a circuit shining out among the flames.* But here he intended neither "circuit" nor "orbit" to be understood in those ways. Instead, in this place, an "orbit" is the single, complete, and finished revolution of a star—that is, the return to the same place after traveling the full circumference of the sphere through which it moves.

<margin>The Circuit</margin>
A "circuit" here, however, is the line encircling the sphere, acting as a path through which both lights run, and within which the lawful wandering of the "straying" stars is confined.

<margin>The wandering stars</margin>
The ancients called these "wandering" <note>original: *errantes*; from which we get the word "planets"</note> because they are carried by their own course, and move with a contrary motion toward the east against the force of the greatest sphere—that is, of the heaven itself...

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

...they roll from the west; and the speed of all is equal, their motion similar, and the manner of their measurement is the same. However, they do not all complete their circuits and orbits in the same amount of time. And thus, this very speed is a thing of wonder: for while it is the same for all—none being able to be swifter or slower than the others—they nevertheless do not all finish their journey in the same span of time. But regarding how different distances function under the same speed, our following points will teach more appropriately. 

Having recounted these things concerning the nature of the stars and the "star-like" mind of humans, the father <note>Aemilius Paullus</note>, wishing his son <note>Scipio Aemilianus</note> to be pious toward the gods and just toward men, added a reward once more. He pointed out the **Milky Way**, the circle owed to the virtuous and filled with the assembly of the blessed. He remembers it in these words: *It was a circle shining with the most brilliant whiteness among the flames, which you (as you received it from the Greeks) call the Milky Way.* 

<margin>The Milky Way</margin>
This "orb" means the same thing as "circle" in the naming of the Milky Way. The Milky Way is one of the circles that surround the heavens; and besides it, there are ten in number, about which we will speak when a suitable discussion of this matter arises. Of all of them, this one alone is visible to the eyes; the others are marked out more by thought than by sight. 

Regarding this Milky Way, many have held differing opinions: some have offered mythical causes for it, others natural ones. But we, keeping silent about the myths, will speak only of those things which seem to pertain to its nature. **Theophrastus** said the Milky Way was a "seam," <note>original: "compagem"</note> because the sphere of heaven is joined together from two hemispheres. And thus, where the edges of both meet, a notable brightness is seen. **Diodorus** believed it was fire of a dense and solidified nature, massed together into a single path along a curved boundary by the separation of the world’s structure. He argued that it admits the gaze of the viewer, whereas the rest of the celestial fire—whose light is spread out with too much thinness—is not subjected to our sight. **Democritus** argued it consisted of innumerable small stars, all of which are crowded together into one space by a thick tract; because the gaps between them are very narrow, they are close to one another on every side, and thus, by the scattering of light diffused everywhere, they show a continuous body of joined light. 

But **Posidonius**, whose definition has gained the consensus of many, says the Milky Way is an infusion of stellar heat, which a curve opposite to the Zodiac turns aside for this reason: 

<margin>The Ten Circles</margin>
since the sun, by never exceeding the boundaries of the Zodiac, left a part of the heaven devoid of its heat, this circle—receding from the sun's path at an angle—might temper the whole universe with its warm bend. In which parts it intersects the Zodiac has been related above. So much for the Milky Way. 

There are, however, ten other circles (as we have said): one of which is the **Zodiac** itself. Among these ten, it is the only one that could possess "width" in the manner we shall describe. 

<margin>The Zodiac Arch</margin>
The nature of the celestial circles is an incorporeal "line," which is conceived in the mind such that it is judged by length alone and cannot have width. But in the Zodiac, the capacity of the signs <note>the constellations of the Zodiac</note> required width. Therefore, as much space as the dimension of width occupied for the upright stars was bounded by two lines. 

<margin>The Ecliptic Line</margin>
A third line drawn through the middle is called the **Ecliptic**, because when the sun and moon complete their course together on this same line, a failure <note>an eclipse</note> must necessarily occur for one of them: for the sun, if the moon then moves beneath it; for the moon, if it is then opposite to the sun. 

<margin>Eclipse of the Sun and Moon</margin>
Therefore, the sun never fails except when it is the thirtieth day of the moon; and the moon does not know failure except on the fifteenth day of its course. For thus it happens: either the cone of the Earth’s shadow stands in the way of the moon (which is positioned opposite the sun to borrow its usual light from it), or the moon itself, moving beneath the sun, repels the sun's light from human sight by its own obstruction. In an eclipse, therefore, the sun itself suffers nothing, but our sight is cheated. The moon, however, truly suffers during its own eclipse by not receiving the light of the sun, by whose benefit it colors the night. Knowing this, **Virgil**, the most skilled in all disciplines, said: *The various eclipses of the sun, and the labors of the moon.* <note>original: "Defectus solis uarios: lunaeq; labores" from Virgil's Georgics</note> 

Although a drawing of three lines both encloses and divides the Zodiac, antiquity—the author of these names—wished it to be called one circle. 

<margin>The Five Circles</margin>
Five other circles are called **Parallels**. The middle and greatest of these is the **Equinoctial** <note>the Equator</note>. Two are near the extremities and are therefore short; one of these is called the **Northern**, the other the **Southern**. Between these and the middle are two **Tropics**, which are larger than the end circles but smaller than the middle; these form the boundary of the "scorched zone" on either side. Besides these, there are two other circles, to which "incomplete rotation" gives a name: those surrounding the Northern pole, and likewise...

# BOOK ONE XVI

...spread out in reverse and intersecting at the summit: they divide the zodiac equally into four parts by following five parallels, so that one of them runs through **Aries** <note>The Ram</note> and **Libra** <note>The Scales</note>, and the other through **Cancer** <note>The Crab</note> and **Capricorn**. However, they believe these do not reach the southern pole. Two others which complete the aforementioned number—the **meridian** and the **horizon**—are not drawn on the celestial sphere, because they cannot have a fixed location; instead, they vary according to the diversity of the observers or their dwellings.

<margin>The Meridian circle</margin>
For the **meridian** is that which the sun designates when it comes directly over the heads of men, creating midday. And because the roundness of the earth does not allow the dwellings of all people to be equal to one another, the same part of the sky does not look down upon everyone’s head. Therefore, there cannot be one single meridian for all people; rather, a unique meridian is created for each individual directly above their own head.

<margin>The Horizon</margin>
Similarly, the viewpoint of each individual creates their own **horizon**. For the horizon is like a boundary of the sky marked out in a circle, consisting of what is seen above the earth. And because the human eye cannot truly reach the ultimate edge of the world, however far one can see by looking around, that creates their own personal limit of the sky which sits above the earth. This horizon, which each person’s sight circumscribes for themselves, cannot contain within itself a length of more than three hundred and sixty **stadia** <term>stadia: an ancient Greek unit of distance; 360 stadia is roughly 40 miles</term>. 

<margin>Measurement of the Horizon</margin>
For the line of sight of one looking out does not exceed one hundred and eighty stadia. But when the vision reaches this distance, failing to go further, it curves back into a circle. And so it happens that this number, doubled from each side, makes the space of three hundred and sixty stadia contained within one's horizon. Always, as much as you leave behind by walking forward from one part of this space, just as much is taken up from the inner part; thus the same horizon is always changed by any movement between places. Furthermore, this view we have described is permitted either by a level plain on land or the calm freedom of the open sea, which presents no obstacle to the eyes. Nor should it trouble you that we often see a mountain placed very far away, or that we look up at the very heights of the heavens. For it is one thing when height thrusts itself upon the eyes, and another when the gaze stretches and extends itself across a flat plane; it is only in the latter that the circle of the horizon is formed. Let these things suffice concerning all the circles by which the heaven is girded.

Let us transfer our discourse to the following matters, from which everything seemed remarkable and wondrous to me as I contemplated it. For there were stars which we have never seen from this place, and their magnitudes were such as we never suspected to exist. Among these, the smallest was that which, being the furthest from heaven and nearest to the earth, shone with a borrowed light. Indeed, the spheres of the stars easily surpassed the size of the earth.

By saying: *From which everything seemed... to me as I contemplated*, he affirms what we said above: that the meeting of Scipio and his parents occurred within the **Milky Way** itself during the dream. There are two primary things he reports admiring regarding the stars: the "newness" <note>meaning their unfamiliarity to an observer on Earth</note> of some, and the great size of all of them. We shall discuss the newness first, and the size afterward. By skillfully adding *which we have never seen from this place*, he shows the reason why they are not seen by us. For the location of our dwelling is so placed that certain stars can never be seen from it, because that very part of the heaven in which they reside can never appear to those living here. For this part of the earth which is inhabited by all men known to us rises toward the northern pole, and the spherical convexity of the earth sinks the southern pole away from us into the depths. 

<margin>The Northern Pole</margin>
Since the space of the heavens always revolves around the earth from east to west, this pole which holds the **Great and Little Bears** <note>the constellations Ursa Major and Minor</note>, whichever way it turns in the world’s rotation, is always above us and always seen by us; it always shows the "Bears fearing to be dipped in the ocean's surface" <note>original Latin: "arctos oceani metuentes aequore tingi"</note>. 

<margin>The Southern Pole</margin>
The southern pole, on the other hand, is sunk away from us because of the position of our dwelling; neither the pole itself is ever seen by us, nor are its stars, with which it undoubtedly marks itself. And this is what the poet <note>Virgil</note>, conscious of nature itself, said:

> This pole is always high above us; but that one,
> Beneath our feet, black **Styx** <note>The river of the underworld</note> beholds, and the deep spirits of the dead.

But while the roundness of the earth creates this difference for those dwelling upon it—parts of the heavens being either always visible or never visible—to one who is in the heavens, everything is visible without...

<margin>The Meridian circle</margin>
For the **meridian** is that which the sun marks when it comes directly over a person's head, creating the middle of the day. And because the <term>sphericity of the earth</term><note>original: "globositas terrae." Macrobius is emphasizing that the Earth is a globe, which was standard knowledge in late Roman scholarship.</note> does not allow the dwellings of all people to be equal to one another, the same part of the sky does not look down upon everyone’s head. Therefore, there cannot be a single meridian for everyone; rather, a unique meridian is created for each person directly above their own head. Similarly, the vantage point of each individual creates their own **horizon**. For the **horizon** is like a boundary of the sky marked out in a circle, representing what is visible above the earth.

<margin>The Horizon</margin>
Human vision cannot truly reach the actual end of the sky; rather, however far each person looks by turning their eyes around, they create their own boundary of the sky that is above the earth. This horizon, which each person’s sight circumscribes for themselves, cannot contain a length of more than **three hundred and sixty stades**<note>A "stade" (stadium) was an ancient unit of distance, roughly 600 feet. 360 stades is approximately 40 miles.</note> within itself.

<margin>Measurement of the Horizon</margin>
For the sight of one looking across does not exceed **one hundred and eighty stades**. But when the vision reaches this distance, failing as it advances, it curves back into a roundness. And so it happens that this number, doubled from both sides, creates the span of three hundred and sixty stades contained within one’s horizon. Always, however much you later move forward from a part of this span, that same amount is taken from the inner part behind you; thus the same horizon is always changing, no matter how much you travel from place to place. Moreover, this line of sight we have described is permitted either by a level plain on land or the calm freedom of the open sea, which presents no obstacle to the eyes. Do not let it disturb you that we often see a mountain at a very great distance, or that we look up at the very heights of heaven. For it is one thing when height forces itself upon the eyes, and another when the gaze stretches and extends itself across a flat plane; it is on the level plane alone that the circle of the horizon is formed. Let these things said about all the circles that gird the heavens suffice. Let us transfer our discourse to the following matters, from which all things seemed distinguished and wonderful to me as I contemplated them. These were the **stars** which we have never seen from this place, and the **magnitudes** of them all, which we never suspected to exist. Among these, the smallest was that which, being the furthest from heaven and nearest to the earth, shone with a borrowed light. Indeed, the globes of the stars easily surpassed the magnitude of the earth.

By saying: *From which, as I contemplated all things,* he confirms what we said above: that the meeting of Scipio and his ancestors took place within the <term>Milky Way</term> itself during the dream. There are two primary things which he reports marvelling at regarding the stars: the **novelty** of some, and the **magnitude** of them all. We shall discuss the novelty first, and the magnitude afterward. He adds fully and learnedly: *which we have never seen from this place,* showing the reason why they are not seen by us. For the location of our habitation is so placed that certain stars can never be seen from it, because the very part of the sky in which they are located can never appear to those living here. For this part of the earth which is inhabited by all men known to us—which we in turn cannot know <note>Referring to the inhabitants of the southern hemisphere, whom the ancients called "Antichthones" or "Antipodes."</note>—rises toward the **northern pole**, and the spatial convexity sinks the **southern pole** deep away from us. Since the space of the heavens always rolls around the earth from east to west, this pole which holds the "Bears" <note>The constellations Ursa Major and Ursa Minor.</note>, whichever way the world's rotation turns it, is always seen by us because it is above us; it always shows the "Bears" fearing to be dipped in the waters of the Ocean.

<margin>The Northern Pole</margin>
<margin>The Southern Pole</margin>
The **southern pole**, on the other hand, is sunk away from us because of the position of our dwelling; it is never seen by us, nor does it show its stars, with which it is undoubtedly adorned. And this is what the poet <note>The "poet" is Virgil.</note>, conscious of nature itself, said:
> This pole is always high above us; but that other,
> beneath our feet, the dark Styx and the deep shades of the dead behold.
<note>original: "Hic uertex nobis ſemper ſublimis: at illum / Sub pedibus ſtix atra uidet maneſq; profundi." Quoted from Virgil's Georgics (1.242-243). The Styx is the river of the underworld; the "manes" are the spirits of the dead.</note>

But while the globosity of the earth causes this difference for the inhabitants—making parts of the heavens appear either always or never—for one who is in the heavens, everything is visible without...
