# XVI
## ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

<margin>The magnitude of the stars</margin>
[Scipio] sees the sky without doubt, with no part of the Earth obstructing his view; for the entire Earth, compared to the magnitude of the heavens, barely occupies the space of a **point** <note>original: "puncti." In ancient and medieval cosmology, the Earth was considered mathematically insignificant—a mere dot—relative to the vastness of the fixed stars.</note>. Thus, for one who had never happened to see the stars of the southern pole from the Earth, they rightly inspired a new wonder when they were seen with a free view, without the hindrance of any earthly barrier. And because he understood the reason why he had never seen them before, he said: "Moreover, these were the stars which we have never seen from this place." By saying "this place," he was demonstratively referring to the Earth, where he was while recounting these things. There follows that discussion where he added what they were: "And these magnitudes are of all those things which we never suspected existed." But why men never suspected the magnitudes which he saw in the stars, he himself revealed by adding: "Moreover, the spheres of the stars easily surpassed the magnitude of the Earth." For when can a man—unless the teaching of philosophy has made him more than a man, or rather, a *true* man—suspect that a single star is larger than the entire Earth? For as they revolve, each one seems hardly able to equal the flame of a single torch. Therefore, the true magnitude of these stars will be believed as asserted if it is established that each one is larger than the whole Earth; which you may recognize in this way:

<margin>The Point</margin>
Geometers have said that a **point** is that which, because of its incomprehensible smallness, cannot be divided into parts, nor is it a part itself, but is merely called a "sign." Physicists have taught that the Earth, compared to the magnitude of the circle through which the sun revolves, occupies the measure of a point. How much smaller the sun is than its own circle has been discovered by the most manifest methods of measurement; it is established that the measure of the sun is the **two hundred and sixteenth part** of the magnitude of the circle through which the sun itself runs. Since, therefore, the sun is a specific part of its circle, while the Earth is a mere point compared to the sun’s circle (which cannot be a "part" without hesitation of judgment), it is certain that the sun is larger than the Earth—if indeed a "part" is larger than that which, by its excessive smallness, cannot even take the name of a part. Truly, it is certain that the circles of the stars above the sun are larger [than the sun's circle], if that which contains is greater than that which is contained. For this is the order of the celestial spheres: each lower one is surrounded by the one above it. Hence he also called the sphere of the moon the last in the heavens and the smallest, being a neighbor to the Earth, since the Earth itself, truly being the very last, fails into a point. If, therefore, the circles of the superior stars are (as we have said) larger than the circle of the sun, and each of these stars is of such magnitude that each occupies its own measure as a part of its circle, then without doubt each is larger than the Earth, which we have already said is a point compared to the sun's circle (which is smaller than the higher ones). Concerning the moon, whether it truly shines with a borrowed light, the following things will teach.

When Scipio's gaze, passing over these things with wonder, had flowed down as far as the lands and lingered there on familiar things, he was again called back to the higher things by a warning from his guide, who showed him the order of the spheres from the very beginning of the heavens in these words:

<margin>The nine globes or orbs</margin>
"All things are connected to you by nine circles, or rather globes, of which one is the outermost celestial sphere which embraces all the others: the supreme God himself, bound and containing the others, in which are fixed those eternal courses of the stars which revolve. Subject to this are seven spheres which turn backward with a motion contrary to the heavens <note>Macrobius is describing retrograde motion and the idea that while the whole sky turns daily from East to West, the planets move independently from West to East.</note>. Of these, that sphere which they name **Saturn** on Earth occupies one globe. Next is that brightness, prosperous and healthful to the human race, which is called **Jupiter**. Then comes the red one, horrible to the lands, which you call **Mars**. Then, beneath the middle region, the **Sun** occupies the place of leader, prince, and moderator of the other lights; the mind of the world and its tempering force, of such magnitude that it illuminates and fills all things with its light. Following this as companions are the courses, one of **Venus**, the other of **Mercury**. And in the lowest orb, the **Moon**, kindled by the rays of the sun, revolves. Below this, however, there is nothing except that which is mortal and fleeting, except for the souls given to the human race by the gift of the gods. Above the moon, all things are eternal. For the ninth, which is the **Earth** in the middle, does not move and is the lowest; and toward it all weights are carried by their own inclination."

A diligent description of the whole world from the highest to the lowest is collected in this place; it forms a certain complete body of the universe, which some have called <term>The All</term> <note>original Greek: "τὸ πᾶν" (to pan); Macrobius uses this term to signify the totality of the cosmos as a single organism.</note>. Hence it is said here: "all things are connected." Virgil indeed called it a "great body" [when he wrote]: *And it mingles itself with the great body.* <note>original: "Et magno se corpore miscet" from Virgil’s Aeneid VI.727, often cited by Neoplatonists to describe the World Soul.</note> In this place, Cicero, having sown the seeds of things to be sought, has left us much to cultivate. Regarding the seven subject globes, he says: "which turn backward with a motion contrary to the heavens." Which...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Cicero’s "Dream of Scipio," moving from the physical size of the stars to the philosophical and mechanical causes of their motion. It explores the concept of the World Soul and the distinction between the "fixed" stars and the "wandering" planets.</meta>

# BOOK ONE XVII

[He] says: he advises us to inquire whether the heavens revolve, and if those seven [spheres] both revolve and are moved by a contrary motion. Or, if this is the order of the spheres which Cicero relates, the authority of Plato <note>original: "Platonica... authoritas"</note> agrees. And if they are truly placed beneath [the highest heaven], in what way are the stars of them all said to traverse the zodiac, since the zodiac is both one and in the highest heaven? Or what reason makes the courses of some shorter and others longer in a single zodiac? For all these things must be asserted in explaining their order. And finally, for what reason are all weights carried toward the earth by their own inclination <note>original: "nutu suo," referring to the ancient concept of gravity where objects "desire" to reach the center</note>, as he says?

The nature, power, and reason of the World Soul <note>original: "mundanæ animæ," the *anima mundi* or vital force that animates the universe</note> teaches that the heaven revolves. Its eternity consists in motion because motion never leaves that which life does not desert. Nor does life depart from that in which it flourishes, being always in motion. Therefore, the celestial body—which the World Soul fabricated for itself to be a participant in immortality—is always in motion so that it might never fail in living. It does not know how to stand still because the soul itself, which impels it, does not stand still. For since the soul, which is an incorporeal essence, is in motion, and the body of the heaven was the first of all things fabricated by the soul, the nature of motion undoubtedly migrated from the incorporeal into this first body. Its power, whole and uncorrupted, does not desert that which it first began to move. Indeed, the motion of the heaven is necessarily revolving because, while it must always be moved, there is no place beyond it toward which an addition might extend; it is agitated by the continuation of a perpetual returning into itself. Therefore, it runs in that which it can or has, and for it to "proceed" is to be revolved, because the one course of a sphere encompassing all spaces and places is to rotate. 

But even so, it seems to always follow the soul, which runs through that very turning. We shall say, therefore, that it never finds [the soul] if it always follows it in this way; or rather, it always finds it, because the soul is everywhere total and everywhere perfect. Why then, if it finds what it seeks, does it not rest? Because the soul is also a stranger to rest. It would stand still if it found a soul that was standing still. But since that toward whose desire it is drawn always pours itself through the universe, the body also always twists itself into it and through it. These few things out of many regarding the secret of celestial volatility, found with Plotinus <note>original: "plotio authore," referring to the Neoplatonist philosopher Plotinus</note> as the authority, will suffice.

However, that he called this outermost globe (the one that revolves so) the "highest" is not to be understood as if he considered the globe itself to be the First Cause and the most omnipotent God. For the globe itself, which is the heaven, is the fabric of the Soul; the Soul proceeded from the Mind; the Mind was created from God, who truly is "He who is." But he called it "highest" in relation to the others in the order which are placed beneath it; wherefore he immediately added that it "restrains and contains the others." 

Regarding God: He is not only an immortal and divine animal, full of renowned reason from that purest Mind, but He either creates or contains all the virtues that follow that first summit of omnipotence. Finally, the ancients called Him Jupiter <note>original: "Iouem"</note>, and among theologians, Jupiter is the World Soul. Hence the saying: *From Jupiter is the beginning, O Muses; all things are full of Jupiter.* This is from Aratus <note>original: "Arato," a Greek didactic poet</note>, whom other poets have borrowed; when he was about to speak of the stars, deciding that the beginning should be taken from the heaven in which the stars reside, he mentioned that one must begin with Jupiter. From this, Juno is called both his sister and his spouse. 

<margin>Why Juno is both sister and spouse of Jupiter. Fixed stars.</margin>

Juno, however, is the Air <note>original: "aer"</note>; and she is called "sister" because the air was created from the same seeds as the heaven, and "spouse" because the air is subject to the heaven. Here it must be understood that besides the two lights [the Sun and Moon] and the five stars which are called "wandering" <note>original: "uagæ," the planets</note>, some say all the rest are fixed in the heaven and do not move except with the heaven. Others, whose assertion is nearer the truth, say that these also proceed by their own motion besides that with which they are carried by the conversion of the heaven. But because of the immensity of the outermost globe, exceeding a believable number, they consume ages in a single circuit of their ambition; and therefore no motion of theirs is perceived by man, since the span of human life is not sufficient to detect even a brief point of such slow progression. Hence Cicero, being ignorant of no sect approved by the ancients, touched upon both opinions at once by saying: *In which are fixed those eternal courses of the stars which revolve.* For he both said they were "fixed" and did not remain silent about them having "courses." Now let us inquire, by arguments leading to the truth, whether those seven globes which are placed beneath are carried by a contrary motion (as he says) to that which the heaven is turned. The Sun and the Moon and the five stars, which take their name from "error" <note>The word "planet" comes from the Greek *planētēs*, meaning "wanderer" or "error."</note>, besides that which they are drawn from the east to the west by the daily [motion] of the heaven...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of celestial mechanics, specifically addressing the counter-intuitive motion of the "wandering stars" (planets) compared to the fixed stars. Having established that the World Soul powers the motion of the heavens, Macrobius now provides empirical proofs for the direction of these movements.</meta>

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO
XVII

...revolution: that [the stars] proceed by their own motion into the East from the West has seemed—not only to those unlearned in secular literature, but also to many initiated in doctrine—to shrink from belief and be judged as something like a marvel. But to those who look more closely, it will be established that this is so true that it can not only be conceived in the mind, but also proven to the eyes themselves. However, so that we may deal with one who stubbornly denies this, come now—whosoever you are who pretends this is not clear to you—let us set aside all the things that contention feigns to destroy faith, or those which truth itself suggests, and change into the parts of a logical division. These wandering stars <note>the planets</note>, along with the two luminaries <note>the Sun and Moon</note>, we shall say are either fixed in the sky—so that like other stars no motion of their own can be judged by our eyes, but they are carried by the force of the world’s rotation—or they are moved by their own progression. Again, if they move, they either follow the path of the heaven from sunrise to sunset, traveling both by the common motion and their own; or they turn with a contrary retreat into the East from the direction of the West. Beyond this (as I suppose) nothing can be, or even be imagined. Now let us see which of these can be proven true. If they were fixed, they would never depart from the same station, but would always be seen in the same places as the others. For behold, among the fixed stars, the Pleiades <note>original: "Vergiliae"</note> never scatter from their own bond, nor do they desert the Hyades which are nearby, or leave the neighboring region of Orion. The structure of the Seven Stars <note>original: "Septentrionum," the Great Bear or Big Dipper</note> is not loosened. The Snake <note>the constellation Draco</note> which glides between them does not change its once-enfolding embrace. These [planets], however, are seen now in this region of the sky, now in that. And often, when two or more have come together in one place, they are afterwards separated both from the place in which they were seen together and from each other. From this, with the eyes themselves as witnesses, it is established that they are not fixed in the heaven. Therefore they move; nor can anyone deny this which experience affirms. We must ask, therefore, whether they revolve from East to West, or in a contrary direction by their own motion. But to us seeking this, not only the most manifest reason but even sight itself will demonstrate the truth.

<margin>The order of the signs of the zodiac</margin>

For let us consider the order of the signs by which we see the zodiac divided or distinguished, and let us take the beginning of that order from any sign we wish. When Aries rises, after it Taurus emerges. Gemini follows this, then Cancer, and the rest in order. If these [planets] therefore proceeded into the West from the East, they would not roll from Aries into Taurus—which is situated behind it—nor from Taurus into Gemini, a later sign; but rather they would proceed from Gemini into Taurus, and from Taurus into Aries by a straight progression consonant with the world’s rotation. Since they roll from the first sign into the second, from the second to the third, and from there to the rest, which are subsequent, it is established without doubt that these stars move not with the heaven, but against the heaven. So that this may be fully clear,

<margin>The course of the Moon</margin>

let us add proof from the course of the Moon, which is more notable for both its clarity and its velocity. The Moon, after it has been renewed by departing from the Sun <note>the New Moon</note>, is seen on about the second day around sunset; and as if a neighbor to the Sun which it recently left, after that has set, it holds the margin of the sky, preceding it above the West. On the third day it sets later than on the second, and so daily it recedes further from the West, so that on the seventh day it is seen in the middle of the sky around sunset. After another seven days, when the Sun sets, the Moon rises; thus in the middle of the month it traverses half the sky—that is, one hemisphere—by receding from the West toward the East. Again, after seven more days, around sunset, it holds the peak of the hidden hemisphere. And the proof of this thing is that it rises in the middle of the night. Finally, when the same number of days have passed, it reaches the Sun again, and the rising of both is seen to be nearby; for having long followed the Sun, it is moved again, and by receding little by little, always returning toward the East, it leaves the West behind. The Sun itself also moves no differently than from West to East; and although it completes its retreat more slowly than the Moon—inasmuch as it traverses one sign in the same time the Moon runs through the entire zodiac—it nevertheless provides manifest evidence of its motion, subject to the eyes. For we prove it is in Aries because, since it is an equinoctial sign, it makes equal hours of sleep and day. When it sets in this sign, we see Libra—that is, the Claws of the Scorpion <note>original: "Scorpii chelas," as Libra was formerly considered the scorpion's claws</note>—rising soon after; and Taurus appears near the sunset. For we see the Pleiades and the Hyades, the brighter parts of Taurus, not long after the Sun sets. In the following month, the Sun retreats into the subsequent sign, that is, into Taurus; and so it happens that neither the Pleiades nor any other part of Taurus is seen that month. For the sign which rises with the Sun and sets with the Sun is always hidden, so much so that even the neighboring stars are concealed by the proximity of the Sun. For the Dog Star <note>Sirius</note> also is then [hidden] because it is near Taurus...

<summary>Macrobius provides astronomical proofs that the planets, Sun, and Moon move from West to East, contrary to the primary rotation of the firmament. He uses the sequential order of zodiac signs and the monthly phases of the Moon as empirical evidence for this planetary progression.</summary>

# BOOK ONE

...is said to be malevolent—as is thought of the stars of Mars and Saturn—or why a more notable reputation for benevolence belongs to Jupiter and Venus among the <term>genethliacs</term> <note>original: "genethliacos"; these are astrologers who cast birth charts</note>, since the nature of divine things is one. I shall bring forward a reason that, as far as I know, has been read in only one place. For Ptolemy, in three books,

<margin>
Where the properties of the stars come from
</margin>

in which all things that are compatible are joined and fitted together, there occurs a "joining competence." Nothing can be compatible with another thing except through these numbers. These are the *epitritus* <note>original: "epitritus"; the ratio of 4:3</note>, the *hemiolius* <note>original: "hemiolius"; the ratio of 3:2</note>, the *epogdous* <note>original: "epogdous"; the ratio of 9:8</note>, the double, the triple, and the quadruple. I wish for you to accept these in this place as if they were the names of numbers. In the following sections, indeed, when we speak of the <term>harmony of the heavens</term>, we shall learn more opportunely what these numbers are and what they are capable of. For now, it is enough to know this: that without these numbers, no bond and no concord can exist. 

Indeed, the Sun and Moon especially govern our life. Since these two powers are proper to perishable bodies—namely, to feel and to grow—the <term>sensory nature</term> <note>original: "æstheticon," from the Greek for "perceptive"</note> comes to us from the Sun, and the <term>vegetative nature</term> <note>original: "phyticon," from the Greek for "growth"</note> comes to us from the lunar sphere. Thus, our life which we enjoy consists of the benefit of both luminaries. However, our conduct and the very ancient record of our actions are referred both to these two luminaries and to the five wandering stars <note>the planets</note>. 

But the intervention of those numbers mentioned above joins and associates some of these stars well with the luminaries, while no bond of number applies others to the luminaries. Therefore, the stars of Venus and Jupiter are associated with both luminaries through these numbers. But the star of Jupiter is joined to the Sun through all these numbers, and to the Moon through many; the star of Venus is joined to the Moon through all, and to the Sun through many. Hence, although both are believed to be beneficent,

<margin>
The star of Jupiter
</margin>

the star of Jupiter is more suited to the Sun, and Venus to the Moon. Therefore, they are more favorable to our lives than if they were not in concord with the luminaries—the authors of our life—by the logic of numbers. The stars of Saturn and Mars do not have such competence with the luminaries, though Saturn looks toward the Sun and Mars toward the Moon by some slight or extreme line of number. Therefore, they are thought to be less favorable to human life, as if they were not joined to the authors of life by a close logic of number. 

Why these stars themselves sometimes provide wealth or fame to men ought to belong to another treatise; here it is enough to have disclosed the reason why one is thought terrible and another salutary. Indeed, Plotinus, in the book titled *How the Stars Act* <note>Enneads 2.3</note>, declares that nothing happens to men by the force or power of the stars, but that those things which the necessity of decree ordains for individuals are merely shown through the transit, station, or retreat of these seven. It is as if birds, either by flying past or standing still, signify future things with their wings or voice without knowing it themselves. Thus, one star will be rightly called "salutary" and another "terrible," since through the former we signify prosperity, and through the latter, inconveniences. 

In all these names which are spoken concerning the Sun, the speech is not extravagant for the sake of empty praise, but true things are expressed by these terms. He is called "Leader and Prince," "Regulator of the other lights," and "Mind and temperament of the world." Plato, in the *Timaeus*, when speaking of the eight spheres, says: "So that there might be a certain measure of speed and slowness through the eight circuits themselves, and that it might be known, God kindled a light in the circuit above the earth in the second place, which we now call the Sun." You see how this definition intends for the light of all the spheres to be in the Sun. 

But Cicero, knowing that the other stars also have their own light, and that only the Moon (as we have often said) lacks its own, clarifies the obscurity of this definition more purely. Showing that the greatest light is in the Sun, he says not only "Leader and Prince and Regulator of the other lights" (thus he knows the other stars are lights as well), but calls him "Leader and Prince," whom Heraclitus calls the "fountain of celestial light." He is the **Leader** because he precedes all in the majesty of light. He is the **Prince** because he so stands out that, because he alone appears in such a way, he is called "the Sun" <note>Macrobius is playing on the Latin word "Sol" (Sun) and "solus" (alone)</note>.

<margin>
From where "Sun" comes
</margin>

He is called **Regulator of the others** because he himself regulates their courses and returns by a certain definition. For there is a certain definition of space which each wandering star reaches as it recedes from the Sun; and when it is forbidden to approach further, it is seen to move backward. And again, when it reaches a certain part in its retreat, he recalls it to its accustomed direct course. Thus the force and power of the Sun...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of celestial mechanics in Macrobius's commentary. Having previously discussed the specific influences of the planets, the author now addresses the fundamental astronomical question of planetary direction, arguing that the planets move "backwards" (West to East) against the daily rotation of the firmament.</meta>

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

...rotation: that it proceeds by its own motion from west to east is judged a monstrosity and contrary to faith, not only by those unlearned in letters, but even by many initiated into doctrine. But to those who examine it closely, it will be so clearly true that it can be grasped not only by the mind but proved by the eyes themselves. However, so that we may deal with one who stubbornly denies this: come, you who pretend this is not clear to you—let us change into logical divisions all the things that either a contentious person imagines to undermine faith, or that truth itself suggests. We shall say these wandering stars, along with the two luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon</note>, are either fixed in the sky—meaning, like other stars, they have no motion of their own judged by our eyes, but are carried by the impulse of the world's rotation—or they move by their own advancement. Again, if they move: either they follow the path of heaven from east to west, traveling both by the common motion and their own; or they turn in a contrary retreat toward the east from the western side. 

Beyond this (as I suppose) nothing can either be, or be imagined. Now let us see which of these can be proven true. If they were fixed, they would never leave the same station, but would always be seen in the same places like the other stars. For behold, among the fixed stars, the **Vergiliae** <note>original: "vergiliæ"; more commonly known today as the Pleiades</note> do not pull apart from their grouping, nor do the **Hyades** <note>A V-shaped cluster of stars in the constellation Taurus</note> desert those stars that are in their neighborhood, nor do they leave the region closest to **Orion**. The frame of the **Great Bear** <note>original: "Septētrionū"; literally "the seven oxen," referring to the stars of the Big Dipper</note> does not dissolve. The **Serpent** <note>original: "Anguis"; the constellation Draco</note> that glides between them does not change its once-wrapped embrace. But these [the planets], indeed, are seen now in this region of the sky, and now in that. And often, when two or more have come together into one place, they are later separated both from the place where they were seen together and from each other. From this, with the eyes themselves providing proof, it is established that they are not fixed in the heavens. Therefore, they move; nor can anyone deny what experience affirms. It must be asked, then, whether they revolve from east to west, or in the contrary direction by their own motion.

<margin>
The order of the signs of the zodiac
</margin>

But to us seeking this, not only the most manifest reason but sight itself will demonstrate it. For let us consider the order of the signs by which we see the zodiac divided or distinguished, and let us take the beginning of that order from any sign we please. When **Aries** rises, **Taurus** emerges after it. The **Gemini** follow this; then **Cancer**, and the rest in order. If these stars, therefore, proceeded toward the west from the east, they would not roll from Aries into Taurus, which is behind its side, nor from Taurus into Gemini, a later sign; rather, they would proceed from Gemini into Taurus, and from Taurus into Aries in a straight approach consistent with the world's rotation. Since, therefore, they revolve from the first sign into the second, from the second to the third, and likewise to the rest which are subsequent; and since the fixed signs are carried along with the heavens, it is established without doubt that these stars move not *with* the heavens, but *against* the heavens.

<margin>
The course of the Moon
</margin>

So that this may be fully clear, let us add an argument about the course of the Moon, which is more notable both for its brightness and its speed. After the Moon has been renewed by leaving the Sun, it is seen around sunset on about the second day; and as if it were a neighbor to the Sun which it recently left, after the Sun has set, it holds the edge of the sky above the west. On the third day, it sets later than on the second, and so every day it recedes further from the west, so that on the seventh day it is seen in the middle of the sky around sunset. After another seven days, when the Sun sets, the Moon rises; thus in the middle part of the month, it measures out half the sky—that is, one hemisphere—by receding from the west toward the east. Again, after another seven days, it holds the peak of the hidden hemisphere at the time of sunset. The evidence for this is that it rises in the middle of the night. Finally, when the same number of days have passed, it is caught by the Sun again, and the rising of both is seen to be near; for as long as it follows the Sun, it is moved again, and receding little by little, it always leaves the west by returning toward the east. 

The Sun itself moves no differently than from west to east; and although it completes its retreat more slowly than the Moon—inasmuch as it traverses one sign in the time the Moon runs through the whole zodiac—it nevertheless provides manifest evidence of its motion, subject to the eyes. For let us suppose it is in Aries; because this is an <term>equinoctial sign</term> <note>A sign where the sun crosses the celestial equator, making day and night equal</note>, it makes the hours of sleep and day equal. When it sets in this sign, we see **Libra**—that is, the Claws of the **Scorpion**—rise soon after; and Taurus appears near the sunset. For we see the Vergiliae and the Hyades, the brighter parts of Taurus, not long after the Sun sets. In the following month, the Sun recedes into the subsequent sign, which is Taurus; and it so happens that neither the Vergiliae nor any other part of Taurus is seen in that month. For a sign that rises with the Sun and sets with the Sun is always hidden, to the extent that even neighboring stars are concealed by the proximity of the Sun. For even the **Dog Star** <note>Sirius</note> is then hidden because it is near Taurus...

<summary>Macrobius provides a detailed astronomical proof that the planets move from West to East by comparing their shifting positions against the fixed constellations and the sequential order of the Zodiac signs.</summary>

<page-num>XIX</page-num>
<header>BOOK ONE XIX</header>
<margin>See XVIII after -></margin>

...is said to be harmful, as is thought of the stars of Mars and Saturn; or why a more notable degree of benevolence is held by Jupiter and Venus among **astrologers** <note>original: "genethliacos"; those who cast horoscopes based on birth charts</note>, since there is but one nature of the divine beings. I shall bring forth a reason that, to my knowledge, has been read in only one place. For **Ptolemy**, in the three books he composed on harmony, revealed the cause which I will briefly explain. <margin>Whence the properties of the stars arise</margin> There are certain numbers through which all things that agree with one another are joined and fitted together; a joining harmony is created, and nothing can agree with another except through these numbers. These are the **sesquitertial** <note>original: "epitritus"; a 4:3 ratio</note>, the **sesquialter** <note>original: "hemiolius"; a 3:2 ratio</note>, the **sesquioctave** <note>original: "epogdous"; a 9:8 ratio</note>, the double, the triple, and the quadruple. I wish for you to accept these here as the names of numbers. In the following sections, when we speak of the harmony of the heavens, we shall more opportunely explain what these numbers are and what they can do. For now, it is enough to know this: that without these numbers, no bond and no concord can exist. 

Our life is especially moderated by the Sun and the Moon. Since these two properties belong to perishable bodies—to feel or to grow—the **sensory nature** <note>original: "æstheticon"</note> comes to us from the Sun, and the **vegetative nature** <note>original: "phyticon"; the power of growth</note> from the Moon, reaching us from their spheres. Thus, our life which we enjoy consists of the benefit of both lights. However, our social interaction and the outcome of our actions are referred both to these two lights and to the five wandering stars <note>The five planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>. But the intervention of the numbers mentioned above joins and associates some of these stars well with the luminaries, while no connection of number applies others to the lights. 

Therefore, the stars of Venus and Jupiter are associated with both lights through these numbers. But the star of Jupiter is joined to the Sun through all these ratios, and to the Moon through many; and Venus is joined to the Moon through all, and to the Sun through many numbers. Hence, although both are believed to be **benefic** <note>favorable or lucky</note>, <margin>The star of Jupiter</margin> the star of Jupiter is more suited to the Sun, and Venus to the Moon; and therefore they accommodate our life more than if they were not in concord by the reckoning of numbers with the luminaries who are the authors of our life. 

The stars of Saturn or Mars do not have such a competence with the luminaries, although Saturn may behold the Sun and Mars may behold the Moon by some distant or extreme line of numbers. Therefore, they are thought to be less favorable to human life, as if they were not joined to the authors of life by a tight reckoning of numbers. Why they themselves nonetheless sometimes provide wealth or fame to men must belong to another treatise; for here it suffices to have opened the reason why one is thought terrible and another salutary. 

And **Plotinus** indeed, in the book entitled *Thus do the Stars*, declares that nothing happens to men by the force or power of the stars, but that those things which the necessity of decree ordains for individuals are shown through the transit, station, or retreat of these seven, just as birds, by flying past or standing still, signify future things with their wings or voice without knowing it themselves. Thus, however, it is right to call this one "salutary" and that one "terrible," since through the former we signify prosperity, and through the latter inconveniences. 

In these many names which are said of the Sun, the speech does not wander in vain nor for the sake of boastful praise; rather, true things are expressed by these terms. He says he is the **"Leader and Prince"** and the **"moderator of the remaining lights,"** the **"mind of the world,"** and its **"temperance."** **Plato**, in the *Timaeus*, when speaking of the eight spheres, says: "So that there might be a certain measure of speed and slowness through the eight circuits themselves, and that it might be known, God kindled a light in the second circuit above the earth, which we now call the Sun." You see how this definition wants the light of all the spheres to be in the Sun. 

But **Cicero**, knowing that the other stars also have their own light, and that only the Moon (as we have often said) lacks its own, more clearly resolves the obscurity of this definition. Showing that the greatest light is in the Sun, he says not only that it is the "leader and prince and moderator of the remaining lights" (thus he knows the other stars are lights too), but calls this leader and prince that which **Heraclitus** calls the **"fount of celestial light."** <margin>The Sun: whence the name</margin> He is the Leader, therefore, because he precedes all in the majesty of light. He is the Prince because he stands out so much that, because he alone appears as such, he is called **Sol** <note>A common ancient etymological play: "Sol" (Sun) derived from "Solus" (Alone)</note>. He is called the Moderator of the rest because he himself moderates their courses and returns by a certain definition. For there is a certain boundary of space which each wandering star reaches as it recedes from the Sun, and as if prohibited from approaching further, it is seen to be driven backward. And again, when it has touched a certain part in its receding, it is recalled to its accustomed direct course; thus the force and power of the Sun...

Having previously touched upon the harmonic ratios of the planets, the text now focuses specifically on the Sun—its role as the "Heart of Heaven" and the geometric methods used by ancient scientists to measure its immense size relative to the Earth.</meta>

<page-num>XIX</page-num>
<header>ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO</header>

...regulates the motions of the other lights by a fixed measure. It is called the **Mind of the World** <note>original: "Mens mundi"</note>; indeed, physicists have called it the **Heart of Heaven** <note>original: "cor cæli"</note>. <margin>The Sun is called the heart of heaven</margin> This is surely because all things that we see happening through the heavens by a settled reason—the day and the night, the changing turns of length and shortness between the two, and the equal measure of both at certain times—and then the mild warmth of spring, the scorching heat of the Crab and the Lion <note>The zodiac signs of Cancer and Leo, representing midsummer</note> in summer, the softness of the autumn breeze, and the force of the cold with a tempering between the two: the course and reason of the Sun dispenses all these things. Rightly, therefore, is it called the heart of heaven, through which all things happen that we see occurring by divine reason. There is also this reason why it is rightly called the heart of heaven: because the nature of fire is always in perpetual motion and agitation. We have reported that the Sun is the source of the **ethereal fire** <note>original: "ignis ætherei"; the pure, celestial flame of the upper heavens</note>. Therefore, what the Sun is in the ether, the heart is in a living creature: its nature is such that it never ceases from motion, for even a brief cessation of its agitation, by whatever chance, would immediately destroy the soul. This concerns why he called it the Mind of the World. But as to why it is also called the **tempering of the world** <note>original: "tēperatio mūdi"</note>, the reason is clear: for it is most certain that not only the Earth, but also the heaven itself—which he truly calls the world—is tempered by the Sun. Thus, its extremities, which have receded furthest from the path of the Sun, lack every benefit of heat and grow numb in a single perpetuity of cold, a point which will be more aptly explained in the following sections. It remains for us to say a few things that must not be passed over concerning its magnitude, which he extolled with a most true proclamation.

<margin>The magnitude of the Sun</margin> Physicists have especially desired to achieve this in every inquiry concerning the magnitude of the Sun: how much larger it can be than the Earth. And **Eratosthenes** <note>A Greek polymath (c. 276–194 BC) famous for measuring the Earth's circumference</note> says thus in his books of dimensions: "The measure of the Earth multiplied twenty-seven times will produce the measure of the Sun." **Posidonius** <note>A Stoic philosopher and scientist (c. 135–51 BC)</note> says this much, much more frequently, and both call upon the evidence of the lunar eclipse to support their case. Thus, when they wish to prove the Sun is larger than the Earth, they use the testimony of the failing Moon. When they attempt to assert the eclipse of the Moon, they borrow proof from the magnitude of the Sun. And so it happens that while each builds its case upon the other, neither builds a case with probability, with mutual testimony always wavering back and forth in the middle; for how can one prove something through a matter that is itself still to be proven? But the **Egyptians**, speaking not at all from conjecture, and having set aside a free argument without calling the lunar eclipse to their defense, wished to prove by what measure the Sun is larger than the Earth, so that they might then finally show through its magnitude why the Moon fails. However, this could by no means be apprehended otherwise unless the measure of both the Earth and the Sun were found, so that a distinction might be made from the comparison. The dimension of the Earth was easily established for eyes investigating by reason; but they saw they could not find the measure of the Sun except through the measure of the heaven through which it runs. Therefore, they first determined to measure that heaven, that is, the path of the Sun, so that through it they might recognize the scale of the Sun. But I ask, if anyone was ever so idle—as if on holiday from all serious work—as to take these matters into his hands, let him not shudder at such a promise of the ancients as if it were near-madness, nor let him laugh. For genius made a way for itself toward a matter that seemed incomprehensible by nature, and through the Earth they found the measure of the heaven. However, so that the reason for the invention may be clear, a few things must first be said according to the rules, so that the approach to the following matters may be better prepared. In every circle or sphere, the middle point is called the **center**. <margin>Center</margin> The center is nothing other than a point by which the middle of the sphere or circle is distinguished by the most certain observation. Likewise, a line drawn from any place on the circle that marks the boundary, into any part of the same circle, must necessarily divide the disk. But that division does not divide the disk into halves in every way. For only that line divides the disk through the middle into equal parts which is drawn from the top to the bottom in such a way that it must pass through the center. And this line, which thus divides the circle equally, is called the **diameter**. <margin>Diameter</margin> Likewise, the diameter of any circle, when tripled and with the addition of a seventh part of itself, makes the measure of the circle that encloses the disk. That is, if the length of the diameter holds seven inches, and you wish to know from that how many inches the circumference of that circle holds, you will triple the seven, making twenty-one. To these you will add a seventh part, which is one, and you will pronounce the measure of this circle to be twenty-two inches, whose diameter extends seven inches. All these things geometry...

<page-num>XVIII</page-num>
<header>BOOK ONE</header>

it [the constellation] is not seen, being hidden by the proximity of the light. And this is what Virgil says:

> The white Bull opens the year with golden horns,
> and the Dog Star sets, giving way to the opposing constellation.
<note>original: "Candidus auratis aperit cum cornibus annum / Taurus:& aduerso cedens canis occidit astro." A quote from Virgil’s *Georgics* describing the start of the agricultural year.</note>

For he does not mean to imply that the Dog Star is carried into its setting as soon as the Bull rises with the Sun—since the Bull is the first to rise—but rather he says it "sets" while the Bull is carrying the Sun, because it then begins to be invisible due to the Sun's nearness. However, at that time, as the Sun is setting, the Balance <note>The constellation Libra</note> is found so much higher that the whole of the Scorpion appears to have risen; yet the Twins <note>Gemini</note>, being nearby, then seem to have set. Again, after the month of the Bull, the Twins are not seen, which signifies that the Sun has migrated into them. After the Twins, it moves back into the Crab <note>Cancer</note>. And then when it sets, the Balance is soon seen in the middle of the sky. Thus it is established that the Sun, having passed through three signs—that is, the Ram <note>Aries</note>, the Bull, and the Twins—has moved back to the middle of the hemisphere. Finally, after the three following months, having traversed the three signs that follow—I mean the Crab, the Lion, and the Virgin—it finds itself in the Balance, which again makes the night equal to the day; and while it sets in that very sign, the Ram soon rises, in which the Sun used to set six months before. We have chosen to put forward its setting rather than its rising because the later signs are seen after sunset. And while we show that the Sun returns to those signs which are usually seen when the Sun is sinking, we demonstrate beyond doubt that it moves back in a motion contrary to that which moves the heavens. These things which we have said concerning the Sun and the Moon will also suffice to assign the retreat of the five stars <note>The "wandering stars," or planets: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury.</note>; for by the same reasoning, by migrating into the later signs, they always turn in a retreat contrary to the world's rotation.

<margin>
The Order
of the 
Spheres
</margin>

Having asserted these things, a few words must be said about the order of the spheres. In this matter, Cicero may seem to differ from Plato; for Cicero says the sphere of the Sun is the fourth of the seven—that is, located in the middle—while Plato records that it holds the place that is second upward from the Moon—that is, the sixth place from the top of the seven. Archimedes and the calculations of the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian astronomers and mathematicians.</note> agree with Cicero. Plato followed the Egyptians, the parents of all philosophical disciplines, who wish the Sun to be located between the Moon and Mercury in such a way that they have discovered and declared the reason why the Sun is believed by some to be above Mercury and above Venus. For even those who think so do not wander far from the appearance of the truth. Indeed, the following reason persuaded them of the opinion of this permutation. From the sphere of Saturn, which is the first of the seven, to the sphere of Jupiter, the second from the top, there is such a great distance of intervening space that the higher one completes the circuit of the zodiac in thirty years, while the one below it completes it in twelve years. Again, the sphere of Mars is so far from Jupiter that it completes the same course in two years. Venus, however, is so much lower in region than Mars that a year is sufficient for it to traverse the zodiac. Now, indeed, the star of Mercury is so close to Venus, and the Sun so near to Mercury, that these three circle their heaven in an equal space of time—that is, a year, more or less. Therefore, Cicero also called these two courses the "companions of the Sun," because in an equal space they never depart far from one another. The Moon, however, has moved down so far from these that what they complete in a year, she completes in twenty-eight days. Therefore, among the ancients, there was no disagreement regarding the order of the three higher ones—which an immense distance clearly and distinctly separates—nor regarding the region of the Moon, which is far removed from all others. But the proximity of these three—Venus, Mercury, and the Sun—confuses their order. However, this reason did not escape the ingenuity of the Egyptians, which is as follows: The circle through which the Sun runs is surrounded by the circle of Mercury as the lower one. That one, in turn, is included by the higher circle of Venus. And so it happens that when these two stars run through the upper arcs of their circles, they are understood to be located above the Sun. But when they travel through the lower parts of their circles, the Sun is considered to be higher than them. Therefore, to those who said their spheres were below the Sun, it seemed so because of that course of the stars which sometimes (as we said) appears lower, and which is truly more notable because it then appears more freely. For when they hold the higher parts, they are more hidden by the rays. And for this reason, that persuasion grew strong, and this order was received into use by almost everyone. Nevertheless, a more clear-sighted observation has discovered a better order, which, besides the investigation of sight, this reason also commends: that the Moon, which lacks its own light and borrows from the Sun, must necessarily have its source... <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing with the idea that the Moon's source of light must be nearby.</note>

...subject to its own light. For this reasoning explains why the moon does not have its own light, <margin>Why the Moon has no light of its own</margin> while all the other stars shine with their own. This is because those stars located above the sun are in the purest **ether**; <term>ether</term> <note>In ancient science, ether was the "fifth element," a pure, undying fire that filled the space of the heavens above the air.</note> in which everything that exists possesses a natural light of its own. This ether, with all its fire, rests upon the sphere of the sun in such a way that the zones of heaven which are far from the sun are oppressed by perpetual cold, as will be shown below. The Moon, however, because it alone is below the sun and very close to the region of **falling things**, <note>The "sublunary" realm—the Earth and its atmosphere—where things are subject to change, decay, and death.</note> being itself devoid of light, could not have light unless it was placed beneath the sun to reflect it. Finally, because the earth is one part of the entire world, and the moon is one part of the ether, they have called the moon an "ethereal earth." Yet it could not be immobile like the earth, because in a sphere that rotates, nothing remains immobile except the center. Of the worldly sphere, the earth is the center; therefore, it alone remains immobile. Furthermore, the earth, having received the sun's light, only becomes bright; it does not reflect it. The Moon, like a mirror, sends forth the light by which it is illuminated, because those parts of it are distinct and dense like air and water. It is considered a torch, and for that reason, it is thickened with extreme density, nor is it penetrated by any light beyond its surface. Although the moon is a boundary, it is a boundary of the most liquid light and ethereal fire; therefore, although it is a denser body than the other heavenly bodies, it is still much purer than earthly matter and is penetrable by the light it receives, so much so that it emits that light again. However, it carries no sense of heat to us, because a ray of light, when it comes to us from its origin (that is, from the sun), carries with it the nature of the fire from which it is born. But when it is poured into the body of the moon and reflects from there, it sends back only brightness, not heat. For even a mirror, when it emits a splendor from itself by the force of a fire placed opposite at a distance, shows only the likeness of the fire while lacking the sensation of heat.

<margin>The Sun in the spheres</margin> We have sufficiently discussed what order Plato or his authorities gave to the sun, or which order Cicero followed when he assigned it the fourth place among the globes, or what reasoning induced the persuasion of this difference, and why Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> said: *the moon, kindled by the rays of the sun, revolves in the lowest orbit.* But to this must be added why Cicero wants the sun to be the fourth out of seven. Now, the fourth among seven is not just "nearly" the middle, but is the middle in every way; yet he did not say the sun was the "absolute" middle, but "almost" the middle, using these words: *Then, below, the sun occupies nearly the middle region.* <note>original: "Deinde subter mediam fere regionem sol optinet."</note> This addition is not without purpose, for it tempers the statement: the sun, occupying the fourth place, will hold the middle region by number, but not by space. For if it is located between three above and three below, it is undoubtedly the middle by number; but when the dimension of the entire space occupied by the seven spheres is inspected, the region of the sun is not found located in the middle of the space, because it is further from the highest point than it is from the lowest extremity. This assertion will be proven by a brief, unambiguous argument. The star of **Saturn**, which is the highest, traverses the zodiac in thirty years; the sun, in the middle, in one year; the moon, the last, in less than a full month. Therefore, there is as much difference between the sun and Saturn as there is between one and thirty. There is as much between the moon and the sun as there is between twelve and one. From this, it appears that the region of the sun does not create a division of the total space from top to bottom exactly at the halfway point. But because he was speaking here of the number, in which the fourth is truly the middle, he pronounced it the "middle"; yet because of the hidden dimension of the spaces, he added the word to temper this definition.

It should be noted that the existence of a star of Saturn, and another of Jupiter, and another of Mars, is not a constitution of nature, but a human persuasion, which gave numbers and names to the stars. For he does not say "that star which is Saturnian," but *that which on earth they name Saturnian*; and *that glow which is called Jupiter's*, and *that which you call Martian*. He expressed in each case that these names were not found in nature, but were human inventions adapted for the sake of distinction. As for why he called the glow of Jupiter "prosperous and salutary to the human race," while calling that of Mars "red and terrible to the earth," one description is drawn from the color of the stars (for Jupiter's shines bright, while Mars' glows red), and the other from the tradition of those who wish for favorable or adverse influences to flow from these stars into the lives of men. For they generally define terrible things as coming from the star of Mars, and salutary things from Jupiter. If anyone should ask the cause of the other—whence comes malice in divine beings, such as the stars—

<page-num>XX</page-num>

->**BOOK ONE**<-

We could prove these matters with geometrical and most evident reasons, were it not for our belief that no one doubts them, and our desire to avoid extending this volume to an excessive length. It must also be understood that the shadow of the earth—which the sun, running below the lower hemisphere after sunset, forces to be cast upward, and from which the darkness over the earth arises—is called **night**. <margin>Night</margin> <note>original: *Nox*</note> This shadow extends sixty times the measurement of the earth's diameter. This length, standing upright reaching to the very circle through which the sun runs, pours back the darkness upon the earth by the exclusion of light. Therefore, we must first reveal how large the diameter of the earth is, so that it may be clear what sixty times that measure amounts to. Once these basics are tasted, the discourse may return to the treatment of the measurements it promised. By the most evident and indubitable dimensions, it is established that the circumference of the entire earth—whether it lies desolate or inhabited—measures two hundred and fifty-two thousand **stadia**. <note>A *stadium* was an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet, though its exact length varied in different regions.</note> Since the circumference holds this much, the diameter undoubtedly has eighty thousand stadia, or not much more, according to the rule of tripling the diameter and adding a seventh part, as we stated regularly above regarding the diameter and the circle. <margin>Circumference of the earth.</margin> <note>original: *Ambitus terrae*. The author is using the ancient approximation for Pi (π) as 22/7 (3.142...).</note> And because to calculate the length of the earth’s shadow we must multiply the diameter of the earth, not its circumference—for it is the diameter that is known to grow upward—you must multiply the eighty thousand stadia of the earth's diameter sixty times. This makes four million, eight hundred thousand stadia from the earth to the sun's path, where we said the earth's shadow reaches. Now, the Earth is located as a center in the middle of the celestial circle through which the sun runs. Therefore, the measurement of the earth's shadow will make up half of the diameter; and if an equal measurement is extended from the other side of the earth to the same circle, the full diameter of the circle through which the sun runs is found. Thus, by doubling those four million, eight hundred thousand, the full diameter of the celestial circle will be nine million, six hundred thousand stadia. Once the diameter is found, the measurement of its circumference is easily revealed to us. For you must multiply this sum which formed the diameter by three, adding a seventh part, as has been said often already; and so you will find the circumference of the entire circle through which the sun runs to be thirty million, one hundred and seventy thousand stadia. Having said these things, by which the measurement of the earth's circumference and diameter is shown, as well as the scale of the circle through which the sun runs and its diameter, we shall now indicate what the measurement of the sun itself is, and how those most wise men discovered it. For just as the size of the circle through which the sun travels could be detected by the furthest point of the shadow, so the measurement of the sun was found through that same circle in the following manner, as the ingenuity of the investigation proceeded. On the day of the **equinox**, <note>original: *aequinoctialis*. The day when day and night are of equal length.</note> before the sun rose, a stone vessel was placed level, fashioned in the likeness of a hemisphere. It was hollowed out with a curved perimeter and marked below with lines for the twelve hours of the day. The shadow of a protruding **stilus** <note>Also known as a gnomon, the vertical rod of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note> marks these hours as it moves with the passage of the sun. Now, the function of such a vessel (as we know) is this: the shadow of the stilus runs from one edge to the other in the same amount of time that the sun measures out half of the heaven from rising to setting—that is, the rotation of one hemisphere. For a full rotation of the entire heaven is completed in a day and a night. Therefore, it is established that as much as the sun moves in its own circle, the shadow moves just as much in this vessel. Thus, as the time of the sun's rising approached, the diligent gaze of an observer stayed fixed upon this levelly placed vessel. And when, at the first ray of the sun which it emitted, the first top of the solar disk emerged, and the shadow descending from the top of the stilus touched the first edge of the curved lip, that very place which received the first fruits of the shadow was marked with a sign. It was then observed for as long as the sun’s disk appeared above the earth, until its upper edge was still seen to rest upon the horizon; and immediately the place to which the shadow had then moved in the vessel was noted. The dimension between both marks of the shadows was taken, which measures the full disk of the sun—that is, the diameter born from its two edges. It was found to be a ninth part of that space which is contained from the top lip of the vessel to the line of the first hour. From this, it is established that in the sun's course, nine repeated passes of its disk make up one hour of equinoctial time.

And because the rotation of the celestial hemisphere, completed in twelve hours, creates the day, and nine times twelve makes one hundred and eight: without doubt, the diameter of the sun is the one hundred and eighth part of the equinoctial hemisphere. Therefore, it is the two hundred and sixteenth part of the entire equinoctial circle. It was proved previously that the circle itself has thirty million and one hundred and seventy thousand **stadia**. <note>A stadium was an ancient unit of length. Macrobius is citing a total circumference of 30,170,000 stadia.</note> Therefore, if you consider the two hundred and sixteenth part of that sum, you will find the measure of the diameter of the sun. That part is approximately one hundred and forty thousand. Thus, the diameter of the sun must be said to be about one hundred and forty thousand stadia. From this, it is found to be nearly double the diameter of the earth. <note>The earth's diameter was previously estimated at 80,000 stadia; 140,000 is slightly less than double, but roughly so in ancient approximations.</note> It is established by the examination of geometrical reasoning that when, between two spheres, one diameter exceeds the other by double, the sphere whose diameter is double is eight times larger than the other sphere. <note>This follows the geometric principle that the volume of a sphere is proportional to the cube of its radius (2 cubed = 8).</note> Therefore, from these things <margin>Size of the Sun</margin> <note>original: *Solis magnitudo*</note> it must be said that the sun is eight times larger than the earth. We have briefly sampled these points regarding the size of the sun, excerpted from many sources. But since we have said that seven spheres are placed below the heaven, with each outer one surrounding those contained within, and they are all far removed both from the heaven and from each other. Now it must be asked: since there is only one zodiac, and it consists of stars fixed in the heaven, in what way are the stars of the lower spheres said to wander within the signs of the zodiac? The reason is not long to find, for it waits at the very entrance of the question. For it is true that neither the sun nor the moon, nor any of the **wanderers**, <note>original: *uagis*. The ancient term for planets, as they appeared to "wander" against the backdrop of fixed stars.</note> are carried through the signs of the zodiac in such a way as to be mixed with their stars; rather, each is said to be in that sign which it had above its head <note>The zenith point directly above the planet.</note> in that region of its own circle running beneath them. This is because reason has divided the circles of the individual spheres into twelve equal parts, just as it divided the zodiac. And whichever planet comes into that part of its own circle which is situated under the part of the zodiac assigned to Aries, it is conceded to have entered Aries itself. A similar observation holds for the stars moving into each individual part. And because the way to understanding is easier through the eyes, let the sight assign what the speech has described. Let there be a zodiac circle, marked with the letter **a**. Within this, let seven other orbits be placed. And let the zodiac be divided from **a** into twelve parts by fixed marks in order, to which the following letters shall be assigned. Let the space enclosed between **a** and **b** be assigned to Aries; that between **b** and **c** to Taurus; that between **c** and **d** to Gemini; to Cancer what follows; and the rest to the others in order. With these established, now let individual lines be drawn downward from each of the zodiac’s marks and letters through all the circles to the very last one. Without doubt, the passage of the lines will divide each orbit into twelve parts. In whichever circle, therefore—whether the sun, or the moon, or any of the wanderers—runs, when it comes to the space enclosed between the lines flowing down from the marks and letters **a** and **b**, it will be said to be in Aries. This is because, positioned there, it will have the space designated for Aries in the zodiac above its head, just as we described. Similarly, into whichever part it moves, it will be said to be in the sign under which it is found. And this very description will teach us by the same shortcut why some planets traverse the same zodiac and the same signs in a longer time, and others in a shorter time. For as often as many orbits are placed within each other, just as the largest is that which is first, and the smallest is that which holds the last place, so it is with the middle ones: the one closer to the top is larger than those below, and the one closer to the last is shorter than those above. Therefore, among these seven spheres, the order of position has assigned to each its degree of speed. Thus, the stars that run through larger spaces complete their circuit in a more prolonged time, and those through narrow spaces in a shorter time. For it is established that none among them proceeds faster or slower than the others. But while the motion of traveling is the same for all, the diversity of the spaces alone creates such a diversity of time. For, to pass over the middle ones for now so that the same things are not often repeated: Saturn [completes] the same signs in thirty years...

## The Beginning of the Circle

<image-desc>A circular diagram representing the celestial spheres and the organization of the cosmos. The outermost ring contains the names of the twelve signs of the zodiac: ARIES, TAURUS, GEMINI, CANCER, LEO, VIRGO, LIBRA, SCORPIUS, SAGITTARIUS, CAPRICORN, AQUARIUS, PISCES. Within the zodiac are seven concentric rings for the planetary spheres: SATURN, JUPITER, MARS, THE SUN, VENUS, MERCURY, THE MOON. The center of the diagram is divided into four concentric layers representing the classical elements: FIRE, AIR, WATER, and EARTH at the absolute center.</image-desc>

The moon completes its circuit and passes through in twenty-eight days: the difference in time is solely due to the size <note>original: *quantitate*</note> of the circles, of which one is the largest and another the smallest. Therefore, each of the other planets either extends or contracts its travel time according to the nature of its space. At this point, a diligent investigator of these matters might find something to ask. Indeed, having inspected the signs of the zodiac, which the provided illustration demonstrates as a support for our confidence, one might ask: "Who found or created the twelve parts of the celestial circle? Especially since no starting point for each individual sign is visible to our eyes?" To this most necessary question, let history itself respond, recounting the deed by which this difficult division was sought out and achieved by the ancients.

For the ancestors of the Egyptians—who are established as the first of all people to dare to examine and measure the sky—enjoyed a perpetual clarity of weather. Always looking up at the sky with a free gaze, they discovered that among all the stars or constellations fixed in the heavens, only five stars <note>Macrobius refers to the five planets visible to the naked eye: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> wandered along with the sun and moon. Yet, these five did not run through every part of the sky at random and without a certain "Law of Error" <note>original: *erroris sui Lege*. The ancients used "error" to mean "wandering," as the planets' paths seem to deviate from the fixed stars.</note> to their movements. Finally, they noticed that these stars never strayed toward the northern axis, nor did they ever sink to the lowest depths of the southern pole; instead, they held all their courses within the boundary of a single <term>oblique circle</term> <note>This "oblique circle" is the Ecliptic, the path the sun appears to follow across the sky, which is tilted relative to the earth's equator.</note>. They noted that these stars did not all go and return at the same pace, but some reached the same place at different times from others. Again, among these, some seemed to approach, some to move backward, and sometimes they appeared to stand still.

After, I say, they saw these things happening among them, they decided to establish certain parts for themselves in that very circle and to mark them with divisions. This was done so that there would be certain names for the places in which the stars lingered, or from which they had departed, or to which they were about to return, which they could announce to one another and transmit to posterity for study. Therefore, they prepared two bronze vessels, one of which had its bottom pierced in the manner of a <term>clepsydra</term> <note>An ancient water clock that measured time by the regulated flow of liquid.</note>. They placed the empty, intact vessel beneath the other, which was filled with water but held by a plug. They then observed one very bright and clearly notable star among the fixed stars as it was rising. As soon as it began to emerge, they quickly withdrew the plug and allowed the water from the upper vessel to flow into the one placed below. It flowed until the end of that night and the following day, and until that...

Following the previous page's introduction to the challenge of dividing the invisible circles of the sky, the author now details the mechanical experiment using water clocks to define the twelve signs of the zodiac and explains the mythological and astrological reasons for their order and planetary rulers.</meta>

-> ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO <-

...on the second night, until the same star returned again to its rising point. As soon as it began to appear, the water that was flowing in was immediately moved aside. Since the observation of the star's journey and return signified a complete rotation <note>original: *conversionem*</note> of the heavens, they established the measure of the sky for themselves based on the quantity of water collected from that flow. This volume was then divided into twelve equal parts using a reliable measurement, and two other vessels of this capacity were prepared so each could hold exactly one of the twelve parts. All the water was then poured back into the original large vessel, after first closing its opening. They placed one of those two smaller capacity vessels under the large one, while keeping the other nearby, ready and empty. 

With these preparations made, on another night, they observed the rising of a constellation <note>original: *sidus*</note>—later given the name Aries—in that part of the sky where they had learned through long observation that the sun, the moon, and the five "wandering stars" <note>The five planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> travel; this path they later called the Zodiac. At the very moment this constellation began to rise, they allowed the water to flow into the vessel placed beneath. Once it was full, they quickly removed it and emptied it, substituting the other similar vessel. They carefully and memorably noted the stars in that location which were rising at the moment the first vessel was filled, understanding that in the time it took for one-twelfth of the total water to flow, one-twelfth of the heavens had ascended. 

From that point where the water began to flow into the first vessel at the start of the rising, to the point that was rising when that same first vessel was full, they declared to be one-twelfth of the sky—that is, one "sign." Likewise, when the second vessel was filled and retracted, they substituted the other one (which had been emptied and prepared) and similarly noted the place that was emerging. From the end of the first sign to the point rising at the end of the second flow of water, the second sign was marked. Thus, by alternating the vessels and marking the boundaries of the rising parts of the sky for each portion of flowing water, they proceeded. When all the water had been consumed through its twelve parts, they had returned to the beginning of the first sign. Doubtless, they then possessed the parts of the sky divided and marked for themselves by certain observations and judgments, achieved through such a clever device. 

This was not accomplished in a single night, but over two; for the entire sky does not rotate in one night, but half rotates during the day and the remaining half during the night. However, the inspection of two consecutive nights did not divide the whole sky; rather, measurements taken at night during different seasons marked both hemispheres in equal turns. They preferred to call these twelve parts "signs" (*signa*), and specific names were added to each for the sake of identification. Because these signs are called *zodia* in the Greek tongue <note>meaning "living things" or "animal shapes"</note>, they called the circle itself the "Zodiac," as if it were the "bearer of signs."

<margin>The origin of the Zodiac</margin> These same men have passed down the reason why they preferred Aries <note>The Ram</note> to be called the first sign, even though in a sphere there is no "first" or "last" point. They say that on the beginning of that day which first shone—that is, when the heavens and the purified elements first broke into this splendor, which is rightly called the "Birthday of the World"—Aries was in the middle of the sky. Because the "mid-heaven" <note>term: *medium caelum* or Midheaven; the highest point in the sky relative to the observer.</note> is like the vertex of the world, Aries was therefore considered the first among all, because it appeared as the head of the world at the first dawn of light. 

They also add the reason why these twelve signs were assigned to the powers of different deities. For they say that in this very "birth-chart" of the world, while Aries (as we have taught) held the mid-heaven, the hour of the world’s birth was carried by Cancer <note>The Crab</note>, which then held the Moon. After this, the Sun rose with Leo <note>The Lion</note>, Mercury with Virgo <note>The Virgin</note>, Venus with Libra <note>The Scales</note>, Mars was in Scorpio <note>The Scorpion</note>, Jupiter occupied Sagittarius <note>The Archer</note>, and Saturn moved in Capricorn <note>The Horned Goat</note>. Thus it came to pass that each of these is said to be the "lord" of the sign in which they are believed to have been when the world was born. Antiquity assigned only one sign each to the two "Luminaries" <note>The Sun and the Moon</note> in which they then resided: Cancer to the Moon and Leo to the Sun. But for the five other stars, ancient tradition added the remaining signs to those they already occupied, so that in the assignment, a second order began from the end of the first. For we said above that Saturn was in Capricorn, the last of all; therefore, the second addition made him the first who had been last. Thus, Aquarius <note>The Water-bearer</note>, which follows Capricorn, is given to Saturn; Pisces <note>The Fish</note> is assigned to Jupiter, who was before Saturn; Aries to Mars, who preceded Jupiter; Taurus <note>The Bull</note> to Venus, whom Mars followed; and Gemini <note>The Twins</note> to Mercury, whom Venus followed.

It also explains the "Thema Mundi," the mythical birth chart of the universe, which establishes the astrological relationship between planets and their ruling signs.</summary>
