# THE COMMENTARY OF MACROBIUS AURELIUS THEODOSIUS, A MAN OF CONSULAR
# and illustrious rank, on the most elegant Dream of Scipio.

## BOOK TWO.

<image-desc>Two woodcut illustrations placed side-by-side. The left illustration depicts a scholarly scene in a workshop: one figure sits at a desk with an open book and compasses, while in the background, figures work at an anvil and with various tools, illustrating Pythagoras' discovery of musical intervals in a blacksmith's shop. The right illustration is a decorative square containing a large, ornate initial "S" intertwined with foliage and featuring a small child or putto figure.</image-desc>

In the previous commentary, Eustathius—my son, dearer and more beloved to me than light—our discourse had proceeded to the course of the starry sphere and the seven placed beneath it. Now let us discuss their music and their harmony <note>original: *modulatiōe*</note>. "What is this," he <note>Scipio the Younger, the narrator of the Dream</note> said, "what is this so great and so sweet sound that fills my ears?"

"This is," he <note>Scipio Africanus the Elder, appearing in the dream</note> replied, "the sound which, though separated by unequal intervals, is yet divided according to a fixed proportion and reason. It is produced by the impulse and motion of the spheres themselves; by tempering high notes with low ones, it creates various harmonies evenly. For such great movements cannot be driven in silence, and nature brings it about that the extremes on one side sound low, while on the other side they sound high. For this reason, the highest course of the starry sky itself—whose rotation is swifter—moves with a sharp, high-pitched sound; while this lowest lunar course moves with the deepest, lowest sound. For the earth, the ninth body, remaining immobile, always clings to the lowest seat, embracing the middle place of the world. Those eight courses <note>The sphere of fixed stars plus the seven planetary spheres.</note>, in which the power of the seven gods is the same, produce sounds with distinct intervals; this number [seven] is almost the knot <note>A "knot" or *nodus* in this context refers to a binding mathematical or cosmic principle that holds reality together.</note> of all things. Learned men, by imitating this with strings and songs, have opened for themselves a return to this celestial place."

Having explained the order of the spheres and described their motion—whereby the seven lower spheres are carried in a direction contrary to the rest of the heaven—it follows that we must here investigate what kind of sound the impact of such great masses produces. For sound must necessarily be born from the very rotation of the spheres. This is because the air, struck by the intervention of the blow itself, emits the force of a crashing sound; nature herself dictates that the violent collision of two bodies must result in sound.

But this sound, which is born from any strike of the air, either brings something sweet and musical to the ears, or it sounds foolish or harsh. For if the strike is moderated by a certain observation of numbers, a composed and self-consistent melody <note>original: *modulamen*</note> is produced. But when a tumultuous collision, governed by no rhythmic measures, rings out, a confused and disordered noise offends the hearing. In heaven, however, it is established that nothing accidental and nothing tumultuous occurs; rather, all things there proceed according to divine laws and fixed reason.

From these points, it has been gathered by unassailable reasoning that musical sounds proceed from the rotation of the celestial spheres, because it is necessary for both sound and motion to occur, and the reason inherent in divine things becomes the cause of the melody within the sound. Pythagoras was the first of all the Greek people to conceive of this in his mind. He understood that something composed, something musical, sounded from the spheres on account of the necessity of reason, which never departs from celestial things. 

But what that reason was, or by what measures <note>original: *modis*</note> it was to be observed, he did not easily grasp. While a long investigation of such a great and secret <note>original: *archanæ*</note> matter fatigued him in vain, chance offered what deep thought did not find. For when by chance he passed by a public place where blacksmiths were softening glowing iron with blows, the sounds of the hammers, responding to each other in a fixed order, suddenly fell upon his ears. In these sounds, the low and high pitches harmonized in such a way that both returned to the listener's sense with a fixed dimension; from various impacts, a single consonant sound was born. 

Thinking that here an opportunity was offered to him to grasp with his eyes and hands what he had long sought in thought, he approached the blacksmiths. Leaning over the work, he gazed quite curiously, noting the sounds produced by the arms of each individual. Since he thought the sounds were to be attributed to the strength of those striking, he ordered that they should exchange hammers with one another. When these were changed, the diversity of sounds left the men and followed the hammers. Then he turned all his care to examining their weights.

<summary>Macrobius begins Book Two by explaining the "Music of the Spheres," arguing that the motion of celestial bodies must produce harmony based on mathematical ratios. He recounts the famous legend of Pythagoras discovering these musical intervals by listening to the varying pitches of hammers in a blacksmith's shop.</summary>

It transitions from the physical observation of planetary motion to the mathematical laws of acoustics.</meta>

<header>ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO</header>

When he <note>Pythagoras</note> had noted for himself the difference in weight held in each hammer, he ordered other hammers to be made, exceeding the weight of the others by more or less. By their strikes, sounds were heard that were in no way similar to the previous ones, nor were they as consonant with each other. Then he realized that the harmony of the voice comes forth by the law of weights. Having collected the numbers in which the harmonious diversity of weights was contained, he turned his investigation from hammers to strings <note>original: *fides*</note>; he stretched sheep intestines or ox sinews with various weights tied to them, just as he had learned existed in the hammers. From these, such a concord resulted as the previous observation, not noticed in vain, had promised—with an added sweetness which the resonant nature of strings provided. Here, Pythagoras, having mastered such a great secret, discovered the numbers from which sounds consonant with one another are born. Thus, when strings were arranged according to this observation of numbers, certain strings were tuned to others in a harmony of corresponding numbers; so much so, that when one was struck with a plectrum <note>a small tool used to pluck a stringed instrument</note>, another, though placed far away but corresponding in numbers, sounded at the same time. From all the nearly infinite variety of numbers, however, only a few—and those incalculable—were found that would unite to produce music.

<margin>The Four-to-Three Ratio</margin>
Moreover, these ratios are six in all: the *epitritus* <note>the sesquitertian ratio, or 4:3</note>, the *hemiolius* <note>the sesquialter ratio, or 3:2</note>, the *duplaris* <note>the double ratio, or 2:1</note>, the *triplaris* <note>the triple ratio, or 3:1</note>, the *quadruplus* <note>the quadruple ratio, or 4:1</note>, and the *epogdous* <note>the sesquioctave ratio, or 9:8</note>. The **epitritus** is when, of two numbers, the larger contains the whole of the smaller plus a third part of it, such as four to three; for in four there is three, and the third part of three, which is one.
<margin>The Fourth</margin>
This number is called the *epitritus*, and from it is born the symphony which is called **The Fourth** <note>original Greek: *Δια Τεσσαρῶν* (Diatessaron)</note>.
<margin>The Three-to-Two Ratio</margin>
The **hemiolius** is when, of two numbers, the larger contains the whole of the smaller plus its half; such as three to two, for in three there are two, and half of them, which is one. And from
<margin>The Fifth</margin>
this number, which is called *hemiolius*, is born the symphony called **The Fifth** <note>original Greek: *Διαπέντε* (Diapente)</note>. The **double**
<margin>The Double Ratio</margin>
ratio is when, of two numbers, the smaller is counted twice in the larger, such as four
<margin>The Octave</margin>
to two; and from this double ratio is born the symphony whose name is **The Octave** <note>original Greek: *Διαπασῶν* (Diapason)</note>.
<margin>The Triple Ratio</margin>
The **triple** ratio is when, of two numbers, the smaller is counted three times in the larger, such as three to one; and from this number proceeds the symphony called **The Octave and a Fifth** <note>original Greek: *Διαπασῶν καí Διαπέντε*</note>.
<margin>
The Quadruple Ratio
The Fourfold
</margin>
The **quadruple** is when, of two numbers, the smaller is counted four times in the larger, such as four to one; which in numbers creates the symphony they call **The Double Octave** <note>original Greek: *Δισδιαπασῶν* (Disdiapason)</note>.
<margin>The Nine-to-Eight Ratio</margin>
The **epogdous** is the number which contains within itself the smaller plus an eighth part of it, such as nine to eight; because in nine there is eight, plus the eighth part of it, which is one. This number produces the sound which musicians have called a **tone**. The ancients indeed wished to call a sound smaller than a tone a **semitone**, but it must not be understood as if it were thought to be a "half-sound," just as we do not take a "semi-vowel" in letters to mean half of a vowel. Furthermore, a tone, by its own nature, cannot be divided into two equal parts. For since it consists of the number nine, and nine can never be divided equally, the tone refuses to be divided into two equal halves. But they called a "semitone" that which is less than a tone. It was discovered to be as small a distance from a tone as these two numbers are from each other: namely, two hundred forty-three and two hundred fifty-six. The ancient Pythagoreans called this semitone a **diesis** <note>original: *dihesin*</note>, but subsequent usage established that a sound smaller than a semitone should be called a *diesis*.
<margin>The Five Symphonies</margin>
Plato called the semitone a **limma**. There are, therefore, five symphonies: **The Fourth**, **The Fifth**, **The Octave**, **The Octave and a Fifth**, and **The Double Octave**.
But this number of symphonies belongs to the music which either the human breath can produce or the human ear can capture. Beyond this, however, the range of celestial harmony extends itself further—namely, up to four times **The Octave and a Fifth**. Let us set aside for now these celestial harmonies and speak of those we have named. The symphony of the **Fourth** consists of two tones and a semitone; so that
<margin>
The Octave

The Double

</margin>
we may leave aside the small fractions which are added, lest we create difficulty. It arises from the *epitritus* <note>4:3</note>. The **Fifth** consists of three tones and a semitone, and it arises from the *hemiolius* <note>3:2</note>. The **Octave** consists of six tones and arises from the double ratio. But **The Octave and a Fifth** consists of nine tones...

...had been: they were assigned.

<margin>The order of the Planets</margin>
It should be noted at this point that in the birth of the world, either by the foresight of nature or by the genius of the ancients, that order was given to the stars which Plato assigned to their spheres: so that the moon would be first; the sun second; above this, Mercury; Venus fourth; then Mars, followed by Jupiter; and Saturn last. Yet, even without the support of this reasoning, the previously mentioned logic commends the Platonic order as superior. From those questions which we proposed to investigate concerning the recently cited words of Cicero—as briefly as was permitted—from the highest sphere, which is called the *aplanes* <note>original: *aplanes*; the Greek term for the "fixed" or "unwandering" sphere of the stars</note>, down to the moon, which is the last of the divine things: we have now (I believe) completed them all. For we have shown that the heavens revolve, and why they revolve so; and an indubitable reason has revealed that the seven spheres are carried in a contrary motion. Furthermore, regarding the order of the spheres themselves, this treatise has found what different people have felt, what caused the disagreement among them, and which opinion is more to be followed. Nor was this left unmentioned: why, among all the stars, the moon alone does not shine without the rays of her brother <note>The Sun</note>. But it has also been made public that the logic of distances compelled the sun to be called "nearly the middle," though not precisely the middle, even by those who placed it fourth among the seven. The meaning of the names by which they are called—such that they are thought only to be praised—has become known. Likewise, the Sun's magnitude, and also the size of the celestial circle through which it runs, along with the size of the earth—how it was grasped and demonstrated—has been shown. We have also resolved how the stars of the lower spheres are said to be carried through the Zodiac (which is above them all), and what reason creates the different cycles, whether fast or slow. Moreover, we have explained why the Zodiac itself is divided into twelve parts, why Aries is considered first, and which signs are under the dominion of each of the gods. But all these things which reach from the summit down to the moon are sacred, incorruptible, and divine: because within them is the *aether* <note>the "fifth element," believed to be the substance of the heavens, distinct from the four earthly elements</note>, which is always the same, never receiving the uneven tide of variation. Below the moon, both air and the nature of change begin together. And just as there is a boundary between aether and air, so the moon is the boundary between the divine and the perishable. However, when it is said that nothing below the moon is divine except for the souls given to the human race as a gift from the gods, it must not be understood to mean that souls are *here* in the sense that they are thought to be born here. Rather, just as we are accustomed to saying the sun is on the earth when its rays come and go, so too the origin of souls is celestial; they are merely exiled here by the law of temporary hospitality.

<margin>The Ray</margin>
Therefore, this region possesses nothing divine of itself, but it receives it; and because it receives it, it also sends it back. It would be said to possess it as its own if it were permitted to hold it forever. But it is established that the souls of the mixed [beings] do not consist of this region alone, since this region would not suffice for the fabrication of the body. For although earth, water, and air are below the moon, a body capable of life could not be made from these alone; there was a need for the protection of aethereal fire to provide the vigor for sustaining life and soul in earthly members—to both create and carry the vital heat.

<margin>The Magnitude of the Sun</margin>
Let it be enough for us to have said these things regarding the air. It remains for us to discuss the necessary facts about the earth, which is the ninth of the spheres and the last of the world. For he <note>Cicero</note> says that the earth, being middle and ninth, does not move and is the lowest; into it, all weights are carried by their own motion. These are truly inseparable causes which are bound together by mutual links; while one creates the other, they are born from each other in turn, and are never separated from the embraces of natural society. Such are the little bonds by which nature has constrained the earth: for all things are carried into it because, as the middle, it does not move. It does not move because it is the lowest. Nor could it fail to be the lowest point into which all things are carried. Let this treatise explain each of these points which the necessity of things has bound together in an inseparable tangle. "It does not move," he says: for it is the *centron* <note>original: *centron*; the center point</note>. In a sphere, we have said that only the center does not move, because it is necessary that a sphere move around something immobile. He added, "it is the lowest." This too is correct, for that which is the center is the middle. In a sphere, it is established that only the middle is the "bottom." And if it is the bottom, it follows that it was truly said that all things are carried into it. For nature always leads weights to the bottom. Indeed, in the world itself, the earth was made so that whatever was the purest and most clear from all the matter out of which all things were made, that held the summit and was called Aether.

<margin>Aether</margin>
The part which had less purity, and in which there was some light weight, became Air, and fell into the second place.

<margin>Air</margin>
After these, that which was still liquid but already thick enough to be felt by the touch, was congealed into the flow of Water. Finally, whatever was vast, impenetrable, and dense from all the wild tumult—scraped away from the purified elements—settled at the bottom. It remained at the lowest point, submerged by perpetual, constricting cold; the distance of the sun caused this refined material to accumulate in the furthest part of the world. Therefore, that which was thus solidified received the name of Earth. A thick air, closer to the earthly cold than to the sun...

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous discussion on the order of the planetary spheres and the nature of the moon, the author now transitions into the mathematical foundations of the "Music of the Spheres." This page recounts the legend of how Pythagoras discovered the numerical ratios that govern musical harmony, moving from physical experiments with hammers to the abstract laws of resonance.</meta>

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

And when he had noted for himself the difference in weight found in each hammer, he ordered other hammers to be made, exceeding the weight of the others by more or less. By the striking of these, the sounds heard were in no way similar to the previous ones, nor were they as harmonious with one another. Then he realized that the concord of the voice arises from the law of weights. Having collected the numbers in which this harmonious diversity of weights was contained, he shifted his investigation from hammers to strings. He stretched the intestines of sheep or the sinews of oxen by binding them with the same varied weights he had learned were in the hammers. Such a harmony resulted from these as the previous observation, noted not in vain, had promised—with the added sweetness which the sonorous nature of strings provides. Here, Pythagoras, having mastered such a great secret, discovered the numbers from which harmonious sounds are born. He did this to such an extent that strings arranged according to this observation of numbers were tuned to the concord of specific, corresponding numerical ratios. Thus, when one string was struck with a plectrum <note>A small tool used to pluck strings, like a modern guitar pick</note>, another string, though placed far away but matching in its numbers, would sound at the same time. Out of all the infinite variety of numbers, only a few—and they are countable—were found to be suitable for producing music.

<margin>Epitritus (4:3)</margin>
There are six of these in all: the *epitritus* <note>original: *epitritus*; the sesquitertial ratio of 4:3</note>, the *hemiolius* <note>original: *hemiolius*; the sesquialter ratio of 3:2</note>, the double, the triple, the quadruple, and the *epogdous* <note>original: *epogdous*; the sesquioctave ratio of 9:8</note>. An *epitritus* is when, of two numbers, the larger contains the whole of the smaller plus one-third part of it—as four is to three. For in four there is three, and the third part of three (which is one). This number is called the *epitritus*, and from it is born the symphony called the **Fourth** <note>original: $\Delta\iota\alpha\ T\epsilon\sigma\sigma\alpha\rho\hat{\omega}\nu$ (*Diatessaron*), meaning "through the four"</note>.

<margin>Fourth</margin>
<margin>Hemiolius (3:2)</margin>
The *hemiolius* is when, of two numbers, the larger contains the whole of the smaller plus one-half of it—as three is to two. For in three there is two and its half (which is one). From this number, which is called the *hemiolius*, is born the symphony called the **Fifth** <note>original: $\Delta\iota\alpha\pi\epsilon\nu\tau\epsilon$ (*Diapente*), meaning "through the five"</note>.

<margin>Fifth</margin>
<margin>Double</margin>
The double number is when, of two numbers, the smaller is counted twice in the larger—as four is to two. From this double number is born the symphony whose name is the **Octave** <note>original: $\Delta\iota\alpha\pi\alpha\sigma\hat{\omega}\nu$ (*Diapason*), meaning "through all"</note>.

<margin>Octave</margin>
<margin>Triple</margin>
The triple, however, is when, of two numbers, the smaller is counted three times in the larger—as three is to one. From this number proceeds the symphony which is called the **Octave and a Fifth** <note>original: $\Delta\iota\alpha\pi\alpha\sigma\hat{\omega}\nu\ \kappa\alpha\acute{\iota}\ \Delta\iota\acute{\alpha}\pi\epsilon\nu\tau\epsilon$ (*Diapason kai Diapente*)</note>.

<margin>Quadruple</margin>
<margin>Quadruple</margin>
The quadruple is when, of two numbers, the smaller is counted four times in the larger—as four is to one. In numbers, this creates the symphony which they call the **Double Octave** <note>original: $\Delta\acute{\iota}\varsigma\Delta\iota\alpha\pi\alpha\sigma\hat{\omega}\nu$ (*Disdiapason*)</note>.

<margin>Epogdous (9:8)</margin>
The *epogdous* is the number which contains within itself the smaller plus its eighth part—as nine is to eight. For in nine there is eight, and additionally the eighth part of it (which is one). This number brings forth the sound which musicians have called the **Tone**. The ancients wished to call a sound smaller than a tone a "semitone," but this should not be understood as if it were a perfect half-sound. Just as we do not take a "semi-vowel" in letters to be exactly half a vowel, a Tone, by its very nature, cannot be divided into two equal parts. Since it consists of the number nine, and nine can never be divided equally <note>Because 9 is an odd number, the Pythagoreans argued it could not be split into two equal integers</note>, the Tone refuses to be divided into two halves. Instead, they called a sound smaller than a tone a "semitone." It was discovered that this semitone differs from a tone by as much as these two numbers differ between themselves: that is, 243 and 256. The ancient Pythagoreans called this semitone a *dihesis* <note>original: $\delta\acute{\iota}\epsilon\sigma\iota\varsigma$</note>, but later usage established that a sound even smaller than a semitone should be called a *dihesis*. Plato called the semitone a *limma* <note>original: $\lambda\epsilon\hat{\iota}\mu\mu\alpha$, meaning "remnant"</note>.

<margin>The Five Symphonies</margin>
There are, therefore, five symphonies: the **Fourth**, the **Fifth**, the **Octave**, the **Octave and a Fifth**, and the **Double Octave**. But this number of symphonies pertains to the music that either the human breath can produce or the human ear can perceive. However, the reach of celestial harmony extends further—even up to four times the **Octave and a Fifth**.

<margin>Octave and Fifth</margin>
For the moment, let us set aside these celestial harmonies and discuss the ones we have named. The symphony of the **Fourth** consists of two tones and a semitone—leaving out the tiny fractions involved in the addition so as not to create difficulty—and it arises from the *epitritus* ratio.

<margin>Double Octave</margin>
The **Fifth** consists of three tones and a semitone, and it arises from the *hemiolius*. The **Octave** consists of six tones and arises from the double ratio. But the **Octave and a Fifth** consists of nine tones...

# BOOK ONE

<margin>The order of the Planets</margin>
...had been: they were assigned. We should note at this point that in the birth of the world, either through the providence of things or the genius of antiquity, this order was given to the stars, which Plato assigned to their spheres: so that the Moon was first; the Sun second; above this Mercury; Venus fourth; then Mars; then Jupiter; and Saturn last. Yet, even without the support of this reasoning, the previous argument abundantly commends the Platonic order. From those questions we proposed to investigate concerning the recently cited words of Cicero—moving with allowed brevity from the highest sphere, which is called the *aplanes* <note>original: *aplanes*; the "fixed" or non-wandering sphere of the stars that forms the outermost boundary of the universe</note>, down to the moon, which is the last of the divine things—we have now (I believe) completed everything. For we have shown that the heaven rotates, and why it rotates so; and certain reasoning has revealed that the seven spheres are carried in a contrary motion. Regarding the order of the spheres themselves, what various thinkers have felt, or what caused the dissension among them, and which opinion is more to be followed, our treatise has investigated. Nor has this been left unsaid: why among all the stars, the Moon alone does not shine without the rays of her brother <note>The Sun</note>. But it has also been made public why a spacious reasoning forced the Sun to be called "nearly the middle," though it is placed in the fourth spot among the seven. What the names signify by which it is called—so that it is thought only to be praised—has become known. Its magnitude as well, and the size of the celestial circle through which it runs alongside the Earth, or how it is demonstrated from the sphere; and how the stars of the subordinate spheres are said to be carried by the Zodiac, which is above them all; or what reason causes the diverse returns, whether swift or slow. Also, the Zodiac itself, into which twelve parts it is divided, and why Aries is considered first, and which signs are under the power of which deities, has been explained. 

But all these things that reach from the summit down to the Moon are sacred, incorruptible, and divine; because in them is the *ether* <note>A fifth element, believed by ancients to be weightless, eternal, and the substance of the heavens</note>, which is always the same spirit, never receiving the unequal heat of variation. Below the Moon, both air and the nature of change begin together. And just as with ether and air, so the Moon is the boundary between the divine and the perishable. However, when it is said that nothing below the Moon is divine except for the souls given to the human race as a gift from the gods, it must not be understood that souls are "here" in the sense that they are thought to be born here. Rather, just as we are accustomed to say the Sun is "on the earth" when its rays arrive and recede, so the origin of souls is celestial. By the law of "temporal hospitality" <note>The philosophical idea that the soul is a temporary guest in the physical body, like a traveler in an inn</note>, the soul is an exile here. Therefore, this region possesses nothing divine of itself, but it receives it; and because it receives it, it also sends it back. It would be said to possess it as its own only if it were permitted to hold it forever. 

But it is not established that the soul is mixed from the material of this lower region, since that region would not suffice even for the fabrication of the body alone. For since Earth, Water, and Air are below the Moon, a body could not be made from these alone that would be fit for life. There was a need for the protection of ethereal fire, which would provide the strength for sustaining life and the soul within earthly limbs, and which would both create and carry the vital heat. Let it be enough for us to have said these things about the air. It remains for us to discuss the necessary things concerning the Earth, which is the ninth of the spheres and the last of the world. For he says: "The Earth, which is central and ninth, does not move and is the lowest; into it all weights are carried by their own motion." 

Those causes are truly insoluble which are bound together by mutual links; and while one creates the other, they are born from each other in turn, never separated from the embraces of natural society. Such are the "little cords" by which nature has constricted the Earth. For everything is carried into it because, as the center, it does not move. It does not move because it is the lowest. And it could not fail to be the lowest since everything is carried into it. Let our treatise explain each of these things which the necessity of nature has woven together inseparably. "It does not move," he says, for it is the *centron* <note>original: *centron*; the mathematical center or hub of a rotating body</note>. In a sphere, we have said that only the center does not move, because it is necessary that a sphere move around something immobile. He added, "it is the lowest." This too is correct: for that which is the center is the middle. In a sphere, it is established that only the middle is the "bottom." And if it is the bottom, it follows that it was truly said that "all things are carried into it." For nature always leads weights toward the bottom. 

For even in the world itself, the Earth was made in this way: whatever was most pure and liquid from all the matter out of which all things were made, that held the summit and was called **Aether**. 
<margin>Aether</margin>
<margin>Air</margin>
The part which had less purity, and in which there was something of light weight, emerged as **Air**, and fell into the second place. After these, that which was still liquid but now bulky enough to resist the touch, was coagulated into the flow of **Water**. Finally, that which remained from the entire "wild tumult"—the vast, impenetrable, dense dregs scraped from the purified elements—settled at the bottom. It remained stuck at the lowest point, submerged by a perpetual, binding frost, which the distance of the sun heaped up at the ultimate part of the world. That which was thus hardened took the name of **Earth**. Thick air, closer to the earthly cold than to the heat of the sun, was assigned to this place.

<meta>Continuity: Following the discussion of the celestial spheres and the placement of the Sun and Moon, the author now focuses on the Earth itself, specifically its position at the absolute center of the universe and the physical laws—such as gravity and atmospheric pressure—that keep it stationary and cause objects to fall toward it from every direction.</meta>

### ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

By the dense pressure of a thick breath <note>original: *spiraminis*; referring to the atmospheric pressure or "pneuma" thought to surround the Earth</note>, it [the Earth] is supported and held together from all sides. It does not allow the Earth to move back or forth, partly because of the force of the air that surrounds it and balances it with equal vigor from every direction, and partly because of the very nature of the sphere’s edge. If the Earth were to deviate even slightly from the middle, it would become closer to one peak of the heavens and leave the bottom behind. It remains in the center for this reason: because that part alone is at an equal distance from any point on the sphere’s surface. Therefore, into this center—which is the lowest point and does not move because it is the core—it is necessary that all weights are carried, just as the Earth itself has settled into this place like a weight. This is proven by countless examples, but especially by the rains, which fall toward the Earth from every part of the air. For they do not fall only onto this surface where we live, but also onto the sides—which create the spherical roundness of the Earth—and onto the other side, which is "below" relative to us; the rain falls there as well. For if the air, thickened by the exhalation of the Earth’s cold, is forced into a cloud and thus breaks into rain—and since the air surrounds the entire Earth—then without a doubt, rain-water flows out from every part of the air (except for the zone scorched by perpetual heat <note>The "Torrid Zone" near the equator, which ancient geographers believed was too hot for rain or life</note>), and it flows down from everywhere onto the Earth, which is the only seat for weights. If anyone rejects this, they must consequently believe that outside of this one surface we inhabit, whatever snow, rain, or hail falls must fall "up" from the air into the sky. For the sky is equally distant from every part of the Earth; it is looked up to from the sides and from the part "below" us with the same immense height as it is from our own dwelling. Unless all weights were carried toward the Earth, the rains that fall outside the sides of the Earth would not fall onto the ground but into the heavens—a notion that exceeds the absurdity of a scurrilous joke.

Let the Earth, then, be a sphere marked with the points **a, b, c, d**. Around it, let there be the circle of air marked with **e, f, g, l, m**. Let a line drawn from **e** to **l** divide both circles (that is, of the Earth and the air). The part we inhabit will be the upper part, and that other part will be beneath our feet. Unless every weight fell toward the Earth, the Earth would receive rain only on a very small part—from **a** to **c**. However, the area of air from **f** to **e** and from **g** to **l** would cast its moisture away into the air and the sky. From the lower hemisphere of the sky, the rain would flow outward, and therefore into a place unknown to nature, as the following diagram shows. But a sober discourse disdains even to refute this; it is so absurd that it collapses without needing a formal argument. It remains, therefore, demonstrated by indubitable reason that all weights are carried by their own motion toward the Earth. These things that have been said here also help us in the discussion of that place which mentions that there are **antipodes** <note>original: *antipodas*; people living on the opposite side of the globe, literally "those with feet opposite"</note>. But here, having brought this continuous treatment to a halt, let us reserve the discussion of the following matters for the second volume of this commentary.

<page-num>XXIII</page-num>
## BOOK TWO

...and a semitone <note>original: *hemitono*; a half-step in a musical scale</note>: and let it be of the triple number <note>The ratio 3:1</note>. The double octave <note>original: *Dis diapason*</note> contains twelve tones and is formed from the quadruple ratio <note>The ratio 4:1</note>. From this, Plato—after he recognized through the succession of Pythagorean doctrine and the divine depth of his own genius—realized that no joining harmony could exist without these numbers. In his *Timaeus*, he established that the World Soul <note>original: *mundi animam*</note> was fashioned through the mixture of these numbers by the ineffable providence of God the Creator. If the meaning of this is applied to this work, it will greatly help our understanding of Cicero’s words, which seem obscure regarding the discipline of music. But lest that which is used to support another explanation be thought difficult in itself, a few things must first be set forth by us, which will simultaneously make the understanding of both clearer. Every solid body extends in three dimensions: for it has length, width, and depth. A fourth dimension cannot be found in any body whatsoever; rather, every solid body is contained by these three. Geometers, however, propose other bodies to themselves, which they call "mathematical," which are to be submitted to thought alone, not to the senses.

<margin>The mathematical body: the point</margin>
For they say a point is an indivisible body, in which neither length, nor width, nor height is detected, since it cannot be divided into any parts. This point, when drawn out, creates a line—that is, a body of one dimension. For it is long without being wide or deep, and is contained by two points at either end that terminate the length alone. If you double this line by adding another, you create a mathematical body that is built from two dimensions, length and width, but lacks height. And this

<margin>Surface</margin>
is what is called a surface <note>original: *superficies*</note> among them; it is contained by four points—that is, two for each line. If indeed these two lines are doubled, so that two are placed beneath two, depth is added: and from this a solid body is created, which without doubt will be contained by eight corners. We see this in a die <note>original: *tessera*; a six-sided gaming cube</note>, which is called a **cube** in the Greek language.

<margin>Monad, Die, Cube</margin>
The nature of numbers is applied to these geometric principles: and the monad <note>original: *monas*; the number one, representing unity</note> is considered a point. For just as a point is not a body but makes bodies out of itself, so the monad is not called a number but the origin of numbers. For the first number is in "two," which is similar to a line produced from a point under the double termination of a point. This number two, when doubled from itself, creates four, in the likeness of a mathematical body [a surface] which extends under four points in length and width. The number four itself, when doubled, creates eight, which number imitates a solid body. Just as we said two lines placed over two lines—with the dimension of eight corners—create the complete solidity of a body, so it is said among geometers that "twice two, twice" <note>2 x 2 x 2 = 8</note> is now a solid body. Therefore, from an even number, the progression up to eight is the solidity of a body; thus, among the principles, he assigned fullness to this number. 

Now it is necessary to examine how this is achieved from an odd number as well. And because the monad is the origin of both even and odd numbers, let the number three be believed to be the first line. This number tripled makes nine, which itself creates a body of length and width, as if from two lines. Likewise, nine tripled provides the third dimension. And so, on the side of the odd number, at twenty-seven—which is three times three, three times <note>3 x 3 x 3 = 27</note>—a solid body is created, just as in the even number "twice two, twice" (which is eight) created solidity. Therefore, to create a solid body on both sides, the monad is necessary, along with six other numbers: three from the even and three from the odd. From the even: two, four, eight; from the odd: three, nine, twenty-seven. Timaeus, therefore, in Plato’s work, announcing the counsel of the Divinity in fabricating the World Soul, says that it was woven through these numbers, which from both even and odd create a cube <note>meaning a "solid" or perfect number</note>—that is, the perfection of the Divinity. This was not because it signified that the Soul had anything corporeal, but so that it might be able to penetrate the universe by animating it; the World Soul was made through the numbers of solidity to fill the solid body of the world. 

Now let us come to the words of Plato himself. For when he spoke of God fabricating the Soul of the world, he said: "He took the first part from the whole fabric. Then he took a double part of the first; then a third, one-and-a-half <note><term>hemiolia</term>: the ratio 3:2</note> of the second but triple the first; a fourth, double the second; a fifth, triple the third; a sixth, eight times the first; and a seventh, twenty-seven times multiplied from the first." After this, he filled the intervals that gaped between the double and triple numbers by inserting parts, so that two means <note>mathematical averages</note> would bridge each interval; from these bonds were born the sesquialtera <note><term>hemiolii</term>: 3:2 ratio</note>, the sesquitertia <note><term>epitriti</term>: 4:3 ratio</note>, and the sesquioctave <note><term>epogdoi</term>: 9:8 ratio, the whole tone</note>.

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

->**IMAGE DESCRIPTION**<-
->A triangular diagram representing the "Platonic Lambda," a tool used to visualize the harmony of the universe. At the peak is the number **6** (VI). Descending the left side are the even numbers **2, 4, and 8** (II, IIII, VIII). Descending the right side are the odd numbers **3, 9, and 27** (III, VIIII, XXVII). Within the center of the triangle, a grid shows the mathematical averages (means) between these numbers, including **8, 9, 12, 18, 16, 27, 24, 36, 32, 54, 64, 108**, and **109** <note>These internal numbers represent the complex arithmetic and harmonic proportions used to calculate musical intervals like fourths, fifths, and octaves.</note><-

These words of Plato <note>Referring to the *Timaeus*</note> were previously understood by no one. They believed the first part to be the monad <note>original: *monadem*; the number one, representing unity</note>; the second part, as I have told you, they considered to be the "dual" number, which is the double of the first; the third is the "ternary" number <note>3</note>, which is a sesquialteral ratio <note>original: *hemiolius*; a 3:2 ratio</note> to two, and triple to one; the fourth is four, which is double the second (that is, double two); the fifth is the "nonary" number <note>9</note>, which is triple the third (that is, triple three); the sixth is the "octonary" <note>8</note>, which contains the first number eight times. But indeed, the seventh part results in twenty-seven, which creates, as we said, the third argument of an odd number <note>3 to the power of 3</note>.

One can observe that this "weaving" of the soul proceeded in a specific order: after the monad (which is both even and odd), the first even number was placed, which is **two**. Then followed the first odd number, which is **three**. In the fourth place came the second even number, **four**. In the fifth place, the second odd number, **nine**. In the sixth place, the next even number, **eight**. In the seventh place, the third odd number, **twenty-seven**.

<margin>Odd numbers are male; even are female.</margin>
This was done because the odd number is considered male and the even number female. From the union of even and odd—that is, from male and female—would be born that which was destined to give birth to the universe. This progression moves toward the "solidity" of each <note>creating 3D cubic numbers like 2³=8 and 3³=27</note>, as if it were to penetrate every solid thing. 

Then, the soul had to be composed of these numbers because they alone contain a "joinable" suitability; she was destined to provide a binding concord to the entire world. For **two to one** is a double ratio; we have already said that the harmony of the *octave* <note>original: *diapason*</note> is born from the double. **Three to two** creates the sesquialteral ratio; from this arises the *perfect fifth* <note>original: *diapente*</note>. **Four to three** is the sesquitertian ratio <note>original: *epitritus*</note>; from this is composed the *perfect fourth* <note>original: *diatessaron*</note>. Likewise, **four to one** is calculated in a quadruple ratio, from which the *double octave* <note>original: *disdiapason*</note> harmony is born. 

Therefore, the World Soul, which impels the body of the universe we see toward motion, must be woven from numbers that create a musical harmony within themselves. This allows the soul to produce musical sounds from the motion she provides by her own impulse, finding the origin of these sounds in the very fabric of her own composition.

Plato says (as we mentioned above) that the God who authored the soul, after weaving together the odd numbers, filled the "gaping" intervals with sesquialterals, sesquitertians, sesquioctaves <note>original: *epogdois*; the 9:8 ratio, or a whole tone</note>, and semitones <note>original: *limmate*</note>. 

Therefore, Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> most learnedly showed the depth of this Platonic teaching in his own words. "What is this," he asks, "what is this sound, so great and so sweet, that fills my ears?" 

"This," he says, "is the sound which, though separated by unequal intervals, is nonetheless distinguished by a fixed and proportional ratio, produced by the impulse and motion of the spheres themselves." 

You see how he mentions "intervals" and testifies that these are "unequal" among themselves, yet he does not deny they are "distinguished by a fixed ratio." This is because, according to Plato's *Timaeus*, the unequal intervals of the numbers are separated by fixed ratios—specifically the sesquialterals, sesquitertians, sesquioctaves, and semitones—in which all melodic principles are contained. 

It should be noted here that these words of Cicero would surely never be open to our understanding unless the logic of these ratios (by which the intervals are distinguished) had been explained first, and unless the Platonic numbers from which the World Soul is conceived were revealed. We must understand why the soul is woven from music-creating numbers. All these things show both the cause of the world’s motion (which only the impulse of the soul provides) and the necessity of musical harmony, which the soul infuses into the motion she creates because that harmony is part of her nature from her very origin.

Here Plato, in his *Republic*, when he treated the rotation of the celestial spheres, says that individual **Sirens** sit upon individual spheres, signifying that a song is offered to the deities by the motion of the spheres. For "Siren" <note>original: *syrem*</note> in the Greek understanding means "one who sings to God." Theologians also call the nine Muses the musical songs of the eight spheres...

# BOOK TWO

...and they wished there to be one greatest encompassing sphere, which consists of all the others. Hence Hesiod, in his *Theogony* <note>original: *theogonia*; Hesiod’s poem on the origins of the gods</note>, calls the eighth Muse "Urania" <note>original: *uraniā*; meaning 'the Heavenly One'</note>: because after the seven wandering spheres <note>The planets</note> which are situated below it, the eighth star-bearing sphere placed above them is called "Heaven" by its own name. And to show that there is a ninth and greatest sphere, which consists of the harmonious whole of all sounds, he added: "And Calliope is indeed the most excellent of them all" <note>original Greek: *καλλιόπη δὴ δὲ προφερεστάτη ἐστὶν ἁπασάων*</note>. By her name, he shows that he calls the ninth Muse the very sweetness of the voice.

<margin>Calliope</margin>
For "Calliope" is the Greek interpretation for "of the best voice"; and to indicate more clearly that she is the one composed of all the others, he assigned to her the name of the whole: namely, "the most excellent of all." For they call Apollo "Musagetes" <note>original: *μουσηγέτον*; Leader of the Muses</note> as if he were the leader and prince of the other orbs: as Cicero himself reports: "the leader, prince, and moderator of the other lights; the mind of the world, and its tempering force."

<margin>The Muses</margin>
Even country folk know that the Muses are the song of the world: for they called them *Camoenae* <note>The Roman name for the Muses</note> as if they were *canenae*, from *canere* <note>to sing</note>. Therefore, theologians, also confirming that the heavens sing, employed musical sounds in sacrifices: which among some were performed with the lyre and cithara, and among others with flutes or other musical instruments. In the hymns to the gods themselves, rhythmic meters were applied to the verses of the songs through "strophe" and "antistrophe": so that through the strophe, the forward motion of the star-bearing sphere might be celebrated, and through the antistrophe, the diverse backward movement of the wandering planets might be proclaimed. From these two movements, the first hymn in nature, to be sung to God, took its beginning.

<margin>The dead are escorted with songs</margin>
The institutions of many nations and regions have also decreed that the dead should be escorted to burial with song, based on this persuasion: that after leaving the body, souls are believed to return to the origin of musical sweetness—that is, to heaven. For this reason, every soul in this life is captivated by musical sounds: so that not only those of more refined character, but even all barbarous nations practice songs, by which they may either be animated to the fire of valor or relaxed into the softness of pleasure. This is because the soul brings into the body a memory of the music of which it was conscious in heaven; thus it is so occupied by the charms of song that there is no heart so fierce or harsh that it is not held by the affection of such delights.

<margin>The fables of Orpheus and Amphion</margin>
From this, I believe, the fables of Orpheus and Amphion took their start—one of whom was said to draw animals lacking reason with his songs, the other to draw even stones. This is likely because they were the first to draw nations that were either barbarous and without the cultivation of reason, or soft with no more emotion than a stone, toward a sense of pleasure through singing.

<margin>What song does</margin>
In short, every state of the soul is governed by songs: so that music is played for the advance to war, and likewise for the retreat; by song, men are both excited and, conversely, calmed toward valor. It grants and takes away sounds; it both instills and withdraws cares. It suggests anger, persuades toward mercy, and even heals the body of diseases. For this is why those offering remedies to the sick are said to "enchant" <note>original: *præcinere*; to sing before or over someone</note> them. Is it any wonder if music has such great dominion among men, when birds

<margin>The Nightingale</margin>
also, such as nightingales and swans and others of that kind, practice song as if by a certain discipline of art? Indeed, some creatures—whether birds, land beasts, or aquatic monsters—run into nets of their own accord when invited by song; and the shepherd's pipe commands rest for the flocks that have gone out to pasture. Nor is it a wonder: for we have said before that the causes of music, with which the World Soul is woven, are inherent within it. This World Soul itself provides life to all living things: "Here is the race of men and cattle, the strength of flying things, and the monsters the sea bears beneath its marble surface" <note>A quote from Virgil's *Aeneid* (6.728-729)</note>. Rightly, therefore, is everything that lives captivated by music: because the heavenly Soul, by which the universe is animated, took its origin from music. While this Soul impels the body of the world into its spherical motion, it produces a sound that is divided by unequal intervals, yet intervals distinct in their reasoning according to a fixed proportion, just as the Soul itself was woven from the beginning. But these intervals—which in an incorporeal Soul are thought to exist only by reason and not by sense—must be investigated to see if a balanced dimension is preserved even in the body of the world itself. And Archimedes indeed

<margin>Archimedes. Measurements from the earth to each planet</margin>
believed he had discovered the number of *stadia* <note>An ancient unit of distance, roughly 600 feet</note> by which the moon is distant from the earth's surface, Mercury from the moon, Venus from Mercury, the sun from Venus, Mars from the sun, Jupiter from Mars, and Saturn from Jupiter; he even thought he had measured by reason the entire space from the orb of Saturn to the star-bearing heaven itself. However, this measurement of Archimedes was rejected by the Platonists, as if double and triple intervals were not...

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

...observing this, they established it as a belief: that as great as the distance is from the earth to the moon, the distance from the earth to the sun is double that; as great as it is from the earth to the sun, the distance from the earth to Venus is triple; as great as it is from the earth to Venus, the distance from the earth to the star of Mercury is four times that; as great as it is from the earth to Mercury, the distance from the earth to Mars is nine times that; and as great as it is from the earth to Mars, the distance from the earth to Jupiter is eight times that; finally, as great as it is from the earth to Jupiter, the distance from the earth to the orb of Saturn is twenty-seven times that. <note>These specific numbers—2, 3, 4, 9, 8, 27—are drawn from Plato's *Timaeus* and represent the two geometric progressions (powers of 2 and 3) used to describe the "binding" of the World Soul.</note> Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who wrote extensively on Plato.</note> included this Platonic persuasion in his books, in which he shed no small amount of light upon the obscurities of the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue regarding the creation of the universe.</note>. He explains that they believed these intervals in the body of the world were created in the image of the Soul's own composition, and that they are filled with <term>sesquitertians</term> <note>original: *epitritis*; a 4:3 ratio, the musical fourth</note>, <term>sesquialterals</term> <note>original: *hemioliis*; a 3:2 ratio, the musical fifth</note>, <term>sesquioctaves</term> <note>original: *epogdois*; a 9:8 ratio, a whole tone</note>, and <term>semitones</term> <note>original: *hemitonis*; a half-step in the musical scale</note>, and are thus limited, and in this way, harmony is produced. The logic of this, woven into the substance of the Soul, is also inserted into the mundane body, which is moved by the Soul. Hence Cicero’s assertion is learned and perfect in every part: he says that the celestial sound is divided by unequal intervals, but intervals nonetheless distinguished by a fixed proportional logic.

<margin>
High and low sound
</margin>
Now the subject reminds us to reconsider the differences in sounds, between the "grave" <note>low-pitched</note> and "acute" <note>high-pitched</note>, and how they are produced. Nature dictates that the extremes at one end sound low, while those at the other sound high. For this reason, that highest, star-bearing circuit of heaven, whose revolution is more rapid, moves with a high-pitched, excited sound. However, this lunar and lowest circuit moves with the deepest, lowest sound. We have said that sound is never produced unless the air is struck. But whether a sound is brought forth as higher or lower is the result of the strike: if it falls with great force and speed, it provides a high sound; if it is slower and more sluggish, it provides a lower sound. A rod serves as evidence: when it strikes the air, if it deals the blow quickly, it makes the sound sharp; if more slowly, it strikes the ear with a lower tone. We see the same in strings: if they are stretched with a tighter pull, they sound high; if looser, they sound lower. Therefore, while the superior orbs are rolled with greater force according to their vast size, and while they strain with a "spirit" <note>original: *spiritu*; here referring to the cosmic breath or ether</note> that is stronger at its origin, they move with a high-pitched, excited sound because of that very speed of revolution, as he says. But this lunar and lowest orb sounds the lowest because it is already turned with a "spirit" that is fainting at its extremity. Indeed, because of the narrowness into which the penultimate orb is squeezed, it is turned with a more gentle force. We prove this no differently in flutes <note>original: *tibiis*; ancient pipe instruments</note>: a high sound is emitted from the holes near the mouth when blown, but a lower sound comes from those far away and near the end. Likewise, a higher sound comes through wider openings, and a lower one through narrow ones. The reason for both causes is the same: because the breath is stronger where it begins and weaker where it ends; and because it drives a greater force through a larger opening, whereas the opposite happens in narrow openings placed far away. Therefore, the highest orb—both as it opens into the immense and as it is driven by a "spirit" that is stronger the closer it is to its origin—emits a high pitch from itself. The voice of the last orb is already broken, both because of the shortness of its space and its great distance from the source. From this, it is also more clearly proven that as the "spirit" recedes downward from its origin, it becomes so much gentler in its impact, until around the Earth—which is the final part of the sphere—it is considered so thick and dense that it is the cause for the Earth always sticking in one seat. Nor is the Earth allowed to move in any direction, being besieged on all sides by the density of the surrounding spirit. That the middle place is the final point in a sphere has already been proven in the preceding pages.

<margin>
The nine spheres of the world-body
</margin>
Therefore, there are nine spheres of the entire mundane body. The first is that star-bearing one, which is called "Heaven" by its proper name and is called *Aplanes* <note>original Greek: *ἀπλανής*; meaning "unwandering" or "fixed"</note> among the Greeks, warding off and containing the others. This one is always rolled from the east toward the west. Below it are the seven which we call "wandering," which are carried from the west toward the east. The ninth is the Earth, without motion. There are eight, therefore, which move; but they make seven sounds which create a harmony from their revolving. This is because the orbs of Mercury and Venus, accompanying the Sun in an equal circuit, follow it almost like satellites; and therefore, by some students of astronomy, they are thought to share the same power. Whence he says: *But those eight circuits, in which the power of two is the same, produce seven sounds distinct by intervals*—which number is the knot <note>A "key" or "binding force"</note> of almost all things. That the number seven is the knot of all things will be fully discussed when...

# BOOK TWO

...regarding these numbers, we spoke earlier. To illuminate (as I believe) the obscurity of Cicero’s words, a succinct treatise by us on music—conducted with as much brevity as allowed—will suffice. For to search for the technical names of strings like <term>netes</term> <note>original: *netas*; the highest string/note in a Greek tetrachord</note> and <term>hypates</term> <note>original: *hypatas*; the lowest string/note</note>, or the subtle minutiae of tones and <term>limmas</term> <note>original: *limatum*; a "limma" is a small musical interval, roughly a semitone</note>, and to assert what stands for a letter, a syllable, or a whole noun in sound: this belongs to a show-off, not a teacher. Indeed, just because Cicero made mention of music in this place, we should not take the opportunity to wander through every possible treatise that could be written on music—which (in my opinion) I do not believe has any limit. Rather, those points should be pursued which can clarify the words you have undertaken to explain; for in a matter that is naturally obscure, he who pours out more than is necessary in his exposition adds darkness rather than removing density. Therefore, we shall make an end to this part of the treatise, adding one thing we think worthy of knowing: that although there are three types of musical melody—the <term>enharmonic</term>, the <term>diatonic</term>,

<margin>
Three types of melody
</margin>

and the <term>chromatic</term>—the first has fallen out of use because of its excessive difficulty. The third is of an infamous softness. Therefore, the middle one, the diatonic, is ascribed to the "Music of the World" in the doctrine of Plato. Nor shall we place this among the things to be passed over: why we do not perceive with clear hearing the music born from the perpetual rotation of the heavens. It is because the sound is greater than can be received by the narrowness of human ears. By a similar nature, the <term>Catadupa</term> <note>The famous waterfalls or cataracts of the Nile at Aswan; ancient writers claimed the roar was so loud the local people became deaf.</note> exclude the magnitude of the crash from the ears of the inhabitants.

<margin>
Why we do not perceive the harmony of the heaven
</margin>

What wonder is it if a sound exceeds our hearing which the impulse of the world's mass emits? It is not for nothing that he [Scipio] says: "Such a great and sweet sound fills my ears." But he wanted it to be understood that if the ears of him who deserved to be present at celestial secrets were filled by the magnitude of the sound, it remains that the senses of other men cannot grasp the hearing of the world's concord. But let us now turn the treatise to what follows. *You see that the earth is inhabited in rare and narrow places, and in those very spots where it is inhabited, vast wildernesses are interspersed; and those who inhabit the earth are not only so interrupted that nothing can pass between them from one to another, but they stand partly oblique, partly transverse, and partly even opposite to us, from whom you can certainly expect no glory.* You perceive, moreover, that this same earth is wreathed and surrounded by certain belts, two of which—most different from each other and supported by the poles of the heaven themselves on either side—you see have frozen with frost; but that middle and largest one is scorched by the heat of the sun. Two are habitable: the southern one, in which those who stand press their footprints opposite to yours <note>This refers to the "Antipodes," people living on the opposite side of the globe.</note>, has nothing to do with your race. But this other one, situated under the North Wind, which you inhabit: see how small a part of it touches you. For all the land that is cultivated by you, narrowed at the poles and broader at the sides, is a certain small island surrounded by that sea which you call the Atlantic, the Great, the Ocean on earth; yet you see how small it is despite such a great name. After the speech of Tullius [Cicero]—led through matters necessary and fit for the present work—described the heaven in which all things are contained, the order and motion of the subordinate spheres, the sound of celestial music explaining modes and numbers, and the air subject to the moon, he now completes the description of the earth itself, sparse in words but fertile in facts. Indeed, by naming the "spots" of habitations and, concerning the inhabitants themselves, calling some interrupted, opposite, oblique, and transverse, he painted the roundness of the terrestrial sphere with words, if not with colors. This also is not without the perfection of learning: that he does not allow us to err like others who believed the earth was encircled by only one ocean. For if he had said "all the earth is a certain small island surrounded by that sea," he would have given it to be understood that there was one circuit of the ocean. But by adding "which is cultivated by you," he left the true division of that sea—about which we shall discuss shortly—to be understood by those desiring to know.

<margin>
Belts or zones of the earth or heaven
</margin>

Regarding the five belts, I pray you do not think the doctrine of the two parents of Roman eloquence, Maro [Virgil] and Tullius [Cicero], disagrees; for while the latter says the earth is wreathed by these belts, the former [Virgil] asserts that the heaven is held by them, which he calls "zones" by their Greek name. That both have reported a pure and true reason, and not one contrary to the other, will be established by the preceding discussion. But so that all things which we have undertaken to explain in this place...

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

...so that these matters may be made clear: we must first speak of the zones <term>cingulis</term> <note>original: *cingulis*; literally "belts," referring to the climatic zones of the Earth</note>. Because once their positions are placed before our eyes, the rest will be easier to understand. First, we must explain how they crown the Earth, and then how they occupy the heavens. The Earth is the ninth and final sphere. This is divided by the horizon—that is, the "final circle" of which we spoke before. Therefore, half of it—the part we inhabit—is under that sky which is above the Earth, and the other half is under that sky which, as it revolves, descends to those places that seem "lower" to us. For being located in the middle, the Earth looks up at the sky from every side. Thus, its smallness in relation to the sky is like a mere point, but to us, it is an immense globosity. It is distinguished by regions that are pressed upon by extremes of either cold or heat, though it possesses a twin-temperate climate between these opposites. For both the northern and southern extremities are frozen with perpetual frost. These are like two belts by which the Earth is girded, but they are short in circumference, as they encircle the very ends of the globe. Both of these are unsuitable for habitation, because that icy numbness provides life for neither animal nor crop; for the body is nourished by the same air that feeds the plants.

<margin>
Northern
Southern
</margin>

The middle belt—and therefore the largest—is scorched by the eternal breath of continuous heat. The space it occupies, which is both wide in circumference and quite long, is made uninhabitable for living things by the excess of its fervor. However, between the extremities and the middle, there are two zones—larger than the ends but smaller than the middle—which are tempered by the climates of both their neighbors. In these zones, nature has granted that inhabitants may draw vital breath.

<margin>
The middle belt
</margin>

<margin>
Two temperate belts
</margin>

Because a concept enters the mind more easily through a diagram than through speech, let there be a globe of the Earth to which the letters **a, b, c,** and **d** are assigned. And around **a**, let **n** and **l** be written; around **b**, **m** and **k**; around **c**, **g** and **i**; and around **d**, **e** and **f**. And let straight lines be drawn from the points we mentioned: that is, from **a** through **g** to **i**; from **m** to **n**; from **k** to **l**; and from **e** to **f**. Thus, two spaces opposite one another—that is, one from **a** to **c** down to the line drawn at **d**—are understood to be frozen with perpetual frost. For **n** is the upper northern extremity, and the lower is the southern. Let the middle part, from **n** all the way to **l**, be the torrid zone. It remains then that the belt from **i** to **n** be tempered by the heat below and the cold above. Likewise, the zone between **l** and **f** receives a temperate climate from the heat above and the frost below.

<columns>2</columns>
Let it not be thought that these lines we have mentioned were just invented by us. For these are the circles of which we spoke above: the northern and southern, and the two tropics. Indeed, the equinoctial line <note>The celestial equator</note> should not be marked in this place where we are speaking of the Earth; it will be added again in a more suitable place. Although these two zones were granted by the gift of the gods to "weary mortals" <note>A poetic reference to humanity</note>, and we have said they are temperate, nevertheless, both zones were not granted to people of our kind. Rather, only the upper one, which is from **i** to **n**, is inhabited by every race of men known to us:

## BOOK TWO

...is understood by reason alone: which, because of a similar climate, is similarly inhabited: but by whom, it has never been permitted for us to know, nor will it ever be. For the scorched <term>torrida</term> <note>The "torrid zone" or the tropics, which ancient Greeks and Romans believed was a wall of fire preventing passage to the southern hemisphere.</note> zone cast between them denies passage for both types of humanity to reach one another. Finally, of the four quarters <term>cardines</term> <note>original: *cardinibus*; literally "hinges" or "turning points," used here to mean the four primary regions of the inhabited world.</note> of our habitation: East, West, and North are called by their own names because they are known to us from our very beginnings. For even if the northern extremity is uninhabitable, it is nonetheless not very remote from us.

<margin>Midday</margin>
But for the fourth quarter of our habitation, this reason gave another name: it is called "Midday" <note>original: *meridies*</note> rather than "Southern" <note>original: *australis*</note>. This is because the term "Southern" properly belongs to that region which proceeds from the other extremity [the South Pole] opposite the North. The place where this quarter begins for us causes it to be rightly called "Midday." Since it begins to be felt from the middle of the earth, where the use of the day is centered, it was named *meridies*—as if it were "mid-day" <note>original: *medi-dies*; Macrobius is explaining the Latin etymology where "d" was changed to "r".</note>—with one letter changed.

<margin>South Wind</margin>
It must be known, however, that the wind which comes to us through this quarter—that is, the South wind <note>original: *auster*</note>—is so cold in its origin that the North wind is as commendable to us for its gentle chill. But because it travels to us through the flame of the torrid zone, it grows hot, mixed with fire; and that which begins cold, arrives hot. For neither reason nor nature would allow that two quarters, pressed by equal frost, should emit blasts of a dissimilar nature. Nor is there any doubt that our North wind reaches those who live adjacent to the Southern zone as a hot wind for the same reason, and that the South wind soothes their bodies with the dual chill of its own breeze.

The same reasoning does not permit us to doubt that through that surface of the Earth too, which is considered "below" us, the entire circuit of the zones which are temperate here is held to be temperate by the same path; and therefore there too those same two zones, distant from one another, are similarly inhabited.

Or let whoever prefers to oppose this belief say what it is that deters him from this distinction. For if the capacity for living is in this part of the lands which we inhabit—because treading the ground we look up at the sky above our heads, because the sun both rises and sets for us, and because we enjoy the surrounding air whose breath we inhale—why should we not believe others live there, where the same conditions are always at hand?

<margin>To breathe</margin>
For those who are said to dwell there must be believed to breathe the same air, because there is the same climate in the continuation of the same zonal circuit.

The same sun is said to set for them at our rising, and it will rise when it sets for us. They will tread the ground just as we do, and they will always see the peak <note>The zenith, or the point of the sky directly overhead.</note>, always see the sky. Nor will there be fear lest they fall from the earth into the sky, since nothing can ever fall upward. (For if to us—to say it as a sort of joke—"down" is where the earth is and "up" is where the sky is, then for them, too, "up" will be what they look at from below, and they are never going to fall into the heavens). I would even affirm that among them, those unskilled in the nature of things think these same things about us; they cannot believe we live in the place where we are, but imagine that if anyone tried to stand under their feet, he would fall. Yet no one among us ever feared he would fall into the sky; therefore, no one among them is going to fall into the upper reaches, just as all weights, by their own inclination, are carried toward the earth as the teachings mentioned above have shown.

Finally, who would doubt that on the sphere of the earth, those things which are called "lower" are opposite to their "upper" counterparts, just as East is to West? For on both sides, it is held by diameters. Since therefore it is established that both East and West are similarly inhabited, what is it that excludes belief in this different habitation as well?

A diligent reader will find all these things in these few words of Cicero. For when he says the earth is "belted and surrounded by its own zones," and when he says "spots of habitations" <note>original: *maculas habitationum*; a reference to Scipio's vision where the inhabited parts of the Earth look like small patches or spots from a great height.</note> are seen on the earth, he does not mean those which are inhabited in our part of the world with some desert places placed between. For he would not add "vast wildernesses cast between" those spots if he were speaking of the wildernesses themselves, between which certain parts are held like spots. But because he calls these four habitable areas—which reason has shown to be two in each of the two hemispheres of the earth—"spots," he rightly added "wildernesses cast between." For just as the part inhabited by us is divided by many wildernesses cast between...
