->### ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO<-

...is distinguished: it must be believed that in those three other habitations there are similar distinctions between desert and cultivated lands. But he [Cicero] also depicted the inhabitants of the four habitations both by the relationship of their location and by the very quality of their stance. For first he says: others besides us inhabit the earth in such a way that, being cut off from one another, they have no ability to travel to each other. These very words declare that he is not speaking of a single race of men separated from us on this surface solely by the intervention of the scorched <term>torrida</term> <note>The tropical zone, believed by ancients to be a barrier of fire.</note> zone. For in that case, he would rather say: "so interrupted that nothing can pass from them to us." But by saying "so interrupted that nothing can pass among them from those to others," he signifies how those races of men are divided among themselves. 

Furthermore, concerning those who truly relate to our part of the world, he added that those who are divided both from us and from each other stand partly "oblique" <note>original: *obliquos*; likely those in the same hemisphere but different longitudes.</note>, partly "transverse" <note>original: *transuersos*; those in the opposite hemisphere but same longitude.</note>, and partly even "opposite" <note>original: *aduersos*; the Antipodes, standing feet-to-feet on the exact opposite side of the globe.</note> to us. Therefore, the "interruption" refers not just to one race being cut off from us, but to all races being divided from one another, which is to be distinguished as follows. 

Those whom the scorched zone separates from us—whom the Greeks call <term>antoikoi</term> <note>original: *αντοικοι*; literally "those who live opposite." These people live in the southern temperate zone, on the same side of the Earth as us but across the equator.</note>—are similarly separated from those who inhabit the lower part of their own zone by the intervening southern frozen zone. Again, those people are sequestered from their own <term>antoikoi</term> (that is, those living in the lower parts of our own belt) by the intervention of the burning zone; and those in turn are removed from us by the rigors of the northern extremity. And because there is no single, neighboring continuity for everyone, but instead wildernesses of heat or cold are cast between them denying mutual passage, he called these parts of the earth which are inhabited by the four races of men "spots of habitation" <note>original: *maculas habitationum*; Cicero uses this term to describe how small and isolated human civilizations appear when viewed from the heavens.</note>. 

Moreover, he himself distinguished how all others are believed to plant their footsteps in relation to ours. He openly pronounced the southern people to stand opposite to us, saying: "Of these, the southern zone, in which those who dwell press their footsteps opposite to us." And they are "opposite" to us for this reason: because they stay in the part of the sphere which is against us. It remains to inquire whom he mentioned as standing "transverse" and "oblique" to us. But there can be no doubt about them: he meant those who hold the lower part of our own zone stand "transverse" to us, while those who have been allotted the slopes of the southern circle are "oblique."

It remains for us to report the spans of the earth itself: how much has been granted for habitation and how much is uncultivated. That is, what the dimension of each individual belt is. So that you may easily understand this, you must return to the description of the orb of the earth which we set down a little while ago, so that through the marks of the written letters, the logic of the dimensions may be more clearly explained. The entire orb of the earth—that is, the circle which encloses the whole circumference, to which the letters **a, b, c, d** are assigned—has been divided by those who have measured with reason into sixty parts <term>sexagesimae</term> <note>Macrobius uses a system of 60 units to measure the 360-degree circumference of the Earth.</note>. 

The whole circumference itself contains two hundred and fifty-two thousand <term>stadia</term> <note>Approximately 25,000 to 30,000 miles, depending on the length of the *stadium* used; this reflects Eratosthenes’ famous calculation.</note>. Therefore, each single sixtieth part extends for four thousand two hundred stadia. Without doubt, half of it—which is from **a** through the east **i** and **a** up to **c**—contains thirty sixtieth-parts and one hundred and twenty-six thousand stadia. A fourth part—which is from **a** to **c**, beginning from the scorched zone—contains fifteen sixtieth-parts and sixty-three thousand stadia. The measurement of this fourth part, once reported, will establish the full dimension of the entire circumference. 

From **a** therefore, up to **p**, which is the middle of the scorched zone, there are four sixtieth-parts, which make sixteen thousand eight hundred stadia. Therefore, the entire scorched zone consists of eight sixtieth-parts and holds thirty-three thousand and six hundred stadia besides. The width of our belt, however, which is temperate—that is, from **a** through to **o**—contains five sixtieth-parts, which make twenty-one thousand stadia. And the span of the frozen zone from **o** to **c** has six sixtieth-parts, which hold twenty-five thousand two hundred stadia. From this quarter of the orb of the lands, the measurement of which we have clearly expressed, you will recognize the magnitude of the other fourth part from **a** to **d** by the same distinction of dimensions. When, therefore, you know how much the surface of the sphere which is toward us holds in its entire half, you will be similarly instructed concerning the measurement of the lower half—that is, from **a** to **d** through **b** up to **c**. For now, because we have painted the orb of the earth on a flat surface, and we cannot express the middle in a plane, we have imitated the spherical swelling by height...

## BOOK TWO

...understanding from the circle: which appears more as a horizon than a meridian. Furthermore, I want you to grasp this in your mind: we have presented this measurement as follows: as if the part from *d.* through *a.* to *c.* were the upper part of the earth, which is the part we inhabit; and the part from *d.* through *b.* to *c.* were the lower part of the earth. This discussion having reached its own conclusion, let us now assert what we promised to prove: that **Virgil** <note>original: "Maronem", referring to Publius Vergilius Maro</note> correctly assigned these belts to the heavens, and **Cicero** correctly assigned them to the earth, and that both said the same thing in harmony, not in disagreement. For the nature of the heavens has distinguished this balance and extremity in different parts of the earth; the quality of either cold or heat, once it has clung to any part of the upper air <term>ether</term>, infects that same part of the earth which it looks down upon as it encircles it. And because they called these diversities, which are bounded by certain limits, "belts" <term>cingulos</term> in the heavens, it is necessary that the same number of belts be understood here on earth as well. Just as in a very small mirror a huge face is shown, its limbs or features are held in a narrow space in the same order that their own size had arranged them in reality. But here too we shall lessen the labor of asserting what is said by placing a picture before your eyes. Let there be a sphere of heaven *a. b. c. d.* And let it enclose within itself the sphere of the earth, to which are assigned *f. x. t. u.* And let there be drawn in the sphere of heaven the northern circle from *i.* to *o.*, the summer tropic from *g.* to *p.*, the equinoctial from *a.* to *b.*, the winter tropic from *f.* to *q.*, and the southern circle from *e.* to *r.* Let the <term>zodiac</term> <note>The path of the sun through the constellations.</note> also be drawn from *f.* to *p.* Again, in the sphere of the earth, let the same limits of the belts be drawn which we described above: at *n.*, at *m.*, at *l.*, and at *k.*

<columns>2</columns>

<image-desc>A circular cosmological diagram representing the celestial and terrestrial spheres. <column-break/>

With these things thus depicted, it will be established without difficulty that the individual parts of the earth borrow their quality regarding excess or balance from the individual parts of the heaven positioned above their summit. For what is above from *d.* to *r.* looks down upon the earth from *f.* to *k.* And what is in heaven from *r.* to *q.* affects the earth from *k.* to *l.* And what is in heaven from *q.* to *p.* produces the same effect on earth from *l.* to *m.* Whatever the quality is from above from *p.* to *o.*, such it is on earth from *m.* to *n.* And whatever it is there from *o.* to *c.*, such it is here from *n.* to *t.*

<column-break/>

In the upper air, both extremities—from *d.* to *r.* and from *c.* to *o.*—are bound by eternal frost. The same is true on earth from *f.* to *k.* and from *t.* to *n.* Again, in heaven from *q.* to *p.*, it seethes with excessive heat. On earth, too, between *l.* and *m.*, there is the same burning heat. Likewise, there are temperate zones in heaven from *o.* to *p.* and from *q.* to *r.* These are also temperate here on earth from *n.* to *m.* and from *l.* to *k.* The equinoctial circle, which is drawn from *a.* to *b.*, cuts through the middle of the scorched zone. That Cicero himself knew that the earthly belts are infected by the celestial ones is shown from his own words. For he says: *"Of which you see two, most distant from each other and supported by the very poles of heaven on either side, are stiff with frost."* <note>A quote from Cicero's "Dream of Scipio" describing the Arctic and Antarctic zones.</note> Behold, they testify that the final cold comes from heaven. He says the same regarding the middle heat: *"But that middle and largest one is scorched by the heat of the sun."* Since, therefore, he clearly places both the frost from the poles of heaven...

<page-type>text</page-type>
# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

...and since he indicated that the heat from the sun comes to the belts of the earth, he showed that these same belts first existed in the heavens. Now since it has been established that there are the same zones or belts (for these are two names for one thing) in heaven and on earth, it must now be said: what cause in the upper air <term>ether</term> creates this diversity of quality? <margin>The Scorched Zone</margin> The Scorched Zone is enclosed by two tropics: that is, from *g.* to *p.* by the summer tropic, and from *f.* to *q.* by the winter tropic. Moreover, we have drawn the zodiac <note>the path of the sun through the constellations</note> from *f.* to *p.* Therefore, let the point *p.* be considered the summer tropic, Cancer, and the point *f.* be Capricorn.

It is established that the sun travels neither further up than Cancer nor further down than Capricorn, but when it reaches the borders of the tropics, it soon returns; hence they are called "solstices" <margin>Solstices</margin> <note>original: "solstitia", from 'sol' (sun) and 'stare' (to stand), meaning the point where the sun seems to stand still before reversing direction</note>. And because the summer tropic is the boundary of our temperate zone, when the sun reaches that limit, it creates summer heat for us, burning the lands below with a greater sensation due to its proximity. Finally, it cannot be doubted that at that time winter returns for the southern people, because then the sun recedes from them by the full extent of its path. Conversely, when it reaches the point *f.*, that is, Capricorn, it brings winter to us by its withdrawal, and returns summer to them by its proximity.

Here it must be noted that the sun enters any house from only three cardinal directions, but never from the fourth. For a window receives the sun from both the east <note>at its rising</note> and the west <note>at its setting</note>. It also receives it from the south, because the entire journey of the sun is in our southern sky, as the previously shown diagram illustrates. But a northern window never truly admits the sun, because the sun never approaches from point *p.* toward *o.*, but always receding from *p.*, it never reaches the limits of the North Pole. Therefore, a ray of the sun is never poured through this cardinal direction.

A shadow of any body will also provide proof of this same fact. For it falls toward the west when the sun rises, and toward the east when it sets. At midday, however, because the sun holds the south, the shadow is cast toward the north. In our habitation, it is impossible for the shadow of any body to fall toward the south, because a shadow is always cast in the opposite direction of the sun. But the sun can never be opposite to the south for us, since it never reaches the northern limits.

Certainly, since that part of the Scorched Zone which is near the temperate zone permits inhabitants, whatever spaces they inhabit there beyond the tropic, they cast a shadow toward the south at that time when the sun holds Cancer. For then the sun becomes northern to them when it holds the tropic, which recedes from them toward the north. <margin>Syene</margin> Now the city of Syene <note>modern Aswan, Egypt</note>, which is the beginning of the province of Thebaid after the deserts of the upper mountains, is situated directly under the summer tropic. And on that day when the sun enters a certain part of Cancer, at the sixth hour of the day (since the sun is then found directly above the city's zenith), no shadow can be cast on the ground there from any object. Nor even the pointer of a sundial that shows the hours, which they call a <term>gnomon</term> <note>original Greek: γνόμονα; the vertical part of a sundial</note>, can create a shadow from itself then. <margin>Lucan</margin> And this is what Lucan <note>a Roman poet</note> wished to say, yet he did not explain it fully as it stands. For by saying: *and Syene which turns shadows nowhere* <note>original: "atque umbras nusquam flectente Siene"</note>, he touched upon the fact but confused the truth. For it does not turn them "nowhere" always, but only at one specific time, which we have recounted with its proper reasoning.

These things having been related, it is certain that the sun never leaves the boundaries of the Scorched Zone, because the zodiac is tilted from tropic to tropic. The cause is therefore manifest why this zone is always subject to flames: namely, because the sun, both source and administrator of all eternal flame, never leaves it. Therefore, both extreme parts—that is, the northern and the southern—to which the sun's heat never reaches, are necessarily weighed down by perpetual frost.

But the proximity of heat and cold from this side and that tempers the two remaining zones (as we have said). Finally, in this very zone which we inhabit, which is entirely called temperate, the parts that are near the scorched belt are nonetheless hotter than the others, such as Ethiopia, Arabia, Egypt, and Libya; in which the heat so thins the body of the surrounding air that it is either never or rarely condensed into clouds, and therefore they have almost no use for rain <note>original: "imbrium", seasonal showers</note>. Conversely, the zone approaches more closely to the boundaries of the cold region, such as the Maeotian marsh <note>the Sea of Azov</note>, or the regions through which the Don <note>Tanais</note> and Danube <note>Hister</note> flow, <margin>Hyperboreans</margin> and all the places above Scythia, whose inhabitants antiquity called Hyperboreans <note>literally "those beyond the North Wind"</note>, as if they had passed beyond the origin of the North Wind <note>Boreas</note> by receding inward; they are weighed down by almost eternal frost, so that it is not easy to explain how great the injury of excessive cold is there. But the places that are in the middle of the temperate zone, since from both excesses...

<summary>Macrobius explains how the sun's movement between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn creates the Scorched Zone and the surrounding temperate and frigid zones. He provides a famous scientific proof using the city of Syene, where shadows disappear at noon during the summer solstice.</summary>

## BOOK TWO

...they recede far from [the heat]: they maintain a true and healthful temperature. The subject reminds us: since we have stated a fact that no one can refute—that both tropics form the boundaries of the zodiac, and the sun can never exceed either tropic by traveling further up or further down—we must look beyond the zodiacal circle. That is, beyond the scorched region which is enclosed by the tropics, the temperate zones begin on each side. Let us investigate what Virgil meant (whom no error of any discipline ever entangled) when he said:

> By the gift of the gods granted, and a path cut through both,
> Where the slanted order of the signs turns. 
> <note>original: "Munere concessae divum: & via secta per ambas: / Obliquus qua se signorum vertitur ordo." From Virgil's Georgics 1.238-239.</note>

For in these verses, he seems to say that the zodiac is led through the temperate zones and that the sun's course is carried through them. This is not right to believe, as the sun's course never exceeds either tropic. Now, therefore, consider what we said: even within the tropic, in that scorched part <note>the Torrid Zone</note> which is near the temperate zone, there are inhabitants. For Syene is under the tropic itself; Meroë, however, recedes 3,800 stades <note>a "stade" was a Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters</note> into the Scorched Zone from Syene; and from there to the land productive of cinnamon, there are 800 stades. And through all these spaces of the scorched region, though they are few, inhabitants enjoy life. Beyond that, however, the land is now inaccessible because of the excessive heat of the sun. 

Since, therefore, so much of the scorched space provides for life, there is no doubt that around the neighboring area of the other temperate zone—that is, the <term>antoikoi</term> <note>those who live in the same longitude but the opposite hemisphere</note>—the borders of the scorched zone have just as much space and an equal mildness. All things are equal on both sides. Therefore, it must be believed that through the "poetic trumpet" (which always extols everything to a greater degree), he said the sun's path was cut "through the temperate zones" because on each side the borders of the scorched zone are similar to the temperate ones, allowing themselves to be inhabited. 

Or perhaps by poetic license, he used one small word in place of another nearly similar one, and preferred to say "through both" (*per ambas*) when he meant "under both" (*sub ambas*). For in reality, the path of the zodiac arrives back and forth *under* both temperate zones, but not *through* them. We know that Homer himself, and Virgil who imitated him in all things, often changed such small words.

<margin>“Through” for “Between”</margin>
Or, what seems more proper to me: by "through both," he wanted "between both" to be understood. For the zodiac turns *between* both temperate zones, not *through* both. He is accustomed to familiarly use "through" (*per*) for "between" (*inter*), just as he does elsewhere: "And the two Bears [constellations] through which, in the manner of a river..." <note>original: "Circum perque duas in morem fluminis arctos." From Georgics 1.244.</note> For the starry snake <note>the constellation Draco</note> does not cut through the Bears, but while it embraces them and comes between them, it turns around them and between them, not through them. Therefore, our understanding can stand firm if we consider "through both" to be said as "between both," following the poet's own habit. 

Nothing else occurs to us for a defense beyond what we have said. But since we have placed in the open the boundaries which the sun's path never exceeds, and it is manifest to all that what Maro <note>Virgil's family name</note> said—who is known to be ignorant of error—it will be for the genius of each individual to find what more can be contributed to resolving this question.

These things having been treated (as I think) with no idle inspection, now we will establish what we promised concerning the ocean. Not by one, but by a double circuit does it flow around the whole body of the earth. Its true and primary passage is unknown to the unlearned kind of men. For that which many think is the only ocean is actually a secondary circuit made by necessity, flowing back from those original borders.

<margin>The Ocean</margin>
Furthermore, its primary "crown" <note>belt of water</note> passes through the hot zone of the earth, girding the upper and lower parts of the lands, following the curve of the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>the celestial equator</note>. From the east it pours back two gulfs: one toward the northern extremity, the other toward the southern. And again, from the west, two gulfs are born together, which flow back and meet those sent from the east at the two extremities we mentioned above. And while they mix with the greatest force and the impetus of the tides, and strike each other in turn, from that very collision of waters is born that famous <term>flow and ebb</term> <note>original: "accessio pariter & recessio"</note> of the ocean. 

And wherever this happens in our sea <note>the Mediterranean</note>, whether in narrow straits or on flat shores, it happens from those borders of the ocean which we now call the Ocean, because our sea flows from them. Moreover, its truer channel (so to speak) holds the scorched zone: and both the ocean itself which follows the equinoctial and the gulfs born from it—which imitate the horizon circle in the curve of their bending—divide all the earth into four parts, and make each habitation (as we said above) an island. For flowing between us and the southern men through the hot zone and girding the whole, and again surrounding the extremes of both regions with its borders, [it makes] two in the upper and lower [hemispheres]...

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

...surface, it creates islands. Hence Cicero <note>original: "Tullius" – Marcus Tullius Cicero, the author of the text Macrobius is commenting upon</note>, wanting this to be understood, did not say: "every land is a certain small island," but "every land which is inhabited by us is a certain small island." This is because each of the four habitable regions <note>Macrobius believed the world was divided into four inhabited quarters separated by oceans</note> is made into its own small island, with the ocean twice—as we have said—surrounding them. All these things can be placed before your eyes by the diagram provided below. From it, you will see the origin of our sea <note>The Mediterranean</note>, which is one part of the whole, and the source of the Red and Indian Seas. You will also find where the Caspian Sea originates, although I am not unaware that there are some who deny that it has an entrance from the Ocean. Nor is there any doubt that the sea similarly flows from the Ocean into that southern temperate zone. However, this ought not to be described by our own testimony, since its location remains unknown to us.

As for what Cicero said—that our inhabitable land is narrow at the poles and wider at the sides—we will be able to notice this in the same diagram. For however much longer the tropical circle <note>the Equator/Tropics</note> is than the northern circle, by that much is the zone narrower at its peaks than at its sides; because its summit is contracted into a narrow space by the shortness of the outermost circle. The extension of the sides, however, is stretched out by the length of the tropic from each part. Finally, the ancients said that our whole inhabitable land, when stretched out, is similar to a <term>chlamys: a short, oblong mantle or cloak worn by ancient Greeks</term>. Likewise, because the whole earth (in which the Ocean also exists) holds the position of a central point relative to any celestial circle, he necessarily added regarding the Ocean: "Which, though called by such a great name, you see how small it is." For although among us it is called the "Atlantic Sea" or the "Great Sea," to those looking down from the heavens it cannot seem great; for in relation to the sky, the earth is a mere sign and a point which cannot be divided into parts. Therefore, the smallness of the earth is so diligently asserted so that the pursuit of fame might be seen as a trivial thing.

# BOOK TWO
### PAGE XXX

Let the brave man understand that greatness cannot exist in such a small space. This teaching will appear no less clearly in what follows: even if the hope of future generations should desire to pass down the praises of each of us—received from our fathers—to those who come after, we still cannot achieve a glory that is eternal, or even long-lasting. This is because of the deluges <note>original: "eluuiones" – periodic world-cleansing floods</note> and conflagrations <note>original: "exustiones" – periodic world-cleansing fires</note> of the earth which must necessarily happen at certain fixed times. <margin>The fruit of virtue</margin> The wise man places the fruit of virtue in his own conscience, while the less perfect man places it in glory. Thus, Scipio, desiring to instill perfection in his grandson, advises him to be content with the reward of conscience and not to seek out glory. In seeking glory, there are two things which are most desired: that it spread as widely as possible, and that it endure as long as possible.

Above, by discussing the narrowness of our habitation, he taught that a very small portion of the whole earth (which occupies the space of a mere point in relation to the heavens) is possessed by humans of our kind. He showed that no one's glory could be spread even across that entire small part, since the fame of the Roman name was not strong enough to swim across the Ganges or cross the Caucasus mountains. Having thus cut away the hope of widely spreading fame by placing the narrowness of our world before our eyes, he now wishes to take away the hope of its duration. He does this so that, as a persuasive teacher, he may fully instill a contempt for glory into the mind of his grandson. He says: "Not even in this very place where the name of a wise and brave man can spread, can the eternity of a name endure." This is because the downfall of things interferes with their longevity, sometimes through the burning of the lands, sometimes through their flooding—matters which we shall discuss further.

In this part of the treatise, he secretly resolves a question that signifies the doubts many have regarding the eternity of the world. For who would easily agree that the world has always existed? Especially when the reliability of history itself confesses that the cultivation and improvement of many things—or even their very invention—is recent. <margin>The eternity of the world</margin> Antiquity remembers, or tells in fables, that the first humans were rude and, in their forest-dwelling neglect, not much different from the harshness of wild beasts. It is handed down that they did not even have the food we use now, but were first nourished by acorns and berries, only later hoping for nourishment from the furrows of the field. Because we think of the beginning of things and of the human race in this way, we believe there was first a Golden Age, and from there nature degenerated through cheaper metals until the Iron Age defiled the final centuries. And lest we seem to borrow everything from fables, who would not think the world began at some point, and that its age is not long, since there is no Greek history of excellent deeds stretching back more than two thousand years? Indeed, before Ninus <note>A legendary king of Assyria, husband of Semiramis</note>, from whom some believe Semiramis was born, nothing remarkable is related in books. If, as the philosophers wish, the world existed from the beginning—or rather before the beginning—why, through an innumerable series of ages, was the culture we use now not discovered? Why was there no use of letters, which alone support the eternity of memory? Why, finally, has the experience of many things reached some nations only recently? For example, the Gauls only learned the cultivation of the vine and the olive when Rome was already growing up. Other nations still do not know many things which we have invented and enjoyed. All these things seem to argue against the eternity of the world, making us think that each thing began gradually from a certain starting point.

But philosophy is the authority that the world has always existed, with God as its founder, yet not "from a certain time." For time could not exist before the world, since the courses of the sun create nothing other than time itself. Human affairs, however, often perish for the most part while the world remains, and then they rise again, returning in cycles of either deluge or conflagration. The cause or necessity of this cycle is as follows. <margin>Ethereal fire is nourished by moisture</margin> Physicists have taught that ethereal fire is nourished by moisture. They assert that beneath the scorched zone of the sky occupied by the path of the sun (that is, the zodiac), the Ocean was placed by nature (as we described above). This was done so that the entire width through which the sun and the five wandering stars <note>The planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> run back and forth might have the nourishment of moisture from below. And they maintain that this is what Homer—the fountain and origin of all divine inventions—allowed the wise to understand under the cloud of poetic fiction: when he wrote of Jupiter and the other gods (that is, the stars) setting out for the Ocean, with the Ethiopians inviting him to a feast. Through this...

<summary>Macrobius argues that human fame is fleeting not only because of geographic limits but because periodic natural disasters (floods and fires) wipe out civilizations. He addresses the philosophical debate on whether the world is eternal or newly created, concluding that while the world is eternal, human society restarts in cycles.</summary>

# DE SOMNIO SCIPIONIS
### PAGE XXX

...they want to suggest that Homer was using a fabled image: that nourishment for the stars is drawn from moisture. For this reason, he said the Ethiopian kings feasted with the celestial gods because no one lives near the shore of the ocean except the Ethiopians, whom the proximity of the sun has scorched to a dark black color. Since heat is nourished by moisture, this alternation occurs: now heat overflows, now moisture. For it happens that fire, having been nourished to its maximum growth, overcomes the moisture it has consumed. And so, a change in the atmosphere’s temperament allows for a conflagration <note>original: "incendio" – a world-purifying fire</note>, and the earth is burned deep within by the unleashed flames. But soon, once the force of the heat is spent, strength gradually returns to the moisture, since a large part of the fire used up in the burning consumes less of the reborn moisture. And again, over a long passage of time, the growing moisture conquers more deeply, so that it pours over the lands in a deluge <note>original: "eluuio" – a world-purifying flood</note>. Then heat resumes its strength after these events, and so it happens: as the world remains amidst these alternating excesses of heat and moisture, the cultivation of the earth and the race of men often perish. When a temperate balance is restored, they are renewed; yet never does either a deluge or a conflagration cover all lands or the entire human race, or burn them away completely. Certainly in Egypt—as Plato confesses in his *Timaeus*—neither an excess of moisture nor of heat has ever caused harm. This is why infinite thousands of years are still read about in the monuments and books of the Egyptians alone. Surely, then, those parts of the earth that survive the destruction become a nursery for restoring the human race. And so it happens that men—not in a brand-new world, but raw men and ignorant of culture, the memory of which was cut off by the destruction—wander upon the earth. Gradually shedding the harshness of their wild wandering, and with nature as their teacher, they begin to accept gatherings and assemblies. At first, there is among them a simplicity ignorant of evil and as yet inexperienced in cunning, which provides the name of the "Golden Age" <note>original: "nomen auri" – referring to the mythical first age of man</note> to those first centuries. From there, as the use of things and arts moves further toward civilization, emulation creeps more easily into their souls; though it begins well, it eventually turns into hidden envy. And from this is born whatever the human race experiences in the centuries that follow. This is the cycle of fail and return that varies in human affairs while the world itself remains unharmed. But what does it matter if those born after you speak of you, when there was no word from those born before? These earlier men were no fewer in number, and were certainly better men; especially since among those very people by whom our name can be heard, no one can maintain a memory of even a single year. For men popularly measure the year only by the return of the sun—that is, the return of a single star. In reality, however, when all the stars have returned to the place from which they once set out, and have brought back the same arrangement of the entire heaven after long intervals, then that can truly be called a "turning year" <note>This is the "Great Year" or "Platonic Year," estimated by ancients to last thousands of years</note>; I hardly dare to say how many human generations are contained within it. For just as once the sun seemed to fail and be extinguished for men when the soul of Romulus <note>The legendary founder of Rome</note> penetrated into these very celestial temples, so too, whenever the sun shall again fail from that same part of the sky and at the same time—with all the signs and stars recalled to that same beginning—consider the year complete. Regarding the desire for this glory: having shown above that it is restricted by geography—lest you think it eternal even within those narrow limits—he now teaches that it is not only devoid of perpetuity, but cannot even spread to the boundaries of one full Great Year.

We shall explain the reasoning behind this assertion. A "year" is not only that which common usage now calls by that name; rather, the emergence of each of the lights or stars through the entire circuit of heaven, from a certain place back to that same place, is its own "year." Thus, a month is the year of the moon, in which it traverses the circle of the sky; for "month" <note>original: "mensis"</note> is named from the moon, because in the Greek language the moon is called *mene*. Finally, Virgil, in his description of the lunar year (which is short) wishing to signify the year which is completed by the course of the sun, says: "Meanwhile the sun rolls round the great year" <note>original: "Interea magnum sol circuvoluitur annum"</note>, calling it "great" only in comparison to the moon's year. For the course of Venus and Mercury is almost equal to that of the sun. But the year of Mars takes almost two years—for in that much time it circuits the heaven; the star of Jupiter consumes twelve years, and Saturn thirty years in the same circuit. These facts

The reason for it is this: all the stars and constellations that seem fixed in the heaven, whose own motion human sight can never feel or detect, are nevertheless moving, even beyond the rotation of the heavens...

# BOOK TWO
### PAGE 31

...by which they are always drawn; their progress in their own approach is so slow that no human life is long enough to detect, through continuous observation, the change in position from where they were first seen. 

<margin>The end of the mundane year</margin>
Therefore, the end of the "Mundane Year" <note>original: "Mundani anni" — often called the Great Year or the Platonic Year</note> occurs when all the stars and all the constellations contained in the *aplanes* <note>original: "aplanes" — the Greek term for the sphere of the fixed stars, which was believed to be immovable relative to itself</note> have returned from a certain point to that same point in such a way that not a single star in the heavens is in a different place than where it was when all the others moved from that spot; their return marks the end of their year. This return is such that the two "lights" <note>the Sun and Moon</note> as well as the five wandering stars <note>the planets: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> are in the same locations and positions they were in at the start of the Mundane Year. This happens (as the physicists claim) after fifteen thousand years have passed. 

Therefore, just as the "year" of the moon is a month, and the "year" of the sun is twelve months, and the other stars have their own years as we mentioned above, so too fifteen thousand years (as we now compute them) make up one Mundane Year. 

<margin>The mundane year</margin>
That year should truly be called the "Revolving Year," which is measured not by the return of the sun alone, but by the return of all the stars in whatever heaven they reside to the same place, concluding under the same description of the entire sky. From this, it is called "Mundane," because the heavens are properly called the *Mundus* <note>The Latin word *mundus* can mean both "world" and "universe" or "the heavens"</note>.

<margin>The World</margin>
Therefore, just as we call the sun's year not only the period from the first of January to the next, but also from the day following the first until that same day, or from any day of any month until its return to that same day; so too everyone makes the beginning of this Mundane Year whenever they decide. Thus, for example, Cicero here establishes the beginning of the Mundane Year for himself from the solar eclipse that occurred toward the end of Romulus’s life <note>Romulus, the legendary founder of Rome, was said to have vanished during a solar eclipse</note>. And although solar eclipses have occurred very often since then, a repeated eclipse is not said to have completed a Mundane Year; rather, it will be completed only when the sun, in its eclipse, is in the exact same location and position, and finds all the stars of heaven and all the constellations back where they were when it was eclipsed at the end of Romulus’s life.

<margin><unclear>Scipio's Dream</unclear></margin>
Therefore, fifteen thousand years after the departure of Romulus (as the physicists assert), the sun will be eclipsed again in such a way that it is in the same sign and the same part of that sign as it was at the beginning under Romulus, with all stars and signs having been recalled to their places. Indeed, at the time Scipio was serving as a soldier in Africa, five hundred and seventy-three years had passed since the departure of Romulus. For in the six hundred and seventh year from the founding of the city <note>607 AUC or 147 BCE</note>, this Scipio triumphed after the destruction of Carthage. 

<margin>When Carthage was destroyed</margin>
From that number, subtract the thirty-two years of Romulus’s reign and the two years that passed between the dream and the end of the war, and five hundred and seventy-three years remain from the departure of Romulus to the time of the dream. Therefore, he signaled with reasonable modesty that not even a twentieth part of the Mundane Year had yet turned. For if anyone counts on their fingers, they will find how many years are left of a twentieth part <note>1/20th of 15,000 is 750</note> from the end of Romulus to Scipio’s military service in Africa, which we said was five hundred and seventy-three years.

<margin>The immortal soul</margin>
"But you," [the elder Scipio says], "strive on: and hold this truth: that you are not mortal, but this body is. For you are not what that physical form declares; rather, the mind of each person is who they are, not that shape which can be pointed to with a finger. Know then that you are a god <note>original: "Deum te igitur scito esse" — a central Stoic and Platonic claim that the rational soul is divine</note>, if indeed he is a god who is vigorous, who feels, who remembers, who foresees, and who rules, moderates, and moves that body over which he is placed, just as that leading God moves this world. And as that eternal God himself moves the world which is mortal in some part, so the everlasting soul moves the fragile body."

Well and wisely did Cicero's Scipio fulfill the order of a true teacher regarding the instruction of his grandson. To briefly review the entire content of the work from the beginning: first, he predicted the time of his death and the impending traps of his kinsmen, so that he might learn to stop hoping for anything from this life, having found it to be so short. Then, so that he would not be crushed by the fear of the predicted death, he showed that a wise and good citizen must migrate into immortality. 

<margin><unclear>The soul is turned from the desire for death</unclear></margin>
When that hope had further carried him toward a desire for dying, there followed the timely dissuasion of his father, Paulus, shutting out his son’s burning haste for a self-sought death. Therefore, once a balance of hoping and waiting was fully planted in the mind of the dreamer on both sides, he could then be raised higher toward divine matters...

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

...they wish to signify the mythic imagery of Homer: that the stars draw their nourishment from moisture. For this reason, he said the Ethiopian kings and the feasts of the gods <note>Homer, in the Iliad, describes the gods traveling to Ethiopia to feast, which ancient commentators interpreted as the sun and stars "consuming" vapors from the ocean</note> were located near the shore of the ocean, because none but the Ethiopians live there, whom the proximity of the sun has scorched to the point of a black complexion. Therefore, since heat is nourished by moisture, this alternation occurs: at one time heat overflows, and at another, moisture. For it happens that when fire is nourished to its maximum growth, it overcomes the moisture it has drawn in. Thus, the changed temperament of the air grants license to a conflagration, and the fire, once let in, burns the earth with a deep blazing. But soon, once the impetus of the heat is spent, the strength of the moisture gradually returns; since a great part of the fire was expended in the conflagrations, it consumes less of the newly reborn moisture. And again, over a long tract of time, the moisture grows so much that it overcomes the heights and pours over the lands in a flood. Afterward, the heat regains its strength again; and so it happens that while the world remains stable between the alternating excesses of heat and moisture, the cultivation of the lands and the human race often perish. When a temperate balance is restored, the world is renewed again. However, neither flood nor fire ever covers all lands or the entire human race, nor does it utterly burn them away. Certainly in Egypt, as Plato admits in the *Timaeus* <note>In Plato's dialogue, an Egyptian priest tells Solon that Egypt is spared from these catastrophes by the rising of the Nile, preserving their ancient records</note>, an excess of moisture or heat has never caused harm. Whence an infinite number of thousands of years are read in the monuments and books of the Egyptians alone. Surely, therefore, those parts of the lands that survive the slaughter become the nursery for restoring the human race. And so it happens that humans wander the earth not as a sophisticated race, but as unrefined and ignorant of culture—the memory of which was cut off by the destruction. Gradually stripped of the harshness of their wandering wildness, they endure gatherings and assemblies under the instruction of nature. At first, there is among them a simplicity that knows no evil and is as yet inexperienced in cunning; this is what grants the name "Golden" to the first ages <note>A reference to the "Golden Age," a mythical era of peace and primordial innocence</note>. From there, as the use of things and arts moves further toward cultivation, emulation creeps into their souls all the more easily, which, beginning well at first, secretly turns into envy. And from this is born whatever the human race experiences in the succeeding ages. This alternation, therefore, varies by the failing of human affairs and their subsequent return within the unharmed world. What difference does it make, then, what is said of you in the speech of those born afterward, when there was no word from those born before—who were not fewer in number and were certainly better men—especially since among those very people by whom our name can be heard, no one can achieve the memory of a single year? For people commonly measure the year only by the return of the sun, that is, of a single star. But in reality, when all the stars have returned to the same place from which they once set out, and have restored the same configuration of the entire sky after long intervals, then can it truly be called a "revolving year"; in which I hardly dare to say how many human generations are contained. For just as the sun once seemed to fail and be extinguished for men when the soul of Romulus <note>The legendary founder of Rome, said to have ascended to heaven during a solar eclipse</note> penetrated these very temples, so whenever the sun fails again at the same part of the sky and at the same time, then—with all the constellations and stars recalled to the same starting point—consider the year completed. Know that not even a twentieth part of this year has yet turned. 

<margin>The Year, the Moon, and the Month. Whence the course of the planets is defined.</margin>
He continues to press the same point, dissuading the desire for glory: having shown above that glory is narrow in its location, now he teaches that it is not only devoid of perpetuity but cannot even be propagated to the limits of one full year. We shall explain the reason for this assertion. The "year" is not only that which common usage now calls it; rather, the measure of each individual light or star—its return from a certain place to that same place through the entire circuit of the sky—is its own "year." Thus, a month is the "year" of the moon, within which it traverses the ambit of the sky; for the month is named from the moon, because in the Greek tongue, the moon is called *mene*. Finally, wishing to signify the year which is completed by the sun's course, Virgil said of the description of the lunar year (which is short): "Meanwhile the sun rolls through the Great Year" <note>Virgil, Aeneid 3.284. Macrobius notes that Virgil uses "Great Year" here somewhat poetically or comparatively</note>, calling it "Great" in comparison to the lunar one. For the course of Venus and Mercury is almost equal to the sun's. But the year of Mars takes almost two years; in that much time, it circles the sky. The star of Jupiter completes its circuit in twelve years, and Saturn in thirty. 

<margin>The Mundane Year. The fixed stars also move.</margin>
These things regarding the "lights" <note>the sun and moon</note> and the wandering stars <note>the planets</note> are already well known, as they are often reported. But the year which is called "Mundane" <note>original: "mundanus," the Great Year of the Universe</note>, which is truly the revolving one because it is created by the rotation of the full universe, unfolds over the most vast ages. The reason for it is as follows: all the stars and constellations that are seen fixed in the sky—whose own motion human sight can never feel or detect—nevertheless do move, even beyond the rotation of the heavens...

# BOOK TWO XXXI

...by which they are always drawn: they are moved forward by their own progress so slowly that no human life is long enough to detect, through continuous observation, the change in position from where he first saw them. 

<margin>The end of the world year</margin>
Therefore, the end of the **world year** occurs when all the stars and all the constellations contained in the *aplanes* <note>original: "aplanes"; referring to the "fixed" outer sphere of stars which, in ancient astronomy, was thought to move extremely slowly compared to the planets</note> have returned from a certain place to that same place, so that not a single star in the sky is in a different position than it was when all the others moved from that spot, to which they have now returned to complete their year. This requires that the two luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon</note>, along with the five wandering stars <note>The planets known in antiquity: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, are in the same locations and sectors they occupied at the beginning of the world year. 

<margin>The world year</margin>
According to the natural philosophers, this happens after fifteen thousand years have passed. Therefore, just as the year of the moon is a month, and the year of the sun is twelve months, and the other stars have their own years as we mentioned above, so fifteen thousand of the years we currently calculate make up one **world year**. That should truly be called the "turning year," which is measured not by the return of the sun (that is, a single star) but by the return of all the stars in whatever heaven they reside to the same place, concluding under the same description of the entire sky. 

<margin>The World</margin>
For this reason, it is called "mundane" (of the world), because the word "world" (*mundus*) is properly the name for the heavens. Therefore, just as we call it a "year of the sun" not only from the first of January to the next, but also from any given day to its return on that same day, so anyone can set the beginning of this world year at whatever point they choose. For instance, here Cicero established the beginning of the world year for himself from a solar eclipse that occurred toward the end of Romulus's life. And although solar eclipses have occurred very frequently since then, a repeated eclipse is not said to have fulfilled the world year; rather, it will be fulfilled only when the sun, in eclipse, is in the exact same place and sector and finds all the stars and constellations of the sky in the same positions they were in when it eclipsed at the end of Romulus’s life. Therefore, fifteen thousand years after the departure of Romulus (as the natural philosophers assert), the sun will eclipse again in such a way that it is in the same sign and the same part of the sky as it was at that first point under Romulus, with all stars and signs having been recalled to their places. 

When Scipio was serving as a soldier in Africa, five hundred and seventy-three years had passed since the departure of Romulus. For in the six hundred and seventh year from the founding of the city <note>607 AUC or 147–146 BCE</note>, this Scipio triumphed after destroying Carthage. 

<margin>The time when Carthage was destroyed</margin>
If you remove from that number the thirty-two years of Romulus’s reign, and the two years that passed between the dream and the end of the war, five hundred and seventy-three years remain from the departure of Romulus until the dream. Therefore, Cicero noted reasonably and truly that "not even a twentieth part of a single world year has yet turned." For anyone who calculates it on their fingers will find how many years are left to reach a twentieth part <note>A 20th of 15,000 is 750; Macrobius is showing that Scipio's 573 years is indeed less than 1/20th of the Great Year</note> from the end of Romulus to Scipio’s military service in Africa, which we said was five hundred and seventy-three years.

"But you," <note>Macrobius is now quoting the spirit of Scipio the Elder speaking to the younger Scipio in Cicero's text</note> "strive on, and hold this truth: that you are not mortal, but this body is. For you are not what that physical form declares; rather, the mind of each person is who they are, not that shape which can be pointed to with a finger. 

**Know then that you are a god** <note>original: "Deum te igitur scito esse"</note>, if indeed he is a god who flourishes, who feels, who remembers, who foresees, and who rules, moderates, and moves that body over which he is placed, just as that lead God rules this world. And as that eternal God moves the world, which is in some part mortal, so the everlasting soul moves the fragile body."

In this, Cicero’s Scipio fulfilled the order of a good teacher regarding the education of his grandson. To briefly review the entire content of the work from the beginning: first, he predicted the time of Scipio's death and the looming traps of his relatives, so that he might learn to stop hoping for anything from this life, which he discovered was not long-lasting. Next, lest he be crushed by the fear of that predicted death, he showed that a wise and good citizen must migrate toward immortality. And when that hope had moved him so much that he desired to die immediately, there followed the timely dissuasion of his father, Paullus, which blocked the son’s burning haste and his appetite for a self-chosen death. With a balance of hope and expectation thus fully planted in the mind of the dreamer, he was then ready to be raised higher toward divine matters...

<summary>Macrobius defines the 'Great Year' (15,000 years) as the time it takes for all celestial bodies to return to a shared starting point and argues that the human soul is a divine, governing force within the body.</summary>
<keywords>Great Year, Mundane Year, astronomy, solar eclipse, Romulus, Scipio Africanus, Carthage, Cicero, immortality of the soul, divinity of the mind</keywords>

# PAGE 80
## ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

Africanus enters the soul of his grandson. He does not allow him to look back at the earth until he first recognizes the nature, motion, and harmony of the heavens and stars; he must know that all these things are the reward for his virtues. Once Scipio’s mind has been strengthened by the eagerness inspired by such a great promise, he is then commanded to despise glory—which among the unlearned is believed to be the great reward for virtue. This is done by showing the smallness of the earth, its narrow boundaries, and the fleeting nature of time. Africanus, therefore, having almost cast off his human form and with a purified mind now capable of grasping his own nature, is here more openly warned to know that he himself is a god. Let this be the culmination of the present work: to make it clear that the soul is not only immortal, but is a god. Therefore, he who had already been received into divinity after leaving the body, about to speak to a man still dwelling in this life, says: **know that you are a god** <note>original: "deum te scito esse"</note>. He does not grant such a great privilege to a human before he can distinguish what he truly is, lest he think that the part of us which is mortal and fragile is also called divine. Since it is Cicero's custom to hide a profound knowledge of things beneath a brevity of words, he now includes a great secret in a short summary. This is the same secret that Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was a major Greek-speaking philosopher of the Neoplatonist school</note>—who was even more sparing with words than Cicero—discussed in an entire book. The title of that work is: *What is an animal? What is a human?* In this book, Plotinus asks: to what part of us do our wills, memories, fears, desires, anger, and pains belong? Finally, he asks whether thoughts and intellect belong to the soul alone, or to the soul using a body. After many arguments presented with a dense abundance of facts (which we must pass over now only so that the volume does not become tiresomely long):

<margin>What is an animal?</margin>
he finally pronounces that an "animal" is an animated body. But he did not leave this neglected or unexamined; he asked by what benefit of the soul and by what path of fellowship it animates the body. He assigns all those passions we mentioned above to the "animal." However, he testifies that the "human" is the soul itself. Therefore, the person who is seen is not the true human; the true human is the one who rules what is seen. Thus, when death comes and the animal part departs, the animation falls away because the body is widowed of its ruler. This is the part of a human that is seen to be mortal. The soul, however, which is the true human, is a stranger to every condition of mortality; so much so that, in imitation of God ruling the world, it rules the body while animating it. For this reason, the natural philosophers <note>the "physici" or early scientists and philosophers of nature</note> called the world a **great man** and man a **brief world** <note>This refers to the concept of the "microcosm" (the human as a small universe) and the "macrocosm" (the universe as a giant organism)</note>. Because of these similarities and other privileges by which the soul is seen to imitate God, both ancient philosophers and Cicero called the soul a god. As for his statement that the world is mortal in a certain part, he is referring to common opinion, by which some things in the world seem to die—such as a lifeless animal, an extinguished fire, or dried-up moisture. For all these things are commonly believed to have perished.

<margin>Nothing dies</margin>
But it is established according to the assertion of true reason—which Cicero himself knows, and Virgil was not ignorant of when he said there is "no place for death"—that nothing within the living world perishes. I mean that of those things which seem to die, only the appearance is changed; the thing itself returns to its origin and into the elements themselves, ceasing to be what it was. Finally, Plotinus in another place, when discussing the composition of bodies and pronouncing that they can be dissolved, raised an objection to himself: "Why then are the elements, whose flow is obvious, not similarly dissolved at some point?" He answered this great and powerful objection briefly: the elements, though they flow, are never dissolved because they do not flow *outward*. While what flows from other bodies departs from them, the flux of elements never departs from the elements themselves. Therefore, in this world, no part is mortal according to the assertions of true reason. But when Cicero said it was mortal "in a certain part," he wanted to lean slightly toward common opinion (as we said).

<margin>Immortality of the soul</margin>
At the end, however, he places the strongest argument for the immortality of the soul: that the soul itself provides the motion for the body. You will find the nature of this in Cicero's own words that follow: *For that which is always moved is eternal; but that which brings motion to something else, and which is itself moved from elsewhere, must necessarily have an end to living when it has an end to motion. Therefore, only that which moves itself never ceases to be moved, because it is never deserted by itself.*

<summary>Macrobius explains the divine nature of the human soul, defining the "true human" as the soul rather than the body and arguing for its immortality through the concept of self-movement. He introduces the Neoplatonic idea of the microcosm, where the human soul rules the body just as God rules the universe.</summary>

Having established the divinity of the soul in the previous section, the text now turns to the philosophical proofs of the soul’s immortality, specifically focusing on the concept of "self-motion" as found in Cicero’s translation of Plato.</meta>

# PAGE 32
## BOOK TWO

For other things that are moved, this is the source, this is the beginning of motion. There is no origin for a beginning <term>principium: the first cause or starting point</term>; for all things arise from a beginning, but the beginning itself cannot be born from any other thing. For it would not be a beginning if it were generated from elsewhere. And if it never arises, it certainly never dies; for if a beginning were extinguished, it would neither be reborn from another, nor would it create anything else from itself, since it is necessary that all things arise from a beginning. Thus, it follows that the beginning of motion comes from that which is moved by itself. Moreover, this can neither be born nor perish; otherwise, the entire sky would collapse and all of nature would necessarily stand still, unable to find any force by which it might be moved by a primary impulse. Since it is clear, therefore, that whatever moves itself is eternal, who is there to deny that this nature has been granted to souls? For everything that is agitated by an eternal impulse is in the soul. Now, that which is "soul" is moved by an internal and its own motion; for this is the unique nature and power of the soul. If the soul is the only thing among all others that moves itself, then it certainly was not born, and it is eternal. This entire passage was translated word-for-word by Cicero from Plato’s *Phaedo* <note>original: "Phedone Platonis"; although the text says the Phaedo, Cicero is actually translating a famous passage from Plato’s Phaedrus (245c–246a)</note>, in which the immortality of the soul is asserted with the strongest arguments. And this is the sum of the arguments: that the soul is immune to death because it moves by its own power.

<margin>
How immortality is understood
</margin>
It must be understood, however, that immortality is understood in two ways: either something is immortal because it is not capable of death by its own nature, or because it is defended from death by the care of another. Of these, the first way refers to the immortality of the soul; the second to the immortality of the world <note>the universe or cosmos</note>. For the soul, by its very nature, is foreign to the condition of death. The world, however, is held in this perpetuity of life by the benefit of the soul. Furthermore, the phrase "always moved" is accepted in two ways: it is accepted both for that which is always moved from the moment it exists, and for that which exists always and is always moved. It is this second way by which we say the soul is always moved. With these things established, the syllogisms <term>syllogism: a logical argument where a conclusion is reached from two linked premises</term> by which the various followers of Plato reason about the immortality of the soul must now be revealed. For there are those who arrive at the single goal of proof through steps of syllogisms, making a certain proposition for the next step from the conclusion of the previous one. Among these, the first argument is this: The soul moves by itself; whatever moves by itself, moves always. Therefore, the soul moves always. The second follows, arising from the end of the first: The soul moves always; whatever moves always is immortal. Therefore, the soul is immortal. And so, in two syllogisms, two things are proved: both that the soul is always moved, as in the first; and that it is immortal, as gathered from the second. Others, indeed, proceed in their arguing up to a third step in this way: The soul moves by itself. That which moves by itself is the beginning of motion. Therefore, the soul is the beginning of motion. Again, from this conclusion a proposition is born: The soul is the beginning of motion. That which is the beginning of motion is not born <note>unbegotten; having no prior cause</note>. Therefore, the soul is not born. In the third place: The soul is not born; that which is not born is immortal. Therefore, the soul is immortal. Still others have reduced their entire reasoning into the shorthand of a single syllogism: The soul moves by itself; that which moves by itself is the beginning of motion; that which is the beginning of motion is not born; that which is not born is immortal; therefore, the soul is immortal. But the final conclusion regarding the immortality of the soul can only stand for one who does not refute the first proposition: that is, that the soul moves by itself. For if this is not accepted in faith, everything that follows becomes weak.

<margin>
Arguments concerning motion
</margin>
The Stoics <note>a school of Hellenistic philosophy that emphasized virtue and harmony with the rational order of the universe</note> indeed agree with this. Aristotle, however, so far disagrees that he attempts to assert not only that the soul is not moved by itself, but that it is not moved at all. He constructs his clever arguments to show that nothing moves by itself, so that even if he grants that something might do this, he confirms that it is not the soul. For he says: If the soul is the beginning of motion, I will show that the beginning of motion cannot be moved. And so he enters into the divisions of his art: first he teaches that in the nature of things there is something immobile, then he tries to show that this is the soul. He says it is necessary that either all things are immobile, or all things are moved, or some of these are moved and some are not. Likewise, he says if we grant both motion and rest, it is necessary that either some things always move and others never move, or all things at once now rest and now move. Regarding these, he says, let us ask what is more true. That all things are not im- <meta>Catchword: im- (continued on next page as "immobile")</meta>

<summary>This page analyzes the logical proofs for the soul's immortality, focusing on the Platonic argument that the soul is a "self-moving" principle and therefore eternal, while also introducing Aristotle's opposing view that the soul is immobile.</summary>
<keywords>immortality of the soul, self-motion, Plato, Cicero, Aristotle, syllogisms, first principle, Stoics, cosmic order</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Macrobius's commentary on the "Dream of Scipio." Following the translation of Plato’s argument for the immortality of the soul via self-motion, Macrobius now begins to contrast the Platonic view with the Aristotelian critique of motion.</meta>

# PAGE 24
## ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

That there are things in motion is evidenced by sight itself: for there are things whose motion we see. Conversely, sight teaches us that not everything is moved: for we recognize things that are stationary. But neither can we say that everything either undergoes motion or is without motion: for there are things whose perpetual motion we see—there is no doubt, for instance, regarding the celestial bodies. It remains then, he says: that just as some things are always in motion, so there must be something that is always immobile. From these points, it is concluded that there is something immobile; no one opposes or refutes this. For this is a true division and does not contradict the **Platonic** school. Nor, if something is immobile, does it follow that this is the soul. Nor does the claim that the soul moves of itself confirm that the universe is moved; rather, it establishes the manner in which the soul moves. 

If indeed there is something else that is immobile, it will have no bearing on what is established regarding the soul. Even **Aristotle**, seeing this, after teaching that there is something immobile, wishes to say that this is the soul <note>Macrobius is referencing Aristotle’s *Physics* and *De Anima*, where Aristotle challenges the idea of the soul as a self-moving number</note>: and he begins to assert that there is nothing which can move of itself, but that all things which are moved are moved by another. If he had truly proven this, nothing would be left to support the **Platonic** school: for how could it be believed that the soul moves of itself, if it were established that nothing can move of itself? In this Aristotelian argument, the order of this division is woven together. 

Of all things that are moved, he says: some move **through themselves** <term>per se: moving by their own inherent nature or power</term>, others **by accident** <term>ex accidenti: moving only because they are contained within or attached to something else that is moving</term>. And those are moved by accident, he says, which, though they do not move themselves, are nevertheless in something that is moved: like a cargo or a passenger resting in a ship. Or even when a part moves while the whole remains still: as if someone standing were to move a foot, a hand, or the head. However, that which moves **through itself** is that which moves neither by accident nor in part, but the whole moves at once: as when fire ascends to the heights. 

And regarding those things that move by accident, there is no doubt that they are moved by another. But I will also prove, he says, that even those things which move through themselves are moved by another. For of all things that move through themselves, some possess another cause of motion within them: such as animals or trees, which are understood without doubt to be moved by another: namely, by a cause that lies hidden within them <note>Aristotle argues that in living things, the soul is the "other" thing that moves the body</note>. For he does not separate the cause of motion from that which is moved. Others, however, are openly moved by another: that is, either by **force** or by **nature**. And by force we say every javelin is moved: which, when it has left the hand of the thrower, seems to be carried by its own motion: but the origin of the motion is attributed to force; for thus we sometimes see the earth carried upward and fire downward: which an external impulse undoubtedly compels. 

By nature, however, heavy things are moved when they are carried downward by themselves, or light things when they are carried upward. But it must also be said that these are moved by another, though it is uncertain by what. For reason, he says, discovers that there is something—I know not what—that moves these things; for if they moved spontaneously, they would also stop spontaneously. Nor would they always travel a single path; rather, they would move through various ways if they were carried by a spontaneous agitation. Since, however, they cannot do this, but the ascent of light things and the descent of heavy things is always assigned <note>original: "depuratus"; here meaning the natural path is fixed or cleared for them</note>, it appears that their motion is referred to a certain and established necessity of nature. 

These and similar points are what **Aristotle** believed he had proven: that everything which moves is moved by another. But the **Platonists**, as will be shown a little later, taught that these arguments were more clever than true. Now there follows his joined division by which he labors to show that the soul cannot move of itself, even if another thing could do this: and he borrows the first proposition of this matter from those points which he considers established. For he says: Since, therefore, it is established that everything which is moved is moved by another, without doubt that which first moves—because it is not moved by another (for it would not be the first if it were moved by another)—must, he says, either be said to stand still or to move itself. 

For if that which moves it is also said to be moved by another, and that again by another, this inquiry will fall into infinity: you will never find the first beginnings if another always precedes those which you thought were first. It remains, therefore, he says, that if that which first moves is not said to stand still, it must be said to move itself: and thus in one and the same thing there will be one part that moves and another that is moved. Since in every motion, he says, these three things are necessary: that which moves, that by which it moves, and that which is moved. Of these three, that which is moved only undergoes motion: it does not also move; while that by which the motion occurs is both moved and moves; but that which moves is not itself moved: so that from the three, that which is in the middle is common, while the two extremes are understood to be contrary to each other.

<summary>This page explores the philosophical debate between the Platonists and Aristotle regarding the nature of motion, specifically whether the soul moves itself or is moved by another. Macrobius outlines Aristotle's categories of motion—per se, accidental, by force, and by nature—as a challenge to the Platonic doctrine of the soul's self-motion.</summary>

# PAGE XXVIII
## ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

That there are **movable things** is evidenced by sight itself, for we see things that are in motion. Conversely, sight also teaches us that **not all things are moved**, as we recognize things that are stationary. But we cannot say that all things merely alternate between undergoing motion and being without motion, because we see things in perpetual motion—as there is no doubt regarding the **celestial bodies**. It remains, therefore, as he says: that just as some things are always moving, so there must be something that is **always immobile**. No one opposes or refutes the conclusion drawn from these observations that there is something immobile. For this is a true logical division and does not conflict with the Platonic school. Indeed, if something is immobile, it does not necessarily follow that this thing is the soul. Nor does the claim that the soul moves by its own power confirm that all things move; rather, it establishes the specific *manner* in which the soul moves. If there is indeed something else that is immobile, it will have no bearing on what is established concerning the soul.

**Aristotle**, seeing this after he taught that there is something immobile, wishes to say that this [the immobile thing] is the soul. He begins to assert that nothing exists which can be moved by itself, but rather that **everything which moves is moved by another**. If he were to prove this truly, nothing would remain to defend the Platonic sect; for how could it be believed that the soul moves by itself if it were established that *nothing* can be moved by itself?

In this Aristotelian argument, a logical division of this kind is woven together. Of all things that move, he says, some move **of themselves** <note>original: "per se"; meaning intrinsically or directly</note> and others move **by accident** <note>original: "ex accidenti"; meaning they move only because they are part of or inside something else that is moving</note>. He says things move by accident which, while not moving on their own, are nevertheless in something that does move—like a piece of luggage or a passenger resting in a ship; or even when a part moves while the whole remains still, as when someone standing still moves a hand, foot, or head.

However, a thing moves **of itself** when it moves neither by accident nor merely in part, but the whole moves at once—as when fire ascends to higher regions. Regarding those things that move by accident, there is no doubt that they are moved by another. "But," he says, "I will prove that even those things which move of themselves are moved by another." For of all things that move of themselves, some possess the cause of motion within them—such as animals or trees, which are understood to be moved by another, namely by a cause that lies hidden within them; for reason separates the cause of motion from that which is moved.

Others, however, are openly moved by another—that is, either by **force** or by **nature**. We say every projectile is moved by force; for when it has left the hand of the thrower, it seems to be carried by its own motion, but the origin of that motion is referred back to the force applied. In this way, we sometimes see earth carried upward and fire downward, which a foreign impulse undoubtedly compels.

By nature, however, heavy things are moved when they are carried downward of themselves, or light things when they are carried upward. But even of this, it must be said that they are moved by another, though it may be uncertain from what source. For **right reason** <note>original: "ratio"; likely "recta ratio"</note> detects that there is some unknown thing that moves these; for if they were moved spontaneously, they would also stand still spontaneously. Nor would they always travel a single path; rather, they would move through various directions if they were carried by a spontaneous agitation. Since they cannot do this—but ascent is always assigned to light things and descent to heavy things—it appears that their motion is referred to a certain and established **necessity of nature**.

These and similar points are what Aristotle believed proved that everything which moves is moved by another. But the Platonists, as will be demonstrated a little later, taught that these arguments were more clever than they were true. Now, a subsequent division of his must be joined, by which he labors to show that the soul cannot move itself even if another thing could do so; he borrows the first proposition of this matter from those points he considers to have been established. For he says: Since it is established that everything which is moved is moved by another, then without doubt that which **moves first**—because it is not moved by another (for it would no longer be considered "first" if it were moved by another)—must be said either to **stand still** or to **move itself**. For if that which moves it were also said to be moved by another, and that one again by another, this inquiry would fall into infinity; you will never find the first beginnings if another thing always precedes what you thought was first.

It remains, therefore, he says, that if that which moves first is not said to stand still, it must be said to move itself; and thus in one and the same thing there will be one part that moves and another part that is moved. Indeed, he says that in all motion these three things are necessary: **that which moves**, **that by which it moves**, and **that which is moved**. Of these three, that which is moved only *is* moved, it does not also move another; while that through which the motion occurs both moves and is moved; but that which [primarily] moves is not itself moved. Thus, out of the three, the middle one is common to both, while the two ends are understood to be opposites of each other.

<summary>Macrobius presents Aristotle’s challenge to Plato’s theory of the soul as a self-mover, detailing Aristotle's classification of motion into intrinsic, accidental, forced, and natural categories. Aristotle argues for a "Prime Mover" that must be immobile to avoid an infinite regress of causes.</summary>
