# PAGE XXXIII
## BOOK TWO

For just as there is that which is moved and does not move: so he says there is that which moves and is not moved: for this reason we have said: that since everything which is moved is moved by another: if anything moves and is itself moved: we will always seek the source of its motion, and we shall never find a beginning. Then, if anything is said to move itself: it is necessary, he says, that we must think it is moved either as a whole by the whole: or a part by a part: or a part by the whole: or the whole by a part: and yet, whether that motion proceeds from the whole or from a part: it will require another author <note>original: "authorem" — here meaning a primary cause or originator</note> for itself. From all these points, the entire **Aristotelian** reasoning gathers into one conclusion in this manner. Everything that moves is moved by another. That which moves first, therefore: either stands still: or is itself moved by another. But if it is moved by another: then it can no longer be called the "first": and we will always seek what moves the first thing: it remains, therefore, that it must be said to stand still. Therefore, that which first moves stands still. Against **Plato**, therefore, who says the soul is the principle of motion: a logical argument <term>syllogismus: a structured form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</term> is composed in this way: The soul is the principle of motion: but the principle of motion is not moved: therefore, the soul is not moved. And this is what he forcefully objected to in the first place: Not content merely to persuade that the soul is not moved: he also presses with other arguments no less forceful. No beginning <note>original: "initium" — the starting point or origin</note>, he says, can be the same as that of which it is the beginning. For among geometricians, the principle of a line is said to be a point, not a line: Among mathematicians, the principle of number is not a number. Likewise, the cause of being born is not itself born: and therefore the cause of motion itself, as a beginning, should not be moved. Therefore the soul, which is the beginning of motion: is not moved. This is also added: It can never happen, he says, that regarding one and the same thing at one and the same time, opposites pertaining to one and the same thing should occur. We know, however, that to move is to act: and to be moved is to undergo <term>pati: the passive state of being acted upon by an external force</term>. To that which moves itself, therefore, two contrary things will happen simultaneously: both to act and to undergo: which is impossible. The soul, therefore, cannot move itself. Likewise he says: If the essence of the soul were motion: it would never rest from motion: for there is nothing that receives the opposite of its own essence: For fire will never be cold: nor will it hardly ever grow warm of its own accord: but the soul sometimes ceases from motion: for we do not always see the body being driven: Therefore, motion is not the essence of the soul, whose opposite it receives. He also says: If the soul is the cause of motion for others: it cannot be the cause of motion for itself. For there is nothing, he says, that is the cause of the same thing for itself as it is for others: just as a doctor or a physical trainer provides health or strength—which the former gives to the sick and the latter to wrestlers—they do not, by this same act, provide it to themselves. Likewise he says: Every motion requires an instrument for its exercise: as the practice of individual arts teaches. Therefore, it must be seen whether the soul also needs an instrument to move itself. But if that is judged impossible: then it will also be impossible for the soul to move itself. Likewise he says: If the soul is moved: without doubt, along with the remaining types of motion, it is also moved from place to place: If this is so: now it enters the body: now again it departs: and it performs this frequently. But we see that this cannot happen. 
<margin>
Types of 
motion.
</margin>
Therefore, the soul is not moved. To these things he also adds: If the soul moves itself: it is necessary that it moves by some type of motion. Therefore, it either moves itself in a place: or it moves by producing itself: or by consuming itself: or by increasing itself: or by decreasing itself: for these, he says, are the types of motion. Let us ask how each of these can happen. If it moves in a place: it either moves in a straight line: or it rotates in a circle with spherical motion: but there is no infinite straight line. For whatever line is understood in nature: it is undoubtedly bounded by some end. If, therefore, the soul moves along a bounded line: it is not always moved: for when it comes to the end: and from there returns again to the beginning: it is necessary that an interval in the motion occurs in that very change of returning. But neither can it rotate in a circle: because every sphere moves around something immobile: which we call the center <term>centron: the fixed midpoint of a circle or sphere</term>. If, therefore, the soul also moves thus: it must either have within itself that which is immobile: and so it would be that the whole of it is not moved: or if it does not have it within itself: another no less absurd conclusion follows: that the center is outside: which cannot be. It is clear from these points, he says, that it does not move in a place. But if it produces itself: it follows that we must say the same thing both exists and does not exist. If indeed it consumes itself: it will not be immortal. But if it either increases or decreases itself, the same thing will be found to be simultaneously both larger and smaller than itself. From these—

# BOOK TWO XXXIII

For just as there is that which is moved and does not move others, so, he says, there is that which moves others and is not itself moved. This is why we said that since everything that is moved is moved by another, if something moves and is itself also moved, we will always be seeking the source of its motion and will never find a beginning. Furthermore, if something were said to move itself, he says it is necessary that we consider it to be moved either as a whole by the whole, or a part by a part, or a part by the whole, or the whole by a part; and yet, whether that motion proceeds from the whole or from a part, it will require another author for itself. From all these points, **Aristotelian** reasoning <note>Macrobius is summarizing arguments found in Aristotle's *Physics* (Book VIII) and *De Anima* (Book I).</note> gathers the following conclusion in this manner: Everything that moves is moved by another. Therefore, that which first moves either stands still or is itself moved by another. But if it is moved by another, it can no longer be called the "first," and we will always be searching for what moves the first; it remains, therefore, that it must be said to stand still. Thus, that which first moves stands still.

Against **Plato**, therefore, who says the soul is the principle of motion, a <term>syllogism</term> <note>A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> is composed in this way: The soul is the principle of motion; however, the principle of motion does not move. Therefore, the soul does not move. And this is what he first violently objected to. Not content with merely persuading that the soul does not move, he presses on with other reasons no less forceful. No beginning, he says, can be the same as that of which it is the beginning. For among <term>geometers</term>, the principle of a line is said to be a point, not a line. Among <term>arithmeticians</term>, the principle of number is not a number <note>In ancient math, 'one' was often considered the source of numbers rather than a number itself.</note>. Likewise, the cause of birth is not itself born; and therefore the cause of motion itself, as a beginning, should not be moved. Therefore the soul, which is the beginning of motion, does not move.

This is also added: He says it can never happen that regarding one and the same thing, at one and the same time, contraries pertaining to that same thing should occur. We know, however, that to move is to act, and to be moved is to suffer <note>original: "pati"; in a philosophical sense, this means to be the passive recipient of an action.</note>. Therefore, to that which moves itself, two contrary things would happen at once: both acting and suffering—which is impossible. The soul, therefore, cannot move itself. Likewise he says: If the essence of the soul were motion, it would never rest from motion; for there is nothing that receives the contrary of its own essence. For fire will never be cold, nor will it ever hardly grow warm of its own accord <note>as it is already heat itself</note>; yet the soul sometimes ceases from motion, for we do not always see the body being moved.

</margin>

Therefore, the essence of the soul is not motion, since it admits the contrary of motion <note>i.e., rest</note>. He also says: If the soul is the cause of motion for others, it cannot be the cause of motion for itself. For nothing, he says, is the cause of the same thing for itself as it is for others; just as a doctor or a physical trainer provides health or strength—which the former grants to the sick and the latter to wrestlers—they do not necessarily provide these things to themselves by this same act. Likewise he says: All motion requires an instrument for its exercise, as the use of individual arts teaches. Therefore, one must see whether the soul also needs an instrument to move itself. But if that is judged impossible, it will also be impossible for the soul to move itself.

He also says: If the soul is moved, it is undoubtedly moved from place to place, along with the other types of motion. If this is so, it now enters the body, then again exits, and does this frequently. But we see that this cannot happen. Therefore, the soul is not moved. To these things he adds: If the soul moves itself, it must move by some genre of motion. Therefore, it either moves itself in space, or moves by generating itself, or by consuming itself, or by increasing itself, or by decreasing itself; for these, he says, are the <term>genres of motion</term> <note>Aristotle identified several types of change as "motion": locomotion, growth, decay, and generation/corruption.</note>. Let us ask how each of these could happen. If it moves in space, it either moves in a straight line or rotates in a circle with a spherical motion. But a straight line is infinite. For whatever line is understood in nature, it is undoubtedly bounded by some limit. If, therefore, the soul moves through a bounded line, it is not always moved; for when it comes to the end and returns from there back to the beginning, a gap in motion must occur in that very change of returning. 

But neither can it rotate in a circle, because every sphere moves around something immobile, which we call the center <note>original: "centron"</note>. If, therefore, the soul also moves thus, it would either have something within itself that is immobile—and thus it would happen that the whole of it is not moved—or if it does not have this within itself, another no less absurd thing follows: that the center is outside of it, which cannot be. It is established from these things, he says, that it does not move in space. But if it generates itself, it follows that we say the same thing both exists and does not exist. If indeed it consumes itself, it will not be immortal. But if it either increases or decreases itself, the same thing will be found to be at once both larger and smaller than itself. From these—

### PAGE XXXIII
### ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

Our own eyes testify to things in motion: for there are things whose movement we can see. Conversely, sight also teaches us that not all things move: for we recognize things that are stationary. But we cannot say that all things simply fluctuate between moving and being at rest: for we see the perpetual motion of certain things: there is no doubt, for instance, regarding the heavenly bodies <note>original: "caelestibus" — referring to the stars and planets which were thought to be in eternal, circular motion</note>. It remains, therefore, he says: that just as some things always move, there must also be something that is always immobile. No one opposes or refutes the conclusion that something must be immobile. For this is a logically sound division and it does not contradict the **Platonic** school. Even if something is immobile, it does not necessarily follow that this "something" is the soul. Nor does the person who says the soul moves itself claim that the entire universe moves; rather, they are defining the specific way in which the soul moves. If indeed there is some other immobile thing, it will have no bearing on what is established concerning the soul.

Even **Aristotle** himself, seeing this after he taught that there must be something immobile, wishes to claim that this principle is the soul <note>original: "hoc esse aīam uult dicere" — This is a complex point where Macrobius interprets Aristotle's "Prime Mover" in relation to the soul's function</note>: and he begins to assert that nothing can move itself, but rather that everything which moves is moved by another. If he had truly proven this, nothing would remain to support the **Platonic** school: for how could it be believed that the soul moves itself if it were certain that nothing at all can move itself? In this **Aristotelian** argument, the order of his reasoning is woven together as follows. Of all things that move, he says, some move by their own nature <note>original: "per se"</note> and others move incidentally <note>original: "ex accidēti" — or by accident, meaning they move only because they are inside something else that is moving</note>. He says things move incidentally when they do not move themselves but are inside something else that does: like cargo or a resting passenger on a ship. Or even when a part moves while the whole remains still: as if someone standing in one place were to shake a foot, a hand, or their head.

A thing moves by its own nature when it moves neither incidentally nor in part, but the whole moves at once: as when fire rises upward. Regarding those things moved incidentally, there is no doubt they are moved by another. But I shall also prove, he says, that even those things which seem to move by themselves are actually moved by another. For of all things that move by their own nature, some possess the cause of motion within them: such as animals or trees, which are understood to be moved by another—namely, by a cause that lies hidden within them. For reason separates the cause of the motion from the object being moved. Others are openly moved by another: that is, either by force or by nature. We say a javelin is moved by force: for when it has left the hand of the thrower, it seems to be carried by its own motion, but the origin of that motion is attributed to force. In this way, we sometimes see earth carried upward and fire downward: an external force, without doubt, compels them against their own nature.

Things are moved by nature when heavy things fall downward or light things rise upward by their own weight. But even here, it must be said they are moved by another, though it may be uncertain what that "other" is. For reason discovers that there is "some certain something" <note>original: "nescio quid" — an unspecified or mysterious force</note> which moves these: for if they moved spontaneously, they would also stop spontaneously. Nor would they always travel a single path; instead, they would move in various directions if they were driven by a spontaneous impulse. Since they cannot do this—light things always ascending and heavy things always descending—it appears their motion is tied to a fixed and established necessity of nature.

These are the arguments by which **Aristotle** believed he had proven that everything in motion is moved by another. But the **Platonists**, as will be shown shortly, taught that these arguments were more clever than they were true. Now we must look at his next division, by which he labors to show that the soul cannot move itself, even if such a thing were possible for something else. He borrows his first premise from what he believes he has already established. For he says: Since it is established that everything in motion is moved by another, then without doubt, the "first mover," because it is not moved by another (for it would not be the "first" if something else moved it), must either be said to stand still or to move itself. For if the thing moving it were also moved by another, and that again by another, the inquiry would fall into infinity: you would never find a starting point if something always preceded what you thought was first. It remains, therefore, he says, that if the first mover is not stationary, it must move itself. Thus, in one and the same entity, there will be one part that moves and another part that is moved. For in all motion, he says, these three things are necessary: that which moves, that *by which* it moves, and that which is moved. Of these three, that which is moved only receives motion and does not give it; that by which motion happens both receives and gives motion; but the primary mover gives motion without receiving it. Thus, the middle element is shared, while the two ends are opposites.

It concludes by introducing the concept of the "Prime Mover" as either a stationary force or a divided entity where one part moves another.</summary>

For just as there is that which is moved and does not move: so too, he says, there is that which moves and is not moved <note>original: "quod mouet: & non mouet"</note>: because of which we said: that since everything that is moved is moved by another: if something moves and is itself moved, we would always be seeking the source of its motion, and we would never find a beginning. Furthermore, if something is said to move itself, he says it is necessary that we think of it as moved either as a whole by the whole, or a part by a part, or a part by the whole, or the whole by a part: and yet, whether that motion proceeds from the whole or from a part, it will require another author for itself. From all of these, the entire **Aristotelian** reasoning is gathered into one in this manner. Everything that moves is moved by another. That which first moves, therefore, either stands still, or is itself also moved by another. But if it is moved by another, it can no longer be called the "first," and we will always have to ask what moves the first thing; it remains, then, that it must be said to stand still. Therefore, that which first moves stands still.

Against **Plato**, therefore, who says that the soul is the principle of motion <note>original: "aīam motus esse principiū"</note>, a syllogism is composed in this way: The soul is the principle of motion: but the principle of motion does not move. Therefore, the soul is not moved. And this is what he violently objected to in the first place. Not content to persuade us only that the soul is not moved, he also presses with other reasons no less violent. No beginning, he says, can be the same as that of which it is the beginning. For among geometers <term>geometras: scholars of geometry</term>, the principle of a line is said to be a point, not a line. Among mathematicians <term>arithmeticos: those who study the properties of numbers</term>, the principle of a number is not a number. Likewise, the cause of being born is not itself born: and therefore the cause of motion itself, as the beginning, is not moved. Therefore the soul, which is the beginning of motion, is not moved.

This is also added: He says it can never happen that concerning one and the same thing, at one and the same time, contraries pertaining to one and the same thing should occur. We know, however, that to move is to act, and to be moved is to be acted upon <note>original: "mouere facere est: & moueri pati est" — a distinction between active doing and passive receiving</note>. Therefore, to that which moves itself, two contrary things would happen at once: both to act and to be acted upon: which is impossible. The soul, therefore, cannot move itself. He also says: If the essence of the soul were motion, it would never rest from motion: for there is nothing that receives the contrary of its own essence. For fire will never be cold: nor will it hardly ever grow warm of its own accord <note>Macrobius means fire is essentially hot, so it doesn't "become" hot, it simply *is* hot</note>; the soul, however, sometimes ceases from motion: for we do not always see the body being agitated. Therefore, motion is not the essence of the soul, since it admits the contrary of motion (rest).

He says further: If the soul is the cause of motion for others, it cannot be the cause of motion for itself. For there is nothing, he says, that is the cause for itself of the same thing which it provides to others: just as a physician or a physical trainer provides health or strength—which the former gives to the sick and the latter to wrestlers—they do not necessarily provide these things to themselves from this same act. Likewise he says: Every motion requires an instrument for its exercise, as the use of individual arts teaches. Therefore, we must see whether the soul also needs an instrument to move itself. But if that is judged impossible, then this too will be impossible: that the soul should move itself. Likewise he says: If the soul is moved, it is moved without doubt by the remaining motions, and is moved from place to place. But if this is so, now it enters the body, and now again it departs, and it performs this frequently. But we see that this cannot happen. Therefore, the soul is not moved.

<margin>Types of motion.</margin>
To these things he also adds: If the soul moves itself, it is necessary that it moves by some type of motion. Therefore, either it moves in place, or it moves by generating itself, or by consuming itself, or by increasing itself, or by decreasing itself: for these, he says, are the types of motion. Let us ask how these individual things can happen. If it moves in place, it moves either in a straight line or it rotates in a circle with a spherical motion. But there is no infinite straight line. For whatever line is understood in nature, it is without doubt terminated by some end. If, therefore, the soul moves through a terminated line, it is not always moved: for when it comes to the end and returns from there back to the beginning, it is necessary that an interval of motion occurs in that very change of returning. But neither can it rotate in a circle: because every sphere moves around something immobile, which we call the <term>centron: the center point of a circle or sphere</term>. If, therefore, the soul also moves in this way, it must either have that which is immobile within itself—and thus it would not be moved as a whole—or if it does not have it within itself, another no less absurd thing follows: that the center is outside of it, which cannot be. It is established from these things, he says, that it does not move in place. But if it generates itself, it follows that we say it both exists and does not exist at the same time. If indeed it consumes itself, it will not be immortal. But if it either increases or decreases itself, the same thing will be found to be at once both larger and smaller than itself.

### ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

...he gathers such a syllogism: If the soul moves itself, it moves by some kind of motion; but no kind of motion by which it might move itself is found; therefore it does not move itself. 
<margin>
Platonist arguments against Aristotle regarding the motion of the soul.
</margin>
Against these so subtle, clever, and plausible arguments, one must be prepared, following the followers of Plato, who undermined the attempt by which Aristotle had tried to wound the so true and so valid definition of his master. Indeed, I am not so forgetful of my own standing or so bold as to resist Aristotle or support Plato from my own genius; rather, just as each of the great men who gloried in being called Platonists left behind one or two defenses for the display of their own works, I have heaped these collected points together into one body of continuous defense, adding whatever was right to feel or possible to understand after them. And because there are two things he [Aristotle] attempted to assert—one, where he says there is nothing that moves from itself; the other, by which he confirms that the soul cannot be this—both must be resisted, so that it may be established that something can be moved from itself, and that it may become clear that the soul is this thing. First, therefore, we must be wary of the tricks of that division in which, by enumerating some things that move from themselves and showing that those are also moved by another (that is, by a cause lurking within), he seems to himself to have proved that all things which move—even if they are said to move from themselves—are nevertheless moved by another. For a part of this matter is true, but the conclusion is false. For we do not deny that there are some things which, though they seem to move from themselves, are known to be moved by another; however, not everything that moves from itself undergoes this necessity of being moved by another. For when Plato says the soul moves from itself—that is, when he calls it a <term>self-mover <note>original: αὐτοκίνητον (autokinēton)</note></term>—he does not want it to be numbered among those things which seem to move from themselves but are moved by a cause lurking within them, as animals are moved by an author who is different but hidden (for they are moved by a soul), or as trees are moved, for even if their driver is not seen, it is clear they are driven by nature lurking within them. 

But Plato says the soul moves from itself in such a way that he does not name another cause, either happening from without or lurking within, as the author of this motion. We shall explain how this should be understood. We call fire "hot," but we also say iron is "hot"; and we name snow "cold" and a stone "cold"; honey is "sweet," but we also call honey-wine "sweet." Yet each of these signifies different things for different subjects. For we take the name of "hot" differently regarding fire than regarding iron, because fire is hot through itself <note>original: "per se"</note> and does not become hot from another. On the contrary, iron does not grow hot except from another. Likewise, snow is cold and honey is sweet because it happened from no other source; yet the coldness in a stone or the sweetness in honey-wine comes from the snow or the honey. Thus, "standing" and "moving" are said of both those things which stand or move by themselves, and those which are stopped or driven by another. But for those things which happen to be moved or stand by another, these also cease to stand and move. However, for those things where "being" and "moving" are the same, they never cease from motion, because they cannot exist without their own essence. Just as iron loses heat, fire truly does not cease to be hot. Therefore, the soul moves from itself, even though animals or trees may seem to move through themselves. For to those, a different cause (though lurking within)—that is, a soul or nature—ministers motion, and therefore they lose that which they took from elsewhere. The soul, however, moves through itself just as fire is hot through itself, with no adventitious cause either heating the latter or moving the former. For when we call fire "hot," we do not conceive of two different things: one which heats and another which is heated; rather, we call the whole thing "hot" according to its nature. When we call snow "cold" or honey "sweet," we do not perceive one thing which provides this quality and another to which it is provided. So also when we say the soul is moved through itself, a twin consideration of the mover and the moved does not follow; rather, we recognize its essence in the motion itself. Because that which is the name of "hot" in fire, the word for "cold" in snow, and the designation of "sweet" in honey, must be understood as the name <term>self-mover <note>original: αὐτοκίνητον (autokinēton)</note></term> regarding the soul, which the Latin translation signifies as "moving through itself." Nor should it confuse you that "to be moved" <note>original: "moueri"</note> is a passive verb; nor, as when "to be cut" is said, are two things considered equally: that which cuts and that which is cut. Likewise, when "to be held" is said, two are understood: that which holds and...

<page-num>XXXIIII</page-num>
<header>BOOK TWO XXXIIII</header>

...that which is held: so here, in the term "to be moved," you should consider it to have a twofold meaning: that which moves and that which is <term>moved</term><note>The Latin word *moueri* is a passive form ("to be moved"), but Macrobius argues it doesn't always imply an external force.</note>. For indeed, to be cut or to be held is a <term>passion</term><note>In ancient philosophy, a "passion" (passio) is any state where something is acted upon by an external agent, rather than being the source of its own action.</note>; therefore, it encompasses the consideration of both the "doer" and the "receiver." However, when "to be moved" is said of things that are moved by another, it similarly represents both considerations. But regarding that which moves by itself—so that it is <note>original Greek: αυτοκίνητον</note> self-moving—when it is said "to be moved," because it moves from itself and not from another, no suspicion of "passion" can be understood. For even though "to stand" may not appear to be a passive verb, when it is said of something that stands because another set it upright—as a spear stands when fixed in the earth—it signifies a "passion." Likewise, although "to be moved" may sound passive, if there is no "doer" involved, there can be no "receiver" of the action. And to make it more absolutely clear that passion is signified by the reality of things rather than the sound of words: behold, when fire is carried to the upper regions, it suffers nothing; but when it is carried downward, it undoubtedly suffers a passion, because it does not endure this unless another force impels it. Thus, though one and the same word is uttered, we say that "passion" is sometimes present and sometimes absent. Therefore, "to be moved" is the same in meaning as "to be hot": when we say iron is hot or a stylus is moved, we admit it is a passion because both states come from elsewhere. But when it is said that fire is hot or the soul moves—because the 
<margin>Essence</margin>essence of the former is in its heat and the essence of the latter is in its motion—no room is left here for passion; rather, the soul is said to move just as the fire is said to be hot. In this place, Aristotle, weaving a clever verbal trick, contends that Plato himself signified two things—that is, the mover and the moved—by saying: "Only that which moves itself, because it never deserts itself, never ceases to be moved." Aristotle proclaims that Plato aptly distinguished the two with these words: "that which moves" and "is moved." But it seems to me that a man so great as Aristotle could not have been ignorant of the truth, but rather, in an exercise of cleverness, he voluntarily engaged in a task suited to his wit. For who would not notice that when one says something "moves itself," two separate things are not to be understood? It is just as when one says <note>original Greek: ἑαυτόν τιμωρούμενος</note> "punishing himself"—is there one who punishes and another who is punished? And when someone says they "lose themselves," "envelop themselves," or "free themselves," it is not necessary for there to be one person acting and another person receiving the action. Rather, this alone is expressed by the meaning of the phrase: that he who punishes himself or frees himself has not received this from another, but has either brought it upon himself or provided it for himself. So also, when it is said of the <note>original Greek: αυτοκίνητον</note> "self-moving" that it moves itself, it is said in order to exclude the estimation of any other mover. Plato, wishing to remove such a thought from the reader's mind, expressed it by what he stated previously: for that which always moves is eternal; that which brings motion to another and is itself moved from elsewhere, having an end to its motion, must necessarily have an end to its living. What could be found more explicit than these words, testifying with clear meaning that what moves itself is not moved from elsewhere? For he says the soul is eternal for this reason: because it moves itself and is not moved from elsewhere. Therefore, "to move itself" signifies this alone: not to be moved by another. Do not think that the same thing moves and the same thing is moved; rather, "to be moved" without another mover is, in itself, "to move." It is therefore clearly established that not everything that is moved is moved by another. Thus, the self-mover cannot be moved by another; nor indeed is it moved by itself in such a way that there is one part moving and another being moved—neither in whole nor in part, as Aristotle proposes. Instead, it is said to move itself for this reason alone: so that it is not thought to be moved by another. Furthermore, that Aristotelian division of motions, which we mentioned above, is more suited to a deceptive argument than a proof. In it he says: "Just as there is that which is moved and does not move, so there is that which moves and is not moved." For it is certain that everything that is moved moves other things—as it is said that a rudder moves a ship, or a ship moves the air surrounding it or the waves. What is there that, while it is being moved, cannot impel something else? If it is not true that things being moved do not move other things, then your premise—that you can find something which moves but is not itself moved—does not hold. Therefore, that division of motions put forward by Plato in the tenth book of the *Laws* is more to be approved. He says: "Every motion is either that which moves itself and others, or that which is moved by another and moves others." The first refers to the soul; the second to all bodies. These two motions are separated by their difference and joined by their shared nature. They have this in common: both the first and the second move other things. But they differ in this: the former is moved by itself, the latter by another. From all these...

He refutes Aristotle’s linguistic critiques by comparing the soul's self-motion to someone "freeing themselves"—an action where the mover and moved are a single, unified identity.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Macrobius's defense of the Platonic definition of the soul as a self-moving entity. Having previously addressed Aristotle's logical objections—specifically that a "first mover" must itself be stationary—Macrobius now methodically dismantles those arguments to prove that the soul’s very nature is motion.</meta>

<page-num>CLXXXI</page-num>
<header>CONCERNING THE DREAM OF SCIPIO</header>

What we have gathered, drawn from the fertile insights of the Platonists, establishes that it is not true that everything which moves is moved by another. Therefore, the <term>principle of motion</term><note>The "principle" (principium) refers to the starting point or origin of any action.</note> cannot be said to stand still out of a necessity to appease some other mover. This is because, as we have said, it can move itself without being moved by anything else. Thus, the <term>syllogism</term><note>A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two shared premises.</note> has been weakened—the one which had been constructed through various and complex divisions. That argument was: "The soul is the principle of motion; the principle of motion does not move; therefore, the soul does not move." It remains then, since it has been established that something can move by itself without an external mover, to show that the soul is this very thing. This will be easily demonstrated if we take our arguments from clear and indubitable facts. Either the soul, the body, or a mixture of both provides motion to a human being. Since these are the three possibilities upon which this inquiry proceeds, and since it is established that this motion can be provided neither by the body nor by the mixture, it remains beyond doubt that the human is moved by the soul. Now let us speak of each individually, and first of the body. It is more manifest than any assertion can make it that no inanimate body moves by its own motion. Furthermore, nothing that is itself immobile can move something else; therefore, the body does not move the human. We must see whether perhaps the very mixture of soul and body provides this motion for itself. But because it is agreed that motion does not belong to the body, if it is also not present in the soul, then no motion can be produced from two things that lack motion. Just as bitterness will not come from two sweet things, nor sweetness from two bitter things, nor will heat be born from a double cold, or cold from a double heat. For every quality increases when doubled; a contrary quality never emerges from doubling similar things. Therefore, motion will not come from two immobile things. Thus, the mixture will not move the human. From this, an unassailable syllogism is gathered from the indubitable light of conceded facts: A living creature moves; however, either the soul, the body, or the mixture of both provides motion to the creature. But neither the body nor the mixture provides motion. Therefore, the soul provides motion. From these points, it appears that the soul is the beginning of motion; and the previous discussion taught that the beginning of motion moves by itself. There is no doubt, therefore, that the soul is <note>original Greek: "αὐτοκίνητον"</note> **self-moving**, that is, it moves by its own power. At this point, that opponent speaks up again and fights with another dispute concerning "beginnings." We shall repeat the same solutions here which we have set out above in the order of objections. He says: "Those things which are born from their beginnings cannot be the same as the beginnings themselves." And for that reason, the soul, which is the principle of motion, should not move, lest the beginning be the same thing as that which is born from the beginning—that is, lest motion seem to have proceeded from motion. To this, there is a ready and absolute response: although we admit that principles and those things which come forth from principles may sometimes differ in some way, they can never be so contrary to each other as "standing still" and "moving" are to one another. For if the beginning of white were called black, and if the origin of moisture were dryness, then good would proceed from evil, and sweet from a bitter beginning. But it is not so, because nature does not allow the beginnings and the subsequent things to disagree to the point of being contraries. However, a difference is sometimes found between them, such as is appropriate between an origin and its progression; as is the case here between the motion by which the soul moves and that by which it moves other things. For Plato did not simply say the soul was "motion," but "self-moving motion." What lies between "self-moving motion" and "motion by which it moves others" is quite clear: for the former has no external author, while the latter is the author of motion for others. It is established, therefore, that it is impossible for beginnings and the things created from beginnings to differ so much that they are contraries, nor, however, was a moderate difference lacking here. Therefore, the principle of motion will not be "standing still," as that opponent gathered with his clever conclusion. To these, a third objection followed (as we remember): that two contrary things cannot happen to one thing at the same time—meaning that because "to move" and "to be moved" are contraries, the soul cannot move itself unless it is moving and being moved at once. But the points asserted above dissolve this: for it is agreed that in the motion of the soul, two separate things are not to be understood (that which moves and that which is moved), since "to be moved by oneself" is nothing other than "to be moved without another moving it." There is no contradiction where what is happening is a single thing, because it is not happening from one to another; indeed, the very motion of the soul is its essence. And for this, a fourth occasion arose (as we related above)...

<summary>Macrobius argues that the soul must be the source of human motion through a process of elimination, concluding that the soul is inherently self-moving (autokinēton). He refutes the idea that a "first mover" must be stationary, asserting that the soul's essence is motion itself.</summary>

<page-num>XXXV</page-num>
<header>BOOK TWO</header>

of the debate. If the <term>essence</term><note>The "essence" (essentia) refers to the fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing that makes it what it is.</note> of the soul is motion, he asks: why does it sometimes rest? For no other thing admits a quality contrary to its own essence. Fire, whose essence is heat, never ceases to be hot. And because the coldness of snow is in its essence, it is never anything but cold. Therefore, by the same reasoning, the soul ought never to cease from motion. But I would like him to say when he suspects the soul ceases? If, he says, by moving itself it must also move the body, then surely when we see the body is not moving, we should understand that the soul also is not moving.

Against this, a twofold defense is at hand. First, because the motion of the soul is not detected only by whether the body is driven. For even when no part of the body is seen to move in a human, yet thought itself—or in any animal, hearing, sight, smell, and the like—as well as dreaming those hoped-for things in rest itself, all these are motions of the soul. Furthermore, who would say the body itself is immobile, even when it does not seem to be driven? Consider the growth of the limbs, or if the age and time for growing has already passed, consider the beating of the heart which is impatient of stopping; consider the orderly digestion of food which, by a natural distribution, provides nourishment between the veins and the organs; consider how the very collection of flowing fluids testifies to the perpetual agitation of the body. Therefore, the soul moves by an eternal motion that is its own, and the body also moves for as long as it is animated by that initial source and cause of motion.

From this arises the spark of his fifth question. If the soul, he says, is the cause of motion for others, it cannot be the cause of motion for itself, because there is nothing that is the cause of the same thing for both itself and others. Truly, although I could easily prove there are many things which are the cause of the same thing for both themselves and others, nevertheless, lest I seem too eager to oppose everything he asserts, I will concede this to be true; for even held as true, it will not harm the assertion of the soul’s motion. For we call the soul the <term>origin</term><note>Latin: *initium*. The starting point or source from which something begins.</note> of motion and the cause; we shall see about the cause later. Meanwhile, it is established that every origin exists within the thing of which it is the origin. Therefore, whatever proceeds into any thing from its origin is found in that origin itself; thus, the origin of heat cannot fail to be hot. Who would deny that the fire itself, from which heat passes into other things, is hot? But fire, he says, does not heat itself, because by nature it is entirely hot. I have grasped what I wanted: for neither does the soul move itself in such a way that there is a distinction between the motion and the mover, but the whole soul is moved by its own motion in such a way that you cannot name any part of it that moves <note>original: "nihil possis spirare quod moveat"</note>.

These things said about the origin shall suffice. Regarding the "cause," since we have freely granted through a spontaneous agreement that nothing should be the cause of the same thing for itself and others, we willingly acquiesce so that the soul, which is the cause of motion for others, might not be seen as the cause of motion for itself. For the soul is the cause of motion for those things which would not move unless it provided it. The soul, however, does not bestow motion upon itself so that it may move, but it is of its own essence that it moves. From this, the question that arises is resolved: for then perhaps I might concede that instruments are required for the exercise of motion when the thing that moves is one thing and the thing being moved is another. In the soul, however, not even a scurrilous joke would dare to seek this without the risk of anger; its motion is in its essence. Just as fire, although it may be moved by some hidden cause within itself, nevertheless reaches for the heavens without the need for any instruments. Much less are these instruments to be sought in the soul, whose essence is its own motion.

In the things that follow, a man so great <note>Macrobius refers here to Aristotle.</note> and otherwise extraordinarily keen, seems like one who is merely cavilling. If the soul moves, he says, then among other types of motion, it also moves from place to place. Therefore, he says, it now exits the body, now enters it again, and is often occupied in this exercise—which we do not see happen; therefore the soul does not move. Against this: there is no one who would not respond without hesitation that not everything that moves also moves from place to place. Finally, a similar line of questioning should be turned back upon him more aptly. Do you say that trees move? Since I think he would agree, he shall be struck by the same wit. If trees move, then doubtless (as you are accustomed to say) among other motions they also move from place to place. But we see they cannot do this by themselves; therefore trees do not move. But so that we can make this <term>syllogism</term><note>A logical argument where a conclusion is reached from two premises.</note> more forceful by an addition, after we have said "therefore trees do not move," we shall add: "but trees do move." Therefore, not everything that moves also moves from place to place. And thus the end escapes into the outcome of a sound conclusion. If, therefore, we admit that trees indeed move, but by a motion suited to them...

He uses the analogy of growing trees to prove that motion does not always require moving from one place to another.</summary>

<page-num>XXXIX</page-num>
<header>ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO</header>

...followed. <note>original: "tuntur" (likely part of 'sequuntur' or 'conceduntur')</note> Shall we deny this to the soul: that it is moved by a motion agreeable to its own <term>essence</term><note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "essence" is the fundamental nature of a being that cannot be changed without the being ceasing to exist.</note>? These and other strong arguments might be stated even if the soul could not move by this spatial kind of motion; but since it indeed animates the body by its arrival and departs from the body by a certain law of established time, who would deny that it is also moved in space (so to speak)? As to the fact that it does not frequently vary its arrival and departure within a single span of time, this is the result of a secret and deliberate arrangement of nature. To keep the life of the living creature bound by certain chains, nature has instilled such a love of the body in the soul that it loves that to which it is joined of its own accord; thus it rarely happens that it departs, even when the law of its time is finished, except mourning and unwillingly.

Having dissolved this objection too (as I believe), let us come to those questions with which he <note>Macrobius is referring to Aristotle here.</note> seems to press us. "If the soul moves itself," he says, "it moves by some kind of motion: must we say then that the soul moves itself in space? Therefore that space is either a circle or a line. Or does it move by separating or consuming? Does it increase or decrease itself? Or let him bring forward another kind of motion by which we may say it is moved."

But all this bothersome heap of questions flows from one and the same cunning of a poorly conceived definition. For because he once proposed to himself that "everything which is moved is moved by another," he seeks all these types of motion in the soul—the kind where one thing is the mover and another is the thing being moved. Yet none of these categories can apply to the soul, in which there is no distinction between the mover and the moved.

"What then is it?" someone will say, "or how is the motion of the soul understood if none of these apply?" Whoever desires to know this will learn it either from Plato’s teaching or from <term>Tully’s</term><note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, whose "Dream of Scipio" serves as the foundation for this commentary.</note>: "Indeed, for all other things that are moved, this is the source <note>original: "fons"</note>, this is the principle of moving." How great the expression of this word is, by which the soul is called the "fount of motion," you will easily find if you conceive in your mind the motion of an invisible thing without an author—and therefore proceeding without beginning and without end and moving other things—for which nothing more similar among visible things could be found than a fountain. A fountain is the beginning of water in such a way that while it creates rivers and lakes from itself, it is said to be born from nothing else.

For if it were born from another, it would not be the principle itself. And just as a source is not always easily discovered, yet from it are poured out the Nile, or the <term>Eridanus</term><note>The Po River in Italy.</note>, or the <term>Hister</term><note>The Danube River.</note>, or the <term>Tanais</term><note>The Don River.</note>. And as you wonder at seeing their swiftness, and seeking within yourself the origin of such great waters, you run back in thought to the source, and you understand all this motion to flow from the first principle of the spring; so when, by considering the motion of bodies—whether they be divine or earthly—you perhaps wish to seek their author, let your mind run back to the soul as if to a source.

Its motion, even without the service of the body, is testified by thoughts, joys, hopes, and fears. For its motion is the discernment of good and evil, the love of virtues, and the desire for vices, from which flow all the channels of things born thereafter. For its motion is whenever we are angry and are armed in the heat of mutual collision, from which the madness of battles gradually proceeds and fluctuates. Its motion is that we are swept into desires, that we are bound by lusts. But if these motions are governed by <term>reason</term><note>original: "ratione"</note>, they become healthy; if they are abandoned, they are both swept headlong and sweep others with them.

You have learned the motions of the soul, which it exercises sometimes without the body's service, and sometimes through the body. If indeed you seek the motions of the <term>World Soul</term><note>The 'Anima Mundi,' the soul that Neoplatonists believed animated the entire universe and directed the stars.</note> itself, look upon the celestial revolutions and the rapid impulses of the spheres lying beneath, the rising or setting of the sun, the courses or retrogressions of the stars: all of which proceed with the soul moving them. Truly, to say that she is immobile—she who moves all things—was not fitting for Aristotle; how great he is in other matters has been proven, but in this he is great only to one whom the power of nature and manifest reason does not move.

Therefore, having taught and asserted the motion of the soul, <term>Africanus</term><note>Scipio Africanus the Younger, the protagonist of the Dream.</note> commands and instructs in these words how its exercise must be used: "**Exercise this [soul] in the best things.**" Now, the best cares are for the safety of the fatherland; stirred and exercised by these, the soul will fly back more swiftly to this seat and its own home. And it will do this more quickly if, even then while it is enclosed in the body, it reaches outward and, contemplating those things which are outside, abstracts itself as much as possible from the body. For as for those who have given themselves over to the pleasures of the body and have offered themselves as its servants, so to speak, and obeying pleasures by the impulse of lusts have violated the laws of gods and men, having slipped out of their bodies, they roll around the earth itself, nor [into this]...

<summary>Macrobius defines the soul as the "fount of motion," using the metaphor of a spring feeding great rivers to explain how an invisible principle moves all physical bodies and celestial spheres. He concludes by relaying Scipio Africanus's advice to exercise the soul in virtuous service to the state to ensure its swift return to the heavens.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page concludes Macrobius's commentary. Following the previous discussion on the nature of the soul's motion, the author now categorizes the types of virtues and explains how this specific work—Cicero’s Dream of Scipio—serves as a complete compendium of all branches of philosophy (Moral, Natural, and Rational).</meta>

<page-num>XXXVI</page-num>
<header>BOOK TWO XXXVI</header>

...they do not return to their place <note>original: "locū" (locum)</note> unless they have been tossed about for many ages. In the earlier part of this work, we said that virtues are sometimes **at leisure** <note>original: "ociofas" (otiosas); referring to the contemplative life of a philosopher</note> and sometimes **active** <note>original: "negociosas"; referring to the busy life of a statesman</note>: the former are suitable for philosophers, the latter for the rulers of republics. Nevertheless, both types of virtue make the person who practices them blessed. These virtues are sometimes divided, but often they are mixed when a mind is found to be capable of both by nature and by training. For if someone is a stranger to all formal doctrine, yet in the republic he is prudent, temperate, brave, and just, he stands out even while removed from the contemplative life; through the vigor of these **active virtues**, heaven nonetheless yields to him as a reward. 

But if someone, within the quiet of their nature, is not fit for action, but is instead carried upward solely by the excellent gift of conscience, and spends their store of learning on the practice of divine disputation—a follower of heavenly things and a wanderer from fleeting, perishable things—he too will be carried to the heights of heaven by these **leisurely virtues**. Yet it often happens that the same heart is sublime in the perfection of both acting and disputing, and attains heaven through both exercises of virtue. 

Let **Romulus** be placed by us in the first category; his life never abandoned the virtues but always practiced them. In the second is **Pythagoras**, who was an artist of discourse rather than action, following only the virtues of doctrine and conscience. In the third and "mixed" category, among the Greeks, let there be **Lycurgus** and **Solon**; among the Romans, **Numa**, both **Catoes**, and many others who both drank deeply of philosophy and established the firmament of the republic. For just as Greece produced many men dedicated solely to the leisure of wisdom, Rome has not been without them. 

Since, therefore, our **Africanus** <note>Scipio Africanus the Younger, the protagonist of the Dream</note>—whom his grandfather just now instructed as a teacher—is of that kind which both borrows a rule for living from doctrine and supports the state with virtues, for that reason the precepts of a twofold perfection are commanded to him. But because he is stationed in the camp and sweating under arms, the **political virtues** are suggested to him first, in these words:

> But the best cares are for the safety of the fatherland; the mind that is stirred and exercised by these will fly more swiftly to this seat and to its own home. 

Then, since philosophy is no less suitable for a learned man than for a brave one, it is added:

> And it will do this more quickly if, even then when it is shut up in the body, it stands out abroad, and by contemplating those things which are outside, it abstracts itself as much as possible from the body. 

For these are the precepts of that doctrine which says that "death" <note>The "philosophical death," or the detachment of the soul's interests from the physical body's needs.</note> is to be desired by those practicing philosophy. From this it follows that those still placed in the body should despise the body as a **foreign burden** (as far as nature allows). He persuasively argues for these virtues now and at the opportune time, after he has declared how great and how divine the rewards owed to virtue are. 

But because a law is called "imperfect" if no penalty is sanctioned for those who stray, he therefore sanctions a punishment at the conclusion of the work for those living outside these precepts. **Hermagoras the Platonist** <note>Likely referring to a Neo-Platonist commentator, though the identification is debated by scholars</note> followed this topic more copiously, numbering infinite ages in which the souls of the guilty, often rolled back into the same punishments, are permitted to emerge from <term>Tartarus</term> <note>The deep abyss in Greco-Roman mythology used as a dungeon of torment for the wicked</note> only late; and at last, having obtained purification, they return to the principles of their nature, which is heaven. 

For it is necessary that every soul return to the seat of its origin. Those who inhabited the body as if it were a foreign land return quickly after the body [is gone], as if to their fatherland. But those who clung to the allurements of bodies as if to their own homes—the more violently they are separated from them, the later they return to the heights.

<margin>Moral, Natural, and Rational philosophy</margin>
But now let us bring an end to the discussion, concluding the dream with this added point which befits the closing: since there are three parts of all philosophy—**moral**, **natural**, and **rational**—and moral is that which teaches the perfected correction of character; natural is that which disputes concerning divine bodies; and rational is when the discourse is about incorporeal things which the mind alone embraces; **Tullius** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the author of the original *Dream of Scipio*</note> omitted none of these three in this dream. 

For that exhortation to the virtues, to the love of country, and to the contempt of glory—what else does it contain but the **moral instructions of ethics**? But when he speaks either of the motion of the spheres, or the novelty and magnitude of the stars, and of the sun's sovereignty, and the celestial circles, and the terrestrial zones, and the situation of the ocean, and reveals the secret of the harmony of the spheres, he commemorates the **secrets of physics**. And when he disputes concerning the motion and immortality of the soul—which is established to be in no way corporeal, and whose essence no sense but **reason** alone perceives—there he ascends to the height of **rational philosophy**. 

Truly, therefore, it must be pronounced that nothing is more perfect than this work, in which the entire integrity of philosophy is contained.

Here, Macrobius shifts from philosophical commentary to a literary and historical compendium, though he continues the theme of intellectual and moral development, now addressed specifically to his son, Eustachius.</meta>

<page-num>XXXXV</page-num>
<header>THE FIRST BOOK OF THE SATURNALIA</header>

# THE FIRST BOOK OF THE SATURNALIA
# Of Macrobius Aurelius Theodosius, a Man of Consular and Illustrious Rank, concerning the Banquet of the First Day. To his son, Eustachius.

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut illustration depicting a banquet (convivium). Five men in classical robes are seated around a wooden table. Two sit on the left, one at the far end facing the viewer, and two on the right. The central figure appears to be speaking or gesturing. On the table are plates with food, including a whole roasted bird, and a large pitcher. To the right of the illustration is a large decorative woodcut initial "M", elaborately historiated with floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>

**M**ANY and various are the things, my son Eustachius, which nature has made dear to us in this life; yet nothing has she bound us to more closely than the love of those to whom we have given life. Nature has willed that our care in educating and instructing them be such that parents can feel no greater pleasure if their desires for their children succeed according to their wishes, nor greater sorrow if the opposite should occur. Hence it is that I, too, value nothing more highly than your instruction. To achieve its perfection, I have chosen to take shortcuts rather than long, winding paths. Being impatient of all delay, I do not merely wish for you to advance through those subjects which you yourself study so diligently; I am also acting so that I may have read for you as well. Whatever I have gathered—either after you were born or before your birth—from various volumes written in both the Greek and Roman languages, all of it shall serve as your "furniture of knowledge" <note>original: "sciētiæ suppellex"; a metaphor for a well-stocked mind</note>. It will be like a sort of literary storehouse <note>original: "pēu" (penu); a larder or pantry</note>, so that whenever the need arises—whether to recall a history that lies hidden from the public in a pile of books, or a memorable word or deed—it may be easily found and brought forth for you.

Nor have I gathered these noteworthy things into a disorganized heap; rather, I have arranged these various matters, drawn from diverse authors and confused in their chronology, into a certain "body" of work. Thus, what I had noted down indiscriminately and mixed together as an aid to my own memory has now come together in an orderly fashion, like the connected parts of a limb. Do not find fault with me if I often explain matters I have borrowed from various readings in the very words used by the authors who first told them; for the present work does not promise a display of eloquence, but a collection of things worth knowing. You ought to be satisfied if you learn of ancient lore—sometimes through my own descriptions, which are not obscure, and sometimes through the faithful words of the ancients themselves—just as each subject suggested itself to be either narrated or transcribed.

Indeed, we ought in a way to imitate the bees, which wander about and pluck flowers, then arrange whatever they have brought back, distributing it through the honeycombs and transforming the various juices into a single flavor by a certain blending and by the unique property of their own breath. We, too, should commit to the pen whatever we have acquired from diverse readings, so that they may coalesce into this same orderly arrangement. For things are better preserved in the mind when they are distinct; yet this distinction is not without a certain "leaven" <note>an agent of transformation, like yeast</note> which seasons the whole, blending the various offerings for the use of a single flavor. Thus, even if it is apparent from where a thing was taken, it will nevertheless appear to be something other than the source from which it was derived. 

We see nature doing this in our own bodies without any effort of our own. The foods we take in, as long as they remain in their own quality and float as solids, are a heavy burden to the stomach; but once they have been changed from what they were, only then do they pass into strength and blood. We should ensure the same for the things that nourish our 
<margin>Digestion</margin>
intellects: whatever we have swallowed, we must not allow it to remain whole, lest it remain foreign; rather, we must cook it into a certain **digested arrangement** <note>original: "digeriē" (digeriem)</note>. Otherwise, these things may enter the memory, but not the intellect. Let us gather from all sources, so that one thing may be made from many, just as a single number is formed from individual units. Let our mind do this: let it hide away all the things it has heard, yet let it show forth the very thing it has produced. Just as those who compose fragrant perfumes take care, above all, that no single scent dominates the mixture, they instead consult the juices of all...

He uses famous metaphors of bees making honey and the stomach digesting food to explain how a scholar must transform varied readings into a unified, personal intellect.</summary>

...of many fragrances into one breath. <margin>Chorus</margin> You see how many voices a chorus consists of, yet one sound is returned from them all. There is a high pitch, a low pitch, and a middle pitch; women's voices are added to the men's, and the sound of the flute is interspersed. In this way, the voices of individuals are hidden, but the voices of all appear, and a harmony is made from discordant parts. I wish this present work to be such. In it are many arts, many teachings, and examples from many ages—but all breathed into one. If you do not despise what you already know, nor avoid what is unknown to you, you will find much here that is a pleasure to read, a refinement to have read, or a benefit to remember. For I believe nothing is inserted into this work that is either useless to know or difficult to grasp. Instead, everything is designed so that your intellect might be <term>more vigorous<note>original: "vegetius" — Macrobius uses this word to mean lively or spirited, likely a play on his son's education being a "living" thing.</note></term>, your memory more supported, your oratory more skilled, and your speech more pure—unless, perhaps, because we were born under a different sky, the vein of the Latin tongue does not support us. <margin>More supported</margin>

What we wish to obtain from those who may eventually spend time learning these things is that they judge fairly and kindly if the native elegance of the Roman mouth is lacking in our speech. But I am being careless, for I might incur the same rebuke that Marcus Cato once leveled at Aulus Albinus, who was consul with Lucius Lucullus. <margin>Aulus Albinus</margin> That Albinus wrote a history of Roman affairs in the Greek language. In the first part of that history, he wrote words to this effect: that no one should be angry with him if anything in those books was written without proper composition or elegance; for, he said, "I am a Roman man born in Latium, and Greek eloquence is most foreign to us." Therefore, he asked for pardon for any lack of quality. When Marcus Cato read this, he said: "Truly, Aulus, you are a great trifler! You preferred to beg off a fault rather than be free of the fault itself. For we usually seek pardon either when we have erred through ignorance or when we have committed a wrong <margin>Pleading for a fault</margin> under the command of another. Who," he asked, "I pray, forced you to commit that for which you had to ask for forgiveness before you even did it?" Now, we shall state the outline we have given to this work, presented in the manner of a prologue.

## The Outline of the Entire Work ### Chapter One.

At the <term>Saturnalia<note>The Saturnalia was an ancient Roman festival in honor of the god Saturn, characterized by gift-giving, banqueting, and a temporary reversal of social norms. Here, Macrobius uses it as a setting for intellectual dialogue.</note></term>, the leading men of the Roman nobility and other learned men gather at the house of Vextius Praetextatus. They dedicate the celebrated holiday to liberal conversation, providing banquets for one another with mutual kindness and not departing from one another except for nightly rest. For throughout the entire span of the holidays, they occupy the better part of the day with serious discussions and engage in dinner-table talk during the evening, so that no part of the day is left empty of something learned or pleasant. But the talk at the table will be more joyful, so that it may have more pleasure and less severity. For just as in other works where banquets are described, so too in that *Symposium* of Plato, the conversation is not of a harsh nature, but is a varied and charming description of desire. In that work, Socrates does not press and entangle his adversary with tight knots as he usually does, but in a manner more of playing than fighting, he gives his opponent a chance to slip away and escape. For it is proper for conversations at a banquet to be as pure in character as they are enticing in charm.

The morning discussion, however, will be more robust, as befits men who are both learned and most illustrious. For the famous men of the past—the Cottas, the Laelii, and the Scipios—will not be the only ones to dispute great matters in the books of the ancients so long as Roman literature exists. Why should it not also be permitted for the men of the present—the Flaviani, the Albini, the Symmachi, and the Eustachii, whose splendor is similar and whose virtue is not inferior—to speak in the same way? And let it not be held against me if one or two of those whom mature age has gathered into this assembly are placed alongside those of a later generation. That this is permitted is shown by the testimony of Plato's dialogues. Indeed, Parmenides was so much older than Socrates that Socrates's childhood barely touched the other's old age, and yet they are shown disputing arduous matters together. Socrates spends an entire famous dialogue in discussion with Timaeus, though it is well known they did not live in the same era. Furthermore, Paralus and Xanthippus, whose father was Pericles, converse with Protagoras in Plato's work during his second visit to Athens, even though that infamous plague had killed them long before.

### Concerning the day or the various ways of distinguishing day and night. Chapter II.

While I was looking for an opening to approach you, Posthumianus, and for the most relaxed times to consult you—since the holidays are now here, which the greater part of the month dedicated to <note>The god of beginnings and transitions, usually associated with January.</note>Janus provides. On almost all other days, which are suitable for pleading legal cases, no hour can be found at all when you are not either defending the business of your clients in the forum or studying their cases at home. Now, however (for I know that you take your holiday not for play but for serious study), if it is convenient to answer what I have come to ask, you will have done something not unpleasant for yourself, in my opinion, and truly most pleasing to me. 

First, I want to ask you this: Were you present at that banquet, which was renewed with continuous hospitality over several days, and at the conversation which you are said to have been among the first to proclaim and adorn with the highest praise? I would have heard part of this myself, had I not left Rome for Naples after those banquets. Recently, however, I was present with others who were marvelling at the strength of your memory, as you often related in order everything that was said then. This one thing, Decius, we ask: as you yourself—since your youth was just ending then—could see, and could hear in part from Albinus, if it has seemed best in the whole course of your life that, as much as you were permitted to rest from defending legal cases, you would devote that same amount of time to the gathering and conversation of learned men and those like yourself. 

For a well-ordered mind cannot rest more usefully or more honorably than in some opportunity for learned and refined conversation, and for asking and answering questions with courtesy. But what was that banquet? Or is it to be doubted that you are speaking of the one held recently at the house of <note>A prominent Roman statesman and leader of the pagan senatorial aristocracy.</note>Vettius Praetextatus by the most learned of the nobles and others, where a pleasing exchange of ideas varied the discussion among the rest? I have come to ask about this very thing; I would like you to explain what kind of banquet it was, from which I do not think you were absent, given the singular friendship everyone has for you.

Indeed, I would have wished to be there, and I do not think it would have been unwelcome to them; but since there were many cases of friends for me to study thoroughly during those days, when I was invited to dinner then, I replied that it was a time for me to <term>meditate, not to eat<note>original: "meditandi non edendi" — a play on words emphasizing his preference for intellectual preparation over physical consumption.</note></term>. I urged them to seek someone else instead, someone involved in no business and free from care. So it happened: for Praetextatus ordered that the eloquent and learned Eusebius, a rhetorician outstanding among the Greeks—that is, among the professors of our age—and not unskilled in <term>Latin learning<note>original: "doctrinæ latialis"</note></term>, be invited in my place. 

From where, then, are those things known to you, which were brought forth and arranged so pleasantly and courteously for the regulation of life with most abundant examples (as I hear) and a wealth of varied learning? Since the <term>winter solstice<note>original: "solsticialis dies" — Macrobius refers to the winter solstice, the time of the Saturnalia festival.</note></term> followed the festival of the Saturnalia, at which those banquets were celebrated, and I was at home with a more cheerful mind, free from forensic care, Eusebius came there with a few of his followers. Immediately, with a beaming face, he said: "Posthumianus, I confess I am bound to you by great gratitude for many reasons, but especially for this: that by asking for an excuse from Praetextatus, you made a place for me at the dinner. Thus I understand that not only is your favor with me, but Fortune itself conspires and breathes so that some benefit might come to me from you." 

"Do you wish," I said, "to restore to us what you so kindly and willingly confess is owed? And to lead this leisure of ours, which we are very rarely permitted to enjoy, so that to those things at which you were then present, we may now seem to be present?" "I will do as you wish," he said. "I will tell you, however, not of the food or drink—though those too were present in abundance and purity—but also what was said by them over so many days, whether at the banquets or especially away from the table, as much as I can recall in my mind." When I heard these things, it seemed to me that I was approaching the life of those who are called blessed by the wise. For even the things said between them the day before I was present... Avie-
