"Who then, and among whom, or from what source did the conversation arise?" Posthumianus was asked. "In this way, I am here as an untiring listener." Then he said: As the day declined toward evening—the day which the <term>Saturnalian festival<note>A major Roman winter festival in honor of the god Saturn, characterized by feasting, role reversals, and gift-giving.</note></term> was about to follow—when Vettius Praetextatus was providing an opportunity for those who wished to meet at his home, there came Aurelius Symmachus and Caecina Albinus, who were most closely joined to each other both in age and in character and studies. Servius—recently a professional among the <term>grammatici<note>Teachers of literature and language.</note></term>, wonderful and lovable for his learning—followed them, looking at the ground with modesty, and appearing like one who wished to remain hidden. When Praetextatus saw them and came forward to meet them, and had greeted them most charmingly, he turned to Furius Albinus, who then happened to be present with Avienus, and said: "Do you wish, my Albinus, since you see those whose arrival is most opportune, and whom we might rightly call the lights of our city, for us to share that matter about which a conversation had begun to arise between us?" "Why should I not most especially want it?" Albinus said. "For no other thing can be more pleasant, either for us or for them, than to speak about learned questions." And when they had sat down, then Caecina said: "What that may be, my Praetextatus, even if I do not yet know, I ought not to doubt that it is best to know, since it has brought us a reason for talking, and you do not allow us to be without it."

"But you ought to know," he said, "that the conversation between us was this: since tomorrow’s day gives the beginning to the festivals dedicated to Saturn, when should we say the Saturnalia begin? That is, when should we consider the tomorrow's day to take its beginning? And indeed, we have tasted some small parts of this dispute among ourselves. But since it is more known that you track down whatever lies hidden in books than that you could deny it through modesty, I want you to proceed to bring into the open whatever learned understanding you have grasped about this which we seek." 

Then Caecina said: "Since to you who bring me into this conversation, neither ignorance denies nor forgetfulness takes away anything from all those things which were worked out by the ancients, I see it as superfluous to bring forward known things among those who know. But lest anyone think I am burdened by the honor of being consulted, I will revolve in a few words whatever my thin memory suggests to me about this." After this, when he saw everyone ready and alert to listen, he began thus: "Marcus Varro, in his book of *Human Affairs* which he wrote *About Days*, says: 'People who are born in these twenty-four hours from midnight to the next midnight are said to be born on one day.' By which words he seems to have divided the observation of days so that he who is born after sunset but before midnight, belongs to that day which the night soon followed. On the other hand, he who is born in the six later hours of the night is seen to be born on that day which dawned after that night."

<margin>Various opinions on the beginning of the day</margin>

"But the same Varro wrote in the same book that the Athenians observe it differently, and they say all that middle time from sunset to the sun setting again is one day. The Babylonians, moreover, differently: for they call that space beginning from the rising sun to its next rising by the name of one day. The Umbrians, truly, say one and the same day is from noon to the following noon. Which indeed," said Varro, "is too absurd. For he who was born at the <term>sixth hour<note>original: "hora sexta" — the Roman way of saying midday or noon when counting from dawn.</note></term> on the <term>Kalends<note>The first day of the Roman month.</note></term> among the Umbrians, his birthday will seem to be both the half of the Kalends and what will be after the Kalends until the sixth hour of that day. But that the Roman people, as Varro said, count individual days from midnight to the next midnight is shown by many arguments. For Roman sacred rites are partly by day and partly by night; and for those which are by day, the time is assigned from the sixth hour of the preceding night <note>original: "ab hora sexta noctis" — midnight.</note>. In addition to this, the ritual and custom of taking <term>auspices<note>Divination by observing the flight or behavior of birds, essential for Roman legal and military actions.</note></term> teaches that the observation is the same. For magistrates, when they must both take auspices and act upon that for which the auspice proceeded on one day, take auspices after midnight and act after the sun has risen; and they are said to have taken auspices and acted on the same day. Moreover, the tribunes of the plebs, who are not allowed to be absent from Rome for a whole day, when they set out after midnight and return after the first torch is lit but before the following midnight, are not seen to have been absent for a day, since they returned before the <term>sixth hour of the night<note>Midnight.</note></term>..."

For the <term>trinoctium<note>A "three-night" absence. According to the Twelve Tables, if a woman stayed away from her husband's house for three nights a year, she prevented him from gaining legal ownership (usucapio) over her through "use."</note></term> could not be completed—the period which, according to the <term>Twelve Tables<note>The foundation of Roman law, written around 450 BCE.</note></term>, she ought to be absent from her husband for the purpose of interruption—because the final six hours of the third night would belong to the next year, which began on the Kalends. > "Damp night," he says, "turns her middle course:
> And the cruel Rising Sun has breathed on me with his panting horses."
By these words, he reminds us that the day which the Romans called "civil" begins at the sixth hour of the night <note>original: "a sexta noctis hora" — অর্থাৎ midnight.</note>. The same poet expressed when the night also begins in his sixth book. For when he had said:
> "By this exchange of talk, Aurora with her rosy chariot
> had already crossed the midpoint of the axis in her heavenly course,"
The poet soon added:
> "Night rushes on: we spend the hours in weeping."
<margin>Division of the civil day</margin> Thus, as a most careful observer of civil definitions, he described the beginnings of day and night. The day is divided as follows: The first period of the day is called the "inclination of midnight" <note>the turning point after midnight</note>. Then comes the "cock-crow" (*gallicinium*). Then the "time of silence" (*conticinium*), when the cocks fall silent and men are also at rest. Then the "dawn" (*diluculum*), that is, when the day begins to be distinguished. Then the "morning" (*mane*), while the day is bright. It is called *mane* either because the beginning of light emerges from the lower places—that is, from the <term>Manes<note>The spirits of the dead or the underworld.</note></term>—or (which seems truer to me) from the omen of a "good name." For the people of Lanuvium also say *mane* for "good," just as among us the opposite is *imane* <note>original: "imanis"</note>, such as a "monstrous beast" or a "monstrous crime," and other things of this kind: not for something good. Then follows the time from morning to midday, which is the middle of the day. After that comes the time already called "declining," and soon the "final hour" (*suprema tempestas*), which is the latest time of the day, as expressed in the Twelve Tables: "Let sunset be the final hour." Then comes the "evening" (*vespera*), which is derived from the Greeks. For they call it *hesperan* <note>original: "εσπέραν"</note> from the star Hesperus; from which Italy is also named *Hesperia*, because it lies to the west. From this time, it is called "first torch," then "bedtime" (*concubia*), and then "dead of night" (*intempesta*), which has no time suitable for conducting business. This is the division of the civil day observed by the Romans. Therefore, when the "coming night" <note>original: "noctu futura"</note> has reached its midpoint, it will be the omen of the Saturnalia, whose custom is to begin on the "morrow's day" <note>original: "die crastini"</note>. Here, when everyone had praised Albinus's memory as if it were a storehouse of antiquity,
<margin>A storehouse</margin> Praetextatus, seeing Avienus whispering to Furius, said: "What is this, my Avienus? What is it that you wish to be revealed to Albinus alone and kept secret from the rest of us?" Then he replied: "I am indeed moved by the authority of Caecina, and I am not unaware that such great learning does not fall into error; yet that novelty of words struck my ears, when he preferred to say 'coming night' (*noctu futura*) and 'on the morrow's day' (*die crastini*) rather than 'in the coming night' (*futura nocte*) and 'on the tomorrow' (*die crastino*), as the rules of grammar require. For *noctu* is not a name but an adverb. Furthermore, 'coming' (*futura*) is a noun <note>acting as an adjective here</note>; it cannot agree with an adverb. <margin>Noctu Nocte</margin> Nor is there any doubt that the difference between *noctu* and *nocte* is the same as between *diu* and *die*. And again, *die* and *crastini* are not in the same case, and unless the case is the same, nouns are not joined in this kind of expression. Furthermore, I wish to know why we should prefer to say *Saturnaliorum* rather than *Saturnalium*. To this, while Caecina remained smilingly silent, Servius was asked by Symmachus what he thought of these matters. He said: 'In this assembly, which is to be revered no less for its learning than for its nobility, I should learn rather than teach; however, I will speak at the command of those ordering me, and <margin>To introduce</margin> I will first introduce the matter of the Saturnalia, and then the others, showing that this way of speaking is not a novelty but an ancient practice. He who says *Saturnalium* relies on a rule. For nouns that take the dative plural in *-bus* never allow their genitive of the same number to increase by a syllable. Instead, it either has the same number, like *monilibus, monilium* or *sedilibus, sedilium*, or it has one syllable fewer, like *carminibus, carminum* or *luminibus, luminum*. Thus, *Saturnalium* is more correctly derived from *Saturnalibus* than *Saturnaliorum*. But those who say *Saturnaliorum* are protected by the authority of great men.'

<header>BOOK ONE</header>

<margin>
On the terms
"Saturnalium" and "Saturnaliorum"
</margin>
For even Sallust, in the third book of his *Histories*, says "of the Bacchanalia" <note>original: "bacchanaliorum"</note>. And Masurius, in the second book of his *Fasti* <note>A calendar or record of festivals and official events.</note>, says: "The day of the Vinalia <note>The Wine Festival</note> is sacred to Jove, not to Venus as some suppose." To cite the grammarians themselves as evidence: Verrius Flaccus, in that short book titled *Saturnus*, says: "The days of the Saturnalia are also held as festivals among the Greeks." And in the same book: "I believe I have written clearly regarding the institution of the Saturnalia <note>original: "saturnaliorum"</note>." Likewise, Julius Modestus in his work *On Festivals* says: "The holidays of the Saturnalia." And in the same book: "Antias relates that Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many religious rites.</note> was the founder of the Agonalia." Yet you will ask: "Can this authority be defended by any rational argument?"

<margin>
Names of the
Festivals
</margin>
Plainly. Insofar as it is not out of place for a grammarian to be brought into conflict with his own <term>analogy<note>In ancient linguistics, 'analogy' refers to the principle that language should follow regular, predictable rules of grammar.</note></term>, I will attempt to unearth by conjecture why it is that they turned away from the usual pronunciation, preferring to say "Saturnaliorum" rather than "Saturnalium." First, I believe that for these names of festival days—which are <term>neuter<note>Nouns that are neither masculine nor feminine.</note></term> and lack a singular form—they wanted a different condition from those names which are shaped in both singular and plural numbers. For Compitalia, Bacchanalia, Agonalia, Vinalia, and others similar to these are names of feast days and are not named in the singular. Or, if you were to speak in the singular number, you would not signify the same thing unless you added the word "festival," such as "the Bacchanal festival" or "the Agonal festival." In that case, the word is no longer a <term>positive noun<note>A primary noun standing on its own.</note></term> but an adjective—what the Greeks call an <term>epithet<note>original: "ἐπίθετον" (epitheton). A descriptive word added to a noun.</note></term>.

They were therefore encouraged to make a distinction in the <term>genitive case<note>The 'possessive' form of a word, usually translated as 'of X'.</note></term>, so that by this <term>declension<note>The variation of the form of a noun, pronoun, or adjective, by which its grammatical case, number, and gender are identified.</note></term> they might express the name of a solemn day. They knew that in several names, even when the <term>dative<note>The grammatical case typically used for the indirect object of a verb.</note></term> ends in *-bus*, the genitive nonetheless ends in *-rum*: as in *domibus/domorum* <note>of houses</note>, *duobus/duorum* <note>of two</note>, *ambobus/amborum* <note>of both</note>. Likewise, when "greens" <note>original: "viridia"</note> is taken as an adjective, they form the genitive in *-ium*, as in "of green meadows" <note>original: "viridium pratorum"</note>. However, when we wish to signify the greenness of a place itself, we say *viridiorum*, as when one speaks of a "beautiful face of green things." In that case, *viridia* is placed as if it were a positive noun, not an accidental quality. Indeed, there was such license among the ancients regarding this genitive form that 

Asinius Pollio frequently used "of the taxes" <note>original: "vectigaliorum"</note>, even though "tax" <note>original: "vectigal"</note> is said no less than "taxes." Furthermore, although we read: "He carried the <term>ancile<note>A sacred shield of the god Mars.</note></term> on his left," the form "of the shields" <note>original: "anciliorum"</note> is also recorded.

<margin>
Days of the
Festivals
</margin>
We must consider, then, whether variety delighted them more than strict adherence to a rule, so that the names of feast days were called thus. For behold: even beyond the vocabulary of solemn days, we find other words declined this way, as the preceding discourse revealed regarding "greenery," "taxes," and "sacred shields." But I also find the names of festivals themselves declined according to the standard rule among the ancients. For Varro says the "day of the festivals" <note>original: "ferialium diem"</note> is named from the food carried to the tombs; he did not say *ferialiorum*. And elsewhere he says *floralium* <note>of the Floral festival</note>, not *floraliorum*, even though he was not signifying the "Floral Games" there, but the festival of Floralia itself. Masurius also, in his second book, says: "The day of the Liberalia <note>original: "liberaliū"</note> is called the Martial Agonium by the <term>pontiffs<note>High-ranking priests in ancient Rome.</note></term>." And in the same book, regarding the night which follows the next day, which is the Lucaria—he did not say *lucariorum*. Likewise, many have said *liberalium*, not *liberaliorum*.

<margin>
Lifeless
and Cheerful
</margin>
From this, it should be pronounced that the ancients indulged in abundance through variety; just as they said *exanimos* and *exanimes* <note>both meaning 'lifeless'</note>, *inermes* and *inermos* <note>both meaning 'unarmed'</note>, and *hilaros* and *hilares* <note>both meaning 'cheerful'</note>. Therefore, it is certain that it is permissible to say both *Saturnalium* and *Saturnaliorum*, since the one is defended by rule and authority, and the other, if not by rule, then by the authority of many. As for the remaining words which seemed new to our friend Avienus, they must be brought forward by the testimony of the ancients. For Ennius—unless he seems a man whose simple style should be rejected by the more polished tastes of our age—used the term "dead of night" <note>original: "noctu concubia"</note> in these words:

> Where the Gauls, having stealthily approached the summit of the citadel at night,
> Suddenly stain the walls and the sentries in the dead of night.

In this passage, it should be noted not only that he said "in the dead of night," but also that he used the phrase "at night" <note>original: "qua noctu"</note>. He placed this in the seventh book of his *Annals*; although in the third book of the same work, he spoke even more clearly.

# OF THE SATURNALIA
<meta>Faint handwritten folio 'XIX' visible at top left.</meta>

<margin>On "tomorrow" <note>original: "Die crastini"</note></margin>
"This night all Etruria will hang by a thread." <note>A famous line from the poet Ennius, used here to show the use of "noctu" (by night).</note>

Claudius Quadrigarius <note>A Roman historian from the 1st century BCE.</note> also, in the third book of his *Annals*, writes: "The Senate, moreover, met by night; by night many were sent home." I think it is not out of place to mention here also that the 'Ten Men' <note>The decemviri, the authors of the Twelve Tables, Rome's earliest law code.</note> in the *Twelve Tables* very unusually used "night" <note>original: "nox"</note> instead of "by night" <note>original: "noctu"</note>. The words are these:
> "If theft be committed by night; if anyone kills him, let him be killed lawfully."

In these words, it should also be noted that they used "him" <note>original: "im"</note> from the pronoun "is," rather than the standard "eum" in the <term>accusative case<note>The grammatical form used for the direct object of a sentence.</note></term>. But even the phrase "tomorrow" <note>original: "die crastini"</note> was not uttered by a most learned man without the authority of the ancients. It was their custom to say "on the fifth day" <note>original: "die quinti"</note> or "on the fifth day" <note>original: "die quinte"</note> as a combined adverb. The evidence for this is that the second syllable is shortened, though it is naturally long when "day" <note>original: "die"</note> is spoken alone. As for what we said regarding the last syllable of that word being written sometimes with an *e* and sometimes with an *i*, this was common among the ancients: they used these letters at the end of words almost interchangeably, such as "pristine" and "pristini" [former], or "procliue" and "procliui" [downward]. Indeed, that verse of Pomponius comes to mind, from the <term>Atellan Farce<note>A type of low-brow, improvised Roman comedy featuring masked stock characters.</note></term> titled *Mevia*:

-> "On this feast day, since I have done nothing, on the fourth day <note>original: "die quarte"</note> I shall die of hunger." <-

<margin>Yesterday <note>original: "Die pristine"</note></margin>
<margin>Yesterday <note>original: "Die pristino"</note></margin>
<margin>On the fourth day [future] <note>original: "Die quarte"</note></margin>
<margin>On the fourth day [past] <note>original: "Die quarto"</note></margin>
"Yesterday" <note>original: "Die pristine"</note> was said in the same way, meaning "on the former day," which is now called "pridie" [the day before], with the order of the compound reversed, as if it were "pristino die." Nor do I deny having read "on the fourth day" <note>original: "die quarto"</note> among the ancients, but this is found referring to the past, not the future. For Gnaeus Marcius, a man of immense learning, says in his *Mimiambs* <note>Poems mimicking scenes from daily life.</note> what we call "three days ago" <note>original: "nudius quartus"</note> in these verses:
> "Recently, on the fourth day <note>original: "die quarto"</note> as I recall, he certainly broke the only water-jar in the house."
Therefore, this distinction should be maintained: we say "die quarto" regarding the past, but "die quarte" regarding the future. But lest we seem to have reported nothing regarding "tomorrow" <note>original: "die crastini"</note>, there is that passage from Caecilius <note>Caecilius Statius, a Roman comic poet.</note> in his second book of *Histories*:
> "If you are willing to give me the cavalry, and you yourself follow me with the rest of the army: on the fifth day <note>original: "die quinti"</note> I will have a cooked dinner ready for you on the Capitol in Rome."
Then Symmachus said: "Your Caecilius took both the story and the word from the *Origins* of Marcus Cato <note>Cato the Elder, the first major Roman prose writer.</note>, where it is written as follows:
> 'Therefore the master of the horse warned the Carthaginian dictator: Send the cavalry with me to Rome; on the fifth day <note>original: "die quinti"</note> a cooked dinner will be ready for you on the Capitol.'"
And Praetextatus added: "I believe it contributes something to demonstrating the custom of the ancients to also compare the words of the Priest, who according to the custom of our ancestors is wont to announce the holidays called the Compitalia." <note>A festival celebrated at the "compita" or crossroads.</note>
<margin>Compitalia</margin>
The words are these:
> "On the ninth day <note>original: "die noni"</note> after the Kalends of January, there shall be the Compitalia for the Roman citizens."

Then Avienus, looking at Servius, said: "Curius, Fabricius, and Coruncanius—most ancient men—or even those older than them, the Horatii triplets, spoke plainly and clearly with their friends. They did not speak the language of the Aurunci, the Sicani, or the Pelasgiians <note>Primitive or legendary early tribes of Italy.</note> who are said to have first inhabited Italy, but used the words of their own age. You, however, speak now as if you were talking with the mother of Evander! <note>Evander's mother, Carmenta, was a prophetess who supposedly brought the alphabet to Rome; this is a joke that the speaker is being too archaic.</note> Do you wish to revive for us words already obliterated for many centuries? You have even incited those excellent men, whose memory is trained by constant reading, to gather such a heap of them. But you boast that antiquity pleases you because it is honest, sober, and modest. Let us live, then, by the morals of the past, but speak with the words of the present!

For I always keep in my memory and my heart that which was written by Gaius Caesar, a man of excellent genius and prudence, in the first book of his *On Analogy*: 'Avoid an unusual and unfamiliar word as you would a reef.' Finally, there are a thousand such words: though they were frequently in the mouth of ancient authority, they have nevertheless been 'discharged' <note>original: "exauthorata"</note> and repudiated by the following age.
<margin>To discharge <note>original: "Exauthorare"</note></margin>
I could bring forth an abundance of these now, were the time of the approaching night not warning us of the necessity of departing. Good words, I pray!" Praetextatus added with his usual moral gravity: "Let us not insolently strike at the reverence due to antiquity, the parent of the arts. Even while you pretend to dislike it, you betray your love for it.
<margin>There is a thousand of words</margin>
For when you say 'there is a thousand of words' <note>original: "mille uerborum est"</note>, what else does your speech savor of but antiquity itself? For although Marcus Cicero, in the speech he composed *In Defense of Milo*, wrote thus..."

"On the former day" <note>original: "die pristine"</note> was said in the same way, which signified the previous day <note>original: "die pristino"</note>, which is now called "pridie." For Gnaeus Marcius, a man of great learning, says in his *Mimes* regarding what we call "four days ago" in these verses: "Recently, on the fourth day <note>original: "die quarto"</note> as I recall, he certainly broke the only water jar in the house." But lest we seem to have reported nothing regarding "tomorrow," there is that passage from Caecilius in the second book of his *Histories*: "If you wish to give me the cavalry, and you yourself follow with the rest of the army, on the fifth day <note>original: "die quinti"</note> I will have a cooked dinner ready for you at the Capitol in Rome." <margin>Compitalia</margin>

Then Avienus, looking at Servius, said: "Curius, Fabricius, and Coruncanius, those most ancient men—or even the triplets, those Horatii older than them—spoke plainly and clearly with their families. Elsewhere he even followed the <term>declension<note>The changing of a word's ending to show its grammatical function.</note></term> of this name. For in the fifteenth book he says:

He clearly shows that "thousand" <note>original: "mille"</note> is a noun and is spoken in the singular number and even takes the <term>ablative case<note>A grammatical case typically used to indicate movement from, or the instrument by which something is done.</note></term>, and that its plural is "thousands" <note>original: "milia"</note>. 
<margin>Thousands</margin>
For "a thousand" <note>original: "mille"</note> is not placed there because "thousands" <note>original: "chilia" / χιλια</note> are spoken in Greek, but because "a thousand" <note>original: "chilias" / χιλιας</note> is. And just as the ancients said "one thousand" <note>one chilias</note> and "two thousands" <note>two chiliades</note>, so they said "one thousand" <note>unum mille</note> and "two thousands" <note>duo milia</note> by a certain and direct logic. In this way, we shall feel the holidays to be more fruitful <note>original: "fœtas"</note> than any business; not "relaxing" the mind, as the saying goes—for Musonius says that to relax the mind is almost like losing it—but soothing it a little, and loosening it with the pleasant and honorable allurements of conversation. If you so decree, you will do a most grateful thing to my household gods by gathering here. Then Symmachus said: "No one who remembers himself to be worthy of this gathering will reject this fellowship, or the leader of the gathering himself. <margin>To boast of.</margin>
of whom our antiquity boasted. I speak of those whom the Athenians once sent as 
<margin>Fine</margin>
ambassadors to the Senate to obtain the remission of a fine which had been imposed on their city because of the devastation of Oropus. That fine had been nearly five hundred talents. Those philosophers were Carneades 
<margin>Carneades Critolaus Diogenes</margin>
from the Academy, Diogenes the Stoic, and Critolaus the Peripatetic. They say that each of them, for the sake of display, declaimed in the most crowded places of the city before a great gathering of men. As it is reported, the eloquence of Carneades was violent and rapid; that of Critolaus was skillful and polished; and that of Diogenes was modest and sober. But when they were introduced into the Senate, they used the senator Gaius Acilius as an interpreter. Yet this friend of ours, though he has mastered all the sects but followed the most probable one, and alone fulfills all these Greek styles of speaking, is nevertheless such a rich interpreter of himself among us that you would not know in which language he completes the work of discussion more easily or more elegantly." All approved the judgment of Quintus 
<margin>Selected</margin>
Aurelius, by which he chose these "picked out" <note>original: "edecumatos"</note> companions; and thus having settled matters, departing first from Praetextatus and then from one another, they each returned to their own home.

# BOOK ONE

...left behind: "Before the estate of Clodius, on which estate, because of those insane foundations, easily a thousand of strong men were occupied [mille hominum versabatur]" <note>original: *mille hominum uersabatur*</note>; not "were occupied" [versabantur], as is usually found in less accurately written books. And in the sixth speech against Antony: "Who, I ask, was found in that year who would enter a thousand of coins [mille nummū] as paid to Lucius Antonius?" Although Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero.</note>, a man of the same age, said in the seventeenth book of his *Human Antiquities*: "it is more than a thousand and a hundred of years" [plus mille et centum annorum est]; nevertheless, they took the confidence for composing it this way <margin>More</margin> only from the authority of their predecessors. For Quadrigarius <note>Quintus Claudius Quadrigarius, a Roman historian of the 1st century BC.</note> wrote thus in the third book of his *Annals*: "There he killed a thousand of men" [mille hominum]. And Lucilius <note>Gaius Lucilius, the early Roman satirist.</note> in the third book of his *Satires*:

> A thousand [mille] to the gate; from the gate it is six to Salernum.

Indeed, elsewhere he even carried out the declension <note>The variation of the form of a word to show its grammatical function.</note> of this noun. For in the fifteenth book he says:

> He who overcomes this one by a thousand of paces [milli passum] and by two,
> Let no Campanian steed follow as a successor.
> He will seem to go with greater space and apart.
> The same author in a new book:
> You are able to seek a hundred with one thousand of coins [milli nummum].

He said "a thousand of paces" [milli passum] instead of "a thousand paces" [mille passibus], and he said "a thousand of coins" [milli nummum] instead of "a thousand coins" [mille nummis]. He clearly shows that "thousand" [mille] is both a noun and is spoken in the singular number, and even takes the ablative case, and that its plural is "thousands" [milia]. For *mille* is not used because of the Greek word *chilia* <note>original: χίλια; a plural adjective meaning 'thousands'.</note>, but because of *chilias* <note>original: χιλιάς; a singular noun meaning 'a group of a thousand'.</note>. And just as the ancients used to say one *chilias* and two *chiliades*, so they said one *mille* and two *milia* <margin>Thousands</margin> by a fixed and direct reasoning. And hey, you! Do you wish to take away the right of voting in the assembly of words from these so learned men, of whom Marcus Cicero and Varro boast themselves to be imitators? And will you cast them down from the bridge like those over sixty? <margin>To cast down from the bridge.</margin> <note>A reference to the Roman proverb *sexagenarios de ponte*, which suggests that those over sixty should be removed from public affairs or, in ancient myth, sacrificed.</note> We would discuss more of this, were it not that the hour compels us, unwillingly, to depart from what we have begun. But do you wish that we spend the following day—which most everyone wastes on the gaming board and dice <margin>Gaming board / Dice</margin>—with these sober stories from the first light until the time of dinner? Let us pass the dinner itself not overwhelmed with cups, nor wanton with dishes, but modest with learned questions and mutual recitals from the dining couch. For thus we shall feel the holidays to be full of benefit above all business, not "relaxing" the mind as they say—for Musonius <note>Musonius Rufus, a Stoic philosopher of the 1st century AD.</note> says that to relax <margin>Full / To relax the mind</margin> the mind is almost like losing it—but soothing it a little and loosening it with the pleasant and honorable allurements of conversation. If you so decide, you will do something most pleasing to my household gods by gathering here.

Then Symmachus <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, a prominent statesman and defender of Roman traditions.</note> said: "No one who remembers himself to be worthy of this gathering will reject this fellowship, or the leader of the gathering himself. But so that nothing may be lacking for the perfection of the group, I propose that there be invited to the same meeting and banquet: Flavianus <note>Virius Nicomachus Flavianus, a historian and friend of Symmachus.</note>, who has proven how much he excels his father (an admirable and charming sight) no less in the elegance of his character and the gravity of his life than in the abundance of his profound erudition. And at the same time Posthumianus, who ennobles the forum with the dignity of his defenses; and Eustachius, who is so great in every kind of philosophy that he alone represents to us the talents of the three philosophers in whom our antiquity took pride. <margin>To boast of.</margin> I mean those whom the Athenians once sent as envoys to the Senate to obtain the remission of the fine <margin>Fine</margin> which it had imposed on their city because of the devastation of Oropus. That fine had been nearly five hundred talents. These philosophers were Carneades from the Academy, Diogenes the Stoic, and Critolaus the Peripatetic <margin>Carneades / Critolaus / Diogenes</margin>, who they say each disputed separately for the sake of display through the most crowded places of the city, with a great gathering of men. The eloquence of Carneades (as it is reported) was violent and rapid; that of Critolaus was clever and polished; that of Diogenes was modest and even sober. But when introduced into the Senate, they used the senator Caelius as an interpreter. Yet this man of ours [Eustachius], although he has attained all the philosophical sects but followed the most probable one, and alone fulfills all these Greek types of speaking, is nevertheless such a rich interpreter of his own thoughts among us that you would not know in which language he more easily or elegantly fulfills the work of discussing." All approved the judgment of Quintus Aurelius [Symmachus], by which he chose the most elite <margin>Elite</margin> <note>original: *edecumatos*, meaning "hand-picked" or "of the highest quality".</note> companions; and when these things were thus settled, they departed together, first from Praetextatus <note>Vettius Agorius Praetextatus, the host of the Saturnalia dialogues.</note>, and then from one another, and each returned to his own home.

# THE SATURNALIA

# ¶ The conversation of the following day. Chapter III.

<margin>
To introduce
To indulge
</margin>
On the following day, all those who had agreed to meet the day before arrived early at the house of Vettius <note>Vettius Agorius Praetextatus (c. 315–384 AD), a high-ranking Roman official and defender of traditional Roman religion.</note>. Praetextatus received them into his library, where he was waiting for them. "I see this will be a most excellent day for me," he said, "since you are all here, and those who were invited to join our gathering have promised to attend. Only Postumianus felt it more important to attend to the preparation of his legal defenses; in his place, I have substituted Eusebius, a Greek rhetorician famous for his learning and eloquence. I have suggested to everyone that, now that the day has dawned, they should indulge us with their company, especially since it is not lawful to be occupied with any public business today. Certainly, no one is seen today wearing the formal toga, the ceremonial robe, the military cloak, or the purple-bordered robe <note>original: *togatus certe uel trabeatus: paludatusue: seu prætextatus*</note>." Then Avienus, as was his habit of interrupting, spoke. "Since you mention your own name, Praetextatus, among the names of various types of clothing," he said, "I am reminded of a question that I think is not merely trivial. Since the wearing of the toga, the ceremonial *trabea*, or the military *paludamentum* has not resulted in people being called by those names as their own, I ask you: why did antiquity claim this name for the purple-bordered garment alone, and what origin did this name acquire?"

# Chapter IIII.

<margin>
Advocate
</margin>
During these words of Avienus, Flavianus and Eustathius—a pair of remarkable friendship—and soon after them Eusebius, entered and made the gathering more lively. After greetings were given and received, they sat down, asking what the topic of conversation was. Then Vettius said, "You have arrived at just the right moment for me while I was looking for someone to advocate for me. Our friend Avienus is raising a question about my name, and he demands its origin as if he were demanding proof of my lineage. For since there is no one who is called by the name 'Togatus' or 'Military-Cloaked' <note>original: *togatus... paludatus*</note> as their own name, he asks why 'Praetextatus' <note>A name derived from the *toga praetexta*, a purple-bordered robe worn by magistrates and free-born children.</note> should be a name. But since 'Know Thyself' <note>original: *γνῶθι σε ἀυτóν* (gnōthi seauton)</note> is inscribed on the door of the Delphic temple and is the famous saying of one of the Seven Sages, what should I be thought to know about myself if I am ignorant of my own name, the origin and cause of which I must now explain? Tullius Hostilius, the third king of the Romans, after defeating the Etruscans, was the first to establish that the curule chair, the lictors, the embroidered toga, and the purple-bordered robe <note>original: *sellã currulem: lictoresq;: & togã pictã: atq; prætextã*</note>—which were the symbols of Etruscan magistrates—should be used in Rome. But in that age, the purple-bordered robe was not used by children. For, like the other things I have listed, it was a garment of honor. But later, Tarquinius Priscus <note>Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth King of Rome, traditionally credited with introducing many Roman customs.</note>, the son of the Corinthian exile Demaratus—whom some say was called Lucumo—the third king after Hostilius and the fifth from Romulus, celebrated a triumph over the Sabines. In that war, he praised his own son, who was fourteen years old and had struck down an enemy with his own hand, in a public speech; he presented him with a golden amulet and a purple-bordered robe, marking the boy as brave beyond his years with the rewards of manhood and honor. For just as the purple-bordered robe belonged to magistrates, so the amulet <note>original: *bulla*</note> was the ornament of those celebrating a triumph, which they wore during the procession, containing within it remedies they believed were most powerful against envy. This custom was then adopted so that the robe and the amulet were used by noble children, to attract omens and prayers for a courage similar to his who first received these gifts in his early years. Others think that the same Priscus, when he was organizing the social ranks with the skill of a far-seeing prince, considered the dress of free-born boys among his primary concerns. He established that patricians should use the golden amulet with the toga bordered with purple, provided that their fathers had held a curule magistracy. For others, it was granted that they only use the purple-bordered robe, but only up to those whose parents had earned their proper military pay on horseback <note>Meaning the children of the Equestrian class, or Roman knights.</note>. However, it was not permitted by any law for the children of freedmen to use the purple-bordered robe, and much less for foreigners who had no connection to the Romans. But later, the robe was granted to the sons of freedmen as well, for the following reason, which Marcus Laelius the Augur records: he says that during the Second Punic War, the board of two men <note>The *duumviri*, officials in charge of religious duties.</note>, by decree of the Senate, consulted the Sibylline Books <note>Ancient prophetic scrolls consulted by the Roman state during crises.</note> because of many omens. Having inspected them, they announced that a supplication must be made on the Capitoline Hill and a ritual banquet for the gods <note>original: *lectisternium*</note> performed using collected donations, so that freedwomen who wore the long robe <note>The *stola*, the traditional dress of a Roman matron.</note> might also provide money for that purpose. Therefore, the prayer was performed, with free-born boys and also the sons of freedmen, as well as girls with both parents living <note>original: *patrimis matrimisq*</note>, reciting the hymn. Because of this, it was granted that the sons of freedmen, provided they were born from a legal mistress of the house, should also wear the robe.

...that they should wear the purple-bordered robe and a leather strap around the neck for the honor of the <term>bulla<note>A protective amulet, usually round or heart-shaped, worn by free-born Roman boys.</note></term>. Verrius Flaccus <note>A famous Roman grammarian and teacher from the time of Augustus.</note> says: When the Roman people were suffering from a plague, the oracle responded that it happened because the gods were being "looked down upon." The city was anxious because the oracle was not understood. It so happened that on the day of the chariot races, a boy looked down upon the procession from an upper room <note>original: *coenaculo*</note> and told his mother in what order he had seen the secret sacred objects arranged in the <term>pilentum<note>A covered, four-wheeled carriage used by priests and matrons for carrying sacred vessels.</note></term>. When the boy reported this to the Senate, they decided that the places where the procession traveled should be veiled; thus the plague was settled. The boy, who had resolved the ambiguity of the oracle, was granted the right to wear the <term>toga<note>The formal woolen garment of a Roman citizen.</note></term> and the <term>prætexta<note>A toga with a purple border worn by magistrates and free-born children.</note></term> as a reward. Those most skilled in antiquity
<margin>Hersilia</margin>
report: During the abduction of the Sabine women, one woman named Hersilia was abducted along with her daughter while she was clinging to her. Romulus gave her as a wife to a certain Hostus from the Latin territory—a man of distinguished valor who had fled to his protection. A boy was born to her before any of the other Sabine women gave birth. Because he was the first to be procreated on hostile ground, he was
<margin>Hostus Hostilius</margin>
called Hostus Hostilius by his mother. He was also honored by Romulus with the golden *bulla* and the purple-bordered robe. For when Romulus had called the abducted women together for consultation, he is said to have promised that he would give a distinguished gift to the infant of the woman who was the first to bear him a Roman citizen.

### Regarding the shape of the bulla. Chapter V.

<margin>The shape of the bulla</margin>
Some believe it was granted to free-born boys that they should fasten a heart-shaped figure in a *bulla* upon their chest, so that looking upon it, they would consider themselves men only if they excelled in their "heart" <note>In this context, meaning "intellect" or "character."</note>. The purple-bordered robe was also added to these boys so that they might be guided by the "blush" of the purple dye toward the modesty proper to their free-born status. We have said where the purple-bordered robe came from and added the reasons why it is thought to have been granted to childhood. Now, the reason why the same habit
<margin>Childhood</margin>
<margin>The purple-bordered garment</margin>
passed into the use of a name must be explained in a few words. Formerly, it was the custom for Senators to enter the Senate house with their sons who were wearing the purple-bordered robe. When a major matter was being consulted upon in the Senate and had been deferred to the following day, it was decided that no one should announce this matter—over which they had deliberated—until it
<margin>The boy Papirius</margin>
had been decreed. The mother of the boy Papirius, who had been in the Senate house with his parent, questioned her son as to what the fathers had done in the Senate. The boy replied that it must be kept secret and it was not permitted to say. The woman became more eager to hear it. The secrecy of the matter and the silence of the boy spurred her mind to investigate. She questioned him more urgently and violently. Then the boy, under pressure from his mother, came up with a plan for a witty and festive lie. He told her it was discussed in the Senate which would seem more useful and more in the interest of the Republic: whether one man should have two wives, or whether one woman should be married to two husbands. When she heard this, she was terrified in her soul; she rushed trembling from the house and reported it to the other matrons. The next day, a huge crowd of mothers of families flocked to the Senate, weeping and pleading, praying that one woman should rather be married to two men than one man to two. The Senators entering the Senate house wondered what this "outburst" from the women meant, and what this
<margin>Outburst</margin>
demand of theirs intended. Not as a small omen, they feared this immodest madness of the respected sex. The boy Papirius removed the public fear. Stepping into the middle of the Senate, he narrated what his mother had insisted on hearing and what he had pretended to his mother, exactly as it had happened. The Senate kissed the boy's loyalty and wit, and made a decree that hereafter boys should not enter the Senate house with their fathers, except for that one Papirius. To that boy, the surname "Praetextatus" was later given as an honor by decree, on account of his wisdom in remaining silent and speaking during the age of the purple-bordered robe <note>original: *in prætextata ætate*</note>. This surname later stuck to our family as a name. Not otherwise were the Scipios named, except that
<margin>Origin of Scipio</margin>
Cornelius, who carried his father (who lacked his sight) as a staff <note>original: *pro baculo*</note>, was surnamed *Scipio* <note>The Latin word *scipio* means a staff or walking stick.</note>, and gave the name from the surname to his descendants. So your friend Messala was named from the surname of Valerius Maximus, who, after he took the city of Messana, the most noble city of Sicily, was surnamed Messala.
<margin>Origin of Messala</margin>
It is no wonder if names were born from surnames, since, on the contrary, surnames are also drawn from proper names: such as Aemilianus from Aemilius, or Servilianus from Servius. Here Eusebius added: "Messala and Scipio—one for piety, the other for valor—as you say, the surnames..."

### PAGE LIX

...perished. But regarding the names **Sow** and **Donkey** <note>original: *Scropha* and *Asina*</note>, which are the surnames of men of no small standing: I want you to tell us where they came from, since they seem closer to insults than to honors. Then he replied: It was neither honor nor injury, but chance that created these names. 

<margin>Why the surname Donkey was given to the Cornelii.</margin>
For the surname **Donkey** was given to the family of the Cornelii because the head of the Cornelia clan, having bought an estate—or perhaps when giving his daughter to a husband—when the guarantors <note>original: *sponsores*</note> solemnly demanded security from him, he led a female donkey <note>original: *asinam*</note> loaded with money into the Forum as a present pledge in place of guarantors. 

<margin>Where the surname Sow began.</margin>
Tremellius, however, was nicknamed **Sow** <note>original: *scropha*</note> by the following event. This Tremellius was at his villa with his household and children. When a neighbor’s sow wandered off, his slaves stole it and killed it. 

<margin>The livestock concerning the sow</margin>
The neighbor, having called upon guards, surrounded the entire area so that the animal could not be carried away. He appealed to the master of the house for his livestock to be restored. Tremellius, who had learned the truth from his farm manager, placed the carcass of the sow under some quilts 

<margin>Quilts</margin>
<term>centones<note>Heavy patchwork blankets or quilts made of scraps of cloth, often used for bedding or to extinguish fires.</note></term> upon which his wife was lying. 

<margin>The Inquiry</margin>
He then permitted the neighbor to conduct a search. When they came to the bedroom, he composed the words of an oath: he swore there was no sow in his villa except for the one—he said—that was lying in the quilts, and he pointed to the bed. This most witty oath gave Tremellius the surname **Sow**.

While these things were being told, one of the household slaves, whose duty it was to meet those wishing to see the master, announced that **Euangelus** was present along with **Dysarius**. 

<margin>The Bitterness</margin>
These two then seemed to surpass all others in Rome who professed the art of medicine. Many of those sitting there showed their disapproval with wrinkled brows. They felt the arrival of Euangelus would be unpleasant for their leisure and unsuitable for such a peaceful gathering. For he was known for a bitter wit and a tongue that was insolently biting; he was bold and uncaring of the offenses he provoked everywhere with his hateful words, which he cast at friends and enemies alike without distinction. 

But **Praetextatus**, being equally calm and mild toward everyone, ordered that they be admitted and sent people to meet them. 

<margin>A convenient arrival</margin>
Following behind them as they entered was **Horus**, a man equally strong in body and mind. After winning many palms as a champion boxer, he had moved on to the study of philosophy. He followed the sect of **Antisthenes**, **Crates**, and **Diogenes** themselves, and was held in high regard among the <term>Cynics<note>A school of philosophy that emphasized living in virtue and agreement with nature, often rejecting social conventions and material wealth.</note></term>. 

But Euangelus, after he entered and found such a great assembly rising to greet him, said: "Is it chance that has drawn all these men to you, Praetextatus, or is there some deeper business at hand that required you to meet by arrangement <note>original: *ex disposito*</note> with witnesses removed? If it is the latter (as I suspect), I would rather leave than mix myself into your secrets, from which my own will would remove me, even if fortune had caused me to stumble upon them."

Then **Vectius**, although he was always firm in his tranquility of mind and enduring of all things, was nonetheless moved by such an insolent question. He said: "If you had considered either me, Euangelus, or these lights of innocence here, you would not imagine any secret among us that could not be made clear to you or even to the common people. For I am not unmindful, nor do I believe any of these men are ignorant of that holy precept of philosophy: 

<margin>One must speak only what can be heard by gods and men.</margin>
**One must speak with men as if the gods were listening, and speak with the gods as if men were listening.** <note>Praetextatus quotes a famous ethical maxim attributed to various philosophers, emphasizing transparency and integrity.</note> The second part of this rule decrees that we should ask nothing of the gods that we would be ashamed to admit wanting to our fellow men. 

We have gathered, in fact, so that we might both honor the sacred holidays and avoid the sluggishness of idleness, turning our leisure into useful business. 

<margin>A contribution</margin>
We have met to spend the whole day sharing learned stories, as if each of us were bringing a <term>symbolum<note>Originally a "contribution" or "token" for a communal meal where everyone brings a dish; here used metaphorically for a "potluck" of intellectual ideas.</note></term>. For if no religious law forbids leading water through channels during sacred festivals, and if divine and human laws permit us to dip sheep in a healthy river, why should it not be considered an honor to religion to dedicate the sacred days to the sacred study of literature? 

But because someone wished for you also to be added to us as gods, please—if you are willing—let us spend the day together in both conversation and dining. I take it as granted that everyone present today will agree to this."

Then Euangelus replied: "To come upon stories when uninvited is certainly not considered shameful; however, to rush unasked into a banquet prepared for others was mentioned by **Homer**—and not without a mark of censure—even in the case of a brother <note>A reference to Menelaus in the Iliad, who arrives at Agamemnon's feast uninvited.</note>. And take care that you do not arrogantly wish for three 'Menelauses' to have happened upon you, when only one befell that great king."

Then everyone, assisting Praetextatus, began to plead and charm them into the common fellowship—asking Euangelus most often and most earnestly, but also those who had entered with him. Amidst these things...

<margin>What the number of guests ought to be.</margin>
Evangelus, calmed by the request of everyone, said: "I believe the book of Marcus Varro <note>A prolific Roman scholar and writer</note> is not unknown to you, from his Menippean satires, which is titled: *You know not what evening may bring* <note>original: *Nescis quid uesper uehat*</note>. In this, he defines the number of guests by this law: that it be neither fewer than the number of the Graces <note>Three goddesses of charm and beauty</note> nor more than the number of the Muses <note>The nine goddesses of the arts and sciences, numbering nine</note>. Here I see, excluding the 'king' of the banquet <note>The host or designated leader of the party</note>, there are as many of you as there are Muses. Why then do you seek to add more to a perfect number?" And Vettius said: "Your presence will provide this for us: so that we may both fulfill the Muses and the Graces, whom it is right to assemble for the festival of the prince of all the gods." When they had sat down, Horus, looking at Avienus—whom he was accustomed to visit more familiarly—said: "In this cult of Saturn, whom you call the prince of the gods, the rite seems to have flowed down from the most religious nation of the Egyptians into the secrets of the temples even until the death of Alexander the Macedonian. After him, pressed by the tyranny of the Ptolemies, they were forced to receive these gods into their worship in the manner of the Alexandrians, among whom they were chiefly honored. Yet they obeyed the command in such a way that they did not entirely confound the observations of their own religion. For because it was never lawful for Egyptians to appease the gods with livestock or blood, but only with prayers and incense; and because for these two newcomers <note>Saturn and Serapis</note> victims had to be slaughtered according to custom, they placed their shrines outside the boundary <note>original: *pomerium*</note>—
<margin>The Boundary <note>original: *Pomeriũ*</note>.</margin>
—so that they might be honored with the solemn blood of sacrifice, yet the urban temples would not be polluted by the death of livestock. Therefore, no town of Egypt receives a shrine of either Saturn or Serapis within its walls. I hear that one of these <note>Serapis</note> was admitted by you with difficulty and hardship; yet you celebrate Saturn with the greatest honor among all others. If, therefore, there is nothing that prohibits me from knowing this, I want it to be brought into the open." Here Avienus, referring the expectation to the 'Pretextate' <note>Praetextatus, the host and leader of the intellectual circle</note>, said: "Although all who are present may excel in equal learning, yet Vettius, uniquely conscious of all sacred matters, can reveal to you both the origin of the cult paid to this god and the cause of the solemn festival." When Praetextatus tried to pass this off to others, everyone obtained from him that he should discourse on it himself. Then, silence having been made, he began thus:

### ❡ The origin of the Saturnalia. Chapter VI.

<margin>Origin of the Saturnalia.</margin>
"It is lawful for me to bring forward into the open that origin of the Saturnalia, not which refers to the secret nature of divinity, but which is either discussed as accepted in fables or opened to the public by philosophers. For the hidden reasons flowing from the source of pure truth are not permitted to be narrated even in the rites themselves. But if anyone attains them, he is commanded to keep them covered within his conscience. Whence, the things which it is lawful to know, our Horus may review with me. Janus held that region which is now called Italy by kingship.
<margin>Janus, king of Italy.</margin>
Who (as Hyginus relates, following Protarchus the Trallian) possessed this land with Camese, also a native, in such shared power that the region was called Camesene and the town Ianiculum <note>A hill in Rome</note>.
<margin>Camesene. Ianiculum.</margin>
Afterward, the kingdom was reduced to Janus alone, who is believed to have displayed a double face so that he might look at those things which were before and those behind his back. Which, without doubt, must be referred to the wisdom and skill of the king, who knew the past and foresaw the future; just as **Forethought** and **Hindsight** <note>original: *Anteuorta* and *Postuorta*</note>, companions of the most fitting divinity, are worshiped among the Romans.
<margin>Forethought. Hindsight.</margin>
Therefore this Janus, when he had received Saturn—who had arrived by a fleet—as a guest, and having been taught by him the skill of the countryside, improved that wild and rude diet from before grain was known, and rewarded him with a partnership in the kingdom.
<margin>Saturn received.</margin>
Since Janus was also the first to stamp bronze coins, he preserved his reverence for Saturn in this too: that since Saturn had been conveyed by ship, Janus expressed the image of his own head on one side, and a ship on the other, so that he might propagate the memory of Saturn even to posterity. That bronze was so stamped is understood
<margin>First stamping of bronze begun by Janus</margin>
today in the game of dice, when boys tossing pennies <note>original: *denarios*</note> into the air, cry out 'Heads or Ships' <note>original: *capita aut nauim*; the Roman equivalent of "Heads or Tails"</note> as a witness of antiquity in the game. That these two reigned together in harmony and founded neighboring towns by their common labor is known from Virgil <note>original: *Maronem*</note>, who relates: 'Ianiculum was the name for this one, Saturnia for that.' It is also evident because posterity dedicated two continuous months to them: so that December would possess the sacred rite of Saturn, and January the name of the other."

<margin>
December is sacred to Saturn, January to Janus. Why Saturnia leads to the Saturnalia.
</margin>
When Saturn suddenly disappeared from sight, Janus devised ways to increase his honors. First, he named the entire land under his rule "Saturnia." Then, he established an altar with sacred rites as if to a god, which he called the Saturnalia. So many ages did the Saturnalia precede the era of the city of Rome. He ordered him to be observed with the majesty of religion, as the author of a <term>better life</term> <note>Meaning the transition from a wild, nomadic existence to settled agriculture.</note>. His statue bears witness to this, to which Janus added a scythe as the emblem of the harvest. To this god is attributed the knowledge of grafting shoots, the cultivation of fruit trees, and all such fertile disciplines. The people of Cyrene also, when they perform divine rites for him, crown themselves with fresh figs and send cakes to one another, believing Saturn to be the discoverer of honey and fruits. 

<margin>
Sterculius Saturn. Total liberty permitted to slaves during the Saturnalia.
</margin>
The Romans also call him <term>Sterculius</term> <note>From "stercus," meaning dung or manure.</note>, because he first provided fertility to the fields using manure. The times of his reign are said to have been the happiest, both because of the abundance of things and because no one was yet distinguished by slavery or freedom—a fact that can be understood from the practice where, during the Saturnalia, total liberty is permitted to slaves. Another cause of the Saturnalia is recorded as follows: those who had been left behind in Italy by Hercules (as some say, in anger because the herd had been poorly guarded; or, as others think, because he left them there on purpose so they might protect his altar and shrine from raids). When they were being harassed by robbers, they occupied a high hill and called themselves "Saturnians," by which name that same hill was also formerly called. And because they felt protected by the name and religion of that god, they are said to have instituted the Saturnalia, so that the observation of the appointed feast might call the minds of their rustic neighbors to a greater reverence for the sacred. Nor am I ignorant of that other cause assigned to the Saturnalia: that the Pelasgians <note>An ancient people of the Greek world.</note> (as Varro records), when they were driven from their homes and sought diverse lands, many flocked to Dodona; and being uncertain where they should settle, they received this response:

> Go, seeking the Saturnian land of the Sicels,
> and the basin of the Aborigines where an island floats;
> when you have mingled with these people, send a tithe to Phoebus,
> and send heads to Hades, and to the Father, lights.
> <note>original: "σείχετε μαιόμενοι σικελῶν σατουρνίαν αἶαν / κ’ἀβοριγινέων κοτύλην οὗ κάσος ὀχεῖται / αἷς ἀναμιχθέντες Δεκάτην ἐπέμψατε φοίβῳ / καὶ κεφαλὰς ᾅδῃ καὶ τῷ πατρὶ πέμπετε φῶτα"</note>

<margin>
Lake Cutilia.
</margin>
Having received this oracle, when they finally reached Latium after many wanderings, they discovered a floating island in Lake Cutilia. For there was a very large patch of turf—whether it was condensed mud or a marshy growth—bound together by brushwood and trees into a wild sort of forest, which wandered about as the waves of the whole "sea" <note>The lake.</note> tossed it. Thus, faith was placed in the god by this sign: that a thing which was high with mountains and vast with fields could nevertheless migrate through the waters. When this miracle was discovered, they learned that these were the seats predicted for them. Having driven out the inhabitants, they occupied the region, consecrating a tenth of the plunder to Apollo according to the response, and erecting a small shrine to Dis <note>Pluto, god of the underworld.</note> and an altar to Saturn. They named his festival the Saturnalia. And for a long time, they believed they were pleasing Dis with human heads and Saturn with the sacrifice of men, because of the oracle which said:

> And send heads to Hades, and to the Father, lights.
> <note>original: "καὶ κεφαλὰς ᾅδῃ καὶ τῷ πατρὶ πέμπετε φῶτα"</note>

But they say that later, Hercules, returning through Italy with the cattle of Geryon, persuaded their descendants to change these ill-omened sacrifices into lucky ones by offering to Dis not the heads of men,

<margin>
Oscilla.
</margin>
but <term>oscilla</term> <note>Small masks or puppets made in the likeness of humans.</note> skillfully modeled to a human image; and honoring the Saturnian altars not by slaughtering men, but by kindling lights. This was because the word <term>phota</term> <note>original: "$\phi\tilde{\omega}\tau\alpha$"</note> signifies not only "man" but also "lights." 

<margin>
Wax candles were sent during the Saturnalia.
</margin>
From this began the custom of sending <term>cerei</term> <note>Wax candles.</note> during the Saturnalia. Others think candles are sent for no other reason than that under this ruler, we were led out from an unkempt and dark life, as if toward the light and the knowledge of the good arts. I also find this in literature: that many, taking the opportunity of the Saturnalia, would greedily demand gifts from their clients, and this burden weighed heavily on the poorer sort. Publicius, a tribune of the plebs, proposed a law that none but wax candles should be sent to the wealthier citizens. Here Albinus Caecina added: "The kind of change in sacrifice you just mentioned, Praetextatus, I find was later celebrated at the Compitalia <note>A festival at the 'compita' or crossroads.</note>, when games were held throughout the city at the crossroads. These were restored by Tarquin the Proud to the Lares and Mania, following a response of Apollo, in which it was commanded that...

<margin>Compitalia</margin>

<margin>The antiquity of the Saturnalia</margin>

Now, a few things must be related concerning the temple of the god itself. Tullius Hostilius, when he had triumphed twice over the Albans and a third time over the Sabines, dedicated a shrine to Saturn in accordance with a vow. The Saturnalia was then first instituted in Rome. Although Varro, in his sixth book *On Sacred Buildings*, writes that King Lucius Tarquinius contracted for the building of the temple of Saturn

at the Forum, but Titus Larcius as dictator dedicated it during the Saturnalia. Nor does it escape me that Gellius writes the Senate decreed the temple of Saturn be built, and that Lucius Furius, a military tribune, oversaw that matter. It has an altar and a dining room before it. There, by the <term>Greek rite</term> <note>The "Greek rite" (Graeco ritu) meant sacrificing with the head uncovered, unlike the typical Roman custom of veiling the head.</note>, divine service is performed with an open head, because they think it was practiced that way from the beginning, first by the Pelasgians and later by Hercules. The Romans wished the temple of Saturn to be the <term>Treasury</term> <note>original: "Aerarium"</note> because, during the time he inhabited
<margin>The Temple of Saturn as the Treasury of Rome</margin>
Italy, it is said that no theft was committed in his lands, or because under him nothing was private property. It was not lawful even to mark or divide a field with a boundary; they sought things for the common good. Therefore, they placed the common money of the people in the house of the one under whom all things were universal to everyone. I should not omit this:
<margin>Tritons on the roof of the temple of Saturn</margin>
that <term>Tritons</term> <note>Mythological sea-creatures, half-man and half-fish.</note> with trumpets were placed upon the roof of the temple of Saturn. This is because, from the commemoration of his era down to our age, history is brought forth and is, as it were, vocal; but before him, history was mute, obscure, and unknown, which the tails of the Tritons, submerged and hidden in the earth, testify. But as for why Saturn himself is seen in
<margin>Why Saturn is seen in chains</margin>
shackles, Verrius Flaccus says he does not know the cause. However, the reading of Apollodorus suggests the truth to me. Apollodorus says that Saturn is bound throughout the year by a woolen bond and released on his feast day, that is, in this month of December. And from this the proverb was said: *The gods have woolen feet.* This signifies that in the tenth month, the seed animated in the womb grows toward life; but until it breaks out into the light, it is held by the soft bonds of nature. <term>Holding back</term> <note>original: "κατέχων" (katechōn)</note>. For as much as the mythologists pull Saturn apart with fictions, the natural philosophers recall him to a certain likeness of truth. They say he cut off the genitals of his father Caelus; when these were cast into the sea, Venus was procreated, who, having formed from the foam of the wave, received the name <term>Aphrodite</term> <note>original: "ἀφροδίτη"; from the Greek "aphros," meaning foam.</note>.
<margin>The origin of Venus</margin>
From this they wish it to be understood that when there was chaos, there was no time. If indeed
<margin>Time</margin>
time is a certain dimension gathered from the revolution of the heavens. Time began from there. From him is thought to be born <term>Cronus</term> <note>original: "κρόνος"</note>, who (as we have said) is <term>Chronos</term> <note>original: "χρόνος", the Greek word for Time.</note>. And since the seeds of all things to be born after the heavens were flowing from the sky, and all the elements which make up the fullness of the world were poured from those seeds, once the world was perfected in all its parts and members, a limit was made by a certain time to the proceeding of seeds from heaven for the conception of elements; for they had already been created full. The eternal propagation of animals, however, was transferred to the faculty of generating from moisture—to Venus—so that through the union of male and female, all things might thereafter be born. <page-num>XXXVIII</page-num>
<header>->ON THE SATURNALIA<-</header>
<sig>f ij</sig>

<margin>The origin of Saturn and the Satyrs</margin>
...the myth of the [castration]: even our own ancestors called him Saturn from the Greek word for the male member <note>original: "παρά τὸ σάθην" (*para to sathen*)</note>, which signifies the virile organ, just as "Saturn" does. From this, they believe the Satyrs were also named—essentially as "sathunoi"—because they are prone to lust. Some think a scythe was attributed to him because Time reaps, manages, and cuts down all things. They say he was accustomed to devouring his own children and then vomiting them back up. This similarly signifies that he is Time, by which all things are alternately created and consumed, and from which they are born anew. That he was driven out by his son: what else is this but the fact that aging times are pushed aside by those born afterward? As for him being "bound": it is because periods of time are connected by a fixed law of nature, or because all fruits are alternated by certain bonds and knots of growth. For myths also claim his scythe fell in Sicily, because that land is exceptionally fertile. And since we have mentioned that Janus reigned together with Saturn, and having already related what the mythologists and natural philosophers think of Saturn, we shall now bring forward what both groups say about Janus. The mythologists report that during the reign of Janus, the homes of all people were protected by religion and sanctity.

<margin>Janus: his origin and why he is two-faced</margin>
For this reason, divine honors were decreed for him; and because of his merits, the entrances and exits of temples were consecrated to him. Xenon also records in the first book of his *Italian History* that Janus was the first in Italy to build temples to the gods and establish the rituals of sacrifices; therefore, he earned a perpetual place in the opening prayers of sacrifices. Some think he is called "two-faced" <term>bifrons</term> <note>Literally "two-fronted" or "two-faced."</note> because he knew the past and foresaw the future. But the natural philosophers <note>The "physici," or those who interpret myths as allegories for natural forces.</note> consecrate him more through arguments of his divinity. For there are those who say that Janus is the same as Apollo and Diana, and they affirm that both deities are expressed in this one power. Thus, Nigidius also reports that among the Greeks, Apollo is worshipped under the name "of the door" <note>original: "θυραῖος" (*thuraios*)</note>, and they celebrate at his altars before their doors, demonstrating that he is the master of exits and entrances. This same Apollo is called by them "of the streets" <note>original: "ἀγυιεὺς" (*aguieus*)</note>, as if he were in charge of the city's ways. For they call the roads that are within the <term>pomerium</term> <note>The sacred boundary of a city.</note> "streets" <note>original: "ἀγυιὰς" (*aguias*)</note>.

<margin>Diana</margin>
Indeed, they attribute power over all "three-way crossroads" to Diana. But among us, the name "Janus" shows that he presides over all doors <note>original: "ianuis"</note>, which is similar to the Greek term "of the door." He is depicted with both a key and a rod, as if he were the guardian of all gates and the ruler of roads. Nigidius proclaimed that Apollo is Janus and Diana is "Jana," with the letter 'd' added, which is often added for the sake of elegance to the letter 'i'—as in the words *redit* (he returns), *redhibet* (he gives back), *redintegrat* (he restores), and similar terms. Some wish to show that Janus is the Sun, and therefore "twin-faced" as the master of both celestial gates, who opens the day as he rises and closes it as he sets. He is invoked first whenever a divine matter is celebrated for any god, so that through him, access may be opened to the one to whom the sacrifice is made, as if he himself transmits the prayers of the suppliants through his gates to the gods. Hence, his image is often fashioned holding the number three hundred in his right hand and sixty-five in his left, to demonstrate the measurement of the year, which is the chief power of the Sun. Others have wanted him to be the World—that is, the Heavens—and said Janus is named from "going" <note>original: "eundo"</note>, because the world is always "going" as it rolls in an orb, and making a beginning from itself, it is brought back into itself.

<margin>Eanus</margin>
Whence Cornificius, in the third book of his *Etymologies*, says that Cicero does not call him Janus, but "Eanus" from "going" <note>original: "eundo"</note>. From this, the Phoenicians also, expressing him in their sacred rites, fashioned a dragon curled into a circle devouring its own tail, to show that the world is nourished from itself and revolves into itself. For this reason, among us, his image looks in four directions, as shown by his statue adorned with medallions <note>original: "faleris"</note>. Caius Bassus, in the book he composed *On the Gods*, says that the two-faced Janus is fashioned as the doorkeeper of both the upper and lower worlds; the same god is four-faced as if embracing all quarters of the world with his majesty. In the most ancient songs of the <term>Salii</term> <note>An ancient college of priests in Rome dedicated to Mars.</note>, he is sung as the "god of gods." Also Marcus Messalla, a colleague of Gnaeus Domitius in the consulship and an <term>augur</term> <note>A religious official who interpreted the will of the gods by observing the flight of birds.</note> for fifty-five years, begins thus concerning Janus: "He who fashions all things and rules the same, he joined the force and nature of water and earth—heavy and prone to slipping into the depths—with the light force of fire and spirit flying into the vast heights, surrounding them with the heavens; which greatest force of the heavens bound together these two disparate forces..."

...and in sacrifices we invoke the Twin Janus, Father Janus, Janus Juno...
