...names: Janus the Sower <note>original: *Janus Consivium*</note>, Janus of the Spear <note>original: *Janus Quirinus*</note>, Janus the Opener <note>original: *Janus Patulcius*</note>, and Janus the Shutter <note>original: *Janus Clusius*</note>. Why we invoke him as the **Twin-faced** <note>original: *geminum*</note> has been explained above. We call him **Father** as if he were the god of gods. We call him **Junonian** because he holds the entry not only to the month of January, but to all months; for all the Kalends <note>The first day of the month</note> fall under the jurisdiction of Juno. Regarding this, Varro writes in the fifth book of his *Human Antiquities* that twelve altars were dedicated to Janus to represent the twelve months. The name **Sower** <note>original: *Consivium*</note> comes from "sowing," that is, from the propagation of the human race, which is sown with Janus as the author. **Quirinus** is used because he is powerful in war, derived from the spear which the Sabines call a *curis*. He is called **Opener** <note>original: *Patultium*</note> and **Shutter** <note>original: *Clusivium*</note> because his doors lie open during war and are closed in peace. The following reason is given for this custom: during the Sabine War, which was fought

<margin>The Janual gate.</margin>
on account of the abducted maidens, the Romans hurried to close the gate located at the foot of the Viminal Hill—which was later called the Janual Gate from this event—because the enemy were rushing into it. After it was closed, it soon opened again of its own accord. When this happened a second and third time, many armed men stood as guards at the threshold because they were unable to keep it shut. While a fierce battle was being fought elsewhere, a rumor suddenly spread that our forces had been routed by Tatius <note>King of the Sabines</note>; for this reason, the Romans guarding the entrance fled in terror. Just as the Sabines were about to break through the open gate, it is said that a massive force of torrents erupted from the temple of Janus through this gate, with gushing waves. Many of the enemy ranks perished, either scalded by the boiling water or swallowed by the rapid whirlpool. Because of this event, it was decreed that during times of war, the doors should be opened as if the god had set out to help the city. So much for Janus. But let us return to the **Saturnalia**. It was considered a sin to begin a war during the Saturnalia; to demand punishment from a criminal during these days is a crime requiring atonement. Among our ancestors, the Saturnalia used to end in a single day, which was the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January <note>December 17th</note>. But after Julius Caesar added two days to this month, the festival began to be celebrated on the sixteenth day. It happened that while the common people were ignorant of the fixed

<margin>The days of the Saturnalia.</margin>
day of the Saturnalia—some celebrating on the day inserted by Caesar and others according to the old custom—the Saturnalia came to be counted as lasting several days. Even among the ancients there was an opinion that the Saturnalia lasted seven days—if it can be called an opinion when it is confirmed by reliable authors. For Novius, the highly esteemed writer of Atellan farces <note>A form of early Roman improvisational comedy</note>, says: "The long-awaited seven days of Saturnalia have come." Mummius also, who revived the long-dormant art of Atellan farce after Novius and Pomponius, says: "Our ancestors, who established many things well, did this best: they made the seven days of Saturnalia occur in the height of the cold." But Mallius says that those who defended themselves under the name and religion of Saturn (as we said above) established three days of festival and called them the Saturnalia. Following this tradition, Augustus ordered in his judicial laws that three days be kept as holidays. Masurius and others believed the Saturnalia fell on only one day, the fourteenth before the Kalends of January. Fenestella confirms their view, saying that the virgin Aemilia was condemned on the fifteenth before the Kalends of January; if the Saturnalia had been happening that day, she would not have pleaded her case at all. Then he added: "The Saturnalia followed that day." Soon after he says: "On the following day, which was the thirteenth before the Kalends of January <note>December 20th</note>, the virgin Licinia was ordered to plead her case." From this he shows that the thirteenth is a working day. The twelfth <note>December 21st</note>, however, is the festival of the goddess **Angeronia**, to whom the pontiffs perform a sacrifice in the chapel of

<margin>The chapel of Volupia; Angeronia.</margin>
**Volupia**. Verrius Flaccus says she is called Angeronia because, when appeased, she drives away anguish and anxieties of the soul. Masurius adds that the image of this goddess is placed on the altar of Volupia with her mouth bound and sealed for this reason: so that those who conceal their pains and anxieties may, through the benefit of patience, arrive at the greatest pleasure <note>original: *voluptas*</note>. Julius Modestus says sacrifice is made to this goddess because the Roman people were once freed from a disease called

<margin>The disease of Angina.</margin>
angina <note>A sore throat or quinsy</note> after a vow was made. On the eleventh before the Kalends <note>December 22nd</note>, the festival is dedicated to the **Lares** <note>Guardian deities of the household and city</note>, for whom the praetor Aemilius Regillus vowed a temple in the Campus Martius during the war against Antiochus. The tenth before the Kalends <note>December 23rd</note> is the festival of Jupiter, which is called the

<margin>Larentinalia.</margin>
**Larentinalia**. Regarding this, since it is pleasant to tell tales, these are the opinions. They say that during the reign of Ancus, the temple warden of Hercules, having nothing to do during the holidays, challenged the god to a game of dice, with the god himself overseeing the hands of both players...

# BOOK ONE, PAGE 90
### THE SATURNALIA

<margin>Acca Larentia</margin>
...on the condition that the loser should pay for a dinner and a prostitute. Since Hercules was the victor, he shut Acca Larentia—the most famous prostitute of that time—inside the temple along with the dinner. The story goes that on the following day, she received a gift from the god after their union: that she should not reject the first opportunity offered to her when she returned home. It so happened that when she left the temple, she was approached by a man named Carutius, who was captivated by her beauty. She followed his wishes and was joined to him in marriage; after her husband's death, she became the owner of all his property. When she herself passed away, she named the Roman people as her heir. For this reason, Ancus Marcius had a statue of her carved in the Velabrum <note>A valley in Rome between the Palatine and Capitoline hills, once a marshy marketplace.</note>, the most frequented part of the city, and a solemn sacrifice was established in her honor,

<margin>Festivals consecrated to Jupiter</margin>
by which sacrifices were made to her departed spirit by a priest <note>original: *flaminem*</note>. These festivals were also consecrated to Jupiter, because the ancients believed that souls are given by Jupiter and returned to him after death. Cato says that Larentia, having grown wealthy from the trade of a prostitute, left the lands of Turax, Semurium, Lincerium, and Solinium to the Roman people after her death; thus, she was deemed worthy of a magnificent tomb and the honor of an annual funeral rite. Macer, in the first book of his *Histories*, confirms that Acca Larentia, the wife of Faustulus, was the nurse of Romulus and Remus. He claims that during the reign of Romulus, she was married to a wealthy Etruscan named Carutius and inherited his wealth, which she later left to Romulus, whom she had raised; because of this devotion, he established the funeral rites and a festival day in her honor. From all these accounts, it can be gathered that the Saturnalia was originally a single day, celebrated only on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January <note>December 17th</note>. On that day alone, after the banquet at the Temple of Saturn,

<margin>The Opalia</margin>
the cry "Saturnalia!" would ring out. This day is now assigned to the Opalia during the Saturnalia, since it was originally dedicated to Saturn and Ops together. They believed this goddess Ops was the

<margin>Ops</margin>
wife of Saturn, and therefore both the Saturnalia and the Opalia are celebrated in this month, because Saturn and his wife are believed to be the discoverers of both grain and fruit. Thus, once all the produce of the fields has been gathered, men worship these gods as the authors of a more civilized life; some are even persuaded that they represent

<margin>The origin of Saturn</margin>
the Sky and the Earth. They say Saturn is named from "sowing" <note>original: *a satu*</note>, the cause of which comes from the sky, and that Ops is the Earth, by whose "help" <note>original: *ope*</note> the nourishment for human life is sought, or perhaps from "work" <note>original: *ab opere*</note>, through which fruits and grains are born. Those who offer vows to this goddess do so while seated, and they intentionally touch the earth, demonstrating that Mother Earth herself is to be sought by mortals. Philochorus says that Cecrops first established an altar to Saturn and Ops in Attica, and worshipped those gods as Jupiter and the Earth. He ordained that the masters of households, once the grains and fruits were gathered, should eat everywhere with their slaves, with whom they had endured the burden of labor in tilling the fields; for he said the god is delighted by the honor shown to slaves in contemplation of their labor. This is why, according to

<margin>Why they sacrifice to Saturn with an uncovered head</margin>
foreign custom, we perform the sacred rite to this god with an uncovered head <note>The Romans usually veiled their heads during sacrifice; baring the head was a Greek custom.</note>. I believe we have now abundantly proved that the Saturnalia used to be celebrated on only one day, that is, the fourteenth day before the Kalends. But later, it was extended to three days, first because of the days added by Caesar to this month, and then by an edict of Augustus, who assigned a three-day holiday to the Saturnalia. Thus, beginning on the sixteenth day, they end on the fourteenth <note>Counting backwards in the Roman style</note>, the day on which they were previously accustomed to occur. But the added celebration of the "Day of Little Seals" <note>original: *Sigillaria*</note> extends the public gathering and religious joy to seven days.

<margin>The Sigillaria</margin>
At this point, Evangelus <note>One of the guests in Macrobius's dialogue, often playing the role of the cynical or rude interloper.</note> said: "This, indeed, I can no longer bear! Our friend Praetextatus <note>The host and lead scholar of the dialogue.</note>, in a pompous display of his own wit and a boastful show of speaking, just a moment ago wanted to claim it as an honor to some god that slaves should eat with their masters—as if the gods truly cared about slaves, or as if any wise man would admit the insult of such a foul association into his own home. And now, he tries to assign a religious duty to the

<margin>Oscilla</margin>
*Sigillaria*, which merely provide clay puppets <note>original: *oscillis fictilibus*</note> as playthings for infants who are still crawling. And because he is considered the prince of the religious, he now mixes in some superstitions as well—as if it were not permitted for us to occasionally disbelieve Praetextatus." When everyone had shuddered at this, Praetextatus said with a smile: "Evangelus, I am willing for you to think me superstitious and unworthy of belief, unless a proven reason demonstrates the truth of both matters to you. And as we speak first of the slaves: do you think they are a race of men in jest, or in earnest? For the gods..."

# BOOK ONE

#### A2

...do the immortals not deign to look upon them with their care or providence? Or perhaps you do not permit slaves to be counted among the number of men? Hear then how much indignation reached heaven concerning the punishment of a slave.

### The History of Atronius Concerning a Punished Slave, Chapter VII.

<margin>The history of Atronius concerning a punished slave</margin>
For in the four hundred and forty-fourth year after the founding of Rome, a certain Atronius Maximus <note>Other historical sources, such as Livy, identify this man as Titus Latinius.</note> drove his slave through the circus before the start of the spectacle; the slave had been beaten and was bound to a wooden yoke <note>original: *patibulo*</note>. For this reason, Jupiter was indignant. He commanded a certain Annius in a dream to announce to the Senate that this performance, so full of cruelty, had displeased him. When Annius ignored the vision, a sudden death took his own son. After a second warning, and because of the same negligence, he himself collapsed into a sudden weakness of the body. Finally, on the advice of his friends, he was carried in a litter <note>original: *lectica*</note> to the Senate and delivered the message. Scarcely had he finished speaking when he immediately recovered his health and walked out of the curia <note>The Senate house.</note> on his own feet. Therefore, by a decree of the Senate and by the Maevian law, a day was added to those Circensian games to appease Jupiter, and it was called the "restoration day" <note>original: *instauraticius*</note>. This was named not from the yoke—as some think from the Greek word <margin>The Restoration day; To restore</margin> *apo tou staurou* <note>original: ἀπό τοῦ σταυροῦ, meaning "from the cross" or "from the yoke."</note>—but from the act of "redintegration" or renewal, as Varro prefers, who says that *instaurare* <term>To restore/renew</term> is like making a thing new again.

Do you see how much care for a slave reached even the highest of the gods? But from where does your great and monstrous disdain for slaves come? As if they are not composed of and nourished by the same elements as you, and do not draw the same breath from the same source. Consider that those whom you call your property were born from the same seeds, enjoy the same sky, and live and die just as you do. They are slaves; rather, they are men. They are slaves; rather, they are fellow-slaves.

<margin>How much the condition of slaves is to be valued</margin>
If you consider that Fortune has equal power over both, you can see him as a free man just as easily as he can see you as a slave. Do you not know at what age Hecuba <note>The Queen of Troy who became a slave after the city's fall.</note> began to serve? Or Croesus? Or the mother of Darius? Or Diogenes? Or even Plato himself? Finally, why do you so dread the name of slavery? He is indeed a slave, but by necessity; yet perhaps he is a slave with a free soul. Will it harm him if you show who is *not* a slave? One serves lust, another greed, another ambition; all serve hope, and all serve fear. Truly, no slavery is more disgraceful than that which is voluntary.
<margin>Disgraceful slavery</margin>

But we trample upon the one lying under the yoke imposed by Fortune as if he were wretched and vile. Yet that yoke which we place upon our own necks, we do not allow to be criticized. You will find among slaves someone stronger than money; you will find a master, out of hope for profit, pressing kisses onto the hands of another's slaves. I shall therefore judge men not by their fortune, but by their character <note>original: *moribus*</note>. Each person gives themselves their character; chance assigns their condition. Just as it is foolish for a man about to buy a horse to inspect not the animal itself but its saddle and bridle, so he is most foolish who thinks a man should be valued by his clothing or by his social condition—which is merely a garment wrapped around us. It is not necessary, my dear Evangelus, that you seek a friend only in the forum or the Senate. If you look carefully, you will find one at home as well. Live with your slave mercifully and kindly; admit him to your conversation and occasionally into your necessary deliberations. For our ancestors, removing all envy from masters and all insult from slaves, called the master the "father of the family" <note>original: *pater familias*</note> and the slaves "the household" <note>original: *familiares*, literally 'members of the family'</note>.
<margin>The counsel of slaves is not to be despised; Household members</margin>

Therefore, let your slaves respect you (believe me) rather than fear you. Someone will say that I am now casting masters down from their high position and, in a way, calling slaves to the cap of liberty <note>original: *pilleum*, a felt cap given to emancipated slaves.</note>, because I said they ought to respect rather than fear. Whoever feels this way forgets that what is enough for the gods is enough for masters; furthermore, he who respects also loves, and love cannot be mixed with fear. From where do you think that most arrogant proverb arose, which people toss about: "As many enemies as there are slaves"? We do not have them as enemies, but we make them so, when we are most proud, most insulting, and most cruel toward them. Our own luxuries force us to reach a state of madness, so that whatever does not respond to our will evokes anger and fury.
<margin>As many enemies as slaves</margin>

For we take on the souls of tyrants toward them, and we wish to exercise our power over slaves not as much as is becoming, but as much as is permitted. For (to pass over other types of cruelty) there are those who, while they distend themselves with the abundance and greed of the table, do not permit the surrounding slaves even to move their lips, not even for the purpose of speaking.

# SATURNALIA

<margin>The loyalty of slaves</margin>
Every murmur is suppressed by the rod; not even accidental sounds are exempt from beatings. A cough, a sneeze, or a hiccup is paid for with great suffering. Thus it happens that those who are not permitted to speak in their master's presence speak about their master behind his back. But those who were allowed to converse not only in their masters' presence but even with them—those whose mouths were not sewn shut—were ready to offer their own necks for their master and turn any imminent danger onto their own heads. They spoke at banquets, but they remained silent under torture. Shall we review the virtues practiced in the hearts of slaves? First, let 

<margin>Vrbinus</margin> 
Vrbinus <note>Also known as Panapio in other accounts; he was a Roman proscribed during the civil wars.</note> come to your mind. When he was ordered to be killed and was hiding in Reate, his hiding place was betrayed. One of his slaves put on his master's ring and clothes and lay in the bedroom into which the pursuers were rushing. He presented his neck to the soldiers as they entered and received the blow as if he were Vrbinus himself. Later, after Vrbinus was restored to his status, he built a monument to this slave with an inscription that spoke of such great merit. 

<margin>Aesopus</margin> 
Aesopus, a freedman <note>A former slave who has been granted or bought his freedom.</note> of Demosthenes, was an accomplice to the adultery that his patron had committed with Julia. Although he was tortured for a very long time, he steadfastly refused to betray his patron, until Demosthenes himself confessed after other accomplices provided proof. And lest you think a secret can only easily be hidden by one person: Labienus was hiding with the help of his freedmen, and although the freedmen were compelled by every kind of torture to reveal him, they could not be forced to do so. And lest anyone say of a freedman that this loyalty was due to the benefit of having received freedom rather than to his natural character, consider the kindness of a slave toward a master even 

<margin>Restio</margin> 
while he himself was being punished by that master. For when Antius Restio was proscribed <note>Placed on a list of state enemies whose property was confiscated and who could be killed for a reward.</note> and was fleeing alone at night, while his other slaves were plundering his goods, one slave—who was still in chains and had his forehead branded <note>original: *inscripta fronte*. Branding was a common punishment for runaway or "bad" slaves.</note> as punishment—was released from his custody after his master’s condemnation. This slave followed the fleeing man and urged him not to fear him, saying that the insult he had suffered should be blamed on fortune, not on his master. He then hid and fed his master through his own efforts. When he later sensed that pursuers were near, he killed an old man whom chance threw in his way and threw him onto a prepared funeral pyre. When the fire was lit, he ran to those searching for Restio, saying that the condemned man had paid the penalty to him—

<margin>Cepio</margin> 
that he had tormented the master much more severely than he himself had been tormented. Because he was believed, Restio was saved. Consider also Caepio, who had been motivated to kill Augustus; after the crime was detected and he was condemned, a slave 
carried him to the Tiber in a chest. He brought him by a night journey to the Laurentine field to his father's villa. Then, when the master was cast ashore by a shipwreck at Cumae, the slave hid him discretely at Naples. When he was caught by a centurion, he could be moved neither by bribes 

<margin>Asinius Pollio</margin> 
nor by threats to betray his master. Also, when Asinius Pollio was harshly forcing the people of Patavium <note>Modern-day Padua.</note> to contribute money and arms, and the masters were hiding because of this, a reward and freedom were offered to slaves who would betray their masters. It is well established that not a single slave was overcome by the reward or betrayed his master. Hear now of a slave who showed not only loyalty, but also an eloquent 

<margin>Grumentum</margin> 
genius for invention. When the city of Grumentum was being pressed by a siege, some slaves left their mistress and fled to the enemy. Later, when the town was captured, they formed a conspiracy and rushed into the house. They dragged out their mistress with faces threatening punishment, loudly declaring to those they met that they had finally been given the opportunity to punish their cruel mistress. While they appeared to be dragging her off to execution, they protected her with services full of devotion. See also in this station of life a greatness of soul that prefers death to a life of mockery. Cluentius Pelignus, an Italian who was seized by his own cohorts 

<margin>Cluentius Pelignus. An Italian</margin> 
lest he be handed over to Pompey, was killed by his slave, who then killed himself so as not to survive his master. When Gaius Gracchus was fleeing from the Aventine Hill, his slave Euporus—or as some record, Philocrates—

<margin>C. Gracchus</margin> 
remained an inseparable companion as long as there was any hope of safety, protecting him by whatever means he could. Then, over the body of his slain master, he poured out his own life, tearing his vitals with a self-inflicted wound. Consider Publius 

<margin>Scipio saved by a slave</margin> 
Scipio himself, the father of Africanus; after he had fought with Hannibal and was wounded, a slave placed him on a horse and, while everyone else was deserting, he alone brought him back to the camp. It might seem like a small thing to have served masters while they lived; but what of the courage found in seeking vengeance for them? For a slave of King Seleucus, while serving a friend of the king who had murdered his master, stabbed him while he was dining to avenge his master. What shall I say of the two virtues which are rare even among nobles...

#### BOOK ONE

A2

<margin>Anaxilaus
Mycitho</margin>
...it is clear that in one servant <note>original: *mancipio*</note> there existed both the pious desire for ruling and the greatness of soul for despising power. Anaxilaus of Messene, who founded Messana in Sicily, was the tyrant of the Rhegians. When he died, leaving behind young children, he was content to entrust them to his slave, Mycitho. This man managed the guardianship with such integrity and held power so mercifully that the Rhegians did not disdain being ruled by a slave. When the boys finally reached adulthood, he handed over both the property and the power to them. He himself, taking only a small travel allowance, departed and grew old at Olympia in the greatest tranquility. To what extent the fortune of a slave has been of benefit to the public is shown by many examples. In the Punic War, when there were not enough men to be enrolled, slaves promised they would fight for their masters; they were received into the state and called <margin>Volones</margin> *Volones* <note>original: *uolones*; meaning "volunteers," from the Latin *uello* (to wish or want)</note> because they did this of their own free will. At Cannae, after the Romans were defeated, eight thousand slaves were purchased and served as soldiers. Even though captives could have been ransomed for less, the Republic preferred to entrust itself to slaves during such a great storm. Furthermore, after the disaster and the famous defeat suffered at Lake Trasimene, freedmen were also called to take the military oath. In the Social War, the efforts of twelve cohorts <note>A cohort was a standard tactical unit of a Roman legion, numbering about 480 men.</note> <margin>When and in which wars slaves were accepted into military service</margin> composed of freedmen were seen to be of remarkable courage. We have also learned that when Caesar replaced fallen soldiers, he accepted slaves from his friends and made use of their brave efforts. Caesar Augustus in Germany and Illyricum recruited many cohorts of freedmen, which he called "Voluntary" cohorts. And lest you think these things happened only in our Republic, when Zopyrion was besieging the Borysthenians, they were able to withstand the enemy by freeing their slaves, granting citizenship to foreigners, and canceling debts <note>original: *tabulis nouis*; literally "new tablets," a common Roman term for debt forgiveness</note>. Cleomenes of Sparta, when only one thousand five hundred Spartans were left who could bear arms, enrolled nine thousand warriors from manumitted <note>Term for the formal act of freeing a slave.</note> slaves. The Athenians also, after their public resources were exhausted, gave freedom to their slaves. And lest you think that such virtues among slaves existed only in the male sex, hear of a deed by slave women that is no less memorable; indeed, you will find no deed more useful to the Republic in any class of nobility. It is so widely known <margin>Festival of the slave women</margin> that the seventh of July <note>original: *Nonis iuliis*</note> is a festival day for slave women that neither its origin nor the cause of its celebration is unknown. For on that day, both free women and slave women sacrifice to Juno Caprotina under a wild fig tree <note>original: *caprifico*</note> in memory of the kind courage which appeared in the souls of the slave women for the preservation of public dignity. After the city was captured and the Gallic uprising had subsided, the Republic was reduced to a meager state. The neighbors, seizing the opportunity to attack the Roman name, placed Posthumius Livius, the dictator of the Fidenates, in command. He sent mandates to the Senate demanding that if they wished the remains of their city to survive, the mothers of families and the virgins should be handed over to him. While the fathers were suspended in a doubtful deliberation, a slave woman named Tutela—or <margin>Tutela or Philothis the slave woman</margin> Philotis—promised that she, with the other slave women, would go to the enemy under the names of their mistresses. Having taken the clothing of matrons and virgins, they were brought to the enemy, with those following them weeping to create a convincing display of grief. When they had been distributed throughout the camp by Livius, they provoked the men with a great deal of wine, pretending that it was a festival day for them. When the men had been <margin>A beautiful deed done by slave women for the Roman People</margin> lulled to sleep, the women gave a signal to the Romans from a wild fig tree that was closest to the camp. When the Romans had overcome them in a sudden raid, the Senate, mindful of the benefit, ordered all the slave women to be set free, provided them with dowries from the public treasury, and allowed them to wear the finery they had used then. The Senate named the day itself the *Nonae Caprotinae* <margin>The Nonae Caprotinae</margin> after that wild fig tree from which they took the signal of victory, and established a sacrifice to be celebrated with an annual solemnity. For this sacrifice, the milk that flows from the wild fig tree is used in memory of the preceding deed. But the slave's nature was not unfit or unequal even to the study of philosophy. Phaedo <note>original: *Phædron*</note>, of the Socratic circle, <margin>Phaedo</margin> was so close to Socrates and Plato that Plato dedicated that divine book on the immortality of the soul to his name. He was a slave of noble form and intellect. Cebes the Socratic is said to have bought him at the urging of Socrates; he kept him in the disciplines of philosophy, and he later emerged as an illustrious philosopher. His very elegant dialogues about Socrates are still read.

# XXXVIIII
### OF THE SATURNALIA

<margin>
Menippus
Polus
Perseus
Mys
Diogenes
</margin>
There were also many others who were slaves and later emerged as famous philosophers. Among them was the famous Menippus, whose books Marcus Varro emulated in his satires—which some call "Cynic" satires, though he himself called them "Menippean." <note>Menippus of Gadara (3rd century BCE) was a Cynic satirist known for mixing prose and verse. Marcus Varro was a prolific Roman scholar.</note> There was also Polus, the slave of the Peripatetic philosopher Philostratus; and the slave of Zeno the Stoic, who was called Perseus; and Epicurus’s slave, whose name was Mys. All were philosophers of no small renown in their time. Then there is Diogenes the Cynic, who, though he had fallen from freedom into slavery, was once being auctioned when Xeniades of Corinth wished to buy him. When Xeniades asked what craft he knew, Diogenes replied, "I know how to command free men." <note>original: *noui hominibus liberis impare*</note> Then Xeniades, 
<margin>Epictetus</margin>
marvelling at this response, set him free and, handing his own sons over to him, said: "Take my children, whom you shall command." Regarding the noble philosopher Epictetus—who was also a slave—the memory is too recent for his story to be lost among the forgotten. Two verses written by him about himself are often quoted, from which you may subtly understand that those who struggle in this life with various hardships are not entirely hated by the gods, but that there are secret reasons which only the curiosity of a few can reach:

->I, Epictetus, was born a slave, and was maimed in body,<-
->and as poor as Irus, yet dear to the immortals.<-
<note>original Greek: *Δοῦλος Ἐπίκτητος γενόμην καὶ σώματι πηρός: καὶ πενίην ἶρος καὶ φίλος ἀθανάτοις.* Irus was the famous beggar in Homer’s Odyssey.</note>

You have now, I believe, a proven case that the name of "slave" is not to be looked upon with disdain, since even Jupiter himself took care for a slave, and it is established that many among them have been faithful, far-sighted, brave, and even philosophers. 
<margin>Sigillaria</margin>
Now I must briefly review the matter of the *sigillaria* <note>The *Sigillaria* was the final part of the Saturnalia festival where people gave small clay figurines (*sigilla*) as gifts.</note>, lest you think I have spoken of things to be laughed at rather than things that are sacred. Epicadus reports that after Hercules killed Geryon, he led the cattle through Italy as a victor. Having built a temporary bridge—which is now called the 
<margin>Sublician bridge</margin>
Sublician bridge <note>The *Pons Sublicius* is the oldest known bridge in ancient Rome, made of wooden beams (*sublicae*).</note>—he cast human effigies into the river, equal in number to the companions he had lost by chance during his wanderings. He did this so that the current might carry them down to the sea and return them to their ancestral lands in place of the bodies of the deceased. From this, the custom of fashioning such likenesses remained part of the sacred rites. However, I consider the origin of this practice to be truer to the one I mentioned a little while ago. After the Pelasgians <note>An ancient people of the Greek world.</note> learned through a more fortunate interpretation that "heads" did not mean living heads, but clay ones, and that the word *phos* <note>original Greek: *φωτός*; a pun playing on the Greek word's double meaning for "man" and "light."</note> signified not only a man but also a light, they began to light wax candles to Saturn instead of human sacrifice, and to bring certain masks <note>original: *oscilla*</note> to the little chapel of Dis which adjoins the altar of Saturn, in place of their own heads. 
<margin>Sigilla</margin>
From this, it was handed down that wax candles should be sent as gifts during the Saturnalia, and that "seals" <note>original: *sigilla*; small figurines</note> should be fashioned by the potter's art and prepared for sale, which people might offer to Saturn and Dis as a substitute for themselves and their families. For this reason, the bustling trade in such items begins at the Saturnalia and occupies seven days—which are all made holidays, though not all are festival days. For we have proven that the festival itself falls in the middle, that is, on the 13th day before the Kalends of January <note>December 17th.</note>, and this has been proven by the claims of others who have more fully recorded the system of the year, the months, the days, and the order organized by Caesar.

---

->In what order the year was, or how it came to be.<-
->Chapter VIII.<-

<margin>Order of the year</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'C' with scrollwork and foliage inside a square border.</image-desc>As he wished to make an end of speaking here, Aurelius Symmachus added: "Proceed, my dear Praetextatus, with such sweet eloquence to discourse upon the year as well, before you experience the nuisance of someone asking. If anyone present happens to be ignorant of the order it followed among the ancients, or how it was later renewed by more certain rules, you yourself seem to have incited the minds of the listeners to learn this by discussing the days added to the month." Then, with the same flow of speech, he wove together the rest. A certain measure of the year always existed among the Egyptians alone; for other nations, it wavered with a differing number of days and an equal measure of error. To be content with mentioning the customs of only a few regions: the Arcadians divided their year into three months; the Acarnanians into six; the rest of the Greeks computed their own year at three hundred and fifty-four days. It is no wonder, then, that in this variety, the Romans also once had their year 
<margin>Of thirty days</margin>
organized into ten months by the authority of Romulus; because the year began in March and was completed in three hundred and four days. Thus six months—namely April, June, August, September, November, and December—consisted of thirty days each; while four others—March, May, July, and October—had thirty-one...

That this was the first month of the year is proven most clearly by this: from March itself, July [Quintilis] is the fifth month, and the following months were named in order according to their number. Also, on the first day of this month, they would light new fire on the altars of Vesta, so that as the year began, the care of tending the renewed fire might begin again. The month 
of April
</margin>
¶ He named the second month April: as some believe, with an aspiration, as if it were "Aphrilis," from the foam <note>original Greek: αφρόν (aphron)</note> from which Venus is believed to have been born. They claim Romulus's reason was this: that he might name the first month after his father, Mars, and the second after Aeneas’s mother, Venus. Thus, those from whom the origin of the Roman name began would especially watch over the beginnings of the year—since even today in our sacred rites we call Mars "Father" and Venus "Mother." Others think that Romulus, either through a higher wisdom or the providence of a certain divine power, ordered the first months such that since the preceding one was dedicated to Mars—a god who is often the killer of men (as Homer says: "Ares, Ares, slayer of men, blood-stained, stormer of walls" <note>original Greek: αρες αρες βροτολοιγε μιαιφονε τειχεσιπλητα</note>)—the second should be dedicated to Venus, who might soothe his violence with her beneficial influence. For even among the twelve signs of the zodiac, which are believed to be the certain dwellings of certain deities, while the first sign, Aries [the Ram], is assigned to Mars, the following one, Taurus [the Bull], immediately received Venus. And again, on the opposite side, Scorpio is so divided that it is common to both gods. Nor is this division thought to lack celestial reason. Indeed, the rear part, armed with a sting as if it were a most powerful weapon, is the dwelling of Mars; but the forward part, which is called the "Yoke" among the Greeks <note>original Greek: ζυγός (zygos)</note> and which we call "The Scales" [Libra], Venus received, who joins marriages as if with a concordant yoke and composes friendships. However, Cingius, in the book he left behind *On the Calendar* [Fastis], says that some ignorantly think the ancients named the month of April after Venus, since no festival day and no notable sacrifice was instituted for Venus during this month by our ancestors. 
<margin>The name of Venus.</margin>
Furthermore, Varro agrees with Cingius, affirming that the name of Venus was not even used among Romans under the kings, whether in Latin or Greek; therefore, the month could not have been named after Venus. But since the sky is usually gloomy and covered with clouds before the spring equinox, and the sea is closed to sailors, and the lands themselves are covered by water, frost, or snow—and all these things "open up" in the spring (that is, in this month)—and the trees, as well as the other things the earth contains, begin to open themselves into buds: for all these reasons, it should be believed the month is rightly called "April," as if it were "Aperilis" [the Opening Month]. Similarly, among the Athenians, the same month is called *Anthesterion* <note>original Greek: ανθεστηριών</note> from the fact that at this time all things flourish. Nevertheless, Verrius Flaccus does not deny that it was later established on this day for matrons to perform a sacrifice to Venus—the reason for which we must pass over, as it does not fit this location.

<margin>The month of May.</margin>
¶ Romulus placed May as the third month, concerning whose name there is broad disagreement among authors. For Fulvius Nobilior, in the *Fasti* [Calendar] which he placed in the Temple of Hercules of the Muses, says that after Romulus divided the people into "Majores" [elders] and "Juniores" [youths], so that one part might protect the state with counsel and the other with arms, he named this month "May" [Maius] and the following "June" [Junius] in honor of both parts. There are those who record that this month passed into our calendar from the people of Tusculum.

# OF THE SATURNALIA
<page-num>LXXXXVII</page-num>

<margin>Menippus</margin>
Not a few other slaves also existed who later emerged as famous philosophers. Among these was Menippus, whose books Marcus Varro imitated in his satires—which some call "Cynic" satires, but he himself called "Menippean" <note>Menippus of Gadara (3rd century BCE) was a Cynic satirist; Varro’s "Menippean Satires" combined prose and verse.</note>. 
<margin>Polus</margin>
There was also Polus, the slave of Philostratus the Peripatetic; and the slave of Zeno the Stoic, who was called Perseus; 
<margin>Perseus</margin>
and Epicurus’s slave, whose name was Mys. These were philosophers of no small renown who lived in that age. 
<margin>Mys</margin>
Even Diogenes the Cynic, although he had passed from freedom into slavery by being sold: when Xeniades the Corinthian wished to buy him and asked what trade he knew, Diogenes replied, "I know how to command free men." 
<margin>Diogenes</margin>
Then Xeniades, marvelling at his answer, set him free and, handing his own sons over to him, said, "Take my children, whom you shall command." Regarding the noble philosopher Epictetus, because he too was a slave, the memory is too recent 
<margin>Epictetus</margin>
to be lost among things forgotten. Two verses written by him about himself are circulated, from which you may understand a deeper meaning: that those who struggle in this life with various hardships are not entirely hated by the gods, but that there are hidden causes which only the curiosity of a few can reach:

> I was Epictetus, born a slave, and crippled in body,
> and a beggar like Irus, yet dear to the immortals. <note>original Greek: Δοῦλοϛ Ἐπίκτητοϛ γενόμην καὶ σώματι πηρόϛ. καὶ πενίην ἶροϛ καὶ φίλοϛ ἀθανάτοιϛ.</note>

You have (I believe) proof that the name of "slave" should not be looked down upon with disdain, since even Jupiter felt concern for a slave, and it is well-established that many of them have emerged as loyal, farsighted, brave, and even philosophers. Now, regarding the *Sigillaria* <term>Sigillaria: A festival of "little seals" or figurines occurring at the end of the Saturnalia</term>, I must review a few points, lest you think I am speaking of things to be laughed at rather than sacred matters. 
<margin>Sigillaria</margin>
Epicadus reports that Hercules, after killing Geryon and driving his herds through Italy as a victor, built a temporary bridge (which is now called the Sublician) 
<margin>Sublician bridge</margin>
and cast human effigies into the river, equal in number to the companions he had lost by chance during his travels. This was done so that the current might carry them to the sea and return them to their ancestral homes in place of the bodies of the deceased. From this, the custom of fashioning such images remained among sacred rites. But to me, the origin of this practice seems more truly that which I recall mentioning a little while ago: that after the Pelasgians <note>The mythical early inhabitants of Greece and Italy.</note> learned a more favorable interpretation—that the oracle meant "clay heads" rather than the heads of living men, and that "light" [phōs] could signify a candle as well as a human life <note>original: "φωτὸϛ" (phōtos). This is a wordplay: in Greek, "phōs" can mean both "man" and "light."</note>—they began to light wax candles to Saturn instead, and to bring certain figurines to the little chapel of Dis <note>The god of the underworld.</note> that stood next to the altar of Saturn, in place of their own lives. From that time, the tradition was handed down that wax candles were sent as gifts during the Saturnalia, and little seals [sigilla] 
<margin>Sigilla</margin>
were fashioned with the art of clay and prepared for sale, which people would offer as a purification for themselves and their families to Dis and Saturn. Therefore, the celebration of such commerce began during the Saturnalia and occupies seven days; however, it makes only some of those days holidays, not all. For we have proven that the festival is in the middle, that is, on the 13th day before the Kalends <note>December 17th.</note>, and this has been proven by other assertions from those who have more fully reported the reckoning of the year, the months, the days, and the arrangement organized by Caesar.

---

### VIII. In what order the year was, and in what order it is now.

<margin>The order of the year</margin>
**W**hen he wished to make an end of speaking, Aurelius Symmachus added: "Proceed, my dear Praetextatus, with such sweet eloquence to also discourse upon the year, before you experience the annoyance of another question. For if anyone among those present is perhaps ignorant of the order it followed among the ancients, or how it was later renewed by more certain rules, you yourself seem to have incited the minds of the listeners to learn this by discussing the days added to the month." Then, with the same flow of speaking, he wove together the rest. A fixed measure of the year always existed among the Egyptians alone; for other nations, it wavered with a different number of days and an equal amount of error. And to be content with reporting the custom of only a few regions: the Arcadians divided their year into three months; the Acarnanians into six; the rest of the Greeks reckoned their own year at three hundred and sixty-four days. It is therefore not surprising that in this variety the Romans also once had their year organized into ten months by the authority of Romulus, because the year began in March and was completed 
<margin>Of thirty days</margin>
in three hundred and four days; so that six months—namely April, June, August [Sextilis], September, November, and December—were of thirty days each, while four—March, May, July [Quintilis], and October—were of thirty-one days each.

# BOOK ONE
<page-num>XLVII</page-num>

...and they were dispatched individually: those who even today have the Nones on the seventh day; the others on the fifth.
<margin>Nones on the seventh; Nones on the fifth</margin>
For those having the Nones on the seventh, the Kalends returned from the Ides on the seventeenth day. But for those having them on the fifth, the start of the Kalends returned on the eighteenth.

---

<margin>March as the first month</margin>
This was the arrangement of Romulus: he dedicated the first month of the year to his father, Mars. That this was the first month of the year is proved most clearly by this: that the fifth month from it is called *Quintilis* <note>The "fifth" month, which we now call July.</note>, and thereafter the months were named by their number. Also, on the first day of this month, they would kindle the new fire on the altars of Vesta, so that as the year began, the care of maintaining the renewed fire began once more. On the entrance of this same month, both in the Palace, the meeting halls, and the houses of the priests, the old laurels were replaced with new ones. In this same month, sacrifices were made both publicly and privately to Anna Perenna <note>An ancient Roman deity of the circle of the year.</note>, so that
<margin>To pass through the year. Wages were paid to teachers in the month of March. Dinners were served to slaves.</margin>
it might be permitted to "pass through the year and the seasons" <note>original: "annare pannareq;". A traditional prayer for a healthy cycle of the year.</note> comfortably. In this month, wages were paid to teachers, which the completed year made due. The political assemblies were inaugurated; taxes were contracted. And the matrons served dinners to the slaves, just as the masters did during the Saturnalia. The women did this at the beginning of the year to invite the slaves to prompt obedience through this honor; the men did it because they were paying thanks for work completed.

<margin>The month of April</margin>
He named the second month April: as some think, with an aspiration, as if "Aphrilis" from the foam which the Greeks call *aphros* <note>original: ἀφρόν</note>, from which Venus is believed to have been born. And they assert this was Romulus's reasoning: that he should name the first month after his father Mars, and the second after Aeneas's mother, Venus. Thus these two especially would preserve the beginnings of the year, from whom the origin of the Roman name came; since even today in sacred rites we call Mars "father" and Venus "mother." Others think Romulus, either by deeper wisdom or by the providence of a certain deity, ordered the first months such that, since the preceding month was dedicated to Mars—a god who is mostly the slayer of men, as Homer says: 
> Ares, Ares, bane of mortals, blood-stained stormer of walls! <note>original Greek: ἆρεσ ἆρεσ βροτολοιγὲ μιαίφονε τείχεσι πλῆθα</note>

the second month should be dedicated to Venus, who would soothe his violence with her kindness. For also in the twelve signs of the zodiac, of which certain homes are believed to belong to certain deities: since the first sign, Aries (the Ram), is assigned to Mars, the following one, Taurus (the Bull), immediately received Venus. And again, from the opposite region, Scorpio is so divided that it is common to both gods. Nor does it seem that the division itself lacks celestial reason. Since the rear part, armed as if with a most powerful weapon (the sting), is the home of Mars; but the first part, which the Greeks call the "Yoke" <note>original: ζυγός</note> and we call Libra (the Scales), Venus received, who joins marriages as if with a concordant yoke and composes friendships. But Cingius, in that book he left concerning the calendar, says that some ignorantly think the month of April was named by the ancients after Venus, since no festival day and no notable sacrifice was established for Venus during this month by our ancestors. Indeed, not even in the songs of the Salii <note>The Salii were the "leaping priests" of Mars.</note> is any praise of Venus celebrated, as there is for the other celestial beings.
<margin>The name of Venus.</margin>
Varro agrees with Cingius, affirming that the name of Venus was not even used among the Romans under the kings, neither in Latin nor Greek, and therefore the month could not have been named after Venus. Instead, since the sky is usually gloomy and covered with clouds before the spring equinox, and the sea is closed to sailors, and the lands themselves are covered with either frost or snow, and all these things "open" in the spring—that is, in this month—and the trees, no less than everything else contained in the earth, begin to "open" themselves into bud; it is rightly to be believed from all these things that the month is called April, as if "Aperilis" <note>Derived from the Latin *aperire*, "to open."</note>, just as among the Athenians the same month is called *Anthesterion* <note>original: ἀνθεστηριών</note> because at this time all things flourish. However, Verrius Flaccus does not deny that it was later established on this day that matrons should perform a sacrifice to Venus; the reason for this matter, since it does not fit this place, must be passed over.

<margin>The month of May.</margin>
Romulus placed May as the third; concerning its name there is a wide disagreement among authors. For Fulvius Nobilior, in the calendar which he placed in the Temple of Hercules of the Muses, says that after Romulus divided the people into elders and youths—so that one part might protect the republic by counsel and the other by arms—in honor of both parts, he called this month May <note>From *maiores*, meaning "elders."</note> and the following month June <note>From *iuniores*, meaning "youths."</note>. There are those who mention that this month passed into our calendars from the people of Tusculum...

<header>OF THE SATURNALIA</header>

...among whom it is even now called the god Maius, who is Jupiter; he is so named from his "greatness" <note>original: "magnitudine"</note> and "majesty" <note>original: "maiestate"</note>. Cingius thinks the month was named after Maia, whom he said was the wife of Vulcan. He uses this as an argument: that the Priest of Vulcan <note>The *flamen uulcanalis*.</note> performs a sacrifice to this goddess on the Kalends of May.
<margin>Maia or Maiesta, wife of Vulcan</margin>
But Piso says that Vulcan’s wife is called Maiesta, not Maia. Others contend that Maia, the mother of Mercury, gave her name to the month; they prove this primarily because in this month all merchants sacrifice to Maia and Mercury together. Some affirm—with whom Cornelius Labeo agrees—that this Maia, for whom a sacrifice is celebrated by the elders <note>The "Maiores," providing an alternative etymological link to the month name May.</note> in this month, is the Earth; they say she obtained this name from her greatness, just as she is called the "Great Mother" in sacred rites. They gather evidence
<margin>A sow is sacrificed to Maia</margin>
for this estimation from the fact that a pregnant sow is sacrificed to her, which is the victim specifically designated for the Earth. They say Mercury is joined to her in these rites because the voice is given to a newborn human only upon contact with the earth; and we know, of course, that Mercury is the master of voice and speech. Cornelius Labeo is the authority who states that a temple was dedicated to this Maia (that is, the Earth) on the Kalends of May under the name of the "Good Goddess" <note>original: "Bona Dea"</note>. He confirms that the Good Goddess and the Earth are the same, which can be shown from the more secret rituals of the sacrifices. This
<margin>Fauna, Ops, and Fatua.</margin>
same goddess is invoked in the books of the pontiffs as the "Good Goddess," and as "Fauna," "Ops," and "Fatua." She is called "Good" because she is the cause of all things good for our sustenance; "Fauna" because she favors <note>original: "fauet"</note> every use of living creatures; "Ops" because life consists of her "help" <note>original: "auxilio"</note>; and "Fatua" from "speaking" <note>original: "fando"</note> because (as we said above) infants born from the womb do not utter a voice until they have touched the earth. There are some who say this goddess has the power of Juno, and therefore a royal scepter is placed in her left hand. Others believe she is Proserpina, and that a sow is sacrificed to her because a sow ate the crop which Ceres gave to mortals.
<margin>Semele.</margin>
Others believe she is the "Earthly Hecate" <note>original: "Χθόνιαν ἑκάτην"</note>, or as the Boeotians believe, Semele. They also say she is the daughter of Faunus, and that she resisted her father’s will when he fell in love with her, such that he beat her with a myrtle rod. When she did not yield to her father’s desire even when he plied her with wine, the father is believed to have transformed himself into a serpent and lay with his daughter. As proof of all this, they offer these facts: that
<margin>Wine is not used in the rites of the Good Goddess.</margin>
it is a religious crime <note>original: "nefas"</note> to have a myrtle rod in her temple; that a vine is spread over her head, with which her father chiefly tried to deceive her; and that wine is not usually brought into her temple under its own name, but the vessel in which the wine is placed is called a "honey-pot" and the wine is called "milk." Furthermore, snakes appear in her temple, neither frightening nor being afraid, wandering indifferently. Some think she is Medea, because every kind of herb is found in her temple, from which the priestesses often provide medicines; and because a man is not allowed to enter her temple on account of the injury she suffered from her ungrateful husband, Jason. Among the Greeks she is called the "Women's Goddess" <note>original: "θεὸς γυναικεία"</note>, whom Varro recorded was the daughter of Faunus. She was so modest that she never left the "women's quarters" <note>original: "γυναικωνῖτιν"</note>, her name was never heard in public, nor did she ever see a man or was seen by a man; for which reason no man enters her temple.
<margin>Women did not participate in the rites of Hercules. Potitius and Pinarius, guardians of the rites of Hercules.</margin>
Hence also, women in Italy are not allowed to participate in the sacrifice of Hercules, because when Hercules was driving the cattle of Geryon through the fields of Italy, a woman replied to him when he was thirsty that she could not provide water because it was the day the goddess of women was being celebrated, and it was not lawful for men to taste from that preparation. Because of this, Hercules, when he was about to perform his sacrifice, forbade the presence of women and commanded Potitius and Pinarius, the guardians of the rites, not to permit any woman to be present. Behold the occasion for the name: having said that Maia and the Good Goddess are the same, it compelled us to bring forth whatever we discovered regarding the Good Goddess.

<margin>The month of June</margin>
June follows May; it is named either from the "Junior" part of the people, as we said above, or (as Cingius thinks) because it was previously called "Junonius" among the Latins. For a long time
<margin>Temple of Juno Moneta.</margin>
it was recorded in the calendars of the people of Aricia and Praeneste under this name; so much so that, as Nilus says in the commentaries on the calendars, this name for the month remained for a long time among our ancestors. But later, after certain letters were worn away, it was called "June" instead of "Junonius." For the temple of Juno Moneta was also dedicated on the Kalends of June. Some have thought the month of June was named after Junius Brutus, who was the first...

XLVIII
HEADER: BOOK ONE
A2

<margin>The goddess Carna</margin>
[Brutus] was made consul of Rome; and it is recorded that in this month—specifically on the Kalends of June <note>The first day of the month.</note>—after the expulsion of Tarquin, he performed a sacred rite to the goddess Carna on the Caelian Hill in fulfillment of a vow. They believe this goddess presides over the human vital organs; they therefore petition her to keep the liver, the heart, and whatever internal viscera there are safe and sound. And because it was through the favor of the heart—through the feigned stupidity of which Brutus was considered fit for his role—that the reform of the public state arose, he consecrated a temple to this goddess who presides over the vitals. Bean mash <note>original: "pulte fabatia"</note> and bacon fat are sacrificed to her, because the strength of the body is greatly bolstered by these things. Indeed, the Kalends of June are commonly called the "Bean Kalends" <note>original: "fabariæ"</note> because in this month mature beans are used in divine rites.

<margin>The Bean Kalends. The month of July.</margin>

### ¶July. Chapter X.

Next follows July, which, although it was called *Quintilis* <note>The "fifth" month, counting from March.</note> by number when Romulus's arrangement held the beginning of the year in March, nevertheless retained that name even after Numa placed January and February before it, even though it no longer seemed to be the fifth month, but the seventh. But later, in honor of the dictator Julius Caesar, by a law proposed by the consul Mark Antony, son of Marcus, it was called July, because Julius was born in this month on the fourth day before the Ides of Quintilis <note>July 12th.</note>.

<margin>The month of August.</margin>

### ¶August. Chapter XI.

Then there is August, which was previously called *Sextilis* <note>The "sixth" month.</note> until it was given to the honor of Augustus by a decree of the Senate, the words of which I have subjoined: "Whereas the Emperor Caesar Augustus entered his first consulship in the month of Sextilis; and celebrated three triumphs in the city; and the legions were led down from the Janiculum and followed his auspices and loyalty; and Egypt was brought under the power of the Roman people in this month; and an end was put to the civil wars in this month; and for these reasons this month is and has been most fortunate for this empire; it pleases the Senate that this month be called August." The same decree of the people <note>original: "plebiſcitū"</note> was made for the same reason, with Sextus Pacuvius, tribune of the plebs, proposing the motion.

<margin>September, also called Germanicus.</margin>

### ¶September. Chapter XII.

The month of September retains its original name, [despite] the title of "Germanicus" <note>Emperor Domitian attempted to rename September "Germanicus" after himself, but the name did not persist after his death.</note>.

<margin>October, also called Domitianus.</margin>

### ¶October. Chapter XIII.

Domitian had indeed invaded October with his own name <note>Renaming it "Domitianus".</note>. But when it was decided that the ill-omened name should be erased from every bronze or stone monument, the months were also stripped of that title used by the tyrant's usurpation. Afterward, the caution of the leaders, avoiding the ill omen of starting others, preserved the ancient names for the months from September all the way to December. This was the annual dimension ordered by Romulus, who (as we have said above) established that the year should have ten months, consisting of three hundred and four days. He arranged the months so that four of them had thirty-one days, and six had thirty. But since this number agreed neither with the course of the sun nor the calculations of the moon, it sometimes happened that the cold of the year occurred in the summer months and, conversely, winter heat occurred. Whenever that happened, they allowed as many days to be added without any month name as would bring it to that time of year when the state of the sky was found suitable for the impending month.

<margin>Division of the year by Numa.</margin>

### ¶Division of the year by Numa. Chapter XIV.

<margin>The god Februus. Likewise the month of February.</margin>
But Numa followed; as much as he could grasp by his own natural talent under a raw sky and in an as-yet unpolished age—or perhaps because he was instructed by the observations of the Greeks—he added fifty days so that the year would extend to three hundred and fifty-four days, in which he believed twelve cycles of the moon were completed. To these fifty added by himself, he added another six taken from those six months that had thirty days—that is, one from each—and having made fifty-six days, he divided them by equal measure into two new months. Of these two, he called the first January and wished it to be the first of the year, as it were the month of the two-faced god looking back at the end of the past year and forward to the beginnings of the future. The second he dedicated to the god Februus <note>A god of purification.</note>, who is believed to have power over ritual cleansings. For it was necessary that the city be purified in that month, in which he ordained that...

<meta>This page continues the technical history of the Roman calendar. Having previously discussed the naming of the months, the author now explains the mathematical reforms of Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome, specifically focusing on the shift toward lucky odd numbers and the complex system of adding extra days to align the lunar year with the sun.</meta>

XVII
HEADER: XVII. THE SATURNALIA

<margin>
How many days the months have
</margin>
...so that the proper rites might be paid to the gods of the underworld <note>The "Di Manes," spirits of the deceased ancestors.</note>. The neighboring peoples soon followed Numa’s arrangement, beginning to calculate their own year with as many days and as many months as Pompilius <note>Numa Pompilius.</note> had decided. But they differed in this one respect: they alternated their months between thirty and twenty-nine days. Shortly after Numa’s time—in honor of the odd number, a secret principle that nature was bringing to light even before the time of Pythagoras <note>The philosopher Pythagoras taught that odd numbers were masculine, finite, and lucky, while even numbers were feminine and unlucky.</note>—he added one day, which he gave to January. This was done so that in the year as a whole, as well as in each individual month (except for February), an odd number would be maintained. For since there are twelve months, if each were counted as either an even or an odd number, they would produce an even total; therefore, by making one month an even number, he made the subtraction of that one day result in an odd total for the others. Consequently, January, April, June, <term>Sextilis</term> <note>The "sixth" month, later renamed August.</note>, September, November, and December were reckoned at twenty-nine days, and they held their <term>Nones</term> <note>One of the three monthly marker days, usually falling on the 5th or 7th.</note> on the fifth day, and their <term>Ides</term> were all calculated seventeen days before the next <term>Kalends</term> <note>The first day of the following month.</note>. March, May, <term>Quintilis</term> <note>Later renamed July.</note>, and October, however, possessed thirty-one days each. The Nones in these months fell on the seventh day. Similarly, after the Ides, seventeen days were counted in each month until the following Kalends. But February alone retained twenty-eight days, as if an even number and a sense of deficiency were appropriate for the gods of the underworld.

### ¶ On Intercalation. Chapter XV.

<margin>
Intercalation
</margin>
<note>Intercalation is the practice of inserting extra days or months into a calendar to keep it synchronized with the seasons.</note> When the Romans, following this distribution of Pompilius, calculated their own year according to the course of the moon just as the Greeks did, they necessarily established an <term>intercalary month</term> in the Greek fashion. For when the Greeks realized they had rashly organized the year into 354 days—since it is apparent from the sun’s course, which completes the zodiac in 365 days and a quarter, that their year was short by eleven and a quarter days—they devised a set method of intercalating. Every eight years, they would intercalate ninety days, from which they formed three months of thirty days each. The Greeks did this because it was laborious and difficult to intercalate eleven and a quarter days every single year. Thus, they preferred to multiply this number by eight; the ninety days that result when the quarter-day and the eleven days are combined eight times are then inserted, distributed into three months as we have said. They called these days "overstepping" <note>original Greek: ὑπερβαίνοντας (*hyperbainontas*)</note> and the months "inserted" <note>original Greek: ἐμβολίμους (*embolimous*)</note>. The Romans decided to imitate this order as well, but in vain; for it escaped their notice that they had added one day to the Greek total (as I mentioned above) in honor of the odd number. Because of this, the total number and the sequence could not align over an eight-year period. But while this error was not yet discovered, they followed the Greek example for eight years, calculating ninety days as if they were a surplus to be poured in. They balanced these intercalations by alternating twenty-two days in some years and twenty-three in others across four intercalations. But every eight years, an excess of eight days resulted from these intercalators, because (as I have already said) the Roman year already exceeded the Greek number by one day each year. Once this error was recognized, this type of correction was introduced: in every third eight-year period, they distributed the intercalary days so that not ninety, but sixty-six days were intercalated, compensating for the twenty-four days that had grown above the Greek total over those years. The month of February was assigned for all intercalations, since it was the last month of the year. In this, they were also imitating the Greeks; for they also inserted surplus days into the last month of their year, as recorded by Glaucippus, who wrote about the sacred rites of the Athenians. However, they differed from the Greeks in one way: the Greeks intercalated after the final month was completed, but the Romans did so before February was finished, specifically after the twenty-third day, once the <term>Terminalia</term> <note>A festival in honor of Terminus, god of boundaries, marking the end of the old religious year.</note> had been celebrated. Then they joined the remaining five days of the month of February after the intercalation—I believe—according to the ancient custom of their religion, so that March would always follow February.

### ¶ On Market Days. Chapter XVI.

<margin>
Market Days
</margin>
But since it often happened that the <term>nundinae</term> <note>Market days held every ninth day (counting inclusively), where rural people came to the city.</note> fell sometimes on the first day of the year and sometimes on the Nones—both of which were considered disastrous for the state—a remedy was devised to avert this. We shall explain this, if we first show why the market days were avoided on all Kalends or Nones. For as often as they occurred...

the year began with a day that was added to the <term>market days</term> <note>original: "nundinis"; these were the "ninth-day" markets where rural people came to the city</note>: that entire year was ill-omened and mournful due to various misfortunes. This belief was especially confirmed by the revolt of Lepidus <note>Marcus Aemilius Lepidus led a rebellion in 78 BCE; the calendar's misalignment was blamed for the ensuing chaos</note>.

## ->On the Nones. Chapter XVII.<-

<margin>The Nones</margin>
<margin>The uncertain birthday of Servius Tullius.</margin>
Furthermore, it was thought that a gathering of the entire multitude should be avoided on the **Nones** <note>The Nones were one of the three monthly marker days in the Roman calendar, usually falling on the 5th or 7th</note>. This was because the Roman people, even after the kings had been driven out, celebrated this day most especially, as they believed it was the birthday of **Servius Tullius** <note>The sixth king of Rome, credited with many populist reforms</note>. Since it was uncertain in which month Servius Tullius had been born, yet it was agreed he was born on the Nones, the people frequented all the Nones with famous celebrations. Therefore, those in charge of the calendar days feared that the gathered crowd might start a revolution out of longing for the king during the market days. They took care to ensure the Nones were separated from the market days. For this reason, that extra day which we said makes the year overflow was left to the judgment of those presiding over the <term>fasti</term> <note>The official calendar of judicial and religious days</note>. They could insert it (intercalate) when they wished, provided they placed it in the middle of the **Terminalia** <note>A festival for the god of boundaries on February 23rd</note> or in the <term>intercalary month</term> in such a way as to divert the crowd from the "suspected" day of the market. And this is what some of the ancients reported: that there was not only an intercalary month among the Romans, but even an **intercalary day**.

<margin>When intercalation was first done. By whom the market days were established.</margin>
When intercalation was first performed is reported differently by various sources. **Licinius Macer** assigns the origin of this practice to **Romulus**. **Antias**, in his second book, contends that **Numa Pompilius** invented it for the sake of religious rites. **Junius** records that King **Servius Tullius** was the first to intercalate, and **Varro** agrees that he also established the market days. **Tuditanus** reports in his fourth book on magistrates that the **Decemvirs** <note>The "Ten Men" who drafted early Roman law</note>, who added two tables to the original ten, asked the people about intercalating. **Cassius** writes that these same men were the authors of it. **Flavius** says that the Consul **Marcus [Acilius Glabrio]** did this in the five hundred and sixty-second year from the founding of the city, shortly before the start of the Aetolian War. But **Varro** argues against this, writing that a very ancient law had been inscribed on a bronze column by the consuls **Lucius Pinarius** and **Furius**, in which mention of intercalation is included. Let this be enough on the origins of intercalation.

However, there was a time when, due to superstition, all intercalation was omitted. Sometimes, through the favor of the priests—who wished to deliberately extend or shorten the days of the year for the benefit of the <term>tax collectors</term> <note>original: "publicanis"; private contractors who collected taxes and stood to gain or lose money based on the length of the fiscal year</note>—days were either added or subtracted. Under the guise of religious observation, a great occasion for confusion emerged.

<margin>The correction of the year made by Gaius Caesar.</margin>
¶ But later, **Gaius Caesar** [Julius Caesar] forced all this wandering and still uncertain inconsistency of time into the order of a fixed definition. He was assisted by **Marcus Flavius** the scribe, who reported each individual day in writing to the Dictator in such a way that their order could be found very easily, and once found, a certain status would persist. Therefore, Gaius Caesar, about to begin the start of the new arrangement, consumed all the days that could still cause confusion. Because of this, it happened that the last **Year of Confusion** <margin>Year of Confusion.</margin> extended to four hundred and forty-three days. After this, imitating the **Egyptians** (the only ones who understood divine matters), he strove to direct the year according to the number of the sun, which completes its course in 365 days and a quarter. For just as the <margin>Lunar year.</margin> **lunar year** is a month, because the moon consumes a little less than a month in its circuit of the zodiac, so the **solar year** must be calculated by this number of days, which it completes when it turns back again to that sign from which it departed. From this, it is called the <margin>Turning year</margin> **turning year**; and it is considered "great," whereas the year of the moon is thought "brief." **Virgil** embraced both of these: *Meanwhile the sun rolls through the great year* <note>original: "Interea magnum sol circūuoluitur annum." From the Aeneid, III.284</note>.

<margin>Where "year" [annus] comes from</margin>
¶ Here, **Ateius Capito** thinks the "year" (*annus*) is named from the circuit of time, because the ancients used to use *an* for *circum* [around]; as **Cato** says in his *Origins of the Orators*: *An terminum* meaning "around the boundary," and *ambire* for "to go around." **Julius Caesar**, therefore, added ten days to the ancient observation so that the year would consist of 365 days, during which the sun illuminates the zodiac. And so that the quarter-day would not be missing, he decreed that every fourth year, the priests who were in charge should intercalate one day in the months and days—specifically in that month and place where the month was intercalated among the ancients, that is, before the last five days of the month of February. He decreed that this should be named <margin>Bissextile.</margin> **Bissextile** <note>original: "bissextū"; referring to the "twice-sixth" day before the Kalends of March, our leap day</note>. However, the ten days which we said were added by him, this arrangement—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Roman calendar's evolution.
