# ->THE SATURNALIA<-

He distributed [the extra days]. In January, **Sextilis** <note>original: "sextilem"; the sixth month of the old calendar, later renamed August</note>, and December, he inserted two days each. In April, June, September, and November, he inserted one day each. However, he added no day to the month of February, so as not to interfere with the religious rites of the gods of the underworld <note>February was traditionally a month of purification and honoring the dead</note>. In March, May, **Quintilis** <note>original: "quintili"; the fifth month, later renamed July in honor of Julius Caesar</note>, and October, he preserved the original status, as they already had a sufficiently full number of days—namely, thirty-one each. Therefore, he also kept the <term>Nones</term> <note>The "Nones" were the 5th or 7th day of the month</note> on the fifth day, just as Numa had established, because Julius changed nothing in these months. 

But for January, August, and December—to which Caesar added two days—although they began to have thirty-one days each after Caesar's reform, they still have their Nones on the fifth day. From their <term>Ides</term> <note>The 13th or 15th day of the month</note>, they count backward nineteen days to the following <term>Kalends</term> <note>The 1st day of the next month</note>. This is because Caesar did not want to insert the added days before either the Nones or the Ides, lest he corrupt the religious observance of those days, which occurred on a fixed date, by a <margin>Postponement</margin> new delay. Nor did he want to insert them immediately after the Ides, so that the proclamation of any festivals would not be violated. Instead, once the festivals of each month were completed, he made a place for the "stranger" days <note>original: "diebus aduenis"; these were the newly added days</note>. 

In January, he placed these on the days we call the fourth and third before the Kalends of February; in April, the sixth before the Kalends of May; in June, the third before the Kalends of July; in August, the fourth and third before the Kalends of September; in September, the third before the Kalends of October; in November, the third before the Kalends of December; and in December, the fourth and third before the Kalends of January. 

Thus it happened that, while all these months to which he added days had previously counted seventeen days back to the Kalends of the following month, after the increase of the added days, those that received two days counted back nineteen, and those that received one counted back eighteen to the return of the Kalends. Nevertheless, the order of the festivals of each month was preserved. For if a festival or holiday was held on the third day after the Ides (which was then called the sixteenth before the Kalends), even after the increase of days, the same religious practice was observed so that it was celebrated on the third day after the Ides. This was true even if, because of the increase, it was no longer called the sixteenth before the Kalends, but the seventeenth (if one day was added) or the eighteenth (if two were added). 

<margin>Legal days</margin> For this reason, he inserted the new days near the end of each month, where he found the end of all the festivals that were in that month. He marked all these added days as **fasti** <note>original: "fastos"; days on which legal and business transactions were permitted</note> to allow greater freedom for legal actions. He designated none of the added days as <term>nefasti</term> <note>days on which public business was prohibited</note>, nor even as <term>comitial</term> days <note>days for public assemblies</note>, so that the addition would not increase the political campaigning of the magistrates. 

Thus Caesar, having established the civil year according to the measurements of the sun, published it by a publicly posted edict. And the error could have stopped there, had not the priests created a new error for themselves out of the very correction itself. For whereas they ought to have intercalated the day which is made up of the <term>quadrants</term> <note>original: "quadrantibus"; the 1/4 day or six hours remaining each year</note> every four years when the year was completed and before the fifth began, they instead intercalated not when the fourth was finished, but when it was just beginning. This error persisted for thirty-six years, during which twelve days were intercalated when only nine should have been.

<margin>Correction of the year made by Augustus</margin> But Augustus eventually corrected this error after it was discovered; he ordered twelve years to pass without an <term>intercalary</term> <note>leap</note> day, so that those three days which had grown in excess through thirty-six years by the faulty haste of the priests could be "swallowed up" by the following twelve years without an intercalation. After this, he ordered one day to be intercalated every five years <note>By Roman inclusive counting, this means every four years</note> at the beginning of the year, according to the arrangement of Caesar. He then commanded this entire order to be engraved on a bronze tablet for eternal preservation. 

Then **Horus** <note>A character in the dialogue, likely representing an Egyptian viewpoint</note> said: "This intercalary day, which is to be inserted before the fifth year begins, indeed agrees with the calculations of Egypt, the mother of the arts. However, it seems laborious to explain it in their months, which all have thirty days. After the twelve months are finished—that is, 360 days—they then return the remaining five days to their year between August and September, attaching every four years the intercalary day made from the quadrants. But here [in the Roman system], the count does not proceed in a continuous increase from the first to the last day of the month; but after the Kalends, it is directed toward the Nones. From there, I hear it turns toward certain Ides. After that, unless I am mistaken—or rather, as you have just reported—it returns toward the following Kalends..."

# BOOK ONE

...to be observed. I would truly like to know what all these things mean. For I do not even hope to keep up with the vocabulary that is added among you every single day, while you name some calendars <note>original: "fastos"; the list of days on which legal business could be conducted</note> and others by various names. I also confess my ignorance regarding your **Nundinae** <note>The Roman market cycle, occurring every nine days; the name literally means "ninth-day affairs"</note>, about which such diligent and cautious observation is described. It is no cause for shame for me, a foreigner, to be ignorant of these things; but even a citizen should not be ashamed to learn them from you, Prætextatus. Then Prætextatus said: "I do not think it is a cause for shame for you, Horus, since you are a native of Egypt, nor even for us whose origin is Roman, to ask about what all the ancients thought was a subject worthy of inquiry. For countless authors have exercised great care in investigating the **Kalends**, **Nones**, and **Ides**, and the various observations of the festivals. Therefore, we shall briefly gather into one place what has been said about these things by everyone."

"When Romulus was organizing the state of his own empire—with a sharp mind, certainly, but a rustic one—he took the beginning of each month from that day on which the new moon happened to be seen. Because it does not happen continuously that it appears always on the same day, but is accustomed to be seen sometimes later and sometimes earlier for certain reasons, it so happened that <margin>The beginning of the month established by Romulus.</margin> when it appeared later, more days were given to the preceding month, or when earlier, fewer were given. The first occurrence of the moon dictated a permanent law of numbering for each individual month. Thus it happened that some months received thirty-one days, others twenty-nine. Nevertheless, it was decided that in all months the **Ides** should fall on the ninth day after the **Nones**, and between the Ides and the following **Kalends**, it was established that sixteen days were to be counted. Therefore, a fuller month had those two days by which it was increased between its own Kalends and Nones. For this reason, for some months the fifth day from the Kalends makes the Nones, and for others, it is the seventh day."

"Caesar, however (as we said above), while guarding the established sacred rites, did not want to change the order of the Nones even in those months to which he added two days; because, once the festivals of the whole month were completed, he carefully inserted his own added days into the divine schedule. Therefore, in ancient times, before the calendar was published for the knowledge of all by the scribe Gnaeus Flavius—against the wishes of the patricians <note>The elite ruling class who previously kept the calendar secret to maintain legal power</note>—this duty was delegated to a minor priest <term>pontifex minor</term>. He was to observe the first appearance of the new moon and report the sighting to the King of Sacrifices <term>rex sacrificulus</term>. Thus, after a sacrifice was celebrated by the King and the minor priest, the same priest, having 'called'—that is, summoned—the common people to the Capitol near the <margin>The Calabra Court</margin> **Curia Calabra** (which is next to the Hut of Romulus), would announce the number of days remaining from the Kalends to the Nones. He would proclaim 'five days' by repeating the word <gloss>original: "καλῶ"; I call</gloss> five times, or 'seven days' by repeating it seven times. 

<margin>The origin of 'Kalends' from 'Calabra' and 'Classis'.</margin> The word *kalo* is Greek and means 'I call.' And it was decided to call the first day 'Kalends' because it was the first of those days that were 'called out' <note>The Latin *Calendae* shares a root with *calare*, meaning to call out</note>. From this, the name was given to the Court itself to which they were called—the *Calabra*—and to the *Classis* <note>fleet or assembly</note>, because the whole people were called into it. Therefore, the minor priest produced the number of days remaining until the Nones by 'calling' them out, because on the day of the Nones, it was necessary for the country folk who were in the fields to flock into the city to receive the reasons for the festivals from the King of Sacrifices and to know what was to be done in that month. <margin>The origin of the 'Nones'</margin> For this reason, some think the Nones were so named as if they were the beginning of a 'new' <note>Latin: *novae*</note> observation; or because from that day, nine days <note>Latin: *novem*</note> are always counted to the Ides—just as among the Etruscans, the Nones were held frequently because they greeted their king every ninth day and consulted him on their own business."

### ->¶ On the Ides. Chapter XVIII.<-

Furthermore, the name of the **Ides** was taken from the Etruscans, among whom that day is called *itis*. Likewise, they interpreted it as 'the trust of Jupiter.' For since we accept Jupiter as the author of light—wherefore the Salii <note>an ancient college of priests</note> sing of him as 'Lucetius' in their hymns, and the <margin>Lucetius, Jupiter, Diespiter, Jupiter's Trust, Jupiter's Festivals</margin> Cretans call the day <gloss>original: "Δία Τὴν ἡμέραν"; Dia the day</gloss>, and the Romans themselves call him 'Diespiter' as the 'Father of Day'—this day is rightly called 'Jupiter's trust.' His light does not end with the setting of the sun, but continues the splendor of day into the night as the moon illuminates it, which is accustomed to happen always at the full moon—that is, in the middle of the month. A day which lacks nocturnal darkness they called 'Jupiter's trust' by an Etruscan name; hence antiquity ordained that all Ides be observed as festivals of Jupiter.

# THE SATURNALIA

<margin>
To divide.
A widow is so named because the Ides are consecrated to Jupiter.
Juno of the Kalends.
Janus of Juno.
Artemis as the moon.
Days following festivals are "black" days.
</margin>

Others think the **Ides** <note>original: "idus"; the middle of the month</note> are so called because on that day the full moon is seen, and were named *vidus* from "seeing" <note>original: "videndo"</note>, with the letter *v* later removed. This is similar to the opposite case where we add a *v* to what the Greeks call *idein* <note>original: "ἰδεῖν"; to see</note> to say our word *videre* <note>to see</note>. Some prefer to think the Ides were named from the Greek word *eidos* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ εἴδους"; from the appearance or shape</note> because on that day the full shape of the moon is revealed. There are those who believe the Ides are named after the "Idulian ox," which the Etruscans call by this name and which is sacrificed to **Jupiter** by the Flamen <note>a high-ranking Roman priest</note> on all Ides. To us, however, that explanation of the name seems closer to the truth: that we call the day the "Ides" because it divides the month. For in the Etruscan language, *iduare* means "to divide," from which we get the word *vidua* <note>widow</note>, as if it were *valde idua*, meaning "greatly divided," or *vidua* meaning "divided from a man." Just as all Ides belong to Jupiter, so the authority of both Varro and the pontifical records confirms that all **Kalends** <note>original: "kalendas"; the first day of the month</note> are assigned to **Juno**. This is even observed by the people of Laurentum in their ancestral religions, for they have added a surname to the goddess from these ceremonies, calling her "Juno of the Kalends." Indeed, on every Kalends from the month of March to December, they pray to this "Goddess of the Kalends." In Rome, too, on all Kalends, the minor pontiff performs a sacred rite to Juno in the Calabra court. Also, the **Regina Sacrorum** <note>Queen of the Sacred Rites</note>, that is, the wife of the **Rex Sacrorum** <note>King of the Sacred Rites</note>, sacrifices a sow or a lamb to Juno in the royal palace. It is from her that we said **Janus** was surnamed "Junonius," because while every entrance is attributed to that god, all the days of the Kalends are seen to be assigned to this goddess. Since our ancestors observed the beginning of the months from the rising of the moon, they rightly assigned the Kalends to Juno, believing the moon and Juno to be the same; or perhaps because the moon travels through the air, which is why the Greeks named the moon **Artemis** <note>original: "ἀρτέμιν"</note> as if she were *aerotomos* <note>original: "ἀεροτόμων"; cutting the air</note>. Since Juno is the ruler of the air, they deservedly consecrated the beginnings of the months—the Kalends—to this goddess. I should not omit this either: that by religious custom, people have become accustomed to avoid the Kalends, **Nones**, and Ides for joining in marriage. For these days, except for the Nones, are holidays <note>original: "feriati"</note>. On holidays, it is a sin for force to be used against anyone; therefore, weddings are avoided then, because force seems to be used against virgins at that time. But Varro reports that **Verrius Flaccus**, a man most skilled in pontifical law, used to say that because the ancients were allowed to cover old ditches on holidays, but it was not lawful to make new ones, holidays were therefore more suitable for widows than for virgins to marry. Someone might ask: why then is the celebration of weddings prohibited on the Nones, if it is not a holiday? The reason for this is also clear. Because the first day of the wedding is given to modesty, it is necessary for the bride to begin to take control of her husband's house and perform sacred rites on the following day. However, all "following days" <note>original: "postriduani dies"</note>—whether after the Kalends, the Nones, or the Ides—are equally "black" <note>original: "atri"; ill-omened or unlucky days</note>. Therefore, they said the Nones were unsuitable for weddings, so that the bride would not inaugurate her wifely freedom or perform a sacrifice on an ill-omened day, when it is forbidden for sacred rites to be celebrated. But since the order of things has led us to the commemoration of days, a few things must also be said about what the inquiry of our friend Horus contains.

## On the division of days. Chapter XIX.

<margin>
The division of days.
Festive days.
Profane days.
Split days.
Holidays and their kinds.
Fixed holidays.
Conceptive holidays.
</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring a figure among winding vines and foliage.</image-desc>**Numa** <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome and founder of many religious institutions</note>, just as he distributed the year into months, so he divided each month into days. He called all days either **festive** <note>original: "festos"</note>, **profane** <note>original: "profestos"</note>, or **split** <note>original: "intercisos"</note>. Festive days are dedicated to the gods. Profane days are granted to men for the administration of both private and public business. Split days are shared between gods and men. On festive days, there are sacrifices, feasts, games, and holidays. On profane days, there are days for legal business <note>original: "fasti"</note>, assembly days <note>original: "comitiales"</note>, adjournment days, fixed days, and battle days. Split days are divided within themselves, not among others. For on certain hours of those days it is lawful <note>original: "fas"</note> to administer the law, and at other hours it is not. For when the sacrificial victim is being slain, it is a sin to speak <note>i.e., to perform legal speech</note>. Between the slaughter and the offering <note>original: "intercæsa et porrecta"</note>, it is lawful to speak. Again, when the offering is burning, it is not lawful. Therefore, we must discuss the division of festive and profane days more broadly. A sacred celebration occurs either when sacrifices are offered to the gods, or when the gods are honored with divine feasts, or when games are held in honor of the gods, or when holidays are observed. There are four kinds of public holidays <term>feriae<note>Religious festivals or holidays where public business was suspended.</note></term>. For they are either **fixed** <note>original: "stativae"</note>, **conceptive** <note>original: "conceptivae"</note>, **ordered** <note>original: "imperativae"</note>, or **market days** <note>original: "nundinae"</note>. The fixed holidays are common to the whole people on certain and established days and months, and are noted in the calendars with fixed observations; on these days the **Agonalia**, **Carmentalia**, and **Lupercalia** are especially observed. Conceptive holidays are those which are announced every year by magistrates or priests for days that are either certain or even uncertain, such as the **Latin Festival**, the **Sementivae**, the **Paganalia**, and the **Compitalia**. Or-

It also introduces Numa Pompilius's categorization of days into festive, profane, and split days based on their suitability for religious or legal business.</summary>

### BOOK ONE

<sig>G iii</sig>

<margin>Appointed festivals.</margin>
<margin>Market days.</margin>
**Appointed festivals** <note>original: "feriae imperativae"</note> are those which the consuls or praetors proclaim at their own discretion. **Market days** <note>original: "nundinae"</note> belong to the common people—that is, the country folk—who gather on these days to look after their own business or trade their goods. Furthermore, there are festivals belonging to specific families, such as those of the Claudian, Aemilian, Julian, or Cornelian families, or any other family that observes its own traditional household celebrations. There are also days for individuals, such as birthdays or the rituals for dealing with lightning strikes. Likewise, there are days for funerals and atonement. Among the ancients, anyone who spoke the names of the deities **Salus Semonia**, **Seia**, **Segetia**, or **Tutilina** <note>these were minor deities associated with sowing, crops, and protection of the harvest</note> observed those days as festivals. Similarly, the **Flaminica** <note>the wife of the Flamen Dialis, the high priest of Jupiter</note> was on holiday whenever she heard thunder, until she had appeased the gods. 

The priests used to assert that a festival was polluted if any work was done after it had been proclaimed and established. Furthermore, it was not permitted for the **King of Sacrifices** <note>original: "rex sacrorum"</note> or the priests to see work being performed on festivals; therefore, they would announce through a herald that no such thing should be done, and anyone who ignored the instruction was fined. Beyond the fine, they asserted that a person who had done something unintentionally on such days should offer a pig as an atonement <note>original: "piaculum"</note>; however, one who worked intentionally could not be purified. This was the firm opinion of **Scæuola** the high priest. 

However, **Umbro** denies that a person is polluted if they have done work pertaining to the gods or for the sake of a sacrifice, or if they have performed a task regarding an urgent necessity of life. Finally, when Scæuola was consulted on what was permitted to be done on festivals, he replied: "That which would cause harm if left undone." Therefore, if an ox fell into a pit and the head of the household rescued it using labor, he was not considered to have polluted the festival; nor was he who shored up a broken roof beam to save it from imminent collapse. 

On this point **Maro** <note>the poet Virgil</note>, who was skilled in all branches of learning, knew that a sheep might be washed either for the sake of cleaning the wool or for curing the mange. He declared that it was permitted to dip a sheep during festivals if it was done as a remedy, writing: *To dip the bleating flock in the healthful stream.* By adding the word "healthful," he showed that it was permitted only for the sake of warding off disease, and not

<margin>Court days</margin>
<margin>Forbidden days</margin>
<margin>Assembly days</margin>
<margin>Adjournment days</margin>
also for the profit of cleaning the wool. So much for festive days and what arises from them, which are also called **forbidden days** <note>original: "nefasti"; days when legal business was banned</note>. 

Now let us speak of the non-festive days and those categories that proceed from them: namely **court days**, **assembly days**, **adjournment days**, **fixed days**, and **battle days**. **Court days** <note>original: "fasti"</note> are those on which the praetor is permitted to speak the three solemn words: *do, dico, addico* <note>"I give, I pronounce, I adjudge"—the legal formula for granting a trial, stating the law, and awarding property</note>. Their opposites are the **forbidden days** <note>original: "nefasti"</note>. **Assembly days** <note>original: "comitiales"</note> are those on which it is legal to conduct business with the people. On court days legal action can be taken, but business cannot be done with the people; on assembly days, both are possible. **Adjournment days** <note>original: "comperendini"</note> are those on which a legal summons <note>original: "vadimonium"</note> may be issued. **Fixed days** <note>original: "stati"</note> 

<margin>Fixed days</margin>
<margin>Summons</margin>
<margin>Plautus</margin>
are those established for the sake of a trial with a foreigner <note>original: "peregrinus"</note>, as **Plautus** says in *The Weevil*: "A fixed day of appointment with an enemy <note>original: "hoste"</note> intervened." In the ancient manner, "enemy" here signifies a "foreigner." I would not separate **battle days** 

<margin>Battle days</margin>
from the "lawful" days <note>original: "iusti"</note>; indeed, there are thirty continuous lawful days during which a red banner is placed on the citadel for the commanded army. **Battle days** are all those on which it is divinely permitted to reclaim property or provoke an enemy. For when the **Latin Festival** is being observed, or during the days of the **Saturnalia**, and even when the **Mundus** <note>a ritual pit representing the entrance to the underworld</note> is open, it is a religious crime to take up battle. Therefore, it was not fitting to begin a war during the time of the Latin Festival—during which a public truce was once established between the Roman people and the Latins—nor during the feast of **Saturn**, who is believed to have reigned without any warlike tumult. Nor should it be done while the *Mundus* is open, for that is a sacred time dedicated to Father Dis <note>Pluto</note> and Proserpina; they thought it better to go to battle only when the jaws of Pluto were closed. 

Regarding this, **Varro** writes as follows: "When the *Mundus* is open, it is as if the door of the sorrowful gods of the underworld stands open. Therefore, it is a religious violation not only to engage in battle, but even to hold a military levy, to set out for war, to weigh anchor, or to take a wife for the sake of having children." The ancients also avoided calling out men for service on days marked by adversity. They also avoided doing so on festivals, as Varro wrote in his books on the augurs in these words: "One ought not to summon men on festivals; if one has summoned them, let there be an atonement." It must be known, however, that the Romans had the freedom to choose the day for fighting if they themselves were initiating the war; but when they were under attack, no day stood in the way of defending either their own safety or the public dignity. 

<margin>Post-festival days</margin>
For what place is there for such observation when the power of choice no longer remains? Our ancestors thought that the **days following festivals** should be avoided for all business; they even condemned them as "black" days, considering the name itself unlucky.

<header>BOOK III OF THE SATURNALIA</header>

## ¶ On the Various Names of Apollo. Chapter XX.

<margin>The various names of Apollo related to the sun</margin>
The name of Apollo is referred to the Sun through a manifold interpretation, the order of which I shall proceed to reveal. Plato writes that the sun was named Apollo <note>original: "ἀπόλλωνα" (Apollona)</note> from "the casting of rays" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ πάλλειν τὰς ἀκτίνας" (apo tou pallein tas aktinas); Latin gloss: "from the hurling of rays"</note>. Chrysippus derives the name Apollo as "not being of the many and common substances of fire" <note>original: "ὡς οὐχὶ τῶν πολλῶν καὶ φαύλων ὀυσιῶν τοῦ πυρὸς ὄντα" (hos ouchi ton pollon kai phaulon ousion tou pyros onta)</note>. For he argues that the first letter of the name <note>the 'A' in Greek often acts as a 'privative' or negation</note> retains the meaning of a denial, "because he is alone and not many" <note>original: "ὅτι μόνος ἐστὶ καὶ οὐχὶ πολλοί" (hoti monos esti kai ouchi polloi)</note>. Indeed, the Latin language also called him "the Sun" <note>original: "solem"</note> because he alone <note>original: "solus"</note> obtained such great brightness. Speusippus, however, argues that his power consists of many fires <note>original: "ὡς ἀπὸ πολλῶν οὐσιῶν πυρὸς αὐτοῦ συνεστῶτος" (hos apo pollon ousion pyros autou synestotos)</note>. Cleanthes derives it "as if he makes his risings from various places" <note>original: "ὡς ἅπαλλῶν τὰς ἀνατολὰς ποιούμενου" (hos hapallon tas anatolas poioumenou)</note>, because he rises from different points as the locations of the earth decline. Cornificius thinks Apollo is named from "revolving" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀναπολεῖν" (apo tou anapolein)</note>, because within the circuit of the world—which the Greeks call the pole <note>original: "πόλον" (polon)</note>—he is carried back to his rising by a joyful impulse. Others think Apollo was named because he "destroys living creatures" <note>original: "ὡς ἀπόλλυντα τὰ ζῶα" (hos apollynta ta zoa)</note>. For he takes away life and oppresses living beings when he sends a pestilence through the excessive intensity of his heat, as Euripides says in his *Phaethon*: **"O golden-shining Sun, how you have destroyed me; hence mortals clearly call you the Destroyer [Apollo]"** <note>original: "ὦ χρυσοφεγγὲς ἥλι’ ὡς μ’ ἀπόλεσας ὅθεν σ’ ἀπόλλων’ ἐμφανῶς κλῄζει βροτός"</note>. Archilochus says the same: **"O Apollo, do you also point out the guilty and destroy them..."** <note>original: "ἀφ’ ἀπόλλων καὶ σὺ τοὺς μαιτίους σήμαινε καὶ σφὰς οὐλλυώ σπερόλλυεις"</note>. Consequently, those burned by disease are called "Apollo-struck" or "Sun-struck" <note>original: "ἀπολλοκοβλήτους καὶ ἡλιοβλήτους" (apollokobletous kai heliobletous)</note>. And since the effects of the moon are similar to those of the sun, both in helping and harming, women afflicted by certain diseases are called "Moon-struck" or "Artemis-struck" <note>original: "σεληνοβλήτους καὶ ἀρτεμιδοβλήτους" (selenobletous kai artemidobletous)</note>. It is for this reason that they decorate images of Apollo with a bow and arrows: so that by the arrows, the force of his emitted rays might be understood. Hence Homer says: **"But when he let fly a sharp arrow at them, he struck."** <note>original: "αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ τάντοισι βέλος ἐχεπευκὲς ἐφιεὶς βάλλε"</note>. This same author is also the source of the public safety <note>original: "sospitatis"</note> which the sun is believed to provide to living creatures through a temperate climate. But because he provides constant health, and a pestilential occurrence from him is rarer, the images of Apollo carry the Graces in the right hand and a bow with arrows in the left; this signifies that he is slower to do harm, and the right hand is more ready to bestow health. For this reason, the power of healing is attributed to him, because the temperate heat of the sun is the flight of all diseases. Indeed, they think he was named Apollo "as driving away diseases" <note>original: "ὡς ἀπελαύνοντα τοὺς νόσους" (hos apelaunonta tous nosous)</note> or from "destroying" them. This sentiment, which also fits the pronunciation of the Latin name, meant we did not change the name of this god; you may understand Apollo as one who wards off evils, whom the Athenians call "the Averter of Evil" <note>original: "ἀλεξίκακον" (alexikakon)</note>.

<margin>Pestilential Apollo</margin>
But the people of Lindos also worship Apollo as "the Pestilential One" <note>original: "λοιμιον" (loimion)</note>, so called because he ended a plague. This same opinion of a saving and medicinal god is also maintained in our own sacred rites. For the Vestal Virgins invoke him thus:

<margin>To invoke</margin>
**Apollo the Healer; Apollo the Paean.** Since, therefore, there are two great effects of this star (that is, the sun)—one by which he aids the life of mortals with temperate heat, the other by which he sometimes sends a pestilential poison by the hurling of his rays—two identical names are used for each effect with specific pronunciations. They call the god **Ieïos** <note>original: "ἰήϊον"</note> and **Paean** <note>original: "παιάνα"</note>. Both names are suited to either effect: "Ieïos" from "to heal" <note>original: "ἰᾶσθαι" (iasthai)</note> and "Paean" from "to stop pains" <note>original: "παυεῖν τὰς ἀνίας" (pauein tas anias)</note>; and conversely, "Ieïos" from "to go" or "to send" <note>original: "ἰέναι" (ienai)</note>—that is, from sending the "sharp arrow"—and "Paean" from "to strike" <note>original: "παίειν" (paiein)</note>. It became established, however, that when they pray for health to be given to them, they pronounce it with the letter 'eta', **"Ieïe Paean"** <note>original: "ἰήϊε παιαν"</note>, meaning "Heal, O Paean." But when they say **"Ie Paean"** <note>original: "ἰε παιαν"</note> with the letter 'epsilon' and an aspiration on the first letter, they signify that this is said against someone in an adverse prayer, **"Strike, O Paean"** <note>original: "βάλλε παιὰν" (balle paian)</note>, that is, "send by striking." They say Latona used this voice when she encouraged Apollo to attack the Python with his arrows (the natural reason for which I shall explain in its proper place). The Delphic oracle is said to have confirmed this cry—"Ie Paean"—to the Athenians when they sought the god's help against the Amazons during the reign of Theseus; for it ordered those about to enter war to invoke and encourage the god as a helper in these very words. Apollodorus, in the fourteenth book of his work *On the Gods* <note>original: "περὶ θεῶν" (Peri theon)</note>, writes that the sun is called "Ieïos" and "Apollo" from "rushing and moving through the universe" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ κατὰ κόσμον ἰεῦθαι καὶ ἰέναι" (apo tou kata kosmon ieusthai kai ienai)</note>, because the sun is carried with force through his orbit. But Timothy writes thus: **"O Sun, you who strike the heavenly pole forever with your rays, send far-shooting..."** <note>original: "σὺ τῶν ἀεὶ πολὸν οὐράνιον ἅμα τοῖς ἀκτίσιν ἥλιε βάλλων πέμψον ἑκαβόλ"</note>

...bringing a <term>Paean</term> <note>A hymn of praise or healing, often addressed to Apollo</note> that takes away the disease with his arrows <note>original: "λον ἔχοροῖσ βέλεθσασ ἀπὸμεῦρασ παιᾶν"</note>. He calls the same god, when presiding over health-giving causes, **Oulios** <note>original: "οὔλιον"</note>, that is, the author of health: as Homer says, "Be whole and hail indeed" <note>original: "οὔλετὲ καὶ μάλα χαῖρε"</note>.
<margin>Vlios Apollo</margin> Menander writes that the Milesians sacrifice to Apollo Oulios for their health. Pherecydes reports that Theseus, when he was being led to Crete to the Minotaur, vowed for his safety and return to **Apollo Oulios and Artemis Oulia**. Nor is it a wonder if twin effects are celebrated with various names: since we accept that other gods also, from the contrary, can be reckoned in the same matter with a double power and name: like Neptune, whom they call at times **Ennosigaios** <note>original: "ἐννοσίχθονα," meaning Earth-shaker</note>, and at other times **Asphalion** <note>original: "ἀσφάλίωνα," meaning the Stabilizer</note>. Likewise Mercury excites and puts to sleep the minds and eyes of men, as the poet says: "He took the wand with which he soothes the eyes of men" <note>original: "εἵλετ' οΔέ ράβΔον Τῇ Τ' ἀνΔρῶν ὄμμαΤα θέλγει"</note>. From which we also adore Apollo, that is the sun: now with surnames signifying safety, now pestilence; although the pestilence which he sends upon the guilty clearly signifies that this god fights on behalf of the good.
<margin>Libystinus Apollo</margin> This is the Apollo **Libystinus** who is celebrated with exceptional religion at Pachynus, a promontory of Sicily. For when the Libyans, about to invade Sicily, had brought their fleet to that promontory, Apollo—who is worshipped there—was invoked by the inhabitants and sent a pestilence upon the enemies; and nearly all being cut off by sudden death, he was surnamed Libystinus. In our annals also, a similar majesty of the presence of the same god is contained. For when games were first celebrated at Rome to Apollo, following the prophecy of the seer Marcius and the <term>Sibylline song</term> <note>Prophetic verses attributed to the Sibyl, consulted by Romans in times of crisis</note>, because of the sudden arrival of the enemy, the common people were excited to arms and ran to meet the foe. At that time, a cloud of arrows was seen to be carried against the adversaries; it both put the enemy to flight and brought the victorious Romans back to the spectacles of the "hospital" god. From this it is understood that the games were instituted for the sake of victory in battle, not for a pestilence, as some think. 
However, this is the reason for that mistaken opinion: because at that time of year, the sun shines directly over the vertex of our habitation. For the sun is in the <term>Tropic of Cancer</term> <note>The summer solstice</note> during the summer; as the sun passes through it, its rays are not sent from afar but are cast down from above, illuminating us with direct brightness. Therefore, it was estimated by some that the **Apollonian Games** were established mainly to propitiate the god of heat; but I find in literature that these games were instituted for the sake of victory, not health (as some writers of annals record). For in the <term>Punic War</term> <note>The great conflict between Rome and Carthage</note>, these games were first instituted from the Sibylline books at the persuasion of **Cornelius Ruffus** the <term>decemvir</term> <note>A member of a ten-man commission</note>, who for that reason was surnamed **Sibylla**; 
<margin>Sybilla, who is also Sylla</margin> and later, with the name corrupted, he first began to be called **Sylla**. Furthermore, it is said that in the songs of the seer Marcius (two volumes of which were brought into the Senate), it was found written thus: "Romans, if you wish to drive the enemy from your land and the plague which comes from distant nations, I advise that games should be vowed to Apollo, which shall be performed annually for Apollo in common. Let that <term>praetor</term> <note>A high-ranking Roman magistrate</note> preside over these games who shall give the highest law to the people and the commons. Let the decemvirs perform the sacrifices with victims according to the Greek rite. 
<margin>Enemies</margin> If you do this rightly, you will always rejoice and your republic will become better. For that god will extinguish your **enemies** <note>original: "perduellos"</note> who peacefully graze upon your fields." From this song, although one day was initially spent on divine matters for the sake of averting the threat, the Senate later decreed that the decemvirs should consult the Sibylline books (so that they might be better instructed regarding the games to be held for Apollo and the correct performance of the divine rite). When the same instructions were found there, the fathers [Senators] voted that games should be vowed and performed for Apollo; and for that purpose, twelve thousand pieces of bronze were given to the praetor, along with two larger sacrificial victims. The decemvirs were commanded to perform the sacrifice according to the Greek rite with these victims: for Apollo, a golden-horned ox and two white golden-horned goats; for Latona, a golden-horned heifer. The people, wearing crowns, were ordered to watch the games in the circus. This is the primary origin handed down for the Apollonian Games. 
Now, from other names of this god as well, let us prove that he is the same as Apollo and the Sun. He is surnamed **Loxias**: as Aenopides says, "because he proceeds through the **oblique circle** <note>original: "λόξον κύκλον" (loxon kyklon), referring to the ecliptic or the sun's slanted path</note> moving from the west to the east." 
<margin>Loxias Apollo</margin> Or as Cleanthes writes: "he moves in spirals, for they are both oblique and straight." 
<margin>Delius Apollo</margin> Or because he sends "oblique rays" <note>original: "λόξους ἀκτῖνας"</note> upon us, as he is in the south while we are to his north. He is surnamed **Delius** from "making manifest"...

...to make all things manifest and clear by his light <note>original: "λα καὶ φανερὰ πάντα ποιεῖν τῶ φωτὶ"</note>: because by illuminating he shows all things clearly. He is called **Phoebus** (as Cornificius says) from a word meaning "to move with force" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ φοιτᾶν βίᾳ"</note>: because he is carried along with power. Most, however, believe he is called Phoebus because of his appearance and brightness, meaning "pure and bright" <note>original: "καθαρὸν καὶ λαμπρὸν"</note>. Likewise, they call him **Phaneta** from the word meaning "to appear," because he appears new each day <note>original: "ἀπό τοῦ φαίνειν ἐπειδὴ φάινεται νέος"</note>: because the sun daily renews itself. Whence Virgil says: "The new morning." The inhabitants of Camirus, who dwell on an island sacred to the sun, sacrifice to Apollo as the "ever-begotten" <note>original: "ἀεὶ γενετῆ"</note>, because he is always being born the same and is always begetting <note>original: "τῶ τὸν αὐτὸν ἀεὶ γίγνεσθαι καὶ ἀειγεννᾶν"</note>: that is, because he is born by always rising, and because he himself begets all things by sowing, warming, bringing forth, nourishing, and increasing them. For **Lycian Apollo**,

<margin>
Lycian
Apollo
</margin>
we receive many reasons for this name. Antipater the Stoic writes that he is called Lycian Apollo from a word meaning "to shine," as the sun illuminates all things <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ λαυκένεσθαι"</note>. Cleanthes notes that he is called Lycian Apollo because just as wolves <term>lupi</term> seize cattle, so he too snatches up moisture with his rays. The ancient Greeks called the first light that precedes the rising of the sun *lyke* <note>original: "λύκην"</note> from the word for time <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ λύκου"</note>; and even today they call the twilight *lycophos*, about which time the poet writes:
> "When it was not yet dawn, but the night was still in twilight." <note>original: "ἦμος δ’ οὐτ’ ἄρ πω ἠώς ἔςι δὲ ἀμφιλύκη νύξ"</note>
The same Homer says: "Pray to Apollo, the light-born, famous with his bow" <note>original: "ἀυχεο δ’ ἀπόλλωνι λύκη γενετῆ κλυτοτόξῳ"</note>: which signifies "him who begets the light" <note>original: "τῷ γέννωντι τὴν λύκην"</note>, that is, who generates light by his rising. For the splendor of the rays, preceding the approaching sun from far and wide and gradually thinning the darkness of the shadows, gives birth to light. Nor did the Romans do any differently than in many other cases from the Greek: thus they seem to have formed the word for light (*luce*) from *lyce*. The most ancient of the Greeks also call the year *lykabanta* <note>original: "λυκάβαντα"</note>: that which is proceeded through and measured by the sun <note>original: "Τὸν ἀπό τοῦ λύκου... βαινόμενον καὶ μετρούμενον"</note>. That the sun is called *lykon* <note>a wolf</note> is evidenced by the city of Lycopolis in the Thebaid, which

<margin>
Origin of
the Wolf
</margin>
worships Apollo and the wolf <note>original: "λύκον"</note> with equal religion: venerating the sun in both. For this animal seizes and consumes all things in the manner of the sun, and seeing with a great sharpness of eyes, it overcomes the darkness of the night. Some think that wolves <note>original: "λύκους"</note> themselves were named from *lyce*, that is, from the first light: because these wild beasts especially observe that time as fit for seizing cattle, which the shepherd drives out from the stalls to pasture after the night's hunger, just before dawn. And they surnamed Apollo "Ancestral" <note>original: "πατρῶον"</note>: not by the specific religion of one race or city, but as the author of the generation of all things, because the sun, by drying up moisture, provided the cause for all things to be generated, as Orpheus says: "Having the mind and wise counsel of a father" <note>original: "πατρὸς ἔχοντα νόον καὶ ἐπίφρονα βουλὴν"</note>. Whence we also

<margin>

</margin>
call Janus "Father," venerating the sun under this name. They surnamed him **Nomius Apollo** <note>original: "νόμιον ἀπόλλωνα"</note>, not from a pastoral duty as in the fable where he is imagined to have pastured the cattle of King Admetus, but because the sun feeds <term>pascit</term> all things which the earth brings forth. Whence he is sung as the shepherd not of one kind, but of all cattle, as in Homer where Neptune says: "Phoebus, you were the herdsman of the slow-footed, curved-horned cattle" <note>original: "φοῖβε σὺ δ’ ἕλικωποδας ἕλικας βοῦς βουκο λέεσκες"</note>; and the same poet signifies a shepherd of the flock, saying:
> "Those which the silver-bowed Apollo pastured in the mountains..." <note>original: "τὰς ἐν φίριν ορε σ’ ἀργυρότοξος ἀπόλλων"</note>
Furthermore, there are temples to him as the shepherd of all: among the Camirians he is **Epimelios** <note>Guardian of flocks</note>, among the Naxians **Poianios** <note>Of the pasture</note>, likewise he is worshiped as the god **Arnokomes** <note>Lamb-haired</note>, and among the Lesbians as **Napaios** <note>Of the dell</note>. And there are many surnames through various cities tending toward the duty of the god as a shepherd. For which reason, as the overseer of the whole flock

<margin>

</margin>
and a true shepherd, Apollo is recognized. He is called **Eleleus** <note>original: "ἐλελεύς"</note>: from a word meaning "to move around the earth" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἑλιττἔσθαι περὶ τὴν γῆν"</note>, because he seems to be rolled around the earth in an eternal circuit; as Euripides says: "O Sun, whirling with your swift horses a flame of much fire" <note>original: "ἥλιε θοαῖσ ἵπποισιν ἑλίσσῶν φλέγοσ πολλοῦ πυρὸσ"</note>; or as Empedocles says: "Because having been whirled around, he attends to the great heaven" <note>original: "οὕνεκα ἑλιθεὶς μέγαν οὐρανον ἀμφιπολέυει"</note>. Alternatively, it is from a word meaning "to bring together and assemble" people when he has risen: because his rising leads men into a gathering.

Likewise, he is **Argyrotoxus** <note>Silver-bowed</note>, because as he emerges above the highest circuit of the world, he is shaped like a certain white and silver arch, from which arch the rays flash out in the manner of arrows. <margin>
Sciallios
Apollo
Thym-
braean
Apollo.
Philesius
Pythius.
</margin>
...he runs <note>original: "θεῖ"</note> because he moves fervently. He is called **Karneios** <note>original: "Καρνεῖόσ"</note> because he is "seen as burning and young" <note>original: "καίόμενοσ ὁρᾶται νέοσ"</note>; or because, while all burning things are consumed, he remains always new, glowing with his own heat. Likewise, he is **Apollo Sciallios** <note>original: "ἀπόλλων σ' κία λλίοσ"</note> because "he makes movements of a different kind" <note>original: "τὰσ' κυνησει ἀλλοίασ' ποιεῖ"</note> for us as he moves from the south. He is **Thymbraeus** <note>original: "θυμβραῖοσ"</note> because "he sends the rain-showers" <note>original: "Τούσ' θάμβρουσ' θεῖσ'"</note>, for he is the god of rain. He is **Apollo Philesius** <note>original: "ἀπόλλων φιλήσιοσ'"</note> because we greet his rising light with love and the most friendly reverence of our eyes. He is **Apollo Pythius** <note>original: "ἀπόλλων πύθιοσ'"</note>, which natural philosophers believe is named not from "inquiring" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ πυθεῖν"</note>—that is, from the consultation of hidden things—but **from "rotting"** <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ πύσειν"</note>—that is, "to putrefy" <note>original: "σ' ηπεῖν"</note>. This process never occurs without the force of heat. From this, they believe the name **Python** <note>original: "πύθων"</note> is derived, even though the Greeks tell fables about this name being given to the god following the slaying of a dragon. However, this myth is not inconsistent with the understanding of a natural secret, as will be revealed if the sequence of events is followed: for the story is told of Apollo being born, just as I promised to explain a little earlier. It is said that Juno stood in the way of Latona when she was about to give birth to Apollo and Diana. But when the birth finally happened, they say a dragon named **Python** <note>original: "πύθων"</note> attacked the cradles of the gods, and Apollo, in his earliest infancy, killed the beast with his arrows. Natural reason demonstrates that this should be understood as follows: after Chaos, when confused deformity first began to shine into the forms of kingdoms and elements, and the earth was still a moist substance swaying in a soft and unstable seat, the heavenly heat gradually grew stronger. As fiery seeds flowed down into it, they believe the stars were produced, and the sun was snatched into the upper regions by the greatest force of heat. The moon, however, being more moist and as if of a female sex, held the lower regions by a certain natural moderate warmth, as if the sun consisted more of the father’s substance and the moon of the mother’s.

<margin>Latona.</margin>
Indeed, the natural philosophers wish for Latona to be seen as the Earth, whom Juno long hindered so that the deities we mentioned might not be born. Juno represents the **Air** <term>Aer</term>, which, being still moist and heavy, stood in the way of the higher Ether <term>Aether</term>, preventing the brilliance of the lights from shining through the density of the airy moisture, as if from the progress of a birth. But the persistence of divine providence won out, which is believed to have assisted the birth. Therefore, on the island of Delos, to confirm the truth of the myth, a Temple of Providence—which they call the **Naon Pronoias** <note>original: "ναον προνοίασ"</note>—is celebrated with fitting religion. For this reason, they are said to be born on an island, because they seem to us to rise out of the sea.

<margin>Why it is called Delos.</margin>
This island is called Delos because the rising and, as it were, the birth of the lights makes all things **evident** <note>original: "δῆλα"</note>—that is, it makes them clear and open. Furthermore, there is a natural explanation for the slaying of the dragon, as Antipater the Stoic writes. For the exhalation of the still-moist earth, moving into the upper regions with a whirling force, and then, after being heated, rolling back down into the lower regions like a deadly serpent, corrupted all things by the power of putrefaction—which is only generated from heat and moisture. By covering the sun itself with a density of darkness, this mist seemed in some way to take away its light. But at last, thinned, dried out, and killed by the divine heat of the rays falling like arrows, it gave rise to the myth of the dragon slain by Apollo.

<margin>The natural reason for the death of Python.</margin>
There is also another reason for the slain dragon. For although the sun's path never departs from the <term>ecliptic line</term>, a certain deflection varies its journey up and down according to the turns of the winds, winding like the coil of a dragon. Whence Euripides says: **"The dragon-born gaze leads the whole, joined in harmony with the four-formed seasons, a vehicle for the many-fruited weapon."** <note>This quote from Euripides refers to the sun guiding the seasons through the zodiacal path.</note> Under this name for the celestial journey, when the sun had finished its course, it was said to have "finished the dragon."

<margin>Natural reason for the death.</margin>
From this, the myth of the serpent's death arose. Moreover, the name "Arrows" signifies nothing other than the casting of rays, which are understood to be longest at that time when the sun is at its highest, finishing its annual course during the longest days of the summer solstice. Thus he is called **Hekabolos** <note>original: "ἑκαβολοσ"</note> and **Hekatabolos** <note>original: "ἑκαταβολοσ"</note>, meaning "Far-darting," as he sends his rays down to the earth from the longest and highest point. These points might have sufficed regarding the surname Pythius, were it not that another reason for the same name presented itself.

<margin>Apollo is called Pythius.</margin>
For when the sun makes the summer solstice in the sign of **Cancer**, which is the limit of the longest day, and from there acts a retreat toward the shortening of the days, he is called Pythius at that time, as if saying: **"As the last of the gods, I run the final course."** <note>original: "ωσ πυματον θεῶν οέσιτελευταιοσ Δρομον τρεχω."</note> This same name suits him when he enters **Capricorn** again and is understood to have completed the final course of the shortest day. And so, in either of these signs, the annual space having been completed, Apollo is said to have "finished the dragon"—that is, his winding path...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of solar theology from Book 1 of Macrobius's Saturnalia. Having previously discussed Apollo's titles related to light and rain, the text now moves to his astronomical roles in the zodiac and his physical representation in eastern cults, finally transitioning into Chapter 21 to argue that Apollo and the god Liber (Dionysus) are one and the same deity.</meta>

### THE SATURNALIA

<margin>The Gates of the Sun.</margin> ...is delayed. Cornificius reported this opinion in his work on etymologies. Therefore, all these things pertain to these two signs—which are called the **Gates of the Sun**: **Cancer** and **Capricorn**. This is because the crab <note>Latin: *cancer*</note> is believed to be an animal that moves backward and sideways; by the same logic, in that sign, the sun begins to perform its backward movement obliquely, as is its custom. As for the habits of the **she-goat** <note>Latin: *capra*</note> in the pasture, it is observed that she always seeks the heights while grazing; and so the sun in Capricorn begins to return from the lowest depths toward the heights.

<margin>Apollo Didymaeus.</margin> They call him **Apollo Didymaeus** <note>original: "ἀπόλλωνα Διδυμαῖον"; "Didymaeus" means "the Twin"</note> because he displays a twin aspect of his divine power, both by illuminating himself and by forming the moon. For indeed, from a single source of light, he illuminates the spaces of day and night with two celestial bodies. Hence, the Romans also worship the sun under the name and appearance of the "Twin Year," using the title of Apollo.

<margin>Apollo Delphius. <gloss>The Clarifier</gloss></margin> They call him **Apollo Delphius** <note>original: "ἀπόλλωνα Δελφίον"</note> because he reveals things that are hidden through the clarity of his light <note>original: "ἐκ τοῦ δηλοῦν ἀφανῆ" — from revealing the unseen</note>. Or, as Numenius prefers: as if he were "one and alone." For he says that in the ancient Greek language, "one" used to be called *delphon*; from this, he says, a brother is called *adelphos* <note>original: "ἀδελφόσ"</note>, meaning "no longer one." 

Furthermore, the people of Hierapolis, who are a nation of the Assyrians <note>This refers to the cult of the sun god at the "Holy City" in Syria, likely representing the deity Hadad identified as Apollo</note>, condense all the effects and virtues of the sun into the appearance of a single bearded statue, <margin>The Statue of Apollo.</margin> and they call this same figure Apollo. His face is shaped with a long beard tapering to a point, with a **calathus** <note>a tall, basket-shaped headdress symbolizing the heavens or fertility</note> rising above his head. The statue is protected by a breastplate. In his right hand, he holds an upright spear, with a small figure of Victory standing upon it. His left hand offers the appearance of a flower; and from the tops of his shoulders, a Gorgon-like cloak <note>the *aegis*</note> fringed with snakes covers his shoulder blades. Nearby, eagles represent the likeness of flight. Before his feet is a female image, to the left and right of which are signs of women. A dragon encircles these with its winding coils.

The downward-pointing beard signifies the rays he casts down from above onto the earth. The golden calathus rising high shows the summit of the ether, where the substance of the sun is believed to reside. By the evidence of the spear and breastplate, the image is linked to Mars, whom the preceding discourse reveals to be one and the same as the sun. Victory testifies that all things are subject to the power of this celestial body. The appearance of the flower provides for the flowering of things, which this god impregnates, generates, nourishes, fosters, and matures. The female figure is an image of the Earth, which the sun illuminates from above. The two equally female signs by which she is surrounded represent **Matter** and **Nature** <note>original: "hylen naturamque"</note> as his servants. The image of the dragon shows the winding path of the star. The eagles, because of the great speed of their flight, demonstrate the height of the sun. <margin>What Minerva represents.</margin> A Gorgon-like garment is added because **Minerva**, whom we accept as the presiding power of this sun, is the sun's own virtue. Just as Porphyry testifies, Minerva is the power of the sun that supplies prudence to human minds. For this reason, this goddess is remembered as having been born from the head of Jove—that is, produced from the highest part of the ether, which is the origin of the sun.

---

-> ## ¶ Concerning Father Liber: how the Sun and Father Liber are the same. Chapter XXI. <-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'H' at the start of Chapter XXI, featuring ornate foliate designs within a square frame.</image-desc>

<margin>Father Liber is also the Sun.</margin> These things which we have said concerning Apollo can also be considered said of **Liber** <note>the Roman name for Bacchus/Dionysus</note>. For Aristotle, who wrote the *Theologumena*, asserts with many other arguments that Apollo and Father Liber are one and the same god. He also says that among the Lyncestians <note>OCR: *ligyreos*; Aristotle refers to the Lyncestae of Thrace/Macedonia</note> in Thrace, there is a shrine consecrated to Liber, from which oracles are given. But in this shrine, the prophets prophesy only after drinking a great deal of unmixed wine, just as oracles are spoken at the Claros shrine after water is drunk. Among the Spartans also, in the sacred rites they call the **Hyacinthia** celebrated for Apollo, they are crowned with ivy in the Bacchic ritual. Likewise, the Boeotians, while remembering that Mount Parnassus is consecrated to Apollo, nevertheless worship both the Delphic oracle and the Bacchic caves on the same mountain as being consecrated to a single god. 

Hence, divine rites are celebrated for both Apollo and Father Liber on the same mountain. Since both Varro and Granius Flaccus affirm this, Euripides also teaches it in these words: <margin>Satyrs.</margin> "Dionysus, girt with thyrsos and fawn-skins, dancing among the pines down Parnassus" <note>original: "Διόνυσοσ θύρσοισ' καὶ νεβρῶν δόραισ' καθάπτοσ' ἐπ' πεύκαισι παρνάσον κατάπηδα χορεύων"</note>. On this mountain, Parnassus, Bacchic rites are held every other year, where a frequent gathering of Satyrs is reportedly seen, and their distinct voices are often heard. Likewise, the clashing of cymbals often reaches the ears of men. And lest anyone think Mount Parnassus is dedicated to different gods, the same Euripides, in his *Licymnius*, writes that Apollo and Liber are one and the same god: "Lord, lover of laurel, Bacchus, Paean, Apollo of the beautiful lyre" <note>original: "Δέσποτα φιλοδάφνε βάκχε παιὰν ἀπόλλων εὐλύρε"</note>. Aeschylus agrees with this same opinion...

It begins a new chapter arguing that Apollo and Dionysus (Liber) are actually the same god, citing classical authors and shared cult sites like Parnassus.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse in Book 1 where the author argues that all the various gods of antiquity are, in fact, different manifestations of the Sun. Having discussed Apollo, the text now transitions into proving that the god Liber (the Roman name for Dionysus or Bacchus) is also identical to the Sun.</meta>

# BOOK ONE

...O Apollo, O Bacchus, O Paean! <note>original: "υσ απόλλον ώβακΧέ ὦπαάντιο"</note> But although it was previously asserted that Apollo and the Sun are one and the same, and it was later taught that Father Liber <note>A Roman deity of fertility and wine, identified with the Greek Dionysus.</note> is the same as Apollo, no doubt arises from this that the Sun and Father Liber must be considered the same divinity. Nevertheless, he establishes this even more firmly with clearer arguments. For in the sacred rites, this observation of the religious mystery is maintained: that when the Sun is in the upper—that is, the diurnal—hemisphere, he is called **Apollo**; but when he is in the lower—that is, the nocturnal—hemisphere, he is considered **Dionysus**, who is also Father Liber. Likewise, they fashion statues of Father Liber sometimes of a boyish age, and sometimes as a young man. Furthermore, they also depict him with a bearded, elderly appearance; such as the one the Greeks call 
<margin>Bacchapaean</margin>
**Bacchapaean**, and also the one they call **Brisseus**; and as the Neapolitans in Campania celebrate him, 
<margin>Brisseus. Ebona.</margin>
giving him the surname **Ebona**. These diversities of ages are related to the Sun: so that he appears as a tiny child at the 
<margin>Winter Solstice.</margin>
**winter solstice**, just as the Egyptians bring him out from the sanctuary <note>original: "ex adyto"</note> on a certain day, because then, on the shortest day, he seems like a small infant. From that point, with the following increases, at the **vernal equinox**, he attains strength similarly to an adolescent, and is adorned with the figure of a young man. Afterward, his age is established in the most full-bodied image of a beard at the **summer solstice**, at which time he reaches the peak of his growth. From there, through diminishments, the god is figured in a fourth form, as if growing old. Likewise, we learn that in Thrace, the Sun and Liber are considered the same, whom they worship with magnificent religious devotion, calling him 
<margin>Sebadius Bacchus.</margin>
**Sebadius**, as Alexander writes; and a temple is dedicated to that god on the hill of Zilmissus in a round shape, the middle of whose roof is open. The roundness of the temple demonstrates the appearance of this star <note>Macrobius refers to the Sun as a star/planet in the ancient astronomical sense.</note>, and light is admitted through the top of the roof so that it may appear that the Sun illuminates everything from the highest point by the admission of light, and because when he rises, all things are opened. Orpheus also, wishing the Sun to be understood, says among other things: "He who agitates the divine ether... whom they now call **Phanes** and **Dionysus** and King **Eubouleus** and **Antauges**, whom others among earthly men call by other names; he first came to light and was called Dionysus because he whirls <note>original: "dineitai"</note> through the vast and long Olympus; but he changed his name and took a surname for every variety according to the changing of time." <note>This is a translation of the corrupted Greek passage in the source, which quotes Orphic hymns equating the Sun with various divine names.</note> He called him **Phanes** from "light" <note>original: "apo tou photos"</note>, that is, from light and illumination, because he is seen by all while seeing all things. **Dionysus**, as the poet himself says, is from "being able to be whirled" <note>original: "apo tou dyneasthai kai periphesthai"</note>,
<margin>Dionysus.</margin>
that is, he is carried around in a circuit. From this, Cleanthes writes that he is so named from "completing" <note>original: "apo tou diany-ai"</note>, because by his daily impetus from the east to the west, he completes the course of the sky by making day and night. The natural philosophers call him **Dionysus** as "the mind of Zeus" <note>original: "Dios noun"</note>, because they said the Sun is the mind of the world. Moreover, the world is called "the sky," which they call **Jupiter**; hence Aratus, when about to speak concerning the sky, says: "From Zeus let us begin." 
<margin>World. Liber.</margin>
He is called **Liber** by the Romans because he is "free and wandering" <note>original: "liber et uagus"</note>, as Naevius says. This is because the wandering Sun, letting loose his fiery reins, joins himself closer to the earth. That same Orphic verse calling him **Eubouleus** <note>meaning "Good Counsel"</note> shows that this god provides good counsel. For if counsels are born from the conception of the mind, and authors believe the Sun is the mind of the world from which the principle of understanding flows into men, they rightly believed the Sun to be the presiding officer of good counsel. Orpheus clearly pronounces that the Sun is Liber in this verse: "The Sun whom they call by the surname Dionysus." That verse is indeed more absolute, but this one by the same poet is more concise: "One Zeus, one Hades, one Sun, one Dionysus." The authority of this verse is founded on the oracle of **Apollo at Claros**, in which another name is also added to the Sun; for in those same sacred verses, among other things, he is called **Iao**. For when the Clarian Apollo was consulted as to which of the gods he should be considered who is called Iao, he spoke thus. The power of this oracle's divinity and the interpretation of the name, by which Father Liber and the Sun signify Iao, was investigated by Cornelius Labeo in the book whose title is *On the Oracle of the Clarian Apollo*. Likewise, Orpheus, demonstrating that Liber and the Sun are one and the same god, writes thus concerning his ornament and dress in the Liberalia <note>Festivals of Liber/Bacchus.</note> rituals. From this Virgil also, writing that Father Liber is the Sun and Ceres is the Moon—who equally, by the nocturnal tempering or the diurnal heat, 
<margin>To govern the fruits.</margin>
govern the fertility of the soil and the ripening of the fruits—says: "If by your gift the earth changed the Chaonian acorn..."

<summary>Macrobius argues that the god Liber (Dionysus) is identical to the Sun, using etymology, Orphic hymns, and solar cycles to explain the god's various ages and names. He links the name "Iao" from the Clarian oracle to this universal solar deity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section of Book I of Macrobius's Saturnalia, which seeks to prove that all the traditional gods of the Roman and Greek pantheons are actually different names or aspects of the Sun. Having just discussed Father Liber (Bacchus/Dionysus), the author now transitions to Mars and Mercury.</meta>

# SATURNALIA
## VI <note>While the original text marks this as Book 6, the content corresponds to Book 1, Chapters 22-23 of the standard edition.</note>

...exchanged the acorn for the rich ear of grain. <note>original: "pingui glandem mutauit arista," a reference to Virgil's Georgics.</note> The same poet soon taught by a worldly example that the Sun is the author of earthly fertility when he said: "It has often been profitable to set fire to sterile fields," <note>original: "Saepe etiam steriles incendere profuit agros"</note> and so forth. For if fire applied by human ingenuity provides manifold aid, what must be attributed to the ethereal heat of the sun?

---

->On Mars. Chapter XXII.<-

<margin>Mars is the same as Liber</margin>
The things that have been said concerning Father Liber demonstrate that Mars is the same as he, and thus the same as the sun; for indeed, many join Liber with Mars, showing them to be one god. Hence Bacchus is surnamed **Enyalios**, <note>meaning "The Warlike"</note> which is among the proper names of Mars. Among the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, a statue of Father Liber is worshipped, distinguished by a spear rather than a *thyrsus* <term>thyrsus: a ritual staff associated with Bacchus, usually topped with a pine cone</term>. But when he holds the thyrsus, what else does he carry but a hidden weapon, whose point is covered by the creeping ivy? This shows that the impulses of war must be bound by a certain bond of patience. For ivy has the nature of binding and obliging. Furthermore, the heat of wine—of which Father Liber is the author—often drives men even to the fury of war. Therefore, because of the heat common to the effects of both, they wished Mars and Liber to be one and the same god. Certainly, the Romans worship both with the title of "Father." They call one "Father Liber," 
<margin>Marspiter</margin>
and the other "Marspiter," <note>original: "Marspitrem"</note> that is, "Father Mars." From this, Father Liber is also proven to be powerful in wars, because they declared him to be the first author of the **triumph** <term>triumph: a ceremonial procession in Rome to celebrate a military commander's victory</term>. Since, therefore, Father Liber is the same as the sun, and Mars is the same as Father Liber, who would doubt that Mars is the sun? The Accitani, a Spanish people, also celebrate a statue 
<margin>Neton</margin>
of Mars adorned with rays with the greatest religious devotion, calling him **Neton**. <note>The OCR reads "Necyn," but the historical name of this local Spanish solar-war god is Neton.</note> And certainly, natural reason requires that the gods who are the parents of celestial heat should differ more in name than in substance and reality. Moreover, the heat by which the mind is inflamed and excited—sometimes to anger, sometimes to virtues, and occasionally to the excess of a temporary madness, through which things wars are born—they have named Mars. The poet <note>Homer</note>, expressing his force and applying it to the likeness of fire, says: "Mars rages like a destructive fire." <note>original: "μαίνεται Δωμάρης ἐγχέσπαλος ηολοον πῦρ"</note> In sum, it must be pronounced that the effect of the sun, by which the fervor of spirits and the heat of blood is excited, is called Mars.

---

->On Mercury. Chapter XXIII.<-

<margin>Mercury is the sun</margin>
Indeed, the arguments previously taught are evidence that Mercury is the sun. For it appears even here that Apollo and Mercury are the same: because among many nations, the star of Mercury is referred to by the name of Apollo. And because Apollo presides over the Muses, Mercury imparts speech, which is the gift of the Muses. Besides this, there are many proofs that Mercury is considered to be the sun. First: because the statues of Mercury are adorned with feathered wings, which thing shows the velocity of the sun. For as we believe Mercury to be the master of the mind, and we understand him to be so named **from interpretation**, <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἑρμηνεύειν" (hermeneuein)</note> so also the sun is the mind of the world. Moreover, the velocity of the mind is the greatest, as Homer says: "as swift as a wing or a thought." <note>original: "ὡς εἴ πτερον ἠὲ νόημα"</note> Therefore, Mercury is adorned with wings as if by the very nature of the sun. The Egyptians resolve this argument more clearly, fashioning winged statues of the sun itself, in which there is not only one color. For they fashion one with a blue appearance, and another clear. Of these, they call the clear one "upper" and the blue one "lower." Now, the name of the "lower" sun is given when it completes its course in the lower hemisphere—that is, in the winter signs; and the "upper" when it circles the summer part of the zodiac. There is the same fiction concerning Mercury under another fable, when he is considered the minister and messenger between the upper and lower gods. 
<margin>Argiphontes</margin>
Furthermore, he is surnamed **Argiphontes** <note>Slayer of Argus</note>, not because he killed Argus—whom they say, adorned with the light of many eyes around the circumference of his head, guarded the daughter of Inachus <note>Io</note>, the mistress of that goddess <note>Juno</note>, who had been turned into the form of a cow—but under a fable of this kind: Argus 
<margin>Argus is called the sky. Mercury is figured in a square state.</margin>
is the sky, distinguished by the light of the stars, in which there seems to be a certain appearance of celestial eyes. Moreover, it was decided that the sky should be called Argus from its brightness and velocity, **from "white" and "swift"**. <note>original: "παρὰ τὸ λευκὸν ταχύ"</note> And it seems to observe the earth from above, which the Egyptians, when they wish to signify it in hieroglyphic letters, place the figure of a cow. Therefore, that circuit of the sky adorned with the lights of the stars is then considered "killed" by Mercury when the sun, by observing the stars in the daytime, as if kills them by its light.

<summary>This page argues for the solar nature of Mars and Mercury, identifying Mars with the sun's heat and spirit, and Mercury with its speed and the "killing" of stars by daylight (symbolized by the myth of Argus).</summary>

BOOK ONE LVI

...by removing the sight of his light from mortals. Most statues of Mercury are also fashioned in a **square shape** <note>These pillar-like statues were known as 'Herms'</note> marked only with a head and erect male organs. This figure signifies that the sun is the head of the world, and the king and creator of fates; all his power consists not in a division of various members, but in the mind alone, whose seat is in the head. The four sides are fashioned for the same reason: because a four-stringed lyre <note>the 'tetrachord'</note> is believed to be attributed to Mercury. Indeed, this number signifies either the four quarters of the world, or the four changes of the seasons by which the year is enclosed, or because the zodiac is divided by the two equinoxes and two solstices. In contrast, the seven strings of Apollo's lyre represent the movements of the seven celestial spheres, over which nature has appointed the sun as moderator. In 

<margin>Apollo's Lyre</margin>
<margin>The Caduceus of Mercury is clear.</margin>
the case of Mercury, it is also clear that the sun is worshipped through the **caduceus** <term>caduceus: the staff carried by Mercury, featuring two entwined serpents</term>; for the Egyptians fashioned it in the likeness of a male and female dragon joined together, consecrated to Mercury. These dragons are bound to one another in the middle of their coils in a knot called the **Knot of Hercules**, before their upper parts, bent back into a circle, join the end of the circle with their eyes pressed together. Afterward, the tails are brought back to the handle of the caduceus, and it is adorned with wings sprouting from that same part of the handle. The Egyptians claim that the symbolism of the caduceus also pertains to the birth of humans, which is called **Genesis**. 

<margin>Genesis. The presiding gods who give to us.</margin>
They record that four presiding gods are present at a person's birth: **Spirit, Fortune, Love, and Necessity** <note>original Greek: <term>Δαίμονα τύχην ἔρωτα ἀνάγκην</term></note>. They wish the first two to be understood as the Sun and the Moon; for the Sun is the author of the spirit, heat, and light, and is the creator and guardian of human life, and therefore is believed to be the *Daimon* <note>Spirit or guiding deity</note> of the one being born. The Moon is *Tyche* <note>Fortune</note>, because she presides over bodies, which are tossed about by the variety of chance events. Love is signified by the kiss of the serpents, and Necessity by the knot. As for why wings are added, that has already been explained above. The coils of the dragons were chosen for these symbols specifically because of the winding path of both celestial bodies.

---

## On Aesculapius. Chapter XXIII.

<margin>Aesculapius is referred back to the sun.</margin>
For this reason, a dragon is also joined to the statues of **Aesculapius** <note>the god of medicine</note> and **Salus** <note>the goddess of Health</note>, because these gods are referred back to the nature of the sun and moon. Aesculapius is the health-giving power from the substance of the sun, coming to the aid of the souls and bodies of mortals. Salus, however, is the effect of the lunar nature, by which the bodies of living beings are helped, being strengthened by a health-giving balance. Therefore, the figures of dragons are joined to their statues because they cause human bodies to regain their former vigor, casting off the skin of weakness just as dragons renew their youth each year by shedding the skin of old age. 

<margin>The Dragon.</margin>
Furthermore, the appearance of the dragon is referred to the sun itself, because the sun always returns from its lowest point—as if from old age—to its height, as if to the strength of youth. That the dragon is among the chief symbols of the sun is also shown by its very name, for it is called a "dragon" from the Greek word *derkein*, which means "to see" <note>original: <term>ἀπὸ τοῦ δέρκειν</term></note>. For they say this serpent possesses the sharpest sight and a vigilant nature, imitating the nature of this celestial body; for this reason, the guardianship of temples, inner shrines, oracles, and treasures is assigned to dragons. It is proved here that Aesculapius is the same as Apollo, not only because he is believed to be born from him, but because the right of divination is also joined to him. For Apollodorus writes in his books titled *On the Gods* that Aesculapius presides over divinations and auguries. This is no wonder, since the disciplines of medicine and divination are closely associated. For a doctor foreknows both favorable and unfavorable things that will happen in the body. 

<margin>A doctor must know the future.</margin>
As Hippocrates says: a doctor ought to speak concerning the sick man about "the things that are, the things that will come to be, and the things that were" <note>original: <term>τὰ τεόντα τὰ νὲ δόμενα καὶ πρωτέοντα</term>; this refers to the doctor knowing the patient's history, current state, and prognosis</note>. This matches the divinations, which know "the things that are, the things that will come to be, and the things that were."

---

## On Hercules. Chapter XXV.

<margin>Hercules is also understood through the sun.</margin>
But Hercules, too, is not foreign to the substance of the sun. Indeed, Hercules is that power of the sun which provides virtue to the human race in the likeness of the gods. Do not think that the Hercules born to Alcmene at Boeotian Thebes was the only one, or even the first called Hercules; rather, he was the last of many, and was deemed worthy of this title and honored with this name because through his excessive bravery he deserved the name of the god who rules over virtue. Furthermore, the god Hercules is worshipped with great devotion even at Tyre. But the Egyptians venerate him with the most sacred and August religion, beyond memory—which among them is the longest—worshipping him as one lacking a beginning. He himself is believed...

# BOOK I
