->OF THE SATURNALIA<-

**Vocabulary:** Giants, Hercules, Theron, Sarapis, Alexander of Macedon, Isis, Attis, Osiris, Adonis, Venus, Proserpina

<margin>Giants.</margin>
...and that he destroyed the giants when they fought for heaven: as if by the power of the gods. As for the giants, what else should we believe them to have been but a certain impious race of men who denied the gods? For this reason, it was thought they wished to drive the gods from their celestial seat. Their feet ended in snake coils, <note>In ancient art, Giants were often depicted with serpent-like legs (anguiped), symbolizing their earth-born nature.</note> which signifies that they thought of nothing upright or heavenly; the entire step and progress of their lives sank down into the infernal regions.

<margin>Hercules. It is clear.</margin>
Against this race, the sun exacted the punishment due through the force of its pestilential heat. Indeed, it is clear even from his name that Hercules is the sun. For what else is "Heracles" but "Heras kleos," that is, the glory of the air? <note>original: "heras.i. aeris cleos". The author uses a Greek etymology: *Hera* (interpreted here as the air) and *kleos* (glory).</note> And what other glory of the air is there except the illumination of the sun? When the sun withdraws, a depth of darkness hides the spirit of the air.

Furthermore, the administration of sacred rites among the Egyptians asserts the manifold power of the god through many rituals, identifying Hercules as <note>original: "τὸν ἐν πᾶσι καὶ Διὰ πάντων ἥλιον"</note> "the sun who is in all things and through all things." An argument of no small weight can also be gathered from events elsewhere on earth.

<margin>Theron, King of Spain.</margin>
For Theron, the king of Hither Spain, when driven by madness to attack the temple of Hercules, led an army of ships. The people of Gades <note>Modern-day Cádiz, Spain, home to a famous temple of the Phoenician Melqart, whom the Romans identified as Hercules.</note> came out against them in long ships. While the battle was joined and the fight was still equal, suddenly the royal ships were turned to flight and, at the same moment, were consumed by a sudden fire. The very few survivors among the enemy reported that lions had appeared to them standing upon the prows of the Gaditanian fleet, and that their own ships were suddenly scorched by rays of light—just like those painted on the head of the sun—sent out against them.

---

### Concerning Sarapis. Chapter XXVI.

<margin>Sarapis, who is also taken for the sun. To boast.</margin>
The city adjacent to Egypt, which boasts Alexander of Macedon as its founder, <note>Alexandria.</note> observes the worship of Sarapis and Isis with a devotion bordering on religious awe. Yet, it testifies that all that veneration is bestowed upon the sun under the name of Sarapis—whether when they place a *calathus* <note>A tall, basket-shaped headdress symbolizing fertility and the heavens.</note> upon his head, or when they add the sign of a three-headed beast to the statue. This beast displays the image of a lion in its middle and largest head. On the right side, the head of a dog rises up with a mild and flattering appearance. The left part of the neck ends in the head of a ravenous wolf. A snake connects these animal forms with its coils, its head returning to the god's right hand, where the monster is seen. Therefore, the lion’s head represents the present time, because its condition is strong and burning between the past and the future. But the past is signified by the wolf's head, because the memory of things gone by is snatched away and stolen. Likewise, the image of the flattering dog designates the outcome of future time, for which hope—though uncertain—flatters us. But to whom would the seasons be subject if not to their own author? His head, adorned with the *calathus*, shows both the height of the stars and the power of his capacity, because all earthly things return to him when they are drawn up by his sent heat.

Receive now what is proclaimed by an oracle concerning the sun or Sarapis. For Sarapis, whom the Egyptians declared the greatest god, was asked by Nicocreon, king of the Cypriots, which of the gods he should be considered. He instructed the king's anxious devotion with these verses: <note>original: "εἷς θεὸς τοῖος Δέμας ἐστὶν οἷον κἀγὼ εἴπω οὐράνιος κόσμος κεφαλὴ γαστὴρ δὲ θάλασσα γαῖα δέ μοι πόδες εἰσὶ τὰ δ’ οὔατα ἐν αἰθέρι κεῖται όμματα τηλαυγὲς λαμπρὸν φάος ἠελίοιο"</note> "A god am I such as I shall describe: the celestial world is my head, the sea my belly, the earth is my feet, my ears lie in the ether, and my eyes are the far-reaching, brilliant light of the sun." From this, it appears that the nature of Sarapis and the sun is one and indivisible. Isis is celebrated with every religious rite as being either the earth or the nature of things underlying the sun. Hence it is that the entire body of the goddess is

<margin>Thickened</margin>
thickened with continuous breasts, because the universe is nourished by the sustenance of either the earth or the nature of things.

### Concerning Adonis, Attis, and Osiris. Chapter XXVII.

<margin>Adonis, who is also taken for the sun. Venus, Proserpina.</margin>
There is no doubt that Adonis is also the sun, as seen in the religion of the Assyrians, among whom the greatest veneration for Venus Architis and Adonis once flourished, which the Phoenicians now maintain. For the natural philosophers have worshipped the upper hemisphere of the earth, the part we inhabit, under the name of Venus. The lower hemisphere of the earth, however, they called Proserpina. Therefore, among the Assyrians or Phoenicians, the goddess is depicted as mourning because the sun, proceeding in its annual path through the order of the twelve signs, enters the part of the lower hemisphere. For of the twelve signs of the zodiac, six are considered upper and six lower. When he is in the lower signs, and therefore makes the days shorter, the goddess is believed to mourn, as if the sun were lost to the temporary snatching of death and detained by Proserpina...

...we have called the deity of the lower circle of the earth and the antipodes <note>The "antipodes" refers to people living on the opposite side of the globe.</note>. Furthermore, they wish it to be believed that **Adonis** was returned to **Venus** when the sun, having conquered the six annual signs of the lower order, begins to traverse the hemisphere of our circle, with an increase of light and of days. Or, they hand down that **Adonis** was killed by a boar, imagining the image of winter in this animal; for the bristly and rough boar delights in damp and muddy places covered with frost, and feeds specifically on the winter fruit, the acorn. Therefore, winter is like a wound to the sun, which diminishes both its light and heat for us—both of which happen to living beings in death. 

An image of this goddess [Venus] is fashioned on **Mount Lebanon** with her head veiled, appearing sad, supporting her face with her left hand within her garment; tears are believed to flow in the sight of those looking on. This image, besides being that of the mourning goddess (as we said), is also of the winter earth: at which time, veiled by clouds and widowed of the sun, she is benumbed; and the springs, like the eyes of the earth, flow more abundantly, and the fields, again widowed of their own cultivation, show a mournful face. But when the sun has emerged from the lower parts of the earth and crosses the boundaries of the vernal equinox <note>The spring equinox, when day and night are of equal length.</note> by increasing the day, then **Venus** is joyful and beautiful: the fields are green with crops, the meadows with grass, and the trees with leaves. Therefore, our ancestors dedicated the month of April to **Venus**. Similarly, the **Phrygians**, with the stories and administrations of sacred rites unchanged, show that the same things are understood regarding the **Mother of the Gods** and **Attis**.

<margin>Why Cybele is carried by lions.</margin>
For who would doubt that the **Mother of the Gods** is considered the earth? This goddess is carried by lions: animals strong in impulse and heat, which is the nature of the sky, by whose circuit the air is contained, which carries the earth. But the sun, under the name of **Attis**, she adorns with both a pipe and a rod. The pipe shows the order of the unequal spirit, because the winds, in which there is no equality, take their own substance from the sun. The rod asserts the power of the sun, who governs all things. That the primary reason for the sun is the focus of these ceremonies can also be understood from this: that according to their ritual, the *descent* <note>original: "κατάβασις" (katabasis)</note> having ended and the simulation of mourning performed, the beginning of joy is celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [March 25],

<margin>Hilaria</margin>
which day they call the **Hilaria** <note>A Roman festival of rejoicing.</note>: the first time the sun extends the day longer than the night. Likewise, under different names, the religious effect is found among the **Egyptians**.

<margin>Osiris.</margin>
When **Isis** mourns **Osiris**, she is in hiding. Neither is **Osiris** anything other than the sun, nor **Isis** anything other than the earth (as we said), or the nature of things. And the same reasoning that turns around **Adonis** and **Attis** also alternates mourning and joy in the Egyptian religion by the turns of the annual administration.

<margin>Hieroglyphic letters.</margin>
Hence the **Egyptians** assert **Osiris** to be the sun: whenever they wish to express him in their hieroglyphic letters, they engrave a scepter, and in it they express the appearance of an eye; and by this sign they show **Osiris**, signifying that this god is the sun, and sublime with royal power looks down upon all things—because antiquity calls the sun the **Eye of Jupiter**.

<margin>The sun is the eye of Jove.</margin>
Among them **Apollo**, who is the sun,

<margin>Horus Apollo. The Hours.</margin>
is called **Horus**. From which also the twenty-four **Hours**, by which day and night are completed, received their name; and the four seasons by which the annual circle is filled are called "hours." The same **Egyptians**, wishing to dedicate a statue in the name of the sun itself, fashioned an image with a shaved head, but with hair remaining on the right side. The preserved hair teaches that the sun in the nature of things is never entirely hidden. The removed hair, with the root remaining, shows that this star, even at the time when it is not seen by us, has the substance for emerging again, just like hair. By the same argument, time is also signified when the light is narrow. When, as if with its increases shaved off, and only a narrow prominence remaining, the sun reaches the minimum space of the day,

<margin>Winter Solstice</margin>
which the ancients called the **winter solstice**, naming it *bruma* from the "brevity" of the days—that is, the *descent* <note>original: "κατάβασις" (katabasis)</note>. Emerging again from these hiding places or narrows toward the summer hemisphere, it is stretched out into increases as if being born, and then it is believed to have reached its kingdom. Therefore, the **Egyptians** consecrated an animal in the zodiac in that part of the sky where the sun boils most strongly with heat in its annual course:

<margin>The Lion.</margin>
and they call the sign of the **Lion** there the "house of the sun" because that animal is seen to derive its substance from the nature of the sun. And first in impulse and heat...

<margin>He surpasses the animals</margin>
...surpasses the animals, just as the sun surpasses the stars. The lion is strong in its chest and the front part of its body, but grows weaker in its hind limbs. Similarly, the sun's power increases in the first part of the day toward midday—or in the first part of the year from spring toward summer—but soon it fades as it is led away, either toward evening (which is the lower part of the day) or toward winter (which is seen as the lower part of the year). Likewise, the lion is always seen with open and fiery eyes, just as the sun looks upon the earth with a perpetually open, fiery, and tireless gaze. Nor is the lion alone in this; indeed, the entire circle of the zodiac is rightly related to the nature of the sun. 

<margin>
The signs of the zodiac are related to the nature of the sun.
**Aries** (The Ram)
</margin>
To begin with **Aries**, there is a great harmony between them. For this animal lies on its left side through the six months of winter, but from the spring equinox <note>The time when day and night are equal, signaling the start of spring.</note> it lies on its right side—just as the sun traverses the right hemisphere from that same time, and the left for the remainder of its circuit. For this reason, the Libyans fashion **Hammon**—whom they believe to be the god of the setting sun—with ram’s horns, which are the animal's greatest strength, just as rays are the sun’s. Indeed, among the Greeks, the ram is called *krios* from the word *keras* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ κέρως κριὸς"; *keras* means horn.</note>. 

<margin>**Taurus** (The Bull)</margin>
Egyptian worship shows that **Taurus** is related to the sun for many reasons: either because at **Heliopolis** <note>The "City of the Sun" in Egypt.</note> they especially worship a bull consecrated to the sun named **Netiron**; or because the **Apis** bull in the city of **Memphis** is received as an image of the sun; or because in the town of **Hermonthis**, in a magnificent temple of **Apollo**, they worship a bull consecrated to the sun named **Bacchis**, which is notable for miracles consistent with the sun's nature. For it is affirmed to change colors every hour, and is said to have shaggy hair growing in the opposite direction <note>Against the "grain" of the hair.</note>, contrary to the nature of all other animals; from this, it is considered an image of the sun shining into the opposite part of the world. 

<margin>**Gemini** (The Twins)</margin>
As for **Gemini**, who are believed to live by alternating deaths, what else do they signify but the one and same sun? Now descending into the depths of the world, now rising again to the highest peak. 

<margin>**Cancer** (The Crab)</margin>
What else does **Cancer**, with its sideways crawl, show but the sun’s path? It never travels in a straight line, but is destined to always move through that oblique path where the order of the signs turns; especially in that sign, where the sun begins to turn away from its high course to seek the lower regions. 

<margin>**Virgo** (The Maiden)</margin>
The **Lion** has already been discussed above. As for **Virgo**, who carries an ear of grain in her hand, what is she but the **Solar Power** <note>original: "Δύναμις ἡλιακὴ" (*Dynamis heliakē*).</note> which weighs down the fruits? Therefore, she is believed to be Justice, who alone allows the growing fruits to reach the use of mankind. 

<margin>
**Scorpio**
**Libra** (The Scales)
**Sagittarius** (The Archer)
</margin>
The whole of **Scorpio**, within which is **Libra**, represents the nature of the sun: it grows numb in winter, but once this has passed, it raises its sting again by its own power, having suffered no permanent natural damage from its winter torpor. **Sagittarius**, which is the lowest and last of all the zodiac dwellings, for this reason "degenerates" from a man into a beast in its hind limbs, as if it were thrust down from the heavens into the underworld by its rear parts. Yet it shoots an arrow, which indicates that even then, the life of all things is preserved by the sun’s rays, even when they come from the lowest part. 

<margin>**Capricorn**</margin>
**Capricorn**, bringing the sun back from the lower parts to the higher, seems to imitate the nature of the goat; for while a goat grazes, it always leaves the low ground to seek the heights of the jutting cliffs. 

<margin>**Aquarius** (The Water-Bearer)</margin>
Does not **Aquarius** show the very power of the sun? For from where would rain fall upon the earth, unless the sun's heat drew moisture to the heights? Its pouring back out is the abundance of rain. 

<margin>**Pisces** (The Fish)</margin>
In the final order of the zodiac, **Pisces** are located. These were consecrated to the sun not by some likeness of their nature, like the others, but as a demonstration of the power of the star; for life is given by the sun not only to creatures of the air and land, but also to those whose lives are submerged in the waters, as if exiled from the sun's sight. So great is the sun's power that it brings life even by penetrating hidden depths.

---

### On Nemesis. Chapter XXVIII.

<margin>Nemesis</margin>
To return the discourse to the sun’s manifold power: what else is **Nemesis**, who is worshiped as a check against pride, but the power of the sun? For such is its nature that it obscures things that are bright and removes them from sight, while it illuminates things that are in the dark and offers them to our view.

---

### On Inuus. Chapter XXIX.

<margin>Inuus</margin>
**Pan** himself, whom they call **Inuus**, allows the wiser among us to understand him as the sun under this guise in which he is seen. The Arcadians worship this god, calling him **the lord of all matter** <note>original: "τὸν πᾶν ὕλης κύριον" (*ton pan hylēs kyrion*).</note>; by this, they do not mean he is the "lord of the woods," but rather the ruler of the entire material substance. The power of this matter comprises the bodies of all things, whether they be divine...

<margin>Essence</margin>
...whether they be earthly: it composes the essence. Therefore, the horns of Inuus <note>Inuus was an ancient Italian deity of the woods, often identified with the Greek god Pan</note> and the long hanging down of his beard show the nature of light; for the sun both illuminates the circuit of the upper sky and sheds light on the lower parts. Whence Homer says of him: "The lord of the silver bow, who mightily brings light to mortals" <note>original: "ἀργυροτόξου ἀνάκτος ὃς ἰφι θέως φέρη κ' δὲ βροτοῖσι"</note>. What the pipe or the staff signify, we have expressed above in the discussion of the attire of Attis. The fact that he ends in goat's feet has this reasoning: because matter, which is stretched out into every substance by the sun’s distribution, after producing divine bodies from itself, finishes in the element of earth. To represent this extremity, the feet of this animal were chosen because it is an earthly creature and yet always seeks the heights while grazing; just so the sun is seen either when it sends its rays down to the lands or when it gathers itself back upon the mountains. The love and delight of this Inuus is believed to be Echo <note>original: "ἠχώ"</note>, who is subject to no one’s eyes; this signifies the harmony of heaven, which is a friend to the sun—being, as it were, the moderator of all the spheres from which that harmony is born—yet it can never be grasped by our senses.

### On Saturn. Chapter XXX.

<margin>Saturn</margin>
Saturn himself, who is the author of time—and is therefore called *Kronos* by the Greeks with a change of a letter, as if it were *Chronos* <note>The author is playing on the Greek words Kronos (the god) and Chronos (Time)</note>—what else is he to be understood as but the sun? For the order of the elements is distinguished by the count of time, revealed by light, bound together by eternity, and distinguished by vision; all of which show the activity of the sun.

### On Jove. Chapter XXXI.

<margin>Jupiter</margin>
Nor does Jupiter himself, the king of the gods, seem to exceed the nature of the sun; rather, it is shown by clear signs that Jupiter and the sun are the same. For when Homer says: "For Zeus [goes to] the Ocean" <note>original: "ζεὺς γὰρ ὃς ὠκεανὸν"</note>, Cornificius writes that the sun is understood by the name of Jove, for whom the wave of the Ocean provides, as it were, a feast. For this reason, as both Posidonius and Cleanthes <note>Famous Stoic philosophers</note> affirm, the sun's path does not recede from the region which is called "scorched" <note>The tropical zone between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn</note> because the ocean runs beneath it, surrounding and dividing the earth. Now, it is established by the assertion of all natural philosophers that heat is nourished by moisture. For as he says: "all the gods followed together" <note>original: "θεοὶ ἁμ̄α πάντες ἕποντο"</note>, the stars are understood, which are carried with him daily toward their setting and rising by the force of the sky. For they say gods are nourished by moisture. They call 

<margin>Star</margin>
the constellations and stars "gods" (*theoi*) from the word *theein* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ θεῖν"</note>, that is, "to run," because they are always in motion; or from *theoreisthai* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ θεωρεύεσθαι"</note>, meaning "to be seen." The poet adds "on the twelfth [hour] of his birth," signifying not the number of days, but of hours, in which they are returned to the rising of the upper hemisphere. The words of Plato from the *Timaeus* <note>The quote actually originates from Plato's *Phaedrus*, though Macrobius attributes it to the *Timaeus*</note> lead our understanding to the same opinion: "The great leader in heaven, Zeus, driving a winged chariot, goes first, arranging all things and caring for them. He is followed by an army of gods and spirits, arranged in twelve parts; but Hestia remains alone in the house of the gods." By these words, he 

<margin>The Sun is the same as Jupiter</margin>
wants the Sun to be understood under the name of Jove as the great leader in heaven, showing the speed of the star by the winged chariot. For in whatever sign of the zodiac he may be, he surpasses all signs and stars; and he seems to lead all the gods who preside over the signs, ordering and adorning all things. Therefore, the other gods are held as his army, distributed through the twelve parts of the zodiac, because he himself occupies the place of the twelfth sign in whichever sign he may be. Now the name of "demons" <note>From the Greek *daimones*, meaning guiding spirits or lesser divine beings</note> is joined with the title of gods either because they are "knowing" <note>original: "Δαίμονες", from a root meaning to know</note> of the future; or (as Posidonius writes in the books titled *On Heroes and Demons*) because their quality is produced and divided from ethereal substance, whether from *daiein* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ Δαίειν"</note>, that is "to burn," or from *daiomenou* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ Δαιομένoυ"</note>, that is "being divided." But when he adds "Hestia remains alone in the house of the gods," it signifies that this one, whom we take to be the earth, remains immobile within the house of the gods (that is, within the world), as Euripides says: "And the earth, where all mortals dwell, is in the ether." From this too it is shown what should be thought of the sun and Jove, since elsewhere it is said "Jove sees all and knows all" <note>original: "πάντα Διῶν Διὸς καὶ πάντα νοήσας"</note> and in another place "the Sun who sees all and hears all" <note>original: "ἥλιος ὃς πάντ' ἐφορᾷ καὶ πάντ' ἐπακούει"</note>. Therefore, both should be worshipped as one power. The Assyrians also [worship] the sun under [the name] of Jupiter...

<margin>He surpasses the animals</margin>
...surpasses the animals, just as the sun surpasses the stars. The lion is strong in its chest and the forward part of its body, but its strength declines in its hindquarters. Similarly, the sun's force increases in the first part of the day toward midday—or in the first part of the year from spring toward summer—but soon it fades as it is led down, either toward sunset (which is the lower part of the day) or toward winter (which is seen as the lower part of the year). Likewise, the lion is always seen with open and fiery eyes, just as the sun looks upon the earth with a perpetually open, fiery, and tireless eye. Nor is it the lion alone; indeed, all the signs of the zodiac are rightly referred to the 
<margin>The signs of the zodiac are referred to the nature of the sun: Aries.</margin>
nature of the sun. To begin with Aries <note>The Ram</note>, there is a great harmony between them. For the ram lies on its left side for the six months of winter, but from the spring equinox, it lies upon its right side—just as the sun travels through the right hemisphere from that same time and through the left for the remainder. For this reason, the Libyans represent Hammon <note>The Egyptian god Amun, identified with Zeus/Jupiter</note>—whom they believe to be the setting sun—with the horns of a ram, for in these the animal is most powerful, just as the sun is in its rays. Even among the Greeks, he is called <term>the ram</term> <note>original: <term>κριός</term></note> <term>from the word for horn</term> <note>original: <term>ἀπὸ τοῦ κέρως</term></note>. 
<margin>Taurus</margin>
That Taurus <note>The Bull</note> is referred to the sun is shown by Egyptian worship for many reasons: either because at Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun"</note> they especially worship a bull consecrated to the sun which they call Mnevis <note>The OCR reads "Netiron," but this is a transcription error for the sacred bull Mnevis</note>; or because the Apis bull in the city of Memphis is received as an image of the sun; or because in the town of Hermonthis, in a magnificent temple of Apollo, they worship a bull consecrated to the sun called Buchis <note>The OCR reads "bacchim"</note>, which is famous for miracles matching the nature of the sun. For it is affirmed to change colors every hour, and it is said to be shaggy with bristles that grow in the opposite direction, contrary to the nature of all other animals—
<margin>Gemini</margin>
whence it is like an image of the sun shining into the opposite part of the world. Moreover, Gemini <note>The Twins</note>, who are believed to live by alternating deaths, what else do they signify but the one and the same sun, now descending 
<margin>Cancer</margin>
into the depths of the world, now rising again to the highest altitude? What else does Cancer <note>The Crab</note>, with its sideways crawl, show but the path of the sun? For its path is never straight, but it is its lot to travel along that path which is slanted as the order of the signs turns. Especially in that sign, the sun begins to seek the lower parts by a slanted course from its highest point. 
<margin>Virgo</margin>
The Lion has already been discussed above. As for Virgo <note>The Maiden</note>, who holds an ear of grain in her hand, what else is she but <term>Solar Power</term> <note>original: <term>Δύναμις ἡλιακὴ</term></note> which is weighed down by the fruits? She is therefore believed to be Justice, who alone ensures that the growing fruits reach the use of mankind. Scorpio, including the Scales <note>Libra</note>, 
<margin>Scorpio and Libra</margin>
represents the nature of the sun, which grows sluggish in winter; once this is passed, it raises its sting again by its own force, the sun's nature having suffered no 
<margin>Sagittarius</margin>
lasting damage from the winter torpor. Sagittarius <note>The Archer</note>, which is the lowest and last of all the zodiacal dwellings, is for this reason depicted as changing from a man into a beast in its hind legs, as if it were thrust down from the heavens into the underworld in its tail-end. Yet it shoots an arrow, which indicates that even then the life of all things is 
<margin>Capricorn</margin>
preserved by the rays of the sun, even when coming from the lowest part. Capricorn, leading the sun back from the underworld parts to the heights, is seen to imitate the nature of the goat, which always seeks the heights of the 
<margin>Aquarius</margin>
overhanging cliffs while it grazes. Does not Aquarius <note>The Water-Bearer</note> show the very power of the sun? From where would rain fall upon the lands if the sun’s heat did not draw moisture to the heights? Its pouring back 
<margin>Pisces</margin>
out is the abundance of rain. In the final order of the zodiac, Pisces <note>The Fish</note> are placed; these were consecrated to the sun not because of some physical likeness like the others, but as a display of the star's power, from which life is given not only to animals of the air and land, but also to those whose lives are submerged in the waters and seem exiled from the sight of the sun. So great is the force of the sun that it gives life even by penetrating hidden places.

### On Nemesis. Chapter XXVIII.

<margin>Nemesis</margin>
And so that the discourse may return to the manifold power of the sun: Nemesis, who is worshipped as a remedy against pride—what else is she but the power of the sun? For her nature is such that she obscures bright things and removes them from sight, while she illuminates those that are in the dark and brings them into view.

The Arcadians worship this god, calling him <term>the Lord of Matter</term> <note>original: <term>τὸν τῆς ὕλο- κύριον</term></note>, meaning to signify not just the master of the woods, but the ruler of all material substance. <margin>Essence</margin>
...whether they be of the earth, they compose an essence. Therefore, the horns of Inuus <note>Another name for the god Pan, often associated with the vitality of nature</note> and the long, flowing descent of his beard demonstrate the nature of light; for the sun illuminates both the circuit of the upper heavens and sheds light upon the lower regions. Regarding this, Homer says of him: <note>original: "ὤρνυσ' ἵνα θανάτοισι φέως φέρη ἠδ' ἐ βροτοῖσι."</note> "He rose so that he might bring light to the immortals and to mortal men." What the pipe or the rod signifies, we have expressed above in the description of Attis. As for the fact that he ends in the feet of a goat, the reasoning for this argument is as follows: because the matter which, by the sun’s distribution, is stretched into every substance, having formed divine bodies from itself, finds its limit in the element of earth. Therefore, as a sign of this extremity, the feet of this animal were chosen because it is both of the earth and yet always seeks the heights while grazing; just as the sun is seen either when it sends its rays down from above to the lands, or when it gathers itself back upon the mountains. The love and delight of this Inuus is believed to be Echo, who is subject to no one's eyes; this signifies the harmony of heaven, which is a friend to the sun—being, as it were, the moderator of all the spheres from which she is born—yet she can never be detected by our senses.

### ->Of Saturn. Chapter 30.<-

<margin>Saturn</margin>
**S**aturn himself, who is the author of times (and for that reason is called by the Greeks, with a change of a letter, *Kronos* <note>original: "κρόνοσ"</note> as if he were *Chronos* <note>original: "Χρόνοσ"</note> or Time), what else is he to be understood as but the sun? For the order of the elements is handed down as distinct in the numerosity of time, revealed by light, bound together, carried through eternity, and distinguished by vision—all of which demonstrate the action of the sun.

### ->Of Jupiter. Chapter 31.<-

<margin>Jupiter</margin>
**N**or does Jupiter himself, the king of the gods, seem to exceed the nature of the sun; rather, it is taught through clear evidence that Jupiter and the sun are the same. For when Homer says: <note>original: "ζεύσ γάρ ἰσ ὠκεανὸν"</note> "For Zeus went to the Ocean," Cornificius writes that the sun is understood by the name of Jupiter, for whom the waves of the Ocean provide, as it were, a feast. For this reason, as both Posidonius and Cleanthes <note>Stoic philosophers</note> affirm, the path of the sun does not recede from that region which is called "burnt" <note>the tropics</note>, because the ocean runs beneath it, which both surrounds and divides the earth. Now, it is established by the assertion of all natural philosophers that heat is nourished by moisture. For when he says: <note>original: "θεόι Δᾶμαπάντες ἔποντο"</note> "And all the gods followed," the stars are understood, which are carried daily by the impetus of heaven with him to their settings and risings, and are nourished by that same moisture. For they call 
<margin>A Star</margin>
the constellations and stars "gods" <note>original: "θεοὺς"</note> from the word "to run" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ θέιν"</note>, that is, "to race" <note>original: "τρέχειν"</note>, because they are always in motion; and from the word "to be seen" <note>original: "κἀπὸ τοῦ θεωρεῦσθαι"</note>. The poet adds "on the twelfth day" <note>original: "Δώδεκάτη γενέτωσ"</note>, signifying not the days, but the number of hours in which they are brought back to the rising of the upper hemisphere. Our understanding is also led to the same conclusion by these words from Plato's *Timaeus* <note>Actually from the *Phaedrus*</note>: <note>original: "ὁ μὲν δὴ ἡγεμὼν ἐν οὐρανῷ ζεύσ ἐλαύνων πτηνὸν ἄρμα πρῶτος πορεύεται Διακόσμῶν πάντα καὶ ἐπιμελούμενος. τω Δε ἕπεταί στρατία θεῶν καὶ Δαιμόνων κατὰ Δώδεκα μέρη κεκοσμημένη μένει δὲ ἑσία ἐν θεῶν οἴκῳ μόνη."</note> "Now the great leader in heaven, Jupiter, driving a winged chariot, goes first, ordering all things and caring for them. And after him follows an army of gods and spirits, marshaled in twelve parts; but Hestia alone remains in the house of the gods." By these words, he wants the sun to be understood 
<margin>The Sun is the same as Jupiter</margin>
under the name of Jupiter, showing the speed of the star with a winged chariot. For in whatever sign it may be, it surpasses all signs and stars; and it is seen to go before all the gods who preside over the signs, as their leader, by ordering and adorning all things. Therefore, the other gods are regarded as his army, distributed through the twelve parts of the signs, because he occupies the place of the twelfth sign in whichever sign he happens to be. Furthermore, he joins the name of "demons" <note>spirits or divine beings</note> with the title of the gods, either because they are "daemons" <note>original: "Δαιμονέσ"</note>, that is, "knowing the future," or as Posidonius writes in the books titled *On Heroes and Demons*: because they have a quality produced and divided from the ethereal substance, whether from "to burn" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ Δαιεῖν"</note>, that is, "to set on fire" <note>original: "καίειν"</note>, or from "being divided" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ Δαιομένους"</note>, that is, "apportioned." As for the addition "but Hestia alone remains in the house of the gods," it signifies that this alone—which we take to be the Earth—remains immobile within the house of the gods, that is, within the world, as Euripides says: <note>original: "καὶ γαῖα μὲν πάντες οἱ βροτοὶ οἴκουσι κλεν ἐν αἰθέρι."</note> "And the earth, where all mortals dwell, is famous in the ether." From this it is also shown what must be thought concerning the Sun and Jupiter, since elsewhere it is said, "all things through Zeus and Zeus knowing all," and in another place, "the Sun who oversees all and hears all." Thus, both must be worshipped as one power. The Assyrians also worship the sun under the name of Jupiter...

<margin>The Heliopolitan</margin>
...by the name of the one whom they call the divine Heliopolitan: they celebrate him with the greatest ceremonies in the city which is named Heliopolis <note>The City of the Sun, located in modern Lebanon, famous for the Temple of Jupiter Baal</note>. 
<margin>Jupiter</margin>
The statue of this god was taken from a town in Egypt also called Heliopolis, during the reign of Senemur among the Egyptians (or perhaps his name was Senepos). It was first brought into that land by Oppias, an ambassador of Delebois, King of the Assyrians, and by Egyptian priests, of whom the leader was Parmetis. It was kept for a long time among the Assyrians before it later migrated to Heliopolis. Why this was done, and by what reasoning it departed Egypt and came to these places where it is now, and why it is worshipped with an Assyrian rite rather than an Egyptian one, I have declined to say, as it does not pertain to the present cause. Now indeed, that this same being is both Jupiter and the Sun is recognized both from the rite of the sacrifices and from his appearance. For the statue stands in gold with a beardless face; the right hand is raised with a whip in the manner of a charioteer, while the left holds a lightning bolt and ears of grain. All of these demonstrate the joined power of Jupiter and the Sun. The religion of this temple is also powerful in divination, which is attributed to the power of Apollo, who is the same as the Sun. 
<margin>On a litter</margin>
For the statue of the Heliopolitan god is carried on a litter <note>original: "ferculo"; a platform or tray used to carry divine images in processions</note>, just as the statues of the gods are carried in the procession of the Circus games; and for the most part, the leading men of the province support it, with their heads shaved, purified by a long period of abstinence. They are carried by a divine spirit, not by their own will, but where the god impels those carrying him—just as we have seen at Antium, where the statues of the Fortunes are moved forward to give responses. Even those who are absent consult this god by sending sealed documents, and he writes back in order to those questions contained within the consultation. 
<margin>Trajan</margin>
Thus also the Emperor Trajan, when he was about to set out from that province for Parthia with his army, being of a very firm religious disposition, was urged by friends—who had already experienced great signs from this divinity—to consult him regarding the outcome of the undertaking. He acted with Roman prudence, first testing the reliability of the religion to ensure no human fraud was involved. First, he sent sealed letters to which he wanted a reply. The god ordered a sheet of paper to be brought, signed while blank, and sent; the priests were stunned by such an act, for they were ignorant of the contents of the letters. Trajan received these with the greatest admiration, because he himself had also dealt with the god using blank tablets. Then, with other letters written and sealed, he asked whether he would return to Rome after finishing the war. The god ordered a centurion’s vine-staff <note>The "vitis" was a staff of office representing a centurion's authority; its breaking here is an omen of death</note> from the gifts dedicated in the temple to be brought out, divided into pieces, wrapped in a shroud, and carried forth. The outcome of the matter became clear upon Trajan's death, when his bones were returned to Rome; for by the fragments, the appearance of the remains was shown, and by the evidence of the vine-staff, the time of the coming downfall was revealed. 

And lest the discourse wander through the names of individual gods, hear what the Assyrians think of the Sun's power. For to the god whom they worship as highest and greatest, 
<margin>Adad, the greatest god of the Assyrians; Atargatis, the goddess</margin>
they have given the name Adad. The interpretation of this name signifies "One." They adore him as the most powerful god. But they join to him a goddess named Atargatis, and they attribute all power over all things to these two, understanding them to be the Sun and the Earth. They do not express their power as divided through many species by a multitude of names, but by the symbols with which they are adorned, they signify the manifold excellence of the twofold divinity. These symbols themselves speak to the nature of the Sun. For the statue of Adad is seen distinguished by downward-slanting rays, by which it is shown that the force of heaven is in the rays of the sun, which are sent down to the earth. The statue of Atargatis is distinguished by rays reclined upwards, showing that from the power of the rays sent from above, whatever the earth produces is born. Beneath the same statue are the forms of lions, showing for the same reason that she is the Earth, just as the Phrygians imagined the Mother of the Gods—that is, the Earth—to be carried by lions. Finally, theologians indicate that the power of the Sun is referred to as the summit of all powers, which they demonstrate in their rites with this very brief prayer, saying: 
<margin>Power of the Sun</margin>
"Sun, almighty ruler of the world, spirit of the world, power of the world, light of the world." <note>original Greek: "Ἥλιε παντακράτορ κόσμου πνεῦμα κόσμου δύναμις κόσμου φῶς"</note> And Orpheus testifies that the Sun is all things in these verses: "Hear me, you who turn the circle of the starry path, O Sun, you who are the glorious Zeus, Dionysus, father of the sea, father of the land, O Sun, creator of all, many-colored with golden light." <note>original Greek: "κέκλυθι πώλου κύκλον... χρυσεο φεγγέσ"</note>

### On the Praises of Virgil. XXXII.

<margin>The praises of Virgil</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'H' depicting a figure sitting in a landscape with a building in the background.</image-desc>When Praetextatus <note>Macrobius’s host and a lead speaker in these dialogues</note> had made an end of speaking, everyone kept their eyes fixed upon him in a state of wonder and amazement. Then, one man praised his memory, another his learning, and everyone praised his religious knowledge—affirming that he alone was privy to the secret nature of the gods, and alone possessed the soul to grasp divine matters and the talent to express them. Amidst this, Evangelus <note>A skeptical character in the dialogue who often challenges the other speakers</note> said: 

“Indeed, I marvel that the power of such great deities could be so easily grasped. But as for your citing our ‘Mantuan’ <note>Virgil, who was born near Mantua</note> as a witness for every point when the conversation turns to divine matters, this is done more out of popular favor than sound judgment. Am I really to believe that when Virgil said, **Liber and nourishing Ceres** <note>original: "Liber & alma Ceres"; Liber is a name for Bacchus</note> **instead of the Sun and Moon**, he did not simply place this there in imitation of some other poet? Did he not say it because he heard it said that way, while remaining ignorant of why it was said? Unless, perhaps, just as the Greeks exalt everything of theirs to the heavens, we also want our own poets to be seen as philosophers—even though Cicero himself, who professed no less a study of philosophy than of oratory, often diminishes the glory he won through his eloquence by his disorganized treatment of facts whenever he disputes the nature of the gods, fate, or divination.”

Then Symmachus <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, a famous Roman statesman and orator</note> said: “As for Cicero, Evangelus—who is impervious to such insults—we shall see to him later. Now, since our business is with Maro <note>Virgil's family name</note>, I want you to answer: do you judge this poet's works to be fit only for the instruction of boys, or do you admit there are other, deeper things within them? For you seem to me to still hold Virgil’s verses in the same way we used to sing them as boys when our teachers read them out to us.” 

“On the contrary, Symmachus,” Evangelus replied, “when we were boys we admired him without judgment. It was not permitted by our teachers, nor by our age, to look for faults. Yet no one can shamelessly deny those faults, since Virgil himself confessed them. For why else, when dying, did he bequeath his poem to the flames <note>A reference to the legend that Virgil ordered the Aeneid to be burned upon his death because it was unfinished</note>, if not to ensure that the stains upon his reputation were kept from posterity? And not without reason: for he blushed at the thought of future judgments, should people read of a mother asking her husband for weapons for a son <note>original: "petitio dẽpcatis filio arma a marito"; refers to Venus asking Vulcan for armor for Aeneas</note> who was born to another, or find a thousand other shameful things—whether they be Greek words, or barbarous ones, <margin>The glory of Virgil.</margin> or faults in the very arrangement of the work.”

When everyone had shuddered at what he said, Symmachus added: “This, Evangelus, is the glory of Maro: it grows by no man’s praise, and is diminished by no man’s blame. Truly, those things you tear apart can be defended by anyone from the common crowd of grammarians; let us not do an injustice to our friend Servius <note>Maurus Servius Honoratus, the famous commentator on Virgil</note>—who in my opinion surpasses the ancient teachers in learning—by asking him to excuse such trifles. But I ask you: even if the poetry in so great a poet displeases you, does it not seem that the rhetorical strength <note>term: "nerui oratorii"; literally 'oratory nerves/sinews', referring to the persuasive power and structure of his language</note>, which is most powerful in him, is worthy of praise?”

At these words, Evangelus first broke into laughter. Then he remarked: “By Hercules, it has finally come to this: you are announcing that Virgil is an orator! It is no wonder, since your ambition recently tried to promote him to the rank of the philosophers.”

“If you are of the opinion,” Symmachus said, “that Maro intended nothing but poetry—even if you would begrudge him even that title—hear what he himself pronounced concerning the multifaceted learning in his work. For a letter of Maro himself, addressed to Augustus, begins thus:

-> I indeed receive frequent letters from you. <-

And further down:

-> Concerning my Aeneas, if by Hercules I already had him in a state worthy of your ears, I would gladly send him. But the undertaking is so vast that I seem to have entered upon such a work almost by a defect of the mind; especially since (as you know) I am also applying other, much more important studies to that work. <-

The abundance of subject matter does not disagree with these words of Virgil. Yet most literary men pass over this 'with unwashed feet' <note>original: "pedibus illotis"; an idiom meaning to approach a subject without preparation or reverence</note>, as if a grammarian were permitted to know nothing beyond the explanation of words. Thus these 'fine' men have set for themselves certain limits of knowledge, like boundaries or sacred precincts <note>term: "pomeria"; the religious boundary of a city</note>, which if anyone dares to step beyond, he must be thought to have looked into the temple of the goddess from which males are barred <note>A reference to the 'Bona Dea', whose rites were strictly for women</note>. But let us, who find 'crude wisdom' <note>original: "crassa minerua"; an idiom for plain or unrefined sense</note> unbefitting, not allow the inner sanctuaries of this sacred poem to remain hidden. Instead, having heard the experts, let us investigate the sense of these secrets and offer the opened inner chambers for celebration. And lest I seem to want to embrace everything alone, I promise that I shall demonstrate the most powerful rhetorical inventions and ideas within Virgil's work. As for Eusebius the orator...”

<summary>In this passage, the dinner guests debate the merits of Virgil, with Evangelus criticizing him as a simple poet with many faults, while Symmachus argues that Virgil is a master of deep philosophy and rhetoric. Symmachus cites a letter from Virgil to Augustus to prove the poet intended his work to be a vast, scholarly undertaking.</summary>
<keywords>Virgil, Cicero, Macrobius, Symmachus, Evangelus, Aeneid, Augustus, rhetoric, literary criticism, Latin literature</keywords>

<page-num>XII</page-num>
<header>OF THE SATURNALIA</header>
<sig>H</sig>

<margin>
The principal praises of Virgil
</margin>
“I do not wish to snatch away the discourse on the art of oratory in Maro <note>original: "Maronem"; a common name for the poet Virgil</note> from the most eloquent among us; for his learning and experience in teaching will carry it out better. I have, however, earnestly requested all the rest of you who are present that each of you contributes whatever special observation he has noted regarding Virgil’s genius, as if to a common fund <note>original: "ex symbolo"; referring to a potluck or shared contribution</note>.” These words produced a wonderful degree of eagerness in all who were present. Everyone rose, desiring to hear the others, yet without realizing that they too would be called upon for the same duty. Thus, moved by mutual encouragement, they were easily and willingly stirred to agreement. Looking at everyone, they began to beg Praetextatus to be the first to reveal his judgment, with the others following in the order in which they happened to be sitting. 

Then Vectius <note>referring to Vettius Agorius Praetextatus, the host</note> said: “Indeed, among all the things for which the fame of Virgil is outstanding, as a constant reader I admire this: that he preserved the law of the priests <note>original: "ius pontificum"</note> with such great learning, as if he had made a profession of it, throughout many and various parts of his work.”

<margin>
Virgil as Chief Priest
</margin>
<margin>
Virgil as the greatest augur
</margin>
“And if the flow of such a great discussion does not fail, I promise it shall come to pass that our Virgil will be claimed as a Chief Priest <note>original: "pontifex maximus"; the highest religious office in Rome</note>.” After him, Flavianus said: “In our poet, I find such a great knowledge of augural law <note>original: "iuris auguralis"; the science of interpreting omens from birds and lightning</note> that even if he were destitute of the learning of other disciplines, this profession alone would raise him to the heights.” 

Then Eustachius said: “I would especially praise how much he has translated from the Greeks—acting with caution and as if he were doing something else <note>original: "tanquam aliud agens"</note>—sometimes with skillful concealment and sometimes with open imitation. That is, unless a greater admiration for his astrology and his entire philosophy should take hold of me, which he, being frugal and sober, sprinkled throughout his work in a way that can never be criticized.” 

Furius Albinus, sitting on one side of Praetextatus, and Cecinna Albinus next to him, both praised the affectation of antiquity <note>the use of archaic language</note> in Virgil—one in his choice of words, the other in his style. 

Avienus said: “I will not take it upon myself to dare to praise any single one of the Virgilian virtues. Instead, by listening to whatever you all say, if anything occurs to me regarding these points, or if something has seemed noteworthy to me in my long reading, I will bring it forward at the appropriate time. Just remember that we must demand of our friend Servius <note>the famous 4th-century grammarian and Virgil commentator</note> that he makes clear whatever seems obscure, as he is by far the greatest of all men of letters.” 

When these things were said and agreed upon by the whole group, Praetextatus, seeing that everyone's face was turned toward him, said: “Philosophy, which is the unique gift of the gods and the discipline of disciplines, must be honored with the opening speech. Therefore, let Eustachius remember that the first place for discussion is granted to him, with all other professions yielding. You, my Flavianus, shall succeed him, so that I may be refreshed by your listening and restore my strength for speaking through a period of silence.” 

Meanwhile, the master of the slave service <note>the head butler or steward</note>—whose care it was to either burn incense to the household gods <note>original: "penates"</note>, or to arrange the pantry and rule the servants of the household affairs—notified the master that the family <note>original: "familiam"; here referring to the household slaves</note> had finished their feast according to the solemnity of the annual custom. For on this festival <note>the Saturnalia</note>, the religious household first honors the servants with a banquet prepared as if for the use of the master; and only then is the table of the father of the family <note>original: "patrisfamilias"; the head of the house</note> prepared anew. 

The head of the servants thus suggested that it was time for dinner and to call the masters. Then Praetextatus said: “Our Virgil must therefore be reserved for the better part of the day, so that we may devote a new morning to inspecting his poem in order. Now the hour warns us that this table should be honored by your presence. But let both Eustachius and after him Nicomachus remember that the duty of the opening speech is reserved for them in tomorrow’s discussion. And Flavianus, I summon you by the law already agreed upon, so that on the following day my household gods may boast in the hospitality of such a great gathering.” 

When all had agreed to this, they withdrew with great alacrity of spirit to dinner, each one remembering and approving one thing or another from what they had discussed together.

# THE SECOND BOOK OF THE SATURNALIA OF MACROBIUS AURELIUS THEODOSIUS, MAN OF CONSULAR RANK AND ILLUSTRIOUS.

<image-desc>A detailed woodcut illustration depicting a banquet or symposium. Several figures, both men and women, are gathered around a table laid with vessels and food. On the left, men in robes and hats appear to be in discussion. On the right, a woman stands pouring or serving from a pitcher. A small dog sits on the floor in the center foreground. The scene is set within a room with architectural details like a window or doorway in the background.</image-desc>

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'H' depicting a man in a robe seated and gesturing toward a child standing before him.</image-desc>HERE, when the modest manner of eating brought an end to the restraint of the courses, and the festive joy began to arise over small cups of wine, Avienus said: "Our friend Maro <note>original: "Maro"; the poet Virgil</note> well and wisely described both a tumultuous and a sober banquet in one and the same verse, changing only a few words. For when luxury is accustomed to proceed with noise amidst royal splendor, he says, 'After the first rest came to the feast' <note>original: "postquam prima quies epulis"; Aeneid 1.723. The 'rest' implies a break in the loud commotion of a grand party.</note>. But when heroes sit down to disciplined meals, he does not bring back 'rest,' because no tumult preceded it. Instead, he says, 'After hunger was removed by the food' <note>original: "postquam exempta fames epulis"; Aeneid 8.184. This implies a meal taken for necessity rather than excess.</note>. This banquet of ours has brought together the modesty of the heroic age and the elegance of our own; its sober splendor and careful thrift are such that I would not hesitate to compare it to Agathon’s banquet <note>The setting of Plato’s *Symposium*</note>, or even—despite Plato’s great eloquence—to prefer it. For our host, the king of this table, is no less than Socrates in his character, and more effective in public affairs than that philosopher. As for the rest of you present, you are so eminent in the study of virtue that no one would think to compare you to the comic poets or to Alcibiades—who was only brave when it came to crimes—or to the others who frequented that famous banquet."

"Speak kindly, I pray," Praetextatus said, "out of reverence for the majesty of Socrates. For who would not agree that the luminaries present here are to be preferred to the others who were at that symposium? But to what point does your example tend, Avienus?"

"Because," he replied, "among those men, there was one who asked for a flute-player to be let in, so that a girl, intentionally more soft than nature intended, might exercise the philosophers with the tuneful sweetness and the slippery charms of her greeting. That was attempted there so that Agathon's victory might be celebrated; but we increase the honor of the god whose festival this is without any mixture of such pleasure. Nor am I unaware that we do not consider sadness or a clouded face to be a virtue, nor do we greatly admire that Crassus whom Cicero, following Lucilius, writes laughed only once in his life <note>referring to Marcus Licinius Crassus 'Agelastus,' the grandfather of the famous triumvir, whose nickname meant 'the one who never laughs'</note>."

When Praetextatus added that playful pleasures were neither customary in his household nor should be brought before such a serious gathering, Symmachus interrupted: "Since the Saturnalia is the 'best of days,' as the Veronese poet <note>The poet Catullus</note> says, we Stoics should not reject pleasure as an enemy, nor should we, like the Epicureans, place the 'highest good' in pleasure. Let us instead devise a cheerfulness that lacks wantonness. And if I am not mistaken, I have found it: let us bring forth the choice jokes of ancient and noble men, drawn from many books, in a mutual exchange."

<margin>Flat-footed mime. Storyteller.</margin>
"Let this be our 'lettered joy' and learned banter, taking the place of the flat-footed mime <note>original: "planipedis"; a low-status comic actor who performed without the high boots of tragedy</note> and the storyteller <note>original: "fabulonis"</note> who tosses about shameless and 'pre-textual' <note>original: "praetextata"; a pun on the *toga praetextata* worn by children and magistrates, implying both 'official' and 'lewd' or 'obscene' in this context</note> words; instead, let it imitate shame and modesty. This practice seemed worthy of care and study to the ancients. Indeed, I first notice two men whom the ancient age produced as the most eloquent—the comic poet Plautus and the orator Tully <note>Cicero</note>—and both of them surpassed all others in the beauty of their jokes. Plautus was so famous in this regard that after his death, comedies that were circulating under uncertain authorship were recognized as being by Plautus because of the abundance of jokes. As for Cicero, who is ignorant of how powerful he was in this matter? He even took care to read the books his freedman composed about his patron’s jokes—books which some think were actually by Cicero himself. Who also does not know that he was often called a 'consular buffoon' by his enemies? Even Vatinius says this in his speech..."

# THE SATURNALIA
## Page I

<margin>Witticisms</margin>
...he set forth. And indeed, I would recount—if it were not too long—in which legal cases he <note>Referring to the orator Cicero</note> protected the most guilty defendants and achieved victory through the use of jokes. For example, consider his defense of Lucius Flaccus, whom he saved from the most obvious charges of extortion through the timeliness of a joke. That specific joke does not survive in his published speeches, but is known to me from the book of Fusius Vivaculus, and it is celebrated among his other witticisms. Yet, I did not happen upon this word <note>original: "dicteria"</note> by chance; I used it intentionally. For our ancestors called jokes of this kind "witticisms" <note>original: "dicteria"; often refers to sharp, biting, or clever remarks.</note>. Cicero himself is a witness to this, for in the second book of his letters to Cornelius Nepos, he says: "Therefore, our ancestors, though all things we say might be called 'sayings,' wanted those things which we speak both briefly and sharply to be called by the specific name of 'witticisms'." Thus speaks Cicero. Indeed, Novius and Pomponius often call jokes "witticisms." Marcus Cato, the famous Censor, was also accustomed to joking cleverly. The authority of such men should shield us from any ill-will, even if we were to engage in such banter ourselves. But since we are merely recounting the sayings of the ancients, we are surely defended by the dignity of the authors themselves. If, therefore, you approve of this pursuit, come now—let us recount whatever such sayings come to each of our minds, stirring our memories in turn. This idea of "contrived sobriety" <note>An intellectual game to keep the mind sharp while drinking.</note> pleased everyone; and so, they urged Praetextatus <note>The host of the banquet</note> to provide the authority of an example by beginning.

---

### ¶ On Witticisms. Chapter I.

<image-desc>Decorative initial Q set within a square woodcut border featuring floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
<margin>
Witticisms
most wittily
told by
many.
The jeer of
Hannibal.
</margin>
When that man—I wish to recount the saying of an enemy, but a defeated one, whose memory restores the glory of Roman triumphs—Hannibal of Carthage, while a fugitive at the court of King Antiochus, joked most wittily. The jest was of this sort: Antiochus was showing off his massive forces in the field, which he had prepared for war against the Roman people. He paraded the army, shimmering with silver and gold ornaments. He brought out chariots with scythes and elephants with towers, and cavalry shining with mobile bits, saddles, and horse-trappings. And there the King, boasting in his contemplation of such a great and well-equipped army, looked at Hannibal. "Do you think," he asked, "that all these things are enough for the Romans?" Then the Carthaginian, mocking the cowardice and lack of fighting spirit of the King's expensively armed soldiers, replied: "I believe these are plainly enough for the Romans, even if they are the most greedy of people." <note>Hannibal's joke is a play on the word "enough." The King meant "enough to defeat them," but Hannibal meant "enough loot to satisfy their greed."</note> Nothing could be said more elegantly or more sharply. The King had asked about the size of his army for the sake of comparison; Hannibal answered regarding it as plunder.

<margin>The Sacrifice of Waste</margin>
Flavianus added: There was a sacrifice among the ancients called "the sacrifice of waste" <note>original: "protervia"</note>. In this ritual, it was the custom that if anything remained from the feast, it should be consumed by fire. There is a joke of Cato's regarding this. For he used to say that a certain Albidius—who had "eaten" <note>i.e., spent on food</note> his entire inheritance and finally lost the only house he had left in a fire—had performed the "sacrifice of waste," because that which he could not eat, he had burned.

---

### ¶ Cicero's Saying against Servilia. Chapter II.

<image-desc>Decorative initial S set within a square woodcut border featuring floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>
<margin>
Cicero's
saying against
Servilia
</margin>
Symmachus then said: Servilia, the mother of Marcus Brutus, when she had acquired a valuable estate for a small price from Caesar (who was auctioning off the property of citizens), did not escape this saying of Cicero’s: "Indeed, so you may know the purchase was even better, Servilia bought this farm with a third deducted" <note>original: "tertia deducta"</note>. Now, Junia Tertia <note>"Tertia" means "The Third"</note> was the daughter of Servilia and the wife of Cassius; the Dictator <note>Julius Caesar</note> was being quite wanton with both the mother and the girl. Thus, the city constantly attacked the luxury of the old adulterer with rumors and jokes, so that his crimes were not only treated seriously but also with ridicule.

---

### ¶ The Shoemaker's Witty Saying. Chapter III.

<image-desc>Decorative initial P set within a square woodcut border with ornamental foliage.</image-desc>
<margin>
Galla, a
shoemaker's
tool
</margin>
After this, Ceccina Albinus spoke: Plancus, perhaps while acting in a friend's legal case, wished to destroy the credibility of a troublesome witness. Knowing the man was a shoemaker, Plancus asked him by what trade he supported himself. The man replied urbanely: "I work with Galla" <note>original: "Gallam subigo"</note>. This is considered a shoemaker's tool <note>An oak gall used for tanning leather</note>, but the witness cleverly turned it into a reproach for adultery through ambiguity. For Plancus was rumored to be involved with a married woman named Mevia Galla.

---

### ¶ The Saying of Antony's Friend. Chapter IV.

<image-desc>Decorative initial S set within a square woodcut border with classicizing scrollwork.</image-desc>
Furius Albinus followed. After the flight from Mutina, when people were asking what Mark Antony was doing, one of his close friends was said to have replied: "What a dog does in Egypt: he drinks and runs." <note>original: "bibit & fugit"</note>. For it is well known in those regions that dogs run while they drink, out of fear of being snatched by crocodiles.

¶ **Chapter V.**
**E**ustachius then spoke. When he had seen Publius Mutius—a particularly ill-willed man—looking even gloomier than usual, he said: "Either something unfortunate has happened to Mutius, or something good has happened to someone else." <note>This is a classic joke about the nature of envy; an envious man is miserable not just because of his own luck, but because of the success of others.</note>

¶ **Chapter VI.**
**T**hen Avienus spoke. When Faustus, the son of Sulla, saw that his sister had two lovers at the same time—Fulvius, the son of a fuller, and Pompeius, whose surname was "Macula" (The Stain)—he said: "I wonder why my sister has a stain, since she has a fuller at hand." <note>original: "Macula" and "Fullonem." A "fuller" was a professional who cleaned and whitened clothes; Faustus is punning that a cleaner should have removed the "stain."</note>

¶ **Chapter VII.**
**H**ere Evangelus spoke. At the house of Lucius Mallius—who was considered the best painter in Rome—Servilius Geminius happened to be dining. When he saw Mallius's sons, who were quite ugly, he said: "Mallius, you do not mold <note>referring to procreation/sculpting</note> the same way you paint." Mallius replied: "That is because I mold in the dark, but I paint in the light."

¶ **Chapter VIII.**
**E**usebius then spoke: Demosthenes, he said, was stirred by the reputation of Lais, whose beauty was then the marvel of Greece. He approached her so that he might enjoy her famous love for himself. But when he heard that her price for a single night was half a talent <note>An enormous sum of money, equivalent to thousands of days' wages for a laborer.</note>, he departed with this saying:
<margin>I do not buy regret at such a price.</margin>
**"I do not buy regret at such a price."** <note>original Greek: "ἀγοράζω τοῦ ούτου μετανοῆσαι" — The OCR here contains a fragmented version of the famous Greek quote usually attributed to Demosthenes: "οὐκ ὠνοῦμαι μυρίων δραχμῶν μεταμέλειαν."</note>

¶ During this, while Servius remained silent out of modesty even though it was his turn to speak, Evangelus said: "You are pronouncing all of us grammarians to be impudent if you want your silence in such matters to be seen as a defense of your modesty. Neither your brow, nor that of Disarius or Horus, will be free from the mark of pride unless you wish to imitate Praetextatus and the rest of us."

¶ Then Servius, seeing that his silence was becoming more embarrassing than speaking, emboldened himself to the freedom of a similar story. Marcus Votacilius Pitholaus, he said, when Gaius Servilius had been consul for only a single day, remarked: "In the past we had priests of Jove; now we have consuls of the day." <note>original: "flamines diales... consules diales." This is a pun on the Latin word "dialis." A "Flamen Dialis" was a high priest of Jupiter, but "dialis" also sounds like "dies" (day), implying the consul lasted only twenty-four hours.</note> And Disarius, not waiting for further reproach of his silence, said:
<margin>Diales, that is, of one day</margin>

¶ **Chapter IX.**
**A**fter him, Horus also spoke: I bring to you a **couplet** <note>original: "Dístichon"</note> by Plato, which he wrote as a young man in sport, at a time when he was also dabbling in tragedies:
<margin>Plato's couplet</margin>
**"My soul was on my lips as I was kissing Agathon; the poor thing came up as if to pass across."** <note>original Greek: "τὴν ψυχὴν ἀγαθῶ καὶ φιλῶν ἐπὶ χείλεσιν ἔιχον ἦλθε ἡ τάλαινα ὡς διαβησομένη"</note> After this, a great cheer arose, and everyone gave themselves over to critical laughter, reflecting on the witticisms flavored with ancient festive spirit that each had brought forward. Symmachus then said: "These verses of Plato—though it is uncertain whether one should admire their antiquity or their brevity more—I remember reading translated into Latin, and in a much more expansive style, even though our language is usually considered shorter and more narrow than the Greek. And (as I recall) these are the words:"

<margin>A kiss</margin>
> While with a parted kiss I kissed my boy,
> And drew the sweet flower of his breath from the open path,
> My soul, sick and wounded, ran to my lips,
> Searching for the passage in his open mouth and soft lips,
> Striving to pass through the journey's end.
> Then, if there had been but a little more delay,
> Stirred by the fire of love in that joining of a kiss, it would have passed through,
> Leaving me behind; and a truly wondrous thing would happen:
> That I should become dead to myself, yet live on, having gone into the boy.

"But I wonder that all of you have kept silent regarding the jokes of Cicero, in which
<margin>Jokes.</margin>

he was most eloquent, as he was in all things. And just as a temple-warden proclaims the responses of his deity, I shall recount the sayings of Cicero as my memory suggests them." Then, with everyone alert and ready to listen, he began:

# THE SATURNALIA
## Page II

...had seen [him]; he said: "Who tied my son-in-law to a sword?" <note>original: "quis inquit generum meum ad gladium alligauit?" This refers to Cicero’s son-in-law Lentulus, who was a very short man. Seeing him wearing a long ceremonial sword, Cicero joked that the man was an accessory to the weapon rather than the other way around.</note>
<margin>Witty remarks</margin>
¶ Nor did he spare his brother Quintus Cicero from similar biting wit. For when he was in the province that Quintus had governed, he saw a shield-portrait of him painted in the traditional style with large features down to the chest—yet Quintus himself was of very small stature. Cicero remarked: "My brother at half-size is larger than the whole man."

¶ During the consulship of Vatinius—which lasted only a few days—Cicero’s notable urbanity was widely shared. He said: "A great portent occurred in the year of Vatinius; for during his consulship, there was neither winter, nor spring, nor summer, nor autumn." <note>A joke on how short the term was; the seasons did not even have time to change.</note> Later, when Vatinius complained that Cicero had been too burdened to come and visit him while he was ill, Cicero replied: "I truly wished to come during your consulship, but the night caught up with me." <note>meaning the consulship ended before the day was out.</note> Moreover, Cicero saw a chance for revenge against Vatinius; for he remembered that Vatinius had once boasted that he had been "carried back from exile on the shoulders of the Republic." Cicero asked him: "Then where did you get those varicose veins?" <note>implying that if he was carried, his legs shouldn't be weary, or mocking his physical condition.</note>
<margin>Caninius the consul</margin>
Caninius Rebilus also served as consul for a single day—as Servius recorded. When he ascended the rostra, he simultaneously entered the honor of the consulship and took his leave of it. Cicero, delighting in every occasion for wit, remarked: "Caninius is a <note>original Greek: "logotheōritos"</note> spectator of a consul." <note>The Greek term suggests someone who holds an office only in name or theory, or one who is merely "watched" rather than acting.</note> Regarding this consul, Rebilus achieved such fame that people would ask under which consuls he had been a consul. <note>An absurdity, as he was consul for so short a time he needed other consuls to date his term.</note> Cicero further quipped: "We have a most vigilant consul in Caninius, who during his entire consulship never saw sleep."

<margin>Pompey</margin>
Pompey the Great was often unable to endure Cicero’s jokes. These were some of the things Cicero said about him: "I know whom I should flee, but I do not know whom I should follow." <note>Referring to his hesitation between the factions of Pompey and Caesar during the Civil War.</note> And when Cicero arrived at Pompey’s camp and people said he had come late, he replied: "I am not late at all, for I see nothing ready here." Later, when Pompey asked where his son-in-law Dolabella was, Cicero replied: "With your father-in-law" <note>Dolabella had sided with Julius Caesar, who was Pompey's former father-in-law.</note>. And when Pompey granted Roman citizenship to a deserter, Cicero said: "O, what a fine man! He promises the citizenship of another city to the Gauls, yet he cannot restore our own city to us." Because of such remarks, Pompey rightly said: "I wish Cicero would go over to the enemy, so that he might fear us."

<margin>Beware that man</margin>
Cicero also bared his teeth with biting wit against Caesar. First, after Caesar’s victory, when asked why he had chosen the wrong side in the conflict, Cicero replied: "The way he belts himself deceived me." <note>original: "Praecinctura me decepit." This is a joke about Caesar's youthful habit of wearing his toga with a loose, flowing belt—a style considered effeminate or a sign of loose morals.</note> Caesar used to joke about this himself, as he would hike up his hem and walk with a soft gait, leading Sulla to prophetically warn Pompey: "Beware of that ill-belted boy."

<margin>Cicero’s remarks on Laberius</margin>
Later, when the playwright Laberius was honored with a gold ring by Caesar at the conclusion of the games, he immediately went to sit in the fourteen rows <note>The section of the theater reserved for the equestrian rank, or knights.</note>, violating the traditional order as he had been stripped of his status as a knight and then restored as a mime. As Laberius passed by looking for a seat, Cicero said: "I would receive you, were I not sitting so cramped." This was both a rejection of Laberius and a joke at the expense of the new Senate, whose numbers Caesar had increased beyond what was right. Laberius did not let this pass without a retort, replying:
<margin>A Senator born.</margin>
"It is a wonder you are sitting cramped, since you are accustomed to sitting on two stools." <note>original: "duabus sellis sedere." A scathing accusation of political inconsistency, suggesting Cicero tried to support both sides of the Civil War at once.</note> This was a reproach of Cicero’s perceived fickleness, for which this excellent citizen was undeservedly ill-spoken of.

¶ At another time, Cicero openly mocked Caesar’s leniency in appointing the Senate. When he was asked by his host Publius Mallius to secure a local senate seat for his stepson, Cicero said in front of a crowd: "In Rome, if he has the right of Pompey, it is difficult." <note>A pun on the town of Pompeii and the political influence of Pompey the Great.</note> Nor did his biting wit stop there; when he was greeted by a certain Andron of Laodicea and asked the reason for his arrival, the man replied that he had come as an envoy to Caesar to petition for the freedom of his fatherland. Cicero expressed the state of public servitude by saying: "If you are successful, plead for our freedom as well." <note>original Greek: "ean eutychēs kai peri hēmōn presbeuson."</note>

<margin>Biting jests.</margin>
There flourished in Cicero an exceeding wit and a serious bite, as seen in this excerpt from a letter to Gaius Cassius, the assassin of the dictator: "I wish you had invited me to dinner on the Ides of March; surely there would have been no leftovers. As it is, your leftovers are now giving me trouble." <note>The "leftovers" refers to Mark Antony, whom the conspirators chose to spare, much to Cicero's later regret.</note> Cicero also joked most charmingly about his son-in-law Pilo and Marcus Lepidus. While Symmachus was still speaking and seemed ready to say more, Avienus interrupted him, as is common in dinner conversations, saying: "Even Augustus Caesar was no less a master of this kind of wit than Cicero, and perhaps not even second to Tullius. And if you are willing..."
