...it will be: I am about to relate some of those things which memory suggests. And he said: "Allow Symmachus to finish explaining what Cicero said concerning those he has already named; Avienus will more opportunely follow with the stories concerning Augustus."

<margin>Piso, the son-in-law of Cicero.</margin>
As Avienus fell silent, Symmachus said: "Cicero, when his son-in-law Piso walked rather effeminately, while his daughter walked quite briskly, said to his daughter: 'Walk as if you were the man.' And when Marcus Lepidus had addressed the 'Conscript Fathers' in the Senate, Tullius said: 'I would not have done so much for [a private matter].' <note>original: "Ego non tantum fecissem..." This refers to the formal address 'Patres Conscripti.' Cicero is joking about the weight of the title compared to the triviality of the speech.</note>
<margin>Eager to speak.</margin>
It was most peculiar. <note>original: "δἰδιότατον" (idiōtaton) - a Greek term for something very personal or peculiar.</note> But go on, Avienus, lest I delay you any further while you are so eager to speak."

## Chapter X.

<margin>The jokes of Augustus</margin>
And he replied: "I say that Augustus Caesar affected a witty style, yet always with a respect for his majesty and modesty, so as never to descend into the behavior of a buffoon. He had written a tragedy called *Ajax*, but because he became dissatisfied with it, he erased it. Later, Lucius, a serious writer of tragedies, asked him how his *Ajax* was doing. He replied: 'He has fallen upon a sponge.' <note>This is a clever pun. In Greek tragedy, Ajax dies by falling on his sword. Augustus "killed" his play by using a wet sponge to wipe the ink from the papyrus.</note>

<margin>The tragedy *Ajax*.</margin>
The same Augustus, when a certain man was nervously offering him a petition—at one moment stretching out his hand and the next pulling it back—said: 'Do you think you are giving a penny to an elephant?'
¶ Again, when Pacuvius Taurus asked him for a gift of money, saying that 'people were already commonly saying he had been given a large sum of money by the Emperor,' Augustus replied: 'But don't you believe them.'

<margin>Salary.</margin>
¶ To another man who had been removed from a prefecture of the cavalry and was demanding a salary in spite of it, saying: 'I do not ask for this for the sake of profit, but so that by your judgment I might seem to have obtained a reward and thus laid down my office honorably,' Augustus struck him back with this saying: 'Tell everyone that you received it, and I will not deny that I gave it.'
¶ His urbanity was also noted regarding Herennius, a young man given over to vices. When Augustus had ordered him to leave the camp and the youth used this supplication: 'How shall I return to my father’s house? What shall I say to my father?' He responded: 'Tell him that I did not like you.'
¶ A soldier who had been struck by a stone during an expedition and had a notable, deforming scar on his forehead was boasting too much of his service. Augustus lightly chastised him thus: 'But when you run away, never look back.' <note>Implying the soldier was hit in the front of the head because he was looking back while retreating.</note>
¶ To Galba, whose body was misshapen by a hunchback, who was pleading a case before him and frequently said: 'Correct in me whatever you find to rebuke,' he replied: 'I can give you advice, but I cannot correct you.' <note>A pun on 'corrigere' meaning both to correct a mistake and to straighten something crooked.</note> When many people were being acquitted despite being accused by Severus Cassius, and the architect of Augustus's Forum was drawing out the expectation of the work for a long time, the Emperor joked: 'I wish Cassius had accused my Forum as well.' <note>Implying the work would have been finished and "discharged" as quickly as the defendants Cassius prosecuted.</note>

<margin>The cruelty of Herod.</margin>
When Vectius had plowed up the monument of his father, Augustus said: 'This is truly cultivating the memory of one's father.' <note>A pun on 'colere,' which means both to honor/revere and to till/cultivate land.</note> When he heard that among the boys under the age of two whom Herod, the King of the Jews, had ordered to be killed in Syria, Herod's own son had also been slain, he said: 'It is better to be Herod's pig than his son.' <note>original: "Melius est Herodis porcum esse quam filium." This is a famous pun on the Greek words for pig (hys) and son (hyios), and the fact that Herod, as a Jew, would not eat or slaughter a pig.</note>
¶ The same Augustus, because he knew his friend Maecenas had a style that was loose, soft, and effeminate, often showed himself to be like that in the letters he wrote to him. In contrast to the discipline of speech he usually maintained in writing, he added many jokes in a familiar letter to Maecenas: 'Farewell, honey of the nations, you who make me tremble, ivory from Etruria, laser of Arezzo, superior diamond, pearl of the Tiber, emerald of the Cilnii, jasper of the potters, beryl of Porsenna, carbuncle—may you have all this, to sum up all the soft endearments of mistresses.' <note>original: "ἵνα συντέμω πάντα μαλάγματα" (hina syntemō panta malagmata). This is a parody of Maecenas's flowery and overly-luxurious prose style.</note>
¶ He was once entertained by a certain man with a dinner that was quite meager and ordinary—for he refused almost no one who invited him. After the meal, therefore, as he was leaving this poor and unadorned display, he whispered only this to the man who was saying goodbye: 'I did not think I was so intimate with you.'
¶ When he complained about the darkness of the Tyrian purple he had ordered to be bought, and the seller said, 'Hold it higher and look up at it,' he used this wit: 'What then? So that the Roman people may say I am well dressed, am I to walk around on my sun-deck?'
¶ To his nomenclator <note>A servant whose job was to remember the names of people the master met.</note> who was complaining about his own forgetfulness and asking: 'Surely you did not send me to the forum...'

# THE SATURNALIA
## Page LXII
<meta>Mirrored page number LXII visible in left margin from preceding page.</meta>

Augustus wittily insulted Vatinius during the latter's youth. Although Vatinius was crippled by <term>gout</term><note>original: "podagra" — a painful form of arthritis often associated in antiquity with wealthy or excessive living.</note>, he wished to appear as though he had shaken off the ailment, boasting that he could walk a mile. Caesar remarked: "I am not surprised; the days have become somewhat longer." <note>A joke suggesting Vatinius walks so slowly that it takes him the entirety of a long summer day to finish a single mile.</note>

When news was brought to him of the enormous debt left by a certain Roman knight who, while he lived, had hidden the fact that he owed over twenty million <term>sesterces</term><note>original: "ducenties" — 20,000,000 sesterces, a staggering sum for a private citizen.</note>, Augustus ordered that the man's bedroom pillow be bought for him at the estate auction. When his staff expressed surprise at the request, he gave this reason: "I must have the pillow for my own sleep, upon which a man who owed so much was able to find rest."

One must not skip over the remark he made in honor of Cato. He happened to visit the house where Cato the Younger had once lived. There, a man named Strabo, seeking to flatter Caesar by speaking ill of Cato’s legendary stubbornness, mocked his character. Augustus replied: "Anyone who does not wish the current state of the republic to be changed is both a good citizen and a good man." Thus, with great seriousness, he both praised Cato <note>Cato was a staunch defender of the old Republic who committed suicide rather than submit to Julius Caesar; Augustus subtly honors his principle while also suggesting that any "good citizen" should now support the stability of the current government.</note> and took care that no one should attempt to start a revolution against himself.

<margin>Jokes against Augustus.</margin>
I am usually more amazed by the jokes that Augustus endured than by those he made himself; for his patience was greater than his legendary eloquence—especially since he bore some remarks that were quite stinging with a calm mind. The sharp wit of a certain provincial man became well known. He had entered Rome looking remarkably like Caesar, and everyone turned their heads to stare at him. Augustus ordered the man to be brought before him and, seeing the resemblance, interrogated him in this way: "Tell me, young man, was your mother ever in Rome?" The youth replied, "No," and then added, not content with a simple answer: "But my father was there often." <note>The Emperor's question implied that his own father had an affair with the boy’s mother; the boy’s retort implies that the Emperor's mother had an affair with the boy’s father.</note>

<margin>Pollio's remark to Augustus.</margin>
During the times of the <term>Triumvirates</term><note>The political alliance between Octavian (Augustus), Mark Antony, and Lepidus.</note>, when Augustus had written mocking <term>Fescennine verses</term><note>A form of ribald, aggressive, and improvised Roman poetry often used to mock public figures.</note> against him, Pollio said: "As for me, I shall keep silent. It is not easy to write against a man who can <term>proscribe</term> you." <note>original: "scribere... proscribere" — a play on words. 'Scribere' means to write; 'proscribere' means to put someone on a death list (proscription) where their property is seized and they are declared outlaws.</note>

<margin>Curtius the Knight</margin>
Curtius, a Roman knight given to excessive luxury, was at a banquet with Caesar. When he was served a very thin, meager thrush, he asked if he might "send" it somewhere. The Princeps replied, "Why not?" and Curtius immediately threw it out the window.

Augustus, without being asked, paid off the debt of a certain senator who was dear to him, amounting to four million sesterces. But in place of an expression of thanks, the senator wrote only this to him: "Nothing for me." <note>A cheeky or perhaps ungrateful response, implying that because the money went straight to the creditors, the senator himself received nothing in hand, or that he expected even more.</note>

Licinius, his freedman, used to contribute large sums of money to his patron when new public works were beginning. Following this custom, he once sent a document with a draft of one hundred thousand sesterces; however, a line had been drawn above the figure so that a portion of the space remained blank below it. Caesar, seizing the opportunity, added another hundred thousand with his own hand, carefully filling the space and mimicking the style of the letters. He thus received a double sum, while the freedman pretended not to notice. Later, when a new project began, the freedman gently threw the act back in Caesar’s face by giving him a document that said: "I contribute to you, Master, for the expense of the new work, whatever shall seem right."

<margin>The patience of Augustus as Censor.</margin>
The patience of Augustus as <term>Censor</term><note>A high magistrate responsible for maintaining the census and overseeing public morality.</note> was also marvelous and much praised. A Roman knight was being scolded by the Princeps for apparently wasting his inheritance. The man proved right there that he had actually increased it. Soon after, the Emperor objected that the knight had not obeyed the laws regarding marriage. The man replied that he had a wife and three children; then he added: "In the future, Caesar, when you inquire about honorable men, entrust the inquiry to honorable men."

He also bore not only the freedom but even the recklessness of a common soldier. In a certain villa, Augustus was spending restless nights because his sleep was frequently broken by the hooting of an owl. He ordered the owl to be caught. A soldier skilled in fowling caught it and, hoping for a massive reward, brought it to him. The commander praised him and ordered a thousand coins to be given. The soldier dared to say, "I'd rather it live," and let the bird go. Everyone marveled that the soldier left without being punished for his defiance.

<margin>The Substitute.</margin>
A veteran who was facing a trial on a set day approached Caesar in public and asked him to stand by him in court. Augustus immediately provided an advocate chosen from his own staff and recommended the litigant to him. The veteran cried out with a loud voice: "But Caesar, when you were in danger during the Battle of Actium, I did not look for a <term>substitute</term><note>original: "vicarium" — a deputy or stand-in.</note> for myself; I fought for you in person!" He then bared his body to show the scars he had received. Caesar blushed, and he came to the court to advocate for the man himself, fearing he might appear not only proud but also ungrateful.

Augustus had been delighted during dinner by the musicians belonging to Turonius Flaccus, a slave-dealer, and he had rewarded them with grain, though he was usually liberal with money for other performers. Later, when Caesar asked for them again during dinner, Turonius excused them by saying: "They are busy with the bad ones." <note>A joke suggesting the musicians were "sick" or "poorly" because they were only fed grain (like cattle) instead of being paid with money to buy proper food.</note>

## BOOK SECOND LXIII
<sig>A2</sig>

<margin>A raven greeting Augustus.</margin>
After the sublime victory at Actium, Augustus was returning home. A man met him among those offering congratulations, holding a raven which he had trained to say: "Hail, Caesar, Victorious Commander." Augustus, marveled by such a dutiful bird, purchased it for twenty thousand <term>sesterces</term><note>original: "nummū" (nummorum). A sesterce was a silver or bronze coin; 20,000 was a significant sum, roughly the annual pay of twenty soldiers.</note>. However, the trainer’s partner, who had received nothing from that generous payment, insisted to Caesar that the man had another raven as well, and he asked that the man be forced to bring it. When it was brought, it chirped the words it had learned: "Hail, Victorious Commander Antony!" Augustus, not at all angered, thought it sufficient to order the man to share the reward with his partner. When he was greeted in a similar way by a parrot, he ordered it to be bought. <margin>A Parrot and a Magpie</margin> Marvelling at the same skill in a magpie, he purchased that one too. 

This example inspired a poor shoemaker to train a raven for a similar greeting. Exhausted by the expense of the bird's food, he used to say to the bird whenever it failed to respond: "Work and expense wasted!" <note>original: "opera & impēsa periit"</note>. Eventually, the raven finally began to speak the dictated greeting. Hearing this as Augustus passed by, the Emperor replied: "I have enough such greeters at home." 

The raven, however, remembered the words it had often heard its master complaining: "Work and expense wasted!" At this, Caesar laughed and ordered the bird to be bought for a price higher than any he had paid before.

It was the habit of a certain <term>Greekling</term><note>original: "graeculus" — a somewhat diminutive term for a Greek person, often implying a clever but lower-status intellectual.</note> to offer a complimentary Greek epigram to Caesar as he descended from the Palace. After he had done this many times in vain, and Augustus saw him about to do it again, the Emperor quickly scribbled a short Greek epigram in his own hand on a piece of paper and sent it to the man as he approached. The Greek, upon reading it, began to praise it, marveling both with his voice and his expression. As he approached the Emperor’s litter, he lowered his hand into a meager pouch and pulled out a few small coins <note>original: "denarios" — silver coins</note> to give to the Prince. He added this remark: <margin>Augustus's generosity to the Greek</margin> "Not according to your fortune, Augustus; if I had more, I would give more." <note>original Greek: "μηκατατην τυχην οηνοε βασσε ἐιπλέον ἐδιδοων"</note> Followed by the laughter of everyone present, Caesar called for his treasurer and ordered one hundred thousand sesterces to be counted out for the Greek.

### On the Morals of Women. Chapter XI.

<margin>Julia, daughter of Augustus.</margin>
Let us also relate some of the witty sayings of his daughter, Julia. But if I am not thought too talkative, I wish first to say a few things about the character of this woman, so that each of you may know that what I bring forward are matters both serious and worth learning. With everyone encouraging him to continue what he had begun, he started on Julia. She was thirty-eight years old—a time of life which (if a sound mind remained) was verging toward old age. However, she abused the indulgence of both fortune and her father. Otherwise, she possessed a love of literature and great erudition—which was easily attained in that household—and furthermore, a mild kindness and a spirit not at all cruel, which won for the woman great favor. Those who knew her vices marveled at such a dual nature. 

Her father had more than once corrected her, though in a speech tempered with both indulgence and gravity, telling her to moderate her excessive finery and her conspicuous entourage. Yet, when he looked at the crowd of his grandsons and their resemblance to their father, Agrippa, he felt ashamed to doubt his daughter’s chastity. Thus, Augustus flattered himself that his daughter merely had a cheerful spirit that reached the appearance of boldness, but was free of guilt; he even dared to believe that she was like the Claudia of old. <note>A reference to Claudia Quinta, a Roman matron who proved her chastity through a miracle.</note> And so, he said among his friends: "I have two delicate daughters whom I must endure: the Republic and Julia." 

Once, Julia came before her father in a rather licentious dress and offended his silent eyes. The next day, she changed the style of her attire and embraced her father with an assumed severity. He, who had contained his grief the day before, could not contain his joy, saying: "How much more appropriate is this dress for the daughter of Augustus?" Julia did not fail to defend herself with these words: "Today I dressed for my father’s eyes; yesterday, for my husband’s."

<margin>Livia and Julia, daughter of Augustus.</margin>
This too is well known: Livia and Julia both drew the people's attention at a gladiatorial show, but with a very different entourage. While Livia was surrounded by grave and serious men, Julia was encircled by a crowd of youth, and quite a luxurious one at that. Her father sent her a note advising her to see how much difference there was between the two leading women. She elegantly wrote back: "These men, too, will grow old with me."

The same Julia had begun to have gray hairs early, which she used to have plucked in secret. The sudden arrival of her father once surprised the hairdressers. Augustus pretended not to notice the gray hairs found on their clothing, and after stretching out the time with other talk, he brought up the subject of age. He asked his daughter whether, after some years, she would rather be gray-headed or bald. When she replied that she would rather be gray, the father caught her in her lie, saying: "Why then do these women make you bald so quickly?"

The text highlights Julia's sharp tongue and her father's struggle to manage her public reputation versus her private conduct.</summary>

# OF THE SATURNALIA
## BOOK SECOND LXIII

And when she replied: "I would rather these be gray hairs," he exposed her lie: "Why then do these girls of yours make you bald so quickly?" <note>Augustus had surprised Julia while her maids were plucking her gray hairs to keep her looking young.</note>

Likewise, when a serious friend had advised Julia that she would do better if she conformed herself to the examples of her father’s frugality, she said: "He forgets that he is Caesar; I remember that I am Caesar’s daughter."

<margin>Populia’s response</margin>
When certain people who were aware of her scandalous behavior wondered how she could give birth to sons so closely resembling her husband Agrippa, since she gave the power of her body so commonly to others, she said: "I never take on a passenger unless the ship is full." <note>original: "Nunq̃. nisi naui plena tollo uectorem." A famous and crude joke; she claimed she only committed adultery when she was already certain she was pregnant by her husband.</note>
There is a similar saying by Populia, daughter of Marcus. When someone wondered why other animals never desired the male except when they wished to become pregnant, she responded: "Because they are beasts."

-> The wit of Caselius <-
### Chapter XII.

<margin>Vatinius pelted by the people; Caselius’s saying.</margin>
But to turn from women to men, and from playful jokes to more respectable ones: Caselius the jurisconsult <note>A legal expert or lawyer.</note> possessed a wonderful wit and a sense of freedom; this joke of his in particular became well known. Vatinius, having been pelted with stones by the people when he was putting on a gladiatorial show, had obtained an edict from the <term>aediles</term><note>Magistrates in charge of public buildings and festivals.</note> that no one should throw anything into the arena except fruit. It happened in those days that Caselius was consulted by someone as to whether a pine nut was a fruit. He replied: "If you are going to throw it at Vatinius, it is a fruit."

Then, to a merchant asking how he should divide a ship with a partner, he is said to have replied: "If you divide the ship, neither you nor your partner will have one."

<margin>Marcus Laelius on Galba; Orbilius the grammarian on the same; Lucius Cecilius.</margin>
Regarding Galba, who was famous for eloquence but whose physical appearance (as I said above) ruined him, a saying of Marcus Laelius was passed around: "Galba’s talent has a bad home." <note>Galba was a hunchback; Laelius is remarking that a great mind is housed in a deformed body.</note> On the same Galba, Orbilius the grammarian made a more biting jest. Orbilius had come forward as a witness against a defendant; Galba, in order to rattle him, pretended not to know his profession and asked: "What trade do you practice?" He replied: "I rub hunchbacks in the sun with oil." <note>Orbilius suggests Galba’s deformity is so great he needs specialized treatment.</note>

When Lucius Cecilius saw that Gaius Caesar gave a hundred thousand <term>sesterces</term> to others who were playing ball with him, but gave only fifty thousand to him alone, he said: "What, do I play with only one hand and not two, that I should receive less?"

<margin>Decimus Valerius</margin>
When Publius Clodius was angry and said to Decimus Valerius, who had not given him the money he sought: "What more are you going to do to me, except make me go to Dyrrachium and back?"—joking about the exile of Cicero. <note>Clodius was responsible for Cicero’s exile to Dyrrachium; Valerius implies that being harassed by Clodius is a predictable, if annoying, rite of passage.</note>

-> Concerning Laberius <-
### Chapter XIII.

<margin>Laberius</margin>
But since both Aurelius Symmachus a little while ago and I just now have made mention of Laberius, if we relate some of his and Publilius’s sayings, we will seem to have avoided the lewdness of mimes at a banquet and instead imitated that fame which they promise to stir up when they are present. Caesar "invited" Laberius, a Roman knight of harsh independence, with five hundred thousand sesterces to go out onto the stage and personally act in the mimes that he used to write. But a power is revealed not only if it invites, but even if it entreats—it compels. Hence Laberius himself testifies in these verses in his prologue that he was forced by Caesar:

> Necessity, whose side-winding path’s force
> Many have wished to escape, and few have been able,
> To where has she thrust me, nearly in my final years?
> Me, whom no ambition, no bribery ever,
> No fear, no force, no authority
> Could move from my status in my youth;
> Look how easily in my old age he shook me from my place,
> The gentle-minded speech of an excellent man,
> Delivered calmly and with flattering words.
> For indeed, since the gods themselves can deny him nothing,
> Who could allow me, a man, to deny him?
> After sixty years spent without a mark of shame,
> I, a Roman knight, have left my hearth and home...

# BOOK FIRST LXIIII

"I return as a mime: surely on this day I have lived one day longer than I ought to have lived. O Fortune, immoderate in good as in evil, if it was your pleasure to break the flowering peak of my reputation with the honors of literature, why did you not bend me when I was still flexible, when my limbs were green and strong, so that I might satisfy the people and such a great man <note>original: "tali cum poteram uiro"; Laberius refers to Julius Caesar, who forced him, a high-ranking Roman knight, to perform on stage—a deep social humiliation.</note>? Why do you cast me down now? What do I bring to the stage? Beauty of form, or dignity of body? The strength of my mind, or the sound of a pleasing voice? As the creeping ivy kills the strength of trees, so old age destroys me in the embrace of years. Like a tomb, I retain nothing but a name."

¶ During the performance itself, he took revenge as often as he could. Dressed in the costume of a slave—a Syrian who, looking as if he had been whipped, rushed forward—he cried out: "Moreover, citizens, we have lost our liberty!" And a little later he added: "He whom many fear must of necessity fear many." At this saying, the entire population turned their eyes and faces toward Caesar alone, noting that his unrestrained power had been pelted by this sharp wit.

<margin>Publius Syrus</margin>
Because of this, Caesar turned his favor toward Publius. This Publius was a Syrian by nationality; when he was brought as a boy to his master’s patron, he earned his favor no less by his wit and talent than by his beauty. For by chance, when his master saw a slave suffering from dropsy <note>A condition involving painful swelling from excess fluid.</note> lying in the courtyard and asked what he was doing in the sun, the boy replied: "He is warming the water." <note>A pun on the fluid build-up in the sick man's body.</note> Later, when a joking question arose over dinner as to what constituted "troublesome leisure," and various people gave different opinions, he said it was "the feet of a man with gout." Because of these and other displays, he was manumitted <note>Formally granted his freedom from slavery.</note> and educated with great care. When he began composing mimes and acting in the towns of Italy to great acclaim, he was brought to Rome for Caesar's games. He challenged all the playwrights who had staged their works at that time to compete with him, one by one, on a given subject. When no one refused, he surpassed them all, including Laberius. Because of this, Caesar, smiling, pronounced his judgment in this way: "Though I favored you, Laberius, you have been conquered by a Syrian." He immediately gave the palm of victory to Publius, and to Laberius he gave a gold ring <note>A symbol of the restoration of his status as a Roman Knight, which he had technically lost by performing on stage.</note> along with five hundred thousand sesterces. Then Publius said to the retreating Laberius: "You who competed as a writer, now support him as a spectator." But Laberius, in the very next competition, inserted these verses into a new mime:

> All cannot be first at all times.
> When you reach the highest step of fame, you will stand
> with difficulty; and you will fall no less quickly than you descended.
> I have fallen; he who follows will fall; praise belongs to the public.

<margin>The elegant maxims of Publius</margin>
The maxims of Publius are considered elegant and most suitable for common use. Of these, I remember these few, each limited to a single verse:

He who gives to a worthy person receives a benefit in the giving.
You should endure, not blame, that which cannot be changed.
He who is allowed more than is fair, wants more than is allowed.
An eloquent companion on the road is as good as a carriage.
Frugality is a misery practiced for the sake of a good reputation.
An heir's weeping is laughter behind a mask.
Patience, when injured too often, becomes fury.
He wickedly accuses Neptune who suffers shipwreck a second time. <note>Neptune was the Roman god of the sea.</note>
Through too much arguing, the truth is lost.

LXIII SATURNALIA

And when she responded, "I would rather be a white-haired father," <note>original: "Ego pater cana esse malo"; Julia is joking with her father, Augustus, who had noticed her attendants plucking gray hairs from her head. She suggests she would rather have a father with gray hair (symbolizing wisdom or simply his natural aging) than be a gray-haired woman herself.</note> he caught her in a lie, saying: "Why, then, do those attendants of yours make you bald so quickly?" 

Likewise, when she heard a serious friend suggesting she would do better if she composed herself according to the examples of her father’s frugality, she said: "He forgets that he is Caesar; I remember that I am Caesar’s daughter."

<margin>Populia's response</margin>
When those aware of her scandals wondered how she could produce children so similar to her husband Agrippa, when she granted the power of her body so commonly to others, she said: "For I never take on a passenger unless the ship is full." <note>A famous, if scandalous, maritime metaphor: Julia (or here, Populia) claims she only indulges in affairs when she is already pregnant, ensuring the paternity of her children remains legally "secure."</note>

There is a similar saying by Populia, daughter of Marcus. When someone wondered why other animals never desired the male unless they wished to become pregnant, she responded: "Because they are animals."

->The Wit of Cascellius. Chapter XII.<-

<margin>Vatinius stoned by the people; Cascellius's saying.</margin>
But to return from women to men, and from playful jokes to more honorable ones: Cascellius, <note>A famous Roman jurist known for his sharp tongue and refusal to bow to the dictators of his age.</note> a legal expert, possessed a wonderful wit and freedom of speech; however, he became especially known for his jokes. When Vatinius was being stoned by the people while he was putting on a gladiatorial show, he had obtained an edict from the aediles <note>city officials</note> that no one should throw anything into the arena except fruit. By chance, during those days, Cascellius was consulted by someone as to whether a pine cone was a fruit. He responded: "If you are going to throw it at Vatinius, it is a fruit."

Then, to a merchant asking how he should divide a ship with his partner, he is said to have responded: "If you divide the ship, neither you nor your partner will have one."

<margin>Marcus Lelius against Galba; Orbilius the grammarian against the same. Lucius Cecilius.</margin>
Regarding Galba, who was famous for his eloquence but whose physical appearance (as I said above) ruined his effect, a saying of Marcus Lelius was circulated: "Galba’s genius has a bad house." <note>original: "ingenium Galbae male habitat"; Galba was famously hunchbacked, and Lelius is joking that his brilliant mind is forced to live in a broken body.</note> Against the same Galba, Orbilius the grammarian mocked him even more bitterly. Orbilius had come forward as a witness against a defendant; Galba, in order to confuse him, pretended not to know his profession and asked: "What trade do you practice?" He responded: "I am accustomed to rubbing hunches in the sun." <note>A cruel joke playing on Galba’s deformity; Orbilius implies that his "job" is dealing with people like Galba.</note>

When Lucius Cecilius saw that Gaius Caesar <note>Julius Caesar</note> gave one hundred thousand sesterces to the others who were playing ball with him, but only fifty thousand to him alone, he said: "What, do I play with only one hand and not two, that I should have less?"

<margin>Decimus Valerius</margin>
When Publius Clodius, in a rage, said to Decimus Valerius—who had not given him the money he asked for—"What more can you do to me?" Valerius replied: "Nothing, except that I might go to Durrachium and come back," <note>A biting reference to Cicero’s exile in Dyrrachium; Valerius is mocking Clodius for his role in Cicero's banishment.</note> playing on the exile of Cicero.

->Regarding Laberius. Chapter XIII.<-

<margin>Laberius</margin>
But because both Aurelius Symmachus a little while ago and I just now have made mention of Laberius, if we relate some of his sayings and those of Publius, we shall seem to have avoided the vulgarity of mimes at our banquet, while still imitating the festive spirit they promise to excite. Caesar "invited" Laberius—a Roman knight of harsh independence—with five hundred thousand sesterces to go out onto the stage and perform the very mimes he was writing. But power doesn't just invite; if it begs, it compels. Hence Laberius testifies in his prologue that he was forced by Caesar with these words:

> Necessity, whose side-long course and force
> Many have wished to flee, but few have been able,
> To what depths have you thrust me, now almost at the end of my years?
> I, whom no ambition, no bribery ever,
> No fear, no force, no authority
> Could move from my status in my youth;
> Behold, in my old age, how easily I am shaken from my place
> By the gentle-minded speech of an excellent man,
> Delivered calmly and with flattering words.
> For indeed, since the gods themselves can deny him nothing,
> Who among men could permit me to deny him?
> After sixty years passed without a stain on my name,
> I, a Roman knight, have left my hearth and home...

Non-everyone can be first at every time.
When you have reached the highest step of fame: you will stand
With difficulty; and you will fall no less quickly than you descend.
I have fallen; he who follows will fall; praise belongs to the public.

<margin>The charming maxims of Publius</margin>
The maxims of Publius are considered charming and most suited for common use. From these, I recall those following, each limited to a single verse.

He who gives a benefit to the worthy receives one in return.
Bear, do not blame, what cannot be changed.
He who is allowed more than is right, wants more than is allowed.
A companionable talker on a journey is as good as a carriage.
Frugality is misery with a good reputation.
The weeping of an heir is laughter behind a mask.
Patience, too often provoked, becomes fury.
He who suffers shipwreck twice wrongly accuses Neptune. <note>Neptune was the Roman god of the sea.</note>
Truth is lost in too much arguing.

->The Wit of Caecilius. Chapter 12.<-

->Concerning Laberius. Chapter 13.<-

<margin>Laberius</margin>
But since both Aurelius Symmachus a little while ago and I just now have made mention of Laberius, if we relate some of his and Publius's sayings, we shall seem to have avoided the coarseness of the mimes even while bringing them to our banquet, and to imitate that festive spirit which they promise to stir up when they are present. Laberius, a Roman knight of sharp-tongued liberty, was invited by Caesar with five hundred thousand sesterces to come out onto the stage and perform in person the mimes he used to write. But power does not only invite, it compels, even when it pleads; hence Laberius himself testifies in these words in his prologue that he was forced by Caesar:

> Many have wished to escape: few have been able;

> Who could allow a mere man like me to say no?
> I, having passed twice thirty years without a stain,
> A Roman knight, having left my household hearth...

### On Pylades the actor. Chapter XIV.

<margin>Pylades the actor</margin>
But since I have once entered upon the subject of the stage, we must not omit the actor Pylades, who was famous in his profession during the time of Augustus, and who trained his pupil Hylas to such a degree of skill that they became rivals. The people were then divided in their support for each of them. <margin>Hylas the actor</margin> When Hylas was dancing a certain song, the conclusion of which was: **"The great Agamemnon"** <note>original Greek: "Τον μέγαν ἀγαμέμνονα"</note>, Hylas acted out the part as if he were measuring someone tall and physically massive. Pylades could not endure this, and shouted from the theater seats: **"You are making him tall, not great!"** <note>original Greek: "συμ’ακρον ὄν με ταποιεῖσ’" — Pylades meant that greatness is a quality of character and command, not physical height.</note> Then the people forced Pylades to dance the same song himself. When he came to the place he had criticized, he represented Agamemnon as a man deep in thought, judging that nothing more becomes a great leader than to think on behalf of all. Later, Hylas was dancing the role of Oedipus, and Pylades corrected the dancer's over-confidence with the word **"Look together"** <note>original Greek: "συβλέπειν" — likely a correction regarding the blind Oedipus's focus or the character's lack of awareness.</note>. When he appeared as Hercules Furens <note>Hercules Driven Mad</note>, and it seemed to some that he was not maintaining the dignified bearing suitable for an actor, he took off his mask and rebuked the mockers, saying: **"I am dancing the part of a mad fool!"** <note>original Greek: "μωρὸν μαινόμενον ὀρχοῦμαι"</note>. In this play, he even shot arrows into the audience. When he performed the same role by order of Augustus in the dining room, he both aimed his bow and released the shafts. Nor was Caesar indignant that he was treated by Pylades in the same manner as the Roman people had been. Because it was said that Pylades had changed the style of that crude dancing which flourished among our ancestors and introduced a more graceful novelty, Augustus asked him what he had contributed to the art of dancing; he replied: **"The sound of Lydian pipes."** <note>original Greek: "λυδῶν συριγγῶν"</note>. When Pylades had incurred the indignation of Augustus because of a riot among the people caused by the rivalry between himself and Hylas, he replied: **"King, let them busy themselves with us."** <note>original Greek: "βασιλεῦ ἔασον αὐτοὺς περὶ ἡμᾶς ἀπολεῖσθαι καὶ εὐκαρίσεισ" — Pylades’s point was that as long as the public was obsessed with theater rivalries, they would not be busy plotting against the Emperor.</note> With these things said and cheerfulness aroused, while the flowering memory and the pleasantness of genius in Avienus were being praised, the servant brought in the second course.

<margin>Desserts</margin>
Then Flavianus said: "Many, I believe, disagree with Varro on this point, who, in that most elegant Menippean satire entitled *You Know Not What the Evening Brings*, removed cakes from the second course. But I ask you, Caecina, to speak the very words of Varro, if they have stuck with you by the benefit of a more tenacious memory." And Albinus said: "The passage of Varro which you command me to recall is in these words: 'Desserts <note>original: "Bellaria"</note> are those things which are most honeyed, but are not honeyed.' For a partnership with sweet things is unfaithful to digestion. **Desserts**, however, signify every kind of second course. For what the Greeks called **pastries** <note>original Greek: "πέμματα"</note> or **sweetmeats** <note>original Greek: "τράγηματα"</note>, our ancestors called *bellaria*. In older comedies, one may also find wines that are sweeter called by this name: 'the desserts of Bacchus' <note>original: "Liberi bellaria"</note>."

### On Wine. Chapter XV.

<margin>Wine is the fuel and incentive of genius and virtue.</margin>
And Evangelus said: "Come, before we must rise, let us indulge in wine, which we shall do by the authority of the Platonic decree; for he judged that it is a kind of fuel and an incentive for genius and virtue if the mind and body of a man glow with wine." Then Eustathius said: "What are you doing, Evangelus? Do you think Plato advised that wine should be drained everywhere, and did not rather approve of a more pleasant and liberal invitation among small cups, which would be done under certain sober 'arbiters' and masters of the banquet? And this is what he determines is not useless to men in the first and second books of the *Laws*. For he thought that minds are refreshed and integrated by moderate and honorable drinking sessions to renew the duties of sobriety; once they are gradually made more cheerful, they become more fit to take up their intentions again. And at the same time, if any errors of affection and desire were deeply present in them, which a reverent shame would otherwise hide, all these are detected without grave danger through the liberty given by wine, and they become more opportune for correction and healing. And Plato also says there: 'Such exercises against the violence of wine are not to be fled from,' nor did he ever think anyone truly continent or temperate enough whose life was not tested amidst the very dangers of error and in the midst of the allurements of pleasure."

### BOOK SECOND

...should be explored. For if one is completely ignorant of the pleasures and graces of banquets and is entirely inexperienced in them, and if by chance, desire, or necessity he is led to participate in such delights, he is quickly charmed and captured, and his mind and spirit lose their footing. Therefore, we must engage. Just as if in a battle line, we must decide at close quarters against these pleasurable things and this license of wine, so that we are not safe from them merely through flight or absence, but rather through the vigor of the mind and a constant presence. Through moderate use, we may protect temperance and self-control. At the same time, as the soul is warmed and refreshed, we may wash away any cold sadness or sluggish shame within it. But because we have mentioned pleasures, Aristotle teaches which pleasures are to be avoided. <margin>Five human senses. Two pleasures.</margin> For there are five human senses, which the Greeks call *aistheseis* <note>original: αἰσθήσεις</note>, through which pleasure is sought for the mind or the body: touch, taste, smell, sight, and hearing. Of all these, the pleasure that is taken immoderately is shameful and wicked. Indeed, that which is excessive in taste and touch—this twin pleasure, as wise men have judged—is the most foul of all. Those who surrender themselves to these two pleasures are called by the Greeks with names of the gravest vice: either *akrateis* <note>original: ἀκρατεῖς — meaning "powerless" over oneself</note> or *akolastoi* <note>original: ἀκολάστους — meaning "undisciplined" or "incorrigible"</note>. We call them either incontinent or intemperate. These two pleasures, taste and touch—that is, of food and of lust—are the only ones we see humans have in common with beasts. Therefore, whoever is occupied by these beastly pleasures is held in the same category as cattle and wild animals. The others, proceeding from the three remaining senses, are unique to humans. I will bring forward the words of the philosopher Aristotle on this matter, so that it may be publicly known what such a famous and illustrious man thinks of these infamous pleasures:

> Why is it that those who exceed in the pleasures of touch or taste, or both, are called incontinent? For those concerned with sexual matters are licentious, as are those concerned with the enjoyment of food; of those pleasures concerning food, some come from the <unclear>tongue</unclear> and some from the pouring into the throat, and we share these in common with the other animals. Because these are common, it is considered shameful <unclear>...</unclear> immediately being called a loser, incontinent, and licentious because of being defeated by the pleasures of the hands [touch]. Of the five senses <unclear>that exist, the</unclear> others are unique [to humans], and one takes pleasure from only two [the lower senses], or at least does not experience the others except by accident.

Who, then, possessing any sense of human shame, would take pride in those two pleasures of mating and eating, which a human shares in common with a pig and a donkey? Socrates indeed used to say that many men wish to live so that they might eat and drink, but he himself ate and drank so that he might live. Hippocrates, a man of divine knowledge, thought of sexual intercourse in this way: that it was a part of a most terrible disease, which our people call the "falling sickness" <note>original: *comitialis* — a Roman term for epilepsy, so named because a seizure was considered a bad omen that would stop a public assembly or *comitia*</note>. <margin>What is intercourse?</margin> For his own words are recorded as follows: sexual intercourse is a minor epilepsy <note>original: τὴν συνουσίαν εἶναι μικρὰν ἐπιληψίαν</note>.

V.I
SATURNALIA

# THE SATURNALIA OF MACROBIUS AURELIUS THEODOSIUS, MAN OF CONSULAR RANK AND ILLUSTRIOUS. Book III.
## ¶ On the Rite of Sacrifices. Chapter I.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration on the left side of the page depicting a ritual or sacrificial banquet. A crowned king sits at the center of a table with several other figures. To the left, an attendant performs a ritual act over a basin. To the right of this woodcut is a large historiated initial 'V' containing a cherub or putto, which begins the first word of the text.</image-desc>

When Aeneas realized he was defiled by much slaughter, he said:
> "Father, take the sacred objects in your hand and our ancestral household gods; for me, having come from such great war and recent slaughter, it is a crime to touch them until I have washed myself in a running stream."
<note>original: "Tu genitor cape sacra manu patriosque penates / Me bello e tanto degressum & caede recenti / Attractare nefas: donec me flumine vivo / Abluero." — Virgil, Aeneid II.717-720. Aeneas recognizes that blood-guilt from battle prevents him from handling holy items until he undergoes ritual purification.</note>

¶ After the burial of his nurse Caieta, he was sailed to that specific part of the coast where the pleasant Tiber river breaks forth into the sea. This was so that, at the very threshold of Italy, he might be washed by the river water <margin>Washing in the sacrifices of the gods above.</margin> and thus, in the purest state possible, he might invoke Jupiter and the Phrygian Mother <note>The "Phrygian Mother" refers to Cybele, a goddess of central importance to the Trojans.</note>. Likewise, when he is about to visit Evander and sails through the Tiber, he finds him performing sacrifices to Hercules; thus purified by the river, he could participate in the rites of hospitality. Even Juno herself complains here, not so much that Aeneas had reached Italy against her will, but that he had gained the desired channel of the Tiber; for she knew that, having been purified by this river, he could rightly perform sacrifices even to her. Indeed, she did not even want him to be able to offer her supplications. Now (since we have shown the purification pertaining to the sacrifices of the gods above in the observations of Virgil), let us see <margin>Sprinkling in the sacrifices of the gods below.</margin> whether the same poet maintained the proper custom regarding the worship of the gods of the underworld. It is established that one about to perform sacrifices to the gods above is purified by the washing of the body (*ablutio*); however, when a sacrifice is to be made to those below, it is considered sufficient if only a sprinkling (*aspersio*) occurs. Regarding the sacrifices for those above, Aeneas says: "until I have washed myself in a running stream." But when Dido institutes sacrifices to the underworld gods, she says:
> "Dear nurse Anna, bring my sister here. Tell her to hasten to sprinkle her body with river water."
<note>original: "Annam chara mihi nutrix huc siste sororem. / Dic corpus properet fluviali spargere lympha." — Virgil, Aeneid IV.634-635.</note>

And elsewhere:
> "She had also sprinkled the feigned waters of the fountain of Avernus."
<note>original: "Sparserat & latices simulatos fontis averni." — Virgil, Aeneid IV.512. Avernus was a lake believed to be the entrance to the underworld.</note>

¶ Likewise, when he reports that Misenus is committed to burial, the same poet says: "Three times he went around his companions with pure water, sprinkling them with a light dew." And even when he depicts Aeneas about to consecrate the branch to Proserpina <note>The Golden Bough offered to the Queen of the Underworld.</note> among the shades, he adds: "Aeneas seizes the entrance, and his body with fresh ¶ water he sprinkles." The precision of words is so familiar to this poet that such careful observation in Virgil is expected; yet he uses no words more properly than those for sacred or sacrificial acts. First, I will not omit a point where many are mistaken: "And he casts forth (*porricit*) the entrails into the salt waves." Some mistakenly read "throws away" (*proiicit*), thinking Virgil meant the entrails should be discarded because he added "into the waves," but that is not so. For according to the discipline of the soothsayers (*haruspices*) and the commands of the priests (*pontifices*), this is the formal word for those sacrificing. As Veranius, in the first book of his commentary on Fabius Pictor, discusses the meaning of this word: "Let them cast forth (*porriciunto*) the entrails to the gods, whether upon the altars, the hearth, or wherever the entrails ought to be given." Therefore, *porricere* (to offer or present), not *proiicere* (to throw away), is the proper word for <margin>To cast forth (*Porricere*)</margin> sacrifice. And because Veranius said "on the altar or hearth or wherever they ought to be given," now the sea must be taken in place of the altar and hearth, since the sacrifice is dedicated to the gods of the sea. For Virgil says:
> "Gods who have command over the sea, whose waters I run upon. For you I shall joyfully place a white bull on this shore before the altars, bound by my vow; and the entrails into the salt waves I shall cast forth (*porriciam*), and pour liquid wine."
<note>original: "Dii quibus imperium est pelagi... extaque salsos / Porriciam in fluctus: & vina liquentia fundam." — Virgil, Aeneid V.235-238.</note>

<summary>This page initiates a deep dive into Roman religious rituals, specifically focusing on Virgil's technical accuracy regarding purification. It distinguishes between the full washing (ablutio) required for celestial gods and the sprinkling (aspersio) used for underworld deities, while also clarifying the specific sacrificial verb "porricere."</summary>

From these examples, he teaches that the entrails <note>original: "exta." The internal organs of a sacrificed animal, used for divination.</note> could be properly "offered" to the sea, rather than merely "thrown" into it. <note>original: "porrici" vs "proiici." The former is a technical religious term for offering to the gods; the latter is a common term for tossing something away.</note> "I shall stand before the altars, bound by my vow." <note>original: "voti reus."</note> This expression is specific to sacred rites: one is called *reus* <note>The "defendant" or "debtor."</note> when, having undertaken a vow, he binds himself to the divine powers; however, he is called *damnatus* <note>The "condemned" or "one who has lost his case."</note> when he has already fulfilled his promised vows. But there is no need for me to provide more on this, since that most learned man, Eustachius, has just now discussed this part more fully.

## On the properties of words. Chapter II.

<margin>
To touch
altars
Altar
Handle
</margin>

And one may often find the profound knowledge of this poet in a single word, which the common people might think was spoken by chance. For we read in many places that a prayer alone cannot "propitiate" <note>original: "litare." To offer a sacrifice that is acceptable to the gods.</note> unless the one who prays to the gods also takes hold of the altar with his hands. Hence Varro, in the fifth book of *Divine Matters*, says that altars were first called *ansae* <note>original: "ansa" means a handle or a loop.</note> because it was necessary for them to be held by those performing the sacrifice. For who could doubt that vessels are usually held by handles? Therefore, by a change of letters, they began to be called *aras* (altars); just as those previously called "Valesii" and "Fusii" are now called "Valerii" and "Furii." The poet followed all this in that verse: "Almighty [Jupiter] heard him as he spoke such words and held the altar." <note>original: "Talibus orante dictis: arasque tenentem / Audiit omnipotens." Virgil, Aeneid IV.219-220.</note> Don't you believe it was added that he was heard not just because he was praying, but because he was also holding the altar? Likewise when he says: "With such words he was praying, and I was holding the altars." Also: "I touch the altars, and I call to witness the fires in the midst and the divine powers." This signifies the same force of the name through the act of grasping.

<margin>
Vitula
the goddess

The Flight of
the People.

Annals
</margin>

The same poet—as profound in knowledge as he is pleasant in genius—interpreted several ancient words which he knew pertained to the proper conduct of sacred rites in such a way that, even with a change in the sound of the word, the full meaning remained. For in the first book of the pontiffs, according to Pictor, this word is used: *vitulari*. Regarding the meaning of this word, Titius reported: "To *vitulari* is to rejoice with the voice." Varro also reports in the fifteenth book of *Divine Matters* that the pontiff is accustomed to *vitulari* in certain sacred rites, which the Greeks call "singing a paean." <note>original: "παιανίζειν" (paianizein). To sing a hymn of praise or victory.</note> How many words of interpretation did the learned elegance of Maro <note>Virgil's family name.</note> express in so few words: "And singing the joyful choir-paean." <note>original: "Laetumque choropaena canentes." Virgil, Aeneid VI.657.</note> For if *vitulari* is to rejoice with the voice (which is "to sing a paean"), has not the perfect explanation of the word been preserved in the phrase "singing the joyful paean"? And to dwell longer on this term: Hylas, in the book he composed concerning the gods, says that a goddess who presides over joy is called *Vitula*. Piso says that Victory is named *Vitula*. He offers this proof for the matter: that on the day after the Nones of July, after a successful action—whereas on the previous day the people were turned to flight by the Tuscans (wherefore it is called the *Populifugia* or "Flight of the People")—after the subsequent victory, a *vitulatio* <note>A ritual of thanksgiving/rejoicing.</note> is performed with specific sacrifices. Some think her name refers to the fact that she is "capable of sustaining life" <note>original: "potens sit vitae tolerandae." A folk etymology linking 'vitula' to 'vita' (life) and 'tolerare' (to endure).</note>; therefore, sacrifices are said to be made to this goddess for the crops, because human life is sustained by crops. From this we notice what Virgil says: "When I perform a *vitula* <note>Usually translated as "heifer," but the author argues it refers to the rite itself.</note> for the crops, you yourself come." He said *vitula* in place of *vitulatio*, which we expressed above as being the name of a sacrifice made on account of joy. Let us remember, however, that it should be read in the ablative case: "When I perform [the rite] with a heifer (*vitula*) for the crops"—that is, when I perform the divine service not with a sheep, nor with a goat, but with a heifer. It is as if he said: "when I have sacrificed a heifer for the crops," which is: "when I have made the heifer a divine matter." He shows Aeneas as a Pontiff even by the name given to the recording of his labors; for power is granted to the Pontiffs to collect the memory of deeds done into a tablet, and they call these "Annals" <note>original: "Annales Maximi." The official records kept by the High Priests of Rome.</note> because they were made by the *Pontifices Maximi*. Hence, in the character of Aeneas, he says: "And there is leisure to hear the annals of our labors." <note>Virgil, Aeneid I.373.</note> And because among the decrees of the pontiffs this is most sought after—what is sacred, what is holy, what is religious—we must ask whether Virgil used these according to their definition, and whether he preserved the property of each term in his usual manner.

## On the Sacred, Holy, Religious, and Profane. Chapter III.

<margin>
That which
is made
Sacred
</margin>

Something is "Sacred" (*sacrum*), as Trebatius reports in the first book of *On Religions*, which has been consecrated and belongs to the gods. The poet, mindful of this definition, almost always added an admonition of the gods when he named something "sacred." "I was bringing sacred offerings to my mother Dione and the gods." Likewise: "The sacred rites of Stygian Jove which I have prepared, having begun them duly." Likewise: "For you, even for you, greatest Juno, he slaughters..."

<sig>I ii</sig>

--- Page 168 ---
<meta>This page continues the scholarly dialogue concerning Virgil’s mastery of religious law, specifically focusing on the precise definitions of "profane," "holy," "religious," and "shrine," as interpreted by authorities like Trebatius, Varro, and Servius Sulpicius.</meta>

->SATURNALIA<-

<margin>What is "profane."</margin>
...bringing the sacred offerings. Nearly everyone agrees that the **profane** <note>original: "profanum"</note> is that which is outside the temple's jurisdiction, as if it were "far from the shrine" <note>original: "porro a fano"</note> and separated from religion. An example of this meaning followed when the poet spoke of both the grove and the sacred inner sanctum of the underworld: "Be gone, oh be gone, you **profane** ones," cries the prophetess, "and withdraw from the entire grove." To this is added what **Trebatius** says: that something is properly called "profane" when it has been converted from a religious or sacred status into the use and ownership of men. The poet observed this most aptly when he wrote: "Faunus, I pray, have mercy," he said, "and you, best Earth, hold fast the steel; if I have always tended your honors, which the followers of Aeneas have made **profane** through war." For he had said earlier: "But the Trojans had removed the sacred trunk without distinction." By this, he shows that what is properly "profaned" is that which, once sacred, has been made common and adapted for human actions.

<margin>What is "holy."</margin>
¶ Something is **holy** <note>original: "sanctum"</note> as the same **Trebatius** reports in the tenth book of his *Religions*: sometimes it is the same as "sacred," and the same as "religious"; sometimes it is something else—that is, it is neither sacred nor religious. Pertaining to this second type is the line: "A **holy** soul, and ignorant of that fault, I shall descend to you." For his soul was not held by the sacred or the religious; he wished to show it was "holy," which is to say "incorrupt." Similarly in that passage: "And you, oh **most holy** wife, happy in your death," in which he embraced the honor of the chastity of an incorrupt wife. From this also come "**holy laws**," which ought not to be "corrupted" by the threat of a penalty <note>original: "sanctione." The Latin "sanctum" is etymologically linked to "sancire," to establish by penalty.</note>. However, as for the first definition of "holy"—that is, not as something different from "sacred" or "religious"—consider this: "Behold, a light **peak** was seen to pour forth light from the top of Iulus’s head." And a little later: "We, trembling in fear, shook out the flaming hair and extinguished the **holy** fires with water from the springs." For here we should take "holy" as if it were "sacred," because they occurred by divine will. Likewise, "And you, oh **most holy** prophetess, foreknower of the future," he calls her nothing else but "sacred," whom he saw as both a prophetess and one full of the god, and a priestess.

<margin>What is "religious." Religion. Ceremony.</margin>
¶ It remains for us to share with **Virgil** what is **religious** <note>original: "religiosum"</note>. **Servius Sulpicius** handed down that "religion" was so named because, on account of its holiness, it is removed and set apart from us, as if named from "leaving behind" <note>original: "relinquendo"</note>; just as "ceremony" <note>original: "cerimonia"</note> comes from "lacking" <note>original: "carendo." An ancient etymological theory suggesting ceremony involves abstaining from common things.</note>. Virgil, observing this, says: "There is a vast, cold grove near the river of Caere, widely **sacred** by the religion of the fathers." And he added this to express the specific nature of religion: "On all sides hollow hills enclosed it, and a forest of dark fir rings it." This circumstance certainly made the grove secret and separated from the common use of the people. And to show it was a "left behind" place, not only by the difficulty of approach, he added its holiness: "The story goes that the ancient Pelasgians consecrated the fields and the herd to the god Silvanus." According to **Pompeius Festus**: "Religious people are those who discern what must be done and what must be avoided."

<margin>To draw off water</margin>
Hence **Maro** <note>Virgil's cognomen.</note> says: "No **religion** has forbidden the drawing off <note>original: "deducere"</note> of streams." When he says "to draw off," it is nothing other than "to clean." For on feast days it is permitted to clean out old, fouled streams, but it is not permitted to dig new ones. In passing, this must also be noted: what he himself threw out as if in passing under the meaning of a single word. For it is cautioned in **pontifical law** that since sheep are usually washed for two reasons—either to cure scabies or to clean the wool—on feast days it is not permitted to wash sheep for the sake of cleaning the wool, but it is permitted if the scabies must be washed away for healing. Therefore, he numbered this also among the permitted things: "And to plunge the bleating flock in the **health-giving** river." If he had stopped there, he would have confused the permitted and the forbidden; but by adding "health-giving," he expressed the cause for the permitted washing.

---

### What a shrine is. Chapter IV.

<margin>What a "shrine" is.</margin>
<note>Decorative initial N within a square frame featuring floral motifs.</note> It is a matter of **pontifical observation** to also use the names of sacred places with appropriate precision. Therefore, let us ask what the priests properly call a **shrine** <note>original: "delubrum"</note>, and how Virgil used this name. **Varro**, in the eighth book of *Divine Matters*, says that some think a shrine is a place where, besides the temple itself, an area is taken up for the sake of the god, such as the temple of Jupiter the Stayer in the Flaminian Circus; others think it is the place in which the likeness of a god has been dedicated. And he added: just as the place in which they fixed a candle was called a *candelabrum*, so the place in which they placed a god was named a *delubrum*. From these things prescribed by Varro, we can understand that he preferred the last definition, which he placed last according to his custom: that from the dedication of a god...

It clarifies how these words distinguish between items for human use, incorruptible things, and items set apart by divine decree.</summary>
<keywords>profane, holy, religious, shrine, Trebatius, Virgil, Saturnalia, Macrobius, Pompeius Festus, Varro, pontifical law, etymology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the scholarly dialogue concerning Virgil’s mastery of religious law, moving from the definitions of "profane" and "holy" to a deeper investigation into the word "shrine" (delubrum), the true identity of the Roman household gods (the Penates), and the specific categories of animal sacrifice.</meta>

[PAGE LXVII]

->BOOK THREE<-

...Cato believed that a **shrine** <note>original: "delubrum"</note> took its name from the **statue** <note>original: "simulacrum"</note> placed within it. Virgil, however, carefully followed both explanations. To begin with the latter: when he was about to name a shrine, he observed the rule of either inserting the proper names of the gods or those things that are appropriate to the gods. For instance: *But the twin snakes escape with a glide to the highest **shrines***. And so that he might soon name the statue, he added: *and they seek the heights of fierce Minerva, hiding under the goddess's feet and beneath the circle of her shield.* Likewise: *We miserable ones, for whom that day is our last, deck the **shrines** of the gods.* But that other opinion concerning the **open space** <note>original: "area"</note> which **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar often cited for his expertise on antiquities and religion.</note> had mentioned earlier, he did not abandon: *First they approach the **shrines** and seek peace through the altars.* And soon after: *Or before the faces of the gods she paces toward the rich altars.* For what else is "pacing" <note>original: "spatiari"</note> than walking about in the **space** <note>original: "spatio"</note> of a wide path? By adding "before the altars," he shows that the open space was taken up for the sake of the gods. Thus, in his usual manner, as if doing something else, he fulfills these hidden meanings.

## What are the Penates. Chapter V.

<margin>The gods called Penates.</margin>
Regarding the specific gods of the Romans—that is, the **Penates** <note>The household gods of the Roman state and individual families, believed to protect the domestic hearth and the food supply.</note>—a not unskillful subtlety has been sprinkled throughout this work. **Nigidius** <note>Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero known for his works on theology and the occult.</note> in the nineteenth book of his *On the Gods* asks whether the Penates are the Trojan gods **Apollo** and **Neptune**, who are said to have built the walls of Troy, and whether **Aeneas** brought them into Italy. **Cornelius Labeo** also estimates the same in his book on the Penates. **Maro** <note>Publius Vergilius Maro, i.e., Virgil.</note> follows this opinion when he says: *Thus speaking, he slaughtered the earned honors at the altars. A bull for Neptune; a bull for you, beautiful Apollo.* Varro, in his productive work *Human Antiquities*, reports that **Dardanus** brought the Penates from **Samothrace** <note>An island in the northern Aegean, famous in antiquity for its Mystery cult.</note> into Phrygia, and Aeneas carried them from Phrygia into Italy. Who the Penates actually are, Varro does not explicitly state in that mentioned book. But those who more diligently dig for the truth have said that the Penates are those through whom we **breathe** <note>Etymological wordplay: "penates" linked to "penitus" (deeply/within) and "penus" (the inner pantry/breath of life).</note> deep within, through whom we have a body, and through whom we possess the reason of our minds. They argue that **Jupiter** is the middle ether, **Juno** is the lower air with the earth, and **Minerva** is the highest peak of the ether. They use this argument: that **Tarquin**, the son of Demaratus of Corinth, having been mystically initiated into the Samothracian religions, joined these three deities in one
<margin>The Great Gods</margin>
temple and under the same roof. **Cassius Hemina** says that the gods of Samothrace—who are the same as the Roman Penates—are properly called **the Great Gods** <note>original: "θεοὺς μεγάλους" (theous megalous)</note>. Our poet, knowing these things, says: *With his companions and his son, the Penates and the Great Gods,* which expresses "the Great Gods." But all these names confirm his own opinion on this whole matter while maintaining the teaching on the aforementioned deities. For when he says: *First adore the power of **Great Juno***, he names her **The Great One** <note>original: "τὴν μεγάλην" (tēn megalēn)</note>. When he says: *May Bacchus, giver of joy, and **Good Juno** be present*, he names her **The Kind One** <note>original: "τὴν χρηστήν" (tēn chrēstēn)</note>. He also called her **The Powerful One** <note>original: "τὴν δυνατήν" (tēn dynatēn)</note> by the name **Powerful Lady**. It is also clear that **Vesta** is either numbered among the Penates or is certainly their companion, so much so that consuls, praetors, or dictators, when they enter office at **Lavinium** <note>A city near Rome where the state Penates were kept; it was the legendary first settlement of Aeneas in Italy.</note>, perform a sacred rite to the Penates and Vesta together. Virgil also, where he spoke through the mouth of Hector, said: *Troy commends her sacred things and her Penates to you,* and soon added: *Thus he spoke, and with his hands he brought forth the fillets, the **Powerful Vesta**, and the eternal fire from the inner sanctuary.* **Hyginus** added in the book he wrote on the Penates that they are called **the Ancestral Gods** <note>original: "θεοὺς πατρῴους" (theous patrōous)</note>. Virgil did not leave this unknown either: *Ancestral gods, preserve this house, preserve my grandson;* and elsewhere: *And the ancestral Penates.*

## The types of sacrificial victims. Chapter VI.

<margin>The types of victims.</margin>
He displays his diligence regarding the practice of sacrifice no less than his knowledge of the gods. For when **Trebatius** <note>Gaius Trebatius Testa, a prominent jurist and friend of Cicero and Horace.</note> teaches in the first book of his *On Religions* that there are two types of **victims** <note>original: "hostiarum"</note>: one in which the will of the god is investigated through the **entrails** <note>original: "exta"</note>, and another in which the **soul** <note>original: "anima"</note> alone is consecrated to the god. Hence, the **soothsayers** <note>original: "haruspices"</note> call these "animal victims." Virgil shows both types of victims in his poem. First, that type by which the will of the deities is shown through the entrails: *He slaughters chosen two-toothed sheep according to custom.* and soon: *and gaping over the opened breasts of the cattle, he consults the breathing entrails.* That other type, which is called an "animal victim" because only its life-spirit is sacrificed, he shows when he makes the victor **Entellus** slaughter a bull to **Eryx**. For as he fulfilled...

# OF THE SATURNALIA

<margin>I pay in full</margin>
...the reasons for a living sacrificial victim; he used the name itself. *Eryx, I give to you this better life in place of death* <note>original: "Hanc tibi eryx meliore m aiam pro morte daretis"; from Aeneid 5.483. Here "life" (anima) refers to the animal victim.</note>. And to show that he meant the fulfillment of a vow, he said: *I pay in full* <note>original: "persoluo"</note>, which is the proper term used for a vow. To demonstrate that the debt to the gods was paid, he signaled it by saying: *The ox is laid low, and trembling, falls lifeless to the ground.* It should also be observed whether he shows that other victim to be "living" <note>original: "animalem"</note> in the passage: *With blood you appeased the winds and a slain maiden, when first you Greeks came to the Trojan shores; with blood you must seek your return, and a Greek life must be offered* <note>original: "Sanguine placastis ventos... animaq; litandum argolica"; Aeneid 2.116-118</note>. For he used the word "life" <note>original: "animam"</note>—that is, the name of the victim—and the word *to sacrifice favorably* <note>original: "litare"</note>, which means to have appeased the divine power through a completed sacrifice.

<margin>
To sacrifice favorably.
</margin>

<margin>
Unyoked victims.
Choice victims.
</margin>
Among these very victims—whether they are "living" or "consultative"—there are some called **unyoked victims** <note>original: "hostiae iniuges"</note>, which are those that have never been tamed or placed under a yoke. Our poet remembers these as follows: *Now it would be better to sacrifice seven bullocks from an untouched herd, and as many chosen sheep according to the custom* <note>original: "Nunc grege de itacto septe mactare iuuēcos... lectas de morē bidentes"; Aeneid 6.38-39</note>. And to express "unyoked" more clearly, he added: *and as many heifers with necks untouched.* The word **choice** <note>original: "eximius"</note> used in sacrifices is also not just a poetic <term>epithet</term> <note>original: "ἐπίθετον"</note>, but a priestly term. Veratius, in his *Pontifical Questions*, teaches that victims are called "choice" either because they are **removed** <note>original: "eximantur"</note> from the herd to be destined for sacrifice, or because they are selected for their **exceptional** <note>original: "eximia"</note> appearance to be offered to the gods. Virgil says: *Four choice bulls of outstanding body* <note>original: "Quattuor eximios præstanti corpore tauros"; Aeneid 4.550</note>. By using "choice" <note>original: "eximios"</note> for those that are removed from the herd and "outstanding body" to show they were selected, he demonstrated both meanings.

<margin>
Victim of the Ambarvalia.
</margin>

<margin>
To purify or circle.
</margin>
An **Ambarvalis victim** is one that, as Pompeius Festus says, is led around the fields <note>original: "circum arua"</note> for the sake of a divine rite by those who perform sacrifices for the crops. Virgil mentions this sacrifice in the *Eclogues*, where he speaks of the deification of Daphnis: *These rites shall ever be yours, both when we pay our solemn vows to the Nymphs, and when we purify the fields* <note>original: "quū luštrabimus agros"</note>. Here, **to purify** <note>original: "lustrare"</note> means to go around. From this "going around" the fields, the name of the victim was acquired. Also in the first book of the *Georgics*: *Thrice let the lucky victim go around the new crops.*

It was observed by those sacrificing that if a victim being led to the altars resisted violently or showed itself unwilling to be moved to the shrine, it should be rejected, because they believed it was being offered to an unwilling god. When it stood still after being offered, they believed it was being given to a willing deity. Hence our poet says: *And the sacred goat, led by the horn, shall stand at the altars.* And elsewhere: *And I shall place before the altars a bullock with a gilded brow.*

<margin>
Why Mezentius is a scorner of the gods.
</margin>
Furthermore, Virgil placed all piety in the sacrifices that must be shown to the gods to such an extent that, for the opposite reason, he called Mezentius a "scorner of the gods." For he was not called a scorner of the gods, as it seems to Asper, because he was impious toward men without respect for the gods. Otherwise, Virgil would have said this much more of Busiris, whom he was content to call "unpraised" though he was far more cruel. But the diligent reader will find the true cause of this most defiant name in the first book of Cato’s *Origins*. For he says that Mezentius commanded the Rutulians to offer to him the **first-fruits** <note>The first part of the harvest, traditionally reserved for the gods.</note> which they used to offer to the gods; and all the Latins, fearing a similar command, made a vow: *Jupiter, if it is more pleasing to you, let us give these things to you rather than to Mezentius, so that you may make us victors.* Therefore, because he had demanded divine honors for himself, he was rightly called a "scorner of the gods" by Virgil. Hence that pious insult by the priest: *These are the spoils and the first-fruits from a proud king*—so that by the name of the defiance for which he paid the penalty, Virgil might mark the spoils taken from him.

The learning of this poet regarding both our own and foreign sacred rites is marvelous. For it is not for nothing that when Aeneas comes to Delos, no victim is slain by him; only when they were departing was a divine rite performed for Apollo and Neptune. For it is well known, as Cloatius Verus teaches in the second book of his *Arrangements*, that there is an altar at Delos where a victim is not slain, but they worship the god only with solemn prayer. The words of Cloatius are these: "There is an altar at Delos..."

<margin>
No victim is slain at the Altar of Apollo in Delos.
Father Apollo.
</margin>
"...of Apollo the **Progenitor** <note>original: "γενήτορος" (genetoros)</note>, upon which no animal is sacrificed; they say Pythagoras worshipped this as if it were unpolluted." The poet shows that this is the altar of the **Progenitor** worshipped by Aeneas, since the leader, having entered the temple, immediately begins prayers without any sacrifice being performed. And to name the "progenitor" more expressly, he says: *Grant, Father, an omen.* But when he soon after sacrifices a bull to Apollo and Neptune, we understand this to have been done at another altar. And rightly...
