# BOOK THREE

...above only the father—because that is what is proper there—and below, what is common, he names Apollo. Cato also mentions this altar in his work *On Raising Children* in these words:
> The nurse did all these things with vervain <note>sacred plants or boughs used in rituals</note> and flutes without sacrificial victims, just as at the altar of **Apollo the Father** <note>original: "Apollinis genitiui"</note> at Delos.
In the same verse, I think it should not be omitted why he said the temple was built of "ancient stone" <note>original: "saxo uetusto"</note>. Velius Longus says this is a change of epithet <note>a descriptive term</note>; for he wants to speak of the antiquity of the temple. Many other commentators have followed him, but it is a weak interpretation to merely note the age of a building. However, Epaphus, a man of vast reading, says in his seventeenth book that it happened at a certain time in Delphi that a temple, previously sacred and untouched, was plundered and burned. He adds that many cities and nearby islands around Corinth were swallowed by earthquakes, but Delos was troubled by this misfortune neither before nor since; instead, it always remains on the same stone. Thucydides, the historian, also teaches the same in his third book. It is no wonder, then, if he shows the island as always protected by the defense of religion, and says that a continuous reverence for the place has accrued to it because of the firmness of that same stone—that is, the island itself. Just as he preserved the specific nature of Apollo the Father by calling him "father,"

<margin>Hercules the Victor</margin>
so too did he take care by calling Hercules "**the Victor**." He says: *The victor Alcides <note>Another name for Hercules, referring to his grandfather Alceus.</note> entered these thresholds.* Varro, in the fourth book of his *Divine Antiquities*, thinks he is called "Victor" because he conquered every kind of animal. In Rome, however, there are two temples of **Hercules the Victor**: one at the Triple Gate <note>Porta Trigemina</note> and the other in the Cattle Market <note>Forum Boarium</note>. Massurius Albinus, in the first book of his *Memorable Deeds*, explains the reason for this title differently. He says: Marcus Octavius Herenus was a flute-player in his early youth; after he lost confidence in his craft, he took up commerce, and having conducted his business well, he dedicated a tithe <note>a tenth part of his profits</note> to Hercules. Later, while sailing for the same purpose, he was surrounded by pirates; he fought most bravely and emerged victorious. Hercules informed him in dreams that he had been saved by his help. Having obtained a site from the magistrates, Octavius dedicated a temple
<margin>Octauius Herenus dedicated a tithe.</margin>
and a statue, and called him "**the Victor**" in the inscribed letters. He therefore gave the god an epithet which contained both the evidence of Hercules' ancient victories and the commemoration of a new story which gave the reason for a recent Roman rite. Nor did he say without purpose in the same place:
> And the Pinarian house, the guardian of the Herculean rite.
For some say that when the Great Altar <note>The *Ara Maxima* in Rome.</note> was burning from a neighboring fire, it was saved by the Pinarii; and for that reason, they say Virgil called the Pinarian house the "guardian of the rite" **by way of distinction** <note>original: "κατὰ Διαστολὴν"</note> from the Potitii, who, corrupted by a bribe from Appius Claudius, betrayed the sacred rites to public slaves. But

<margin>The Pinarii and Potitii</margin>
Veratius, an expert on pontifical law, says in the book he wrote *On Supplications* that Hercules—because the Pinarii arrived last when the meal was already finished and the diners were already washing their hands—instructed that neither they nor their descendants should ever taste anything from the tithe to be consecrated to him. Instead, they should be present only for the purpose of serving, not for the feast. He says they are called "guardians of the rite" as if they were ministers <note>servants</note>; as Virgil himself says elsewhere: *But Opis, the guardian of Trivia, has long since been in the mountains,* meaning she is a minister.
Unless, perhaps, he called "guardian" one who has prohibited and restrained herself from the rites, as he says elsewhere:
<margin>Guardian</margin>
> And the guardian of thieves and birds, with his willow sickle, the Hellespontine Priapus, keeps watch.
Here, certainly, "guardian" signifies a protector and a restrainer of birds and thieves. *When these things were said, he ordered the feast and the removed cups to be replaced, and he himself placed the men on a grassy seat.* It is not without reason that he said "**seat**" <note>sedili</note>. For it is a specific observation that in the rites of Hercules, one feasts **sitting**. And Cornelius Balbus, in the eighteenth book of his *Explanations* <note>original: "ἐξηγητικῶν"</note>, says:
<margin>
Feasting while sitting at the rites of Hercules.
</margin>
At the Great Altar, it is observed that no **couch-banquet** <note><term>lectisternium</term>: A ritual where images of gods were placed on couches and offered a meal.</note> takes place. In that same place, it is maintained that everyone performs the rites with an **uncovered head**. This is done so that no one in the temple of the god might imitate his appearance. For there, the god himself is with an uncovered head. Varro says this is a Greek custom, because either Hercules himself, or those left by him who established the Great Altar, sacrificed according to the Greek rite. Gaius Balbus added more to this: he says this is done because the Great Altar was established before the arrival of Aeneas in Italy, who invented this rite of veiling the head. Even those things which are passed over carelessly by the common crowd of readers are not lacking in depth. For when he was speaking of the son of Pollio, he added that which pertained to his own leader:
<margin>
A ram clothed in an unusual color portends happiness for the emperor.
</margin>
> But the ram himself in the meadows will now change his fleece, now with sweetly blushing scarlet, now with saffron yellow.
Furthermore, it is handed down in the **books of the Etruscans** <note>The *Libri Tagetici*, ancient manuals of prophecy and ritual.</note> that if this animal should be clothed in an unusual color, it portends to the ruler a happiness in all things...

<margin>I fulfill my vow</margin>
...the reasons for the "animal" sacrificial victim: he used the term himself. *This better soul, Eryx, I give to you instead of the death* <note>original: "Hanc tibi eryx meliorẽ aiãm pro morte"</note> of a man. And to show that the spoken vows were being completed, he said, "I fulfill" <note>original: "persoluo"</note>, which is the proper word for a vow. To show the gods had accepted the payment, he signified it by saying: *The bull falls lifeless and trembling on the ground.* <note>original: "Sternit̃ exanimisq; tremens procũbit humi bos"</note> It is also worth seeing if he shows that specific victim to be an "animal" sacrifice: *With blood you appeased the winds and with a slain maiden, when first you Greeks came to the shores of Troy; with blood you must seek your return, and sacrifice with a Greek soul.* <note>original: "Sanguine placastis uentos & uirgine cæsa... animaq; litandum argolica"</note> For he used "soul" <note>original: "animam"</note> as the name for the victim, and "to sacrifice" <note>original: "litare"</note>

<margin>To propitiate</margin>
which means to have appeased the divine power once the sacrifice is performed.

<margin>Unbroken victims. An exceptional victim.</margin>
Among these very victims, whether animal or consultative, there are some called "unbroken victims" <note>original: "hostiæ iniuges"</note>, which means those that have never been tamed or placed under a yoke. Our poet remembers these as well: *Now it would be better to sacrifice seven bullocks from an untouched herd, and as many chosen ewes according to custom.* <note>original: "Nũc grege de itacto septẽ mactare iuẽcos... totidẽ lectas de mor̃ bidẽtes"</note> And to express "unbroken" more clearly, he added: *and as many heifers with necks untouched by the yoke.* The term "exceptional" <note>original: "eximii"</note> in sacrifices is also not just a poetic epithet <note>original: "ἐπίθετον"</note>, but a priestly instruction. Veratius, in his *Pontifical Questions*, teaches that victims are called "exceptional" either because they are "exempted" <note>original: "eximantur"</note> from the herd to be destined for sacrifice, or because they are chosen for their "exceptional" appearance to be offered to the gods. Here Virgil says: *Four exceptional bulls of surpassing body.* <note>original: "Quattuor eximios præstãti corpore tauros"</note> Where he shows that those who are "exempted" are "exceptional," and those who are "chosen" are "of surpassing body."

<margin>The Ambarval victim.</margin>
The "Ambarval victim" <note>the victim led around the fields</note> is, as Pompeius Festus says, that which is led around the fields for the sake of divine service by those who perform rituals for the crops. Mention of this sacrifice is found in the *Bucolics* <note>Virgil's Eclogues</note>, where he speaks of the deification of Daphnis: *These shall always be yours, both when we pay our solemn vows to the Nymphs, and when we purify the fields* <note>original: "quũ lustrabimus agros"</note>;

<margin>To purify.</margin>
where "to purify" <note>original: "lustrare"</note> means to go around. For it is from this "going around" the fields <note>original: "ambiendis aruis"</note> that the name of the victim was acquired. But also in the first book of the *Georgics*: *And let the lucky victim go three times around the new crops.*

It was observed by those performing sacrifices that if a victim being led to the altar resisted violently and showed itself unwilling to be moved to the shrine, it should be rejected, because they thought it was being offered to an unwilling god. However, one that stood still when offered was thought to be given to a willing deity. Hence our poet says: *And the sacred goat, led by the horn, shall stand at the altar.* <note>original: "Et ductus cornu stabit facer hircus ad aras"</note> And elsewhere: *And I shall place before the altars a bullock with a gilded forehead.*

Here is that pious insult of the priest: *These are the spoils and the first fruits from a proud king* <note>original: "primitiæ"</note>; so that by the name of his defiance, for which he paid the penalty, Virgil might mark the armor stripped from him.

### BOOK THREE

I iiii

...above, he calls him only "father," which is his specific title there, while below he names him Apollo, which is more common. Cato also mentions this altar in his work *On the Education of Children* in these words: "The nurse performed all these things with leafy branches and flutes without animal victims, as they do at the ancestral altar of Apollo." <note>original: "ut deli ad Apollinis genitiui arā"</note> In the same verse, I think it should not be omitted why he said the temple was built of "ancient rock." <note>original: "saxo uetusto"</note> Velius Longus says this is a change of epithet; for he wants to signify the antiquity of the temple. Many other commentators have followed him, but it is a cold interpretation to merely note the age of a building. Epaphus, however, a man of vast reading, says in his seventeenth book: that it once happened at Delphi that the temple, previously sacred and untouched, was plundered and burned; and he adds that many cities around Corinth and nearby islands were swallowed by earthquakes, but Delos was neither before nor after harassed by this misfortune, but always remained on the same rock. Thucydides the historian also teaches the same in his third book. It is no wonder, then, if he shows the island was always safe by the protection of religion and says that a continuous reverence for the place has accrued to it because of the stability of that same rock—that is, the island. Thus he preserved the specific nature of Apollo the Begetter by calling him "father."

<margin>Hercules the Victor</margin>
He took the same care by calling Hercules "the Victor." He says: *These thresholds the victor Alcides entered.* <note>original: "Hæc inquit limina uictor Alcides subiit"</note> Varro, in the fourth book of his *Divine Antiquities*, thinks Hercules was called "Victor" because he conquered every kind of living creature. At Rome, however, there are two temples of Hercules the Victor: one at the Triple Gate <note>Porta Trigemina</note> and another in the Cattle Market. <note>Forum Boarium</note> Massurius Albinus, in the first book of his *Memorable Deeds*, explains the reason for this title differently. He says that Marcus Octavius Herenus was a flute player in his early youth; after he lost confidence in his art, he took up trade, and having succeeded well, he consecrated a tenth <note>term: <term>profanavit</term> — in this context, the legal act of setting aside a portion of private goods for public/religious use</note> to Hercules. Later, while sailing for business, he was surrounded by pirates, fought most bravely, and emerged the victor. Hercules informed him in his dreams that he had been saved by the god’s own help. Octavius, having obtained a site from the magistrates, dedicated a temple and a statue to him, and titled him "Victor" in the inscribed letters.

<margin>Octavius Herenus Consecrated.</margin>
He gave this epithet to the god so that it might contain both the evidence of Hercules' ancient victories and the commemoration of a new story which gave cause for a recent Roman rite. Not without reason did he say in the same place: *And the Pinarian house, guardian of the Herculean rite.* <note>original: "Et domus herculei custos pinaria sacri"</note> For some say that when a neighboring fire was raging, the Great Altar <note>the Ara Maxima</note> was saved by the Pinarii; and therefore Virgil called the Pinarian house the "guardian" of the rite "by way of distinction" <note>original: "κατὰ διαςολὴν"</note> from the Potitii, who, corrupted by a bribe from Appius Claudio, betrayed the sacred rites to public slaves. But Veratius the Pontiff, in that book he wrote *On Supplications*, says that the Pinarii had arrived last, after the meal had been eaten.

<margin>The Pinarii and Potitii</margin>
When the others were already washing their hands, Hercules commanded that neither they nor their descendants should thereafter taste anything from the tenth consecrated to him, but should be present only for the purpose of serving, not for the feast. As ministers, therefore, they are called "guardians" of the rite, just as Virgil himself says elsewhere: *But Opis, guardian of Trivia, has long since sat in the mountains* <note>original: "At triuiæ custos iā dudum in montibus opis"</note>—the same as "minister." Unless perhaps he called her "guardian" because she withheld and restrained herself from the rites, as he says elsewhere: *And let the guardianship of Hellespontic Priapus, guardian against thieves and birds, keep watch with his willow hook.* <note>original: "Et custos furū atq; auīū... hellespontiaci seruet tutela priapi"</note>

<margin>Guardian</margin>
Here, certainly, "guardian" signifies a prohibitor of birds and thieves. *When these things were said, he orders the feast and the removed cups to be replaced, and he himself places the men on a grassy seat.* <note>original: "Hæc ubi dicta: dapes iubet & sublata reponi Pocula: gramineoq; uiros locat ipse sedili"</note> It is not for nothing that he said "seat." For it is a specific observation that in the rites of Hercules, people feast while sitting. And Cornelius Balbus, in the eighteenth book of his *Interpretations* <note>original: "ἐξηγητικῶν"</note>, says: "At the Great Altar, it is observed that no ritual reclining <note>term: <term>lectisternium</term> — a Roman ritual where images of gods were placed on couches as if feasting</note> takes place."

<margin>They feast while sitting at the rites of Hercules</margin>
It is also observed in the same place that all perform the rites with heads uncovered. This is done so that no one in the temple of the god should imitate his appearance, for there the god himself has his head covered. Varro says this is a Greek custom, because either Hercules himself or those left by him who established the Great Altar sacrificed according to the Greek rite. Gaius Balbus added this further point: he says it is done because the Great Altar was established before the arrival of Aeneas in Italy, who invented this rite of veiling the head. Even those things which are passed over carelessly by the common sort of readers do not lack depth. For when he was speaking of the son of Pol-

<margin>A ram clothed in an unusual color portends happiness for the Emperor.</margin>
-lio, he added something that would pertain to his own Prince: *But the ram himself in the meadows will change his fleece, now with sweetly blushing purple, now with saffron yellow.* <note>original: "Ipse sed in pratis aries iam suaue rubenti Murice: iam croceo mutabit uellera luto"</note> Moreover, it is recorded in the book of the Etruscans: if this animal should be clothed in an unusual color, it portends to the ruler the success of all things.

<header>SATURNALIA</header>

...with happiness and bounty. Beyond this, there is a book by Tarquinius <note>likely Tarquinius Priscus or a legendary source of Etruscan divination</note>, transcribed from the Etruscan book of portents: there it is found that if a sheep or ram is speckled with purple or golden color, it increases the bounty and supreme happiness for the leader of that order and race. It propagates the race and progeny in distinction and makes them more joyful. Therefore, a state of this kind is prophesied for the emperor in his transition. 

Regarding the words and individual details of the sacred rite, which signify things sought from on high, it will be permitted to notice from this:
<margin>What is "Sacred."</margin> "The Fates laid their hand upon him and consecrated him to the weapons of Evander." <note>A reference to Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book 10</note> For whatever is destined for the gods is called "sacred." However, it cannot reach them unless the soul has been freed from the burden of the body, which cannot happen except by death. Thus, he appropriately makes Halesus <note>a Greek hero in the *Aeneid*</note> "sacred" because he was about to meet his end. And here Virgil has followed the precision of both human and divine law. For by the "laying on of hands," he designated a near-possession, and by the word "consecration," he fulfilled the observance of divine law. In this place, it does not seem foreign to report on the condition of those men whom the laws command to be "sacred" to certain gods; for I am not unaware that it seems strange to some that, while it is a sin for other sacred things to be violated, it was lawful for a "sacred man" to be killed. The reason for this matter is as follows: The ancients allowed no sacred animal to remain within their borders but drove them away to the borders of the gods to whom they were sacred. Indeed, they believed the souls of "sacred men"—whom the Greeks call "immortals" <note>original: $\alpha\theta\alpha\nu\alpha\tau o\upsilon\varsigma$ (*athanatous*)</note>—were owed to the gods. Therefore, just as they did not hesitate to send away from themselves what could not be sent to the gods themselves, so they thought the souls which they judged "sacred" could be sent to heaven, wishing them to go there as soon as they were widowed from the body. Trebatius <note>a Roman jurist</note> also disputes this custom in the ninth book of his *On Religions*. I have omitted his example so as not to be long-winded. For whoever has the heart to read it, let it suffice that both the author and the order of the volume have been shown.

### ¶ On things in Virgil that are corrupted by poor pronunciation. Chapter VII.

<image-desc>Ornamental initial 'N' in a square woodcut border, featuring foliate patterns.</image-desc>
<margin>God as masculine and feminine</margin> We corrupt the dignity of several things that were most skillfully brought forth by poor pronunciation; for example, some read: "I depart, and with the *goddess* <note>original: *dea*</note> leading, I am cleared between the flames and the enemies," whereas Virgil most learnedly said: "with the *god* <note>original: *deo*</note> leading," not the goddess. For even in the works of Calvus, Aeterianus affirms it should be read: "And Venus, the powerful *god*," not goddess. Evidence of this is also found in Cyprus, where there is a statue with a bearded body but feminine clothing, yet with the scepter and stature of a man. And they 
<margin>Aphroditus</margin> think the same being is both male and female. Aristophanes calls this being "Aphroditus" <note>original: $\alpha\phi\rho o\delta\iota\tau o\nu$ (*aphroditon*), a masculine form of Aphrodite</note>; Laevius also speaks thus: "Therefore, adoring the nourishing Venus, whether it is female or male, just as the nourishing moon is." Philochorus also affirms in his *Atthis* that this same being is the Moon, and that men perform sacrifices to it in feminine clothing, and women in masculine clothing, because the same being is considered both male and female.

¶ This was also said by Virgil concerning the wisdom of religion: "He fell breathless and left his life among the airy stars." For Hyginus, in his work *On the Properties of the Gods*, when speaking of the stars and planets, says that birds should be sacrificed to them. Virgil therefore learnedly said the soul of the bird remained among those deities to whom it was given for a favorable sacrifice.

¶ Nor does he allow any name to be empty which could be accidental; he called her "of the Mother." By changing a part of the name "Casmilla," she became "Camilla." For Statius Tullianus, in the first book of his *On the Names of Things*, says that Callimachus stated that the 
<margin>Camillus. Camilla.</margin> Etruscans call Mercury "Camillus," by which name they signify a "servant of the gods." From this, Virgil says Metabus called his daughter Camilla, a servant of Diana. For even Pacuvius, when speaking of Medea, says: "Hail, guest, the long-awaited servant <note>original: *camilla*</note> of the heavenly ones, you arrive." The Romans also call noble and prepubescent boys or girls *camilli* and *camillae*, the ministers of the priests and their wives <note>original: *flaminum* and *flaminicarum*</note>.

<margin>Custom.</margin> ¶ It is also fitting not to overlook this observation of his. "It was a custom," he says, "in Hesperian Latium, which the Alban cities immediately held sacred; now Rome, the greatest of things, honors it." Varro, 
<margin>Habit</margin> in his *On Customs*, says that "Custom" <note>original: *Mos*</note> is a judgment of the mind which "Habit" <note>original: *Consuetudo*</note> ought to follow. Julius Festus, in the thirteenth book of *On the Signification of Words*, says: "Custom is an ancestral institution pertaining to the religions and ceremonies of the elders." Therefore, Virgil followed both authors: first, that which is...

<meta>This page continues the discussion in Book Three of Macrobius’s *Saturnalia* regarding the religious and legal precision of the poet Virgil. The previous page discussed the definition of "sacred" and the ritual significance of certain animals; here, the text transitions into the definitions of "custom" versus "habit" and the secret Roman rituals for summoning gods from enemy cities.</meta>

<page-num>LXIX</page-num>
<header>BOOK THREE</header>

Regarding **Varro**, since he had said that "custom" <note>original: *mos*</note> precedes and "habit" <note>original: *consuetudo*</note> follows: after he said **"it was the custom,"** he added: **"which the Alban cities continuously observed: and now Rome, the greatest of all things, observes,"** by which he demonstrates the persistence of habit. And since **Festus** says that this pertains to ceremonies, **Maro** <note>a common name for the poet Virgil, Publius Vergilius Maro</note> taught this same thing by adding the word "sacred": **"the sacred [custom] which the Alban cities continuously observed."** Custom therefore preceded, and the worship of that custom followed: which is habit. And here he fulfilled Varro’s definition. By then adding "sacred," he showed that the custom was dedicated to ceremonies, just as Festus asserted. He preserved this same idea in the twelfth book when he said: **"I shall add the custom and the rites of the sacred things,"** in which he aptly shows that custom consists of sacred rites. But he followed the historical truth in these verses: **"The custom was in Hesperian Latium"** <note>Western Latium, i.e., Italy</note> and so forth. For he preserved the succession of kingdoms. Indeed, first the Latins ruled, then the Albans, and then the Romans. Therefore, he first said "the custom was in Hesperian Latium," and afterwards "which the Alban cities continuously observed as sacred"; then he added: "now Rome, the greatest of all things, observes it."

¶ **"All the gods, by whom this empire had stood, departed, leaving behind their shrines and altars."** <note>A famous line from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book 2</note> This pronouncement was uttered concerning the most ancient custom of the Romans and their most hidden sacred rites. For it is established that all cities are under the protection <term>tutela: the Roman belief that every place was guarded by a specific deity</term> of some god, and it was a secret Roman custom, unknown to many, that when they besieged an enemy city and considered that it could finally be captured, they would call forth the guardian gods with a specific chant <term>evocatio: the ritual "calling out" of an enemy's gods to persuade them to desert to Rome</term>. This was because they either believed the city could not otherwise be taken, or, if it could, they considered it a divine sin <note>original: *nefas*</note> to hold gods as captives.

For this reason, the Romans themselves wished both the god under whose protection the city of Rome exists and the Latin name of the city itself to be unknown. But the name of the god has been included in some books of the ancients, though they disagree among themselves; and thus, through those who investigate antiquity, whatever is thought about this has become known.
<margin>
Angerona
</margin>
For some have believed it to be **Jupiter**; others the **Moon**; there are those who believe it is **Angerona**, who commands silence with a finger pressed to her lips. Others, however, whose authority seems firmer to me, have said it is **Ops Consivia** <note>an ancient Roman goddess of the earth and abundance</note>. Truly, the name of the city itself is unknown even to the most learned, as the Romans took care lest they themselves should suffer the same fate through a hostile "calling forth" <note>evocatio</note> if the name of their protector were made public—a thing they knew they had often done against the cities of their enemies.

<margin>
The chant for the calling forth of the gods.
</margin>
But we must see to it that we are not confused by what some have thought, who believe that by one single chant both the gods are called out of a city and the city itself is "devoted" <term>devotio: a ritual curse consigning a city or army to the gods of the underworld</term>. For I found in the fifth book of "Hidden Matters" by **Sammonicus Serenus** both chants, which he claimed to have found in a very ancient book by a certain **Furius**. Moreover, the chant by which the gods are called forth when a city is surrounded by a siege is of this kind: 

"Whether it be a god or a goddess under whose protection the people and state of Carthage are, and you especially, who have taken up the protection of this city and people: I pray to you, I venerate you, and I ask for grace from you, that you might desert the people and state of the Carthaginians, leave behind their places, temples, sacred things, and city; that you might depart from them and cast fear, dread, and forgetfulness upon that people and state; and that you, having been handed over, might come to me and my people at Rome; and that our places, temples, sacred things, and city might be more acceptable and approved by you; and that you might be set over me and the Roman people and my soldiers, so that we may know and understand it. If you do so, I vow that I will build temples and hold games for you."

Over these same words, sacrifices must be made, and the authority of the entrails <note>original: *extorum* - refers to the practice of haruspicy, or reading animal organs</note> must be seen to promise that these things will happen.

Truly, cities and armies are "devoted" in this way once the divine powers have already been called forth. But only dictators and commanders-in-chief have the power to "devote" with these words:
<margin>
Words for the devotion of cities and armies.
</margin>
"Father Dis, or Jove's Shades <note>original: *Iovis manes* - a rare term for the spirits of the dead or a chthonic Jupiter</note>, or by whatever other name it is lawful to call you: I ask that you fill that city of Carthage and the army which I feel myself to be naming with flight, dread, and terror; and that you lead away those who bear arms and weapons against our legions and army; that you deprive them of the light of the world above. And that you hold the army of the enemies, their cities and fields, which I feel myself to be naming, as devoted and consecrated according to those laws by which enemies are most especially devoted; and those I..."

# THE SATURNALIA
### PAGE 19.1

<margin>
Cities devoted to destruction by the Roman people
</margin>

"...as proxies for me, by my honor and my office, and for the Roman people, our armies and our legions, I devote <note>The ritual of *devotio* was a formal vow by a Roman general to sacrifice himself and the enemy to the gods of the underworld in exchange for victory.</note> them: so that you may allow me, my honor, my command, and our legions and army—who are engaged in these affairs—to remain safe and sound. If you do this in such a way that I may know, feel, and understand it: then whenever and wherever anyone makes this vow, let it be rightly performed. By three black sheep, Mother Earth, and you, Jupiter, I call you to witness." When he says "Earth," he touches the ground with his hands; when he says "Jupiter," he lifts his hands toward heaven; when he says he accepts the vow, he touches his chest with his hands. In the records of antiquity, I have found these towns were so devoted: the Stonii, Fregellae, Gabii, Veii, and Fidenae. These were within Italy. Additionally, there were Carthage and Corinth, as well as many armies and towns of enemies among the Gauls, Spaniards, Africans, Moors, and other nations of which the ancient annals speak. It is for this reason—because of this ritual of "calling forth" <note>The *evocatio*, a ritual inviting an enemy's protective gods to leave their city and come to Rome.</note> and the departure of the deities—that Virgil says: **"The gods all departed, leaving behind their shrines"** <note>original Latin: *Excessere omnes adytis relictis Dii*</note>. And to show they were the guardian spirits, he added: **"by whom this empire had stood."** Furthermore, to show not just the "calling forth" but also the power of "devotion," in which Jupiter is primarily invoked (as we have said), he says: **"Fierce Jupiter has transferred everything to Argos."** Does it not seem proven to you that without knowledge of divine and human law, the depth of Maro <note>Virgil</note> cannot be understood?

¶ At this point, while everyone was agreeing with a single voice that the poet’s learning and the speaker’s explanation were equal, Evangelus <note>A character in the dialogue who acts as the "devil's advocate" or critic of Virgil.</note> cried out that he had suffered in silence long enough and could no longer hide the truth: he must expose the wounds of Virgil’s ignorance to everyone. "I too once withdrew my hand from the schoolmaster's rod," <note>An idiom meaning 'I am also an educated man.'</note> he said, "and I too have studied the basics of pontifical law. From what I know, it will be clear that Maro was ignorant of this discipline. For why would he say: **'I was slaughtering a bull on the shore for the King of the Sky-dwellers'** <note>original Latin: *Caelicolum regi mactabam in littore taurum*; referring to Aeneas sacrificing a bull to Jupiter.</note> if he knew that it is forbidden to sacrifice a bull to this god? Or if he had learned what Atteius Capito 

<margin>
To which gods a bull is sacrificed.
</margin>

recorded? His words from Book One of *On the Law of Sacrifices* are these: 'Therefore, it is not permitted to sacrifice a bull, a boar, or a ram to Jupiter.' Indeed, Labeo <note>Antistius Labeo, a famous Roman jurist.</note> stated in his sixty-eighth book that a bull is only to be sacrificed to Neptune, Apollo, and Mars. Look here: your 'priest' Virgil does not even know what animal to slaughter at which altar, even though this is known even to temple attendants, and the diligence of the ancients did not keep it secret." To this, Praetextatus replied with a smile: "To which gods bulls should be sacrificed—if you are willing to listen to Virgil—he himself will teach you: **'A bull for Neptune, a bull for you, fair Apollo.'** Do you see Labeo’s own words in the poet’s work? Therefore, just as that passage is learned, this other one is clever. For he shows that the sacrifice was not favorable <note>original: *non litatum*, meaning the gods did not accept the offering.</note>, and because of it, there followed: **'A monster horrific to speak of and wondrous to see.'** Thus, looking toward the future, he intentionally made an improper sacrifice. But he also knew that this error was not beyond atonement. For Atteius Capito—whom you stationed in battle against Maro—added these words: 'If anyone happens to sacrifice a bull [to Jupiter], let him offer an expiatory sacrifice' <note>original: *piaculum*</note>. Therefore, the act is not a sacrilege that cannot be purified, though it is unusual. And it was committed not out of ignorance, but to create a place for a future omen."

<margin>
Wine is not offered to Ceres.
</margin>

¶ Evangelus retorted: "If illicit acts are excused by their outcomes, then tell me, I pray: what 'monster' was to follow when he ordered a libation of wine for Ceres, which is forbidden in all her rites? He says: **'For her, dilute the honeycombs with milk and mild Bacchus'** <note>Virgil uses 'Bacchus' as a metonym for wine.</note>. Even Plautus could have taught him that wine is not offered to Ceres; in his play *The Pot of Gold*, he says: 'Strobiles, are they going to perform a wedding for Ceres? Since I see they've brought no wine?' But this 'priest' and 'pontiff' of yours is ignorant of both what should be sacrificed and what should be poured. And so he doesn't miss a chance to wander into error regarding libations, in the eighth book he says: **'Gladly they pour libations on the table, and pray to the gods'**—whereas they ought to have poured the libation on the altar according to custom, not on the table. To respond to your second question first," Praetextatus said, "I admit you have raised a fair point regarding the practice of libating on a table. You would have even increased the difficulty if you had noted Dido libating on a table in a similar way: **'She spoke, and poured the honor of the liquid onto the table.'** Indeed, even Publius Tertius, when discussing the rites of sacrifices at length, said this passage was a question for him, yet he did not resolve his hesitation with a researched reason. <meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page, shifting from the rituals of destroying enemy cities to the specific details of Roman religious law as depicted in Virgil's poetry. The speakers are analyzing whether Virgil accurately described the use of tables as altars and the specific priesthoods and greenery associated with the worship of Hercules.</meta>

# BOOK THREE

<margin>A dedicated table serves the function of an altar.</margin>
It is well known, and I shall make it public: for in the Papirian Law <note>A collection of sacred laws attributed to the early Roman priest Sextus Papirius.</note> it is clearly stated that a dedicated table can serve in place of an altar. For example, it says that in the temple of Juno Populonia, there is a "venerable table." In shrines, some items belong to the category of "vessels," others to "sacred furniture," and others to "ornaments." Those that are vessels act as the tools with which sacrifices are always performed. The table holds the primary place among these objects, for upon it the feasts, libations, and small offerings are placed. Ornaments, however, are shields, crowns, and votive gifts of this sort. Such gifts are not dedicated at the same time the shrines are consecrated; however, a table and small altars are usually dedicated on the same day as the temple buildings themselves. Therefore, a table dedicated with this ritual in a temple possesses the function of an altar and the religious sanctity of a sacred couch <note>term: pulvinar <gloss>a sacred cushioned seat used in Roman ritual for the statues of gods to "sit" upon during feasts</gloss></note>. Thus, in the story of Evander <note>The king who hosted Aeneas on the future site of Rome</note>, a proper libation is performed because it takes place at that table which, according to religious custom, had been dedicated along with the Great Altar <note>original: Ara Maxima; the ancient altar of Hercules in the Forum Boarium in Rome</note>, in a sacred place, and during the very rites in which they were feasting. But in the banquet of Dido, which is clearly only a royal feast and not a sacred one, the libation took place at a human table in a dining room, not in a temple. Because that table was not consecrated, the poet says only the queen performed the libation, as she had the power and permission to perform such a customary act, but there was no ritual necessity for others to do so. Here, however, everyone joyfully performs a libation at the table and prays to the gods; the poet recorded that this was done by everyone together while feasting in the temple and sitting at a single sacred table, because he knew it was the correct procedure. Regarding that verse: **"For whom you dissolve honeycombs with milk and mild wine,"** <note>original: "Cui tu lacte favos & miti dilue baccho"</note> I will briefly resolve why Virgil <note>original: "Maro"</note> is criticized. The poet, an expert in matters of learning and a seeker of elegance in words, knew that libations are made to Ceres with honey-wine; he added "dissolve the honeycombs with mild wine," meaning that the wine begins to mellow when it is turned into honey-wine. For here he called the wine "mild" just as elsewhere he calls it "tamed," saying: **"the wine will tame the harsh flavor."** You will not deny it is well known that on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January <note>December 21st</note>, they sacrifice to Hercules and Ceres with a pregnant sow, loaves of bread, and honey-wine.

"By Hercules, Praetextatus, you have mentioned Hercules quite opportunely! In whose sacred rites Virgil here committed a double error."

> Then the Salii come to the songs around the flaming altars,
> Their temples bound with branches of poplar.

<margin>Salii</margin>
¶ "For he assigned the Salii <note>A college of priests usually dedicated to Mars, the god of war</note> to Hercules, whom antiquity dedicated only to Mars; and he names 'poplar crowns,' when at the Great Altar they bind their heads only with laurel, and no other foliage. We see a laurel crown on the head of the City Praetor when he performs the divine rite for Hercules. Even Terentius Varro <note>A prolific Roman scholar often cited by Macrobius</note> testifies in that satire titled *On the Thunderbolt* <note>original Greek: περὶ κεραυνοῦ</note> that the ancestors were accustomed to vow a tenth to Hercules. They did not let ten days pass without 'pollucating' <note>term: pollucere <gloss>to offer a formal banquet to a god, specifically Hercules, and share the leftovers with the public</gloss></note> the people, sending them away to a 'scot-free' feast <note>original Greek: ἀσύμβολον; a meal provided without the guests having to pay a share</note> while wearing a laurel crown. Is this not a double error, Vectius?" But I say that Virgil erred in neither. First, regarding the type of foliage: it is true that those sacrificing at the Great Altar are now crowned with laurel. But this custom began long after the founding of Rome, after laurel began to grow on the Aventine Hill. Varro explains this in the second book of *Human Antiquities*. Laurel was taken from the nearest mountain by those performing the rites because the nearby location offered the opportunity. Therefore, our Virgil correctly looked back to the times when Evander, before the city was founded, celebrated the rites at the Great Altar and used the poplar, which is most pleasing to Hercules <note>original: "Alcidae"</note>.

<margin>Hercules is the same as Mars; the Salii.</margin>
Furthermore, he assigns the Salii to Hercules because of the depth of his higher learning; among the pontiffs, this god is considered the same as Mars. Indeed, Varro's Menippean satire titled *This is Another Hercules* <note>original Greek: ἄλλος οὗτος Ἡρακλῆς</note> affirms this: for when he speaks at length about Hercules, he proves he is the same as Mars. The Chaldeans also call the star of Hercules what everyone else calls the star of Mars. There is also a book by Octavius Hersennius titled *On the Family Rites of the Tiburtines*, in which he teaches that the Salii were established to perform rites for Hercules on certain days and after taking the auspices.

<margin>Window</margin>
Likewise, Antonius Gnipho, a learned man whose school Cicero used to attend after his work in the forum, proves that the Salii were given to Hercules in that volume where he discusses what a "window" is and what a "door" is—a small opening in a shrine—using which word Ennius also...

# BOOK THREE OF THE SATURNALIA

...was used: by suitable (as I believe) authors and certain reasons, the error that was thought to exist on both sides has been defended. If there are other things that disturb us, let us bring them into the open, so that this comparison of ours—not Maro’s <note>Maro is the family name of the poet Virgil.</note>—may resolve the error.

Then Evangelus said: "Has it never occurred to you, Praetextatus, that Virgil has wandered 'across the whole sky' (as they say) <note>original: "toto... cælo errasse"; a Latin idiom for being completely mistaken.</note> when he had Dido perform her sacrifice for her marriage? For he says: 'She slaughters chosen ewes according to custom to Ceres the Law-giver, to Phoebus, and to Lyæus.' <note>Lyæus is a title for Bacchus, the god of wine. These lines are from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book 4.</note> And then, as if he had just woken up, he added: 'To Juno before all others, who has the marriage bonds in her care.' Hear also the words of Marcus Varro <note>A famous Roman scholar and writer on agriculture.</note> from his third book *On Agriculture*: when he was speaking about raising peacocks in a villa, he said thus: 'Quintus Hortensius is said to have been the first to serve these at an augural dinner.' <note>A banquet held to celebrate the inauguration of a priest into the College of Augurs.</note> Which the good men of the time praised more as a matter of luxury than of strictness. Following his example, many quickly raised their prices, so that their eggs sold for five denarii <note>term: denarius <gloss>the standard silver coin of Rome; five denarii was an exorbitant price for a single egg.</gloss></note> each, and the birds themselves easily for fifty."

<margin>First use of peacocks.</margin> Behold, a thing not only to be wondered at, but even shameful: that peacock eggs should sell for five denarii, which today—I will not say are cheaper—but are simply not for sale at all. This Hortensius used to water his plane trees with wine, to such an extent that in a certain legal action he had against Cicero, he requested a favor from Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> to swap his turn to speak. For he said he needed to leave for his villa immediately so that he could personally pour wine onto a plane tree he had planted at Tusculum. 

<margin>Quintus Hortensius the effeminate.</margin> But perhaps Hortensius does not suffice as the mark of his century: a man otherwise openly soft, and placing all his pride in his appearance. For he was painstakingly neat in his dress. And to ensure he walked out well-attired, he would study his face in a mirror; looking at himself there, he would arrange the toga on his body so that an artistic knot would bind the folds—not placed by chance, but by industry—and the drape, flowing by design, would wrap around his side just so. Once, when he was walking along, elaborately prepared for show, he brought a lawsuit against his colleague for damages because, having met him in a narrow passage, his colleague had accidentally brushed against him and ruined the 'structure' of his toga; he considered it a capital offense that a fold on his shoulder had changed its place. 

Therefore, putting this aside, I come to men of triumphal rank, whom luxury conquered even though they were victors over nations. And I shall remain silent about Gurges, named for 'devouring' his inheritance <note>original: "Gurges"; the nickname of Quintus Fabius Maximus, meaning 'the Whirlpool' or 'Glutton'.</note>, because he compensated for the vices of his earlier life with the distinguished virtues of his later years. 

<margin>Gurges the glutton.</margin> Into what pit of luxury and pride did Metellus Pius <note>A high-ranking Roman general and statesman.</note> fall through a series of successes? 

<margin>Metellus Pius.</margin> And so as not to delay with many words, I have subjoined the very words of Sallust <note>The famous Roman historian.</note> regarding him. "But Metellus, returning to Further Spain after a year with great glory, was watched by men and women alike flocking from everywhere along the roads and rooftops. And the quaestor Caius Urbinus and others, knowing his desires, when they invited him to dinner, provided beyond the custom of Romans and even of mortals: with houses decorated with tapestries and insignia, and stages built for the display of actors; at the same time, the ground was sprinkled with saffron, and other things were done in the manner of a most famous temple. Furthermore, as he sat on a platform, a statue of Victory was lowered with a mechanical sound of thunder to place a crown on his head. Then, as he approached, they offered incense as if to a god. A 'painted toga' <note>term: toga picta <gloss>an all-purple toga embroidered with gold, usually worn only by generals during a triumph.</gloss></note> was often his garment as he reclined. The banquets were most exquisite, sought not only through the whole province, but from across the seas from Mauretania—many kinds of birds and wild beasts previously unknown—by which things he had detracted somewhat from his glory, especially among old and holy men who judged that heavy pride unworthy of the Roman Empire." This was written by Sallust, a most serious critic and censor of others' luxury.

<margin>A most lavish Pontifical dinner.</margin> Understand that luxury was not absent even among the most serious persons. For I report the most ancient dinner of a pontiff <note>A high-ranking priest of the Roman state.</note>, which was recorded on the fourth day of the calendar of that Metellus, the Chief Priest, in these words: "On the ninth day before the Kalends of September <note>August 24th.</note>, the day on which Lentulus was inaugurated as the Flamen of Mars <note>term: Flamen Martialis <gloss>the high priest dedicated specifically to the god Mars.</gloss></note>, the house was decorated; the dining rooms were spread with ivory couches; in two dining rooms the pontiffs reclined: Quintus Catulus, Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, Decimus Silanus, Gaius Caesar the King of Sacred Rites <note>term: Rex Sacrorum <gloss>a high-ranking priest who performed the religious duties formerly held by the kings of Rome. This "Gaius Caesar" is the famous Julius Caesar.</gloss></note>, Publius Scaevola, Sextus Quintus Cornelius, Publius Volumnius, Publius Albinovanus, and Lucius Julius Caesar the Augur, who inaugurated him. In the third dining room sat Popilia, Perpenia, Licinia, and Arruncia, the Vestal Virgins, and his own wife Publicia, the Flaminica..." <note>The wife of a Flamen, who held her own sacred duties and attended religious feasts.</note>

<margin>Teal.</margin>
boiled teal, hares, roasted poultry, starch-paste, and breads flavored with pitch. Even then, luxury was condemned, given that the dinner of the high priests was made of so many things. Indeed, the very types of food were shameful to speak of: for 
<margin>The Trojan Pig</margin>
Cincius, in his speech supporting the Fannian Law <note>A law passed in 161 BCE to limit expenditure on banquets.</note>, reproached his own era because they brought the "Trojan pig" to the tables. They called it this because it was stuffed with other animals enclosed within it, just as the famous Trojan Horse was pregnant with armed men. This lack of restraint in gluttony also demanded that hares be fattened, according to Varro, who, when speaking of hares in the third book of *On Agriculture*, says: "This too was recently established: that hares should be fattened, when certain people take them from the hare-warren and make them fat in cages and enclosed places." If this seems strange to anyone—that hares were customarily fattened in that age—let them hear what is worthy of even greater wonder: fattened snails! The same Varro reports this in the same book. I have indicated where those who wish to read the words themselves should look. I am not saying now that we should be preferred or compared to antiquity; but I have answered the rebuking Horus, asserting the truth: that in those centuries, there was a greater concern for delicacies than in ours.

Furius Albinus, a man no less skilled in antiquity than Cinna, added: "I wonder," he said, "that you did not mention how great an abundance of sea-derived riches used to be procured; by relating this, you would demonstrate the great sobriety of our own banquets." And Cecinna said: "Bring forth into our midst what you have found in your reading regarding this part as well. For you excel all others in the memory of ancient times." And Furius began thus:

"Antiquity is something that must always be adored by us (if we are wise). For those were the centuries that gave birth to this empire through either blood or sweat—which nothing but an abundance of virtues could have achieved. But as must be confessed, in that abundance of virtues, that age was also not without its vices, some of which have been corrected in our century by a sobriety of morals. I had intended to speak of the luxury of that time regarding sea-wealth, but because in the assertion of our improvement, various things suggest themselves to be brought forward one after another, I will not omit the topic of fish, but I will postpone it; meanwhile, I shall remind you of another form of decadence which we now lack. Tell me, Horus, you who reproach us with antiquity: before whose dining room do you remember seeing a female or male dancer today? Yet among those ancients, dancing was eagerly sought after even by honorable people. Behold, for instance, let me begin from that time which was considered to have the best morals. Between the two Punic Wars, freeborn—I say 
<margin>Dancing at the table</margin>
freeborn sons of senators—would go to a dancing school, and there they were said to dance while holding 
<margin>Castanets</margin>
castanets <note>original: "crotala"; small percussion instruments similar to finger cymbals or castanets.</note>. I say nothing of how even matrons did not consider dancing to be dishonest. But among the virtuous women too, there was a care for dancing, provided it was not curious to the point of professional perfection. For what does Sallust say? 'She sang and danced more elegantly than is necessary for an honest woman' <note>referring to Sempronia in Sallust’s *War of Catiline*.</note>. Thus he himself reproached Sempronia, not because she knew how to dance, but because she knew it *too* well. That the sons of nobles—and what is a sin to say, their virgin daughters too—counted the practice of dancing among their studies, Scipio Africanus Aemilianus is a witness, who in his speech against the judicial law of Tiberius Gracchus, says: 
<margin>Reproach of dancing</margin>
'They are taught dishonest tricks with effeminate dancers <note>original: "cynedulis"</note>, and they go to the school of actors with the sambuca <note>A triangular stringed instrument.</note> and the psaltery; they learn to sing, which our ancestors wanted to be considered a disgrace for freeborn people. They go,' I say, 'to the dancing school among effeminates, both virgins and freeborn boys. When anyone told me these things, I could not bring my mind to believe that noble men were teaching their children such things. But when I was led to the dancing school, by my faith, I saw more than five hundred boys and girls in that school. Among them (for which I pitied the Republic) I saw one boy wearing the *bulla* <note>term: bulla <gloss>a locket worn by freeborn Roman children as an amulet and mark of status.</gloss></note>, the son of a candidate, no less than twelve years old, dancing with castanets—a dance which a shameful little slave could not dance with any decency.' You see how Africanus groaned because he had seen the son of a seeker of office (that is, a candidate) dancing with castanets; whom even then the hope and the plan for obtaining office could not restrain..."

### ¶ That several people drew their surnames from fish. Chapter VIII.

<margin>The surname Murena. Sergius Orata. Suspended baths.</margin>
But the name of the Licinii has reminded me to transition from the dancing of the ancients to the maritime luxury of their prey: for it is well established that they were surnamed "Murena" because they took excessive delight in this fish <note>The *murena* is the moray eel.</note>. Marcus Varro agrees with this opinion, asserting that the Licinii were called Murenas in the same way that Sergius Orata was surnamed: because those fish which are called *auratae* <note>The gilt-head sea bream.</note> were his favorites. This is the Sergius Orata who first had "suspended baths" <note>Original: *balneas pēsiles*. An early form of underfloor heating where the floor was raised on pillars.</note>; the first to install oyster-beds in the Baian district; the first to judge the best flavor to be in the Lucrine oysters. He lived, moreover, in the age of that eloquent Lucius Crassus, whose weight and seriousness Cicero teaches us. Yet that Crassus, a man of censorial rank—for he was censor with Gnaeus Domitius—though he was held to be more eloquent than others and was a leader among the most famous citizens, nevertheless mourned in black raiment for a *murena* that had died in the fishpond of his house, as if it were a daughter. Nor was this a secret, for his colleague Domitius brought this up against him in the senate as if it were a shameful crime. Nor did Crassus blush to confess it, but even went further (if it please the gods): the censor boasted, claiming that he had done a pious and affectionate thing. Moreover, that those most noble Roman leaders—Lucius Philippus and Hortensius, whom Cicero calls "fishpond-fanciers" <note>Original: *piscinarios*. A term used mockingly for those more concerned with their fish than the state.</note>—kept their ponds stuffed with the most precious fish, is also indicated by what Marcus Varro relates in his book *On Agriculture*. Marcus Cato—the one who later died at Utica—when he had been left as heir in the will of Lucilius, sold the fish from his fishpond for forty thousand sesterces. *Murenae* were even summoned to the fishponds of our city from as far as the Sicilian Strait, which looks from Messana toward Rhegium. For in that place, they are believed by the extravagant to be the best, by Hercules,
<margin>The Floaters.</margin>

...they become easy to catch. And if I wished to list how many and how great the authors are who have made Sicilian moray eels <note>Original: *murenas*. The Mediterranean moray was a highly prized delicacy in ancient Rome, often kept in private seaside ponds.</note> famous, it would be a long task. It is well known that the villa of this Hirius, although it was not large or sprawling, was sold for four million sesterces <note>Original: *quadragies ſextertium*. ### On the Sturgeon. Chapter IX.

<margin>The Sturgeon fish.</margin>
Neither did the sturgeon, which the seas nourish for the extravagant, escape being a delicacy of that age. And to make it clear that the name of this fish was famous during the Second Punic War, hear how Plautus mentions it in the play titled *Baccharia* through the character of a parasite:
> "What mortal was ever blessed with such great fortune 
> as I am now: for whose belly this procession is carried.
> Even now, the sturgeon that previously lay hidden for me in the sea:
¶ whose side I shall return to the hiding places of my teeth and hands."
And lest the poet be considered a witness of little value, take Cicero as an advocate, showing what honor this fish held among Publius Scipio Africanus the Elder and Munatius. These are the words of Cicero in his dialogue *On Fate*: "For when Scipio and Pontius were together at Lavernum, a sturgeon happened to be brought to Scipio, a fish which is rarely caught. But it is a fish (as they say) of primary nobility." However, when Scipio had invited one or two of those who had come to greet him, and it appeared he was about to invite more, Pontius whispered into his ear: "Scipio, watch what you are doing; that sturgeon is for only a few men." <note>Original: *paucorũ hominũ eſt*. A phrase used to describe something too exclusive or refined for a large crowd.</note> Nor do I deny <note>Original: *iſicias*, likely a typo for *inficias*.</note> that in the times of Trajan, this fish was not held in great price, according to Pliny the Younger, who said in his *Natural History* when speaking of this fish: "It is in no way held in honor, which I certainly wonder at, since it is rarely found." But this frugality did not last long. For in the times of Emperor Severus, who made a show of his harshness of character, Samonicus Serenus—a man learned for that age—when he wrote to his prince and spoke of this fish, first cited the words of Pliny I placed above, and then added: "Pliny (as you know) reached the age of Emperor Trajan. There is no doubt that his statement that this fish was of no honor in his time is true. However, I make it clear by testimonies that it was prized among the ancients, or rather, I see that its popularity has returned to feasts as if by legal recovery." <note>Original: *poſtliminio*. A legal term referring to the restoration of rights to someone returning from captivity; here used metaphorically for a fashion returning to favor.</note> For by your grace, when I am present at the sacred banquet, I notice this fish is brought in by wreathed attendants with a flute player. But as for what Pliny says about the sturgeon's scales, Nigidius Figulus, the greatest investigator of nature, shows it to be true. In the fourth book of his *On Animals*, it is written: "Why other fish have scales facing back, while the sturgeon's are facing forward." Samonicus notes these things, while praising the foulness of his prince's banquets, recognizing the veneration the fish received: being brought in by wreathed men with the song of a flute player, as if it were a procession not for a delicacy, but for a deity. But so we might wonder less 
<margin>Pricing the Mullet fish</margin>
that the sturgeon was usually valued at a heavy price: Asinius Celer, a man of consular rank (as the same Samonicus reports), bought a single mullet for seven thousand coins. In this matter, the luxury of that age can be estimated all the more, since Pliny the Younger denies that in his time a mullet exceeding two pounds in weight was easily found. Yet now we see larger weights everywhere, and we do not know these insane prices. Nor was that gluttony <note>Original: *ingluuies*. A strong term for excessive, wasteful eating.</note> content with the bounty of its own sea. For Optatus, the prefect of the fleet,

...the greatest public benefit turned on this: for five years he devoted his efforts to ensuring that if anyone happened to catch a

Yet Marcus Varro shows that it was so; when enumerating the best foodstuffs produced in various parts of Italy, he awards the palm to the Tiber fish in these words from the eleventh book of his *Human Affairs*: "For food, the following are the best: the Campanian fields produce the grain; the Falernian region, the wine; Cassinum, the oil; Tusculum, the figs; Tarentum, the honey; and the Tiber, the fish." These are Varro’s words on all the fish of this river in general; but among them, as I said above, the 
<margin>The wolf-fish (sea bass).</margin>
wolf-fish held the chief place—and specifically the one caught between the two bridges <note>Original: *inter duos pontes*. This refers to the stretch of the Tiber between the Sublician and Aemilian bridges, where the water was swiftest—and where the city's main sewer, the Cloaca Maxima, emptied.</note>. This is shown by many others, but especially by Caius Titius, a man of Lucilius’s generation, in the speech he gave in favor of the 
<margin>The Fannian Law.</margin>
Fannian Law <term>Lex Fannia: a sumptuary law passed in 161 BC to limit the amount spent on banquets and the number of guests.</term>. I provide his words here not only as evidence of the wolf-fish caught between the two bridges, but also because they easily reveal the morals by which most men lived at that time. Describing spendthrift men wandering into the forum to judge while drunk, and the things they usually say to one another, he speaks thus: "They play at dice with zeal, drenched in perfumes and surrounded by harlots. When it is the tenth hour <note>Roughly 4:00 PM in the Roman day.</note>, they order a boy to be called to go to the assembly to inquire what has happened in the forum: who spoke against a law, who spoke for it, what the tribes have ordered, or what they have forbidden. Then they go to the assembly themselves, lest they lose their own lawsuit by absence. As they go, there is no wine-jar in the alleyway that they do not fill <note>An idiom suggesting they were urinating frequently due to their heavy drinking.</note>, for they have bladders full of wine. They arrive at the assembly and order the case to be stated. Those whose business it is tell their story. The judge calls for witnesses. He himself goes out to urinate. When he returns, he says he has heard everything. He calls for the tablets. He looks at the writing. He can hardly keep his eyelids open because of the wine. When they go into deliberation, this is the speech: 'What business have I with these triflers? Let us rather drink honey-wine mixed with Greek wine, and eat a fat thrush and a good fish—a genuine wolf-fish caught between the two bridges!'" Thus says Titius. But even Lucilius, that sharp and violent poet, shows that he knew this fish was of excellent flavor when caught between the two bridges, and he calls such a man a "plate-licker" 
<margin>Plate-lickers.</margin>
<note>Original: *catillonem*. Derived from *catillus*, a small dish; it implies someone who licks the plates clean like a dog.</note>, namely one who hunts for filth right next to the riverbanks. Strictly speaking, however, those were called *catillones* who, when they came to the final feast of Hercules <note>Original: *poluctum Herculis*. A public banquet following a sacrifice to Hercules.</note>, would lick the small dishes. 
These are the verses of Lucilius:
> Furthermore, whatever each man wished to be served was prepared:
> One man was led by the lights and the platter of fattened birds;
> Another by a "plate-licker" caught between the two Tiber bridges.

It would be a long matter if I wished to list how many instruments of gluttony were either devised by their ingenuity or crafted with great effort. And these, no doubt, were the reasons why so many laws concerning dinners and expenses were brought before the people, and why it began to be commanded that men should eat lunch and dinner with their doors open. Thus, with the eyes of the citizens as witnesses, a limit might be placed on luxury. The 
<margin>The Orchian Law. The Fannian Law.</margin>
Orchian Law was the first of all laws regarding dinners to reach the people; it was proposed by Caius Orchius, a tribune of the plebs, upon the advice of the Senate in the third year after Cato had been Censor <note>181 BC.</note>. I skip its words because they are lengthy, but its main point prescribed the number of guests. This is the Orchian Law, against which Cato later cried out in his speeches, because more guests were being invited to dinner than its prescription allowed. When the increasing necessity of the situation called for a new law, the Fannian Law was passed twenty-two years after the Orchian Law, in the year after the founding of Rome—according to the opinion of Gellius—five hundred and eighty-eight <note>161 BC.</note>. Concerning this law, Samonicus Serenus reports thus: "The Fannian Law reached the people with the immense consensus of all ranks of the most holy Augustus. Neither the praetors nor the tribunes brought it forward, as they did most others, but the consuls themselves passed it based on the counsel and opinion of all good men, at a time when the Republic, through the luxury of banquets, was suffering greater damage than can be believed..."

### PAGE LXXIII

...exposed to harm. Indeed, matters had reached such a point that many freeborn boys, enticed by gluttony, would sell their chastity and their freedom. Many of the Roman commoners would come into the assembly soaked in wine and, while drunk, deliberate on the safety of the Republic. Thus says Sammonicus <note>Serenus Sammonicus was a Roman scholar and physician known for his vast library and writings on social history.</note>. However, the severity of the **Fannian Law** <note>Original: *lex Fannia* (161 BC). This was one of the earliest "sumptuary laws" designed to limit the cost of banquets.</note> surpassed the **Orchian Law** in this regard: under the earlier law, only the number of guests was restricted, and according to it, anyone was permitted to consume their entire estate among a few friends. But the Fannian Law set a limit on expenses at one hundred <term>asses</term> <note>The *as* was a bronze Roman coin. A limit of 100 asses was a strict attempt to curb the cost of a single meal.</note>. For this reason, it is called the "Hundred-As Law" by the poet Lucilius in his usual witty manner.

Eighteen years after the Fannian Law, the 
<margin>
The Didian Law.
</margin>
**Didian Law** followed. There were two reasons for its passage. The first and most important was so that all of Italy, not just the city of Rome, would be bound by the sumptuary law; for many believed that the Fannian Law applied only to the citizens within the city walls, and not to itself broadly. Secondly, it ensured that not only those who provided the lunches or dinners at great expense, but also those who had been invited and were present, would be subject to the penalties of the law.

After the Didian, the 
<margin>
The Licinian Law.
</margin>
**Licinian Law** was introduced by Publius Licinius Crassus the Wealthy. So much zeal was spent by the leading citizens in proposing and approving it that the Senate issued a decree commanding that, as soon as it was promulgated and before it was confirmed by the 
<margin>
The three-market-day period.
</margin>
<term>trinundinum</term> <note>The *trinundinum* was a mandatory 17-to-24-day waiting period (three market days) between the announcement of a law and the final vote.</note>, it should be observed by everyone as if the people’s assembly had already approved it. This law, with a few changes, agrees in most points with the Fannian Law. For in passing it, the authority of a new law was sought because the fear of the older law had faded away. 

By Hercules, this is just as happened with the **Twelve Tables** themselves; when their antiquity began to be held in contempt, the very things guarded by those laws were transferred into the names of other lawmakers. But the gist of the Licinian Law was that on the Kalends, the Nones, and the Roman market days, it was permitted for each person to spend only thirty *asses* per day on food. On other days which were not excepted, no more should be served than three pounds of dried meat and one pound of salted fish, along with whatever was produced from the earth, the vine, or the tree. 

I see what still stings. Was this, then, the judgment of a sober age, where the expense of dinners was coerced by such a legal prescription? Not so. For sumptuary laws were proposed by individuals because they sought to correct the vices of the entire state. And unless people were living with the worst and most wasteful habits, there certainly would have been no need to pass such laws. There is an old saying: "Good laws are born from bad habits." 

<margin>
The Cornelian Law.
</margin>
Following these came the 
<margin>
The sumptuary law which is also a food law.
</margin>
**Cornelian Law**, also a sumptuary law, which the dictator Cornelius Sulla brought forward. In this law, it was not the magnificence of banquets that was prohibited, nor was a limit placed on gluttony, but rather lower prices were imposed on goods. And by what goods, good gods! What exquisite and almost unknown types of delicacies! What fish and what choice morsels he names there! And yet he established lower prices for them, so that I might venture to say the cheapness of the foodstuffs incited men's minds to procure a greater supply of provisions, and even those with small means could serve their gluttony. I will say plainly what I feel: he seems to me exceedingly luxurious and wasteful to whom such great things are set out at feasts, even if they are free. 

Thus, this age is so much more prone to every kind of incontinence that most of these things included in the Sullan law as common knowledge are things none of us have ever even heard of. After Sulla died, the consul Lepidus passed a "food law" himself. For Cato calls sumptuary laws "food laws." From then, after a few years had passed, another law reached the people, proposed by **Antius Restio**. 
<margin>
The Law of Antius Restio.
</margin>
Although it was an excellent law, the stubbornness of luxury and the firm conspiracy of vices rendered it useless, though no one officially repealed it. However, a memorable story is told of Restio, the proposer of the law: as long as he lived, he never dined out again, so that he would not become a witness to the contempt for the law which he himself had passed for the public good.

To these laws I would add the edict on expenses proposed by **Antony**, who was later a Triumvir, if I did not think it unworthy to grant a place among those restraining expenses to Antony—whose usual costs for a dinner were surpassed only by the value of the 
<margin>
Cleopatra's luxury at banquets.
</margin>
pearl consumed by his wife **Cleopatra**. For while Antony, believing that whatever was produced by sea, land, or even sky was born to satisfy his own voracity, would thrust it down his throat, and being captivated by such things, wished to turn the Roman Empire into an Egyptian kingdom; his wife Cleopatra, who did not deign to be surpassed by the Romans even in luxury...

...the highest level of public benefit was at stake in this matter: for five years he devoted his efforts to ensuring that if anyone happened to catch a **parrotfish** <note>Original: *scarus*. A highly prized fish in antiquity, often imported from the Aegean to the Italian coast to stock the local waters.</note> among other fish, they would immediately return it to the sea unharmed and uninjured. When it is the tenth hour <note>Roughly 4:00 PM in the Roman day.</note>, they order a boy to be called to go to the <term>comitium</term> <note>The open-air public meeting space in the Roman Forum.</note> to inquire what has been done in the forum: who has argued for a law, who has argued against it, what the tribes have ordered, or what they have forbidden. From there, they go to the assembly place so they do not lose their own lawsuit by default. While they go, there is no jar in the alleyway that they do not fill, for they have bladders full of wine. They arrive at the assembly looking somber; they order the case to be stated. Those whose business it is tell the story. The judge calls for witnesses. He himself goes to urinate. When he returns, he says he has heard everything. He calls for the tablets. He looks at the writing. He can barely keep his eyelids open because of the wine. When they go into deliberation, this is the talk: 'What business have I with these triflers? Why don't we rather drink honey-wine mixed with Greek wine and eat a fat thrush and a good fish—a genuine wolf-fish that was caught between the two bridges?'"

Specifically, however, those were called **plate-lickers**
