### PAGE LXXIII

...detriments were suffered. Indeed, things had reached such a point that many noble boys, enticed by gluttony, would sell their chastity and their freedom. Many of the Roman plebeians would come to the assembly soaked in wine, and while drunk, they would deliberate on the safety of the republic. So says Sammonicus <note>Serenus Sammonicus, a scholar and polymath of the 2nd century AD, often cited for his knowledge of Roman customs.</note>. However, the severity of the **Fannian law** <note>The *Lex Fannia* (161 BC) was a significant attempt to limit banquet spending.</note> surpassed the **Orchian law** in this regard: under the former, only the number of diners was restricted, and it was still permitted for anyone to consume their entire estate among a few guests. But the Fannian law set a limit on expenses at one hundred *asses* <note>The *as* was a standard Roman bronze coin; one hundred was considered a modest amount for a feast.</note>. For this reason, the poet Lucilius <note>Gaius Lucilius, the "father" of Roman satire.</note>, in his witty manner, calls it the "hundred-asser" (*centussis*). Eighteen years after the Fannian law, the **Didian law** followed. 

<margin>
The Didian Law.
</margin>

The reasons for its passage were twofold. The first and most important was so that the entirety of Italy—not just the city of Rome—would be bound by sumptuary law; for the Italians believed the Fannian law had been drafted not for them, but only for the citizens within the city. Secondly, it ensured that not only those who provided lunches or dinners at great expense would be subject to the law’s penalties, but also those who had been invited to them and had merely attended. 

<margin>
The Licinian Law.
Three market days.
</margin>

After the Didian, the **Licinian law** was introduced by Publius Licinius Crassus "the Rich." Such great zeal was spent by the aristocrats to pass and approve this law that the Senate issued a decree: that as soon as it was promulgated—even before it was confirmed by the *trinundinum* <note>A period of three Roman market days (roughly 24 days) required by law for a proposal to be public before it could be voted upon.</note>—it should be observed by everyone as if it had already been approved by the people’s vote. In truth, this law agrees with the Fannian law in most respects, with a few changes. For in its passing, the authority of a new law was sought because the fear of the older law was fading away. By Hercules, this is just as happened with the **Twelve Tables** <note>The foundational laws of Rome, established c. 450 BC.</note> themselves: once they began to be held in contempt for their antiquity, those same provisions guarded by those laws were transferred into the names of other lawmakers. But the summary of the Licinian law was this: that on the Kalends, the Nones, and the Roman market days, it was permitted for each person to spend only thirty *asses* for the sake of eating. On other days which were not excepted, no more was to be served than three pounds of dried meat and a pound of salt-fish, as well as whatever is produced from the earth, the vine, or the tree. I see what causes a sting here. One might ask: "Is this the judgment of a sober age, where the expense of dinners was restrained by such a prescription of laws?" Not so. For sumptuary laws were brought forward by individuals to correct the vices of the entire state. Indeed, if people were not living with the worst and most extravagant habits, there certainly would have been no need to pass such laws. It is an old saying: **"Good laws are born from bad morals."** <note>Original Latin: *Leges bonae ex malis moribus procreantur*. A common Roman legal maxim suggesting that legislation is a reaction to social decay.</note>

<margin>
The Cornelian Law.
</margin>

The **Cornelian law** followed these, which was itself a sumptuary law proposed by the Dictator Cornelius Sulla. In this law, it was not the magnificence of the banquets that was prohibited, nor was a limit placed on gluttony, but rather lower prices were imposed on goods. And on what goods, good gods! On every exquisite and almost unknown kind of delicacy! What fish, what morsels did he not name there? And yet he established lower prices for them. I would dare to say that the low cost of these foods incited men’s minds to prepare vast quantities of provisions, so that even those with small means could serve their gluttony. I will say plainly what I feel: he seems to me exceptionally luxurious and prodigal for whom such great things are provided at feasts, even if they are cheap. Thus this age is so much more prone to every kind of incontinence that many of these things—which were included in the Sullan law as commonly known—none of us has ever encountered, even by hearsay. 

<margin>
The sumptuary law also known as the food law.
The law of Antius Restio.
</margin>

After Sulla died, the consul Lepidus passed a "food law" himself—for Cato calls sumptuary laws "food laws." Then, after a few years had passed, another law reached the people, introduced by **Antius Restio**. Although this law was excellent, the stubbornness of luxury and the firm alliance of vices rendered it useless, without anyone even repealing it. However, a memorable story is told of Restio, the author of the law: that for as long as he lived, he never dined out again, so that he would not become a witness to the contempt shown for the law he himself had carried for the public good. To these laws I would add the edict on expenses proposed by **Antony**, who was later a Triumvir, were I not to think it unworthy to grant a place among those restraining expenses to Antony—whose usual spending on a single dinner was surpassed by the estimated value of a single pearl consumed by his wife Cleopatra. 

<margin>
Cleopatra’s luxury in banquets.
</margin>

For while Antony believed that whatever was produced in the sea, on the land, or even in the sky was born to satisfy his gluttony, and subjected it all to his gullet and teeth—and for that reason, being captivated, wished to turn the Roman Empire into an Egyptian kingdom—his wife Cleopatra did not deign to be outdone even by the Romans in luxury.

->OF THE SATURNALIA<-

<margin>Cleopatra’s Pearl.</margin>
She challenged Antony with a bet that she could spend ten million sesterces <note>original: "sestertium centies"; roughly equivalent to the annual wages of 10,000 soldiers, an astronomical sum for a single meal.</note> on a single dinner. This seemed incredible to Antony. Without delay, he took the bet, a challenge worthy of the kitchen-minded Munatius Plancus <note>Lucius Munatius Plancus, a prominent Roman politician known for his shifting loyalties and love of luxury.</note>, who was chosen as the judge of this honorable contest. The next day, Cleopatra prepared a dinner for the waiting Antony that was certainly sumptuous, but not one that Antony would marvel at, as he recognized everything being served as part of their daily abundance. Then the Queen, smiling, asked for a bowl, into which she poured a small amount of sharp vinegar. She then hurriedly took a pearl <note>term: "unio" (literally 'unique'); a large, high-quality pearl found alone in a shell.</note> from one of her ears and dropped it in. Once it had quickly dissolved—as is the nature of that stone—she swallowed it. And since she had won the bet by this act (for the single pearl was undeniably worth ten million sesterces), she reached her hand toward the pearl on her other ear to do the same, had not Munatius Plancus, the most severe judge, quickly pronounced Antony defeated. As for the size of that pearl, it can be gathered from the fact that the one which remained was later taken to Rome after the Queen was conquered and Egypt captured. It was cut in two, and from the one pearl, two were made, which were placed on the statue of Venus as a marvel of magnitude in the temple called the 
<margin>The Pantheon temple.</margin>
Pantheon.

### On the Walnut. Chapter 10.

<margin>The Walnut.</margin>
While Furius was still speaking, the sweetmeats <note>original: "bellaria"; dainties or desserts served at the end of a meal.</note> brought in for the second course provided the starting point for a new conversation. Symmachus, handling two nuts with his hand, said: "I would like to hear from you, Servius, why nuts have such varied names, what their origin is, or why so many fruits are called by this one name. Yet they are distinct both in name and in flavor. I want you to first explain those nuts that occur to your memory from your frequent reading." Servius replied: "That nut, the walnut <note>original: "iuglans"</note>, is thought by some to be named from 'helping' <note>original: "iuvando"</note> and from 'acorn' <note>original: "glans"</note>. However, Gaius, in his book on the *Signification of Words*, records this: the walnut tree was named just as if it were 'Jupiter's acorn' <note>original: "Iovis glans"</note>. For that genus of tree has nuts that are of a sweeter flavor than the common acorn. The ancients, who considered this fruit excellent and similar to an acorn, and the tree itself worthy of a god, called it 'Jupiter’s acorn,' which is now called 'walnut' with the letters compressed. Cloatius and Verrius, in their books on Greek derivations, record it this way: 'walnut' <note>original: "iuglans"</note> is as if it were 'God-acorn' <note>original: "diuglans"</note>, that is, the *acorn of Zeus* <note>original: "Διὸς βαλανος" (Dios balanos)</note>, as Theophrastus says. The Greeks also call this the 'Royal nut' <note>original: "basilicam" / "βασιλικὸν"</note>."

### On the Hazelnut. Chapter 11.

<margin>
The Royal nut.
The Hazelnut or Praenestine nut.
The Hazel tree.
The Carstani people.
The Pontic nut.
</margin>
This hazelnut <note>original: "nux auellana"</note>, or Praenestine nut, which is the same thing, comes from the tree called the hazel <note>original: "corylus"</note>, of which Virgil said: 'plant the hazel.' There is a nation of people near the territory of Praeneste who are called the Carstani, who speak of *unripe nuts* <note>original: "αωρων καρυων" (aoron karuon)</note>. Varro mentions this in his philosophical dialogue titled *Marius on Fortune*: 'the same, namely, the Praenestine nuts.' There is also that passage in Naevius in the play *The Soothsayer*: 'Who was it yesterday at your house, the guests from Praeneste and Lanuvium? Both were received with food as was fitting; to one was given an empty, soggy dish, to the others, nuts were poured out on the slope.' Furthermore, the Greeks call this the 'Pontic nut,' as each nation gives this nut a name from the place where it grows most abundantly.

### On the Chestnut. Chapter 12.

<margin>
The Chestnut nut, also called Heracleotic.
The Greek nut, which is also called the Almond and the Thasian.
The Molluscan nut, which is also the Peach.
</margin>
The chestnut nut, of which Virgil says: 'And chestnut nuts,' is also called the Heracleotic nut. For the learned man Oppius, in the book he wrote on *Wild Trees*, says this: 'This Heracleotic nut, which some call the chestnut.' Likewise the Pontic nut, and even those called 'Royal walnuts,' produce buds and flowers at the same time as the Greek nuts. Now I must say what the 'Greek nut' is—and saying this, he took an almond from the dish and showed it—'This is the Greek nut, which is also called the almond <note>original: "amygdala"</note>.' But this same nut is also called the Thasian nut. Cloatius is a witness to this in the fourth book of his *Arrangement of Greek Words*, when he says: 'The Greek nut is the almond.' Acca, indeed, in her *Supplication*, says: 'Add the Greek nut and as much honeycomb as you please.' Although the winter season forbids it to us, since we are speaking of nuts, we should not leave the 'Molluscan' nut unmentioned. Plautus mentions it in *The Casket Comedy* <note>original: "Cistellaria" (OCR says "calcedo")</note> when he says: 'The Molluscan nut hung over the roof-tiles.' Behold, Plautus names it indeed, but he does not explain what the Molluscan nut is."

There is also the peach <note>original: "perficum"; an archaic term for the peach, *Prunus persica*</note> as it is commonly called; it is also called the "molluscan nut," evidently because it is softer than all other nuts. A suitable witness to this fact is Sueuius, a man of great learning, in his idyll titled *The Salad* <note>original: "moretum"; a poem describing the preparation of a rustic herb-and-cheese spread</note>. > Partly peaches—a name that is carried down
> For this reason: because those who once in fierce battles
> Against the King of Pontus, named Alexander the Great <note>The poet Sueuius appears to confuse Alexander the Great with later Roman wars against Eastern kings like Mithridates, or perhaps refers to the peach's Persian origins during Alexander's era.</note>
> Brought them back to their own Persia. After their return,
> They sowed this kind of tree in the chosen Greek lands,
> Giving new fruits to mortals.
> This is the molluscan nut, lest anyone should err in ignorance."

### ¶ On the Tarentine Nut. Chapter XIII.

<margin>Tarentine nut. Tarentum.</margin>
The Tarentine nut is so named because it is so soft that it breaks almost as soon as it is touched. Regarding this, in the book of Favorinus <note>a Roman philosopher and polymath</note>, it is found: "Some speak of Tarentine sheep or nuts which are from Tarentum, which in the Sabine tongue means 'soft.'" This is why Varro also thinks they are called Tarentines in his first book *To Libo*. Horace also seems to fall into this error when he says: "And soft Tarentum."

### ¶ On the Pine Nut. Chapter XIIII.

<margin>Pine nut.</margin>
The pine nut gave us these kernels which have been set before us. Plautus says in *The Casket Comedy* that he who wants the kernels from the nut must break the nut. And since we see apples <note>term: "mala"; in Latin, this broad category included many fleshy fruits like peaches, quinces, and pomegranates, not just what we call apples today.</note> mixed in with the desserts, we must discuss the kinds of apples after the nuts. There are writers on agriculture who divide nuts and apples thus: they call "nut" any fruit covered by a hard shell on the outside with the edible part inside. But an "apple" is that which has the edible part on the outside and encloses something hard within. According to this definition, the peach, which the poet Sueuius previously counted among the nuts, should rather be counted among the apples. Having established this, the types of apples must be enumerated, which Cloatius, in the fourth book of his *Arrangement of Greek Words*, lists so diligently. The types of apples are: the Armenian [apricot], the quince, the citron,
<margin>Kinds of apples. Peach. Citron.</margin>
the honey-quince, the codiriuan, the must-apple, the Martian, the orbicular, the pomegranate-like, the early-ripener, the shriveled, the Punic [pomegranate], the peach, the Quirian, the Psivian, the red, the Scandian, the wild, the Sirutian, the Tiburtine, and the Verian. You see the peach is counted among the apples by Cloatius; it has kept the name of its origin, even though it has long been a sprout of our own soil. As for what Cloatius says, the peach itself is an apple, according to Virgil: "The lucky apple than which none is more excellent," <note>referring to *Georgics* 2.126</note> and so forth. And so that no one doubts Virgil said this about the citron, hear what Oppius says in his book *On Wild Trees*: "The citron tree is likewise an apple, as is the peach; one is produced in Italy, the other in Media." And a little later, speaking of the citron, he says: "It is most fragrant; placed among clothes, it kills moths. It is also said to be an antidote to poisons; when ground and drunk with wine, it saves those drinking it by the purging of its powers. Citron-apples are produced in the province at all times; for some are picked, while others ripen." You see here both the citron named and all the signs provided which Virgil spoke of, although Virgil did not use the name "citron." For Homer also calls the citron *thyon* <note>original: "θύον"; an aromatic wood or fruit</note>, showing it to be a fragrant fruit: "they call it thyon" <note>original: "θύον αποκαλούση ο Δωδει"</note>. And what Oppius says about placing the citron among clothes, Homer also signifies when he mentions "garments" <note>original: "ειματα"</note>. Hence the poet Naevius says in *The Punic War*: "A citron-scented garment."

### ¶ On Pears. Chapter XV.

<margin>Citron-scented garment. Kinds of pears.</margin>
As for these pears we see, a numerous variety of names distinguishes them. For Cloatius describes their names as follows: the Antian, the gourd-pear, the Ciritan, the Cerviscan, the stony, the Crustuminian, the Deciman, the Greekling, the Lollian, the Lanuvian, the Laurel-pear, the Lateresian, the Marapian, the Milesian, the Myrtle-pear, the Nevian, the orbicular, the Pcian, the reddish, the Signine, the Tullian, the Tician, the Turrinian, the early-ripener, the Volemium, the medlar-pear, the late-sown, the late-Sextilian, the late-Tarentine, and the late-Valerian.

LXXXI

THE SATURNALIA

<margin>
Varieties of figs.
</margin>
**D**ried figs also remind us to list the varieties of figs. On this subject, the same Cloatius <note>Cloatius Verus, a Roman grammarian who wrote on technical vocabulary</note> instructs us, following others. For he enumerates the various types of figs according to his diligent custom: the African, the little-white, the reed-fig, the left-handed black, the marsh-fig, the Augustan, the twice-bearing, the Carian, the Chalcidian, the white, the black, the Calpurnian, the Chian, the gourd-fig, the hard-skinned, the Herculean, the Lavian, the player-fig, the
<margin>
The lucky and unlucky fig.
Lucky and unlucky trees.
</margin>
Leptoludian, the Marsic, the Numidian, the dusky, the Pompeian, the early-ripener, the Tellan, and the black. It should be known that the white fig is among the lucky trees, whereas the black is among the unlucky ones. The pontiffs <note>high-ranking priests in Rome who oversaw religious law</note> teach us both. For Veranius <note>an author on pontifical law</note> says regarding pontifical terminology: "Those trees are considered 'lucky' <note>original: "fœlices"</note> which are: the oak, the winter-oak, the holm-oak, the cork-tree, the beech, the hazel, the mountain-ash, the white fig, the pear, the apple, the vine, the plum, the cornelian cherry, and the lotus." However, Tarquinius Priscus <note>the legendary fifth King of Rome</note> says the following in his book on trees: "The trees that are under the protection of the 'averting' gods <note>gods who turn away evil, such as Apollo or Mars</note> are named 'unlucky' <note>original: "infœlices"</note>. These include the blood-red shrub, the lucky-colored black fig—even though it bears black berries and black fruit—as well as the holly, the wild pear, the butcher's broom, the bramble, and the brier. It is fitting to order that the portents of omens be burned with these." Furthermore, why do we find the fig separated from 'pomes' <note>generic term for fleshy fruits</note> by reliable authors, as if it were not a pome? Afranius says in *Selius*: "Pome, vegetable, fig, grape." And also Cicero in the third book of his *Oeconomicus*: "He neither plants the vine, nor does he diligently cultivate what is planted; he has neither olives, figs, nor pomes." Nor should it be ignored that the fig is the only one of all trees that does not flower. The word 'milk' <note>original: "lactis"</note> is specifically used for the sap of figs. Unripe figs are called *grossi*; the Greeks call these *olynthous* <note>original: "ὀλύνθους"</note>. Marcus Attilius says: "Among thousands of such figs you will not see an unripe one." And a little later he says: "You may take from another the unripe figs flowing with milk." And Postumius Albinus in the first book of his *Annals* says of Brutus: "And while he was pretending to be a fool and a 'Brutus' <note>the name Brutus literally meant 'dullard' or 'heavy'</note>, he used to eat little unripe figs with honey."

Just as these are the varieties of grapes: the Aminean—named from the region, for there were Amineans where Falernum is now—the little-donkey, the dark-grape, the white-producer, the Albena, the bee-grape, the Apician, the cow-breast <note>original: "bumamia"; likely the "bumastos" or "cow-breast" grape due to its size</note>—or as the Greeks say *boumastos* <note>original: "βόνια θοσ," likely a printer's error for "βουμαστοί"</note>—the hard-skinned, the wild-vine, the black-pith, the Maronian, the Mareotic, the Numentan, the early-ripener, the Pramnian, the Psithian, the capped-grape, the Rhodian, the garland-grape, the Venus-grape, the speckled-grape, and the Lagean. During these discussions, Praetextatus remarked: "I would wish to listen to our servant <note>referring to the reader or the one providing the technical lists</note> longer, but the hour warns us that we should go and enjoy the dawn-light speech of Symmachus at his home." And so the party dispersed.

---

->On emotional speech.<-

### Chapter I.

<margin>Speeches of passion.</margin>
Now let us see by what tone of speech <term>pathos</term> <note>original: "pathos"; the Greek word for emotion or suffering, used here as a technical term for emotional rhetoric</note> is expressed. And first, let us ask what is taught about such speech by the rhetorical art. For it is necessary that emotional speech be directed either toward indignation or toward pity, which are called <term>oiktos and deinosis</term> <note>original: "οἶκτος καὶ Δείνωσις"; Greek rhetorical terms for "pity" and "vehemence" or "indignation"</note> by the Greeks. One of these is necessary for the accuser, the other for the defendant. It is also necessary that it have an abrupt beginning, since it is not fitting for those who are truly indignant to begin in a gentle manner. Therefore, in Virgil, the goddess Juno begins thus: "Why do you force me to break the deep silence?" <note>Aeneid 10.6</note> And elsewhere: "Am I to desist from my undertaking, defeated?" <note>Aeneid 1.37</note> And elsewhere: "Alas, the hated race and the fates of the Phrygians contrary to our own!" <note>Aeneid 7.293</note> And Dido: "Shall we die unavenged? But let us die," she says. <note>Aeneid 4.659</note> And again: "O Jupiter, will he go?" <note>Aeneid 4.590</note> He says this here. And Priam: "But to you, for your crime," he exclaims, "for such daring deeds." <note>Aeneid 2.535</note> Not only should the beginning be such, but every emotional speech should (if possible) fluctuate with both short sentences and frequent changes of rhetorical figures, much like the tide of a boiling rage.

Let one Virgilian speech, therefore, serve as our example: "Alas, the hated race." It begins with an <term>ecphonesis</term> <note>original: "ecphoneſi"; an emotional exclamation</note>. Then follow short little questions: "Did they not fall on the Sigean plains? Could the captives not be captured? Did burning Troy consume the men?" Then follows <term>hyperbole</term>: "They found a way through the midst of the battle-lines and through the midst of the fires." Then <term>irony</term>: "But I believe my divine powers at last lie exhausted; I have rested, not sated by hatred." Then she complains of her own ineffective daring: "Daring to follow them through the waves and to oppose myself to the fugitives on the whole sea." After this comes a second hyperbole: "Exhausted against the Teucrians <note>the Trojans</note>: the powers of both sky and sea." Then come scattered complaints: "What did the Syrtes or Scylla do for me? What did the vast Charybdis profit?" 

Then an argument "from the lesser" <note>original: "a minore"; a logic-based rhetorical device</note> is joined, so that the emotion may be increased: "Mars was able to destroy the immense race of the Lapiths." Since Mars is a "lesser" person than Juno, this follows: "But I, the great wife of Jove..." Then, when she had compared the causes, consider with what force the goddess said: "Wretched me, who turned myself into all things." She did not say "I cannot destroy Aeneas," but "I am defeated by Aeneas." Then she steels herself for harm; and as is characteristic of one who is angry, even if she despairs that her plan can be fully perfected, she is yet content merely to hinder:

> "If I cannot bend the heavens, I will move the underworld. <note>original: "Flectere ſi nequeo ſuperos: acheronta mouebo" - Aeneid 7.312</note>
> Let it be that it will not be granted to bar him from the Latin kingdoms:
> Yet it is permitted to drag it out and add delays to such great matters.
> Yet it is permitted to cut off the peoples of both kings."

After these things, at the very end—which angry people do gladly—she curses: "You shall be dowered with Trojan and Rutulian blood, O maiden." And immediately she adds a suitable argument from a similar case: "Nor was the daughter of Cisseus <note>Hecuba, who dreamed she gave birth to a torch</note> alone pregnant with a torch, having brought forth wedding fires." You see how often he changed the speech and varied it with frequent figures; because anger, which is a brief madness, cannot maintain one single continuous sense while speaking. 

Nor are speeches moving the listener to pity lacking in the same author. Turnus says to Juturna: "Was it so that you might see the cruel death of your wretched brother?" And the same character, when he increases the ill-will toward the one who killed his friends: "I myself saw Muranus before my eyes, calling me with his voice." And again, when he made his own fortune appear miserable so that he might not be spared as a conquered man: "You have conquered; and the Ausonians have seen me, conquered, stretching out my palms." The same says: "Those whom I would least wish." And there are the prayers of others begging for life: "By you, by the parents who bore you such as you are," and similar phrases.

OF THE SATURNALIA
Page LXXI

<margin>Emotional appeal through pity: and according to age.</margin>

## On the condition of emotional speech, Chapter II.

<image-desc>Ornate decorative initial 'N' in a square frame, featuring intricate foliate designs and scrolls.</image-desc>
Now let us speak of the condition of <term>pathos</term> <note>original: "pathos"; a Greek term for the quality in art that evokes pity or sadness</note>: that which is found either in age or in physical weakness and the other qualities that follow. Virgil maintained this skillfully: so that he might move an emotional appeal of pity from every stage of life. From infancy: "The souls of infants weeping at the very threshold." <note>original: "Infantūqƺ animæ flentes in limine primo"; Aeneid 6.427</note> From boyhood: "Unhappy boy and an unequal match for Achilles." <note>original: "Infelix puer atqƺ impar cōgressus achilli"; Aeneid 1.475</note> And "the little Iulus was stretching his hands toward his father." <note>original: "Et parūuūqƺ patri tēdebat iulum"; Aeneid 2.674</note> This shows that the danger is no less pitiable in a small child than in a son. And "does his wife survive, and the boy Ascanius?" <note>original: "Et superest cōiunx ne excusaƭ ascaniusqƺ pueri?"; Aeneid 2.597</note> And elsewhere: "and the misfortunes of little Iulus." <note>original: "parui casus iuli"; Aeneid 10.524</note> From youth indeed: "Youths placed on funeral pyres before the eyes of their parents." <note>original: "Impositiqƺ rogis iuuenes ante ora parentū"; Aeneid 6.308</note> "And downy cheeks, and the paleness in a youthful body." <note>original: "Pubētesqƺ genæ iuuenili in corpore pallor"; Aeneid 9.754</note> From old age: "Pity the old age of Daunus." <note>original: "Dauni miserere senectæ"; Aeneid 12.934</note> And "the unhappy Aletes is led along, worn out by time." <note>original: "Et Ducitur infelix æuo confectus aletes"; Aeneid 9.246</note> And "he defiles his white hair with much dust." <note>original: "Et caniciē multo deformat puluere"; Aeneid 12.611</note>

<margin>Emotional appeal through fortune.</margin>
¶ He also moved an emotional appeal from the state of fortune: sometimes to pity, sometimes to indignation. Toward pity: "Once the proud ruler of so many peoples and lands of Asia." <note>original: "Tot quōdā populis terrisqƺ superbū regnatorē asiæ"; Aeneid 2.556</note> And Sinon: "And we too have carried some name and glory." <note>original: "Et nos aliqd nomēqƺ decusqƺ gessimus"; Aeneid 2.89</note> And "Once most wealthy in Ausonian fields." <note>original: "Et Ausoniis olim ditissīmus aruis"; Aeneid 10.563</note> Toward indignation indeed from the words of Dido: "And will the stranger have mocked our kingdoms?" <note>original: "Et nostris illuseris aduena regnis"; Aeneid 4.591</note> For he elegantly increases her sense of injury from the contempt shown by Aeneas. And Amata: "Is Lavinia given to be led by Teucrian exiles?" <note>original: "Exulibus ne datur ducenda lauinia teucris?"; Aeneid 7.359</note> And Numanus: "Twice-captured Phrygians." <note>original: "Bis capti phryges"; Aeneid 9.599</note>

<margin>Emotional appeal through weakness.</margin>
¶ He moved emotional pity also from physical weakness. "Since the father of the gods and king of men blasted me with the winds of his thunderbolt and touched me with fire." <note>original: "Ex quo me diuū pater atqƺ hoīum rex Fulminis afflauit uentis: & contigit igne"; Aeneid 2.648. This refers to Anchises, who was crippled by Zeus.</note> And elsewhere: "And nostrils lopped off with a shameful wound." <note>original: "Et truncas inhonesto uulnere nares"; Aeneid 6.497</note> And concerning Mezentius: "He raises himself upon his sick thigh." <note>original: "Attollit in ægrum se fæmur"; Aeneid 10.856</note> And "Hither and thither the head hung from each shoulder." <note>original: "Et Huc caput atqƺ illuc humero ex utroque pependit"; Aeneid 9.436</note> And "Your severed right hand, Larides, seeks its owner." <note>original: "Et te decisa suum laride dextera quærit"; Aeneid 10.395</note> And "the fierce man, with straps passed through his swollen feet, in bloody dust." <note>original: "Et acerqƺ cruento Puluere perqƺ pedes traiectus lora tumentes"; Aeneid 2.272-273, describing the body of Hector.</note>

<margin>Emotional appeal through place.</margin>
¶ He frequently moved emotional pity from the place: "While I drag out my life in the woods among the desert lairs of beasts and homes." <note>original: "Quū uitā in siluis inter deserta ferarum Lustra domosqƺ traho"; Aeneid 3.646</note> "And I wander the deserts of Libya." <note>original: "lybiæ deserta peragro"; Aeneid 1.384</note> And "But we others shall go hence to thirsty Africans. Some of us will reach Scythia and the swift Oaxes of Crete." <note>original: "Et At nos hinc alii sitiētes ibimus afros. Pars scythiam & rapidū cretæ ueniemus oaxē"; Eclogues 1.64-65</note> And that excellently and briefly: "Three times he had dragged Hector around the Trojan walls." <note>original: "Ter circū iliacos raptauerat hectora muros"; Aeneid 1.483</note> Trojan—that is, the walls of his fatherland, which he himself had defended, for which he had fought effectively for the space of ten years. And this: "We flee the fatherland." <note>original: "Nos patriā fugimus"; Eclogues 1.4</note> And "When I leave the tears and ports of the fatherland." <note>original: "Et littora quū patriæ lachrymās portusqƺ relinquo"; Aeneid 3.10</note> And "Dying, he remembers sweet fields." <note>original: "Et dulces moriens reminiscitur agros"; Aeneid 10.782</note> And "The Laurentine shore holds Mimas, unknown... his home was in high Lyrnesus, his grave on Laurentine soil." <note>original: "Ignarū laurens habet ora mimanta Lyrnesi domus alta solo laurente sepulchrum"; Aeneid 10.704-706</note> And so that he might show Agamemnon was unworthily slain, he invoked the place: "He met death just inside the first threshold." <note>original: "Prima iter limina dextra oppetiit"; Aeneid 11.267</note> And this: "Within the walls of the fatherland and amid the safety of homes." <note>original: "Mœnibus in patriis atqƺ iter tuta domorū"</note> Truly, a sacred place moves the chief emotional appeal. He brings in the slain Orpheus and makes his death more pitiable because of the place: "Among the sacred rites of the gods and the nightly revels of Bacchus." <note>original: "Inter sacra deū nocturniqƺ orgia bacchi"; Georgics 4.521</note> And in the destruction of Troy: "Through the houses and religious thresholds of the gods." <note>original: "Perqƺ domos & religiosa deorum limina"; Aeneid 2.487</note> Also the abduction of Cassandra, or the violation which a sacred place makes more pitiable: "Behold, she was being dragged from the temple and the inner shrines of Minerva." <note>original: "ecce trahebaƭ a tēplo adytisqƺ mineruæ"; Aeneid 2.404</note> and elsewhere: "He fell at the altar of the god powerful in arms." <note>original: "Diue armipotentis ad arā pcubuit"</note> And Andromache, when she spoke of the death of Pyrrhus, so that she might express the hatefulness of the killer: "He catches the unwary man and cuts him down at his father's altars." <note>original: "Excipit icautū patriasqƺ obtruncat ad aras"; Aeneid 3.332</note> And Venus, when Aeneas is tossed on the sea by the anger of Juno, complains with indignation about the place to Neptune: "Having dared this in your realms?" <note>original: "In regnis hoc ausa tuis"; Aeneid 1.141</note>

<margin>Emotional appeal through time.</margin>
¶ He often created emotional appeal for himself from the time: "Before they could taste the pastures of Troy and drink from the Xanthus." <note>original: "Prius q̃ Pabula gustassent troiæ xāthūqƺ bibissēt"; Aeneid 1.472</note> And Orpheus, pitiable from long grief: "They say he wept for seven whole months in order." <note>original: "Septem illum totos perhibent ex ordine mēses"; Georgics 4.507</note> And Palinurus: "Scarcely on the fourth light did I see Italy." <note>original: "Vix lumine quarto prospexi Italiam"; Aeneid 6.355</note> And Achaemenides: "Now the third horns of the moon are filling with light." <note>original: "Tertia iā lunæ se cornua lumine complent"; Aeneid 3.645</note> And "Now the seventh summer turns since the fall of Troy." <note>original: "Septima post troiæ excidium iam uertitur æstas"; Aeneid 1.755</note>

<margin>Emotional appeal through cause.</margin>
¶ Emotional appeal from the cause is frequent in his work; for truly, the reason often makes a matter seem either atrocious or pitiable. As Cicero says against Verres <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the famous Roman orator, prosecuting the corrupt governor Verres</note>: about the one who asked for money from parents for the burial of those killed in prison. For this was unworthy not so much because money was requested or exacted, but because of this specific reason. And Demosthenes, when he complains that someone was circumvented by malice, increases the indignation from the cause. He says, "He circumvented the arbitrator who had judged between me and him with integrity." Therefore, Virgil also excellently drew emotion from this topic. He says, "Galaesus is killed in the battle." This in itself is not worthy of pity in a time of war, but he added the cause: while he was [striving for] peace...

<meta>catchword: my</meta>

By citing famous examples like the death of Hector or the exile of Aeneas, the author demonstrates the rhetorical power of adding specific human details to a narrative.</summary>

...presents itself in the middle. In another place, the poet says: "He lays low the unlucky man." <note>original: "Sternit infelix"; Aeneid 12.541</note> Then he adds a cause that makes the situation more piteous: "by a wound intended for another." <note>original: "aliēo uulnere"; i.e., when the weapon had been sent toward someone else</note> And when he wished to describe Palamedes being unworthily slain: "Whom the Greeks, under a false charge of treason, sent down to death, innocent as he was, by an unspeakable judgment, because he forbade the war." <note>original: "Quē falsa sub pditione pelasgī. Insontē infandī iudicio: qa bella uetabat Demifere neci"; Aeneid 2.82-85</note> And Aeneas, to show the greatness of his own fear, skillfully established the cause: "Fearing equally for his companion and his burden." <note>original: "Pariter comitiq; oneriq; timēte"; Aeneid 2.729</note> Why did Iapyx live without glory, having despised all other skills, as the poet says? He provides the cause: "That he might prolong the fate of his dying parent." <note>original: "Ille ut depositi pferret fata parētis"; Aeneid 12.395</note> Of the same kind is the line: "Your own piety deceives you, unwary one." <note>original: "Fallit te incautū pietas tua"; Aeneid 10.812</note> For this cause made him a victim to his enemies and thus pitiable. But when Aeneas urges that the slain be buried, what cause does he put forward? "Those who with their blood won this country for us." <note>original: "Qui sanguine nobis. Hanc patriam pepere suo"; Aeneid 11.24-25</note> Furthermore, indignation is also demonstrated by a cause, as in this instance: "Groaning much at his disgrace and the blows of the proud victor." <note>original: "Multa gemens ignominiam plagasq; superbi Victoris"; Virgil, Georgics 3.226</note> Then: "The loves he lost while unavenged." <note>original: "Tum quos amisit inultus amores"; Aeneid 10.396</note> And this, from the cause of an indignant person’s emotion: "Does that grief touch the sons of Atreus alone? Is it permitted for Mycenae alone to take up arms?" <note>original: "An solos tangit atridas Iste dolor? solisq; licet capere arma mycenis?"; Aeneid 9.138</note> And this: "But you, Alban, should have stood by your word." <note>original: "At tu dictis albane maneres"; Aeneid 8.643. Referring to Mettius Fufetius, who betrayed an alliance.</note> And all those other lines: "This one sold his country for gold." <note>original: "Vendidit hic auro patriam"; Aeneid 6.621</note> And: "Those who were slain for adultery; nor did they share a portion with their own." <note>original: "Quiq; ob adulterium cæsi: Nec partem posuere suis"; Aeneid 6.612</note>

<margin>Pathos from manner and from matter</margin>
To move <term>pathos</term> <note>the quality that evokes pity or sadness</note>, the poet did not overlook those two categories which rhetoricians call "manner" and "matter." Manner is when I say: "he killed him openly or secretly." Matter is when I say: "with a sword or by poison." Demosthenes, speaking of manner, creates ill-will against Meidias by saying he was "struck with a buskin" <note>Demosthenes, Against Meidias; the buskin was a high-heeled boot worn by tragic actors</note>; Cicero says of Verres that "a certain naked man was placed upon a statue by him." <note>Cicero, Against Verres 2.4.86</note> Virgil speaks no less vividly: "He dragged him, trembling, to the very altars, and sliding in the abundant blood of his son." <note>original: "Altaria ad ipsa tremēte Traxit: & in multo lapsantem sanguine nati"; Aeneid 2.550-551</note> And: "He buried his sword up to the hilt." <note>original: "Et capulo tenus abdidit ensem"; Aeneid 2.553</note> And all those descriptions are from manner: "And a huge vulture with a hooked beak tearing at the immortal liver," <note>original: "Rostroq; immanis uultur adunco Immortale iecur tondens"; Aeneid 6.597. Referring to the punishment of Tityos.</note> and so on. And: "Those over whom a black flint, just about to slip, hangs like one already falling." <note>original: "Et quos super atra silex iam iā lapsura cadenti imminet assimilis"; Aeneid 6.602</note> But he also often stirs mercy from manner, as concerning Orpheus: "They scattered the youth over the wide fields." <note>original: "Latos iuuenē sparfẽ re per agros"; Georgics 4.522</note> And this: "The south wind overwhelmed them, rolling the men and the ship in the water." <note>original: "Obruit auster aqua inuoluens naueq; uirosq;"; Aeneid 1.115</note> And: "Others roll a huge stone." <note>original: "Et faxū ingēs uoluūt alii"; Aeneid 6.616</note> And: "Indeed, he even joined dead bodies to living ones." <note>original: "Mortua quin etiā iūgebat corpora uiuis"; Aeneid 8.485. Referring to the king Mezentius.</note> And in the *Georgics*: "Nor was the way of death simple," <note>original: "Nec uia mortis erat simplex"; Georgics 3.482</note> and the rest regarding the description of the plague. But "matter" also moves pathos among rhetoricians, as when Cicero complains of a flame "made from green wood," and someone "killed there, trapped by the smoke." <note>Cicero, Against Verres 2.5.117</note> This is from "matter," because here he used smoke as the material for killing, just as another uses a sword or another poison; and therefore the sharpest pathos is moved from this. He does the same when he complains of a "Roman citizen being beaten with whips." You will find the same in Virgil: "But the omnipotent father hurled his bolt through the thick clouds; not he with torches and the smoky light of brands," <note>original: "At pater omnipotens densa inter nubila telū Contorsit: nō ille faces & fumea tædis"; Aeneid 6.592-593. Comparing Jupiter’s true lightning to Salmoneus's fake torches.</note> and so on. He elegantly mocked the matter of that one [Salmoneus], but from the true and powerful matter of the father, he expressed wrath. We shall indeed enumerate the individual things from which pathos is born among rhetoricians, in which we will show the practice of Maro <note>Virgil's cognomen or family name</note>. But sometimes Virgil uses two or more categories joined in one matter to increase the pathos, as in the case of Turnus, from his age: "Pity a long-lived parent." <note>original: "Miserere parentis Longæui"; Aeneid 12.932</note> From location: "Whom now, sad, his fatherland Ardea divides by a great distance." <note>original: "Quem nūc mœstum patria ardea longe diuidit"; Aeneid 7.411-412</note> And concerning Cassandra, from manner: "behold, she was being dragged." <note>original: "ecce trahebatur"; Aeneid 2.403</note> From her physical appearance: "The virgin daughter of Priam with disheveled hair." <note>original: "Passis priameia uirgo crinibus"; Aeneid 2.403</note> From location: "From the temple and shrines of Minerva." <note>original: "A templo adytisq; mineruæ"; Aeneid 2.404</note> And concerning Agamemnon, from his fatherland: "The Mycenaean himself." <note>original: "Ipse mycenæus"; Aeneid 11.266</note> From fortune: "Leader of the great Achaeans." <note>original: "Magnorum ductor achiuū"; Aeneid 11.267</note> From necessity: "Of his wife." <note>original: "Coniugis"; Aeneid 11.267</note> From location: "The adulterer lurked just inside the first threshold." <note>original: "Prima inter limina subfedit adulter"; Aeneid 11.268</note> He is also accustomed to move pathos silently, as if through a definition; when he seeks to move pity, it is not said clearly, but is given to be understood, as when Mezentius says: "Now the wound is driven deep." <note>original: "Nūc alte uulnus adactum"; Aeneid 10.850</note> For what else is to be understood from this, except that this "deep wound" is to lose his son? And again the same: "This was the only way by which you could destroy me." <note>original: "Hæc uia sola fuit qua perdere posses"; Aeneid 10.879</note> But here, "to perish" must be understood as losing his son. And when Juturna complains that she is forbidden to help her brother: "Am I immortal?" <note>original: "Immortalis ego"; Aeneid 12.882</note> For what follows is that it is not immortality to live in grief. These things, as I have said, have the force of a definition and were elegantly introduced by the poet.

### ¶ Pathos from similarity. Chapter III.

<margin>Pathos from circumstances.</margin>
There are also in the rhetorical art these categories for moving pathos, which are called "circumstances" <note>original: "circa rem"</note>; and they are very suitable for moving the emotions: the first of which is from...

PAGE LXXXI.

# OF THE SATURNALIA

<margin>Pathos from example</margin>
Pathos is also derived from a similar example. Of this, there are three species: the example, the parable, and the image. In Greek, these are <term>paradeigma</term> (example), <term>parabole</term> (comparison), and <term>eikon</term> (image). Regarding the example, Virgil writes:
> If Orpheus could summon the ghost of his wife, 
> relying on his Thracian lyre and tuneful strings. 
> If Pollux redeemed his brother by an alternating death. <note>Aeneid 6.119–121. Aeneas argues that if these heroes were allowed to visit the underworld, he should be too.</note>

<margin>Pathos from fortune</margin>
¶ Why mention Theseus? Why the great Hercules? Even Antenor could escape from the midst of the Greeks. All these instances move us to pity because it seems unworthy that something granted to others should be denied to the speaker. Next, see how the poet increases the sense of resentment: *If Orpheus could summon the ghost of his wife.* You have a different cause here: there it was for a wife, here for a father; there to summon her back, here merely to see him. There, Orpheus relied on his Thracian lyre. Here, Aeneas’s own pity is mocked. *If Pollux redeemed his brother by an alternating death.* Thus he goes and returns on the path so many times. This is already a matter of degree, for it is more to go often than to go once. *Why mention Theseus? Why the great Hercules?* Here, because of their illustrious status, he has nothing to diminish or increase. Instead, he boasts that what shone in them is common to him as well: *And my lineage, too, is from supreme Jove.* <note>Aeneid 6.123</note> Similar to this is the pathos derived from indignation. For what does Juno say? "Was Pallas able to burn the fleet of the Greeks?" Now, this is a greater thing—

<margin>Offense</margin>
—to burn a victorious fleet than the mere remains of fugitives. Then she diminishes the cause: *For the offense and madness of one man, Ajax son of Oileus.* <note>Aeneid 1.39-41</note> She diminishes it by calling it an "offense" <note>original: "noxa"</note>, which is a term for a light fault. And she says "of one man," which could easily be forgiven, and a "madman," so that it might not even be a crime. And elsewhere: "Mars was able to destroy the race of the Lapiths." Note the same observations: it was an entire "race" and a "monstrous" one. Then another

<margin>Pathos from place</margin>
example: "The father of the gods himself yielded ancient Calydon to the rages of Diana." He uses "ancient" so that more honor is added through its antiquity. Then in both cases, he diminishes the cause: *What crime did either the Lapiths or Calydon commit to deserve such things?* <note>Aeneid 7.304-307</note>

<margin>Pathos from parable</margin>
Indeed, the parable, since it is more suited to a poet, very often moves pathos when he wishes to introduce someone either piteous or angry. To move pity: *Like the mourning nightingale under the shade of a poplar.* <note>Georgics 4.511</note> Or: *Like a flower harvested by a maiden's thumb.* <note>Aeneid 11.68</note> There are many other pathetic parables in which he evokes pity. What about anger? *And just as a wolf lying in wait at a full sheepfold, while he growls at the pens.* <note>Aeneid 9.59</note> And: *Like the bellowing of a wounded bull as it flees the altar.* <note>Aeneid 2.223</note> Anyone who looks will find many other similar examples.

<margin>Pathos from image</margin>
The image, which is the third part of similarity, is well-suited for moving the emotions. This occurs when either the physical form of an absent person is described, or one is fashioned that does not exist at all. Virgil did both elegantly. The first regarding Ascanius: *O, the only remaining image of my Astyanax to me! Just so did he carry his eyes, his hands, his face.* <note>Aeneid 3.489-490; Andromache speaks to Ascanius about her lost son.</note> But he fashions an image when he says: *Whom fame followed, her white loins girt with barking monsters.* <note>Aeneid 3.424-428; describing Scylla.</note> But the former "fame" is <term>oiktron</term> (piteous), while the latter is <term>deinosin</term> (horrific); that is, the first moves us to mercy, the second to horror. Just as elsewhere: *And Discord goes rejoicing in her torn robe, whom Bellona follows with her blood-stained whip.* <note>Aeneid 8.702-703</note> And all those things he said about form. But this one is exceedingly pathetic: *Impious Rage sitting within upon savage weapons, bound behind his back with a hundred bronze knots, shall roar horribly with his bloody mouth.* <note>Aeneid 1.294-296</note>

## ¶ Pathos from the lesser. Chapter IV.

<margin>Pathos from a lesser cause</margin>
We have spoken of pathos from similarity; now let us speak of pathos placed by the poet from the "lesser." Certainly, when something is proposed that is great in itself, and then something is shown to be even "lesser" than that which we wish to amplify, an infinite pity is moved. As in this instance: *O happy beyond all others, maiden daughter of Priam, ordered to die at a hidden tomb beneath the high walls of Troy.* <note>Aeneid 3.321-323; referring to Polyxena.</note> First, by saying she is "happy," she makes a comparison to herself; then she establishes it from the place: *at a hostile tomb*; and from the manner, which is no less bitter: *ordered to die.* Thus these things are to be understood: though she died at a hostile tomb, though she was ordered to die, she is still "happier" than I am, because she did not endure any lot of slavery. Similar to this is: *O three and four times blessed!* <note>Aeneid 1.94</note> And what he says of Pasiphae: *Of Proetus—*

It begins a new chapter on how Virgil creates pathos by comparing a character's tragic fate to someone even "lesser" or "happier," such as Polyxena's death versus Andromache's slavery.</summary>

It moves from comparisons of "the lesser" to "the greater," and explores how addressing inanimate objects or expressing doubt can heighten a reader's feelings.</meta>

...they lost their wits and filled the fields with false lowings <note>original: "falsis mugitibus." This refers to the daughters of Proetus, who in mythology were cursed with madness and believed they were cows.</note>. Then, to show that this suffering was of a lesser degree, he adds: *Yet no such foul couplings of beasts followed.* Is this not a powerfully emotional argument from the lesser to the greater? So too when the prophet Helenus warns of many horrors: *He predicted these griefs to me, but not the dread Celaeno.* <note>Aeneid 3.712-713. Celaeno was a Harpy who prophesied famine; Aeneas argues that even her terrifying curses were less painful than the death of his father, Anchises.</note> What do we understand here, except that all the hardships he had endured seemed minor compared to the death of his father.

### Pathos from the Greater. Chapter V.

<margin>pathos from the greater</margin>
Some have denied that a matter can be amplified "from the greater" <note>Latin: *a maiore*. A rhetorical device where an event is compared to a larger catastrophe to emphasize its emotional weight.</note>. However, Virgil introduced this elegantly regarding Dido’s death. He wrote: *Not otherwise than if all Carthage or ancient Tyre should fall, with the enemy let in.* <note>Aeneid 4.669-671</note> For he suggested that the grief from the death of one woman was no less than if the entire city—which would undoubtedly be a greater disaster—had collapsed. Homer did the same.

<margin>pathos from the unexpected</margin>
¶ Among orators, there is also a suitable technique for stirring emotion called "the unexpected" <note>Latin: *praeter spem*.</note>. Virgil employed this frequently: *We, your own progeny, to whom you promise the citadel of heaven...* and so on. And Dido says: *If I was able to expect such great grief, I will also be able to endure it, sister.* <note>Aeneid 4.419</note> Aeneas says to Evander: *And now he, much captured by vain hope, perhaps makes vows.* <note>Aeneid 11.49-50. Aeneas laments that Evander is still praying for a son who is already dead.</note> And that famous line: *A stranger to our land—something we never feared—should say as the possessor of our little field: "These are mine; you old inhabitants, move on."* <note>Eclogue 9.2-4. This refers to the historical trauma of Roman soldiers seizing farmers' lands.</note> Yet I find that one can also move the emotions through that which was already expected, as Evander says: *I was not ignorant of how much new glory in arms means...*

<margin>pathos from similarity of feeling</margin>
Orators call it <term>homoiopatheia</term> <note>From the Greek for "empathy" or "shared feeling."</note> whenever emotion arises from a similarity of suffering, as in Virgil: *To you also, Anchises was such a father.* <note>Aeneid 10.824</note> And: *The image of his father’s piety struck him.* And Dido says: *A similar fortune has driven me also through many labors.*

<margin>pathos toward inanimate and silent things</margin>
¶ There is also that method for stirring emotion in which speech is directed either to inanimate things or to the silent <note>This refers to animals or objects that cannot speak back.</note>; orators use this frequently. Virgil handled both very emotionally. Either when Dido says: *Sweet relics, while fate and the god allowed...* <note>Aeneid 4.651. Dido addresses the clothes and bed left behind by Aeneas before she dies.</note> or when Turnus says: *Now, O earth, hold the steel of the best of men.* And elsewhere: *Now, O spear, never having failed my call.* And: *Rhaebus, we have lived long, if anything is long for mortals.* <note>Aeneid 10.861. The warrior Mezentius speaks to his horse, Rhaebus, as if to a friend before their final battle.</note>

<margin>pathos from doubt</margin>
¶ Hesitation—which the Greeks call <term>aporia</term> <note>A state of being at a loss or in doubt.</note>—also creates emotion among orators. For it is the mark of one in pain or anger to doubt what to do next. *Behold, what am I doing? Shall I, mocked, again try my former suitors?* <note>Aeneid 4.534</note> And that about Orpheus: *What should he do? Where should he go, his wife snatched away twice?* And of Nisus: *What should he do? With what force, with what weapons should he dare to rescue the youth?* And Anna is moved: *Deserted, what shall I seek first? My sister as a companion?*

<margin>pathos from witnessing</margin>
¶ The testimony of a thing seen <note>Latin: *attestatio*.</note> also moves emotion among rhetoricians. Virgil carries this out as follows: *When he saw the head of the snowy Pallas supported, and his face, and the wound gaping in his smooth chest...* And: *Blood filled the fold of his garment.*
> And dying, he rolls in his own blood.
> And he perceives the cruel mother showing her son's wounds.
> And the pale faces of the men hung with grim gore.
> Euryalus rolls in death: and the blood goes through his beautiful limbs.
> And I myself saw when two bodies from our number... <note>Aeneas describing the Cyclops Polyphemus devouring his companions.</note>

<margin>pathos through hyperbole</margin>
Hyperbole <note>Original: *hyptole*. An intentional exaggeration used to emphasize a point.</note>—that is, excess—creates emotion through which either anger or mercy is expressed. Anger, as when it is said someone should have died a thousand times; as in Virgil: *I myself would have given my guilty soul through every kind of death.* Mercy, when he says: *Daphnis, they say even the Carthaginian lions groaned at your death.* Beyond these, emotion is born from excess, whether of a lover's nature or another kind: *If this light is not already longer to me than a whole year.* And separately: *To burn the ships of Turnus before the sacred pine shall give...* And: *Not if he should pour the earth into the waves.*

### Of Exclamation. Chapter VI.

<margin>pathos through exclamation</margin>
Exclamation, which among the Greeks is called <term>ekphonesis</term>, moves the emotions. This occurs sometimes from the voice of the poet, and sometimes from the person he introduces as a speaker. From the poet’s own voice is:
*Mantua, alas, too near to wretched Cremona!* <note>Eclogue 9.28. A famous lament regarding the land confiscations that affected Virgil's home region.</note>

LXXVI

HEADER: THE SATURNALIA

*Unhappy, however posterity will bear those deeds.* <note>original: "Infelix ut cũq; ferent ea facta nepotes." From Aeneid 6.822, referring to Brutus executing his sons.</note> *Love was your crime,* and other similar phrases. Truly, from the persona of another: *May the gods reserve such things for his own head and his race.* And: *Gods, repay such things with favor, if with a pious mouth I demand punishment.* And: *Gods, avert such a plague from the lands.*

<margin>Pathos through silence.</margin>
¶ The opposite of this figure is <term>aposiopesis</term> <note>original: "ἀποσιώπησις," a rhetorical device where a sentence is deliberately broken off.</note> which is a form of silence. For just as in the previous figure we say things by shouting them out, here we withdraw things by keeping silent out of anger. However, the listener is still able to understand what is meant. This is especially fitting for those who are angry, such as Neptune: *Whom I—! But it is better to calm the troubled waves.* <note>Aeneid 1.135. Neptune stops himself before finishing his threat against the winds.</note> And Mnesteus: *Nor do I strive to win. And yet, oh—! But let those whom you have granted this, Neptune, surpass me.* And Turnus: *And yet, oh—! if only some of our usual courage were present.* And in the *Bucolics*: *We know both who was with you—while the goats looked askance—and in what shrine—but the easy-going nymphs just laughed.* <note>Eclogues 3.8-9</note> Even pity can be stirred by this figure, as seen with Sinon: *Until, with Calchas as the servant... But why do I revolve these unwelcome things in vain?*

<margin>Pathos from repetition</margin>
¶ Pathos is also born from repetition, which the Greeks call <term>epanaphora</term> <note>original: "ἐπαναφοράν," the repetition of a word at the beginning of successive clauses.</note>, when sentences begin with the same names. From this, Virgil writes: *The voice itself and the cold tongue called "Eurydice!" even as the soul fled. "Ah, poor Eurydice!" he called; and the riverbanks echoed "Eurydice!" along the whole stream.* <note>Georgics 4.525-527</note> And again: *To you, sweet spouse; to you alone on the shore; of you as the day arrived; of you as it departed, he sang.* And: *The grove of Angitia wept for you; the Fucine lake with its glassy wave wept for you; the clear lakes wept for you.*

<margin>Pathos through rebuke</margin>
¶ <term>Epitimesis</term> <note>original: "ἐπιτίμησις," a sharp rebuke or reproach.</note>, which is a rebuke, also contains pathos; that is, when we refute things using the very same words: *Is Aeneas away in ignorance? Let him be away and ignorant!*

### THE SATURNALIA OF MACROBIUS AURELIUS THEODOSIUS, CONSULAR AND ILLUSTRIOUS MAN. Book V.

Afterward, when Eusebius <note>A character in the dialogue, often representing a learned rhetorician.</note> had been quiet for a short while, everyone declared among themselves with a harmonious murmur that Virgil should be considered no less an orator than a poet. In his work, they argued, there was shown both a great discipline of ornamentation and a diligent observation of the rhetorical art.

Then Avienus said: "I wish for you to tell me, best of teachers: if we concede (as we must) that Virgil was an orator, and if someone now wished to master the art of speaking, would they profit more from Virgil or from Cicero?"

"I see what you are doing," said Eusebius, "and what you intend—where you are trying to drag me. You want to lead me to the very place I least want to go: to a comparison between Maro <note>Virgil's cognomen.</note> and Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note>. You have asked modestly which of them is more excellent, since it follows that the one who is himself most excellent would contribute the most to a student. But I ask you to release me from this high and profound necessity, because it is not for us to settle such great matters between them."

LXXVIII

->BOOK FIVE LXXVIII<-

<margin>Praise of Virgil</margin>
...disputes: I would not dare to appear as the author of such a judgment in either direction. I will only dare to say this: that the eloquence of the Mantuan <note>Virgil, who was born in Mantua.</note> is multifaceted and multiform, and it embraces every kind of speaking. For look: in your Cicero, there is one single tenor of eloquence—that abundant, torrential, and copious style. However, the nature of orators is not simple or singular; one flows and overflows, while another strives to speak briefly and concisely. One who is thin, dry, and sober loves a certain frugality of speech; another delights in fat, brilliant, and florid oratory. In such a great diversity among all others, Virgil alone is found to have forged his eloquence from every genre.

### How many types of speaking there are. Chapter I.

<margin>Four types of speaking</margin>
Avienus replied: I would clearly wish for you to teach me these differences using examples of specific people. Eusebius said: There are four types of speaking. The **Copious**, in which Cicero dominates. The **Brief**, in which Sallust reigns. The **Dry**, which is attributed to Fronto. The **Rich and Florid**, in which Pliny the Second <note>Pliny the Younger.</note> once luxuriated, as does our own Symmachus <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, a famous 4th-century orator and friend of the author.</note> now, who is second to none of the ancients. But in Maro <note>Virgil's family name.</note> alone will you find these four types. Do you wish to hear him speaking with such brevity that brevity itself could not be more narrowed or contracted? *And the fields where Troy once was.* <note>original: "Et campos ubi troia fuit." From Aeneid 3.11.</note> Look how with the fewest words he <margin>Swallowed up</margin> drained and swallowed up a massive city; he did not even leave behind a ruin. Do you wish for him to speak of this same thing most copiously? *The final day has come and the unavoidable time of Dardania: we have been Trojans; Ilium has been, and the great glory of the Teucrians. Cruel Jupiter has transferred everything to Argos; the Greeks rule in the scorched city. O fatherland! O Ilium, home of the gods, and the walls of the Dardanians famous in war! Who could explain the slaughter of that night? Who could unfold the deaths in speaking? Or who could equal our labors with tears? An ancient city falls, having ruled for many years.* <note>A compilation of lines from Aeneid 2. The Teucrians and Dardanians are Trojans; Argos represents the Greeks.</note> What spring, what torrent, what sea has flooded with as many waves as he has here with words? Bring forth now that **Dry** type of elocution: *As Turnus, flying ahead, had preceded the slow column, accompanied by twenty chosen horsemen; and where he is present unexpectedly, whom a Thracian horse with white spots carries, and a golden helmet with a red crest covers.* <note>Aeneid 9.47-50.</note> How about this same thing with what elegance, what **Florid** oratory is produced when he pleases? *By chance the sacred chorus of Cybele, and once a distinguished priest, was shining from afar in Phrygian arms, and was urging on a foaming horse, which a hide covered with bronze scales like feathers, joined with gold. He himself, bright in foreign rust-color and purple, was twisting Gortynian arrows from a Lycian bow; his tunics were embroidered with a needle, and his legs had foreign coverings.* <note>Aeneid 11.768-777. "Rust-color and purple" refers to expensive dyes.</note> But these indeed are separate from each other. Do you wish to see how Virgil himself mixes these four types of speaking, and makes one most beautiful temperament out of all that diversity? *Often it has also been profitable to burn sterile fields, and to burn light stubble with crackling flames. Whether from there the earth conceives hidden strengths and rich food; or whether every vice is cooked out of them by the fire, and useless moisture sweats out. Or whether that heat relaxes more paths and blind openings through which the sap may come into the new grass. Or whether it hardens more and constricts the gaping veins, lest the thin rains or the sharper power of the rapid sun, or the penetrating cold of the North Wind, should scorch it.* <note>Georgics 1.84-93. This is a technical passage on farming that uses balanced, rhythmic language.</note> Behold a type of speaking which you will find nowhere else: in which there is neither headlong brevity, nor infinite abundance, nor meager dryness, nor fat luxuriance.

### Styles of Speaking. Chapter II.

<margin>Two styles of speaking</margin>
There are, furthermore, two styles of speaking, different in their distinct character. One is **Mature** and **Grave**, such as is assigned to Crassus. Virgil uses this when Latinus gives instructions to Turnus: *O youth of outstanding mind, as much as you yourself surpass in fierce virtue, so much is it right for me to consult for you,* and so on. <note>Aeneid 12.19-21.</note> The other is contrary to this, **Fiery**, **Erect**, and **Hostile**, such as Antony used. You will not seek this in vain in Virgil: *Not such were the words you were giving a moment ago; die, and brother, do not desert brother.* <note>Aeneid 10.599-600. These are the words of Mezentius or Aeneas in the heat of battle.</note> Do you see how his eloquence is distinguished by the variety of all things, which indeed it seems to me Virgil—not without a certain...

LXXXVI

->SATURNALIA<-

"Unhappy, however those deeds may affect posterity" <note>original Latin: "Infelix ut cũq; ferent ea facta nepotes." From Virgil's Aeneid 6.822.</note>. "Your crime is love" <note>original: "Crimẽ amor uestrum."</note>, and other similar phrases. In the voice of another: "May the gods boil back [this fury] upon his own head and race." And: "Gods, restore such things to the grateful, if I demand punishment with a pious mouth." And: "Gods, avert such a plague from the lands."

<margin>Emotional power through silence.</margin>
The opposite of this figure is *aposiopesis* <note>A rhetorical device where a sentence is deliberately broken off and left unfinished, the ending to be supplied by the imagination.</note>, which is silence. For just as in the previous case we say things by shouting, here we withdraw things through silence due to anger. Yet the listener is still able to understand. This is especially suitable for those who are angry, such as Neptune: "Whom I—but it is better to calm the stirred waves." <note>Neptune stops himself mid-threat against the winds.</note> And Mnestheus: "I do not strive to win. Although oh!—but let those overcome to whom you, Neptune, have granted this." And Turnus: "Although oh!—if any of the usual courage were present." And in the *Bucolics* <note>Virgil's Eclogues.</note>: "We know both who [did it] to you—while the goats looked askance—and in what shrine—but the easy nymphs laughed." But pity is also stirred by this figure by Sinon: "Until Calchas, being the assistant... But why do I revolve these ungrateful things in vain?"

<margin>Emotional power from repetition.</margin>
Pathos also arises from repetition, which the Greeks call *epanaphora* <note>The repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses.</note>, when sentences begin with the same names. Hence Virgil: "The voice itself and the cold tongue called 'Eurydice' as the soul fled. 
> Ah, wretched Eurydice! The banks along the whole river echoed: 'Eurydice.'" 
And that famous passage:
> "Thee, sweet spouse, thee by himself on the lonely shore, 
> thee as the day arrived, thee as it departed, he sang." 
And that:
> "Thee the grove of Angitia, thee the Fucine lake with glassy wave, 
> thee the liquid lakes wept for."

<margin>Emotional power through rebuke.</margin>
*Epitimesis* <note>A Greek rhetorical term for a sharp rebuke or censure.</note>, which is a rebuke, also contains pathos; that is, when we refute something using the very same words: "Is Aeneas away unaware? Let him be away unaware."

AFTER THESE things, when Eusebius had rested a little, everyone declared with a harmonious murmur that Virgil should be considered no less an orator than a poet; for in him was shown such great discipline of ornament and such diligent observation of the rhetorical art. 

Then Avienus said: "I want you to tell me, best of teachers: if we grant (as is necessary) that Virgil was an orator, if someone now wished to pursue the art of oratory, would he profit more from Virgil or from Cicero?" 

"I see what you are doing," said Eusebius, "what you intend, and where you are trying to drag me—namely, to where I least want to go: to a comparison of Maro <note>Virgil.</note> and Tully <note>Cicero.</note>. For you have asked modestly which of them is more excellent, since necessarily the one who excels most will contribute the most. But I want you to release me from that deep and profound necessity, because it is not for us to settle such great [matters] between them..."

disputes: Nor would I dare to appear as the authority for such an opinion in either direction. I will only venture to say this: that the eloquence of the Mantuan <note>Virgil, who was born near Mantua.</note> is multifaceted and varied, and it embraces every kind of speaking. Look, for instance—in your Cicero, there is but one tenor of eloquence: that overflowing, torrential, <margin>Praise of Virgil</margin> and abundant style. ### On the Styles of Speaking. Chapter I.

<margin>Four styles of speaking</margin>
Avienus replied: I would wish you to teach me these differences more clearly through the examples of specific people. Eusebius said: There are four styles of speaking. The **Copious**, in which Cicero is the master. The **Brief**, in which Sallust reigns. The **Dry**, which is attributed to Fronto. The **Rich and Florid**, in which Pliny the Younger once delighted, and now our own Symmachus—inferior to none of the ancients—luxuriates. But you will find these four styles within the single person of Virgil. Do you wish to hear him speaking with such brevity that brevity itself cannot be more tightened or contracted? "And the fields where Troy once was." <note>original Latin: "Et campos ubi troia fuit." From Aeneid 2.325.</note> Look how, in a few words, <margin>He consumed</margin> he swallowed and consumed a massive city; he did not even leave behind its ruins. Do you wish for him to speak of this very same thing most copiously? "The final day has come and the unavoidable time of Dardania; we Trojans have been; Ilium has been, and the great glory of the Teucrians. Fierce Jupiter has moved everything to Argos; the Greeks rule in the scorched city. O fatherland! O Ilium, home of the gods, and the walls of the Dardans famous in war! Who can unfold the slaughter of that night? Who can explain the deaths in speaking? Or who can equal the labors with tears? An ancient city falls, having ruled for many years." <note>original Latin: "Venit ſumma dies..." from Aeneid 2.324-363.</note> What fountain, what torrent, what sea has flooded with as many waves as he has here flooded with words? Grant me now that "dry" style of speech: "As Turnus, flying ahead, had preceded the slow column, accompanied by twenty chosen horsemen; and where he is present unexpectedly, whom a Thracian horse with white spots carries, and a golden helmet with a red crest covers." <note>original: "Turnus ut anteuolans..." from Aeneid 9.47-50.</note> How is this same thing brought forth with what ornament and what florid speech when he pleases? "By chance, Chloreus, sacred to Cybele and once a priest, shone from afar in distinguished Phrygian arms. And he urged on a foaming horse, which a skin covered with bronze scales like feathers, joined with gold. He himself, bright in foreign rust-color and purple, turned Gortynian arrows from a Lycian bow; his tunics and the foreign coverings of his legs were embroidered with a needle." <note>original: "Forte facer cibele choreus..." from Aeneid 11.768-777. Note the shift from the functional description of Turnus to the highly decorative description of Chloreus.</note> But these styles are indeed separate from one another. Do you wish to see how Virgil himself mixes these four types of speaking, and makes from all that diversity a single, most beautiful temperament? "Often also it has been useful to burn sterile fields, and to burn light stubble with crackling flames. Whether from there the earth conceives hidden strengths and rich food; or whether every vice is cooked out of them by the fire, and the useless moisture sweats out. Or whether that heat opens more paths and blind vents where the sap may come into the new herbs. Or whether it hardens the soil more and constricts the gaping veins, lest the thin rains or the fiercer power of the rapid sun, or the penetrating cold of the North wind, should burn it." <note>original: "Sæpe etiam ſteriles incendere profuit agros..." from Georgics 1.84-93.</note> Look at a style of speaking which you will find nowhere else: in which there is neither headlong brevity, nor infinite abundance, nor hungry dryness, nor fat luxuriance.

### The Manners of Style. Chapter II.

<margin>Two manners of style</margin>
There are, furthermore, two manners of speaking, differing in their moral character. One is **mature and grave**, such as is assigned to Crassus. Virgil uses this when Latinus gives instructions to Turnus: "O youth of outstanding spirit, as much as you yourself surpass in fierce virtue, so much is it right for me to consult for you," and so on. <note>original: "O p̄stans animi iuuenis..." from Aeneid 12.19-21.</note> The other, contrary to this, is **ardent, upright, and hostile**, such as Antony used. You will not seek this in vain in Virgil either: "You did not give such words a moment ago; die! And brother, do not desert your brother." <note>original: "Haud talia dudum Dicta dabas: morere. & fratrē ne deſere frater." From Aeneid 10.597-600.</note> Do you see how his eloquence is distinguished by the variety of all styles, which indeed it seems to me Virgil, not without a certain foreknowledge...

It also explores his ability to shift between different moral tones, from the grave maturity of a statesman to the fierce heat of a warrior.</summary>
