# OF THE SATURNALIA

...[college] by which he prepared himself for the advancement of all: he mixed these styles by design. <note>The speaker, Eusebius, is finishing a point about how Virgil deliberately blended different rhetorical styles to appeal to every kind of reader.</note> This was provided not by a mortal, but by a divine genius; indeed, he followed no other leader than Nature herself, the mother of all things. He displayed this style just as there is harmony in music from discordant notes. Truly, if you inspect the world itself closely, you will find a great similarity between that divine work and this poetic work. For just as the eloquence of Maro <note>Virgil’s family name was Maro.</note> is suited to the characters of all—now brief, now copious, now dry, now florid, sometimes all at once, occasionally smooth or torrential—so the earth itself is here joyful with crops and meadows, there bristling with forests and crags; here dry with sands, there watered by springs; and part is opened to the vast sea. Forgive me, and do not call me too bold for comparing Virgil to the nature of things. For it seemed to me that within him, if I were to say it, he mixed the diverse styles of the ten rhetors who flourished in Attic Athens. <note>The "Ten Attic Orators" were the canonical models of Greek prose, including famous figures like Demosthenes and Lysias.</note>

¶ Then Evangelus, appearing as if mocking, said: "You do well to compare a poet from the Mantuan countryside to God the Creator! I would assert that he had not even read those Greek rhetoricians you mentioned. For how could a Venetian <note>Mantua, Virgil's birthplace, was located in the Roman province of Cisalpine Gaul, often associated with the Veneti people of Northeast Italy.</note> born to rustic parents and raised among woods and shrubs possess even a slight knowledge of Greek literature?"

¶ And Eustachius said: "Be careful, Evangelus, lest you believe any of the Greeks drew as much Greek learning from the highest authors as the skill of Maro either attained or arranged within his work. For besides that ample abundance of philosophy and astronomy which we discussed above, there are no small number of other things he drew from the Greeks and wove into his poem as if they had been born there."

¶ And Praetextatus said: "I beg you, Eustachius, that you might wish to share these things with us as well, as much as your suddenly stirred memory allows." Everyone followed Praetextatus and called upon Eustachius to discourse. He began thus:

¶ "Do you think I am going to speak of the things Virgil drew from the Greeks that are commonly known? That he made Theocritus <note>A Greek poet from Sicily, the father of pastoral poetry and model for Virgil's *Eclogues*.</note> his model for his pastoral work, Hesiod for his rural work <note>The author of *Works and Days*, the model for Virgil's *Georgics*.</note>, and that in the *Georgics* themselves he took the signs of fair and stormy weather from the *Phaenomena* of Aratus? Or that he transcribed the destruction of Troy, along with his Sinon and the wooden horse and all the other things that make up the second book, almost word for word from Pisander? <note>Pisander of Camirus was an early Greek epic poet; Macrobius here makes the famous claim that Virgil's account of the fall of Troy was largely translated from him.</note> Pisander stands out among Greek poets for a work that, beginning from the marriage of Jupiter and Juno, gathered all the histories that occurred in the intervening ages up to his own time into a single series, making one body out of diverse gaps in time. In that work, among the other histories, the destruction of Troy was related in this manner. By faithfully translating these things, Maro fashioned for himself the ruin of the Trojan city. But I pass over these and similar things as they are chanted to schoolboys. Now, has not the *Aeneid* itself borrowed from Homer? First the wanderings from the *Odyssey*, then the battles from the *Iliad*—though the necessary order of events changed the order of the work. For in Homer, the Trojan War was waged first, and then the wandering happened to Ulysses as he returned from Troy. In Maro, however, the navigation of Aeneas preceded the wars that were later waged in Italy. Again, when Homer wanted to make Apollo hostile to the Greeks, he built his case from the injury to a priest. Here, in order to make Juno hostile to the Trojans, Virgil prepared a heap of causes for himself. Nor am I going to relate this next point with great care, although I believe it has not been observed by everyone: that although he promised in the first verse that he would bring Aeneas forth from the shores of Troy—'Who first from the shores of Troy, a refugee by fate, came to Italy and the Lavinian shores' <note>original Latin: "Troiae qui primus ab oris Italiam fato profugus lauinaque uenit Littora." *Aeneid* 1.1.</note>—when he comes to the door of the narration, he brings Aeneas’s fleet out not from Troy, but from Sicily: 'Scarcely out of sight of the Sicilian land, they joyfully set sail into the deep.' <note>original Latin: "Vix e conspectu siculae telluris in altum Vela dabant laeti." *Aeneid* 1.34.</note> He wove this entire structure based on Homeric styles. For he himself, avoiding the likeness of historians—whose law is to begin from the start of events and produce a continuous narrative until the end—followed poetic discipline and began from the middle of things, returning to the beginning later. Therefore, [Homer] does not begin describing the wandering of Ulysses from the Trojan shore, but makes him first sailing from the island of Calypso, and leads him in his own person to the Phaeacians. There, at the banquet of King Alcinous, Ulysses himself narrates how he came from Troy all the way to Calypso."

Eustachius argues that Virgil's mastery of poetic structure—specifically beginning "in the middle of things"—is a sophisticated imitation of Homeric and other Greek epic techniques.</summary>

# BOOK FIVE
### A2

...[after the] Phaeacians, the poet <note>Homer, in the *Odyssey*</note> describes the navigation of Ulysses again up to Ithaca in his own persona. Following him, Maro <note>Virgil</note> leads Aeneas from Sicily; in describing his navigation, he leads him to Libya. There, at the banquet of Dido, Aeneas himself narrates his voyage from Troy as far as Sicily; and he added in a single verse what the poet had already described at length: "Departing hence, a god drove me to your shores." <note>original: *Hic me digressum uestris deus appulit oris.* (Aeneid 3.715)</note> After Africa, the poet again describes the journey of the fleet as far as Italy itself in his own persona: "Meanwhile Aeneas already held the middle of the sea with his fleet, certain of his path." <note>original: *Interea medium æneas iam claſſe tenebat Certus iter.* (Aeneid 5.1)</note> Indeed, the entire Virgilian work is formed as if from a mirror of the Homeric work. For even the storm is described with wonderful imitation. Let anyone who wishes compare the verses of both: just as Venus takes the place of Nausicaa, the daughter of Alcinous. Dido herself reflects the image of King Alcinous celebrating a banquet. Scylla also, and Charybdis and Circe are fittingly touched upon; and in place of the cattle of the Sun, the Strophades islands are fashioned. Instead of the consultation with the dead <note>the *nekyia* in the Odyssey</note>, a descent to them with the company of a priestess is introduced. There Palinurus corresponds to Elpenor; the hostile Dido to the hostile Ajax; and the warnings of Anchises to the counsels of Tiresias. 

Now the battles of the *Iliad* and the description of wounds—not without perfection of discipline—and the double enumeration of reinforcements, and the forging of arms, and the variety of the funeral games, and the blow struck between kings and the broken treaty, and the night reconnaissance, and the embassy bringing back a refusal from Diomedes; after the example of Achilles, the lamentation over Pallas as over Patroclus; and the dispute, just as between Achilles and Agamemnon, so between Drances and Turnus. For in both cases, one was thinking of his own advantage, the other of the public good. The single combat of Aeneas and Turnus is as that of Achilles and Hector; and the captives destined for the underworld, as there for Patroclus, here for Pallas: "Four youths created at Sulmo, and as many whom Ufens rears, he seizes alive as offerings for the dead, to sacrifice to the shades." <note>original: *Quattuor hic iuuenes: totidem quos educat uſens Viuentes rapit inferias: quos immolet umbris.* (Aeneid 10.517-519)</note> 

Furthermore, in place of the Homeric Lycaon—who, caught among those fleeing, it is no wonder if he fled to prayers, yet Achilles did not spare him because of the pain of Patroclus' death—under a similar condition, Magus is introduced in the midst of the tumult. "Then from afar he had aimed his hostile spear at Magus." And when he, embracing his knees, had sought his life as a suppliant, he replied: "Turnus first did away with those dealings of war, even then when Pallas was slain." <note>original: *Belli commertia turnus ſuſtulit iſta prior iam tum pallante perempto.* (Aeneid 10.532)</note> But even the insult of Achilles against Lycaon himself, once slain, is transferred by Maro to Tarquitus: He <note>Achilles</note> says:

> "Lie there now among the fish, who will lick the blood from your wound without care, nor will your mother place you on a bed and wail over you, but the swirling Scamander shall carry you into the broad lap of the sea." <note>original Greek: *Homer, Iliad 21.122-125*</note> 

And so forth. But here our poet <note>Virgil</note> says: "Lie there now, you who were to be feared," and the rest. <note>original: *Iſtic nunc metuende iace.* (Aeneid 10.557)</note> And if you wish me to bring forth the verses themselves translated almost word for word: although my present memory does not supply them all, I will note those that present themselves.

> "He brought the string to his breast and the iron point to the bow." <note>original Greek: *Homer, Iliad 4.123*</note>

How much more concisely the richer language <note>Greek</note> explained the whole matter! Your poet, though he used a longer period, said the same thing:

> "He drew it far back, until the curved ends met together, and now with level hands he touched the point of the iron with his left, and his nipple with the string in his right." <note>original: *Aeneid 11.859-862*</note>

<column-break/>

> "When at last we left that island and no other land appeared, but only sky and sea, then the son of Cronos set a dark cloud above the hollow ship, and the sea grew dark beneath it." <note>original Greek: *Homer, Odyssey 12.403-406*</note>

### PAGE 81

"No longer does any land appear, the sky is everywhere and the sea is everywhere; the wave stood round, arched in the shape of a mountain." <note>original: *Nec iam amplius ulla Apparet tellus cælum undiqƺ & undiqƺ pontus Curuata in molis faciem circūstetit unda.* (Aeneid 3.192–193)</note>

And concerning the abyss of Tartarus, he <note>Homer</note> says:
"As far beneath Hades as the heaven is from the earth." <note>original Greek: *Τοσσον ενερσ’ Αιδεω οσον ουρανος εστ’ απο γαιης.* (Iliad 8.16)</note>

Virgil renders this as:
"Twice as much the abyss opens downward; it stretches beneath the shadows as far as the upward gaze to the ethereal Olympus of heaven." <note>original: *Bis patet in præceps tantum: tenditqƺ sub umbras Quantus ad æthereum cæli suspectus olympum.* (Aeneid 6.578–579)</note>

"But when they had put away the desire for drink and food." <note>original Greek: *αυταρ επει ποσιος και εδητυος εξ ερονεντο* (Iliad 1.469)</note>

"After hunger was banished and the love of eating repressed." <note>original: *Postqƺ exempta fames:& amor compressus edendi.* (Aeneid 8.184)</note>

"Thus he spoke in prayer, and Zeus the counselor heard him. To him the Father granted one thing, but the other he denied: he granted that he should drive the war and the battle from the ships, but he denied that he should return safe from the fight." <note>original Greek: *ωσ’ εφατευχομενος...* (Iliad 16.249–252)</note>

"Apollo heard, and in his mind he granted that part of the vow should succeed: part he scattered into the winged breezes." <note>original: *Audiit & uoti phœbus succedere partem Mente dedit: partem uolucres dispersit in auras.* (Aeneid 11.794–795)</note>

"And his children’s children who shall be born in the time to come." <note>original Greek: *και παιδων παιδες τοι κεν μετοπισθε γενονται* (Iliad 20.308)</note>

"Here the house of Aeneas shall rule over all shores: both the children of his children and those who shall be born from them." <note>original: *Hic domus æneæ cunctis dominabitur oris: Et nati natorum & qui nascentur ab illis.* (Aeneid 3.97–98)</note>

And elsewhere he <note>Homer</note> says:
"And then his knees and his dear heart were loosened, and deeply moved, he spoke to his great-hearted spirit." <note>original Greek: *και τοτε δηνηδυμος...* (Odyssey 5.297–298)</note>

From these two lines, he <note>Virgil</note> fashioned one:
"Straightway Aeneas’s limbs are loosened with a chilling fear." <note>original: *Extemplo æneæ soluuntur frigore membra.* (Aeneid 1.92)</note>

"Break the spear of Diomedes, and grant that he himself fall headlong before the Scaean gates." <note>original Greek: *αξον δ’ εγχος Διομηδεος...* (Iliad 6.306–307)</note>

"O Tritonian maiden, powerful in arms, present in war: break with your hand the weapon of the Phrygian pirate, and stretch him headlong on the ground, and cast him down beneath the very gates." <note>original: *Armipotens præsens belli tritonia uirgo...* (Aeneid 11.483–485)</note>

"At first she rears her head small, but then she fixes her head in heaven and walks upon the earth." <note>original Greek: *ητο λιγη πεν πρωτα...* (Iliad 4.442–443)</note>

"She walks upon the ground and hides her head among the clouds." <note>original: *Ingrediturqƺ solo & caput inter nubila condit.* (Aeneid 4.177)</note>

He <note>Virgil</note> says of sleep:
"A sweet and deep repose, most like to peaceful death." <note>original: *Dulcis & alta quies placidæqƺ simillima morti.* (Aeneid 6.522)</note>

"Yes, by this scepter, which shall never put forth leaves or shoots, since first it left its stump in the mountains, nor shall it bloom again; for the bronze has stripped it of both leaves and bark. Now in turn the sons of the Achaeans carry it in their hands, those who judge and guard the laws by the authority of Zeus. And this shall be a great oath for you." <note>original Greek: *ναι μα τόδε σκῆπτρον...* (Iliad 1.234–239)</note>

"As this scepter (for by chance he was holding a scepter in his right hand) shall never produce branches with light foliage nor shade, once it has been cut from its lowest root in the woods and lacks its mother-tree; it has laid down its hair and arms <note>In poetic Latin, the "hair and arms" of a tree refer to its leaves and branches.</note> to the steel; once a tree, now the hand of the craftsman has enclosed it in beautiful bronze and given it to the Latin fathers to carry." <note>original: *Vt sceptrum hoc...* (Aeneid 12.206–211)</note>

It focuses on descriptions of nature, prayers to the gods, and the famous "oath by the scepter" taken from Achilles and adapted for Latin kings.</summary>

->**BOOK FIVE**<-

But now, if it seems right, I shall step away from this comparison of translated verses, so that a uniform narrative does not produce boredom through satiety, and the conversation may turn to other things no less suited to the present cause. "Proceed, I beg you," said Avienus, "to investigate everything that he took from Homer. For what is more pleasant than to hear two primary prophets speaking the same thing? 

<margin>Three impossible things.</margin>
For since these three things are considered equally impossible: to snatch the lightning-bolt from Jove, or the club from Hercules, or a verse from Homer; even if it could be done, it would nonetheless befit no other person: either to hurl the lightning besides Jove, or to contend in strength besides Hercules, or to sing what Homer sang. In this, he <note>Virgil</note> acted opportunely by transferring what the earlier prophet had said into his own work, making it so that they are believed to be his own. Therefore, you will do what everyone wishes if you would communicate with this assembly whatever our poet <note>Virgil</note> borrowed from yours <note>Homer</note>." 

"Give me, then," said Eustachius, "the volume of Virgil; because by looking at his individual passages, I shall more promptly be reminded of the Homeric verses." And when a servant, by the command of Symmachus, had brought the book sought from the library, Eustachius opened it at random. And while he looked at the verses which chance had offered, he said: "See yourself moving toward the city of Dido <note>Carthage</note> from Ithaca <note>the home of Odysseus</note>."

> There is a place in a long deep inlet: an island creates a harbor 
> by the barrier of its sides: by which every wave from the deep 
> is broken and divides itself into receding ripples. 
> Here and there vast cliffs and twin crags loom 
> into the sky: beneath whose peak the safe waters 
> are silent far and wide: then a backdrop of shimmering woods 
> from above: and a dark grove overhangs with trembling shade: 
> Beneath the face of the opposite cliffs is a cave of hanging rocks: 
> within are sweet waters and seats of living stone: 
> the home of the Nymphs. Here no chains hold 
> the weary ships: no anchor binds them with its hooked bite.
> <note>original: *Est in secessu longo locus...* (Aeneid 1.159–169)</note>

> There is a certain harbor of Phorcys, the old man of the sea,
> in the land of Ithaca; and two projecting 
> headlands are in it, steep and sheer, sloping toward the harbor, 
> which shelter the great wave from the harsh winds 
> outside; but within, the well-benched 
> ships remain without a mooring-rope when they reach the point of anchorage. 
> Moreover, at the head of the harbor is a long-leafed olive tree, 
> and near it is a lovely, misty cave 
> sacred to the nymphs called Naiads. 
> Within are bowls and two-handled jars 
> of stone; and there the bees store their honey.
> <note>original Greek: *φορκυνος Δετις εσι λιμην...* (Odyssey 13.96–104)</note>

When Avienus had asked that he should not mark them scattered here and there, but in order from the beginning, Eustachius, having turned the pages back with his hand to the bottom <note>the start of the roll</note>, began thus:

> For to you, Aeolus, the father of the gods and king of men 
> has given the power both to soothe the waves and to raise them with wind: 
> I have twice-seven nymphs of excellent body: 
> of whom Deiopea, who is the most beautiful in form, 
> I shall join to you in stable wedlock and dedicate as your own.
> <note>original: *Aeole nanq; tibi...* (Aeneid 1.65–73)</note>

The storm stirred up for Aeneas by Aeolus, with the speech of the leader <note>Aeneas</note> lamenting his fate, is described from the storm and speech of Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note>, in which Neptune took the place of Aeolus. Since the verses in both places are many, I have not inserted them. Whoever wishes to read will find the beginning from this verse.

"And now no longer does any land appear, the sky is everywhere and everywhere the sea. The wave stood around, curved into the shape of a massive heap." <note>original Latin: *Nec iam amplius uulla Apparet tellus...* from Aeneid 3.192. Virgil is here imitating Homer's description of the open sea.</note> And concerning Tartarus, that one <note>Homer</note> says:
"As far beneath Hades as heaven is from the earth." <note>original Greek: *Τόσσον ἔνερϑ' Αϊδεω...* from Iliad 8.16.</note>
"Twice as far it lies open headlong: and it extends under the shadows as great as is the upward look to the ethereal heaven of Olympus." <note>original Latin: *Bis patet in præceps...* from Aeneid 6.577. Virgil doubles the distance to emphasize the depth of the underworld.</note>
"But when they had put away the desire for drink and food." <note>original Greek: *αυταρ επει ποσιος...* from Iliad 1.469.</note>
"After hunger was taken away and the love of eating suppressed." <note>original Latin: *Poſtq exempta fames...* from Aeneid 1.216.</note>
"So he spoke praying, and Zeus the counselor heard him. To him the father granted one part, but the other he denied: he gave him the pushing back of war and battle, but he denied his returning safe from the battle." <note>original Greek: *ως εφατ' ευχομενος...* from Iliad 16.249.</note>
"Apollo heard and granted in his mind that part of the vow should succeed: part he dispersed into the flying breezes." <note>original Latin: *Audiit & uoti phœbus...* from Aeneid 11.794.</note>
"And let the children of children who are born after them rule." <note>original Greek: *και παιδων παιδες...* from Iliad 20.307.</note>
"Here the house of Aeneas shall rule over all shores: both the children of children and those who shall be born from them." <note>original Latin: *Hic domus æneæ...* from Aeneid 3.97.</note>
And elsewhere that one <note>Homer</note> says:
"And then his knees and dear heart were loosened." <note>original Greek: *και τότε δὴ λύτο γούνατα...* from Iliad 21.114.</note>
"Aghast, he spoke then to his great-hearted spirit." <note>original Greek: *ὀχϑήσας δ' άρα εἶπε...*</note>
Here <note>Virgil</note> has fashioned one from two:
"Immediately Aeneas’ limbs are loosened with cold." <note>original Latin: *Extemplo æneæ ſoluuntur frigore membra* from Aeneid 1.92. Macrobius notes that Virgil combined the physical collapse and the emotional distress found in two different Homeric lines.</note>
"Break then the spear of Diomedes and grant that he himself fall prone before the Scaean gates." <note>original Greek: *ἄξον δὴ ἔγχος Διομήδεος...* from Iliad 6.306.</note>
"O present Tritonian maiden, powerful in arms, break the weapon of the Phrygian pirate with your hand: and stretch him prone on the ground: and pour him out under the gates themselves." <note>original Latin: *Armipotens præſens belli tritonia uirgo...* from Aeneid 11.483. Virgil adapts a prayer to Athena/Minerva.</note>
"She is small at first when she raises her crest, but then she fixes her head in heaven and walks upon the earth." <note>original Greek: *ητο λιγη μεν πρῶτα...* from Iliad 4.442, describing Discord.</note>
"She enters upon the ground and hides her head among the clouds." <note>original Latin: *Ingrediturq ſolo...* from Aeneid 4.177, describing Fame.</note>
That one <note>Virgil</note> says of sleep:
"Sweet and deep rest, most like to placid death." <note>original Latin: *Dulcis & alta quies...* from Aeneid 6.522.</note>
"Yes, by this scepter. Which shall never grow leaves and branches, since it first left its stump in the mountains, nor shall it bloom again: for the bronze has stripped it of leaves and bark. Now the sons of the Achaeans carry it in their hands as judges, they who protect the laws from Zeus; and this shall be a great oath for you." <note>original Greek: *ναὶ μὰ τόδε σκῆπτρον...* from Iliad 1.234, the oath of Achilles.</note>
"As this scepter—for by chance he was carrying a scepter in his right hand—shall never pour out shoots with light foliage nor shade, since once cut from the lowest stump in the woods it lacks its mother: and it laid down its hair and arms to the iron: once a tree, now the hand of the craftsman has enclosed it in beautiful bronze, and given it to the Latin fathers to carry." <note>original Latin: *Vt ſceptrum hoc...* from Aeneid 12.206. Virgil adapts the famous Homeric oath regarding a wooden scepter that can never again grow green to symbolize the finality of an oath.</note>

# BOOK FIVE LXXX

But now, if it seems right, I shall leave off this comparison of translated verses: so that a uniform narrative does not breed distaste through satiety, and the discourse may turn to other things no less suited to the present cause. "Go on, I pray," said Avienus, "investigate all that Virgil has taken from Homer. For what is sweeter than to hear two preeminent poets saying the same thing?"

<margin>Three impossibilities.</margin>
"Because since these three things are considered equally impossible: to snatch the thunderbolt from Jove, the club from Hercules, or a verse from Homer. Even if it could be done, it would suit no other: either to hurl the bolt except Jove, or to compete in strength except Hercules, or to sing what Homer sang. Here, by opportunely transferring what the prior poet had said into his own work, Virgil made it so they are believed to be his own. Therefore, you will fulfill the wish of all if you share with this gathering whatever our poet has borrowed from yours." 

"I yield then," said Eustachius. "Give me the volume of Virgil; for by inspecting his individual passages, I shall be more promptly reminded of the Homeric verses." When a servant, by the order of Symmachus, had brought the book sought from the library, Eustachius opened it at random. And while he looked at the verses which chance had offered, he said, "See how you are migrating from Ithaca to the city of Dido, to the harbor."

There is a place in a long recess: an island makes a harbor
By the barrier of its sides: by which every wave from the deep
Is broken and divides itself into the drawn-back inlets.
On this side and that are vast rocks: and twin cliffs threaten
Into the sky: beneath whose peak the safe waters lie
Silent far and wide: then a scene with shimmering woods
From above: and a dark grove looms with bristling shade:
Under the opposite face is a cave with hanging rocks:
Within are sweet waters: and seats of living stone:
The home of the Nymphs. Here no chains hold the weary ships,
No anchor binds them with its hooked bite.
<note>original Latin: "Est in secessu longo locus..." from Aeneid 1.159-169. Virgil is describing the harbor at Carthage where Aeneas lands.</note>

There is a harbor of Phorkys, the old man of the sea,
In the land of Ithaca; and there are two projecting
Sheer headlands in it, sloping toward the harbor,
Which break the great wave of the harsh winds
From the outside; and inside, the well-benched ships
Remain without a mooring-rope when they reach the limit of the anchorage.
But at the head of the harbor is a long-leafed olive tree,
And near it is a lovely, dark cave,
Sacred to the nymphs who are called Naiads.
And within are mixing-bowls and jars
Of stone; and there the bees store their honey.
<note>original Greek: "φόρκυνος δέ τ’ ἔστι λιμὴν..." from Odyssey 13.96-106. Macrobius presents this to show that Virgil’s description of Carthage is modeled on Homer’s description of Ithaca.</note>

And when Avienus had asked that he not note them sporadically but in order from the beginning: Eustachius, having drawn the leaves back to the start with his hand, began thus:

"Aeolus, for to you the father of gods and king of men
Has given the power to soothe the waves and raise them with the wind:
I have twice seven nymphs of excellent body:
Of whom Deiopea, who is most beautiful in form,
I will join to you in stable wedlock and dedicate as your own."
<note>original Latin: "Aeole nanq; tibi..." from Aeneid 1.65-73. This is Juno’s speech to the wind god Aeolus.</note>

¶ The storm of Aeneas, stirred up by Aeolus, with the speech of the leader lamenting his situation, is described from the storm and speech of Ulysses, where Neptune held the place of Aeolus. Since the verses are many on both sides, I have not included them. He who wishes to read them will have the beginning from this verse. <note>Macrobius explains that the entire sequence of the storm in Aeneid Book 1 is a structural imitation of Ulysses' ordeal in the Odyssey.</note>

<summary>Eustachius discusses the difficulty of imitating Homer, famously comparing it to stealing Hercules' club, before demonstrating how Virgil’s description of the Carthaginian harbor and the storm of Aeolus were modeled on the Odyssey.</summary>

### PAGE XXXI

"When these things were said: he struck the hollow mountain with his turned spear..." <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.81, describing Aeolus striking the mountain to release the winds.</note>

And in Homer, from the fifth book of the *Odyssey*:
"So speaking, he gathered the clouds and stirred the sea, grasping the trident in his hands; he roused all the blasts of every kind of wind." <note>original: *Odyssey* 5.291-293; here Poseidon stirs the storm against Odysseus.</note>

"As soon as the nurturing light was given, he resolved to go forth and explore the new places: to seek what shores he had reached by the wind, who held them (for he saw they were uncultivated), whether men or wild beasts, and to report his findings to his companions." <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.305-309; Aeneas exploring the coast of Libya.</note>

"Sitting up, he pondered in his mind and heart: 'Woe is me, to what land of mortals have I come now? Are they violent and wild, and not just? Or are they hospitable to strangers and have a god-fearing mind? But come, I will try it myself and see.'" <note>original: *Odyssey* 6.117-121; Odysseus waking up on the island of Scheria.</note>

"None of your sisters have been heard or seen by me—O, how <gloss>quam</gloss> <note>The scribe used an abbreviation 'q' with a stroke for the Latin word 'quam'.</note> shall I address you, maiden? For your face is not mortal, nor does your voice sound human; O, surely a goddess! Are you the sister of Phoebus, or one of the blood of the nymphs?" <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.326-329; Aeneas addressing his mother Venus, who is disguised as a huntress.</note>

"I clasp your knees, O Queen; are you a god or a mortal? If you are a god, one of those who hold the wide heaven, I liken you most closely to Artemis, the daughter of great Zeus, in beauty and stature and form." <note>original: *Odyssey* 6.149-152; Odysseus addressing the princess Nausicaa.</note>

"O goddess, if I were to go back and trace from the first beginning, and if there were leisure to hear the annals of our labors, the evening star would compose the day and close Olympus before I finished." <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.372-374.</note>

---

"But Venus hedged them as they walked with a dark air, and the goddess poured a thick mantle of mist around them, so that no one might see them, nor anyone be able to touch them, or cause a delay, or demand the reasons for their coming." <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.411-414; Venus hiding Aeneas and Achates as they enter Carthage.</note>

"And then the noble Odysseus rose to go to the city; but Athena poured a thick mist around him, being kindly disposed toward Odysseus, lest any of the great-hearted Phaeacians, meeting him, should challenge him with words and ask who he was." <note>original: *Odyssey* 7.14-17.</note>

"Just as on the banks of the Eurotas or along the ridges of Cynthus, Diana leads her dances, followed by a thousand mountain nymphs crowding here and there; she carries a quiver on her shoulder and, as she walks, she towers above all the goddesses; joys thrill the silent breast of Latona. Such was Dido; such she bore herself happily." <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.498-502; the famous simile comparing Queen Dido to the goddess Diana.</note>

"Even as Artemis the archer moves over the mountains, either along the ridges of Taygetus or Erymanthus, taking her delight in the wild boars and swift deer; and with her the nymphs, daughters of Zeus the aegis-bearer, play..." <note>original: *Odyssey* 6.102-105; the original simile comparing Nausicaa to Artemis.</note>

## PAGE LXXXI

...the country-dwellers play; and Leto rejoices in her heart, for [Artemis] holds her head and brow above them all, and is easily recognized, though all are beautiful. So did the unwed maiden stand out among her attendants. <note>original: Homer, *Odyssey* 6.102-109. This describes the princess Nausicaa appearing like the goddess Artemis among her servants.</note>

Aeneas stood forth and shone in the clear light, like a god in face and shoulders; for his mother herself <note>Aeneas’s mother is the goddess Venus.</note> had breathed upon her son a beautiful head of hair, the purple light of youth, and joyous beauty in his eyes. Just as hands add grace to ivory, or when silver or Parian marble is set in yellow gold. <note>original: Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.588-593. Virgil adapts the Homeric "beautification" motif here.</note>

Athena, daughter of Zeus, made him taller to look upon and stouter, and from his head she sent down curling locks like the hyacinth flower. As when a man overlays silver with gold—a craftsman whom Hephaestus and Pallas Athena have taught every kind of art, and he completes graceful works—so she shed grace upon his head and shoulders. <note>original: Homer, *Odyssey* 23.156-162. Athena beautifies Odysseus so he may appear regal to his wife Penelope.</note>

"I am present here before you, the one you seek: Aeneas the Trojan, snatched from the Libyan waves." <note>original: Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.595-596.</note>

---

All fell silent and held their gaze intently. "O Queen, you command me to renew an unspeakable sorrow: how the Greeks overthrew the Trojan wealth and the pitiable kingdom." <note>original: Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.1-4. Aeneas begins his famous account of the fall of Troy to Queen Dido.</note>

"But your heart was turned to ask about my tearful sorrows, so that I might groan and weep even more." <note>original: Homer, *Odyssey* 9.12-13. This is the Greek parallel where Odysseus begins his own long flashback to King Alcinous.</note>

Part of the crowd stood amazed at the deadly gift to the unwed Minerva <note>The "deadly gift" is the Trojan Horse, ostensibly an offering to the goddess Athena/Minerva.</note> and they wondered at the mass of the horse; and first Thymœtes urged that it be led within the walls and placed in the citadel, whether out of treachery or because the fates of Troy were already leading that way. But Capys, and those whose minds held a better opinion, ordered that the Greek traps and suspected gifts be cast into the sea or burned with flames placed beneath, or that the hollow hiding places of the belly be pierced and probed; the uncertain crowd was split into opposing factions. <note>original: Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.31-39. The Trojans debate what to do with the Wooden Horse.</note>

So it stood, while they sat around it and spoke many undecided things; and three plans pleased them: either to cleave the hollow wood with the pitiless bronze, or to drag it to the summit and cast it down the rocks, or to let it remain as a great offering to appease the gods. <note>original: Homer, *Odyssey* 8.505-509. Homer’s description of the Trojans debating the fate of the Horse, which Virgil expanded.</note>

Meanwhile the sky turns, and night rushes from the ocean, wrapping in its great shadow both the earth and the heavens. <note>original: Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.250-251.</note>

---

Ah me, what a sight he was! How changed from that [Hector]... <note>original: Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.274. Aeneas describes his dream of the mangled ghost of the Trojan hero Hector.</note>

### THE SATURNALIA

...Hector: who returned wearing the spoils of Achilles, or having hurled Trojan fires at the Greek ships <note>original: "Hectore: qui rediit exuuias indutus achillis: / Vel danaum phrygios iaculatus puppibus ignes." Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.275-276. This refers to Hector's ghost appearing to Aeneas in a dream.</note>:

->And the young Coroebus<-

The son of Mygdon: who by chance had come to Troy in those days, burning with a mad love for Cassandra; as a son-in-law, he brought aid to Priam and the Trojans <note>original: "Mygdonides: illis qui ad troiam forte diebus / Venerat infano cassandræ incensus amore: / Et gener auxiliū priamo phrygibusq; ferebat." Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.342-344. Coroebus was a prince hoping to marry the prophetess Cassandra.</note>.

Thus was fury added to the spirits of the youths. Then, like scavenging wolves in a black fog, whom the reckless hunger of the belly has driven blind, and whose abandoned cubs wait with dry throats: through weapons, through enemies we go toward certain death, and we hold our way through the middle of the city; black night flies around us with its hollow shadow <note>original: Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.355-360. This famous simile compares the desperate Trojan survivors to starving predators.</note>.

---

Just as one who, treading on the ground, has pressed an unforeseen snake in the rough briars, and suddenly flees in fear as it rises in anger and swells its dark blue neck: not otherwise did Androgeus depart, trembling at the sight <note>original: Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.379-382. Androgeus, a Greek, mistakenly addresses the Trojans and recoils when he realizes his error.</note>.

As when a man sees a snake in a mountain glen and shrinks back, and trembling seizes his limbs, and he withdraws, and paleness takes his cheeks: so did the god-like Alexander <note>Alexander is another name for Paris, the Trojan prince.</note> shrink back into the throng of lordly Trojans, fearing the son of Atreus <note>original: Homer, *Iliad* 3.33-37. Macrobius provides the Greek source to show how Virgil imitated Homer’s snake imagery.</note>.

Just as when a snake, having fed on poisonous herbs, comes into the light—whom the cold winter was hiding swollen beneath the earth—now, having cast its old skin, fresh and glistening with youth, it rolls its slippery back with its chest held high, towering toward the sun, and flickers with its three-forked tongue in its mouth <note>original: Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.471-475. This describes the Greek warrior Pyrrhus as he prepares to break into the palace.</note>:

Not so when a foaming river has burst its banks and gone forth, overcoming the opposing barriers with its whirlpool: it is carried raging into the fields in a mass, and throughout all the plains it drags the herds and their stalls <note>original: Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.496-499. A simile for the Greeks flooding into King Priam's palace.</note>.

Thrice I attempted there to throw my arms around her neck; thrice, grasped in vain, the image escaped my hands, like light winds and most similar to a winged dream <note>original: "Ter conatus ibi collo dare brachia circum / Ter frustra comprēsa manus effugit imago / Par leuibus uentis uolucriq; simillima somno." Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.792-794. Aeneas describes his failed attempt to embrace the ghost of his wife, Creusa.</note>.

Thrice I sprang forward, and my heart urged me to embrace her; thrice she flew from my hands like a shadow or even a dream <note>original: "τρὶς μὲν ἐφορμήθην ἐλέειν τέ με θυμὸς ἀνώγει / τρὶς δέ μοι ἐκ χειρῶν σκιῇ εἴκελον ἢ καὶ ὀνείρῳ / ἔπτατο." Homer, *Odyssey* 11.206-208. This is the Greek source for Virgil's lines above, describing Odysseus trying to embrace his mother in the underworld.</note>.

Here is another storm for Aeneas, and there for Ulysses, told in numerous verses by both authors. But Virgil's begin thus:

After the ships held the deep, and no longer did any land appear <note>original: "Postq̃ altū tenuere rates: nec iā amplius ullæ." Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.192.</note>.

->He says:<-

Accept these too, boy, which may be memorials to you of my hands' work <note>original: "Accipe & hæc manuum tibi quæ monumenta mearum / Sint puer." Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.486-487. These are the words of Andromache to Aeneas’s son, Ascanius.</note>.

The South winds stretch the sails; we flee over the foaming waves, where the wind and the pilot called our course <note>original: "Tendunt uela noti: fugimus spumantibus undis / Qua cursum uentusq; gubernatorq; uocabāt." Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.268-269.</note>.

Scylla besets the right side; restless Charybdis the left; and three times she sucks the vast waves into the broken abyss of her whirlpool, and again casts them up to the air in turn, and lashes the stars with the water. But a cave confines Scylla in dark hiding places, thrusting out her faces and dragging ships onto the rocks. Her face is first that of a human, a maiden with a beautiful breast down to the waist; her lower part is a sea-monster <term>pistris: a mythical sea creature, often depicted as a shark or sea-dragon</term> with a massive body, the tails of dolphins joined to a belly of wolves. It is better to survey the limits of Sicilian Pachynus, delaying there and bending a long course around, than once to have seen the misshapen Scylla in her vast cave and the rocks echoing with her dark-blue hounds <note>original: Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.420-432. Virgil describes the hazards of the Strait of Messina between Italy and Sicily.</note>.

->Homer on Charybdis and Scylla.<-

For on one side was Scylla, and on the other divine Charybdis terribly sucked down the salt water of the sea. Whenever she vomited it forth, like a cauldron on a great fire she would all seethe and bubble in turmoil, and the spray [flew] upward <note>original: "ἔνθεν μὲν γὰρ Σκύλλη ἑτέρωθι δὲ δῖα Χάρυβδις / δεινὸν ἀνερροίβδησε θαλάσσης ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ / ἤτοι ὅτ᾽ ἐξεμέσειε λέβης ὣς ἐν πυρὶ πολλῷ / πᾶσ᾽ ἀναμορμύρεσκε κυκωμένη ὑψόσε δ᾽ ἄχνη" Homer, *Odyssey* 12.235-238.</note>

...onto the peaks of the cliffs on both sides it fell. But whenever she would swallow back the salty water of the sea, all within was mixed in a turmoil. And the rock around roared terribly, and beneath the earth appeared, dark with sand <note>original: "ακροισι σκοπελοισιε παμφοτεροισιν επιπτεν / αλλοτε η ανυις αναβρωξειε γε αλμυρον υδωρ / παση η. Το δε φανεσκε κυκωμενη αμφι δε πετρη / δεινον βεβρυχει υπενερθε δε γαια φανεσκε / ψαμμω κυανεη." Homer, *Odyssey* 12.238-242. This describes the terrifying whirlpool monster Charybdis.</note>.

O you, who are the only image left to me of my Astyanax: just so he used to carry his eyes, his hands, his face <note>original: "O mihi sola mei super astyanactis imago: / Sic oculos: sic ille manus: sic ora ferebat." Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.489-490. Andromache speaks to Aeneas’s son, Ascanius, seeing in him a haunting resemblance to her own lost son.</note>.
For such as his were the feet, and such the hands, and the cast of his eyes, and the head, and the hair above <note>original: "κεινου γαρ τοιοιδε ποδες τοιαι δε χειρεσ / οφθαλμων τε βολαι κεφαλη τεφυπερθε τε χαιται." Homer, *Odyssey* 4.149-150. Menelaus notices how much Telemachus looks like his father, Odysseus.</note>.
Thrice the cliffs gave a roar amidst the hollow rocks. Thrice we saw the spray dashed up and the dripping stars <note>original: "Ter scopuli clamorem inter caua saxa dedere. / Ter spumam elisam: & rorantia uidimus astra." Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.566-567. Aeneas describes the violent sea near the rocks of Scylla.</note>.

---

->Like a deer hit by an arrow:<-
->Whom, unaware, a shepherd hunting with darts has pierced from afar<-
->Among the Cretan woods, and has left the winged steel<-
->Without knowing it: she wanders in flight through the woods and<-
->Glades of Dicte; the lethal shaft remains fixed in her side.<-
<note>original: "Qualis coniecta cerua sagitta..." Virgil, *Aeneid* 4.69-73. This famous simile compares the love-struck and doomed Queen Dido to a wounded deer.</note>

---

He had spoken. The other prepared to obey the command of his great father: and first he binds the golden sandals to his feet, which carry him aloft, whether over the waters or the land, together with the rapid breeze. Then he takes his wand. With this he calls forth pale souls from the Underworld; others he sends down to gloomy Tartarus. He gives sleep and takes it away, and unseals the eyes from death. Relying on this, he drives the winds and swims through the murky clouds <note>original: "Dixerat. ille patris magni parere parabat..." Virgil, *Aeneid* 4.238-246. Mercury (Hermes) prepares to deliver a message from Jupiter to Aeneas.</note>.
So he spoke, and the messenger, the slayer of Argus, did not disobey. Straightway he bound his beautiful sandals beneath his feet, immortal and golden, which carried him over the waters and over the boundless earth as swift as the blasts of the wind. And he took his wand, with which he charms the eyes of men whom he will, and others again he awakens from sleep. Holding this in his hands, the strong slayer of Argus flew <note>original: "ως εφατου δ' απιθησε Δι ακτορος αργειφοντης..." Homer, *Odyssey* 5.43-49. This is the Greek source for the description of Hermes's flight.</note>.
And just as when the Alpine North winds strive among themselves, now from this side, now from that, to uproot an ancient oak of mighty strength with their blasts: a creaking follows, and the leaves deeply cover the ground as the trunk is shaken. The tree itself clings to the rocks, and as far as its peak reaches toward the ethereal airs, so far does its root reach toward the Underworld <note>original: "Ac ueluti annosam ualido quum robore quercum..." Virgil, *Aeneid* 4.441-446. Virgil uses this simile to describe Aeneas standing firm against Dido's pleas, like an oak tree against a storm.</note>.

And now the early Dawn, leaving the saffron bed of Tithonus, began to sprinkle the lands with new light <note>original Latin: "Et iam prima nouo spargebat lumine terras / Tithoni croceum linquens aurora cubile." Virgil, *Aeneid* 4.584-585 and 9.459-460. The poet uses this formulaic description of daybreak to signal a shift in the action.</note>.
And Dawn rose from her bed from beside noble Tithonus, that she might bring light to immortals and to mortals <note>original Greek: "Ἠὼς δ' ἐκ λεχέων παρ' ἀγαυοῦ Τιθωνοῖο / ὤρνυθ' ἵν' ἀθανάτοισι φόως φέροι ἠδὲ βροτοῖσι." Homer, *Iliad* 11.1-2 and *Odyssey* 5.1-2. Virgil’s "saffron bed" is a direct nod to Homer’s "noble Tithonus."</note>.

---

When the ships held the deep sea, and no land was any longer in sight, but everywhere was the sea and everywhere the sky: a dark rain-cloud stood over his head, bringing night and storm, and the wave shuddered in the darkness <note>original Latin: "Vt pelagus tenuere rates: nec iam amplius ulla / Occurrit tellus: maria undiq; & undiq; cælum: / Olli cæruleus supra caput astitit imber / Noctem hyememq; ferens: & inhorruit unda tenebris." Virgil, *Aeneid* 5.8-11. This describes the onset of a storm as Aeneas leaves Carthage.</note>.

---

And he poured wine from the bowls, and called upon the soul of great Anchises, and the spirits released from the underworld <note>original Latin: "Vinaq; fundebat pateris: animamq; uocabat / Anchislæ magni: manesq; acheronte remissos." Virgil, *Aeneid* 5.98-99. Aeneas performs these rites at his father's tomb.</note>.
Drawing wine from a golden bowl, he poured it on the ground and soaked the earth, calling upon the soul of the poor Patroclus <note>original Greek: "οἶνον ἀφυσσάμενος χαμάδις χέε δεῦ δέ γαῖαν / ψυχὴν κικλήσκων Πατροκλῆος δειλοῖο." Homer, *Iliad* 23.218-221. Achilles performs a similar libation for his fallen friend.</note>.

---

To him he gave a triple-layered coat of mail, woven with smooth hooks and gold, which the victor himself had stripped from Demoleos near the swift Simois beneath lofty Troy <note>original Latin: "Leuibus huic hamis confertam auroq; trilicem / Loricam: quam demoleo detraxerat ipse / Victor apud rapidum simoenta sub ilio alto." Virgil, *Aeneid* 5.259-261. This refers to the prize given during the funeral games.</note>.
To him I will give a silver-studded breastplate, a beautiful Thracian one, which I stripped from Asteropaeus <note>original Greek: "τῷ μὲν ἐγὼ δώσω θώρηκα ἀργύρεον / καλὸν ὀρήϊκιον τὸν μὲν ἀξερόπαιον ἀπήυρων." Homer, *Iliad* 23.560-562. Achilles offers a similar prize of captured armor.</note>.

---

And the contest of the runners is similar in both authors; and because the verses are rhythmic in both, the reader will find passage similar to passage. These are the beginnings:
When these things were said, they took their places, and suddenly at the signal— <note>original Latin: "Hæc ubi dicta locum capiunt: signoq; repente." Virgil, *Aeneid* 5.315.</note>
So he spoke, and they all then became hushed in silence <note>original Greek: "ὡς ἔφαθ' οἱ δ' ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ." Homer, *Iliad* 7.92. This is a common formula for the reaction of a crowd.</note>.
But when each was arranged together with their leaders <note>original Greek: "αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κόσμηθεν ἅμ' ἡγεμόνεσσιν ἕκαστοι." Homer, *Iliad* 3.1.</note>.

---

The contest of the boxers begins in this one:
Immediately each stood up, raised on his tiptoes <note>original Latin: "Constitit idigitos extemplo arrectus uterq;." Virgil, *Aeneid* 5.426. This describes Entellus and Dares.</note>. In that one:
Both holding up their strong hands together, they fell upon each other, and their heavy hands were mingled together <note>original Greek: "ἂν τὰ δ' ἀνασχομένω χερσὶ στιβαρῇσιν ἅμ' ἄμφω / σύν ῥ' ἔπεσον σύν δὲ σφι βαρεῖαι χεῖρες ἔμιχθεν." Homer, *Iliad* 23.685-686. This describes the boxing match between Epeius and Euryalus.</note>.

---

If you wish to compare those competing with arrows, you will find these beginnings in both:
Immediately Aeneas invited them to compete with the swift arrow: <note>original Latin: "Protinus æneas celeri certare sagitta:" Virgil, *Aeneid* 5.485.</note>
But he set forth for the archery competition gray iron, and he laid down ten double-axes and ten single-axes <note>original Greek: "αὐτὰρ ὁ τοξεύειν τιθήεντα σιδήρῳ / κὰδ δ' ἔτιθη δέκα μὲν πελέκεας δέκα δ' ἡμιπέλεκκα." Homer, *Iliad* 23.850-851.</note>.

---

It will be enough to have mentioned the main headings of the passages where there is a long narrative; the reader will find the source from which each arose.
He had spoken, and vanished into thin air like smoke <note>original Latin: "Dixerat. & tenues fugit ceu fumus in auras:" Virgil, *Aeneid* 5.740. The ghost of Anchises disappears from Aeneas.</note>.
And the soul went beneath the earth like smoke, twittering <note>original Greek: "ψυχὴ δὲ κατὰ χθονὸς ἠΰτε καπνὸς ᾤχετο τετριγυῖα." Homer, *Iliad* 23.100-101. The ghost of Patroclus leaves Achilles.</note>.

---

"Aeneas, where then do you rush? Where do you hurry off to?" he said. "Whom do you flee? Or who keeps you from our embrace?" <note>original Latin: "Aeneas quo deinde ruis? quo proripis inquit? / Quem fugis? aut quis te a nostris complexibus arcet?" Virgil, *Aeneid* 5.741-742.</note>

---

Thrice he had attempted to put his arms around his neck <note>original Latin: "Ter conatus erat collo dare brachia circum." Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.792 and 6.700. This poignant line emphasizes the physical impossibility of touching a ghost.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the comparative analysis of Virgil and Homer, transitioning from the funeral games of Book 5 of the Aeneid into the descent into the underworld in Book 6. The author, likely Macrobius in his Saturnalia, demonstrates how Virgil's descriptions of death, burial rites, and underworld punishments are meticulously crafted echoes of Homer’s Odyssey and Iliad.</meta>

<header>THE SATURNALIA</header>

Three times the image, grasped in vain, escaped the hands. <note>original Latin: "Ter frustra compressa manus effugit imago." Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.701. This describes Aeneas attempting to embrace the ghost of his father, Anchises.</note>
Three times I rushed forward, and my heart urged me to embrace her; three times she flitted from my hands like a shadow or a dream. <note>original Greek: "τρὶς μὲν ἐφορμήθην, ἐλέειν δέ με θυμὸς ἀνώγει / τρὶς δέ μοι ἐκ χειρῶν σκιῇ εἴκελον ἢ καὶ ὀνείρῳ / ἔπτατο." Homer, *Odyssey* 11.206-208. Virgil imitates Odysseus’s attempt to embrace his mother, Anticleia.</note>

The burial of Palinurus <note>Aeneas's pilot who fell overboard.</note> is modeled on the burial of Patroclus. In this way, he [Virgil] begins:
First, rich with pine-knots and cleft oak. <note>original Latin: "Principio pingue tædis & robore secto." Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.214. This describes the preparation of the funeral pyre for Misenus, though the author here links the scene to the themes of Palinurus.</note> He [Homer] says it thus:
The mourners remained there and piled up the wood; they made a pyre a hundred feet long on this side and that. <note>original Greek: "κηδεμόνες δὲ πάρ᾽ αὖθι μένον καὶ νήεον ὕλην, / ποίησαν δὲ πυρὴν ἑκατόμπεδον ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα." Homer, *Iliad* 23.163-164. This describes the massive pyre built for Achilles' companion, Patroclus.</note> And elsewhere.

Truly, how similar are the very insignias of both tombs?
But the pious Aeneas raised a tomb of massive size and placed upon it the hero’s own arms, his oar and trumpet, under the airy mountain which is now called Misenus after him, and preserves his name eternal through the ages. <note>original Latin: "At pius æneas ingenti mole sepulcrum / Imposuit:suaq; arma uiro remumq; tubamq; / Monte sub aerio:qui nunc misenus ab illo / Dicitur:æternumq; tenet per secula nomen." Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.232-235. This explains the legendary origin of Cape Miseno.</note>
But when the dead man had burned and the armor of the dead, we heaped up a mound and, dragging up a gravestone, we fixed the well-shaped oar on the very top of the mound. <note>original Greek: "αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ νεκρός τ᾽ ἐκάη καὶ τεύχεα νεκροῦ, / τύμβον χεύαντες καὶ ἐπὶ στήλην ἐρύσαντες, / πήξαμεν ἀκροτάτῳ τύμβῳ εὐῆρες ἐρετμόν." Homer, *Odyssey* 12.13-15. Odysseus performs this burial for his companion Elpenor.</note>

Then Sleep, the brother of Death: <note>original Latin: "Tum consanguineus leti sopor." Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.278. A personification found at the entrance to the underworld.</note>
There he met Sleep, the brother of Death... and sweet Sleep fell upon his eyelids, deep and unawakening, most like unto death. <note>original Greek: "ἔνθ᾽ Ὕπνῳ συμβλήτο, κασιγνήτῳ Θανάτοιο... καί τῷ νήδυμος ὕπνος ἐπὶ βλεφάροισιν ἔπιπτεν / νήγρετος ἥδιστος, θανάτῳ ἄγχιστα ἐοικώς." Homer, *Iliad* 14.231 and *Odyssey* 13.79-80. The Greeks viewed Sleep (Hypnos) and Death (Thanatos) as twin brothers.</note>

Therefore, I pray you by the pleasant light of heaven and the air, by your father, by the hope of rising Iulus, snatch me from these evils, unconquered one! Or cast earth upon me—for you can—and seek out the Velian harbor. <note>original Latin: "Quod te per cæli iocundum lumen & auras / Per genitorem oro per spes surgentis Iuli / Eripe me his inuicte malis:aut tu mihi terram / Iniice: nãq; potes:portusq; require uelinos." Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.363-366. The ghost of Palinurus begs Aeneas for burial so his soul can find rest.</note>
Now I beseech you by those behind us, not present, by your wife and the father who reared you when you were little, and by Telemachus, the only son you left in your halls: do not leave me behind unwept and unburied when you go... lest I become a cause of divine wrath against you. But burn me with my armor... and heap up a mound for me on the shore of the gray sea. <note>original Greek: "νῦν δέ σε τῶν ὄπιθεν γουνάζομαι, οὐ παρεόντων, / πρὸς ἀλόχου καὶ πατρός, ὅς ἔτρεφε τυτθὸν ἐόντα, / Τηλεμάχου θ᾽, ὃν μοῦνον ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἔλειπες... μή μ᾽ ἄκλαυτον, ἄθαπτον, ἰὼν ὄπιθεν καταλείπειν, / νοσφισθείς, μή τοί τι θεῶν μήνιμα γένωμαι, / ἀλλά με κακκῆαι σὺν τεύχεσιν, ἅσσα μοί ἐστιν, / σῆμά τέ μοι χεῦαι πολιῆς ἐπὶ θινὶ θαλάσσης." Homer, *Odyssey* 11.66-75. The ghost of Elpenor makes a similar plea to Odysseus.</note>

And one might see Tityos, the foster-child of all-bearing earth, whose body is stretched across nine whole acres; a huge vulture with hooked beak plucks at his immortal liver and his vitals fruitful for punishment; it gropes for its feast and dwells deep within his breast, nor is any rest given to the fibers that grow anew. <note>original Latin: "Nec non & tityon terræ omnipotentis alumnum / Cernere erat:per tota nouem cui iugera corpus / Porrigitur:rostroq; immanis uultur adunco / Immortale iecur tondens:fæcundaq; pœnis / Viscera:rimaturq; epulis:habitatq; sub alto / Pectore:nec fibris requies datur uulla renatis." Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.595-600. Tityos was a giant punished in Tartarus for attempting to rape Latona.</note>
And I saw Tityos, son of glorious Earth, lying on the ground; he lay across nine acres. Two vultures, one on either side, were tearing his liver, reaching inside the caul; he could not keep them off with his hands. For he had dragged away Leto, the honored consort of Zeus, as she was going to Pytho through the lovely Panopeus. <note>original Greek: "καὶ Τιτυὸν εἶδον, Γαίης ἐρικυδέος υἱόν, / κείμενον ἐν δαπέδῳ: ὁ δ᾽ ἐπ᾽ ἐννέα κεῖτο πέλεθρα: / γῦπε δέ μιν ἑκάτερθ᾽ ἐπαμένω ἧπαρ ἔκειρον, / δέρτρον ἔσω δύνοντες: ὁ δ᾽ οὐκ ἀπαμύνετο χερσίν: / Λητὼ γὰρ ἥλκησε, Διὸς κυδρὴν παράκοιτιν, / Πυθώδ᾽ ἐρχομένην διὰ καλλιχόρου Πανοπῆος." Homer, *Odyssey* 11.576-581.</note>

Not if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths, a voice of iron, could I encompass all the forms of crimes or run through all the names of punishments. <note>original Latin: "Non mihi si linguæ centum sint:oraq; centum / Ferrea uox:omnis scelerum comprendere formas: / Omnia pœnarum percurrere nomina possem." Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.625-627. The Sibyl tells Aeneas that the horrors of Tartarus are too numerous to describe.</note>

<header>BOOK FIVE</header>

<note>The header says "Book Five," but the content focuses on Virgil's later books. In the Renaissance edition of Macrobius being translated here, this likely refers to the fifth book of his *Saturnalia*, which is dedicated to Virgil’s use of Homer.</note>

The multitude I could not tell nor name, not even if I had ten tongues and ten mouths, an unwearying voice, and a heart of bronze within me. <note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 2.488-490. This is the famous "Invocations of the Muses" where the poet admits the scale of the Greek army is beyond human counting.</note>

Hence groans are heard, and the rages of lions refusing their chains, and wild things roaring in the night: bristly boars and bears in their pens raging, and the shapes of huge wolves howling. <note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 7.10-14. Virgil describes the island of Circe as Aeneas sails past.</note>
**Whom from the face of men the cruel goddess with powerful herbs**
**Circe had clothed in the faces and backs of wild beasts.** <note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 7.19-20.</note>

They found in the glades the well-built halls of Circe, of polished stone in a place of wide outlook. Round about it were mountain wolves and lions, whom she herself had enchanted after giving them evil drugs. <note>original Greek: Homer, *Odyssey* 10.210-213. This is Virgil’s direct source for the description of the transformed beasts.</note>

What do you seek? What cause for your ships? Or what lack has carried you over so many blue waters to the Ausonian shore? Whether driven by wandering from the path or by storms, such as sailors often suffer on the high sea. <note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 7.196-198. King Latinus greets the Trojans.</note>

Strangers, who are you? Whence do you sail the watery paths? Is it for business, or do you wander aimlessly, like pirates who roam over the sea, risking their lives and bringing evil to foreigners? <note>original Greek: Homer, *Odyssey* 9.252-255. Virgil mimics the formulaic greeting found in the *Odyssey*.</note>

When they return from pasture, and through their long necks
**they give forth melodic measures; the river and the Asian marsh resound far off**
when struck. <note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 7.699-701. Virgil compares the marching troops to a flight of singing swans.</note>

As the many tribes of winged birds—of geese, or cranes, or long-necked swans—in the Asian meadow around the streams of Cayster, fly here and there, glorying in their wings, and with a clang they settle, and the meadow rings. <note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 2.459-463. Virgil borrows the "Asian meadow" (a region in Lydia) directly from this Homeric simile.</note>

She would fly over the tops of the untouched grain, nor would she have harmed the tender ears in her course; or through the middle of the sea, suspended on the swelling wave, she would make her way, nor dip her swift soles in the water. <note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 7.808-811. A description of the warrior-maiden Camilla’s supernatural speed.</note>

And when they would skip over the grain-giving earth, they ran over the top of the stalks of grain and did not break them; and when they would skip over the broad back of the sea, they would run over the crest of the breaking surf of the gray salt water. <note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 20.226-229. Homer uses this image to describe the divine horses of Erichthonius.</note>

Aeneas together with the Trojan youth feeds upon the back of a whole ox and the sacrificial entrails. <note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.181-183. A scene of ritual feasting with King Evander.</note>

To them Agamemnon, lord of men, sacrificed a five-year-old male ox to the almighty son of Cronos... and he honored Ajax with the whole length of the chine. <note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 7.313-322. Homeric heroes, like Virgil’s, receive the choice cut of the "back" or "chine" as a mark of honor.</note>

After hunger was removed and the desire for eating suppressed,
King Evander says. <note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.184-185.</note>

But when they had put away the desire for food and drink, the old man first began to weave his counsel for them. <note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 1.469 and 7.324. Virgil adopts this standard epic transition almost word-for-word.</note>

# THE SATURNALIA

## BOOK FIVE

<note>original: LIBER V. LXXXI. While the header reads "Book Five," this refers to the fifth volume of Macrobius's *Saturnalia*, a 5th-century AD work where a group of scholars discusses the greatness of the poet Virgil. This specific book is famous for documenting Virgil's "thefts" and adaptations from the Greek poet Homer.</note>

Evander is awakened from his humble roof by the nurturing light:
And the morning songs of birds beneath the eaves.
The elder rises: and clothes his limbs in a tunic:
And binds his feet in Tyrrhenian sandals:
Then to his side and shoulders he fastens the Tegeaean sword:
Throwing back the panther skin hanging from his left.
And likewise two guardians from the high threshold
Proceed: and the dogs accompany their master’s step.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.454–462. This passage describes King Evander waking up in his modest home on the site of what would later become Rome.</note>

He rose from his bed and clothed himself in a soft tunic,
beautiful and new. Around him he cast a great cloak,
and beneath his glistening feet he bound his fair sandals,
and about his shoulders he slung a silver-studded sword;
he went forth from his chamber. And in his hand he held a bronze spear,
not alone, for two swift dogs followed along with him.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Odyssey* 2.2–11. Macrobius places this here to show that Virgil modeled Evander’s morning routine directly on Telemachus’s rising in the *Odyssey*.</note>

"O if only Jupiter would bring back my past years to me:
Such as I was when, beneath the very walls of Praeneste,
I leveled the front line, and as victor burned heaps of shields,
and sent King Erulus with this right hand down to the underworld:
to whom at birth his mother Feronia had given three lives—
horrible to tell—three sets of armor to be wielded,
three times he had to be laid low in death: yet then this right hand
took all those lives and stripped him of just as many sets of arms."
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.560–567. Evander expresses the universal longing of an old man for his youthful strength.</note>

"Would that I were young, and my strength was as firm as
when a strife was stirred between the men of Elis and us
over a cattle-raid, when I slew Hippomenes..."
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 7.132–135. This is Nestor’s speech. Virgil imitates the "Old Man's Regret" trope where an elder recalls a specific, supernatural feat of his youth.</note>

---

Just as when the Morning Star, bathed in the wave of the Ocean:
Whom Venus loves above all other fires of the stars:
Has lifted his sacred face to heaven and dissolved the darkness.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.589–591. This beautiful simile compares the young Pallas, son of Evander, to the star Lucifer (the light-bringer).</note>

---

"Behold the gifts perfected by the skill of my husband's art,
promised to you: so that soon, my son, you will not hesitate
to challenge either the proud Laurentines or fierce Turnus to battle."
She spoke, and <term>Cytherea</term> <note>An epithet for the goddess Venus, referring to her birth near the island of Cythera.</note> sought the embrace of her son:
She placed the radiant arms beneath an oak tree facing him.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.612–616. Venus presents the armor forged by the god Vulcan to Aeneas.</note>

But when he had fashioned the shield, both great and sturdy,
he fashioned then for him a breastplate brighter than the gleam of fire;
and he fashioned for him a heavy helmet, fitted to his temples,
beautiful and richly wrought, and upon it he set a crest of gold;
and he fashioned for him greaves of pliant tin.
But when the famed <term>Lame God</term> <note>Hephaestus, known as Vulcan to the Romans.</note> had labored and finished all the armor,
he took it and laid it before the mother of Achilles.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 18.609–617. This describes the forging of Achilles’ armor by Hephaestus, the primary source for Virgil’s description of Aeneas’s armor.</note>

He, joyful at the goddess's gifts and such great honor,
cannot be satisfied; and he turns his eyes over every piece:
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.617–618. Aeneas’s reaction to his new armor.</note>

He rejoiced as he held in his hands the god’s glorious gifts;
and when his heart was satisfied with gazing on the intricate work—
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 19.18–19. Here, Achilles views the armor forged by Hephaestus. Virgil mimics the "joy of the hero" at seeing the craftsmanship.</note>

Iris, glory of the sky: who sent you down to earth for me,
driven from the clouds?
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 9.18–19.</note>

Nor does this grief touch the sons of Atreus alone.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 9.138. The "sons of Atreus" are the Greek leaders Agamemnon and Menelaus.</note>

But you, oh chosen ones: who prepares to cut the rampart

<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 9.146–147.</note>

For what remains, men, take care of your bodies, happy with things
well done: and expect a battle to be prepared.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 9.156–158. This refers to the ritual of eating and resting before combat.</note>
Now go to your meal, so that we may join together for the war.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 9.708–709.</note>
So he spoke, weeping; at the same time he took from his shoulder
his gilded sword, which Lycaon the Gnosian had made with wondrous skill
and fitted into a handy ivory sheath.
Mnestheus gave to Nisus the skin and spoils of a shaggy lion;
faithful Alethes exchanged helmets.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 9.303–307. This describes the gifts given to the heroes Nisus and Euryalus before their mission.</note>
To the son of Tydeus, the battle-staying Thrasymedes gave
a two-edged sword—his own had been left at the ship—
and a shield. About his head he set a helmet of bull-hide,
without peak or crest, which is called a "skull-cap,"
and protects the heads of vigorous youths.
And Meriones gave Odysseus a bow and a quiver
and a sword.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 10.255–260. Virgil models the Roman gift-giving on this Greek scene where Diomedes (son of Tydeus) and Odysseus prepare for their own night raid.</note>

Forthwith they marched out armed; as they went, the whole band
of leaders, both young and old, escorted them with prayers.
And also the beautiful Iulus—
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 9.308–310.</note>
When the two had donned their terrible armor,
they went on their way, and left all the leaders there.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 10.272–273.</note>
Having gone out, they crossed the ditches; and through the shadow of the night
they sought the enemy camp, yet they were destined to bring death to many
before [their own end]. Everywhere they saw bodies scattered across the grass
by sleep and wine. Chariots were tilted up on the shore;
among the reins and wheels lay men together with their armor
and their wine. The son of Hyrtacus spoke first:
"Euryalus, we must dare with the right hand; now the deed itself calls.
Here is our path. You, keep watch and look far off,
lest any hand rise up against us from behind.
I will lay these lands waste and lead you by a wide path."
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 9.314–323. Nisus, the son of Hyrtacus, speaks to his young friend as they enter the camp of the sleeping Rutulians.</note>
So the two went forward through the slaughter and the dark blood.
Quickly they came upon the ranks of Thracian men;
these were sleeping, overcome by weariness, and their gear [lay beside them].
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 10.297–299. This is the Greek equivalent, where Odysseus and Diomedes infiltrate the Thracian camp.</note>

### OF THE SATURNALIA

Their beautiful armor lay on the ground by them, arranged in goodly order in three rows; and beside each man was his pair of horses.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 10.473–475. This describes the camp of the Thracians during the night raid by Odysseus and Diomedes.</note>

And a little later:
When Odysseus saw them, he showed them to Diomedes:
"This is the man, Diomedes, and these are the horses 
of which Dolon, whom we slew, told us.
Come now, put forth your mighty strength; you must not stand
idle with your weapons, but unloose the horses;
or you slay the men, and the horses shall be my care."
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 10.477–481.</note>

But he could not ward off dark death by bird-signs.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 9.328. This refers to the death of Rhamnes, a seer who could not foresee his own death during the night raid.</note>
But he did not escape black death through his omens.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 2.859. This refers to the death of Ennomus the augur. Virgil has clearly mirrored the irony of the "prophet who dies anyway."</note>

And now early Aurora, leaving the saffron bed of Tithonus,
was sprinkling the earth with new light.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 9.459–460.</note>
Dawn rose from her bed by the side of noble Tithonus,
to bring light to immortals and to mortals.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 11.1–2. Tithonus was the mortal lover of the Goddess of Dawn; Virgil preserves this mythological detail.</note>

When the news reached the mother of Euryalus: how the shuttle was dashed from her hands and the wool fell; how she ran wailing along the walls and through the ranks of men, tearing her hair; how she poured out her grief in cries of lamentation—he <note>Virgil</note> took all of this from Andromache lamenting the death of her husband <note>Hector</note>.

O you truly Phrygian women—for you are not Phrygian men!
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 9.617. This is a taunt used against the Trojans; calling men "women" of their nation was a grave epic insult.</note>
O you boasters, you women of Achaea, no longer Achaean men!
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 2.235.</note>

What other walls, what other battlements do you have beyond these?
Shall one man, O citizens, fenced in on all sides by your 
ramparts, cause such carnage throughout the city with impunity? 
Shall he send so many of our finest youths to the Underworld? 
Do you feel no pity or shame for your unhappy fatherland, 
your ancient gods, and the great Aeneas?
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 9.781–787. This is a speech of rebuke given by the Trojan leader Pandarus (or here, likely Turnus's impact on the Trojans), urging the soldiers to fight back against a single hero.</note>

---

They hurl darts from their hands: just as beneath dark clouds 
the Strymonian cranes give signals and traverse the air 
with a cry, fleeing the south winds with a joyful clamor.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.264–266. "Strymonian" refers to the river Strymon in Thrace, famous for its cranes.</note>
The Trojans marched with clamor and shouting, like birds; 
even as the clamor of cranes arises before the sky, 
when they flee from winter and unspeakable rain, 
and with a clamor they fly toward the streams of the Ocean.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 3.2–5.</note>

The crest on his head blazes, and a flame 
pours from the top of his helmet, and his golden shield-boss casts forth vast fires. 
Just as when in the clear night blood-red comets 
glow mournfully, or the burning heat of Sirius 
arises—he who brings thirst and diseases to weary mortals 
and saddens the sky with his sinister light.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.270–275. Sirius is the "Dog Star," associated with the "dog days" of summer heat and illness.</note>
He kindled from his helmet and shield an unwearying fire, 
like the star of autumn, which shines brightest...
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 5.4–5. Referring to Diomedes’s armor. Macrobius illustrates how Virgil expanded Homer’s simple star simile into a more ominous description of comets and the plague-bearing Sirius.</note>

[The star] shines all-bright, as if bathed in the waters of the Ocean.
Such a fire did he kindle from the hero’s head and shoulders.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 5.6–7. This describes the goddess Athena kindling a flame from Diomedes’ helmet and shield, making him shine like the autumn star Sirius.</note>
**And elsewhere,**
shining like the star that rises in late summer,
whose rays shine clearly among the many stars in the darkness of the night,
the star that men call the Dog of Orion.
Brightest of all is he, but he is wrought as an evil sign,
and brings much fever to wretched mortals.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 22.26–31. This describes Achilles as he runs across the plain, comparing his terrifying brilliance to the Dog Star (Sirius), which was believed to bring heat and disease.</note>

Each man has his own day set: a brief and irretrievable time
of life is given to all.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.467–468. These are the words of Jupiter comforting Hercules over the impending death of Pallas.</note>

The fates call, and he has reached the goal of his allotted age.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.472. Referring again to Pallas’s destiny.</note>

"The many talents of silver and gold you mention,
save them for your children. Turnus was the first

<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.524–536. Aeneas, fueled by rage over the death of his friend Pallas, refuses the ransom of the suppliant Magus. Virgil here transforms Aeneas into a cold, relentless warrior.</note>

Take me alive, son of Atreus, and accept a worthy ransom!
Many treasures lie in the house of my wealthy father:
bronze and gold and well-wrought iron.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 6.46–48. The plea of Adrastus to Menelaus, which Virgil adapted for Magus.</note>
Take me alive! I will pay a ransom for myself, for there is within 
bronze and gold and well-wrought iron;
from these my father would grant you a boundless ransom,
if he should hear I were alive at the ships of the Achaeans.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 10.378–381. A similar plea made by the spy Dolon to Odysseus and Diomedes.</note>

Like a hungry lion often roaming the high stalls—
for a frantic hunger drives him—if by chance he sees a fleeing
roe-deer or a stag with high-towering horns,
he gapes immensely and rejoices; his mane bristles, and he clings
leaning over the entrails; foul blood bathes

So does the eager Mezentius rush into the thick of the enemy.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.723–729. Virgil uses this vivid, predatory simile to describe the Etruscan king Mezentius on the battlefield.</note>

As a lion rejoices when he lights upon a great carcass,
having found either a horned stag or a wild goat,
when he is hungry...
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 3.23–25. Virgil’s "hungry lion" is a direct expansion of this Homeric image, where Menelaus is compared to a lion seeing Paris.</note>

The earth is sprinkled with tears, and the armor is sprinkled too.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 11.191. Describing the funeral of Pallas.</note>
The sands were wet, and the armor of the men was wet [with tears].
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 23.15. Describing the mourning for Patroclus. Virgil imitates the "weeping objects" to emphasize the depth of the grief.</note>

### OF THE SATURNALIA

With tears

> The raging Turnus himself is girded for battle;
> And now he has put on his red-orange bronze breastplate,
