> Just as a purple flower, when cut by the plow,
> Withers as it dies; or as poppies with weary necks
> Lower their heads, when they happen to be weighed down by rain.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 9.435–437. Virgil uses this delicate image to describe the death of the young warrior Euryalus.</note>

> And as a poppy in a garden drops its head to one side,
> Weighed down by its seed and the rains of spring.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 8.306–307. Homer uses this to describe the death of Gorgythion, struck by an arrow.</note>

And these matters must indeed be left to the judgment of the readers, so that they may judge for themselves what they ought to feel regarding the comparison of both poets. If, however, you ask my opinion: I will not deny that Virgil, in translating, sometimes refined the material into a more condensed form, as in this following passage.
<note>The speaker here is Eustathius, one of the interlocutors in Macrobius's dialogue, who argues for Virgil's stylistic superiority in specific instances.</note>

> Such is the labor that busies the bees in early summer
> Through the flowery countryside beneath the sun, when they lead out
> The grown young of the race; or when they pack the liquid honey
> And stretch the cells with sweet nectar;
> Or receive the burdens of those arriving; or, forming a column,
> Drive the drones, a lazy herd, away from the enclosures.
> The work seethes, and the fragrant honey smells of thyme.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.430–436. Virgil uses the bee colony as a metaphor for the industrious building of Carthage.</note>

> Even as the tribes of swarming bees go forth
> From a hollow rock, always coming anew,
> And fly in clusters over the flowers of spring;
> Some flit in throngs here, and some there.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 2.87–90. Homer uses the bees to describe the massive, disorganized movement of the Achaean troops.</note>

Do you see how the bees are described as workers by Virgil, but as wanderers by Homer? One expresses the bustle and the sheer variety of flight; the other captures the duty of their innate craft.
In these verses too, Maro <note>Virgil's cognomen</note> stood out as the more resourceful translator.

> O companions (for we are not ignorant of evils before),
> O you who have suffered heavier things: God will give an end to these too.
> You have approached the Scyllaean rage and the deep-sounding
> Cliffs; and you have experienced the Cyclopean rocks.
> Recall your spirits: and dismiss your gloomy fear;
> Perhaps one day it will be a joy to remember even these things
> Through various misfortunes... and so forth.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.198–204. Aeneas encouraging his shipwrecked men.</note>

> O friends, for we are not at all unacquainted with evils;
> Surely this is no greater evil coming upon us than when the Cyclops
> Penned us in his hollow cave by his brute strength;
> Yet even from there, by my counsel and courage and wit, we escaped.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Odyssey* 12.208–211. Odysseus encouraging his men as they approach Scylla and Charybdis.</note>

LXXXVII
### BOOK FIVE

"...we escaped. And I think that one day we shall remember even these things."
<note>original Greek: Odyssey 12.212. These are the words of Odysseus (Ulysses) to his crew after escaping the Cyclops.</note>

**C** Ulysses reminded his companions of a single trial. Here, the hope for release from present evil is encouraged by the outcome of two past misfortunes. Furthermore, the former spoke somewhat obscurely; the latter more aptly: *perhaps even these things will one day be a pleasure to remember*. But even what our poet added is of a stronger consolation. For he animated his men not only by the example of escaping, but also by the hope of future happiness: promising through these labors not only peaceful dwellings, but also kingdoms. It is also a pleasure to examine these verses:

> And just as when on the highest mountains an ancient ash tree,
> Which the farmers, having hacked it with steel and frequent axes,
> Strive to uproot; it continually threatens to fall,
> And, trembling in its foliage, it nods with its shaken crown,
> Until, little by little, overcome by its wounds, it gives
> A final groan, and torn from the ridges, it drags down ruin.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.626–631. This simile describes the final fall of Troy.</note>

> He fell as an oak falls, or a poplar,
> Which in the meadow builders have cut with newly sharpened axes,
> To be a felloe for a beautiful chariot;
> It lies drying by the river bank.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 13.389–391 (and 16.482–484). Homer uses this to describe the death of a warrior.</note>

With great refinement, your author [Virgil] expressed the difficulty of cutting through the massive bulk of a tree. Truly, the Homeric tree is cut down with no trouble at all.

> Not slow to act, Palinurus rises from his bed, and all
> The winds he explores, and catches the air with his ears.
> He notes all the stars gliding in the silent sky:
> Arcturus, the rainy Hyades, and the twin Bears,
> And he surveys Orion, armed with gold.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.513–517. Palinurus is the master-pilot of Aeneas’s fleet.</note>

> But he, sitting, steered skillfully with the rudder,
> Nor did sleep fall upon his eyelids
> As he watched the Pleiades and late-setting Boötes,
> And the Bear, which they also call by the name of the Wagon,
> Which turns in the same place and watches Orion.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Odyssey* 5.270–275. Odysseus is navigating his raft away from Calypso’s island.</note>

**C** A <term>gubernator</term><note>A pilot or helmsman of a ship.</note> who explores the sky must frequently turn his neck back and forth to ensure safety from different regions of the heavens. Virgil [Maro] painted this marvelously, as if with colors. For because <term>Arcturus</term> is near the north, while <term>Taurus</term>—in which the <term>Hyades</term> and <term>Orion</term> are located—is in the southern region, he described a frequent turning of the neck in Palinurus as he consulted the stars. *Arcturus*, he says: behold, he looks toward the northern part. Then the *rainy Hyades*: behold, he is turned toward the south. *The twin Bears*: again he turns his gaze to the north. *And he surveys Orion, armed with gold*: once more he reflects himself toward the south. Indeed, with the word *circumspicit* [surveys/looks around], he shows the variety of one turning himself back and forth repeatedly. Homer introduces his pilot looking only once at the <term>Pleiades</term>, which are in the southern region, and once at <term>Boötes</term> and the Bear, which are at the northern pole.

> Neither was a goddess your parent, nor Dardanus the founder
> Of your race, you traitor; but the shivering Caucasus bore you
> On its hard crags, and Hyrcanian tigers offered you their teats.
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 4.365–367. Dido’s famous curse to Aeneas as he prepares to abandon her.</note>

> Pitiless one, the knight Peleus was not then your father,
> Nor was Thetis your mother; but the grey sea bore you
> And the towering cliffs, because your mind is unbending.
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 16.33–35. Patroclus rebukes Achilles for his lack of pity for the suffering Greeks.</note>

**C** Virgil more fully included not only the ancestry, as did the one he followed, but also the upbringing...

<meta>This page continues Macrobius's systematic comparison of the poets Homer and Virgil in Book 5 of the Saturnalia. Having previously discussed similes of falling trees, the text now examines how Virgil elaborates on Homeric themes, specifically regarding the influence of a nurse's milk on character, the intensity of chariot races, and the imagery of boiling water.</meta>

LXXXXII
### SATURNALIA, BOOK 5

He also censures the nature of his upbringing as something beastly and harsh. For he added from his own invention: **"And Hyrcanian tigers offered their teats,"** <note>original Latin: "Hyrcanæque admorunt ubera tygres" from Virgil’s *Aeneid* 4.367. Dido says this to Aeneas to suggest he has no human mercy.</note> because, clearly, in the formation of character, a great part is held by the nature of the nurse and the quality of her milk. When this milk is poured into the tender infant and mixed with the still-fresh seed of the parents, it shapes a single disposition from this dual bonding. Hence it is that the providence of nature, preparing a likeness between the children and the parents from the very act of nursing, caused an abundance of nourishment to be born at the same time as the birth itself. For after that craftsman-like blood has fashioned and nourished the whole body in its inner chambers, and as the time for birth approaches, that same blood rises to the upper parts of the mother's body and whitens into the nature of milk, so that the one who was the creator is now the same nourisher, recognized by the newborn. Therefore, it is not believed without reason that just as the power and nature of the seed are effective in shaping the likeness of body and mind, so too are the qualities and properties of milk effective in the same matter. Nor is this observed in humans alone, but in livestock as well. For if kids are perhaps nourished by the milk of sheep, or lambs by the milk of goats, it is generally established that in the former, a coarser wool grows, and in the latter, a softer hair. Even in trees and crops, the power and influence of the water and soil that nourish them is often greater for either diminishing or increasing their quality than the nature of the seed itself that is sown. And you may often see a lush and shining tree languish from the poor juice of the earth if it is transferred to another place. Therefore, to condemn his character, that which Virgil added was missing in Homer.

-> Not so headlong in a two-horsed contest do the chariots <-
-> Seize the field and rush forth, poured from the starting gate; <-
-> Nor do the charioteers so shake the flowing reins over <-
-> The unrestrained teams, and leaning forward, they hang over the lash. <-
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 5.144–147, describing a ship race by comparing it to a chariot race.</note>

-> And he always drove with the whip from the shoulder; and the horses <-
-> Were lifted high as they swiftly completed the course. <-
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 23.362–363.</note>

¶ The Greek poet mentions only the horses running under the animating whip, although it could not be said more elegantly than what he added: **"were lifted high,"** by which he expressed the great momentum the course could give. But Maro <note>Virgil's cognomen or family name</note> described both the chariots rushing from the starting gate and the fields being seized with wonderful speed; and having taken a brief seed from the Homeric whip, he painted the charioteers shaking the flowing reins and hanging forward over the lash, nor did he leave any part of the four-horse teams untouched, so that he might give a full description of the contest.

-> Just as when with a great sound a flame <-
-> Of twigs is applied to the sides of a surging cauldron, <-
-> And the waters leap with the heat; the power of the water rages within, <-
-> And the smoky stream overflows high with foam; <-
-> Nor can the wave now contain itself; the black vapor flies to the breezes. <-
<note>original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 7.462–466, describing the boiling rage of Turnus.</note>

-> As a cauldron boils within, urged by much fire, <-
-> Melting the lard of a tenderly-fed pig, <-
-> Bubbling up on all sides, and dry wood lies beneath it. <-
<note>original Greek: Homer, *Iliad* 21.362–364, describing the river Xanthus being scorched by Hephaestus.</note>

¶ The Greek verses contain mention of the cauldron bubbling with much fire, and these words adorn that whole passage. For he expressed the springs emerging from every side quite elegantly. In the Latin verses, the whole parade of the event is described: the sound of the flame. And through this, he said: **"the waters leaping with heat"** and **"the smoky stream overflowing with foam,"** and that it **"raged within,"** with a variety of descriptive abundance. He added after everything: **"nor can the wave now contain itself,"** by which he expressed what always happens in practice from an excess of heat applied beneath. Therefore, the refinement of the poetic trumpet holds itself well, comprising everything that happens in this matter.

LXXXVIII

### BOOK FIVE

They throw open the gate that had been entrusted to the commander's authority,
Relying on their weapons: and of their own accord, they invite the enemy within the walls:
They themselves stand inside, to the right and left, like towers,
Armed with steel, their tall heads gleaming with shimmering crests.
Just as two airy oaks, near flowing rivers—
Whether on the banks of the Po, or by the pleasant Adige—
Rise up together; they lift their unshorn heads to the sky
And nod with their lofty tops.
<note>original Latin: *Aeneid* 9.675–682. Virgil describes the giant brothers Pandarus and Bitias guarding the Trojan camp.</note>

Fools! They found two men, the best of all, at the gates,
The stout-hearted sons of spear-wielding Lapiths;
They stood like high-headed oaks in the mountains
Which withstand the wind and rain every day,
Fixed firm by great, long-stretching roots;
So these two, trusting in their hands and strength,
Awaited the approach of great Asius and did not flee.
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 12.127–134. Homer describes the heroes Polypoetes and Leonteus.</note>

The Greek soldiers Polypoetes and Leonteus stand before the gates and remain unmoved as the enemy Asius approaches, just like fixed trees. Thus far is the Greek description. However, Virgil’s version makes Bitias and Pandarus throw the gate open of their own accord to offer it to the enemy—which was what they desired—so that the enemy might enter the camp and thereby fall into their power. And he calls the twin heroes "towers" at one moment, then describes them gleaming with the light of their crests. Nor did he omit the comparison to trees, but he described it more richly and more beautifully. I would not deny that this was expressed more elegantly by Maro <note>A common name for the poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro).</note>.

> For him, a harsh rest presses upon his eyes, and an iron
> Sleep: his lights are closed in eternal night.
> <note>original Latin: *Aeneid* 10.745–746. A description of death in battle.</note>
> So falling there, he slept a sleep of bronze.
> <note>original Greek: *Iliad* 11.241. Homer’s shorter, famous description of death.</note>

In some passages, the brilliance of both poets is almost equal, such as:

The rapid hoof scatters bloody
Dews: and gore is trampled into the mixed sand.
<note>original Latin: *Aeneid* 12.339–340.</note>

And gleaming with brazen light.
<note>original Latin: *Aeneid* 2.470.</note>

One part seeks the seeds of fire.
<note>original Latin: *Aeneid* 6.6.</note>
<gloss>seeds of fire</gloss>
<note>original Greek: *Odyssey* 5.490.</note>

Just as if someone had stained Indian ivory with bloody purple.
<note>original Latin: *Aeneid* 12.67. A simile for a blush or a wound.</note>
As when some woman stains ivory with crimson.
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 4.141.</note>

If it is necessary for that unspeakable head to reach the harbor
And swim to land:
And if the decrees of Jove so demand, and this end remains fixed:
Yet let him be harassed by the war and arms of a bold people,
Driven from his borders, torn from the embrace of Iulus,
Let him beg for aid, and see the unworthy deaths of his people;
Nor, when he has surrendered himself under the laws of an unfair
Peace, may he enjoy his kingdom or the desired light:
But let him fall before his day, and lie unburied in the middle of the sand.
<note>original Latin: *Aeneid* 4.612–620. Dido’s famous curse against Aeneas, foretelling his future struggles and death.</note>

but if it is his fate to see his friends and reach
his well-built house and his own fatherland,
may he come late and in a wretched state, having lost all his comrades,

<note>original Greek: *Odyssey* 9.532–535. This is the curse the Cyclops Polyphemus levels against Odysseus, which Virgil echoes in the curses of Dido and the struggles of Aeneas.</note>

Running her fine-toothed shuttle through the delicate web.
<note>original Latin: *Aeneid* 7.10–14. Virgil describes the island of the sorceress Circe.</note>
She of the lovely hair dwelt within; they found her there.

### BOOK FIVE
### M

He strikes him down as he is speaking and leaves him as a trunk on the ground.
<note>original Latin: *Dicere deturbat terræ: truncoque reliquit* from Virgil’s *Aeneid* 10.555. Virgil is describing the death of Tarquitus.</note>
These two verses were translated from that source:
> Indeed, he was just about to touch his chin with his sturdy hand
> to beg for mercy, but the other struck him in the middle of the neck,
> rushing forward with his sword, and cut through both tendons;
> and as he was still speaking, his head was mixed with the dust.
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 10.454–457. Homer describes Diomedes killing the spy Dolon. Virgil condenses Homer’s four lines into one short, punchy phrase.</note>

Observe the excessive speed maintained with such weight, a level of exertion that Maro’s efforts could not quite reach. In the chariot race, Homer signaled with what light he followed one chariot slightly leading and another almost joined to it:
> And quickly then
> the swift-footed horses of Pheres' grandson drew ahead,
> and Diomedes’ stallions of the breed of Tros chased after,
> not at all far behind, but very close;
> for they always seemed about to step onto the chariot,
> and with their breath the back and broad shoulders of Eumelus
> grew warm; for their heads leaned over him as they flew.
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 23.375–381. This describes the intense proximity of the horses during the funeral games for Patroclus.</note>

They grow wet with the foam and the breath of those following.
<note>original Latin: *Humescunt spumis flatuque sequentum* from *Aeneid* 5.326. Virgil’s adaptation of the Greek scene above.</note>
More wonderful still is the speed of one following the leader in a footrace in the same poet:
> His feet struck the footprints before the dust could settle around them.
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 23.763. Describing Odysseus following Ajax so closely that he steps in his tracks before the dust fills them.</note>

The sense of this verse is as follows: If someone happens to run through loose dust, when the foot is lifted from the ground by the runner, a footprint is undoubtedly seen marked; and yet, swifter than thought, the dust that had been kicked up by the blow of the foot pours back over the footprint. For the divine poet <note>Referring to Homer.</note> says that the one following was so close that he occupies the predecessor’s footprint before the dust could pour back into it. But here <term>Maro</term> <note>Virgil</note>, wishing to signify the same thing, says:
And now Diores rubs heel with heel.
<note>original Latin: *Calcemque terit iam calce Diores* from *Aeneid* 5.324. Virgil describes the runner Diores pressing closely against Helymus.</note>
See also Homer’s refinement in this: "And he, falling back, lay on his back."
<note>original Greek: *η και ανακλινθεις πεσεν υπτιος* from *Odyssey* 18.398.</note>
That man <note>Virgil</note> says: He laid down his neck, bent back.
<note>original Latin: *Ceruicem inflexam posuit*.</note>
Let us also compare these verses, if it seems right:
> The chariots at one moment would hug the bountiful earth,
> and at another would leap up into the air.
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 23.368–369.</note>

Now low, and now raised sublime in the air
They seem to be carried through the thin breeze.
<note>original Latin: *Aeneid* 5.144–145. Virgil’s description of the rowing race, though using chariot-like imagery.</note>
> She holds her head and forehead above them all.
<note>original Greek: *Odyssey* 6.107. Describing the goddess Artemis among her nymphs.</note>

And as she walks, she towers above all goddesses.
<note>original Latin: *Gradiensque deas supereminet omnes* from *Aeneid* 1.501. Virgil’s description of Diana, used as a simile for Queen Dido.</note>
> Tell me now, Muses, who have your homes on Olympus,
> for you are goddesses, and are present, and know all things.
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 2.484–485. The famous invocation before the Catalog of Ships.</note>

For you remember, goddesses, and you can relate.
<note>original Latin: *Et meministis enim diuæ: et memorare potestis* from *Aeneid* 7.645.</note>

---

At the same time he raises horrific cries to the stars,
Like the bellowing when a wounded bull flees the altar
And has shaken the uncertain axe from its neck.
<note>original Latin: *Aeneid* 2.222–224. Describing the agonizing cries of Laocoön as he is attacked by the serpents.</note>
By inspecting the "thread" <note>Referring to the literary style or texture.</note> of each here, one perceives how great a distance lies between them. But this is no less elegantly done: that when speaking of a bull drawn to sacrifice, he mentions both Apollo and Neptune.

->### ON THE SATURNALIA<-
<meta>Mirrored page number 91 at top left from facing page.</meta>

**Virgil** himself testifies that divine rites are performed with a bull for these two deities in particular:
**"A bull for Neptune; a bull for you, beautiful Apollo."**
<note>original Latin: *Taurum neptuno: taurum tibi pulcher apollo* from *Aeneid* 3.119.</note>

> As when a destructive fire falls upon a thick wood 
> on the peaks of a mountain, and from afar its gleam is seen;
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 2.455–456.</note>
> and as when mountain-flowing torrents 
> into a meeting-place of waters cast their mighty flood 
> from great springs within a hollow ravine, 
> and from afar the shepherd in the mountains hears the roar.
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 4.452–455.</note>

**"Just as when a flame falls on the standing grain when the south winds rage: or a rapid torrent from a mountain stream**
**levels the fields: levels the happy crops and the labors of oxen,**
**and drags the forests headlong. The dazed shepherd, unaware, from a high**
**rock hears the sound."**
<note>original Latin: *Aeneid* 2.304–308. Virgil is describing the fall of Troy.</note>

Virgil violated two distinct parables in order to make one, drawing fire from one source and a torrent from another; and he failed to fulfill the dignity of either.

> As when two winds stir the fishy sea, 
> Boreas and Zephyrus, which blow from Thrace 
> coming suddenly; and at once the black wave 
> crests, and they pour out much seaweed along the sea.
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 9.4–7.</note>

**"As when a storm breaks and diverse winds**
**clash: Zephyrus and Notus and Eurus, joyful with eastern**
**horses: the woods creak; and with his trident**
**foaming Nereus rages and stirs the waters from the lowest depth."**
<note>original Latin: *Aeneid* 2.416–419.</note>

He removes the flaw from this passage which he incurred in the one above, by constructing one parable more clearly from two Greek ones.

> To them, far-working Apollo sent a favorable wind.
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 1.479. The word used for favorable is *ikmenos*.</note>
**"A wind rising from the stern follows them as they go."**
<note>original Latin: *Prosequitur surgens a puppi uentus euntis* from *Aeneid* 3.130.</note>

What our author <note>Homer</note> called "favorable," your author <note>Virgil</note> says is **"rising from the stern,"** which is quite graceful. However, the epithets which our author applied to the wind are so many and so apt that they elevate the verse.

> And seizing two together, he dashed them like puppies against the earth,
> and their brains flowed out on the ground, and wetted the earth.
> These he cut limb from limb and prepared his supper;
> and he ate like a mountain-bred lion, nor did he leave 
> the entrails, or the flesh, or the marrowy bones.
<note>original Greek: *Odyssey* 9.289–293. This describes the Cyclops Polyphemus eating Odysseus's men.</note>

**"He feeds on the entrails of the wretched and on dark blood."**
**"I myself saw when he, lying back in the middle of the cave,**
**seized with his great hand two bodies from our number**
**and smashed them against the rock."**
<note>original Latin: *Aeneid* 3.622–625.</note>

**Maro** <note>Virgil</note> provided a bare and brief account of the deed. In contrast, **Homer** mixed in <term>pathos</term> <note>emotional appeal</note> and matched the cruelty of the act with the pain of the telling.

> And after her I saw Iphimedeia, wife of Aloeus,
> who said she had lain with Poseidon,
> and bore two sons, though they were short-lived:
> Otus like a god, and far-famed Ephialtes,
> whom the grain-giving earth bred as the tallest 
> and by far the most beautiful, after famous Orion.
> For at nine years old they were nine cubits wide and nine tall.
<note>original Greek: *Odyssey* 11.305–312. This describes the Aloadae, giants who tried to storm heaven.</note>

<summary>Macrobius compares specific passages from Homer and Virgil, critiquing Virgil's tendency to combine multiple Homeric similes into single, shorter descriptions. He argues that while Virgil is sometimes graceful, he often loses the emotional depth and vividness (pathos) found in Homer's original Greek epics.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the comparison between the Greek poet Homer and the Roman poet Virgil. The speaker, likely Eustathius in the context of Macrobius’s Saturnalia, is demonstrating how Virgil’s attempts to condense Homeric similes often result in a loss of descriptive power and grandeur.</meta>

### BOOK FIVE
->XC<-

> They were nine cubits in breadth, but in height they were nine fathoms; and they even threatened the immortals in Olympus that they would raise the din of furious war; they were eager to pile Mount Ossa upon Olympus and upon Ossa Pelion with its shaking leaves, so that heaven might be accessible.
<note>original Greek: *Odyssey* 11.311–315. This describes the Aloadae, giant sons of Poseidon who attempted to storm heaven.</note>

¶ **"From here I saw the twin Aloadae, those giant bodies: who attempted to tear down the great heavens with their hands and to cast Jove down from his high kingdoms."**
<note>original Latin: *Hinc & aloidas geminos imania uidi Corpora: qui manibus magnũ rescindere cælum Aggressi: superisq̃ ioue de trudere regnis.* from Virgil's *Aeneid* 6.582–584.</note>
Homer measured the size of their bodies in both height and width, and depicted their limbs with a grand circuit of words. Your poet [Virgil] simply says "giant bodies" and adds nothing further, not daring to touch upon the specific names of measurements. Homer expressed the effort of their mad construction in the piling of mountains. Virgil, by saying they "attempted to tear down," merely spoke of their effort against heaven. Finally, if you compare the description of the location itself, you will find a shameful difference in quality.

> As when on an echoing shore the wave of the sea rises wave after wave under the driving of the West Wind; at first it crests out at sea, but then it breaks upon the land and bellows loudly, and around the headlands it curves and peaks and spits out the foam of the sea.
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 4.422–426.</note>

¶ **"As when the wave first begins to whiten on the sea: little by little the sea raises itself, and lifts its waves higher: then from its very bottom it rises toward the sky."**
<note>original Latin: *Fluctus uti primo cœpit quum albescere ponto: Paulatim sese tollit mare: & altius undas Erigit: inde imo consurgit ad æthera fundo.* from *Aeneid* 11.624–628.</note>
While the former [Homer] describes the movement of the sea and the waves from their very beginning at the shore, the latter [Virgil] flies right past it. Then, regarding what Homer says:

->**at first it crests out at sea**<-
<note>original Greek: *ποντω μεν τα πρωτα κορυσεται* from *Iliad* 4.424.</note>

¶ Virgil turned this into **"Little by little the sea raises itself."** Homer says that the waves, in their increasing size, are curved high and dashed against the shores, spitting out the spray of the gathered filth—a description so vivid that no painting could represent it more expressively. Virgil merely leads the sea from the bottom all the way to the heavens. Virgil had spoken, and confirmed his word by the Stygian streams of his brother [Pluto], by the banks burning with pitch and black whirlpools: **"He nodded, and made all Olympus tremble with his nod."**
<note>original Latin: *Annuit: & totũ nutu tremefecit olympũ.* from *Aeneid* 9.104–106.</note>

> The son of Cronos spoke and nodded with his dark brows, and the ambrosial locks of the lord flowed from his immortal head, and he shook great Olympus.
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 1.528–530.</note>

¶ Phidias <note>A famous Greek sculptor of the 5th century BCE.</note>, when he was crafting the statue of Olympian Jupiter, was asked what model he used to imitate the divine likeness. He replied that he found the archetype of Jupiter in these three verses of Homer. For he gathered the whole countenance of Jupiter from the description of the eyebrows and the hair—both of which you see are omitted by Virgil. To be sure, Virgil did not remain silent about the shaking of Olympus by the majesty of the nod. However, he took the oath from another part of Homer, so that the "thinness" of his translation might be compensated by this addition: **"A boy marking his face with the first unshorn youth."**
<note>original Latin: *Ora puer prima signans intonsa iuuenta* from Virgil's *Aeneid* 7.666.</note>
The omitted grace of the beginning of puberty made the Latin description less pleasing.

> As when among dogs and hunters a boar or lion turns about, exulting in his strength; and they, lining themselves up like a wall, stand against him and hurl frequent spears from their hands; but his noble heart never fears nor is it afraid, though his bravery kills him; and he turns frequently, testing the ranks of men; wherever he rushes, the ranks of men give way.
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 12.41–48.</note>

¶ **"Like a wild beast, which, enclosed by a dense circle of hunters, rages against the weapons, and, not unaware of death, flings itself forward and is carried by a leap over the hunting spears."**
<note>original Latin: *Vt fera: quæ densa uenantum septa corona Cōtra tela furit: seseq̃ haud nescia morti Iniicit & saltu supra uenabula fertur.* from Virgil's *Aeneid* 9.551–553.</note>
You see how the Latin comparison has been contracted into such a narrow space that nothing could be more meager; the Greek, by contrast, with its wealth of both words and details, has filled out the splendor of a true hunt. In the face of such a great difference, it is almost embarrassing to compare them.

The focus remains on Virgil’s "imitatio" (imitation) of Homeric passages and where the Roman poet is perceived to fall short of the original Greek's power and logic.</meta>

# OF THE SATURNALIA
->XC<-

> "Fence spear with spear, shield with shield, buckler with buckler, helmet with helmet, and man with man."
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 13.130–131. Homer describes the Greek ranks closing together in a solid phalanx.</note>

Not otherwise do the Trojan ranks and the Latin ranks clash: foot stays fixed to foot and man crowded against man.
<note>original Latin: *Haud aliter troianæ acies aciesq; latinæ Concurrunt: hæret pede pes densusq; uiro uir.* from Virgil's *Aeneid* 10.359–361.</note>
How great a difference there is between these two passages, I leave for the reader to judge.

> "For a bird came upon them as they were eager to cross over, a high-flying eagle, skirting the host on the left, carrying in its talons a blood-red, monstrous snake, alive and still gasping, and it was not yet forgetful of the fight. For it struck the eagle as he held it, upon the breast by the neck, bending backward; but the eagle let it fall to the ground, pained by the agony, and dropped it in the midst of the throng, and then with a cry it flew away on the gusts of the wind."
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 12.200–207. This describes an omen seen by the Trojans before attacking the Greek wall.</note>

"Just as when a golden eagle, flying high, carries a snatched-up snake, entangles its feet, and clings with its talons. But the wounded serpent twists its sinuous coils, bristles with its raised scales, and hisses with its mouth, rising up tall; she, no less, attacks the struggling creature with her hooked beak, while simultaneously beating the air with her wings."
<note>original Latin: *Vtque uolans alte raptum quuum fulua draconem Fert aquila: implicuitque pedes atque unguibus hæsit. Saucius at serpens sinuosa uolumina uersat. Arrectisque hor ret squammis: & sibilat ore: Arduus in surgens: illa haud minus urget obunco Lucta tem rostro: simul æthera uerberat alis.* from Virgil’s *Aeneid* 11.751–756.</note>
Virgil describes only the eagle’s prey; he fails to notice the omen of the Homeric eagle, which, by coming from the left, prohibited the victors from advancing, and which, after being bitten by the captive snake, dropped its prey in pain. By performing a <term>solistimum tripudium</term> <note>original: "tripudio solistimo". In Roman divination, this was an "excellent dance" or a favorable sign occurring when food fell from a sacred bird's mouth to the ground; here, the snake falling is interpreted as a dark reversal of that sign.</note> with its cry testifying to its pain, it flew past—all of which signified the reversal of victory.

With these details omitted, which gave soul to the parable, only a lifeless body remains in the Latin verses. "Small at first through fear, soon she lifts herself into the breezes, walks upon the ground, and hides her head among the clouds."
<note>original Latin: *Parua metu primo mox sese attollit i auras: Ingrediturq; solū: & caput iter nubila cōdit.* from Virgil's description of *Fama* (Rumor) in *Aeneid* 4.176–177.</note>

> "She who is small at first when she crests her head, but then she fixes her head in heaven while walking upon the earth."
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 4.442–443. Homer is describing *Eris* (Strife/Discord).</note>

<margin>A comparison of Contention and Fame</margin>
Homer said that <term>Strife</term> <note>original Greek: *εριν* (Eris).</note> begins from a small size and afterwards grows until it reaches the sky. Virgil said the same thing about Fame, but inappropriately. For the logic behind "Contention" and "Fame" is not equal. Even if Contention proceeds to mutual destruction and war, it is still Contention; it remains the same thing that grew. But when Fame spreads into the immense, it ceases to be Fame and becomes the knowledge of a thing already known.

For who would still call it "fame" once a matter is known from the earth to the sky? Furthermore, he could not even match the hyperbole. Homer said "heaven"; Virgil said "breezes and clouds." This, however, was his method—not to equal everything he transcribed from his author, although he wanted to insert an imitation of some Homeric passage into every part of his work. Yet human strength cannot everywhere equal that divinity [of Homer], as in that passage which I want us to weigh together in common judgment. Minerva gave to her fighting Diomedes a burning glow of flames, and during the slaughter of enemies, the brilliance of his head or armor threatens on behalf of the soldier.

> "She kindled from his helmet and shield an untiring fire, like the star of late summer which shines most brightly when it has bathed in the Ocean; such a fire she kindled from his head and shoulders."
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 5.4–7. Referring to the Aristeia (moment of peak glory) of the hero Diomedes.</note>

Virgil, admiring this beyond measure, used it excessively. For now he says of Turnus: "The bloody crests tremble atop his head, and his shield sends out flashing lightning bolts." Now he says the same of Aeneas: "A peak of flame burns on his head, a flame is poured from his crests and top; and the bronze shield-boss vomits vast fires." How inappropriately this is placed is apparent here: Aeneas was not yet even fighting, but was simply appearing as he arrived on his ship. In another place: "Whose high helmet, hairy with a triple mane, supports a Chimaera breathing out Etnean fires from its jaws." And what of the fact that Aeneas, having recently received the arms from Vulcan and placed them on the ground, marvels at the helmet "terrible with its crests and moving flames"?

...with a different greed for enjoyment, to see the [splendor] of this place: which, as we mentioned above, he was seized by.

¶ He [Virgil] wished to maintain <note>The OCR reads "seruo," likely a contraction or error for "servare" (to preserve/maintain).</note> a similar reverence for Jupiter when he speaks. For although in the first book, and in the fourth, and in the ninth, Jupiter says certain things without any cosmic commotion; yet finally, after the quarrel of Juno and Venus, he [Virgil] wrote, with him [Jupiter] speaking: "The high house of the gods falls silent; and the earth is still, shaken from its foundation, and the high ether. Then the west winds subsided; the sea presses down its calm waters."
<note>original Latin: *Deum domus alta silescit: & tremefacta solo tellus silet arduus æther. Tum zephyri posuere: premit placida æquora pontus.* From *Aeneid* 10.101–103. Macrobius notes that Virgil only introduces this cosmic silence for Jupiter later in the poem, unlike Homer who is more consistent.</note>
As if the same thing does not happen when he spoke a little while before without any obedience from the whole world. A similar opportunity occurs in the same scales of Jupiter, which he took from that passage:

> "And then the Father [Zeus] stretched out the golden scales, and placed in them two fates of death that brings long woe—one for Achilles and one for Hector, tamer of horses. Taking them by the middle, he raised them; and Hector’s fated day sank down, and he went to the house of Hades, and Phoebus Apollo left him."
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 22.209–213. This is the climactic moment where the gods decide Hector must die.</note>

For although Juno had already predicted regarding Turnus:

> "Now I see the youth meeting unequal fates; the day of the Fates and the hostile light approach."
<note>original Latin: *Nunc iuuenem imparibus uideo concurrere fatis: Parcarumque dies & lux inimica propinquat.* From *Aeneid* 12.149–150. The "Parcae" are the three Fates of Roman mythology.</note>

And although it was manifest that Turnus would certainly perish, yet later:

> "Jupiter himself holds up two scales with equal balance, and imposes the diverse fates of the two."
<note>original Latin: *Iuppiter ipse duas æquato examine lances Sustinet: & fata imponit diuersa duorum.* From *Aeneid* 12.725–726.</note>

<margin>Virgil is an excessive emulator of Homer</margin>
¶ But these and other things are to be forgiven in Virgil, who in his zeal for Homer exceeds the proper limit through excess. And in truth, he could not help but seem lesser in some respects, since he used this one archetype throughout his entire poetry. For he fixed his eyes sharply upon Homer, so that he might emulate not only his magnitude, but also his simplicity, the presence of his speech, and his silent majesty. From this comes the varied magnification of the different characters among his heroes; from this, the intervention of the gods; from this, the authority of the mythical; from this, the natural expression of emotions; from this, the pursuit of ancient descriptions; from this, the weight of parables; from this, the sound of a rushing oration; and from this, the peak of individual things with splendor. Indeed, Virgil’s imitation of Homer is so sweet to him that he even imitated faults in the verses—which are ignorantly criticized by some—I mean those which the Greeks call [defective].

¶ These [defects] he did not avoid, also approving of the Homeric style; such as the "acephalous" <term>acephalous: literally "headless" verses, which begin with a short syllable where a long one is expected by the meter</term> verses in his work: "he batters the gates" <note>original: *arietat in portas*</note>; "a path woven with blind walls" <note>original: *parietibus textum cæcis iter*</note>; and similar ones. As also those which have short syllables in the middle of a verse instead of long ones: "And the hard posts with a bar" <note>original: *Et duros obice postes*</note>. "Father Latinus himself [considers] the plan and great undertakings" <note>original: *Consilium ipse pater & magna incepta latinus*</note>. Other syllables are longer [than expected]: "Indeed, immediately all things" <note>original: *Quin protinus omnia*</note>. "He boils away the moisture with fire" <note>original: *Vulcano decoquit humorem*</note>. "And they mix the foam of silver and living sulfur" <note>original: *Et spumas miscent argenti uiuaque fulphura*</note>. "And the rough arbutus" <note>original: *Et arbutus horrida*</note>. There are in Homer verses similar to those "plucked and shaved" <note>original: *uulsis ac rasis* — referring to verses that feel thin or more like common speech than high poetry</note>, and differing not at all from common speech. These also he [Virgil] loved as if they were heroically unpolished:

> "Love conquers all: and let us yield to love."
<note>original Latin: *Omnia uincit amor: & nos cedamus amori.* From *Eclogues* 10.69.</note>
> "Naked you will lie, Palinurus, on an unknown shore."
<note>original Latin: *Nudus in ignota palinure iacebis arena.* From *Aeneid* 5.871.</note>

There are pleasant repetitions which he did not avoid, such as:

> "Pan even if he should contend with me, with Arcadia as judge; Pan even if he should say he was defeated, with Arcadia as judge."
<note>original Latin: *Pan etiam arcadia mecum si iudice certet: Pan etiam arcadia dicat se iudice uictum.* From *Eclogues* 4.58–59.</note>

¶ He also confessed how much he admired Homeric epithets by imitating them; and a thousand such words, with which the varied majesty of his divine song sparkles like stars. To these, he responds from your own [works]: "Ill-advising hunger" <note>original: *Male suada fames*</note>. "Golden-haired branches" <note>original: *Auricomos ramos*</note>. "Hundred-fold twin Briareus" <note>original: *Centum geminus briareus*</note>. Add also "smoke-bearing night" <note>original: *fumigeram noctem*</note>, and whatever the diligent reader recognizes in almost every single verse. Often Homer, in the middle of narrating, directs his speech as if to someone. Virgil did not omit this either: "You might see them migrating, and rushing from the whole city." <note>original: *Migrantes cernas: totaque ex urbe ruentes.* From *Aeneid* 4.401.</note> And the whole...

<meta>This page continues the comparison between Homer and Virgil from Book Five of Macrobius’s *Saturnalia*. Having previously discussed how Virgil imitates Homer’s descriptions of the gods, the speaker (Eustathius) now examines how Virgil emulates Homer’s technique of inserting "backstories" or historical flashbacks into the narrative to provide context without following a strictly chronological (historical) timeline.</meta>

# THE SATURNALIA
->M iii<-
<note>This "M iii" is a signature mark used by early printers to keep the pages of a book in the correct order during binding.</note>

...with Mars in motion, you would see Leucas boil. And you would believe the Cyclades were torn up and swimming in the sea. And you would see them long to wash in vain.
<note>These lines refer to Virgil’s description of the Battle of Actium as depicted on Aeneas's shield in *Aeneid* 8.675–692. The imagery suggests a battle so intense that islands seem to be uprooted.</note>
Likewise, that divine poet <note>Referring to Homer.</note> opportunely recalls events that happened a little or much earlier into the sequence of his narrative; he does this so that he might both avoid a "historical style"—by not simply listing events in chronological order—and yet not deprive us of the knowledge of past events. Achilles had destroyed Thebe, a city of Asia, and many others before he became angry. But Homer’s work took its beginning from the wrath of Achilles. Therefore, so that we would not be ignorant of what happened before, a timely narration of those events is provided. Likewise, so that we might not be ignorant of which leader the Greek fleet followed to find the Trojan shore (which was unknown to them), when he speaks of the seer Calchas, he says:

> "And he led the ships of the Achaeans to Ilium, by his seer-craft, which Phoebus Apollo gave him."
<note>original Greek: *καὶ νήεσσ' ἡγήσατ' Ἀχαιῶν Ἴλιον εἴσω ἣν διὰ μαντοσύνην τήν οἱ πόρε Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων*. From *Iliad* 1.71–72.</note>

And Calchas himself tells of the omen that occurred to the sailing Greeks regarding the serpent that preyed upon the sparrows—from which it was announced that the army would remain in enemy territory for ten years. In another place, the same old man <note>Referring to Nestor, known for his long-winded wisdom.</note>—as old age is friendly to and talkative in recounting tales—relates ancient matters.

<margin>Virgil
imitated and
emulated
all of this</margin>
**And following things. Virgil most beautifully emulated this whole style.** For I remember [the lines regarding] Priam, son of Laomedon, visiting the realms of his sister Hesione; and indeed I remember Teucer coming to Sidon; and [Evander saying], "As I was when I laid low the first rank beneath the walls of Praeneste."
<note>These are allusions to Virgil's use of "flashbacks" in the *Aeneid* (8.157, 1.619, and 8.561) to fill in the history of his characters.</note>
And the whole narrative concerning the theft and punishment of Cacus <note>A famous episode in *Aeneid* Book 8 where Hercules kills a fire-breathing giant.</note> did not remain silent about the most ancient things; rather, as an imitator of his master [Homer], Virgil brought them to our knowledge. For they say that Cycnus, in grief for his beloved Phaethon... and similar things. But where the auxiliary forces are enumerated—which the Greeks call a *catalog* <term>catalog: a formal list of ships, leaders, or troops</term>—having tried to imitate that same author of his, 

<margin>He deviated</margin>
he deviated a little in some respects from Homeric gravity. First, because Homer, having bypassed Athens and Lacedaemon, and even Mycenae itself (from which the leader of the army, Agamemnon, came), placed Boeotia at the head of his catalog. He did this not because of any special dignity of that place, but because he chose a very well-known promontory <note>The port of Aulis in Boeotia, where the Greek fleet gathered.</note> for the start of his list. Proceeding from there, he describes now the inland regions, now the adjacent coastal ones. He approaches each site of connected places with the discipline of a traveler on a journey. Nor does he permit the continuity of regions in his book to "gape" with any leap; instead, proceeding in this orderly manner, he eventually returns to where he started, and thus encompasses the entire list.

By contrast, Virgil observes no order in commemorating the regions, but tears the sequence of places apart with leaps. First, he brings Massicus from Clusium and Cosa. Abas follows him, accompanied by a band from Populonia and Elba. After these, Pisa sent Asilas. 
<note>Macrobius is criticizing Virgil's "Catalogue of Italians" in *Aeneid* 10. He notes that Virgil jumps around the map of Italy rather than following a logical path.</note>
How far apart these parts of Etruria <note>Modern-day Tuscany and Umbria.</note> are is too well known to need noting. Then soon he returns to Caere, and Pyrgi, and Graviscae—places very close to the City [Rome]—to which he gave Astur as leader. From here, he snatches us away to Cycnus in Liguria, and Ocnus in Mantua. 

But not even in the catalog of Turnus’s allies, if you wish to run through the locations in your mind, will you find that he followed the continuity of regions. Furthermore, Homer commemorates everyone whom he lists in his catalog later in the story, even while they are fighting, whether they meet a fortunate or sinister fate. And when he wants to speak of those killed whom he did *not* include in the catalog, he introduces not the name of an individual man, but the name of a "multitude." Whenever he wants to signify a great slaughter, he says a "harvest of men" was made, not easily adding a specific name to anyone who was not previously introduced in the catalog...

<summary>Macrobius compares the narrative structures of Homer and Virgil, specifically how they handle historical "backstories" and the geographic organization of their military catalogs. He praises Homer’s logical, travel-like progression while noting Virgil’s more fragmented, "leaping" geography.</summary>

# BOOK FIVE
### PAGE XCII

...in the battle line: or he subtracts from it. But our Maro <note>A common nickname for the poet Publius Virgilius Maro, known today as Virgil.</note> neglected the strictness of this observation. For he both omits those named in his catalogue during the actual scenes of war, and names others in battle who were never mentioned before. He stated that a thousand bands of youths came under the leader **Massicus**, those who left the walls of Clusium and the city of Cosa. Then, **Turnus** <note>The primary antagonist of the *Aeneid*.</note> flees on a ship which was brought by King **Osinius** from the shores of Clusium—yet he never named Osinius before. And now it seems unfitting for a king to serve under Massicus. Furthermore, neither Massicus nor Osinius appear at all in the heat of the war. This is also true of those he mentions elsewhere: the brave **Gyas** and the brave **Sergestus**. Likewise the fair **Equiculus**, and the martial **Haemon**, and the most valiant **Umbro**, and **Virbius**, the most beautiful offspring of Hippolytus; none of these earned a place among the ranks of the combatants by either a glorious or a shameful mention in the fighting. **Astur**, and likewise **Cupavo**, and **Cygnus**—distinguished by the myths of Cygnus and Phaethon—contribute nothing to the fight; meanwhile, **Abas** and **Sacrator**, who are completely unknown, are fighting, as is **Atinas**, who was never mentioned before.

Furthermore, among those he does name, there is often a careless confusion on his part. In the ninth book, **Asilas** strikes down **Corinaeus**. Then in the twelfth book, Corinaeus kills **Ebusus**: "Corinaeus, meeting him, snatched a charred brand from the altar, and as Ebusus came on to strike..." <note>A reference to *Aeneid* 12.298–299.</note> So too **Numa**, whom **Nisus** killed; later **Aeneas** pursues the "brave Numa." Aeneas strikes down **Camers** in the tenth book, but in the twelfth, the goddess **Juturna** takes on the form of Camers. **Camilla** kills **Chloreus** in the eleventh book, yet Turnus kills him in the twelfth. **Palinurus** is called the "son of Iasius," and **Iapyx** is called the "son of Iasius"; I wonder if they are brothers? **Hippocoon** is called the "son of Hyrtacus," and then again an "son of Hyrtacus" strikes down Corinaeus—though it is possible two men had the same name.

Where, in these cases, is that caution of **Homer**? 
<margin>The two Ajaxes</margin>
With him, since there are two men named **Ajax**, he sometimes says, "He led the Locrians, Ajax the son of Oileus," <note>original Greek: Λοκρων ΑΗγΕμονευε ΟΙληοσ τα Αιασ. From *Iliad* 2.527.</note> and other times, "Telamonian Ajax." <note>original Greek: Τελαμωνιοσ αιασ.</note> And so on elsewhere.

He never ceases to separate those joined by a common name with distinguishing titles, lest the reader be forced to grapple with suspicions regarding a variation in naming. 

Furthermore, in his catalogue, Virgil took care to avoid causing boredom—something Homer did not worry about in the same way, as he often repeated the same phrasing. Virgil, however, varies his phrasing, as if avoiding repetition like a disgrace or a crime: "First to enter the war from the harsh Tuscan shores..." "Next to him, his son Lausus..." "After these, the chariot famous throughout the fields..." "Then the twin brothers..." "Nor was the founder of Praeneste absent..." "But Messapus, tamer of horses..." "Behold, from the ancient blood of the Sabines..." "Here come the Agamemnonian troops..." "And you, from the mountainous..." "Indeed, the priest came from the Marrubian race..." "There went the offspring of Hippolytus..." <note>These are the opening phrases of various entries in Virgil's catalogue of Italian heroes in *Aeneid* 7.647–782.</note>

Perhaps someone might think these varied forces are to be preferred to that divine simplicity of Homer. But I know not how that repetition uniquely suits Homer. It is worthy of the genius of the ancient poet and appropriate for an enumeration. In a place where he was merely listing names, he did not bend himself out of shape, nor did he twist things minutely by drawing out his pen through variations for each individual. Instead, he stands in the habit of those taking a census, as if counting men arranged in a battle line. This should be done with little more than the words of the numbers. And yet, he varies excellently where it is necessary regarding the names of the leaders. Indeed, Maro so admired that "congestion" of the list in Homer that he expressed it in such a way that I would almost say he translated it more elegantly.

# OF THE SATURNALIA

The Auruncan bands, the Rutulians, and the ancient Sicanians,
The Sacranian battle lines, and the Labicians with painted shields.
Those who plow your glades, O Tiber, and the sacred shore
Of Numicus; who work the Rutulian hills with the plowshare
And the Circean ridge; over whose fields Jupiter Anxurus
Presides: and so forth. <note>original: "Aruncæq manus... & cætera." These lines are from Virgil's Aeneid, Book 7, describing various Italian tribes.</note> Both poets, in their catalogues, after the narration of difficult matters or names, insert a story in more pleasant verses so that the reader’s mind may be refreshed. Homer, while enumerating the regions and names of cities, makes room for myths which exclude the "horror of satiety" <note>A phrase meaning the boredom or exhaustion caused by too much dense information.</note>.

And the rest: by which he prolonged the pleasantry. Virgil, following the "author" <note>Referring to Homer as the primary model for all epic poetry.</note> in this, tells myths now of Aventinus, now of Hippolytus in the first catalogue. In the second, the story of Cygnus serves him; and thus the interwoven beauty cures the tedium of the narrations. Indeed, in all the books of the *Georgics* <note>Virgil's famous four-part poem on agriculture and nature.</note> he did this same thing with the greatest elegance. For after the precepts—which by their nature are a hard subject—so that he might renew the reader's mind or hearing, he concluded each book with the insertion of a story summoned from elsewhere: the first on the signs of storms; the second on the praise of rural life; the third ends in the plague of the cattle. The end of the fourth is the story of Orpheus and Aristaeus—no idle narration. <note>The tragic story of the musician Orpheus trying to rescue Eurydice from the underworld.</note> Thus, the Homeric imitation shines in every work of Maro.

<margin>The Maxims of Virgil.</margin>
Homer so stuffed all his poetry with <term>sententiae</term> <note>Wise sayings or moral maxims used to provide weight to a text.</note> that his individual <term>apophthegms</term> <note>Concise, pithy observations or "soundbites" of wisdom.</note> serve as proverbs in everyone's mouth. Such as: *For no man ever yet knew his own parentage* <note>original: "οὐ γὰρ πω τις ἑὸν γόνον αὐτὸς ἀνέγνω" from the Odyssey.</note>; *For the children of fools are made like their fathers* <note>original: "μωρῶν γάρ τοι παῖδες ὁμοῖοι πατράσι γίνοντο."</note>; *For the mind of the eternal gods is not always nourished [by the same things]* <note>original: "ὀυ γὰρ τ’ αἴθ’ α θεῶν τρέφεται νόος αἰὲν ἐόντων."</note>. And countless others, which are brought forth as maxims. Nor would you look for these in vain within Virgil. *We cannot all do everything.* *Love conquers all.* *Unrelenting labor conquers all.* *Is it then so very wretched to die?* *To each is set his day.* *Whether it be deceit or valor, who would ask in an enemy?* *And what each region produces, and what each refuses.* *The accursed hunger for gold.* <note>original: "Auri sacra fames." One of Virgil's most famous indictments of greed.</note> And, lest I bore you by recounting known things, a thousand such maxims are either in everyone's mouth or meet the reader's eye.

In some matters, I do not know if by chance or by choice, Virgil departs from the Homeric sect regarding "Fortune." Homer preferred not to know Fortune, and commits the rule of all things to a single decree which he calls *Moira* <note>original: "μοῖραν," meaning Fate or Destiny.</note>; so much so that this word *Tyche* <note>original: "τύχη," meaning Chance or Luck.</note> is not named in any part of the Homeric volume. On the contrary, Virgil not only knows and remembers her, but even attributes omnipotence to her; whereas the philosophers who name her intended her to have no power of her own, but to be the minister of the decree or of Providence. And in myths or in histories, he sometimes does the same.

Aegeon in Homer is an aid to Jove. But the verses of Maro arm him against Jove. Eumedes, the offspring of Dolon, is famous in war and resembles his parent in spirit and hand, whereas in Homer, Dolon is unwarlike and uses trickery. <note>Virgil portrays Eumedes as a hero, while Homer portrays his father Dolon as a coward who was caught and killed during a night-raid.</note> Homer admits no mention of the Judgment of Paris. That same poet [Virgil] presents Ganymede not as a cupbearer, but as one snatched by Jove to be a rival to Juno...

# BOOK FIVE XCIII

...relates that the cupbearer <note>The youth Ganymede, whom Jupiter brought to Olympus to serve the gods.</note> was taken up to heaven by the gods as if it were a point of honor. Virgil, however, commemorates that such a great goddess <note>Juno, the queen of the gods.</note> grieved because she was defeated in a beauty contest judged by Paris—a thing which is disgraceful for any honorable woman—and that she vexed his whole race because of the abduction of a favorite.

Sometimes he imitates his author <note>Virgil's primary model, Homer.</note> so subtly that he only changes the arrangement of the description, making it seem like something else. Homer, with great spirit, makes Father Dis <note>The god of the underworld, also known as Hades or Pluto.</note> himself leap up from his throne in terror at the shaking of the earth and cry out in a certain way.

Virgil placed this not as a direct narration, but as a parable, so that it might appear as something else: *“Not otherwise than if the earth, gaping deep within, should reveal the infernal seats and unlock the pale kingdoms hated by the gods, and from above one might see the bottomless pit, and the shades tremble as light is let in.”* <note>Original: "Non secus ac si qua penitus... light is let in." From Virgil's Aeneid 8.243–246.</note> He also stole this while pretending otherwise. For when that author [Homer] had said the gods live without labor <note>original: "θεοὶ ρειαζωοντες" (theoi rheia zoontes)</note>, Virgil said the same thing most secretly: *“The gods in the halls of Jove pity the empty anger of both, and that there are such great labors for mortals”*—labors which they themselves, of course, lack.

<margin>The fourth book of the Aeneid is taken from Apollonius, the writer of the *Argonautica*.</margin>
What Virgil gained from Homer is most clear from this: where the necessity of the story required from Virgil an arrangement for the beginning of the war—which he did not have from Homer, since Homer made the anger of Achilles his beginning, which happened in the tenth year of the war—Virgil labored for a new invention. He made a stag, wounded by chance, the cause of the turmoil. When he saw this was too slight and childish, he increased the grief of the country folk so that their impulse would suffice for war. But neither the servants of Latinus—especially those tending the royal stable—nor Latinus himself (who had entered a treaty with the Trojans and knew of the gifts of horses and a chariot team) should have waged war against a son-in-law of the gods. What then? The greatest of the goddesses [Juno] descends from heaven and summons the greatest of the Furies from the depths of hell. They scatter snakes as if they were performers on a stage itching for madness. He leads the Queen [Amata] out from the inner rooms of matronly respect and forces her to run through the middle of the city. Not content with this, she seeks the woods, calling the rest of the mothers into her fellowship of madness. The once-modest chorus of Bacchantes <note>Followers of Bacchus (Dionysus), known for their wild, ecstatic rituals.</note> celebrates insane rites. What more? I would have preferred Virgil to have followed his author in this part as well, or any other of the Greeks.

I did not say “another” in vain, for he did not harvest his vintage from the vines of just one man, but turned to his own use whatever he found worthy of imitation anywhere. Thus, from the fourth book of the *Argonautica* by the writer Apollonius, he shaped the entire fourth book of his *Aeneid*, transferring the love and lack of restraint of Medea toward Jason to Dido. He arranged this with such an elegant authorial hand that the story of the wanton Dido—which the whole world knows is false <note>The historical Dido lived centuries after the Trojan War and was known for her lifelong chastity.</note>—nevertheless maintains the appearance of truth through so many centuries. It flies through the mouths of all boys; painters and sculptors, who imitate figures woven with fictional threads, use this theme above all in making statues as the unique subject for beauty; nor is it less celebrated by the constant gestures and songs of actors. The beauty of the narration was so powerful that everyone—though conscious of the Phoenician queen’s chastity and well aware that she laid hands on herself to avoid a loss of modesty—nevertheless winks at the story. While their consciences grumble at the truth of the matter, they prefer to celebrate as true what the sweetness of the poet’s invention has poured into human hearts.

Let us see if he also touched upon Pindar, whom Horace <note>original: "Flac." (Quintus Horatius Flaccus).</note> admits is inaccessible to imitation. Small and dewy things that he took from there, I leave aside. But one place, which he tried to transcribe almost in its entirety, I want to share with you, because it is worthy of our closer inspection.

<margin>Etna in imitation of Pindar.</margin>
When he wished to emulate Pindar's poem written about the nature and blazing of Mount Etna, he labored over such thoughts and words that he became more unusual and more "swollen" <note>Meaning bombastic or overly grandiose.</note> in this passage than Pindar himself, who was already considered to have an excessively rich and fat eloquence. And so that you yourselves...

I will make you the judges of what I say: I shall recite as much of Pindar’s poem concerning Mount Etna as my memory allows.

<note>original Greek: "κιο̄ν δ᾽ οὐρανία...". This is from Pindar's Pythian Odes 1.19–26.</note>
"Pillar of heaven, snow-capped Etna, nurse of sharp snow all year long, from whose depths belch the purest fountains of unapproachable fire; in the daytime her rivers pour forth a glowing stream of smoke, but in the darkness of night, the ruddy, rolling flame carries rocks to the deep level of the sea with a crashing roar. That monster <note>Typhon, the giant imprisoned beneath Etna.</note> sends up the most terrible springs of fire."

Now hear Virgil’s verses, so that you may say he more truly began the description than perfected it:

> The harbor, sheltered from the winds’ approach, is vast
> In itself; but nearby Etna thunders with horrific ruins.
> Sometimes it bursts forth a black cloud to the heavens,
> Smoking with a pitchy whirlwind and glowing ash;
> It raises globes of flames and licks the stars.
> Sometimes, groaning, it vomits forth uprooted rocks
> And the mountain's own bowels, and heaps up
> Liquefied stones into the air, boiling from its lowest bottom.

In the beginning, Pindar, following the truth, stated the facts as they are perceived by the eyes: that Etna smokes by day and flames by night. Virgil, however, while laboring to capture the roar and sound of words, confuses both times without making any distinction. That Greek author [Pindar], imitating the very fountains of the language, brilliantly described the vomiting of fire, the flowing rivers of smoke, and the tawny, twisting volumes of flame carrying rocks into the stretches of the sea like fiery rivers. But your Virgil, wishing to interpret "a glowing stream of smoke" <note>original: "ρὁον καπνοῦ αἴθωνα"</note>, piled words together crudely and excessively: "a black cloud with a pitchy whirlwind and glowing ash." For he said that a black cloud smokes with a pitchy whirlwind and *white-hot* ash. Things that are "white-hot" <note>original: "candentia"</note> are not usually smoky, nor are they black—unless, perhaps, he used "white-hot" in a common and improper sense to mean "burning" rather than "shining."

<margin>White-hot.</margin>
For the word *candens* (white-hot) is derived from *candor* (whiteness/brightness), not from *calor* (heat). Furthermore, his claim that rocks are "vomited and raised up" and then immediately "liquefied," and that they "groan" and are "heaped into the air"—this was neither written by Pindar nor ever heard of in any story. Of all things called "monstrous," this description is the most monstrous.

The Greek accusative of such names ends in *e*; for if anyone thinks he said "Diomede" in the Latin fashion, the metrical health of the verse will be lacking. Furthermore, he preferred to title all his poems in Greek: *Bucolics*, *Geor...*

# BOOK FIVE

...the *Georgics* and the *Aeneid*: names whose formation is foreign to the rules of Latin. But enough of those matters, many of which are known to all, and some to quite a few Romans. I come now to other matters which, unearthed from the inner sanctuaries of Greek literature, are known to no one except those who have drunk deeply of Greek learning. For this poet <note>Virgil</note> was as scrupulously and painstakingly learned as he was secretive and almost clandestine about it; he translated many things in such a way that it is difficult to recognize where they were translated from. In the beginning of the *Georgics*, he placed these verses:

> Liber and nourishing Ceres, if by your gift the earth
> Swapped Chaonian acorns for the rich ear of grain,
> And mixed Acheloian cups with the discovered grapes.

<margin>Why Achelous is accepted as water.</margin>
The cohort of grammarians teaches nothing more of these verses to their students than this: that it was by the work of Ceres that men ceased their ancient diet and used grain instead of acorns; and that Liber <note>Another name for Bacchus/Dionysus</note>, as the discoverer of the vine, provided wine for human drink, to be mixed with water. But as to why Virgil, when he wished water to be understood, named the river Achelous in particular, no one asks, nor does anyone suspect there was any special erudition involved. We, having scrutinized this more deeply, have noticed that the learned poet spoke according to the custom of the most ancient Greeks, as authority will show. Among them, "Achelous" was used specifically to signify water. Nor was this done without reason, for the cause of this practice has also been recorded with care. But before I set forth the cause, I shall show, by the testimony of an ancient poet, that this manner of speaking was widespread: that they said "Achelous" for any kind of water. Aristophanes, the old comic poet, says in his comedy *Cocalus*: "He was heavy with wine," he says, "to which no water [Achelous] had been added"—that is, pure wine. Why they were accustomed to speak this way, Ephorus, a most famous writer of histories, shows in his second book with these words:

<note>original Greek: "The oracle at Dodona almost always commanded people to sacrifice to the Achelous..."</note>

Can it be shown more clearly that "Achelous" was used by the ancient Greeks for any water whatsoever? Hence Virgil, most learnedly, says that Father Liber mixed wine with "Achelous." And although there is enough witness to this matter, having produced the words of Aristophanes the comic poet and Ephorus the historian, we shall nevertheless proceed further. For Didymus the grammarian, by far the most learned, having posited the cause which Ephorus stated above, added another as well in these words:

<note>original Greek: "...because it is the oldest of rivers..."</note>

Although these things are abundantly sufficient to prove the ancient custom—where the use of speaking was such that Achelous was considered a common name for all water—nevertheless, the authority of Euripides, the most noble writer of tragedies, shall be added to these. Didymus the grammarian placed this in those books he wrote on <term>Spurious Lines in Tragedies<gloss>original Greek: Τραγῳδουμένων ἀθέτους</gloss></term>, in these words:

<note>original Greek: "Achelous's water..." used in a general sense.</note>

<margin>The Hernici people</margin>
In the seventh book <note>of the *Aeneid*</note> are those verses in which the Hernici people and their city Anagnia—most noble as it then was—are enumerated: "Those whom rich Anagnia feeds."

> Those whom father Amasenus feeds: not for all of them
> Do arms or shields or chariots resound. The greater part
> Sling balls of livid lead. Part carry two darts
> In their hand; and they have tawny caps from wolf-skin
> For head-cover; they set the steps of the left foot
> Bare; a raw-hide boot covers the other.

<margin>The custom of going to war with one foot bare.</margin>
<margin>The Pelasgian Hernicus</margin>
That this custom existed in Italy—to go to war with one foot shod and the other bare—I have never found anywhere else as far as I know; but I shall now make it plain, on the authority of a wealthy source, that this was a custom of some of the Greeks. In this, one must truly marvel at the hidden diligence of this poet. For when he had read that the Hernici (to whom Anagnia belongs) were descended from the Pelasgians, and were so named from a certain Pelasgian leader of theirs named Hernicus, he applied a custom which he had read regarding the Aeto...

# BOOK FIVE
### THE SATURNALIA

...he assigned the things he had read to the Hernici: who are an ancient colony of the Pelasgians <note>The Pelasgians were a mythical or prehistoric people considered the original inhabitants of Greece</note>. Indeed, Julius Hyginus <note>A scholar and friend of the emperor Augustus</note> proves with no few words in the second book of his *On Cities* that a Hernican man and Pelasgian leader was the forefather of the Hernici. Furthermore, the most famous tragic writer, Euripides, shows that it was a custom of the Aetolians <note>A people from central Greece</note> to go into battle with only one foot shod. In his tragedy titled *Meleager*, a messenger is introduced describing the attire of each of the leaders who had gathered to catch the boar. In that play are these verses:

<note>original: "In eo hi uersus sunt." — The Latin text implies Greek verses follow here, which were often omitted or printed in a different font in early editions.</note>

You can see very clearly that these words of Euripides were preserved by Maro <note>Virgil’s family name</note>. For Euripides says:

<note>original: "Ait enim ille:" — Again, Greek text is implied here.</note>

And Virgil also spoke of that same foot being bare: *They set down the bare footprints of the left foot.* <note>original: "Vestigia nuda sinistri instituere pedis." — From the Aeneid, VII.689</note> In this matter—so that my diligence may be further proven to you—I will not keep silent about a fact known to very few: Euripides was criticized by Aristotle. Aristotle contended that this was a result of Euripides' ignorance, for the Aetolians do not have the *left* foot bare, but the *right*. Rather than simply asserting this, I will provide Aristotle’s own words from the second book of his work *On Poets*, which I mentioned above. In that book, speaking of Euripides, he says:

<note>original: "Aristotelis uerba ponam... [Greek implied]"</note>

¶ Although this is the case, you see nonetheless that Virgil preferred to follow the authority of Euripides rather than Aristotle. For I can hardly believe that a man so painstakingly learned was ignorant of these facts. He rightly preferred Euripides; for he has a great familiarity with the writers of Greek tragedies, as can be seen from what we have already discussed and from what will be said shortly. In the fourth book <note>of the Aeneid</note>, describing the death of Elissa <note>Another name for Queen Dido of Carthage</note>, he says that a lock of hair was cut from her with these words:

> Not yet had Proserpina <note>Queen of the Underworld</note> taken the golden lock from her head,
> Nor yet condemned her life to the Stygian Underworld.

<margin>Hair is cut from the dying</margin>

¶ Then Iris, sent by Juno, cuts the lock of hair and brings it to the Underworld. Virgil does not invent this story out of nothing, as Aurelius Cornutus—otherwise a most learned man—thinks. Cornutus added a note to this passage in these words: "Where does this story come from, that hair must be taken from the dying? He has simply become accustomed to inventing things in the poetic manner, such as the Golden Bough." These are the words of Cornutus. But I am ashamed that such a great man, so learned in Greek literature, was ignorant of Euripides' most famous play, *Alcestis*. In this play, Orcus <note>Death personified</note> is introduced on stage carrying a sword, with which he cuts the hair of Alcestis, and he speaks thus:

<note>original: "[Greek implied]"</note>

¶ It has been revealed (in my opinion) whom Virgil followed when he introduced the story of the cutting of the hair. Moreover, they use the word *hallow* <note>original: "ἁγνίσαι" (agnisai)</note> to mean "to consecrate to the gods"; thus our poet says in the person of Iris:

> This offering, as commanded, I carry to Pluto, and I release you from that body.

¶ Now, because I have proven almost everything I said above by the authority of the tragic poets, I will also note a point drawn from Sophocles. In the fourth book, Virgil depicts Elissa <note>Dido</note>, after she has been abandoned by Aeneas, fleeing as if to the songs and incantations of priestesses and witches; and among other things, he says that for the sake of soothing her love, herbs were sought which had been *cut with bronze sickles*. Is this matter not worthy of investigation? How did the idea of bronze sickles come to Virgil's mind? I will therefore set down Virgil's verses, and then those of Sophocles which Maro emulated.

> Herbs sought by moonlight, harvested with bronze sickles...

---

C These are the words of Sophocles. Without a doubt, Virgil brought forward the "bronze sickles" based on this author. In general, many things indicate that bronze was customarily used for divine matters, especially in those rites where people wished to soothe someone, or curse them, or even drive out diseases. I will pass over that line from Plautus when he says: "The village has a copper-fever" <note>original: "Mecū habet pagus morbus æs." — A reference to copper coins or perhaps a specific localized illness</note> and elsewhere in Virgil: "The sounds of the Curetes and the clashing bronze." <note>original: "Curetum sonitus crepitantiaq; æra." — From the Georgics, IV.151, referring to the rattling used to attract bees.</note> But I will set down the words of the most diligent and learned Carminius, who <margin>A bronze plowshare used in marking the walls of a city.</margin> in his second book *On Italy* says: "I find in their rituals of passage that the Tuscans <note>The Etruscans</note> were once accustomed to use a bronze plowshare when they founded cities; and among the Sabines, bronze razors were used for shaving priests." After these words of Carminius, it would be a long task if I wanted to list how many places the most ancient Greeks were accustomed to use the sounds of bronze as a most powerful thing. But for the present work, it is enough to have shown that the bronze sickles were introduced by Maro <note>Virgil</note> following the example of a Greek author.

> In the ninth book, Virgil placed these verses:
> There stood the son of Arcens in splendid armor,
> His cloak embroidered with the needle and bright with Iberian rust <note>original: "ferugine clarus hibera" — Iberian rust refers to a specific dark purple or charcoal-colored dye</note>,
> Distinguished in face; his father Arcens had sent him,
> Raised in the grove of his mother around the Symaethian
