<margin>The Palici gods</margin>
C Who is this Palicus god, or rather, who are these gods? I have found the Palici (for there are two) in almost no Latin author that I know of; but Maro <note>Virgil</note> dug this story out of the innermost Greek literature. For first, just as the Symaethus river, which he mentions in these verses, is in Sicily, so too are the Palici gods worshipped in Sicily; Aeschylus the tragic writer, a Sicilian man, was the first of all to commit them to writing. He also expressed the interpretation of their name—which the Greeks call etymology—in his verses. But before I place the verses of Aeschylus, the story of the Palici must be explained in a few words. In Sicily there is the Symaethus river. <margin>Symaethus river.</margin> Near it, the nymph Thalia, pregnant by the embrace of Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, prayed that the earth might gape open for her out of fear of Juno; and so it was done. But when the time for the maturity of the infants she had carried in her womb arrived, the earth was opened, and two infants emerged from the womb of Thalia; they were called Palici from the Greek "to come back again" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ πάλιν ἱκέθαι" — From 'palin' (again) and 'hikesthai' (to come)</note>, because they had first sunk into the earth and then returned from there. Not far from there are small lakes, <margin>The Crater lakes.</margin> but immensely deep, always bubbling with the gushing of waters: which the inhabitants call "craters" <note>original: "crateras" — literally 'mixing bowls', referring to the shape of volcanic pools</note>, and they call them by the name "Delli." They consider them brothers, and they are held in the highest worship; especially concerning the demanding of an oath near them, a present and effective divine power is shown. For when proof of a denied theft or something of this kind is sought, and an oath is required from a suspect, both parties approach the craters after being cleansed of all contagion; a guarantor is first taken from the person who is to swear, concerning the payment of what was sought, if the outcome should condemn him. There, having invoked the divine power of the place, the swearer would make a testimony of what he was swearing. If he did so faithfully, he would depart unharmed. But if a bad conscience underlay the oath, the false swearer soon lost his life in the lake. This matter so commended the religion of the brothers that the craters were called "implacable." Nor is the temple of the Palici without divination. For when a sterile year had dried up Sicily, by divine...

# THE SATURNALIA

Warned by an oracle of the Palici <note>Sicilian twin deities of geysers and the underworld</note>, the Sicilians celebrated a certain sacrifice to a hero, and fertility returned. Out of gratitude for this, the Sicilians heaped every kind of crop upon the altar of the Palici. Because of this abundance, the altar itself was called "the fat one" <note>original Latin: "pinguis"</note>. This is the complete history of the Palici and their brothers found only in Greek literature, which Virgil <note>referred to here as "Maro," his family name</note> drew upon no less than Latin sources. A book of elegies by Aratus is also mentioned, in which he says the following about a certain poet named Diotimus:

<margin>The town of Gargara</margin> From these verses, the name of the citizens also became known, for they are called Gargareans. Since it is established that "Gargara" can be understood either as a mountain peak or as a town situated at the foot of that same mountain, Virgil <note>The author refers to Virgil's *Georgics* 1.103</note> is speaking not of the mountain top, but of the town. Let us investigate why he used Gargara as a place for fertile crops. It is well known that all of Mysia <note>A region in northwest Asia Minor (modern Turkey)</note> is occupied by rich grain fields, specifically due to the moisture of the soil. Thus Virgil, in the aforementioned verses, after he had said, "moist solstices," added: "no land boasts so much of its cultivation as Mysia," as if to say: "Every region that has had the benefit of timely moisture will equal the fertility of the fields of Mysia." But when Homer mentions it, he designates the field lying below the mountain as "moist." For "many-fountained" <note>original Greek: *polypidax*</note> signifies a place abounding in springs. From this, there was such a great abundance of crops in Gargara that whoever wanted to express a great number of anything would name "Gargara" to represent an immense multitude. Alcaeus is a witness to this, who says the following in his tragedy *In the Heavens*:

->As you see, he clearly used "Gargara" to mean a multitude. Nor is Aristomenes any different.<-

Aristophanes the comic poet, however, using a compound word made of "sand" and "Gargara" <note>original Greek: *psammagargara*</note>, attempts to express an innumerable number—as is his witty way. For in his play *The Acharnians*, he says:

<note>The OCR text for the Greek quote is missing or implied as a gap here</note>

Moreover, Varro often used the term on its own to mean "many" in his *Menippean Satires*. But Aristophanes added "Gargara" to signify an infinite count. According to this, therefore, the sense of these verses is as follows: Since the season of the year is such that the winter is clear and the solstice is rainy, the fruits turn out best. These conditions are so necessary for the fields that without them, even those naturally fertile fields of Mysia would not live up to the reputation for fertility that they have. He adds "Gargara" specifically to "Mysia" because that city, located at the lowest roots of Mount Ida, is irrigated by the waters flowing down from Ida, and thus it might seem not to require summer rains very much. To lend credit to this perception—that not only the province of the mountain Gargara but the fields of all Mysia are damp—Aeschylus can be summoned as a witness.

We have said what he drew from the Greeks in this passage. We shall add this, moreover, for the sake of its pleasantness, and so that it may be clear that our Virgil drew ornaments for himself from every source of antiquity: from where he said "grain is happiest in winter dust" <note>Latin: *hiberno laetissima pulvere farra*</note>. In a book of very ancient songs, which was said to have been composed before everything else written by the Latins, this old rustic chant is found: "In winter dust, in spring mud, great grain, Camillus <note>likely referring to a *camillus*, a young boy serving in religious rites, rather than the famous general</note>, you shall reap."

<margin>Various shapes of cups</margin> Virgil mostly uses Greek names for drinking vessels, such as *carchesia*, *cymbia*, *canthari*, and *scyphi*. Regarding *carchesia*: "Take the *carchesia* of Maeonian wine; let us pour to the Ocean," he says.
And elsewhere: "Here, duly pouring two *carchesia* of pure wine to Bacchus."
Regarding *cymbia*: "We bring boat-shaped *cymbia* foaming with warm milk."
Regarding the *cantharus*: "And the heavy *cantharus* was hanging by its worn handle."

Regarding the *scyphi*: "And the sacred *scyphus* filled his right hand." No one asks what shape these are or why he mentioned them, being content to know that they are cups of this sort. And indeed, the *scyphi* and *canthari* are common names among the public and may be passed over. But concerning the *carchesia* and *cymbia*, which I am not sure you would ever find among the Latins, and which are very rare even among the Greeks, I do not see why people should not be compelled to ask what these new and foreign Greek names mean. A *carchesium* <note>a tall, thin-waisted drinking cup with handles reaching from the rim to the base</note> is a cup known only to the Greeks. <margin>Carchesium</margin> Pherecides mentions it in his books of histories, and says that Jupiter gave it to Alcmene as a price for their union.

...[he is recorded] to have given a golden *carchesium* <note>A tall, slender Greek drinking cup with a "waisted" middle</note> as a gift. But the Roman playwright Plautus left behind an unusual name for it, saying in his play *Amphitryon*: "a *patera* was given," even though the shape of these two vessels is very different. 
<margin>Patera</margin> For a *patera* <note>A shallow, flat libation bowl, similar to a saucer</note>, as the name itself suggests by its sound, is flat and open. A *carchesium*, however, is tall and compressed around its middle section, moderately handled with the handles reaching from the top to the very bottom. Asclepiades, however, a man exceptionally learned and diligent among the Greeks, believes that *carchesia* are named after naval matters. For he says the lower part of a ship's sail is called a *patera*, but the part around the middle is generally called the "neck" <note>original Greek: *trachēlon*</note>, while the topmost part is named the *carchesium*. From there, it spreads out into both sides of the sail, and those parts are called "horns" <note>the yardarms of a ship</note>. Nor is Asclepiades the only one to mention this cup; other illustrious poets do as well, such as Sappho, who says... and Sophocles in the play titled...

<margin>Cymbia</margin> These things concern the *carchesia*, which are unknown to Latin speech and celebrated only in Greece. But you will not find the *cymbia* <note>Small, boat-shaped cups</note> in our language either. It is mentioned by only a few Greek authors. Philemon, a very famous comic poet, says in *The Apparition*:

->Anaxandrides the comic poet also says in a Greek play:<-

Demosthenes also mentions it in the speech *Against Meidias*. These *cymbia*, as the shape of the name itself indicates, are a diminutive form of *cymba* <note>A small boat or skiff</note>; this is a type of ship in both Greek and Latin, with our language deriving the word from theirs. Indeed, I have noticed among the Greeks many types of cups named after naval things: as he taught above regarding the *carchesia*, so these *cymbia* cups are tall and similar to ships. Eratosthenes, a man by far the most learned, mentions this cup in a letter to Agetor of Lacedaemon in these words: "There were..."

<margin>Cissimbium</margin> There were those who thought the *cymbium* was named from *cissimbium* <note>An ivy-wood cup</note> by shortening the word. Many make mention of the *cissimbium* (not to mention Homer, who records this cup being given to the Cyclops by Ulysses). Some wish for the *cissimbium* to be specifically a wooden cup made of ivy, that is, from *kissos* <note>Greek for ivy</note>. And Nicander of Colophon in the first book of his *Hialicon* says:

But Callimachus also mentions this cup:

However, those who think the *cissimbium* made of ivy should not be called "only of ivy" <note>original Greek: *oios ek kissou*</note> seem to rely on the authority of Euripides, who says in *Andromache*:

<margin>Cantharus</margin> So much for the *cymbium*. It follows that since we said above that the *cantharus* <note>A large, deep drinking cup with high handles, often associated with Bacchus</note> is both a type of cup and a type of ship, this should be proven with examples. Regarding the cup, the matter is well known, even from Virgil himself, who most appropriately assigns the personal cup of Father Liber <note>Bacchus</note> to Silenus. But as we promised above, we must also show that it was accustomed to be used for a ship. Menander says in *The Shipmaster*:

<margin>Scyphus</margin> "And a sacred *scyphus* <note>A large, deep, two-handled drinking cup</note> filled his right hand." The *scyphus* is the cup of Hercules, just as the *cantharus* belongs to Father Liber. 
<margin>Hercules the heavy drinker</margin> Indeed, the ancient sculptors did not depict Hercules with a cup without reason—sometimes even staggering and drunk. This is not only because that hero is said to have been a heavy drinker, but also because of an ancient story: that Hercules crossed the immense seas, using a cup as if it were a ship, driven by the winds. But I will say a few things from the Greek antiquities about both matters. And as for this hero being a "heavy drinker"—not to mention things commonly known—there is this clear proof which Ephippus introduces in *Busiris*, showing Hercules speaking thus:

# BOOK FIVE
### THE SATURNALIA

<margin>The Chalice</margin>
There is also a story, not very well known, that a certain nation of men near Heraclea was established by Hercules, called the *Cylicraes* <note>original: *Cylicraon*</note>, a name composed from the Greek phrase *from the cup* <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ κύλικος</note>. We call this kind of drinking vessel a *calix* <note>a chalice</note> by changing a single letter. Moreover, Panyassis <note>OCR: *Piniastis*. Panyassis was an epic poet and relative of Herodotus</note>, an excellent Greek writer, says that Hercules—having been guided to Erytheia, an island of Spain—sailed there in a cup. Pherecydes <note>A 6th-century BCE mythographer</note> is also an authority on this; I have refrained from including their exact words, as they are closer to fables than history. I believe, however, that Hercules did not cross the seas in a literal cup, but in a ship named the *Scyphus* <note>The name of a deep Greek drinking cup</note>; just as we asserted above regarding the *cantharus* and the *carchesium*, and the *cymbia* derived from *cymbae* <note>small boats</note>, all these terms are actually the names of ships.

Virgil also sometimes borrows names from the most ancient Greek histories. You know that in his work, one of Diana’s companions is called Opis. This name is perhaps applied thoughtlessly by the common people, or thought to be a fiction by those ignorant of the poet’s deep learning—as if he wished to assign to Diana's companion a title that ancient Greek writers had originally given to the goddess Diana herself. But Virgil writes:

<margin>Opis the nymph</margin>
> Meanwhile, Opis, swift among the heavenly seats,
> One of the virgin companions and the sacred band,
> Diana <note>referred to here by her mother's name, Latonia</note> called to, and gave forth these sad words from her mouth. **And below:**
> But now for a long time Opis, the guardian of the Crossroads <note>referred to as Trivia, an epithet of Diana/Hecate</note>, has been in the mountains.

He calls Opis a companion and associate of Diana. But hear where Virgil received this name: as I said, he took what he had read as an epithet for the goddess herself and applied it to her companion. Alexander Aetolus, an excellent poet, in the book titled *The Muses*, relates with what great zeal the people of Ephesus—having dedicated the temple of Diana—offered prizes so that the most talented poets of that time would compose various songs to the goddess. In these verses, Opis is not a companion of Diana, but Diana herself is called Opis. He speaks (as I said) about the Ephesian people:

<image-desc>A rectangular area in the center of the page where a woodcut illustration from the reverse side (verso) of the leaf is visible through the paper, depicting two figures in classical robes.</image-desc>

It appeared (unless I am mistaken) that Opis was a name for Diana, and Virgil, out of his immense learning, transferred this name to her companion.

"All the gods have departed, leaving their shrines and altars." No one asks where Virgil got this idea, but it is certain he drew it from Euripides, who in his play *The Trojan Women* introduces Apollo—when Troy was about to be captured—saying these very things.

Those verses show where Virgil adopted the idea that the gods depart from a city that has already been captured. Nor is it without the authority of Greek antiquity when he says: "She herself hurled the swift fire of Jove from the clouds." 
For Euripides introduces Minerva asking Neptune for winds against the Greek fleet, saying that he ought to do what Jupiter did, from whom she received the lightning bolt to use against the Greeks.
In Virgil, Pan is said to have lured the Moon into the deep woods, calling her with the "snowy gift of wool." 
"If it is worthy of belief, with such a snowy gift of wool," and so forth. Regarding this passage, Valerius Probus, a most accomplished scholar, notes that he does not know this history or fable, or which author it refers to. I wonder that this escaped Probus. For Nicander <note>A 2nd-century BCE Greek poet/physician</note> is the author of this story; a poet whom Didymus—the most learned of all grammarians who are or ever were—calls a "teller of fables." Knowing this, Virgil added the phrase: "if it is worthy of belief," thus admitting he was using a "fabulous" author.
In the third book, one reads in passing, without asking where it was translated from: "What the omnipotent Father predicted to Phoebus, Phoebus Apollo predicted to me," and so on. In such places, grammarians, to excuse their own ignorance, attribute these connections to Virgil's natural genius rather than his scholarship. They do not say he borrowed from others, lest they be forced to name the authors. But I assert that our most learned poet followed Aeschylus, the most eminent writer of tragedies, who in the play which is titled in Latin *The Priestess* <note>original: *Sacerdotis*</note>, says the following:

<margin>
Virgil cannot be rightly understood without Greek learning.

Is this not a clear fact: that Virgil adopted the same method as Apollo, who prophesies those things which Jupiter speaks to him? Has it not been proven to you that just as Virgil cannot be understood by one who is ignorant of the sound of the Latin tongue, so too he cannot be understood by one who has not drunk deeply of Greek learning to the point of absolute satiety? For if I did not fear creating a sense of weariness, I could fill enormous volumes with those things he translated from the most profound Greek learning. But the examples already provided for the matter at hand will suffice.

# CONSULAR AND ILLUSTRIOUS MAN. Book VI.

At this point, Praetextatus remarked: "Eustachius has arranged in a wonderful manner the elements of Greek antiquity that Virgil inserted into his poem. But we remember that Furius, Caecina, and Albinus—by far the most learned men of our age—promised they would set forth what the same Maro <note>Virgil</note> drew from ancient writers. The time now suggests that this should be done."

<margin>
Calathis
<note>Wicker baskets</note>
Of a vow
</margin>
When this pleased everyone, Furius Albinus spoke: "Although I fear that, in my desire to show how much our Virgil profited from the reading of the ancients—and which 'flowers' he gathered from everyone, or what ornaments he took from various sources to beautify his poem—I may provide an opportunity for the unlearned or the malicious to find fault. Such people might reproach so great a man for usurping what belongs to others, not considering that this is the very fruit of reading:

<margin>Canistris <note>Reed baskets</note></margin>
to emulate those things which you approve of in others, and to convert those things you most admire among the sayings of others into your own use through a timely derivation. This is something our own writers have often done among themselves and from the Greeks, and the most excellent of the Greeks have often done among themselves. To say nothing of foreigners, I could teach many examples of how much the authors of the old libraries compiled from one another. However, I will prove this at another opportune time (if you are willing); for now, I will bring forward one example

<margin>Scyphus <note>A large cup</note></margin>
which will almost suffice to prove my point. Afranius, a writer of *togatae* <term>togata: A Roman comedy focusing on Roman characters and life, named after the toga worn by the actors</term>, in that specific play titled *The Compitalia*, responded quite unabashedly to those who accused him of taking many things from Menander <note>A famous Greek playwright of the New Comedy period</note>. He said: 'I confess I have taken them, and not only from him, but from wherever anyone had something that suited me—something I believed I could not do better myself—even from a Latin author.' If this partnership, this commonality of material, is permitted among all poets and writers, who can turn it into a crime for Virgil if, to refine himself, he borrowed certain things from the ancients? Indeed, he should be thanked on this account: by transferring certain things from them into his own work, which is destined to last forever, he ensured that the memory of the ancients was not entirely deleted—whom (as the present time shows) we have begun to hold not only as unread, but even as objects of ridicule. Finally, through his judgment in transferring and his method of imitating, he achieved a result where those things found in his work..."

...whether we have read it in another’s work, or we prefer it to be his own, or we wonder that it sounds better here than where it was first produced. I shall, therefore, speak first of those lines which he drew from others, whether as half-verses or as almost complete ones. After this, I shall discuss entire passages transferred with only slight variation, or where the meaning was so transcribed that the source shines through. I will also address other passages that were altered, yet in such a way that their origin is not unknown. Following these, I will demonstrate that certain elements taken from Homer were not taken by Virgil directly from Homer, but rather other writers took them first, and he then translated them from those authors whom he had undoubtedly read.

<note>original: "Rumoreſqz ferunt uarios:ac multa requirunt."</note>
They spread various rumors, and ask many things.

->**Virgil**<-
<note>original: "Nomine quēqz uocans reficitqz in prælia pulſos."</note>
Calling each by name, he restores those driven back into battle.

->**Furius in his tenth book**<-
<note>original: "Nomine quēqz ciet. dictorum tempus adeſſe:"</note>
He rouses each by name. [He reminds them] that the time for their words has arrived.

He records this. Then, further down:
<note>original: "Confirmat dictis:simulatqz exuſcitat acris / Ad bellandum animos:reficitqz ad prælia mentes."</note>
He encourages them with words, and at the same time rouses their fierce spirits for war, and restores their minds for battle.

->**Virgil**<-
<note>original: "Dicite pierides:non omnia poſſumus omnes."</note>
Speak, <term>Pierides</term>: we cannot all do all things. <note>The Pierides is a traditional title for the Muses.</note>

->**Lucretius in his fifth book**<-
<note>original: "Maior erat natus:non omnia poſſumus omnes."</note>
He was older by birth; we cannot all do all things.

->**Virgil**<-
<note>original: "Diuerſi circunſpiciunt:hoc acrior idem."</note>
From different places they look around; all the more fierce for this.

->**Pacuvius in his Medea**<-
<note>original: "Diuerſi circunſpiciimus:horror percipit."</note>
From different places we look around; a shudder seizes us.

->**Virgil**<-
<note>original: "Ergo iter inceptum peragunt rumore ſecundo."</note>
Therefore they complete the journey begun with favorable applause. <note>The phrase "rumore secundo" implies the popular support or favorable shouts of a crowd.</note>

->**Suevius in his fifth book**<-
<note>original: "Redeunt referuntqz petita rumore ſecundo."</note>
They return and bring back the things sought with favorable applause.

->**Virgil**<-
<note>original: "Nunquam hodie effugies: veniam quocunque vocaris."</note>
"Never today shall you escape; I will come wherever you are called." <note>A line from Virgil's Eclogues (3.49).</note>

->**Naevius in *The Trojan Horse***<-
<note>original: "Nunquam hodie effugies: quin mea manu moriare."</note>
"Never today shall you escape without dying by my hand." <note>Gnaeus Naevius was one of the earliest Roman playwrights and epic poets.</note>

->**Virgil**<-
<note>original: "Vendidit hic auro patriam: dominumque potentem / Imposuit: fixit leges pretio atque refixit."</note>
"This man sold his country for gold and imposed a powerful master; he fixed and then unfixed laws for a price." <note>From the Aeneid, Book 6. This refers to the crime of political corruption.</note>

->**Varius, *On Death***<-
<note>original: "Vendidit hic latium populis: agrosque quiritum / Eripuit: fixit leges pretio atque refixit."</note>
"This man sold Latium to foreign peoples and snatched away the fields of the Roman citizens; he fixed and then unfixed laws for a price." <note>Lucius Varius Rufus was a contemporary of Virgil; this shows how Virgil adapted Varius's phrasing regarding the making and breaking of laws.</note>

->**Virgil**<-
<note>original: "Ut gemma bibat: & sarano dormiat ostro."</note>
"So that he may drink from a jeweled cup and sleep on Sarrian purple." <note>Aeneid 6.606. "Sarrian" refers to the city of Tyre, famous for its purple dye.</note>

->**Varius, *On Death***<-
<note>original: "Incubet & tyriis: atque ex solido bibat auro."</note>
"He reclines on Tyrian fabrics and drinks from solid gold."

->**Virgil**<-
<note>original: "Talia saecla suis dixerunt currite fusis."</note>
"Run, oh spindles, the Fates said to their own eras." <note>From the Eclogues (4.46).</note>

->**Catullus**<-
<note>original: "Currite ducentes subtegmina currite fusi."</note>
"Run, oh spindles, drawing out the threads, run." <note>From Catullus 64, the "Marriage of Peleus and Thetis."</note>

->**Virgil**<-
<note>original: "Felix heu nimium felix si littora tantum / Nunquam dardaniæ tetigissent nostra carinæ."</note>
"Happy, alas, too happy, if only the Dardanian ships had never touched our shores." <note>Dido's lament in the Aeneid (4.657-8). "Dardanian" is a poetic name for Trojan.</note>

->**Catullus**<-
<note>original: "Iuppiter omnipotens utinam non tempore primo / Gnosia cecropiæ tetigissent littora puppes."</note>
"O almighty Jupiter, if only in that first time the Cecropian ships had not touched the Gnosian shores." <note>From Catullus 64. "Cecropian" refers to Athens and "Gnosian" to Crete.</note>

->**Virgil**<-
<note>original: "Magna ossa lacertosque exuit."</note>
"He stripped bare his massive bones and arms." <note>Aeneid 5.422.</note>

->**Ennius in Book 17**<-
<note>original: "Magna ossa lacertique apparent homini."</note>
"Massive bones and arms appear on the man." <note>Ennius was considered the father of Roman epic poetry.</note>

->**Virgil**<-
<note>original: "Placidam per membra quietem Irrigat."</note>
"He pours a peaceful rest through the limbs." <note>Aeneid 1.691-2. Virgil uses the verb "irrigat" (to irrigate/water) metaphorically for sleep.</note>

->**Furius in his first book**<-
<note>original: "Mitemque rigat per pectora somnum."</note>
"And he pours a mild sleep through the breast."

->**Lucretius in Book 4**<-
<note>original: "Nunc quibus ille modis sonus per membra quietem Irrigat."</note>
"Now, in what ways that sound pours rest through the limbs."

->**Virgil**<-
<note>original: "Camposque liquentes."</note>
"And the liquid fields." <note>A poetic description of the sea.</note>

->**Lucretius in Book 6, on a similar description of the sea**<-
<note>original: "Et liquidam molem camposque natantes."</note>
"And the liquid mass and swimming fields."

->**Virgil**<-
<note>original: "Et geminos duo fulmina belli scipiadas."</note>
"And the two Scipios, two thunderbolts of war." <note>Aeneid 6.842-3.</note>

->**Lucretius in Book 3**<-
<note>original: "Scipiades belli fulmen carthaginis horror."</note>
"Scipio, a thunderbolt of war, the horror of Carthage."

->**Virgil**<-
<note>original: "Et ora tristia tentantum sensu torquebit amaror."</note>
"And bitterness will twist the grim faces of those tasting it with the sensation." <note>From the Georgics (2.246-7).</note>

->**Lucretius in Book 2**<-
<note>original: "Foedo pertorquet ora sapore."</note>
"It twists the face with a foul taste."

# BOOK SIX

->**Virgil says:**<-
<note>original: "Morte obita qualis fama est uolitare figuras."</note>
"The story goes that after death, figures flit about like ghosts." <note>From the *Aeneid*, Book 10. Virgil is describing the phantom of Aeneas.</note>

->**Lucretius in Book 1:**<-
<note>original: "Cernere uti uideamur eas audireq; coram, / Morte obita quorum tellus amplectitur ossa."</note>
"So that we seem to see and hear them face to face, though the earth embraces their bones now that death has passed." <note>From *De Rerum Natura* (On the Nature of Things). Virgil adapts the phrasing regarding the state of the soul after death.</note>

->**From this also comes that line of Virgil:**<-
<note>original: "Et patris anchisæ græmio complectitur ossa."</note>
"And he embraces the bones of his father Anchises in his bosom." <note>From the *Aeneid*, Book 5.</note>

->**Virgil:**<-
<note>original: "Ora modis attolens pallida miris."</note>
"Raising his face, pale in a wonderful and strange way." <note>From the *Aeneid*, Book 1. This describes the ghost of Sychaeus appearing to Dido.</note>

->**Lucretius in Book 1:**<-
<note>original: "Sed quædam simulacra modis pallentia miris."</note>
"But certain phantoms, pale in a wonderful and strange way." <note>Virgil adopts Lucretius's specific rhythmic ending "modis... miris" to evoke a sense of supernatural dread.</note>

->**Virgil:**<-
<note>original: "Tum gelidus toto manabat corpore sudor."</note>
"Then a cold sweat flowed over his whole body." <note>From the *Aeneid*, Book 3.</note>

->**Ennius in Book 16:**<-
<note>original: "Tunc timido manat ex omni corpore sudor."</note>
"Then from his trembling body, sweat flows everywhere." <note>Ennius was the "father" of Roman hexameter poetry; Virgil frequently refined his older, rougher verses.</note>

->**Virgil:**<-
<note>original: "Labitur uncta uadis abies."</note>
"The oiled fir-wood glides upon the shallows." <note>From the *Aeneid*, Book 8. This refers to a ship, as fir was a common material for shipbuilding.</note>

->**Ennius in Book 14:**<-
<note>original: "Labitur uncta carina:uolat super impetus undas."</note>
"The oiled keel glides; its momentum flies over the waves."

->**Virgil:**<-
<note>original: "Ac ferreus ingruit imber."</note>
"And an iron rain falls thick." <note>From the *Aeneid*, Book 12. A metaphor for a dense volley of arrows or spears.</note>

->**Ennius in Book 8:**<-
<note>original: "Hastati spargunt hastas: fit ferreus imber."</note>
"The spearmen scatter their spears; an iron rain begins."

->**Virgil:**<-
<note>original: "Apicem tamen incita summum Hasta tulit."</note>
"Yet the swift spear carried away the very top of his crest." <note>From the *Aeneid*, Book 12.</note>

<note>original: "Tamen inde uolans secū abstulit hasta Insigne."</note>
"Yet the flying spear took the crest away with it from there."

->**Virgil:**<-

"The dusty horseman rages; all cry out for arms." <note>From the *Aeneid*, Book 9.</note>

->**Ennius in Book 6:**<-
<note>original: "Ballatū pecudes quatit:omnes arma requirunt."</note>
"The bleating of the flock shakes them; all cry out for arms."

->**Virgil:**<-
<note>original: "Nec uisu facilis nec dictu affabilis ulli."</note>
"Neither easy for any to look upon, nor affable in speech." <note>From the *Aeneid*, Book 3, describing the Cyclops Polyphemus.</note>

->**Accius in *Philoctetes*:**<-
<note>original: "Quem neq; tueri contra neq; affari queas."</note>
"Whom you can neither look upon directly nor speak to." <note>Accius—written here as "Actius"—was a famous Roman tragic playwright.</note>

->**Virgil:**<-
<note>original: "Aut spoliis ego iam raptis laudabat opimis: / Aut leto insigni."</note>
"I shall now be praised either for the rich spoils I have taken, or for a noble death." <note>From the *Aeneid*, Book 10.</note>

->**Accius in *The Judgment of the Arms*:**<-
<note>original: "Nam tropheū ferre me a forti uiro pulchrum est. / Si autē & uincar:uinci a tali nullum est probrū."</note>
"For it is a fine thing for me to carry a trophy taken from a brave man. But if I am defeated, there is no shame in being conquered by such a man."

->**Virgil:**<-
<note>original: "Nec si miserum fortuna finonem / Finxit:uanū etiā mendacemq; improba finget."</note>
"Though Fortune has made Sinon miserable, her wickedness shall not also make him false and a liar." <note>From the *Aeneid*, Book 2. Sinon is the Greek spy who convinces the Trojans to bring the wooden horse inside the city.</note>

->**Accius in *Telephus*:**<-
<note>original: "Nam si a me regnum fortuna atq; opes"</note>
"For if Fortune [has taken] the kingdom and wealth from me..."

# SATURNALIA

<note>The text begins with a fragment likely from an older poet, possibly Ennius or Accius, which serves as the thematic precursor to the Virgil quote below.</note>
[He] was able to snatch [fortune away], but was unable to snatch away virtue.

-> **Virgil** <-
<note>original: "Disce puer uirtutem ex me uerumq; laborem: Fortunam ex aliis."</note>
"Learn, my boy, virtue and true labor from me; learn of fortune from others." <note>From the *Aeneid*, Book 12. Aeneas is speaking to his son, Ascanius, before returning to battle.</note>

-> **Accius in *The Judgment of the Arms*** <-
<note>original: "Virtuti is par:dispar fortunis patris."</note>
"He is equal in virtue, but unequal to the fortunes of his father." <note>Accius (here spelled "Actius") was an early Roman tragic poet. This line refers to Ajax or his son.</note>

-> **Virgil** <-
<note>original: "Iam iam nec maxima iuno: Nec saturnius hæc oculis pater aspicit æquis."</note>
"Now, now, neither greatest Juno nor the Saturnian father <note>Jupiter</note> looks upon these things with impartial eyes." <note>From the *Aeneid*, Book 4. Dido's lament.</note>

-> **Accius in *Antigone*** <-
<note>original: "Iam iam neq; dii regunt Neq; profecto deum summus rex omnibus curat."</note>
"Now, now, neither do the gods rule, nor indeed does the highest king of the gods care for all things."

-> **Virgil** <-
<note>original: "Nū capti potuer capī? nū icēsa cremauit Troia ui ros?"</note>
"Could those who were captured not be captured? Did burnt Troy consume its men?" <note>From the *Aeneid*, Book 7. Juno expresses her frustration that the Trojans (Teucrians) seem impossible to destroy.</note>

-> **Ennius in Book 10, when they were speaking of Pergamum <note>Troy</note>** <-
<note>original: "Quæ neq; dardaniis campis potuere perire. Nec quum capta capi.nec quū combusta cremari."</note>
"Those who could neither perish on the Dardanian plains, nor be captured when the city was taken, nor be consumed when it was burnt." <note>Ennius was the 'father' of Roman epic poetry; Virgil frequently adapted his rugged hexameters into a more polished style.</note>

-> **Virgil** <-
<note>original: "Multi præterea quos fama obscura recondit."</note>
"Many others besides, whom obscure fame hides." <note>From the *Aeneid*, Book 5.</note>

-> **Ennius in *Alexander*** <-
<note>original: "Multi alii aduētāt:pauptas quoq; obscurat noīas"</note>
"Many others arrive; poverty also obscures their names."

-> **Virgil** <-
<note>original: "Audentes fortuna iuuat."</note>
"Fortune favors the bold." <note>From the *Aeneid*, Book 10. A famous maxim attributed here to Virgil, but shown to have older roots.</note>

-> **Ennius in Book 7** <-
<note>original: "Fortibus est fortuna uiris data."</note>
"Fortune is given to brave men."

-> **Virgil** <-
<note>original: "Recoquant patrios fornacibus enses Et curuæ rigidum falces conflantur in ensem."</note>
"They re-forge their fathers' swords in the furnaces, and the curved pruning-hooks are melted down into stiff swords." <note>A combination of phrases from the *Aeneid* and the *Georgics* describing the transformation of tools of peace into weapons of war.</note>

-> **Lucretius in Book 5** <-
<note>original: "Inde minutatim processit ferreus ensis. Versaq; in obscurum species est facilis æneæ."</note>
"Then, little by little, the iron sword came forward, and the shape of the bronze sickle fell into disrepute." <note>Lucretius describes the technological progression from the Bronze Age to the Iron Age in his philosophical epic *On the Nature of Things*.</note>

-> **Virgil** <-
<note>original: "Pocula sunt fontes liqdi atq; exercita cursu flumia"</note>
"Their cups are clear springs and rivers exercised by their course." <note>From the *Georgics*, Book 3, describing the simple life of animals.</note>

-> **Lucretius in Book 5** <-
<note>original: "Adsedare sitim fluuii fontesque uocabant."</note>
"The rivers and springs called them to quench their thirst."

-> **Virgil** <-
<note>original: "Quos rami fructus:quos ipsa uolentia rura Sponte tulere sua:carpsit."</note>
"He plucked the fruits which the branches and the willing countryside itself bore of their own accord." <note>From the *Georgics*, Book 2.</note>

-> **Lucretius in Book 5** <-
<note>original: "Quod sol atq; imbres dederat:qd' terra crearat. Sponte sua:satis id placarat pectora donum."</note>
"What the sun and rains had given, what the earth had created of her own accord—that gift was enough to please their hearts."

After considering these verses translated from others, either in their entirety or in part, or those in which he changed words as if staining them with a different dye: I shall now compare passage to passage. I do this so that you may perceive in your mind from whence they were formed, as if you were recognizing them in a mirror.

-> **Virgil** <-
<note>original: "Nec sum animi dubius uerbis ea uincere magnū Quā sit:& angustis hūc addere rebus honorē."</note>
"Nor am I doubtful in my mind how great a task it is to master these things in words, and to add honor to such humble themes." <note>From the *Georgics*, Book 3.</note>

# BOOK SIX

But a sweet love carries me away through the steep, deserted heights of Parnassus <note>A mountain in Greece sacred to the Muses</note>; it is a joy to travel over the ridges where no track of those who came before turns down a gentle slope toward Castalia <note>The sacred spring of the Muses on Parnassus; Virgil is claiming poetic originality here, though the text below argues he is imitating Lucretius. From *Georgics*, Book 3.</note>.

### Lucretius in Book One.

Nor does it escape my mind how obscure these matters are; but a great hope of praise has struck my heart with a sharp thyrsus <note>A staff associated with Bacchus, symbolizing divine inspiration</note>, and at the same time has struck a sweet love for the Muses into my breast. Now, inspired by this with a vigorous mind, I wander through the trackless places of the Muses <note>original: "Pieridum"</note>, trodden by no one’s foot before. <note>From *De Rerum Natura*, Book 1. Note the striking similarity in the "sweet love" and "trackless places" imagery used by Virgil above.</note>

Take also another passage of Virgil <note>original: "Maronis"</note> from which he had drawn a comparison, so that you may find the same "color" and a sound almost similar to the previous passage in both instances.

### Virgil.

If a high house with proud doors does not vomit from its whole building a huge wave of morning callers; nor do they gaze open-mouthed at doorposts inlaid with beautiful tortoiseshell. <note>From *Georgics*, Book 2. This describes the ostentatious wealth of the city in contrast to the simple country life.</note>

### And soon after.

But there is secure rest and a life that knows not how to deceive, rich in varied resources; there is leisure in broad estates: living caves and lakes; and cool valleys <note>original: "tempe"</note>; the lowing of cattle and soft sleep under a tree are not absent there; there are glades and the haunts of wild beasts, and a youth capable of enduring labor and accustomed to having little.

### Lucretius in Book Two.

If there are no golden statues of youths throughout the halls, holding fire-bearing torches in their right hands so that lights may be supplied for nocturnal banquets; nor does the house shine with silver and glitter with gold; nor do the gilded and paneled ceilings echo the lyre; when yet, stretched out among themselves on the soft grass near a stream of water under the branches of a tall tree, they pleasantly care for their bodies with no great wealth: especially when the weather smiles, and the seasons of the year sprinkle the green grass with flowers. <note>Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura* 2.24–33. Virgil clearly modeled his praise of country life on this Epicurean description of simple pleasure.</note>

### Virgil.

Neither the shadows of deep groves nor soft meadows can move his mind; nor the river which, rolled through the rocks, seeks the plain purer than amber. <note>From *Georgics*, Book 3, describing a dying ox unmoved by nature’s beauty.</note>

### Lucretius in Book Two.

Nor can the tender willows and the grass vigorous with dew and any rivers lapping at the top of their banks delight the mind and turn away the sudden care. <note>Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura* 2.362–364. Here Lucretius describes a mother cow grieving for her lost calf, a scene Virgil adapted for his dying ox.</note>

Regarding the plague itself, which appears in the third book of the *Georgics*: the whole "color" and almost all the outlines are drawn from the description of the plague found in the sixth book of Lucretius. For the Virgilian passage begins:

"Here once from a disease of the sky a pitiable season arose..." <note>Virgil, *Georgics* 3.478.</note>

<meta>This page continues the philological comparison between the poets Virgil and Lucretius. The speaker in Macrobius’s *Saturnalia* is demonstrating how Virgil’s description of a cattle plague in the *Georgics* (Book 3) closely mirrors Lucretius’s description of the Plague of Athens in *De Rerum Natura* (Book 6).</meta>

<header>THE SATURNALIA</header>

...a season: and the heat of autumn glowed through its whole duration, and gave every kind of cattle and every wild beast over to death. <note>From Virgil’s *Georgics*, Book 3. Virgil is describing a devastating plague that struck the Noric Alps.</note>

Lucretius indeed begins in this way:

This manner of disease and death-bearing heat once rendered the fields fatal in the borders of Cecrops <note>original: "Cecropis." Cecrops was the mythical founder of Athens; Lucretius is referring to the famous Plague of Athens</note>, and laid waste the roads and emptied the city of its citizens. <note>From *De Rerum Natura*, Book 6.</note>

But since it would be far too long to set down the entire passage from both authors, I will select certain excerpts from which the similarity of the twin descriptions may be clearly seen. 

Virgil says:

Then indeed their eyes are burning, and the breath, drawn from deep within, is sometimes heavy with a groan; and now with a long-drawn sob they stretch their flanks; from the nostrils flows black blood, and the rough tongue presses against the squeezed throat.

->Lucretius says:<-

In the beginning, they carried a head burning with heat, and both eyes red with a suffused light. The throat also would sweat within with black blood, and the path of the voice would be blocked and closed by ulcers. And the tongue, the interpreter of the mind, would drip with gore, weakened by ills, heavy in movement, and rough to the touch.

->Virgil says this:<-

These signs they give in the first days before death. 

And as for what signs they gave, he related them above; that is: 

Drooping ears; in that same spot a fitful sweat, and that indeed is cold as they are about to die; the skin is hard and resists the hand that touches it.

->Lucretius says:<-

And many other signs of death were given then: the mind of the spirit disturbed in sorrow and fear; a gloomy brow; a fierce and furious look; furthermore, ears anxious and full of ringing sounds; thick breathing, or a deep breath rising only rarely; and a shining moisture of sweat soaking the neck; thin, small spits of a shriveled saffron color; and a salty cough barely uttered through the hoarse throat.

->Virgil:<-

It was helpful to pour in the liquid of Lenaeus <note>original: "Leneos." A title for Bacchus, god of wine; thus, wine</note> through an inserted horn; that seemed the only salvation for the dying. Soon, however, this very thing led to their end.

->Lucretius says:<-

Nor was any certain method of a common remedy given. For what had allowed one to breathe in the vital air and to look upon the temples of heaven, this very thing was destruction to others, and prepared their death.

->Virgil says:<-

Furthermore, it no longer matters that the fodder is changed.

<meta>This page continues the philological comparison between the poets Virgil and Lucretius, as well as earlier Roman authors like Ennius and Accius. And the sought-after arts of healing do harm; the masters of medicine have given up. <note>From Virgil’s *Georgics*, Book 3. The "masters" refers to the legendary healers like Chiron and Melampus who could not stop the plague.</note>

->Lucretius says:<-

Nor was there any rest from the evil: the weary bodies lay low; medicine muttered in silent fear. <note>From *De Rerum Natura*, Book 6. Lucretius describes the helplessness of doctors during the Plague of Athens.</note>

->Virgil says:<-

The very air is not fair even to the birds; and they, falling headlong, leave their life beneath a high cloud. <note>Virgil, *Georgics* 3.523. The plague is so pervasive it even taints the sky.</note>

->Lucretius says:<-

Yet not at all easily did any bird appear in those places, nor did the sad generations of wild beasts leave the woods; most were languishing with disease and they were dying. <note>Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura* 6.1215.</note>

Do not the members of this description seem to us to have flowed from one source? <note>The speaker is pointing out that Virgil’s description of the cattle plague is clearly modeled on Lucretius’s description of the human plague.</note> But again, I compare other passages.

->Virgil:<-

They rejoice, drenched in the blood of brothers, and exchange their homes and sweet thresholds for exile. <note>Virgil, *Georgics* 2.510. This refers to the horrors of civil war.</note>

->Lucretius in the third book:<-

With civil blood they forge their wealth, and greedy, they double their riches, piling slaughter upon slaughter; cruel, they rejoice in the sad death of a brother. <note>Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura* 3.70.</note>

->Virgil:<-

Many things have been restored to a better state by time and the varied labor of a changing age; visiting many in turn, fortune has played with them, and placed them again on solid ground. <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 11.425.</note>

->Ennius in the eighth book:<-

One day in war finishes many things. And again, many fortunes fall back by chance. Fortune has by no means followed anyone forever. <note>From the *Annales* of Quintus Ennius (239–169 BC), the "father of Roman poetry."</note>

->Virgil:<-

O youth of outstanding spirit: the more you yourself surpass in fierce courage, the more it is right for me to consult carefully, and in fear, to weigh every chance. <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 12.19. King Latinus is speaking to the hero Turnus.</note>

->Accius in his *Antigone*:<-

The more I understand you to be of that sort, the more it is right for me, Antigone, to consult and spare you. <note>original: "Actius." Lucius Accius was a famous Roman tragic playwright. This is a fragment from his lost play based on the Greek myth of Antigone.</note>

->Virgil:<-

O light of Dardania, O most faithful hope of the Trojans, and so forth. <note>original: "O lux dardaniæ spes o fidissima teucrum." From *Aeneid* 2.281. Aeneas addresses the ghost of Hector.</note>

->Ennius in his *Alexander*:<-

O light of Troy, brother Hector, why are you thus wretched with your torn body? Or who has treated you thus before our watching eyes? <note>From Ennius’s lost play *Alexander*, concerning the Trojan War.</note>

->Virgil:<-

The Lapiths of Pelethronium gave the reins and the circles, placed on the back; and taught the horseman under arms <note>Virgil, *Georgics* 3.115. The Lapiths were a legendary tribe from Pelethronium (a region of Mt. Pelion in Thessaly) credited with inventing the bridle and the "circle" or ring-maneuver for training horses.</note>

# THE SATURNALIA

There are other passages of many verses which Maro <note>A common medieval and Renaissance name for the poet Virgil, whose full name was Publius Vergilius Maro.</note> transferred into his own work from the ancients with the change of only a few words. And because it would be a long task to transcribe all the verses from both sources, I will simply note the ancient books so that anyone who wishes may marvel at the similarity of the passages by reading and comparing them. In the first book of the *Aeneid*, a storm is described; Venus complains to Jupiter about the dangers facing her son, and Jupiter consoles her with the prospect of future prosperity. This entire scene is taken from Naevius <note>Gnaeus Naevius (c. 270–201 BCE), an early Roman dramatist and epic poet.</note> from the first book of the *Punic War*. For there, Venus likewise complains to Jupiter while the Trojans are laboring in a storm, and the words of Jupiter consoling his daughter with hope for the future follow. Likewise, regarding Pandarus and Bitias opening the gates, the passage is taken from the fifteenth book of Ennius, who described two Histrians <note>A tribe from the Istrian peninsula.</note> breaking out during a siege through a gate and dealing slaughter to the besieging enemy. Nor did Virgil refrain from "plundering" Cicero <note>original: "Tullio copilando"—referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> as long as he could gather ornaments for himself from every side. 

*O fame, great and greater still in arms, Trojan man!* <note>original: "O fama ingens ingētior armis Vir troiane"—from Virgil's *Aeneid* 11.124.</note>

Surely he means this: that Aeneas surpassed his own reputation through his brave deeds, whereas usually fame is greater than the reality. This sentiment appeared in Cicero's *Cato* in these words: "as is usually the case to the contrary, so that all things seemed greater in reality than in fame." For it often happens that expectation is surpassed by knowledge, and the ears by the eyes. Likewise, the passage "next to this, but next after an interval" <note>original: "pximus huic loco: sed pximus iteruallo."</note> echoes Cicero in the *Brutus*: "Therefore Lucius Philippus approached the two greatest men, Crassus and Antonius; he was next, but after a long interval, yet still next." 

There are certain things in Virgil which are believed to have been transferred from Homer, but I shall show that they were taken from our own Roman authors, who had previously drawn these things from Homer into their own poems. This is the ultimate tribute to Homeric praise: that even when so many have been on guard against him, and the collected strength of all has joined hands against him, he remained unmoved like a rock in the sea. Homer says this regarding the brave fight of Ajax. Ennius, in his fifteenth book, transfers this passage to the fight of the tribune Caelius with these verses:

> From all sides they converge; spears like rain
> Pierce the tribune’s shield; the boss rang out
> From the bronze sound of the helmets; but no one could
> Tear apart his body with the iron aimed from every side.
> He constantly breaks and shakes off the overflowing spears;
> Sweat covers his whole body, and he labors greatly.
> Nor is there a chance to breathe as the iron flies.
> The Histrians, hurling spears from their hands, kept up the pressure.

From this, Virgil composed the same passage concerning the trapped Turnus <note>A primary antagonist of the *Aeneid*.</note> with a more elegant grace:

> Therefore the youth could neither stand his ground with his shield
> Nor did his right hand prevail; so from all sides, overwhelmed 
> By cast weapons, his hollow temples rang with a constant
> Clanging from his helmet, and the solid bronze gaped under stones.
> The crests were struck from his head, nor could the shield-boss
> Withstand the blows; both the Trojans and the lightning-like 
> Mnestheus himself redouble their spears. Then from his whole body 
> Sweat flows like pitch (nor is there power to breathe); 
> A wearying panting shakes his exhausted limbs.

->Homer says:<-
<note>Homer's original Greek describes the density of the phalanx in the *Iliad*.</note>

->Furius in his fourth Book of Annals:<-

> Foot is pressed by foot, point by point, **man by man.**

->From this Virgil says:<-

> Foot clings to foot, and man dense with man. <note>original: "Hæret pede pes: densusq; uiro uir"—from *Aeneid* 10.361.</note>

<summary>This page analyzes Virgil’s literary "borrowings," arguing that many of his famous scenes and similes were actually adapted from earlier Roman poets like Ennius and Naevius, who had themselves adapted them from Homer.</summary>
<keywords>Virgil, Maro, Ennius, Homer, Naevius, Cicero, Aeneid, literary imitation, poetic influence, Saturnalia, Roman epic, philology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Virgil's literary borrowings, shifting from structural scene-copying to the adaptation of specific verses and metaphors. The dialogue highlights how Virgil drew from early Roman poets such as Hostius and Ennius, as well as the Greek tradition of Homer, to craft his epic style.</meta>

### BOOK SIX

->This is from Homer.<-

Following him <note>Homer</note>, the poet Hostius in the second book of his *History of the Istrian War* <note>original: "belli historici"—referring to the *Bellum Histricum*, an epic poem by Hostius (2nd century BCE) about the Roman conquest of Istria.</note> says:
> Not if I had a hundred tongues and as many mouths and voices flowing like liquid. <note>original: "Non si mihi linguæ centum atq; sint ora totidem uocelq; liquatæ."</note>

->From this, Virgil says:<-

> Not for me, even if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths... <note>original: "Non mihi si linguæ centum sint oraq; centum"—from *Aeneid* 6.625.</note>

There is a Homeric description of a fleeing horse, in these words: <note>The text omits the Greek quote from the *Iliad* but provides the Roman adaptations below.</note>

->Ennius drew from this:<-

> And then just as a horse who, driven from the stalls,
> has broken his bonds with his great spirit: and then
> carries himself through the blue fields and happy meadows of the plain
> with his chest held high: often he shakes his high mane:
> the breath from his warm soul drives white foam. <note>original: "Et tum sicut equus qui de præsepibus actus / Vincla suis magnis animis abrupit..."—Ennius was the "father" of Roman epic poetry.</note>

->Virgil:<-

> Just as when, having broken his bonds, he flees the stalls... <note>original: "Qualis ubi abruptis fugit præsepia uinclis"—from *Aeneid* 11.492.</note> and so forth.

Let no one think the ancient poets are worthless because their verses seem rough <note>original: "scabri"—meaning gritty or unpolished.</note> to us. For that style alone pleased the ears of Ennius’s age, and the following age labored long so that it might settle into this softer style we now prefer. But let me not delay Cecinna <note>Aulu-Caecina Severus, one of the interlocutors in this dialogue.</note> any further; let him reveal what he remembers Maro <note>Virgil</note> having transferred from antiquity.

¶ Then Cecinna discussed how much Virgil sought out from antiquity in either words or passages; Furius, as one mindful of the abundance of both old and new authors, joined in. I will endeavor to show that this most studious poet <note>Virgil</note> judged the individual words of the ancients most aptly and inserted chosen words into his own work. These words seem new to us only because of our neglect of antiquity; for instance, look at:
<margin>“Additus” used for “hostile”</margin>
*addita*: used for “inimical” or “hostile.” Who would not think the poet, by his own judgment, wished to manufacture a new word for himself meaning "affixed" and thereby "hostile"? Yet Lucilius <note>Gaius Lucilius (d. 103 BCE), the inventor of Roman satire.</note> had already said this in his ninth book with these words:
> If a praetor is not **set against** <note>original: "additus"</note> me and does not harrass me,
> it would not be bad if that one man had stretched me out as I say.

->Virgil:<-

> In the morning, he **pours forth** <note>original: "uomit"—literally "vomits."</note> a wave of visitors from all his halls. <note>A description of a wealthy man’s morning reception (salutatio) in *Georgics* 2.462.</note>
<margin>To pour forth</margin>
He uses *vomit* (“pours forth”) beautifully and in the ancient manner. For Ennius says:
> And the Tiber river **vomits** <note>original: "uomit"</note> rocks into the sea.
From this, even now, we call the *vomitoria* <note>term: vomitoria — wide exits in ancient theaters and amphitheaters designed to allow large crowds to exit (pour out) rapidly. They are not, as myth suggests, rooms for vomiting during feasts.</note> in the spectacles, from which people, entering in a mass, pour themselves into the seats.
<margin>Vomitoria in the spectacles</margin>
<margin>Agmen</margin>
¶ To use *agmen* <note>term: agmen — usually a "column" of soldiers on the march.</note> for a certain motion or flow is not inelegant, as in: “the Tiber flows in a smooth **stream**” <note>original: "leui fluit agmine tybris"</note>; indeed, it is an ancient usage.
For Ennius says in his fifth book:
> Because through the pleasant city a river flows in a smooth **stream**.
¶ As for what he says: “to burn with **crackling** flames,” he did not use a new word, but Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BCE), author of *On the Nature of Things*.</note> placed it first in his sixth book.
<margin>With crackling flames</margin>
> Nor is any thing more consumed by the Delphic laurel of Phoebus
> with a terrible sound and a **crackling** <note>original: "crepitante"</note> flame.
<margin>The field bristles.</margin>
“You, iron-hearted with spears: **the field bristles**” <note>original: "horret ager"</note>: “the field bristles” is a marvelous expression. But Ennius also has it in his ninth book.

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of Virgil’s poetic vocabulary. While the previous page focused on structural borrowings from epic predecessors like Hostius and Ennius, this page examines how Virgil adapted specific metaphors and archaic terminology from early Roman poets and prose writers like Lucretius, Cicero, and Cato the Elder to enrich the texture of the *Aeneid* and *Georgics*.</meta>

### BOOK SIX OF THE SATURNALIA

The army bristles with sharp weapons on both sides. <note>original: "Horrefcit telis exercitus afper utrūq;"—referring to the imagery of weapons standing up like bristles on an animal.</note> And in the play *Erectheus*: <note>Erectheus was a tragedy by the early Roman poet Ennius.</note>
> They raise their arms, the weapons bristle. <note>original: "Arma arrigunt horrefcunt tela."</note> 
And in his poem *Scipio*:
> With long spears scattered, the field shines and bristles. <note>original: "Sparfis haltis lōgis cāpus fplendet & horret."</note> 
But before all these, it was Homer. <note>Virgil, Ennius, and others drew this "bristling" metaphor from the Greek epics of Homer.</note>

<margin>Quivering light</margin>
The sea shines under a quivering light. <note>original: "Splendet tremulo sub lumine pontus"—from Virgil’s *Aeneid* 7.9.</note> The phrase "quivering light" is expressed vividly from the very image of the thing itself. But Ennius was there first, in his play *Menalippe*: 
> Thus the earth and the hollow blue of the sky shine with quivering light. <note>original: "Lumen fic tremulo terra & caua cærule candēt."</note>
And Lucretius in his sixth book: 
> Moreover, the moisture of the water tosses with the sun's rays and thins into light from the quivering heat. <note>original: "Præterea solis radiis iactat aqu huor. & i lucē tremulo rarefcit ab æftu."</note>

<margin>Shady arbors</margin>
Here the white poplar leans over the cave, and flexible vines weave shady arbors. <note>original: "Hic candida populus antro imminet & lentæ texunt umbracula uites"—from Virgil's *Eclogues* 9.41-42.</note> There are those who mistakenly believe the word *umbracula* <note>shady places or arbors</note> was coined by Virgil; however, Varro <note>a famous Roman scholar</note> in the tenth book of his *Divine Antiquities* says that this kind of "shady arbor" was granted to certain magistrates in the town. And Cicero in the fifth book of *On the Laws*: "Do you wish then (since the sun already seems to have declined a little from midday, and this whole place is not yet fully shaded by these young trees) that we go down to the Liris? <note>a river in central Italy</note> And let us pursue the remaining matters in those alder-tree arbors?" Similarly, in his work *Brutus*: "But as if in the shady arbors of that most learned man, Theophrastus." <note>Theophrastus was a Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle.</note>
> They cross the fields in a run: and the deer gather 
> their dusty columns in flight; <note>from *Aeneid* 4.154</note>
Because he says "they cross" <note>original: "transmittunt"</note> elegantly in place of "they go across." So too Lucretius in his second book: 
> And the knights fly around: and suddenly, across the middle,
<margin>To cross over</margin>
> they cross the fields, shaking them with a powerful charge. 
And even Paestanus Jubonensis <note>an obscure Roman writer</note> says: "We crossed the horses on foot," which means "we went across."

<margin>To flow down to the ground</margin>
> Following her example, the whole cohort left 
> their horses and flowed down to the ground. <note>original: "Ad terram defluxit equis"—from *Aeneid* 11.500-501, describing Camilla's cavalry dismounting.</note> 
So Furius <note>Furius Bibaculus, a Roman poet</note> says in his first book: 
> He, suddenly bound by a heavy wound, released the horse's 
> reins and flowed down to the ground in a fall, and his 
> bronze armor gave back a sound. 
"Then the soil began to harden and to shut out Nereus from the sea." <note>original: "Tum durare solum & difcludere nerea ponto Cœperit"—from *Eclogues* 6.35. "Nereus" is a poetic name for the sea.</note> This word "to shut out" <note>original: "discludere," meaning to separate or divide</note> strikes our ears as if it were new. But Lucretius used it first in his fifth book: 
> From that place, the parts began to scatter, and like things 
> to be joined with like: and to separate the world. <note>original: "difcludere mundum"</note>

<margin>A fine-spun song</margin>
Tityrus, it is proper for a shepherd to feed fat sheep, but to sing a fine-spun song. <note>original: "deductū dicere carmen"—from *Eclogues* 6.4-5.</note> "Fine-spun" <note>original: "deductum," literally "drawn out" like wool thread</note> is positioned elegantly here to mean thin and subtle. Likewise, Afranius <note>a Roman comic playwright</note> in *The Maiden* replied in just a few words: 
> With a sad, thinned voice: and saying he was not able. 
It was said similarly in the works of Cornificius: 
> To me, as I was chattering with a thinned voice. 
But these usages flowed from this source: Pomponius, in the Atellan farce titled *The Kalends of March*, says: 
> You must thin your voice, so that your words seem like a woman's. 
> Just order one to be brought: I will give back a voice thin and quivering; 
And below: 
> Even now, I shall thin my voice.

<margin>Jutting rocks</margin>
And we skirt the jutting rocks of Pachynus. <note>original: "Proiectaq faxa pachynni Radimus"—from *Aeneid* 3.699. Pachynus is a cape in Sicily.</note> If "jutting" <note>original: "proiecta"</note> is spoken according to common custom, it means "cast away" or "worthless." If according to the ancients, it means "thrown forward." Elsewhere he says: 
> While he steadies himself with his foot 
> thrust forward for the fight. 
But Sisenna <note>OCR "Silenna," referring to the historian Lucius Cornelius Sisenna</note> also said in his second book: 
> And the Marsi come closer: and so, with their shields 
> thrust forward as cover, they throw stones in a contest against the enemy. 
And in the same work: 
> There was an old and massive 
> holm-oak tree: which covered the greater part of the high ground with its jutting branches. 
And Lucretius in his third book: 
> However great the outspread size of the body.

<margin>Seasonable pine</margin>
And to fell a seasonable pine from the woods. <note>from Virgil's *Georgics* 1.256</note> He took this word "seasonable" <note>original: "tempestivam"</note> regarding the pine from Cato, who said: 
> When you dig up a pine nut: take it out during a waning moon 
> in the afternoon, without a south wind. Then indeed it will be 
> seasonable, when its seed is mature.
He also inserts Greek words into his work, but he was not the first to dare this: for among the ancient authors...

<meta>This page continues the philological analysis found in Book 6 of Macrobius’s *Saturnalia*, specifically focusing on how the poet Virgil borrowed and refined vocabulary from earlier Roman poets like Ennius, Lucretius, and Naevius. # BOOK SIX

<margin>Lamps</margin>
...followed with great boldness. "Lamps hang from the golden paneled ceilings." <note>original: "Depēdēt lychni laq̄aribus aureis" — from Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.726.</note> Just as Ennius wrote in his ninth book: "Twelve lamps of light." <note>original: "Lychnorū lūina bis sex."</note> And Lucretius in his fifth book: "Likewise, those nightly terrestrial lights for you, the hanging lamps." <note>original: "Quin ét nocturna tibi terrestria q̄ sunt lumia pēdētes lychni."</note> Lucilius in his first book also wrote: "Furthermore, the goose-footed lamp-stands, and as I said, the lamps before the feet of the bed and the lanterns." <note>original: "Porro chænopoda... lychnosq;... ante pedes lecti atq; lucernas." The term "chaenopoda" refers to lamp-stands shaped like the feet of a goose.</note>

<margin>Bright air (Aethra)</margin>
And regarding the phrase: "Nor did the pole shine with stars in the bright air," <note>original: "Nec lucidus æthra sydera polus." Virgil uses the Greek-derived word 'aethra' for the upper atmosphere.</note> Ennius had said it first in his sixteenth book: "Meanwhile the torch of the sun sets; the ocean is overwhelmed by the red-streaked bright air." <note>original: "Interea fax occidit: oceanūq; rubra tracti obruit æthra."</note> And the same author in his *Thyestes*: "To be carried high through the flaming bright air as a burning torch." <note>original: "Flāmineā p æthrā alte feruidā ferri facē."</note> 

As for "The skillful works of Circe," <note>original: "Dædala Circæ."</note> Lucretius had previously said: "The skillful earth." <note>original: "Dædala tellus." The word 'daedala' implies something intricately or artistically made, named after the mythical craftsman Daedalus.</note> 

"The woods and great Olympus re-echo," <note>original: "Reboant siluæq; & magnus olympus."</note> which is found in Lucretius: "Neither do the harps re-echo in the paneled and gilded ceilings." <note>original: "Nec cythara reboāt laq̄ata aurataq; tecta."</note> But the older poets used this linguistic license more broadly, while Virgil used it more sparingly. For they even used terms like *pausa* (pause), *machaera* (sword), *acotiam* (remedy), *malace* (calm sea), and other similar Greek loans. 

<margin>Wild Oxen
Curved
Vaulted ceiling</margin>
The ancients also used Punic and Oscan words; in imitation of them, Virgil did not reject foreign words, as in that passage: "The forest-dwelling wild oxen continually..." <note>original: "Siluestres uri assidue."</note> For *Uri* is a Gallic word signifying wild oxen. Also: "And the curved ears under their shaggy horns." <note>original: "Et camuris hirtæ sub cornibus aures."</note> *Camurus* is a foreign word meaning "turning back on itself." And perhaps we have also shaped our word for a vaulted ceiling, *camera*, based on this same logic. 

There are also many epithets in Virgil which are believed to have been created by him; but I will show that these too were drawn from the ancients. Some of these are simple, such as *Gradivus* (the marcher) or *Mulciber* (the softner); others are compounds, such as *Arcitenens* (the bow-bearer) or *Vitifator* (the vine-planter). But first I shall speak of the simple ones.

<margin>Mulciber (Vulcan)</margin>
"And the distinct Africans, whom Mulciber [forged]." <note>original: "Et distinctos mulciber afros."</note> *Mulciber* is Vulcan, who becomes the fire that softens and tames all things. <note>The name is derived from 'mulcere,' meaning to soften or stroke.</note> Accius in his *Philoctetes* writes: "Alas, Mulciber, you have forged arms with your hand joined to a lazy man." <note>original: "Heu mulciber arma ignauo iuncta es fabricatus & manu."</note> And Egnatius in the first book of *On the Nature of Things*: "Finally, Mulciber himself, reaching the highest points of heaven, touches them." 

<margin>Butting kids</margin>
"And the butting kids leap upon the flowers." <note>original: "hædiq; petulci floribus insultent."</note> Lucretius in his second book:
> Moreover, the tender kids with their trembling voices
> Recognize their horned mothers, and the butting lambs.
<note>original: "Præterea teneri tremulis in uocibus hædi / Corniferas norunt matres agniq; petulci." The term 'petulcus' refers to an animal prone to butting with its head.</note>

<margin>Liquid fire</margin>
That which he says in the *Bucolics* might seem to be of the greatest audacity: "And at the same time, liquid fire," <note>original: "Et liquidi simul ignis."</note> used for "pure" or "bright," or perhaps for "flowing" and "abundant"—unless Lucretius had used this epithet before him in his sixth book:
> For this reason also it happens that that mobile,
> Golden heat of liquid fire flies down to the earth.
<note>original: "Deuolet in terram liquidi calor aureus ignis."</note>

<margin>Bitter (sad)
Long-eared hare</margin>
The translation of "sad" (*tristis*) to mean "bitter" is a fitting metaphor, as in: "the bitter lupins." <note>original: "tristeq; lupini."</note> And Ennius used it thus in the fourth book of his *Sabines*: "He seeks neither bitter mustard nor the mournful onion." <note>original: "Neq; triste quæritat sinapi: neq; cepe mœstū."</note> 

Virgil is not the first to employ "long-eared hares" (*auritos lepores*); rather, he follows Afranius, who says in his prologue in the character of Priapus: "For as for what the common folk proclaim, that I was born of a long-eared parent, it is not so." 

And to add the compound epithets: as Virgil says:
<margin>Incense-burning
Bow-bearing</margin>
> She saw, when she placed gifts upon the incense-burning altars.
<note>original: "Vidit thuricremis quum dona imponeret aris."</note>
Lucretius had already said in his second book:
> For often before the beautiful shrines of the gods
> A calf falls, slaughtered beside the incense-burning altars.

"As the pious bow-bearer..." <note>original: "Quā pius arcitenens." An epithet for Apollo.</note> Naevius used this epithet in the second book of the *Punic War*: "Then the mighty in arrows, the renowned bow-bearer, the Pythian Apollo sprung from holy Delos."

->The same elsewhere:<-

> When you, the bow-bearing goddess, mighty with arrows...

But also Hostius in the second book of the *Istrian War*:
> Divine Minerva and at the same time the unconquered Apollo, the bow-bearer, son of Latona.

<margin>Forest-dwelling</margin>
"Also the forest-dwelling Fauns." <note>original: "Etiam syluicolæ fauni."</note>
Naevius in the first book of the *Punic War*:
> Forest-dwelling men, unskilled in war.

Accius in the *Bacchae*:
> Forest-dwellers visiting unknown places.

<margin>Sail-flying</margin>
> Looking down upon the sail-flying sea.
<note>original: "Despiciens mare ueliuolum." A vivid compound describing the sea covered in sailing ships.</note>

# OF THE SATURNALIA

### Livius in *Helena*.
You who have measured the high seas of the deep with sail-flying ships. <note>original: "Tu qui permenfus ponti maria alta ueliuola." The word "ueliuola" (sail-flying) describes ships that "fly" using sails.</note>

### Ennius in the fourteenth book.
**When from afar they see the enemies approach with the winds on sail-flying ships.** <note>original: "Quum procul afpiciunt hostes accedere uentis Nauibus ueliuolis."</note>

### The same author in *Andromache*.
**And he snatches the sail-flying ships from the deep.** <note>original: "Rapit & ex alto naues ueliuolas."</note>

<margin>Vine-planter</margin>
**The vine-planter keeping his curved sickle under the image.** <note>original: "Vitifator feruans curuam sub imagine falcem." *Vitifator* is a compound for one who plants or tends vines.</note>

### Accius in *The Bacchae*.
**O Father Dionysus, best vine-planter, born of Semele, the joyful.** <note>original: "O Dionise pater optime uitifator semela genitus euchia."</note>

<margin>Night-wandering</margin>
**And nourishing Phoebe in her night-wandering chariot.** <note>original: "Almaque curru Noctiuago phœbe." Phoebe is a name for the Moon; "noctiuago" means wandering through the night.</note>

### Egnatius, *On the Nature of Things*, book one.
**Dewy Phoebe, as the night-wandering stars glided away, was driven from her place and yielded to the high lights of day.** <note>original: "Roscida noctiuagis astris labentibus phœbe / Pulsa loco cessit concedens lucibus altis"</note>

**You [conquered] the invincible, cloud-born, two-limbed ones.** <note>The "cloud-born" and "two-limbed" refer to the Centaurs, famously born from a cloud and having the bodies of both man and horse.</note>

### Cornificius in *Glaucus*.
<margin>Two-limbed</margin>
**To pierce the two-limbed Centaurs.** <note>original: "Centauros fodere bimembres."</note>

<margin>Goat-born</margin>
**And the goat-born flock through the grass with no guardian.** <note>original: "Caprigenumque pecus nullo custode per herbas."</note>

### Pacuvius in *Paulus*.
**Truly, the stride is larger for the goat-born flock.** <note>original: "Quauis caprigeno pecori grandior gressio est."</note>

### Accius in *Philoctetes*.
**Worn by the hooves of the goat-born.** <note>original: "Caprigenum trita ungulis."</note>

### The same author in *The Minotaur*.
**Whether he was born of bull-born seed or human.** <note>original: "Taurigeno semine ortum fuisse: an humano."</note>

Virgil used these epithets and others like them quite appropriately. For an arrow, he used "flying iron"; and for the Romans, the "toga-wearing race." One of these was used by Suevius, the other by Laberius. For Suevius says in his fifth book: **"The flying weapon of the birds."** <note>original: "Volucrūque uolatile telum."</note> And Laberius in *The Ephebe*: **"You seek to take away the license and lust of the toga-wearing lineage."** <note>original: "Licentia ac libidine ut tollā petis togatae stirpis."</note> The same author further on says: **"Therefore the dominion of the toga-wearing race was expanded by help."** <note>original: "Iccirco ope dilatatum est dominium togatae gentis."</note>

¶ As for the "figures" <note>A "figure" is a rhetorical or poetic device where words are used in a non-literal or unconventional way.</note> which he drew from antiquity, if you wish, I will list them as my sudden memory suggests. But now I want Servius <note>Servius was a famous 4th-century grammarian and commentator on Virgil.</note> to say what he has noted in Virgil that was shaped by the poet himself, rather than accepted from the ancients—or things used in a new but fitting way through poetic daring. For in explaining this same poet daily to the Roman youth, he must have a more ready knowledge of these annotations.

### Virgilian Figures.

The choice pleased everyone. For the remainder of the time, they stood in support and encouraged Servius to note those things which he had stored up. He began thus: "This venerable poet added much grace to the Latin language by shaping sometimes the words and sometimes the senses, such as these: **'Substituted for the mother, she created stolen bastards,'** <note>original: "Supposita de matre nothos furata creauit."</note> as if she herself created those whom she only caused to be born. Or: **'A place fresh with warm slaughter,'** <note>original: "Tepidāque recentem Cæde locum."</note> where 'fresh with slaughter' is a novel expression. And he says this: **'And the companions withdrew on the commanded sea,'** <note>original: "& socii cesserunt æquore iusso."</note> instead of saying they withdrew because they were commanded. And: **'About to sprinkle the flames with slaughtered blood,'** <note>original: "Et cæfo sparsurus sanguine flāmas."</note> referring to blood poured from those who were slaughtered. **'As victor, he paid the gods' vows at the first dawn,'** <note>original: "Vota deum primo uictor soluebat eo."</note> for vows that were made *to* the gods. **'And grant me as a companion for my son in the tomb.'** <note>original: "& me consortem nati concede sepulchro."</note> Another would have said: 'grant me as a companion to the son *of* the tomb.' **'And she, hastening her path along the bow of a thousand colors,'** <note>original: "& Illa Viam celerans per mille coloribus arcum."</note> that is, through the bow of a thousand colors. **'And here others cast spoils torn from the slain Latins into the fire,'** <note>original: "& Hic alii spolia occisis direpta latinis Coniiciunt igni."</note> instead of 'into the fire.' **'He escapes the weapons with his body and watchful eyes.'** <note>original: "Corpore tela modo atq; oculis uigilantibus exit."</note> 'He escapes the weapons' for 'he avoids' them. And: **'The old man released eyes whitening in death,'** <note>original: "Senior leto canentia lumina soluit."</note> using 'whitening' for the senility of old age. **'In the cave of a hollowed tree,'** <note>original: "Exesæ arboris antro."</note> for a hollow space. And: **'He plows a foul forehead with wrinkles'**; 'plows' is said not excessively, but beautifully. **'Thrice he carries the forest around with him in the bronze covering,'** <note>original: "Ter secum ærato circumfert tegmine syluam."</note> using 'forest' to mean a thicket of spears. And: **'The man of the flock,'** <note>original: "Vir gregis."</note> for the ca...

And "not otherwise than those to whom Mezentius is a cause of wrath": <note>original: "Haud aliter iuste quibus est Mezentius iræ."</note> to be an "object of hatred" is the common usage; to be "an object of wrath" is the invention of Maro <note>Virgil’s family name.</note>. Likewise he begins to speak of two:

Virgil starts with the plural "kings" but focuses the action on the singular Latinus.</note> as it is in Homer.

"I confess I urged Juturna to help her wretched brother": 
¶ Where it is customary to say: "I urged Juturna." <note>Virgil uses a specific grammatical case (the dative) that was unusual for this verb.</note> And "The city which I build is yours." <note>original: "Vrbem qua statuo uestra est." Indeed, what poetic indignation: "By Jove, shall he go?" he says here: what pity: "O fatherland, O household gods snatched in vain from the enemy." And that trepidation: "Quickly, bring the iron!
