What of that invention of new meanings: such as "deceptive weapons": and "to arm iron with poison." And "to soften wild habits by cultivation": "they have stripped off their woodland spirit": and "the driven spear drank deep of the virgin's blood": <note>original: "uirgineūqꝫ alte bibit acta cruorem."</note> as in Homer concerning the spear:

And "the tow lives under the hard oak, moving with slow smoke": and "the barking of dogs rages into the air": and "Father Inachus pouring a river from his engraved urn": and "fixed in the veins." "They place their life in the wounds." And whatever he said about bees in the likeness of brave men: so that he might also add to them customs and pursuits: peoples and battles. Why more? so that he might even call them citizens <note>original: "Quirites." A term strictly for Roman citizens, used here for bees to show their organized society.</note>: the day would fail me if I wished to pursue everything shaped by Virgil. But from these things which have been said: the diligent reader will note all similar instances.

<meta>This page continues the discussion in Book 6 of Macrobius’s Saturnalia, where the dinner guests are debating the linguistic choices of the poet Virgil. The previous page ended with examples of Virgil’s poetic metaphors; here, the character Avienus challenges the scholar Servius on Virgil's use of specific words that seem too "weak" or "contradictory" for their context.</meta>

# THE SATURNALIA, BOOK SIX

Behold <note>original: "Ecce" (OCR "cato"). A common misreading in early printed editions.</note> for us, as Eustachius just murmured, he says: he is eager to ask Servius many things about Virgil, the explanation of which pertains to the duty of a teacher of literature. He hopes for some time to be granted so that he might be made more certain by a more learned man concerning obscure and doubtful points. And Praetextatus said: "I approve, my dear Avienus, <margin>You doubt:</margin> that you do not allow the things about which you are in doubt to remain hidden from you. Therefore, let our most learned teacher be entreated by us to allow himself to have this business with you, because what you desire to hear will benefit us all in common. Do not delay any longer in opening the way for Servius to discourse upon Virgil." Then Avienus, turning entirely toward Servius, said: "I wish you to tell me, greatest of teachers, why is it that although Virgil was always anxiously diligent in choosing words suited to the merit or the atrocity of his subject, he yet placed a word carelessly and meanly in these verses: *That she harassed the Dulichian ships with barking monsters around her white waist.* <note>original: "Candida succinctā latrantibus inguina mōstris / Dulichias uexasse rates." From Virgil's *Eclogues* 6.75, describing the monster Scylla.</note> For 'harassed' <note>original: "uexasse."</note> is a word for a light and small inconvenience, not fitting for so atrocious an event, where men were suddenly snatched and mangled by a most savage beast. But I have also caught another instance of this kind: *Who does not know of hard Eurystheus? Or the altars of the unpraised Busiris?* <note>original: "Quis aut eurysthea durū? aut illaudati nescit busiridis aras?" From *Georgics* 3.4. Busiris was a mythical Egyptian king who sacrificed foreigners.</note> For this word, 'unpraised' <note>original: "illaudati."</note>, is not suitable to express the detestation of a most wicked man. One who was accustomed to sacrifice men of all nations is not merely 'unworthy of praise,' but is worthy of the detestation and execution of the entire human race. Nor does this word seem to me to come from Virgilian diligence: *A tunic scaly with gold.* <note>original: "Per tunicā squalentē auro." From *Aeneid* 11.488.</note> For it is not fitting to say 'squalid' or 'rough' with gold, since the filth of squalor is contrary to the brightness and splendor of gold."

And Servius replied: "Concerning the word 'harassed,' <margin>Harassed.</margin> I think it can be answered thus: 'harassed' <note>original: "uexasse."</note> is a heavy word, derived from the force of 'to carry' <note>original: "uehere."</note>, in which there is already a certain force of another's will. For one who is 'carried' is not his own master. But 'harassed,' which is derived from it, is without doubt a word of much more vast power and motion. For he who is struck and snatched <margin>To tax / To toss / To shake</margin> and dragged hither and thither is properly said to be 'harassed.' Just as 'to tax' <note>original: "taxare," meaning to touch repeatedly or sharply.</note> is more intense and frequent than 'to touch,' from which it is undoubtedly derived; and 'to toss' <note>original: "iactare"</note> is much more extensive and broad than 'to throw' <note>original: "iaccere"</note>, from which the word is drawn. 'To shake' <note>original: "Quassare"</note> also is heavier and more violent than 'to quiver' <note>original: "quatere" or "to shake lightly."</note>. Therefore, just because it is commonly said that someone we see struggling with smoke or wind or dust is 'harassed,' the true force and nature of the word ought not to perish; it was observed as was fitting by the ancients, who spoke properly and with precision. The words of Marcus Cato are found in the speech he wrote *Concerning the Achaeans*: 'When Hannibal was mangling and harassing the land of Italy.' Cato said Italy was 'harassed' by Hannibal because no kind of calamity or cruelty or savagery could be found which Italy did not endure at that time. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero.</note> says in his fourth book against Verres: 'Which was so despoiled and plundered by that man, not as if by some enemy—who would nevertheless retain some laws of religion and custom in war—but so that it seems to have been harassed by barbarian pirates.'

Regarding the 'unpraised' man, <margin>Unpraised</margin> it seems two things can be answered. One is of this sort: No one is of such afflicted character that he does not occasionally do or say something that can be praised. Whence this very ancient verse is celebrated as a proverb. <note>He refers to a lost proverb about even the worst person having some merit.</note> But indeed, he who in every matter and at all times lacks all praise, he is 'unpraised,' and he is the worst and most foul of all. And just as the privation of all fault makes one 'blameless,' <margin>Blameless</margin> so 'blameless' <note>original: "inculpatus."</note> is a mark of absolute virtue. Therefore, 'unpraised' is the limit of extreme malice. Thus Homer is often accustomed to praise not by naming virtues, but by removing vices. This is his way.

Epicurus also, in a similar way, defined the greatest pleasure as the privation and removal of all pain in these words. <note>Macrobius refers to the Epicurean idea that the absence of pain is the highest physical state.</note>

By the same reasoning, the same Virgil called the Stygian marsh 'unlovable.' <note>original: "inamabilem."</note> For just as he detested the 'unpraised' **by way of privation** <note>original Greek: "κατὰ στέρησιν."</note> of praise, so he detested the 'unlovable' through the **privation** <note>original Greek: "στέρησιν."</note> of love. In another <margin>What 'to praise' signifies</margin> way, 'unpraised' is defended thus: In the ancient language, 'to praise' <note>original: "laudare."</note> signifies 'to name' or 'to call.' Thus in civil legal actions, an authority is said 'to be praised' <note>original: "laudari."</note>, which means to be named. 'Unpraised' is therefore as if 'un-praisable'—that is, never to be named. Just as formerly by common counsel [the text cuts off...]

<summary>Avienus critiques Virgil’s use of words like "uexasse" (harassed) and "illaudatus" (unpraised) as being too mild for violent contexts, but Servius defends them through etymology and ancient legal definitions.</summary>

# BOOK SIX, PAGE 107

->BOOK SIX, PAGE 107<-

It was decreed in Asia that no one should ever, at any time, name the man who had burned the temple of Diana at Ephesus <note>original: "templum Dianae ephesiae inciderat." This refers to Herostratus, who burned the temple in 356 BCE to ensure his name would be remembered; the Ephesians responded with a decree of *damnatio memoriae*.</note>. The third point remains among those which were criticized: that he spoke of a "tunic stiff with gold" <note>original: "tunicam squalentem auro." From Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.314.</note>. This, however, signifies a wealth and density of gold woven in the appearance of scales.

<margin>Stiff/Rough</margin>
For "to be stiff" <note>original: "squalere"</note> is said from the abundance and roughness of scales <note>original: "squamarum"</note> which are seen on the skins of serpents or fish. For this reason, the same poet demonstrates this in several other places. He says: *A skin covered in bronze scales with gold like plumage protected him.* <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 11.770-771.</note> And in another place: *And now indeed, dressed in a reddish breastplate, he bristled with bronze scales.* <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 11.487-488.</note> Accius, in his *Pelopidae*, writes thus: *The scales of that serpent were fringed with stiff gold and purple.* Therefore, whatever was too heavily packed or pressed down by another thing, so as to strike viewers with a shivering awe by its strange appearance, was said "to be stiff" <note>original: "squalere"</note>. Just as on neglected and scaly bodies, a deep accumulation of filth is called "squalor" <note>original: "squalor"</note>.

<margin>Filth</margin>
By the frequent and constant use of this meaning, the whole word has become so tainted that "squalor" has begun to be used for nothing else but filth. Avienus said: "I am pleased to be corrected, for I thought ill of those excellent sayings. But in this verse, something seems to me to be missing: *He himself sat girt with the Quirinal staff and the small robe.* <note>original: "Ipse quirinali lituo paruaque sedebat succinctus trabea." Virgil, *Aeneid* 7.187-188.</note> If we concede that nothing is missing, it remains that he was 'girt with a staff and a robe,' which is most absurd; for the staff is a short rod, curved in its thicker part, which the augurs use.

<margin>The Staff</margin>
I do not see how one can be seen to be 'girt' with a staff." Servius replied that this was said in a way that many things are usually said through an omission <note>original: "per defectionem," a grammatical figure where words are left out.</note>, as when it is said: *M. Cicero, a man of great eloquence,* and *Roscius, an actor of the highest grace.* Neither of these is full or complete, yet they are heard as full and complete. As Virgil says in another place: *Butes of a massive body,* meaning "having a massive body." And likewise elsewhere: *He threw into the middle twin gauntlets of massive weight,* and similarly: *A house bloody with gore and feasts.* So, therefore, this too should be seen as having been said: *He himself with a Quirinal staff,* that is, "holding a Quirinal staff." This would be not at all surprising if it had been said: *Picus was with a Quirinal staff,* just as we say *the statue was with a large head.* Often "is" and "was" and "has been" are absent with elegance, without harm to the meaning. But since mention has been made of the staff <note>original: "lituus"</note>, it must not be overlooked that we have noticed a question could be asked: whether the augural staff is named from the trumpet <note>original: "tuba"</note>, or the trumpet is called a *lituus* from the staff of the augurs. For both are of equal shape and equally curved at the end. But if (as some think) the trumpet was called a *lituus* from its sound, from that verse of Homer, "clear-sounding" <note>original: "λιγεβίος" (ligyps), meaning shrill or clear.</note>, it is necessary that the augural rod be called a *lituus* from its similarity to the trumpet. However, Virgil uses that word for a trumpet, as in: *And with the trumpet he went into famous battles with the spear.* <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.167.</note> Avienus added: "*Hasten your flight* <note>original: "Maturate fugam." Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.137.</note>; what this means is not quite clear to me.

<margin>To Ripen / Hasten with care</margin>
For flight seems to me contrary to 'ripeness' <note>original: "maturitati"</note>; therefore, please teach me what should be thought of this word." And Servius said: "Nigidius <note>Nigidius Figulus, a famous Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero.</note>, a man distinguished in the disciplines of all good arts, says that 'to ripen' <note>original: "maturare"</note> is that which is neither too early nor too late, but something in the middle and tempered. Nigidius spoke well and properly. For both in grain and in fruit, those things are called 'ripe' <note>original: "matura"</note> which are neither unripe nor fallen and overcooked, but temperately grown in their own time. The Divine Augustus used to express this Nigidian interpretation elegantly in two Greek words. For they say he was accustomed to say in conversation and write in letters: *Hasten slowly* <note>original: "σπεῦδε βραδέως" (speude bradeōs).</note>, by which he advised that both the speed of industry and the slowness of diligence should be applied to a task together. From these two contraries comes 'maturity' <note>original: "maturitas"</note>. Thus, Virgil introduces Neptune commanding the departure of the winds: so that they may depart so quickly as if in flight, and yet maintain a moderation of blowing in their retreat, as if departing 'ripely,' that is, temperately. For he fears lest in the departure itself they harm the fleet, while they return with too much rush as if through flight. The same Virgil most skillfully separated 'to ripen' <note>original: "maturare"</note> and 'to hurry' <note>original: "properare"</note> as if they were full opposites in these verses: *If ever a cold rain keeps the farmers indoors, many things which would soon have to be hurried under a clear sky, are granted to be ripened.* <note>Virgil, *Georgics* 1.259-261.</note> He divided these two words well and elegantly. For in the hurrying of rural work through the seasons and...

# PAGE LIII

->SATURNALIORUM<-

...rains: since there is leisure by necessity, work can be done in a timely manner <note>original: "maturari"</note>; but during clear weather, since the time presses, it is necessary to hurry. Indeed, when one must signify something done more forcefully and hastily, it is more correctly called "prematurely done" <note>original: "praemature factum"</note> than "maturely." As Afranius said in his comedy of Roman life <term>togata: a genre of Roman comedy depicting Roman rather than Greek characters and settings</term> titled *The Suitor*: "You seek dominion, seeking it prematurely and prematurely ripe." <note>original: "appetis dominatum: Petens praemature praecocem."</note> In this verse, it should be noted that he says *praecocem* and not *praecoquem*. For the nominative case is not *praecoqs* but *praecox*.

<margin>Premature</margin>

<margin>Prematurely ripe / Early-ripening</margin>

At this point Avienus asks again: Since Virgil rescued his Aeneas—a man pious above all—from the contagion of a horrific sight in the Underworld, and made him hear their groans rather than see the torments themselves, yet freely led him into the fields of the pious, why did he describe that part of the place where the wicked were confined with only this verse: *The vestibule before the entrance and in the very throat of Orcus*? <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.273: "Vestibulum ante ipsum primisque in faucibus Orci."</note> For he who sees the vestibule and the "throats" <note>original: "fauces," referring to a narrow entry passage</note> has, without doubt, already entered the house itself; or if something else is to be understood by the word "vestibule," I desire to know it.

To this Servius replied: There are many words we use commonly, yet we do not clearly notice what they signify according to their true properties; such is "vestibule," a famous and common word in speech, yet its clear meaning is not expectedly understood by all who use it easily. For they think the vestibule is the forward part of the house which they call the "atrium." But Caecilius Gallus, a most learned man, in his second book *On the Significance of Words Pertaining to Civil Law*, says that the vestibule is not in the house itself, nor a part of the house, but a vacant space before the door of the house, through which the entrance and access to the doors of the house are made from the road. For the door itself was made far from the road with an intervening area that was vacant.

<margin>Vestibule</margin>

What the reason for this word might be is often asked; but what I have read in suitable authors I will not be reluctant to bring forward. The particle *ve-*, like certain others, signifies sometimes intensification and sometimes diminution. For *vetus* [old] and *vehemens* [vehement]—the former is composed from the greatness of age, the latter from excessive impulse and force of mind. However, *vecors* [senseless] and *vesanus* [insane] signify the deprivation of health and heart.

<margin>Old<br/>Vehement<br/>Senseless<br/>Insane</margin>

We said above that those who built large houses in ancient times used to leave an empty space before the door, which was between the doors of the house and the road. In that place, those who had come to greet the master of the same house would wait before being admitted; they stood neither in the road nor within the house. Therefore, from that "standing" <note>original: "consistione"</note> in a large place and a kind of "stabling" <note>original: "stabulatione," implying a place to wait like horses in a stall</note>, those spaces were called "vestibules," in which there was much standing by those arriving before they were let into the house. Others agree that vestibules are as we said, but they disagree on the sense of the word. They refer it not to those who arrive, but to those who dwell in the house, because they never stay there, but come to this place only for the sake of passage when going out or returning. Therefore, whether it is understood by increase (according to the first group) or by decrease (according to the second), it is certain that the vestibule is the area that divides the house from the road. The "throats" <note>original: "fauces"</note> are the narrow path through which the vestibule turns from the road.

<margin>Throats / Narrow passages</margin>

Thus, when Aeneas sees the throat and vestibule of the house of the wicked, he is not inside the house, nor is he polluted by contact with the accursed and cruel building, but from the road he sees the places located between the road and the building.

"What were the *bidentes* sacrificial victims?" asked Avienus. I once asked one of the flock of grammarians, and he replied that *bidentes* <note>A term for sacrificial sheep.</note> were sheep, and thus the word "woolly" was added so they might be more clearly demonstrated to be sheep. "Let it be that sheep are called *bidentes*," I said. "But I wish to know the reason for this epithet in sheep." And he, without hesitation, said that sheep are called *bidentes* because they have only two teeth.

<margin>Sacrificial victims</margin>

Then I said, "Where on earth, I ask you, have you ever seen sheep that naturally have only two teeth? For such a thing would be a portent <note>original: "ostentum," an omen or supernatural freak of nature</note> to be averted by rituals." Then he, moved and irritated by me, said, "Seek rather those things which should be asked of a grammarian. For concerning the teeth of sheep, ask the shepherds..."

# BOOK SIX

...pursued: "I laughed at the witticisms of that worthless fellow," and so forth. But I ask you, as one who is intimately familiar with the nature of his words. Then Servius said: regarding the number of teeth he imagined, I should not reprimand him, since you yourself have already laughed. But I must take care that this notion does not creep in: that *bidentes* <note>original: "bidentes," typically referring to sacrificial sheep</note> is merely an epithet for sheep. For Pomponius, that distinguished poet of Atellan farces <term>Atellan farce: a form of early Roman improvisational comedy</term>, wrote this concerning the Transalpine Gauls: *Mars, I vow to sacrifice to you—if ever I return—a two-year-old boar.* <note>original: "Mars tibi uoueo facturum: si unquam rediero: bidente: uerre." Note that Pomponius uses the term for a pig/boar, not a sheep.</note> Furthermore, Publius Nigidius, in the book he composed on entrails, says that they are called *bidentes*—not just sheep, but all two-year-old beasts <note>original: "bimas," meaning two winters old</note>. Yet he did not say why they are so named. But in the commentaries pertaining to pontifical law, I have read that they were first called *bidennes* <note>meaning "two-year-olds"</note>. The letter 'd' was inserted superfluously (as often happens), just as *redire* <note>to return</note> is said instead of *reire*, and *redamare* <note>to love back</note> instead of *reamare*, and *redarguere* <note>to refute</note> for *rearguere*. For the letter 'd' is usually interposed to manage the gap <term>hiatus: the jarring sound of two vowels meeting</term> between two vowels. Therefore, they were first called *bidennes* as if to mean *biennes* <note>two-year-olds</note>; and through long usage of speech the word was corrupted, and from *bidennes* they were called *bidentes*. Hyginus, however, who was not ignorant of pontifical law, wrote in the fifth book of his works on Virgil that sacrificial victims were called *bidentes* because, due to their age, they had two higher teeth, by which it was clear they had transitioned from a younger to a more mature age.

<margin>Horseman and riding</margin>
¶ Avienus asks again regarding these verses: *The Pelethronian Lapiths gave bits and circles to those mounted on their backs, and taught the rider under arms to leap upon the soil and gather proud steps:* <note>Virgil, *Georgics* 3.115-117</note> why did Virgil attribute the duty of the horse to the rider? For leaping on the soil and gathering steps are clearly the actions of the horse, not the rider. Servius replied: this question of yours arises from a careless reading of the ancients. Because our generation has abandoned Ennius and the entire ancient library, we are ignorant of many things that would not be hidden if the reading of the ancients were familiar to us. For all ancient writers used the term "rider" <note>original: "equitem"</note> for both the man sitting on the horse and for the horse when it was carrying the man; and they used "to ride" <note>original: "equitare"</note> not only for the man, but also for the horse. Ennius says in the seventh book of his *Annals*: *At last, with great force, the four-footed rider and the elephants throw themselves forward.* <note>original: "Denique ui magna quadrupes eques; atque elephanti proiiciunt sese."</note> Is there any doubt that he called the horse itself a "rider" <note>equitem</note> here, since he added the epithet "four-footed"? Thus also "to ride" <note>equitare</note>, which is a verb derived from the noun for rider, was said of both the man using the horse and the horse walking under the man. For Lucilius, a man exceptionally knowledgeable in the Latin language, says that a horse both runs and "rides" in this verse: *Indeed, we see this horse run and ride.* <note>original: "Nempe hunc currere equum nos atque equitare uidemus."</note> Therefore, also in the works of Maro <note>Virgil</note>, who was a diligent student of ancient Latinity, it must be understood thus: *and taught the rider under arms.* That is, they taught the horse carrying the man to leap upon the soil and gather proud steps.

¶ Avienus added: *When now the horse stood, woven with maple beams* <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.15-16, referring to the Trojan Horse</note>—he wished to know whether he named this type of wood in the construction of the horse by chance or by design. For although it may be within poetic license to put one type of wood for any wood, Virgil is not usually fond of the recklessness of license, but prefers to choose the force of certain reason in things or names.

<header>The SATURNALIA, Book VII</header>

# THE SATURNALIA OF MACROBIUS AURELIUS THEODOSIUS, A MAN OF CONSULAR AND ILLUSTRIOUS RANK

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut illustration on the left depicts six men in long robes and hats gathered in conversation. Some point towards bushes on the right. Above the illustration is a text label: "THIS REPROVES THE CARES AND EMPTY VOWS OF MEN". To the right of this woodcut is a large ornate decorative initial 'P' featuring a winged putto figure amidst foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>

**P**RECIOUS little time had passed after the first courses of the banquet were cleared away; as the smaller wine cups were being circulated here and there, Prætextatus <note>Vettius Agorius Praetextatus (c. 315–384 AD), a prominent Roman aristocrat and priest</note> remarked: "It is usually said that food makes those who consume it quiet, while drink makes them talkative. Yet we remain silent even amidst our cups, as if a gathering such as this ought to lack serious or even philosophical discussions."

And Symmachus <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, a famous Roman statesman and orator known for his letters</note> replied: "Do you truly feel this way, Vectius? That philosophy should be present at feasts? Or should she, like a stern and overly modest matron of the house, be kept within her inner chambers <margin>Inner Chamber</margin> and not mingle with Bacchus <note>original: "libero," another name for Liber/Bacchus, the god of wine</note>, for whom even domestic outbursts are familiar? Philosophy is of such modesty that she admits no noise—not just of words, but not even of thoughts—into the sanctuary of her quietude. Let her teach us that it is fitting to guard our hidden modesty within our own walls. Or should I think that philosophy ought to be brought out to a place where even the art of rhetoric—a popular profession—blushed to go? 

<margin>Isocrates</margin> For Isocrates, the Greek orator who first forced free-flowing words to follow rhythmic patterns, when he was asked by his companions at a banquet to bring forth something from the fountain of his eloquence, begged to be excused. 'That which the present place and time require,' he said, 'I do not know; that which I know is neither fit for the present place nor time.'" 

To these words, Eustachius <note>A philosopher character in the dialogue, likely representing Neo-Platonic views</note> replied: "I approve of your intention, Symmachus, in that you revere philosophy with such great respect that you believe she should only be worshipped within her inner sanctuary. But if she is exiled from feasts for this reason, then her children <note>original: "alumnae," literally 'foster children' or those she has nurtured</note>—I mean integrity and modesty, and no less piety along with sobriety—must also depart. 

<margin>Inner Chamber</margin> For which of these would I call less venerable? Thus it would happen that, with such a chorus of matrons banished, the freedom of feasts would be surrendered solely to concubines—that is, to vices and crimes. But far be it from philosophy, which treats the duties of the banquet so carefully in her schools, to shrink from the banquets themselves! It is as if she could not demonstrate in practice what she is accustomed to teach in words, or as if she did not know how to keep to a limit—she who established the boundaries for every action in human life. Nor do I invite philosophy to the table in such a way that she does not moderate herself, for her very discipline is to teach moderation in all things. Therefore, to settle the matter between you and Vectius as if by an arbitrator's judgment: I shall indeed open the doors of the dining rooms to philosophy. But I promise she will be present in such a way that she does not exceed the measure of management known to her and her followers." 

Then Furius said: "Since our age has produced you, Eustachius, as the sole follower of philosophy, please tell us the 'mode of management' you grant her while she dines with us." 

And Eustachius replied: "First, I know she will observe this: that she considers the character of the guests present. If she finds several experts, or at least lovers of her wisdom, among the company, her speech regarding..."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the beginning of Book VII of the *Saturnalia*. Following Prætextatus and Symmachus’s initial remarks about whether philosophy belongs at a dinner party, the text now explores how a wise person should adapt their conversation to the company present, using historical and literary examples to illustrate the balance between silence and speech.</meta>

<page-num>CXI</page-num>
<header>BOOK SEVEN</header>

<margin><unclear>Athenaeus, who [compiled] in Book 3...</unclear> <note>Likely a reference to the author Athenaeus and his work *The Deipnosophists* (The Banquet of the Learned), which shares similar themes.</note></margin>
...[it will not easily] be disturbed. Just as a few "mute" letters <note>consonants</note> scattered among many vowels are easily tamed into the fellowship of a single voice, so too do the few unlearned guests, rejoicing in the company of the experts, either harmonize where they can or are captivated by listening to such matters. However, if the majority are strangers to the training of this discipline, the wise—who will be fewer in number—should decree a "masking of themselves" <note>original: "dissimulationem sui"</note>. They should allow the talkativeness more pleasing to the majority to join the group, lest the rare nobility of thought be disturbed by the more tumultuous crowd. This is one of the virtues of philosophy: whereas an orator is proven only by speaking, a philosopher philosophizes no less by keeping silent for a time than by speaking. Therefore, if only a few learned men are present, they will migrate into the consensus of the unrefined company, keeping the notion of truth safe and resting within themselves, so that any suspicion of discord may vanish.

<margin>Pisistratus</margin>
Nor is it a wonder if a learned man does what Pisistratus, the tyrant of Athens, once did. When he failed to gain the assent of his sons after giving them right counsel, and was therefore in a state of feud with his children, he discovered that his rivals were rejoicing over this. They hoped that from that discord a revolution might be born in the house of the ruler. Calling a general assembly of the citizens, he said: "I was indeed angry with my sons for not acquiescing to their father’s will; but it has since seemed more fitting to my paternal devotion that I should concede to my children's opinion." Let the city know, therefore, that the king's offspring are in harmony with their father. By this fiction, he snatched hope away from those plotting against the peace of the ruler. Thus, in every walk of life, and especially in the joy of a banquet, everything that seems out of tune <note>original: "absonum"</note> must be reduced to a single harmony of sound, while preserving innocence.

<margin>Agatho's Banquet</margin>
Such was the banquet of Agatho <note>The setting of Plato’s *Symposium*</note>, because it featured Socrates, Phaedrus, Pausanias, and Eryximachus. Such was that dinner which the most learned Callias gave <note>The setting of Xenophon's *Symposium*</note>—I mean the one with Carneades, Antisthenes, and Hermogenes and others like them; it heard no word that was not philosophical. But on the other hand, the table of Alcinous or Dido <note>References to the *Odyssey* and the *Aeneid*</note>, being suited only for luxuries, had men like Iopas at the latter, or someone like Polyphemus <note>A possible manuscript error or obscure reference; typically Demodocus is the bard at Alcinous's court</note> at the former, singing to the lyre. Nor were there lacking dancing men at Alcinous's, or Bitias at Dido's, drinking the wine so deeply that he drenched himself in its overflowing excess. If someone had mixed deep sermons of wisdom into the dinner-tales among the Phaeacians or the Carthaginians, would he not have lost the grace appropriate to those gatherings and rightly moved them to laughter? Therefore, his first observation will be to evaluate the guests. Then, where he sees a place open to him, he will not speak of the "secrets of his own depth" amid the cups, nor will he raise thorny and anxious questions, but rather useful and easy ones. For just as among those who practice dancing in the middle of a feast, if someone—in order to exercise himself more—challenges his companions to a foot-race or a boxing match, he would be banished from the cheer of the group as someone inept; so too at the table, one must philosophize when the time is right. Thus, the bowl of liquid born for joy should be tempered by a mixture not only of the Nymphs <note>water</note>, but also of the Muses <note>poetry and learning</note>. For (as must be confessed) in every gathering one must either be silent or speak. Let us ask whether silence or timely speech is more fitting for banquets. For if, as the judges of the Areopagus <note>The high court of Athens, known for its solemnity</note> judge in silence, it were always necessary to be silent during a feast, there would be no further question of whether one should philosophize at the table. But if banquets are not to be mute, why is dishonest speech permitted while honest speech is forbidden? Especially since words gladden a feast no less than the sweetness of wine. For if you look deeper into the hidden wisdom of Homer, that "soothing drug" <note>original: "delinimentum"; referring to the drug Nepenthe</note> which Helen mixed into the wine was not a herb, nor a juice from Ida, but the "opportunity for storytelling" <note>original: "narrandi opportunitas"</note>, which turned the guest, forgotten of his sorrow, toward joy. For she told of the famous deeds of Ulysses while his son was present:

> I could not tell or name them all,
> As many as are the labors of the stout-hearted Odysseus,
> But what a deed that strong man did and dared... <note>original Greek: "πάντα μὲν οὐκ ἂν ἐγὼ μυθήσομαι οὐδ' ὀνομήνω / ὅσσοι Ὀδυσσήος ταλασίφρονος εἰσὶν ἄεθλοι / ἀλλ' οἷον τόδ' ἔρεξε καὶ ἔτλη καρτερὸς ἀνὴρ" — Homer, Odyssey 4.240-242</note>

It contrasts the intellectual feasts of Socrates and Agatho with the more hedonistic banquets of the Phaeacians and Carthaginians.</summary>

->Take shame in your hearts, Achaeans, as you drink.<-
<note>original: "Αἰδῶ ἐνὶ φρένεσὶν πάσχετε πώματα Χαιοὶ." A variation of a line from Homer’s *Odyssey* used here to illustrate a moral point during a banquet.</note>

Therefore, by recounting his father’s glory and his specific brave deeds, he made the son’s spirit more eager; and in this way, he was believed to have mixed a remedy against grief into the wine. You may ask, "What does this have to do with philosophy?" On the contrary, nothing is so closely related to wisdom as adapting one's speech to specific places and times, bringing it into the open after evaluating the character of those who are present. For some are stirred by recounted examples of virtues, others by benefits, and some by modesty; so that even those who were acting otherwise might come to self-improvement after hearing such things often. Furthermore, for those entangled in vices—if the order of conversation at the banquet requires it—philosophy will strike them without them even feeling it. Just as <margin>In what way Bacchus strikes</margin>Father Liber <note>Another name for Bacchus, the god of wine.</note> strikes with his thyrsus <note>A staff topped with a pinecone and wrapped in ivy.</note> by the slanting of the surrounding ivy while the point remains hidden, so the philosopher will not act as a public censor at a feast to openly punish vices. Otherwise, those vulnerable to such criticism will fight back, and the banquet will be thrown into such a tumult that they might seem to be under a harsh decree of this sort: "For the rest, men, joyfully tend to your bodies after things have gone well, and expect a battle to be prepared." <note>A quote from Virgil's *Aeneid* (9.157), suggesting that if a host is too harsh, the guests will prepare for a fight rather than a meal.</note> Or as Homer said more briefly and expressively:

<note>The source text omits the specific Homeric line here, but the context implies a call to eat and be merry before a struggle.</note>

Therefore, if an opportunity for a necessary reprimand arises, it should proceed from the philosopher in such a way that it is both upright and effective. Is it any wonder if a wise man strikes those who, as I said, do not feel it, since he sometimes reprimands in such a way that the one being corrected is actually cheered? He will show the power of philosophy—which speaks nothing foolishly—not only in his stories but also in his questioning. Therefore, let no honorable act, place, or gathering exclude philosophy; she adapts herself so that she appears necessary everywhere, as if it were a sin for her to be absent.

And Avienus said: "You seem to be introducing two new disciplines to me: that of questioning and that of reprimanding, so that eagerness is stirred on both sides in those to whom the speech is directed—even though pain usually follows a reprimand, even a just one. Please make these points, which you have only lightly touched upon, clearer by explaining them further."

"First," Eustachius replied, "I want you to hold this: I was not speaking of that kind of reprimand which looks like an accusation, <margin>The *scomma*</margin> but that which is like a taunt. The Greeks call this a <term>scomma</term> <note>A witty, stinging jest or gibe that contains a hidden truth.</note>. It is no less bitter than an accusation if it is brought forth at the wrong time. But from a wise man, it will be delivered in such a way that it does not lack sweetness. And to answer you first regarding questioning: a questioner who wishes to be pleasant asks things that are easy for the person being questioned to answer, and which he knows the person has learned through diligent practice. For everyone rejoices when they are provoked to bring their own learning into the open, because no one wants what they have learned to remain hidden—especially if it is knowledge they sought with great labor, familiar to only a few and unknown to most, such as astronomy, logic, or other similar subjects. For then they seem to reap the fruit of their labor, when they obtain an occasion for making public what they have learned without the mark of showing off—a mark that is absent when one does not force himself on others, but is invited to speak. On the other hand, it is a cause of great bitterness if you question someone in front of many people about something they have not mastered. For they are forced either to deny they know it—which people consider a total loss of face—or to answer rashly, committing themselves to the random outcome of truth or falsehood. From this, the betrayal of ignorance often arises, and the victim blames this entire misfortune of his shame on the questioner.

Furthermore, those who have traveled over seas and lands do not rejoice when they are asked about things unknown to many, such as the layout of lands or the shape of a sea; they answer gladly and describe the places, now with words, now with a drawing-rod, thinking it most glorious to place before the eyes of others what they themselves have seen. What of leaders and soldiers, who are always <margin>The urge to talk</margin> eager to speak <note>original: "dicturiunt," a playful term for a repetitive urge to tell stories.</note> of their own brave deeds and do not keep silent for fear of sounding arrogant? If they are invited to relate these things, do they not think the price of their labor has been paid in full, considering it a reward to tell what they have done to a willing audience? Indeed, this kind of storytelling ha- <note>The text cuts off mid-word "habet" (has/holds), matching the catchword "ha-" from the original.</note>

...possesses a certain flavor of glory: so that if enviers or rivals happen to be present, they might disrupt such questioning by making a noise, or prevent those stories from being told—which usually bring praise to the narrator—by introducing other tales. Furthermore, a man who has escaped past dangers or completely finished his hardships is very pleasantly provoked to recount them. For he who is still detained by them, even a little, shudders at the reminder and fears the report. Therefore, Euripides <note>An Athenian playwright (c. 480–406 BCE) known for his tragedies.</note> expressed this well; for he added the word **"having been saved"** <note>original Greek: σώθεντα (*sothenta*)</note> to show that the pleasure of the telling begins only after the end of the evils. And our poet <note>Referring to Virgil, the Roman epic poet.</note>, by adding the word "one day," says what else but that the memory of settled labor will be pleasing in the future, after misfortunes have been measured out? **"Perhaps one day it will be a joy to remember even these things."** <note>A famous line from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (1.203), spoken by Aeneas to encourage his men.</note> Nor would I deny that there are types of evils that the one who suffered them does not wish to remember even after they are over. Such a person is no less offended when questioned than when he was in the midst of the evils themselves: such as one who has experienced the executioners and the torture of his limbs, or one who has endured unfortunate bereavements, or one who once suffered a shameful mark from the censors. <note>The "censorial mark" (*nota censoria*) was a public disgrace recorded by Roman officials for perceived immorality.</note> Beware of asking about these, lest you seem to be throwing them in his face. Instead, if you can, often provoke him to speak who was favorably received when reciting, or who freely and successfully carried out an embassy, or who was kindly and affably received by the emperor; or if someone escaped alone when nearly the entire fleet was seized by pirates, whether by his wits or his strength. For a long narrative of such things can hardly satisfy the speaker's desire. It is also helpful if you ask someone to speak of the sudden good fortune of his friend, and how much honor has increased for him; things which he did not dare to keep silent or speak of on his own, fearing now a charge of boasting, now of malice. Let him who delights in hunting be questioned about the extent of the forest, the winding of the animal dens, and the outcome of the hunt. If a religious man is present, give him the opportunity to report by what observances he earned the help of the gods, and how much fruit he gained from the ceremonies; because they consider this a kind of religion: not to keep silent about the benefits of the divine powers. Add to this that they wish to be thought of as friends to the gods. If, however, an old man is present, you have an occasion where you may seem to have conferred the greatest favor upon him if you question him even about things that do not pertain to him at all. For talkativeness is a familiar companion to this age. Knowing this, Homer <note>The legendary author of the *Iliad* and *Odyssey*.</note> caused a whole heap of questioners to be presented to Nestor <note>The king of Pylos, famous in Homer's epics for his wisdom and very long, rambling stories about his youth.</note> all at once:

<margin>
Talkativeness is a familiar trait in old men.
</margin>
**H**e gathered so many seeds for speaking by questioning that he might satisfy the "itch" of old age. And Virgil’s Aeneas, showing himself grateful for everything toward Evander <note>An old king in the *Aeneid* who assists Aeneas.</note>, provided him with various occasions for storytelling. For he does not ask about only one or two things, but **"gladly seeks out and hears, one by one, the monuments of the men of old."** And you know how many things Evander, captured by these consultations, recounted.

**W**hen he said these things, the favor of everyone followed. But soon Avienus added: "I would pray that all of you, who are the most learned of the learned here, would encourage Eustachius by your exhortation to reveal what he said a little while ago regarding the **jest** <term>original: *scomma*; a witty, often biting remark or taunt</term>." And with everyone provoking him to this, he wove the following together: "Besides **accusation** <note>original Greek: κατηγορία (*categoria*)</note>, which is a formal speech <note>original Greek: λόγος (*logos*)</note>, and besides **slander** <note>original Greek: Διαβολὴν (*diabolēn*)</note>, which is a malicious reporting, there are two other names among the Greeks: **reproach** <note>original Greek: λοιδωρία (*loedoria*)</note> and **jest** <note>original Greek: σκόμμα (*scomma*)</note>. For these, I find no exact Latin words, unless 
<margin>
Reproach
Jest
</margin>
perhaps you say that **reproach** is a direct insult used as a rebuke. For I might almost call a **jest** a 'figurative bite,' because it is often covered by deception or urbanity, so that it sounds like one thing, but you understand another. However, it does not always lead to bitterness, but sometimes it is even sweet to those at whom it is thrown. This is a type of speech that a wise or otherwise sophisticated person especially practices, particularly between tables and wine cups, where provocation to anger is easy. For just as a light touch pushes someone standing on a precipice, so too when someone is influenced by wine, a small pain—whether silly or harsh—incites them into a fury. Therefore, one must abstain more cautiously at a banquet from the **jest**, which has a hidden injury within itself. For such words stick all the more tightly than direct reproaches, just as barbed hooks are more tenaciously fixed than straight points. Most especially, words of this kind move the laughter of those present, and the injury is confirmed by this type of assent. For a reproach is like this: 'Have you forgotten that you used to sell salted fish...'"

...should you? A witty jibe <note>original: "scomma"</note>, as we have often said, is a hidden insult; it is of this sort. We remember when
<margin>
Insult
Witty jibe
</margin>
you used to wipe your nose with your arm. For although the same thing is said in both cases, the former is an open insult <note>original: "lœdoria"</note> because it is a direct and proven reproach; the latter is a witty jibe, because it is phrased figuratively. Octavius, who appeared to be of noble birth, said to Cicero while he was reciting: "I do not hear what you are saying." Cicero responded, "Surely you used to have well-pierced ears." This was said because Octavius was of Libyan origin, and it is the custom of those people to pierce their ears. Toward the same Cicero, Laberius—when he was not received into the seating area by him, with Cicero saying, "I would receive you if we were not sitting so narrowly"—said with less stinging wit: "And yet you used to sit on two stools," <note>original: "duabus sellis sedere"</note> reproaching so great a man for his slippery loyalty <note>A jab at Cicero’s shifting political allegiances between Caesar and Pompey.</note>. But that which Cicero said—"if we were not sitting so narrowly"—is a witty jibe against Gaius Caesar, who admitted so many people into the Senate indiscriminately that the fourteen rows <note>The reserved seating for the equestrian order in the theater.</note> could not hold them. Therefore, a wise man should abstain above all others from this kind of humor, which is pregnant with insult, during a banquet. There are other witty jibes that are less harsh, like the bites of a toothless beast; such as when Tullius <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> spoke regarding a consul who held the consulship for only a single day. "It is common," he said, "to have priests of Jupiter <note>original: "flamines diales." A pun: "Dialis" refers to Jupiter, but also sounds like the Latin "dies" for day.</note>; now we have consuls of a day." And regarding the same man: "Our consul is most vigilant, for in his entire consulship he saw no sleep." And to the same man, who was complaining that Cicero had not come to visit him: "I was coming," he said, "but night caught up with me." These and similar remarks have more urbanity and less bitterness, as are those regarding certain bodily defects that cause little or no pain: such as if you speak of someone’s baldness or their nose, whether it has a curved bridge or a Socratic depression. For the less these things are misfortunes, the gentler the pain they cause. On the contrary, the loss of
<margin>
Theocritus of Chios
</margin>
eyes is never mentioned without a stir of emotion. Indeed, King Antigonus killed Theocritus of Chios, whom he had sworn he would spare, because of a witty jibe the man said about him. For when Theocritus was being hurried to Antigonus as if to be punished, and his friends were consoling him and offering hope that he would certainly experience the king's mercy once he came before his eyes, he replied: "Then you are telling me that the hope of my safety is impossible." <note>Theocritus was mocking the fact that King Antigonus was one-eyed.</note> Now, Antigonus was deprived of one eye, and this misplaced wit deprived the slanderer of his life. Nor would I deny that philosophers also have sometimes fallen into this kind of jibe through indignation. Lucius Quintus the praetor had recently returned from his province; he had observed a great integrity of the praetorship, which you might wonder at in the time of Domitian. When he, being ill, told a friend sitting by him that he had cold hands, the friend said with a smile: "And yet you brought them back 'hot' from the province just a short while ago." <note>A pun on "hot" hands meaning hands that have stolen or taken bribes.</note> Quintus laughed and was delighted, since he was entirely free from any suspicion of theft. Conversely, if this were said to a man who felt guilty while recollecting his thefts, it would have embittered the listener. When Socrates challenged Critobolus, a youth of famous beauty, to a comparison of their forms, he was joking, not mocking. Certainly, if you say to a man of accomplished wealth, "I will rouse your creditors against you," or to an exceptionally chaste man, "Prostitutes are grateful to you because you have enriched them with constant generosity," they will surely be delighted, knowing that their conscience is not burdened by these words. Just as, on the contrary, there are those things which provoke under the guise of praise, as I distinguished a moment ago. For if I say to a very cowardly man, "You are to be compared to Achilles or Hercules," or to a man of famous injustice, "I place you above Aristides in equity," without a doubt both will take these words, sounding of praise, as a mark of their own reproach. The same witty jibes can in the same way either please or bite, according to the diversity of the persons present. For there are things which, if cast at us in front of friends, we can hear gladly, but in front of a wife or parents or teachers...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 110 regarding social etiquette and humor at a banquet. Having defined the "scomma" or witty jibe as a potential source of offense, the speaker now explains when such humor is acceptable and transitions the conversation toward more intellectual "banquet questions" concerning science and health.</meta>

<page-num>111</page-num>
<header>BOOK SEVEN</header>

...we would not want any witty jibe <note>original: "scomma"</note> to be spoken against those present, unless perhaps it is of such a kind that their own judgment would willingly accept it. For instance, if one were to tease a young man in the presence of his parents or teachers, suggesting he might go mad from his constant vigils and nightly readings; or in the presence of his wife, joking that he acts foolishly by being so devoted to her, choosing no other beauty but hers. For these remarks, even toward those they are directed at, pour a sense of cheer over those present. A jibe is also commended by the condition of the speaker: if he is in the same situation, such as if a poor man mocks another for his poverty, or one of obscure birth mocks another of obscure birth. For Tharshius Amphias, when he had become powerful after being a gardener and had said something to a friend about his low-born status, immediately added: "But we too are from the same seeds," and thus he made everyone equally happy. Direct jibes pour joy into the person they are directed at if you reproach a brave man as if he were wasteful of his own safety and willing to die for others; or if you charge a generous man with squandering his property by looking out for himself less than for others. In this way, Diogenes used to praise his master, Antisthenes the Cynic, as if by reproaching him. He would say: "He himself made me a beggar instead of a wealthy man, and made me live in a tub <note>A reference to the famous barrel or large jar where Diogenes resided.</note> instead of a grand house." He said these things better than if he had said: "I am grateful to him because he made me a philosopher and a man of perfected virtue." Therefore, although there is only one name for a "jibe," it contains different effects. For this reason, among the Spartans—amidst their other strict institutions of life—this kind of exercise was also established by Lycurgus: so that young men might learn to speak jibes without a "bite" <note>original: "sine morsu"</note> and to endure what was said against them by others. And if any of them had fallen into indignation because of such a remark, he was no longer permitted to speak against another. Therefore, since you see, my dear Avienus (for your youth must be guided, which is so teachable that it grasps what must be said), since you see, I say, that the nature of jibes is a double-edged thing, I advise that in banquets—where anger lies in wait for joy—you should abandon such talk and instead either propose or solve "banquet questions." <margin>Playful</margin> This genre was not considered so playful by the ancients that even Aristotle wrote something about them, as did Plutarch and your own Apuleius. Nor should it be despised, as it earned the attention of so many philosophers.

<margin>Feeding</margin> ¶ And Praetextatus said: "Since this kind of questioning also befits an elderly age, why does he advise it only for the youth? Come now, all of you who are present, let us chat about these things suitable for a banquet—not only about feeding, but also whatever pertains to the nature of bodies or other matters, especially since our friend Disarius is present, whose art and learning can contribute much to this kind of inquiry. Let us draw lots (if it seems right) so that each person in order may propose a question they think should be solved." At this, <margin>Prologue</margin> all agreed. They deferred the opening speech to Praetextatus, praying that since he was beginning, a model for questioning would be established for the others from the thread of his consultation.

<margin>Whether simple or multiple food is easier to digest.</margin> ¶ Then he said: "I ask whether simple food or a variety of food is easier to digest, for we see many following the former and some the latter. And there is a certain haughty and stubborn temperance, which, as if showing itself off, wishes to be seen in opposition to pleasant and charming appetite. Since, therefore, one is censorious and the other delicate, I would certainly like to know which is more suitable for maintaining health. And a witness need not be sought from far away, since Disarius is here, who understands what is suitable for human bodies no less than Nature herself, the author and nurse of this fabric. I would like you to say, then, what the reasoning of medicine <note>original: "medicinae ratio"</note> persuades regarding this matter." Disarius replied: "If some common person from the unlearned masses had consulted me on this question—since common minds are captured more by examples than by reason—I would have been content to remind him of the training of cattle. Since their food is simple and uniform, they are much healthier than human bodies; and among them, those who become entangled in diseases are the ones who are stuffed with composite mashes and various seasonings (so that they may become fattened). He would not doubt thereafter, once he noticed that health is familiar to animals using simple food, while those that are fattened grow sick and become weighed down by a composite variety. Perhaps I would have made him more attentive with another example: to consider that no physician was ever so bold in the care of the sick..."

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on social humor and witty jibes (scomma) to a scientific dialogue regarding health and physiology. The speakers are now debating the merits of a simple versus a varied diet, a common topic in ancient symposiac (banquet) literature.</meta>

<page-num>111</page-num>
<header>THE SATURNALIA</header>

...negligence: such as giving a person with a fever a varied and not a simple meal. It is so well established how easy to digest a uniform diet is, that it suffices for a person even when their nature is weak. Nor would a third example be lacking to show that a variety of foods should be avoided, just as a variety of different wines is usually avoided. For who doubts that he who makes use of different wines falls into a sudden drunkenness, even before the sheer quantity of drink demands it? 

But with you, Vectius <note>Vectius Agorius Basilius Albinus, a Roman aristocrat and one of the interlocutors in the dialogue.</note>—who alone has managed to obtain the perfection of all disciplines—the matter must be treated not so much by examples as by reason, which could not remain hidden even if I were silent. Indigestions <note>original: "cruditates," referring to undigested food or "raw" humors in the stomach.</note> occur either by the quality of the juice <note>original: "succi," meaning the chyle or the liquid state of food after the first stage of digestion.</note> into which the food turns, if it is not suited to the humor which the body has obtained, or by the sheer quantity of the food itself, when nature is not sufficient to cook all that has been heaped together. And first, let us look at the quality of the juice.

<margin>Injury</margin>
He who takes simple food easily learns through experience by which juice his body is either helped or burdened. For he does not doubt by the quality of which food he is possessed when he has eaten only one; and thus it happens that an injury <note>original: "noxa"</note> whose cause has been detected is easily avoided. But he who is nourished by manifold food suffers from diverse qualities arising from the diversity of juices. Nor do the humors born from the variety of matter agree with one another, nor do they produce clear or pure blood when they are turned by the service of the liver and pass into the veins with their own inner turmoil. Hence arises the source of diseases: they are born from the discord of humors fighting against one another. Furthermore, because not all things that are eaten have one nature, they are not all cooked at the same time; rather, some are cooked faster and others more slowly, and thus it happens that the order of the subsequent digestions is disturbed.

<margin>The four digestions of food</margin>
For there is not just one digestion of the food we take; rather, so that it may nourish the body, it undergoes four digestions. All people—even those who are dull-witted—perceive one of these; a more hidden reasoning discovers the others. So that this may be clear to all, I must trace the cause back a little further. There are four powers in us which have received the task of administering nourishment.

<margin>Of the jaws. Of the throat.</margin>
One of these is called *dektikē* <note>original: "δεκτικὴ," meaning "receptive."</note>, which draws down the foodstuffs prepared by the jaws. For what would push such thick material through the narrowness of the throat unless a more hidden force of nature swallowed it? Once swallowed, however, they do not descend all the way to the bottom by a continuous fall through a void in the body through successive passages; nor are they expelled exactly as they were received. Rather, they await the beneficial service of digestion.

<margin>The care of digestions</margin>
The second care belongs to the power which is the "retainer," called *katadektikēn* <note>original: "καταδεκτικὴν," likely a variation of *kathektikē*, the "retentive" faculty in Galenic medicine.</note>. The third is called *alloioōtikē* <note>original: "ἀλλοιωτικὴ," meaning "transformative."</note> because it changes the food from one thing into another. All other powers obey this one, because it takes care of the digestions. For the belly has two openings. The upper one is upright and receives what is swallowed, hiding it in the bag of the belly. This is the stomach <note>The ancients often referred to the esophagus or the cardiac orifice of the stomach as the "stomachus."</note>, which has deserved to be called the "head of the household" <note>original: "paterfamilias"</note>, as if it alone governs the whole living creature. For if it becomes sick, life is in jeopardy, as the passage of nourishment falters; nature has granted it a "will" and a "refusal" as if it were capable of reason. The lower opening, however, is sent downwards and inserted into the adjacent intestines, and from there is the way of expulsion.

<margin>Waste</margin>
Therefore, the first digestion takes place in the belly by the transformative power <note>original: "uirtute ἀλλοιωτικὴ"</note> turning whatever has been accepted into juice. The dregs of this are the waste products <note>original: "retrimēta"</note>, which glide through the intestines when the lower orifice hands them over; this expulsion is managed by the office of the fourth power, whose name is *apokritikē* <note>original: "ἀποκριτικὴ," the "secretory" or "expulsive" faculty.</note>.

<margin>What the liver is</margin>
Therefore, after the food is reformed into juice, the care of the liver now follows. For the liver is congealed blood, and therefore it possesses a native heat which turns the prepared juice into blood. And just as turning food into juice is the first digestion, so the passing of juice into blood is the second digestion.

<margin>The Spleen. Why the right parts are stronger, the left less so.</margin>
The heat of the liver arrives to administer this; it disperses the blood into its own individual members through tubes. That part which is the coldest of the digested materials is poured back into the spleen <note>original: "lyenē"</note>; for just as the liver is the home of heat, the spleen is the home of cold. Indeed, for this reason all the right-hand parts of the body are stronger and the left-hand parts are weaker, because heat—which is the receptacle of blood and spirit—rules the former.

<margin>How urine is made</margin>
The third digestion then occurs. For it purifies the received blood in a certain way, and whatever is watery in it, the veins pour back into the bladder; but the clear, pure, and nourishing blood is administered to each individual member of the whole body. And thus it happens that while the belly alone receives the food, its nourishment is dispersed through all the passages of the limbs, nourishing even the bones, the marrow, the nails, and the hair.

<margin>Waste</margin>
And this is the fourth digestion, which happens in the individual limbs, while that which is given to each limb becomes the actual nourishment for that limb. Yet, even in this material that has been purified so many times, waste products are not lacking; when all the limbs are in their proper health...

<summary>This page outlines the ancient medical theory of the four digestions, explaining how food is transformed from "raw" matter into juice, then blood, and finally the substance of the body's limbs and organs. It argues against a varied diet, claiming it causes "discord" among the bodily humors and leads to disease.</summary>

<page-num>112</page-num>
<header>BOOK SEVEN 112</header>

...vanish through hidden passages. If, however, any part of the body should become ill, those waste products which we called "dross" slide into it as if into a weaker vessel. And here are born the causes which it is the custom for doctors to call rheums <note>original: "ῥεύματα" (rheumata), meaning a flow or flux of humors.</note>. For if there should be an abundance of the final juice <note>the final product of digestion before it is assimilated into the body</note> greater than is right, that part of the body which is healthier repels it from itself, and it undoubtedly slides into a weak part which lacks the strength to push it away. Wherefore the reception of this foreign matter distends the place where it falls, and here pains are created. This is therefore the threefold cause either of gout <note>original: "podagra," specifically gout of the foot.</note> or of any disease arising from a confluence: that is, an abundance of humor, the strength of the limb repelling it, and the weakness of the limb receiving it. Since, therefore, we have asserted that four digestions take place in the body, one of which depends on the other—and if the preceding one is impeded, there is no effect in the following one—let us return in our minds to that first digestion which is completed in the belly; it will be found what sort of impediment arises from a multifaceted diet.

<margin>Causes of diseases</margin>
For the nature of different foods is different: there are some that are digested more quickly and others more slowly. Therefore, when the primary digestion turns into juice, because all the things taken in are not converted at the same time, that which was converted first turns sour while the other things are converted more slowly; we often feel this through belching. Other things also for which digestion is slow are like damp wood, which creates smoke when urged by fire; so do those things smoke under the pressing heat of nature while they are cooked more slowly—if indeed this does not escape the sense of the one belching. But simple food does not have a controversial delay, as it is turned into a simple juice. Nor is that digestion disturbed while all parts succeed one another according to the established measurement of moments. But if someone (since nothing is more impatient than ignorance) should disdain to hear these reasons, thinking that digestion is not hindered except by the sheer quantity of food, and does not wish to treat the quality, here too a multifaceted diet is found to be a cause of diseases. For a variety of side-dishes receives various seasonings by which the throat is provoked beyond what is necessary for nature. Thus a heap is formed, while more is desired because of a craving of the appetite, or certainly while small tastes of each are taken. Hence Socrates was accustomed to persuade that those foods or drinks should be avoided which lead the appetite beyond the point of quenching thirst or hunger. Finally, let the variety of eating be repudiated for this very reason: because it is full of pleasure, which must be avoided by the serious and the studious. For what is so contrary as virtue and pleasure? But I shall make an end to this disputation, lest I seem to accuse this very banquet in which we are—although it is sober—nevertheless because it is varied.

When these things had pleased Praetextatus and the others with one accord, Evangelus <note>a frequent "devil's advocate" and cynic in these dialogues</note> exclaimed: "Nothing is so unworthy to be tolerated as how the Greek language holds our ears captive, and we are forced to assent to the roundness of their words, circumvented by the volubility of their speech, because it acts as a tyrant upon the listeners to extort their faith. And because we confess ourselves unequal to these labyrinths of speaking, come, Vectius, let us urge Eustachius that, having taken up the contrary side of the dispute, he might wish to communicate with us whatever can be said in favor of a varied diet, so that this violent tongue may succumb to its own weapons, and a Greek may snatch this applause from a Greek—as if a crow were to dig out the eyes of another crow <note>a proverb meaning one of the same kind attacking another</note>." And Symmachus said: "Evangelus, you have demanded a pleasant thing rather bitterly. For to dare to speak against things so copiously and elegantly devised is a matter that holds a useful pleasure; but we ought not to seek this as if we were laying snares for geniuses or envying glorious treatises. Nor do I deny that I also could have sung a palinode <note>a song or poem retracting a previous statement</note>. For it is a rhetorical exercise to treat commonplaces on either side by an alternation of inventions. But because perhaps it is easier for things reported by other Greeks to respond to the inventions of Greeks, we all pray you, Eustachius, that by repelling the thoughts and inventions of Disarius with their contraries, you might restore in full the discharged charm of banquets." After he had long declined this duty, he finally succumbed to the encouragement of so many urging nobles whom it was not right to oppose.

"I am forced," he said, "to declare war on two of my dearest friends: Disarius and continence. But having obtained pardon from your authority as if from a praetor’s edict, I shall profess myself the patron of the gullet (since it is necessary). First, Disarius began to capture our wits with examples that are more beautiful than true, as I shall show. For he says that beasts use simple food, and therefore are more difficult to overcome by diseases than men because of their health. But I shall prove both to be false. For it is not the case that food is simple for animals..."

<page-num>112</page-num>
<header>OF THE SATURNALIA</header>

...nourishment for mute animals <note>In antiquity, "mute animals" was a standard way to refer to all non-human creatures</note>: nor are diseases any further removed from them than from us. The sheer variety of the meadows they graze upon bears witness to this; in these meadows are herbs both bitter and sweet, some nourishing a hot "juice" <term>succus: the liquid essence of food during digestion</term> and others a cold one. No kitchen could season dishes with such diversity as nature has varied within these herbs. Eupolis is well known, a poet who should be counted among the elegant writers of Old Comedy. In his play entitled *The Goats*, he introduces goats boasting of the abundance of their food in these words: "We graze upon every kind of woodland growth." <note>original Greek: "βοσκόμεθ' ὕλης ἀπαντοδαπῆς"</note> Does that "simplicity" of food seem right to you, where so many bushes and shrubs are enumerated—no less different in their internal juices than they are in name? 

As for the claim that humans are more easily seized by diseases than cattle, I am content with Homer as my witness; he records that the plague began with the cattle, since the disease fell more easily upon the captured herds before it could creep into the men. Furthermore, the brevity of their lives is evidence of how much weakness exists in mute animals. For which of those animals with which we are familiar can equal the years of a human? Unless, perhaps, you go back to those fables told about crows and ravens. Yet we see those birds gaping after every corpse, lying in wait for every kind of seed, and pursuing the fruits of trees. Indeed, they possess no less gluttony than the legends tell of their long lives. 

The second example (if I remember correctly) is that doctors usually offer simple, not varied, food to the sick. But you offer this (in my opinion) not because it is easier to digest, but because it is less appetizing; the desire to eat withers away from the boredom of uniform nourishment, as if nature—weakened by illness—were not sufficient for the task of concocting <term>concocting: the ancient medical term for "cooking" or processing food in the stomach</term> many different things. Therefore, if one of the sick should desire more of even that simple food, you take it away from the one who still wants it. Thus, by your own design, it is the *quantity* rather than the *quality* that is being controlled. 

As for your persuasion that variety should be avoided in eating just as in drinking, this contains the traps of a hidden deception, because it is colored with the appearance of similarity. However, the logic for food is far different. For who was ever wounded in the mind by eating too much? Yet this happens in drinking.

<margin>Why wine intoxicates.</margin>
One who is stuffed with food is heavy in the stomach or belly; but one infused with wine is like a madman. I believe this is because the thickness of food, remaining in one place, waits for the assistance of digestion, and only then, once processed, does it gradually glide into the limbs. But drink, being lighter by nature, soon seeks the heights and strikes the brain, which is located at the top of the head, with a spray of hot vapors. For this reason, varied wines are avoided, lest a substance which rushes to seize the head should wound the seat of judgment with such diverse and sudden heat. But no such similarity or reason persuades us that such a thing is to be feared in a variety of foods. 

As for that discussion in which you arranged the order of digestions in such a brilliant and varied discourse: I do not deny that everything said regarding the nature of the human body was eloquently put, and it does no harm to the question at hand.

<margin>I agree.</margin>
I disagree with only this: your claim that various juices produced from a variety of foods are contrary to our bodies, seeing as our bodies themselves are constructed from contrary qualities. For we consist of the Hot and the Cold, and of the Dry and the Moist. Simple food, however, which possesses only its own juice, emits a quality of only one kind. But we know that "like is nourished by like." Tell me, I pray, from where will the other three qualities of the body be nourished? Empedocles is a witness that individual things draw toward themselves that which is similar to them, when he says: <note>The text here alludes to Empedocles' theory that "like perceives/nourishes like."</note>

Moreover, I often hear you quoting the words of your Hippocrates with admiration: <note>Hippocrates was the legendary "Father of Medicine."</note> "If man were not a single thing, he would never feel pain; for there would be nothing from which he could suffer if he were a unity."

Therefore, if man is not "one thing," he must not be nourished by "one thing." For even God, the Creator of all, did not wish the air which surrounds us and which we draw in by breathing to have a simple quality—such that the spirit is either only cold or only hot—nor did he doom it to continuous dryness or perpetual moisture. This is because a single quality could not nourish us, who are fabricated from a mixture of four. Thus, He made Spring hot and moist. Summer is dry and hot. Autumn is dry and cold. Winter is equally moist and cold. So too the elements, which are our beginning principles, consist of diversities and nourish us. For Fire is hot and dry; Air is moist and hot; Water similarly...

<summary>The speaker refutes the idea that a simple diet is more natural by pointing out that animals eat a variety of plants and that the human body, composed of four distinct "qualities" (Hot, Cold, Dry, Moist), requires a diverse diet to maintain its balance.</summary>
