...moist and cold. Earth is equally cold and dry. Why then do you reduce us to a uniform diet, when nothing in us, nor around us, nor in those things from which we are made is uniform? As for your claim that food turns acidic or sometimes produces fumes in the stomach because of variety—if you want us to believe this, you must demonstrate either that one who eats a variety of foods always suffers these things, or that one who eats simply never suffers them. But if he who enjoys a copious table often feels no such vice, and he who restricts himself to a single food often endures what you accuse, why do you assign this to variety rather than to perpetual greed?
<margin>Harm</margin>
For even from a simple dish, a greedy man suffers the harm of indigestion <term>cruditas: the state of undigested or "raw" food in the stomach</term>; whereas a moderate man enjoys the benefit of digestion even with a varied meal. But you will say: "excess itself is born from the variety of foods, as the palate is tickled and provoked into taking more than is necessary." Again, I return to what I have already said: indigestion comes from the *amount*, not from the *quality*. For he who is master of himself observes a limit. Even at a Sicilian or Asian table <note>Sicilian and Asian (specifically from Asia Minor) banquets were legendary in the Roman world for their extreme luxury and excess</note>, a person lacking restraint exceeds his limit, even if he feeds only on olives or garden herbs. And yet that man with the copious spread, if he maintains moderation, is in possession of health; conversely, he who eats only pure salt becomes "insane" <note>likely meaning "unhealthy" or "physically distressed" here</note> if he attacks that very thing voraciously. Finally, if you think variety in what we consume is harmful, why do you compose those medicinal potions which you pour into human innards through the mouth out of such contrary and mutually repugnant mixtures?
You mix poppy juice <note>original: "succo papaveris," referring to opium</note> with euphorbium, mandrake, and other herbs of "shouted-about" coldness <note>meaning herbs widely known for their cooling properties</note>, tempered with pepper. Nor do you abstain from monstrous flesh, introducing into your cups the testicles of beavers <note>original: "testiculos castrorum." This refers to castoreum, a secretion from beaver scent glands used in ancient medicine</note> and the venomous bodies of vipers, with which you mix whatever India nourishes and whatever herbs are carried from the lands where noble chalk is produced. Since these remedies are made for the protection of life—as food maintains life and medicine restores it—why do you labor to provide variety for the latter, while casting the former into the squalor of uniformity? After all this, you launched into a "buskined" <note>original: "cothurnati sermonis," referring to the high-soled boots worn by tragic actors; meaning a pompous or overly solemn style of speech</note> censure of pleasure, as if pleasure were always the enemy of virtue, and not only when it has collapsed into luxury by scorning the middle path. For what does the slave himself do—eating only when forced by hunger and drinking only for thirst—except to take pleasure from both? Therefore, pleasure is not immediately infamous by its name alone; rather, let the manner of its use be either honorable or reprehensible. It is not enough to accuse pleasure; it should also be praised. For food which is taken with pleasure is drawn by desire into the stomach and hidden away, the stomach snatching it with wide-open expectation; and while it is enjoyed spiritedly, the stomach soon digests it. This does not happen equally with foods that no sweetness of their own commends. Why then do you accuse variety as if it were a mere provocation of gluttony, when it is the health of a man that his appetite be vigorous? For when appetite fails, he languishes and becomes closer to danger. For just as at sea, pilots fly past by reefing their sails into a smaller measure when their wind is too strong—restraining the blast when it is too great—
<margin>Appetite is tickled</margin>
but are unable to rouse a dormant wind; so too, when the "anger" and appetite are tickled and grow, they are tempered by the pilot-rudder of reason. If they should fail once and for all, the animal is extinguished. If, therefore, we live by food, and appetite alone commends that food to us, we must work at the "invention" of variety so that this appetite may always be provoked, provided that reason is at hand to temper it within the boundaries of its own moderation. Remember, however, that I am present at a charming banquet, not an anxious one. I do not admit variety in such a way that I approve of instances where summer snows
<margin>For show.</margin>
and winter roses are sought. When variety serves more for show than for use, every secret of the woods is searched and foreign seas are disturbed. For it happens that even if the observed moderation does not wound the health of those consuming it, the luxury itself is a sickness of character.

**W**hen these words had been favorably received, Disarius said: "Eustathius, you have followed Dialectic; I have followed Medicine. Whoever wishes to choose what to follow should consult experience, and practice will teach what is more useful for health." After this, Flavianus spoke: "I have always heard other physicians saying the same: that wine should be reckoned among hot things. But just now, when Eustathius touched upon the causes of drunkenness, he proclaimed the heat of wine. However, as I have often reflected on this myself, the nature of wine has seemed to me closer to cold than to heat; I bring this into the open, along with the reasons that draw me to this estimate, so that it may be your place to judge my opinion."
<margin>Wine is naturally cold.</margin>
"Wine, as far as my opinion goes, is naturally cold; yet it is capable of, or even craving for, heat when it is moved toward hot things. For iron, too, though it is cold to the touch, while..."

He eventually poses a question to the physician Disarius based on the works of Aristotle.</meta>

...they wash "cold copper" <note>original: "ψυχρὸν χαλκὸν ὅλουσι" — a Greek poetic fragment or proverb referring to the naturally cold state of metal</note>: yet if it endures the sun, it grows hot, and the external heat expels its native cold. Let us investigate whether reason persuades us that this is so with wine. Wine is applied to the internal parts either as a compress or as a drink. When poured upon the skin, it is used to treat the surface. Even doctors do not deny that it is cold; yet they proclaim it to be hot in the internal organs, even though it does not descend in such a state, but rather grows warm when mixed with hot things.

Indeed, I wish for them to answer: why do they offer wine to a sick person whose stomach is failing through exhaustion, in order to restore its strength through constriction <term>constrictione: the "tightening" or "binding" effect associated with cold substances in ancient medicine</term>? Unless, by its own coldness, it compels the exhausted stomach to pull together and collects what has been dissipated. And when they apply heat to an exhausted stomach (as I said) so that the exhaustion does not increase further, they do not prohibit the drinking of wine, changing the failure into strength through this cure.

I will provide another piece of evidence that wine's nature is not one of immense heat. For if someone unknowingly drinks aconite <note>Aconitum: monkshood, a highly toxic plant known in antiquity as a "cold" poison that killed by chilling the heart</note>, I do not deny that he is usually cured by a large draught of undiluted wine. For when poured into the internal organs, the wine draws heat to itself, and as if it were already hot, it fights back against the cold poison. However, if the aconite itself is given as a drink ground up with wine, no treatment can save the drinker from death. In that case, the wine, being cold by nature, increases the coldness of the poison by its mixture. It no longer grows warm in the internal parts because it is not free, but mixed; or rather, having been turned into something else, it descends into the organs.

Furthermore, wine is given to those exhausted by excessive sweating or a loose belly, so that in both ailments it might constrict the passages. Doctors smear the sleepless with cold things: sometimes with poppy juice, sometimes with mandrake or similar things, among which is wine. For sleep is usually induced by wine, which is nothing other than evidence of great coldness. Furthermore, all hot things provoke sexual desire, excite the seed, and favor procreation. Yet after drinking much undiluted wine, men become more sluggish for intercourse. They say it is not even suitable for conception because an excess of wine, being cold, makes the seed thin or weak.

Indeed, this provides the most manifest proof of my estimation: whatever happens to those who are excessively chilled happens also to the drunk. For they become trembling, pale, and heavy, with a spirit that leaps tumultuously. Their joints and limbs shake. There is the same numbness of the body in both; the same stumbling of the tongue. Indeed, for many, that disease which the Greeks call <term>paralysis <note>original: "παραλυσιν"</note></term> occurs from too much wine just as it does from much cold. Consider also what kinds of cures are provided for the drunk. Are they not ordered to lie under many blankets so that their extinguished heat may be revived? Are they not led to warm baths? Is the heat of the body not excited in them at the time of their anointing? Finally, those who are frequently drunk age quickly. Some are marked by baldness or gray hair before the proper time of their life; these things only happen from a lack of heat. What is colder than vinegar, which is simply wine gone bad? This alone, out of all liquids, violently extinguishes a growing flame, since through its cold it overcomes the heat of the element. I shall not pass over this either: those fruits of trees are colder whose juice imitates the flavor of wine, such as apples—whether simple, pomegranates, or quinces—which Cato calls <term>cotonea</term>.

I have said these things because the topic has often moved and exercised me when I was debating it; I wanted to bring into the open what I have come to think about wine. However, I do not omit the consultation due to me. I address you, Disarius: I want you to resolve what has occurred to me to ask. I remember reading in a Greek philosopher (if I am not mistaken, it was Aristotle) in the book he composed *On Drunkenness*: that women rarely fall into drunkenness, but old men do frequently. He did not add the cause of either this frequency or that rarity. And because this entire question pertains to the nature of bodies—the knowledge of which is the duty of your industry and profession—I want you to reveal the causes of this matter, which he stated as an opinion, if indeed you agree with the philosopher.

<margin>
Why women are more rarely and old men more frequently intoxicated.
</margin>

¶ Then he <note>Disarius the physician</note> said: Aristotle is right in this as in other things, and I cannot but agree with a man with whose discoveries nature itself does not disagree. Women, he says, rarely get drunk, but old men do frequently. This twofold opinion is full of reason, and one part depends on the other. For when we have learned what defends women from drunkenness, we already hold what frequently impels old men toward it. For a woman's body and an old man's body have been allotted contrary natures. A woman has a body that is extremely moist. This is shown by the smoothness and brightness of her skin; it is shown by the specific, regular purgations...

The physician Disarius is concluding his explanation of why women are less susceptible to drunkenness, after which the characters Symmachus and Horus debate the "natural temperature" of the female body—a central topic in ancient biology.</meta>

...evacuations that unburden the body of excess fluid. Therefore, when consumed wine falls into such a large amount of moisture, it loses its strength and becomes diluted; it does not easily strike the seat of the brain because its intensity is extinguished. But this reasoning also supports the truth of the opinion: that the female body, being assigned to frequent purgings <term>purgationibus: a reference to the menstrual cycle, viewed in ancient medicine as a necessary "cleansing" of the body</term>, is pierced with many pores. This allows it to lie open to channels and provides paths for the moisture flowing toward its exit in evacuation. Through these pores, the vapor of the wine quickly vanishes.

In contrast, the body of old men is dry, which is proven by the roughness and scaly nature of their skin. This is also why this age is less prone to weeping—which is itself a sign of dryness. In them, the wine meets no resistance from opposing moisture; it clings to the parched body with its full strength and soon occupies the places that provide a man with his senses. There is no doubt that the bodies of the elderly are hard; thus, the natural channels in these tougher limbs are blocked, and once wine is swallowed, no exhalation occurs. Instead, everything ascends to the very seat of the mind. This is why even sober old men suffer from the same afflictions as drunkards: trembling limbs, stuttering tongues, excessive talking, and outbursts of anger—conditions to which young men are subject when drunk, and old men when sober. Therefore, if they experience even a slight impact from wine, they do not merely "catch" these ills; rather, they stir up those traits that have already taken hold of them by reason of their age. 

When Disarius's discussion had been approved by everyone, Symmachus added: "While the entire reasoning Disarius found regarding the rarity of female drunkenness is well-regarded, one point was overlooked by him: because of the excessive coldness in their bodies, the swallowed wine grows cold and is so weakened that its power, having grown faint, cannot stir up the heat from which drunkenness is born."

<margin>That the nature of women is hotter than that of men. Why hair exists on the man and not on the woman.</margin>

To this Horus replied: "Truly, Symmachus, you are mistaken in thinking the nature of women is cold; I will easily prove it is hotter than a man's (if you are willing). The natural moisture in the body, as one passes the age of childhood, becomes harder and sharpens into hair. This is why the pubes, the cheeks, and other parts of the body are then covered. But in the female body, because heat dries up this moisture, there is a lack of hair; and therefore the body of this sex remains continuously smooth and soft. There is also this evidence of heat in them: the abundance of blood, the nature of which is fervor. Lest it burn the body if it lingers, it is removed by frequent purging. Who, then, would call them cold? Who can deny they are full of heat, since they are full of blood? 

Furthermore, although the custom of burning the bodies of the deceased is no longer used in our age, literature teaches that in the time when the honor of fire was given to the dead, if it happened that several bodies were to be burned together, the funeral attendants were accustomed to add one female body for every ten male bodies. With the help of that one—as if she were by nature flame-like and thus quickly ignited—the others would catch fire. Thus, the heat of women was not unknown to the ancients. Nor will I keep silent on this: since heat is always the cause of generation, females are ready for procreation earlier than boys because they are hotter. Indeed, according to public law, the twelfth year in a female and the fourteenth in a boy defines the age of puberty. What more? Do we not see women, when the cold is extreme, content with a modest garment, not wrapped in many coverings as men usually are? Evidently, their natural heat resists the cold that the air brings against them."

->Response to the preceding points.<-

<margin>Why eunuchs lack hair.</margin>

To this, Symmachus said with a smile: "Our Horus tries well to appear as an orator instead of a Cynic <note>Horus is a Cynic philosopher, known for bluntness; Symmachus teases him for using clever rhetorical arguments</note>, for he turns the very senses by which the coldness of the female body can be proven into their opposites. For the fact that hair does not occupy them as it does men is due to a lack of heat. For it is heat that creates hair. This is why eunuchs lack it; no one would deny their nature is colder than men's. Also, in the human body, those parts are most covered which have more heat within. But the body of women is smooth, as if condensed by natural coldness. For density accompanies chill, and smoothness accompanies density. As for the fact that they are frequently purged, this is a sign not of much moisture, but of defective moisture <note>original: "uitioſi humoris" — referring to "corrupt" or "unhealthy" fluids</note>. For that which is expelled is undigested and raw; and because it is weak, it flows out and has no place to stay, but nature drives it out as if it were harmful and more cold. This is especially proven because women, when they are being purged, also happen to feel a chill. From this, it is understood that what flows out is cold, and therefore it does not remain in the living body, as if extinguished by a lack of heat..."

That a woman’s body might provide pleasure to "burning" men is not an argument for her own heat, but rather for her fatty flesh, which is similar to oil <note>The speaker suggests that fat acts as a fuel for male heat rather than being a source of heat itself</note>. This would not happen to them if it were from heat alone. Furthermore, the fact that they reach the age of generation <note>sexual maturity</note> quickly is not a sign of great heat, but of a weaker nature; just as small, thin apples ripen more quickly, while robust ones ripen later. But if you wish to understand the true nature of heat in generation, consider that men persevere much longer in the ability to generate than women do in the ability to bear children. This is an indubitable proof of the cold or heat in either sex: for the same force is extinguished more quickly in a colder body, while it persists longer in a warmer one. As for men enduring the cold of the air more easily, it is their own cold that allows this, for "like rejoices in like." Conversely, the reason a woman’s body does not shudder at the cold is due to a habit of nature, as they are significantly colder. But let each judge these matters as they wish. 

I, however, come now to consult a great authority; and regarding what I consider worth knowing, I ask the same Disarius—a man who is a very dear friend to me and most learned in these and other matters. Recently I was at my villa in Tusculum <note>Tusculano: a popular resort area for the Roman elite, where Cicero also had a famous estate</note>, while the vintage fruits were being gathered for the annual festival. It was possible to see the rustic slaves permitted to drink deep of the must <term>mustum: freshly pressed grape juice that has not yet fermented into wine</term>, whether squeezed out by press or flowing freely; yet they were not seized by drunkenness. I wondered at this especially in those whom I knew were driven to madness by even a little wine. I ask: what is the reason that must either causes drunkenness very slowly, or not at all?

---

**A**s for this, Disarius replied: Everything that is sweet satisfies quickly, and does not hold a long-lasting grip on one's desire. Instead, a sense of "horror" <note>in this context, a physical aversion or "cloying" sensation</note> succeeds satiety. In must there is only sweetness (*dulcedo*), but no "pleasantness" (*suauitas*); for wine is sweet in its infancy, but when it matures, it is more pleasant than sweet. That there is a distance between these two things, Homer is certainly a witness, for he says:

<margin>Why must does not intoxicate.</margin>

> "He calls honey sweet (*dulce*), and wine pleasant (*suaue*)." <note>original: "Vocat. n. mel dulce: & uinũ suaue."</note> Therefore, since must is not yet pleasant but only sweet, the body's natural aversion does not allow enough of it to be consumed to cause drunkenness.

I add another natural reason: sweetness is inherently resistant to drunkenness. Indeed, physicians force those who are distended to a dangerous degree to vomit using a great deal of wine; and after the vomiting, to counter the wine-fumes remaining in the veins, they offer bread smeared with honey. Thus, sweetness defends the man from the evil of drunkenness. Therefore, must does not intoxicate because it contains only sweetness. But it is also defended by this suitable reason: must is heavy, and by its weight and the mixture of gas and water, it quickly slides down into the intestines and passes through; it does not remain in the places vulnerable to drunkenness. Once it has descended, it undoubtedly leaves behind in the man both qualities of its nature: one which is in the gas, and the other in the substance of the water.

<margin>Must naturally contains water within it.</margin>

But the gas, being roughly as heavy, sinks to the bottom; the quality of the water, however, not only fails to drive one to madness itself, but if any vinous strength remains in the man, the water dilutes and extinguishes it. That water is present in must is shown by this: when it ages, the volume decreases, but it becomes sharper in strength; this is because the water which softened it has exhaled, and the pure nature of the wine remains free with its own strength, no longer softened by the presence of diluted moisture.

The word *isitium* comes from *infections* <note>Albinus is offering a folk etymology, suggesting the word comes from "inserting" or "infecting" the meat with seasonings</note>; through the loss of a letter, it obtained the name it has now. And Disarius replied: That is precisely why this kind of food is difficult to digest—the very reason you think digestion was provided for in advance. For the lightness which the pounding provides causes it to float upon the liquid food it finds in the middle of the stomach; it does not adhere to the lining of the stomach, by whose heat digestion is promoted. Similarly, meat that has been ground and shaped will float when cast into water. From this, it is understood that it does the same in the moisture of the stomach, withdrawing itself from the necessity of digestion. It is "cooked" there as slowly as things are finished when dissolved by the vapor of water rather than by fire. Furthermore, while it is being vigorously pounded, much air is folded into it, which first in the sto...

<margin>Tougher meats are sometimes more easily digested than tender ones.</margin>
"I also have this to ask," Furius said. "What is the reason that some people digest tougher meats more easily than tender ones? For while they quickly 'cook' <note>original: *coquant*; here meaning to digest through internal heat</note> chunks of beef, they struggle to digest tough fish." To this, Disarius replied: "The cause of this is an excessive force of heat within the person. If this heat encounters a suitable material, it engages it freely and consumes it quickly in the struggle. However, it either passes over light material as if it were hidden, or turns it into ash rather than into <term>juice <note>original: *succum*; refers to chyme, the fluid result of digestion</note></term>. It is just as great oaks are turned into glowing pieces of charcoal by fire; yet if straw falls into a fire, soon only its ash remains to be seen. You have another similar example: a more powerful millstone crushes larger grains, but lets those that are smaller pass through whole. Likewise, a fir or an oak is torn up by a mighty wind, but no gale easily breaks a reed."

<margin>Why mustard and pepper, when applied to the skin, cause a wound, but do not hurt when swallowed.</margin>
¶ When Furius, delighted by these explanations, wished to ask more out of curiosity, Cecinna Albinus intervened. "I too desire to have a little business with Disarius’s eloquent learning. Tell me, I pray you," he said, "what is the cause that mustard and pepper, if applied to the skin, cause a wound and pierce the area; yet if swallowed, they inflict no injury upon the body of the stomach?" Disarius answered: "These substances are both sharp and hot, and they blister the surface they are applied to because they use their power in its entirety, without the admixture of any other thing, to do harm. But if they are received into the stomach, their force is dissolved by the washing of the gastric fluids, making them more dilute. Furthermore, they are turned into juice by the heat of the stomach before they can do harm in their whole state."

<margin>Cold wines in Egypt.</margin>
<margin>Why water in wells smokes in winter and grows cold in summer.</margin>
¶ Cecinna added: "While we are speaking of heat, I am reminded of something I have always thought worth asking: Why in Egypt, which is the hottest of all regions, is the wine produced not of a hot nature, but of a—I might almost say—cold quality?" To this, Disarius replied: "It is known to you by sight, Albinus, that waters drawn either from deep wells or from springs smoke in winter and grow cold in summer. This happens for no other reason than that the air surrounding us is hot due to the season, and so the cold is plunged down into the depths of the earth and affects the waters whose source is at the bottom. Conversely, when the air presents winter, the heat, plunging into the interior, gives vapor to the waters rising from the bottom. Therefore, what alternates everywhere else by the variety of the seasons is always the case in Egypt, where the air is always in a state of heat. For the cold, seeking the depths, wraps itself around the roots of the vines and imparts such a quality to the juice rising from them. Thus, the wines of a hot region lack heat."

<margin>Why hot water becomes hotter when moved.</margin>
<margin>Why air moved by a fan in summer acquires cold.</margin>
¶ "Our discussion," said Albinus, "having once entered upon the subject of heat, does not easily depart elsewhere. I wish you would tell me, therefore, why someone who enters hot water is burned less if they remain still, but if they move the water by their own agitation, they feel a greater heat—and the water burns more every time a new motion is added to it?" Disarius said: "The hot water that clings to our body soon offers a gentler touch, either because the skin has grown accustomed to it or because it has received cold from us. But motion applies 'new' water to the body, and since the habituation I just mentioned ceases, the novelty always increases the sensation of heat." "Why then," Albinus asked, "in summer, when hot air is moved by a <term>fan <note>original: *flabro*; a fan or bellows</note></term>, does it not acquire heat but cold? For the same reasoning ought to increase the fervor through motion in this case as well." "The reason is not the same," said Disarius, "for the heat of water and the heat of air. For water is of a more solid body and is a thick material which, when moved, attacks the surface it is applied to with its full force. Air, by motion, is dissolved into wind, and having been made more fluid by agitation, it becomes a breeze. Furthermore, as a breeze, it removes that which was surrounding us—and what was around us was heat. Therefore, when the heat is removed by the breeze, it follows that the agitation provides an incoming sensation of cold."

# SATURNALIA

<margin>Why those who spin in a circle suffer from dizziness.</margin>
...do they experience a darkening of the eyes? Finally, if they persist, they fall down, even though no other bodily motion imposes such a necessity. To this, Disarius replied: "There are seven bodily motions," he said. "One moves forward, another backward; one turns to the right or to the left; one moves upward, another downward; and the last rotates in a circle. Of these seven motions, only one is found in divine bodies: I speak of the spherical motion, by which the heavens, the stars, and the other <term>elements <note>In ancient cosmology, the stars and planets were thought to be composed of a 'fifth element' or aether, moving in perfect circles.</note></term> are moved. For earthly animals, those other six motions are primarily familiar, though the seventh is occasionally employed. But while those six are direct and harmless, the seventh—which produces rotations—disturbs the internal balance through repeated turning. It entangles the <term>breath <note>original: *spiramentum*; here referring to the 'pneuma' or vital spirit believed to carry sensory information</note></term> in the fluids of the head, which serves the brain as it governs all the senses of the body like a pilot. This breath, which surrounds the brain, provides each sense with its power and grants strength to the nerves and muscles of the body. Therefore, when it is disturbed by dizziness and oppressed by agitated fluids, it grows faint and abandons its service. From this, those who are caught in rotations experience duller hearing and obscured vision. Finally, because the nerves and muscles receive no strength from it—as if the source were failing—the entire body, which is supported by them and held upright in strength, is deserted by its supports and collapses into ruin. However, habit—which experience has declared to be a 'second nature'—assists those who are often engaged in such motion. For the 'breath' of the brain, which we mentioned just before, becomes accustomed to a thing that is no longer new; it does not fear the motion nor abandon its duties. Thus, for those who are used to it, this agitation is harmless."

Evangelus <note>Evangelus is portrayed in this dialogue as a cynical and confrontational guest, often challenging the experts.</note> then said: "I have you trapped now, Disarius, and if I am right, you shall not escape today. For I have often heard your colleagues in the medical art—and you yourself—saying that the brain has no sensation; that like the bones, the teeth, and the hair, the brain is without feeling. Is it true that you usually say this? Or will you refute it as a falsehood, Disarius?" 

"It is true," Disarius replied. 

Evangelus continued: "Look, you are cornered. Even if I grant you that there is anything in a human being without sensation besides the hair—which is not easily proven—why did you say just a moment ago that all the senses are served by the brain, when you yourself admit that the brain possesses no sensation? Can the audacity of this contradiction be excused? Or is it merely the well-known glibness of your tongue?"

<margin>How the brain, which lacks sensation, provides sensation to the whole body. The membrane <note>original: *omentum*</note>.</margin>
And Disarius, smiling, said: "The nets in which you hold me trapped, Evangelus, are too loose and too wide. See, you shall watch me escape from them without any effort. It is a work of nature that things that are either too dry or too moist do not receive sensation. Bones, teeth, nails, and hair are so thickened by excessive dryness that they are not penetrable by the effect of the soul, which provides sensation. Fat, marrow, and the brain are so full of moisture and softness that this same effect of the soul—which dryness cannot receive—cannot be held by such softness. Therefore, sensation could not exist in the teeth, nails, bones, and hair, nor in the fat, marrow, and brain. And just as the cutting of hair causes no pain, so too if a tooth, a bone, fat, the brain, or marrow were cut, all sensation of pain would be absent. 

'But,' you will say, 'we see people tormented when bones are cut, and men are racked with the pain of teeth.' Who would deny this is true? But when a bone is cut, it is the <term>membrane <note>original: *omentum*; here used broadly to refer to the periosteum or other protective linings</note></term> placed upon the bone that brings the torture as it suffers the incision. Once the doctor’s hand passes through that, the bone itself and the marrow it contains have an insensitivity to cutting similar to that of hair. And when there is a toothache, it is not the bone of the tooth that is in pain, but the flesh that contains the tooth. For even the nail, as far as it grows out beyond the flesh, is cut without sensation; but that which adheres to the flesh causes pain if cut—not by its own body, but by the body of its seat. Likewise, while hair is cut at the top, it knows no pain; but if it is pulled out, it receives sensation from the flesh it is leaving. And the brain, which either racks a man or frequently kills him when touched, brings this pain not by its own sensation, but by its 'clothing'—that is, the membrane. Therefore, I have explained which things in a human are without sensation and why this is so. The remaining part of my debt is to explain why the brain, though it has no sensation, governs the senses. But I will attempt to be 'solvent' regarding this as well, if I can. The senses of which we speak are five: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. These are in the body..."

...or around the body: these motions are familiar only to perishable bodies. For no sensation exists in a divine body. The soul, however, is distinct from every body: even if a body be divine, the soul is yet more divine. Therefore, if the dignity of divine bodies disdains sensation as something suited only to the perishable, the soul is of even greater majesty, such that it has no need of sense for itself. 

However, so that a human being may exist and be a living animal, the soul provides the power that illuminates the body. Furthermore, it illuminates the body by inhabiting it, and its habitation is in the brain. Since its nature is spherical and it comes to us from on high, it occupies that part of the human being which is also spherical <note>The human head was often compared to the spherical shape of the heavens in ancient philosophy.</note>; yet the soul itself lacks sensation, which is not necessary for its own existence. But because sensation is necessary for the living animal, the soul places a **breath** <note>original: *spiramentum*; refers to the 'pneuma' or vital spirit believed to be the medium of thought and sensation.</note> within the cavities of the brain to carry out its effects. 

The nature of this breath is such that it both introduces and governs the senses. From these cavities—which our ancestors called the "ventricles" of the brain—are born the seven **pairs** <note>original: *syzygiai* (συζυγίαι)</note> of nerves; you may call this by whatever Latin name you wish, but we call them a **coupling** <note>original: *syzygiam*</note> of nerves when two nerves emerge together and end at a specific location. These seven pairs of nerves, rising from the ventricle of the brain, fulfill the role of pipes, leading the sense-giving breath to their respective locations by natural law, so that they may pour sensation into the nearby and distant members of the animal. 

The **first** of these nerves seeks the eyes and gives them recognition, sight, and the discernment of colors. The **second** spreads into the ears, through which the knowledge of sounds is born in them. The **third** is inserted into the nostrils, providing the power of smelling. The **fourth** occupies the palate, through which tastes are judged. The **fifth**, by its power, fills the entire body; for every part of the body discerns the soft and the rough, the cold and the hot. The **sixth**, traveling from the brain, seeks the stomach, for which sensation is most necessary, so that it may crave what is lacking, reject what is superfluous, and, in a sober person, moderate itself. The **seventh** **pair** <note>original: *syzygia* (συζυγία)</note> of nerves pours sensation into the spinal cord, which is to the animal what the keel is to a ship. It is so primary in its use and dignity that it has been called the "long brain" by physicians. 

Finally, from this spinal cord, just as from the brain, various channels are born, serving the power of the soul for three purposes. For there are three things that the body of an animal receives from the soul’s providence: that it may live; that it may live fittingly; and that its immortality may be sought through succession. For these three purposes, as I have said, the work of the soul is provided through the spinal cord. For the strength of the heart and liver and the service of breathing—all of which pertain to living—are supplied from the spinal channels we mentioned. So too, the power for the nerves of the hands, feet, and other parts through which one lives fittingly is provided from there. And so that succession may be cared for, nerves are supplied from that same spinal cord to the private parts and the womb, so they may fulfill their work. Thus, no part of the body in a human being exists without the breath located in the ventricle of the brain and without the benefit of the spinal cord. In this way, it happens that while the brain itself lacks sensation, sensation nevertheless proceeds from the brain into the entire body.

"Well done!" said our friend Evangelus, our **little Greek** <note>original: *Gracculus*; a slightly condescending term for a Greek-speaker, here used playfully.</note>. "He has shown us the hidden things of nature so clearly that we seem to see with our eyes whatever he has described in speech. But I now yield to Eustachius, whose turn to ask a question I have snatched away. Let Eustachius now—or Eusebius, the most eloquent of men—or whoever else wishes, step forward for the exercise of inquiry. We shall meet again later with more leisurely freedom."

<margin>Why gray hair appears first on the front of the head. Why baldness appears on the front of the head.</margin>

Then Eusebius said: "Disarius, I must have a discussion with you about age, at whose door we are both now almost knocking. Homer calls men **gray-templed** <note>original: *poliokrotaphous* (πολιοκροτάφουσ)</note>. I ask whether he means to signify the whole head by a part, in the manner of a poet, or if by some reason he assigns gray hair specifically to this part of the head?" 

Disarius replied: "In this, that divine poet was as wise as in all other things. For the front part of the head is moister than the back, and therefore gray hair is frequently accustomed to begin there." 

"And if the front part," Eusebius said, "is moister, why does it suffer from baldness, which does not happen except by dryness?" 

"That is a timely objection," said Disarius, "but the reason is not obscure. Nature made the front parts of the head more porous, so that whatever superfluous or smoky vapors were around the brain might vanish through many channels. This is why we see on the dry skulls of the dead certain **sutures** <note>original: *futuras*; likely an OCR error for *suturas*, the fibrous joints between the bones of the cranium.</note> by which the hemispheres, as...

<margin>
Those with curly hair turn gray slowly.
</margin>

However, baldness arises from that dryness which occurs through a bad "mixture"—which the Greeks are accustomed to calling *krasis* <note>original: κρᾶσίν (*krasin*); this refers to the specific balance or "temperament" of the four humors in an individual.</note>. Hence, those with curly hair—who are so tempered that they have drier heads—turn gray slowly but quickly pass into baldness. On the other hand, those with thinner hair are not so easily stripped of it, as the moisture which is called phlegm <note>original: φλέγμα (*phlegma*); one of the four bodily humors, characterized as cold and moist.</note> nourishes it; but they experience early graying. 

<margin>
Why gray hairs are white.
</margin>

For gray hairs are white because they imitate the color of the moisture by which they are nourished. If, then, an abundance of moisture in the elderly dyes the hair gray, why has old age earned a reputation for extreme dryness? He said: Because in old age, once the natural heat has been extinguished by the passage of time, the body becomes cold; and from that cold, chilly and superfluous humors are born. Otherwise, the vital liquid has been dried up by long life. Thus, old age is "dry" in the sense that this later stage of life is made heavier by wakefulness—whereas sleep, which occurs mostly from moisture, is born from a non-natural humor. Just as there is much moisture in infancy, which is humid due to an abundance of natural (not superfluous) moisture. The same reasoning explains why childhood does not allow for graying, even though it is very moist; it is because it is not humid from phlegm born of cold, but is nourished by that natural and vital moisture. For that humor which is either born from the coldness of age or contracted by the occasion of some defect is as harmful as it is superfluous. We see this in women, where if it is not frequently discharged, it threatens the extremities. We see this in eunuchs, bringing weakness to their legs; their bones, as if always swimming in superfluous moisture, have lacked natural strength, and therefore they are easily twisted when they cannot bear the weight of the body placed upon them—just as a reed is bent by a weight placed upon it.

And Eusebius said: "Since the discussion of superfluous moisture has dragged us from old age all the way to eunuchs, I wish for you to tell me: why is their voice so sharp that, unless you see them, you might not know whether a woman or a eunuch is speaking?" 

<margin>
Why the voice in women and eunuchs is thinner.
</margin>

He replied that the abundance of superfluous moisture causes this as well. For it makes the windpipe <note>original: ἀρτηρίαν (*arterian*); in ancient anatomy, this specifically referred to the "rough artery" or trachea.</note> through which the sound of the voice rises thicker, narrowing the passage of the voice; and therefore the voice is sharp for both women and eunuchs, but deep for men, for whom the transition of the voice has a free and entirely open passage. Moreover, it is clear that in both eunuchs and women, nearly the same abundance of troublesome moisture is born from an equal coldness, because the bodies of both often grow fat. Certainly, the breasts of both grow large in a nearly similar way.

After these things were said, when the order of the conversation now called upon Servius to ask a question, he—pressed by natural modesty—blushed so deeply that his color betrayed him. And Disarius said: "Come now, Servius, most learned not only of the youths who are your peers, but of all the elders as well: 

<margin>
Embolden.
</margin>

embolden <note>original: *commascula*; literally "make masculine" or "toughen up."</note> your brow and set aside that modesty which the redness on your face indicates; discuss freely with us whatever occurs to your inquiries, for you will contribute no less to our learning than if you were answering the consultations of others." 

<margin>
Why blushing from shame arises in the face.
</margin>

When Disarius had stirred the long-silent Servius with frequent encouragements, Servius said: "I ask this of you, which you said has happened to me: what is the cause that makes redness arise in the body from the shame of the soul?" And he replied: "It is nature; when it encounters something worthy of honest shame, it penetrates deep in search of the blood; when this blood is moved and spread abroad, the skin is dyed, and from this, redness is born. Natural philosophers <note>original: *physici*; refers to those who study the physical world and medicine.</note> also say that nature, touched by shame, spreads the blood before it like a veil, just as we see a blushing person frequently place their hand before their face. You cannot doubt these things, since redness is nothing other than the color of blood." 

<margin>
Why those rejoicing blush.
</margin>

Servius added: "And why do those who rejoice blush?" Disarius said: "Joy happens from the outside. Nature hastens toward this with a swift course; the blood, following along as if possessing the alacrity of its own integrity, dyes the skin. And from this, a similar color is born." He asked further: "On the other hand, for what reason do those who fear turn pale?"

...fears those things touching the body: it submerges itself entirely into the depths, just as we also do when we are afraid, seeking hiding places and locations to conceal us. Therefore, descending entirely so as to lie hidden, the soul draws the blood with it, which it uses as a chariot <note>original: "velut curru"; a Platonic metaphor where the soul is seen as a charioteer driving the body or its vital fluids.</note> to be carried. Once this blood is submerged, a thinner moisture remains in the skin, and from this, the person grows pale. 

<margin>Where trembling comes from.</margin>
<margin>Why those who are afraid suffer a loosening of the body.</margin>

For this reason, those who are afraid also tremble, because the power of the soul, fleeing inward, abandons the nerves by which the strength of the limbs was maintained; and thus they are shaken by the "leap" of fear. Here, a loosening of the bowels also accompanies fear: because the muscles, by which the passages of waste were closed, are deserted by the power of the fleeing inward soul and relax the bonds by which the waste was contained until the proper time for digestion. After these things were said, Servius gave his respectful assent and fell silent.

<margin>Lard: Why salt preserves meat.</margin>

¶ Then Avienus said: "Since the order of the discussion brings me to a similar consultation, the conversation must be brought back to the banquet—from which it has wandered too far—and transferred to other questions. Often salted meat is served, which we call lard <note>original: "laridum"; bacon or salt pork.</note> (as I believe, as if it were 'largely dry' <note>original: "large aridum"; a characteristic ancient folk etymology.</note>). I have decided to ask myself by what logic the addition of salt preserves meat for long-term use. Although I might estimate this for myself, I prefer to be informed by him who cares for bodies." 

And Disarius replied: "Every body is by its own nature dissolvable and prone to decay, and unless it is contained by some bond, it easily flows away. They are contained, however, as long as the soul is present through the reciprocity of the air, by which the receptacles of the spirit are quickened, while they are always nourished by the new food of breathing. When this ceases through the departure of the soul, the limbs decay, and the whole body, worn out by its own weight, is crushed. Then even the blood, which as long as it possessed heat gave vigor to the limbs, turns toward corruption as the heat departs; it does not remain within the veins but is pressed outward, and thus, through the loosened pores, a foul decay flows out. 

<margin>Salt is dry and hot.</margin>

The salt mixed into the body prevents this from happening. For it is by nature dry and hot: it contracts the flowing of the body with its heat, and either restrains or absorbs the moisture with its dryness. Surely it is easy to learn from this that moisture is dispersed or consumed by salt: for if you make two loaves of bread of equal size, one sprinkled with salt and the other without salt, you will find the one lacking salt to be heavier in weight—evidently because the moisture remains in it due to the lack of salt."

<margin>Decanted wine is stronger but more unstable.</margin>

¶ "I also wish this to be asked of my friend Disarius: why is decanted <note>original: "defecatum"; wine that has been cleared of its dregs or lees.</note> wine stronger in its potency but weaker in its permanence? It quickly affects the drinker, yet if it sits, it is easily changed and spoiled." 

Disarius said: "The reason it quickly affects the drinker is this: the more liquid it is made by being purged of its dregs, the more penetrable it becomes in the veins of the drinker. However, it is easily changed because, being supported by no foundation, it lies open on all sides to harm. For the dregs <note>original: "fex"; the lees or sediment of the wine.</note> are like its root, for sustaining and nourishing the wine and providing it with strength."

<margin>Why dregs stand at the bottom in others, but on the surface in honey.</margin>
<margin>Why the freshest honey and the oldest wine are best.</margin>
<margin>Things to be moistened.</margin>

¶ And Avienus said: "I also ask this: why do the dregs sink to the bottom in all liquids except honey? Is honey the only one that spits the dregs to the top?" 

To this, Disarius replied: "The matter of the dregs, being thick and earthy, surpasses other liquids in weight; but it is surpassed by honey. Therefore, in the others, it sinks to the bottom by its gravity; but in honey, being lighter, it is overcome and pushed upward from its place. Since from these things that have been said, similar questions suggest themselves: Why, Disarius, are honey and wine considered best at different ages—honey when it is freshest, and wine when it is oldest? There is even a proverb used by gluttons: 'The honey-wine <note>original: "mulsum"; a popular Roman beverage made of wine and honey.</note> that you would temper well should be mixed with new Hymettian honey and old Falernian wine.' <note>Hymettus was a mountain near Athens famous for honey; Falernian was the most prestigious wine of Italy.</note>"

He replied: "Because they are different in their internal nature. For the nature of wine is moist, and that of honey is dry. If you doubt this statement, consider the effect of medicine. For those parts of the body that are to be moistened are bathed in wine; those that are to be dried are cleansed with honey. Therefore, as length of time absorbs something from both, the wine becomes purer <note>original: "meracius"; unmixed or more potent.</note> and the honey drier; and thus the honey is deprived of its juice, just as the wine is freed from its water."

<margin>Why half-full vessels of wine turn to sourness, while a sweeter flavor is gained for oil.</margin>

¶ "Nor is this which follows unlike the previous questions: why is it that if you keep vessels of wine and oil half-full for a long time, the wine is almost always corrupted into sourness, while on the contrary, a sweeter flavor is gained for the oil?" 

Disarius said: "Both are true. For into that vacuum which lacks liquid at the top, outside air enters, which elicits and absorbs even the thinnest moisture. When that is dried out, the wine—as if despoiled of its strength, whether it was naturally weak or strong—is either sharpened by sourness or constricted by bitterness. Oil, however, above the vacuum..."

...the moisture having been dried, as if the mold <note>original: "mucore"; refers to the slimy or moldy residue that can appear on curing meat.</note> that lay hidden in it were wiped away: it acquires a new sweetness of flavor. Avienus spoke again: "Hesiod <note>An ancient Greek poet; this refers to a passage in his *Works and Days* regarding the consumption of wine.</note> says that when one reaches the middle of the jar <note>term: "dolii" (a dolium was a large earthenware storage jar used for wine, oil, or grain)</note>, one should be sparing; but he says one should use the other parts to satiety: undoubtedly meaning that the best wine is that which remains in the middle of the jar. 

<margin>Why wine is best in the middle of the vessel. Why oil is best at the top of the vessel. Why honey is best at the bottom of the vessel.</margin>

But this is also proven by experience: in oil, the best is that which floats on top; in honey, that which is at the bottom. I ask, therefore, why oil at the top, wine in the middle, and honey at the bottom are believed to be the best." Without hesitation, Disarius said: "Honey that is the best is heavier than the rest. Therefore, in a vessel of honey, the part at the bottom certainly excels in weight, and for that reason, it is more precious than that which floats above. Conversely, in a vessel of wine, the lower part is not only turbulent from the mixing of dregs, but also inferior in taste. However, the top part is corrupted by its proximity to the air, by the mixture of which it becomes diluted. This is why farmers, not content to have stored the jars under a roof, bury them and protect them with coatings smeared on the outside, removing as much as possible the contagion of the air from the wine. It is so clearly harmed by air that it can hardly protect itself in a full vessel, which is less accessible to the air. Furthermore, if you do not draw from it, and yet open a space for the admission of air, all the rest that remains is corrupted. The middle part, therefore, is as far from the boundary of either extreme as it is removed from harm, being neither turbulent nor diluted."

<margin>Why a drink seems stronger to those fasting than to those who have eaten. Why a drink relieves hunger somewhat, but food does not relieve thirst.</margin>

Avienus added: "Why does the same drink seem stronger <note>original: "meracior"; literally "more unmixed," referring to the potency of the wine.</note> to one who is fasting than to one who has taken food?" And he replied: "Hunger empties the veins; fullness obstructs them. Therefore, when a drink flows deep within through the emptiness—because it finds the veins neither dulled by food nor made more dilute by mixing—it is felt by a stronger taste as it travels through the void. This also I must know," said Avienus: "Why does he who drinks while hungry find his hunger somewhat relieved? Yet he who takes food while thirsty not only does not master his thirst, but rather kindles the desire for drink." "The cause is well known," said Disarius. "For nothing hinders a liquid, once taken, from spreading everywhere to all parts of the body and filling the veins. And thus the hunger, which emptiness had created, is refreshed by the remedy of the drink, as if it were no longer entirely empty. Food, however, being more solid and bulky, is not admitted into the veins except gradually after being processed. Therefore, it provides no comfort to the thirst it finds; rather, it absorbs whatever external moisture it encounters, and thus the lack of it, which is called thirst, increases." Avienus said: "Nor will I leave this unknown: why is there greater pleasure when thirst is extinguished by drink than when hunger is settled by food?" And Disarius replied: "This is also clear from what was said before. For the entire draft of a drink penetrates the whole body at once, and creates one great and sensible pleasure in the senses of all the parts. Food, however, by a small supply, comforts the lack only gradually. Therefore, its pleasure is diminished by being spread out in many ways."

<margin>Why those who devour greedily are more easily satisfied. Satiety.</margin>

"I add this also (if it seems right) regarding thirst: why do those who devour more greedily reach satiety more easily than those who eat the same things quietly?" "That answer is brief," he said. "For where food is devoured greedily, much air is brought in with the victuals because of the gaping of the mouth and the frequency of breathing. Therefore, when air has filled the veins, it serves instead of food to cast off the appetite. Unless I am being troublesome, Disarius, allow one chattering excessively out of a desire for learning to ask: why do we compress 

<margin>Why hot foods are more easily tolerated by the mouth than the hand. The belly.</margin>

foods that are quite hot more easily with the mouth than we can endure them with the hand? And if any of them are more burning, so that they might be chewed longer, we swallow them instantly, and yet the belly is not harmfully burned." And he replied: "The internal heat which is in the belly is, as it were, much greater and more vehement; it surrounds and weakens whatever hot thing it receives by its own magnitude. Therefore, it is better, if you bring something burning to the mouth, not to gape as some do—lest you provide strength to the heat with new breath—but to compress the lips for a little while, so that the greater heat which brings aid from the belly and mouth may compress the lesser heat. The hand, however, is helped by no heat of its own to enable it to carry a burning thing."

<margin>Why snow water is harmful. Harm. Harm.</margin>

"For a long time now," said Avienus, "I have longed to know why water which is brought to a snowy chill by being surrounded by globes of snow is no less harmful in drink than water melted from the snow itself. For we know how many and how great are the harms that arise from drinking the moisture of snow." And Disarius: "Add something further before you thirst: for water melted from snow, even if it is heated by fire and drunk warm, is just as harmful as if it were drunk cold..."

...cold. Therefore, it is not by coldness alone that snow-water is harmful, but for another reason which I shall not be reluctant to reveal, following the authority of **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC) was a Greek philosopher whose works on natural science, such as his *Problemata* (Physical Problems), are frequently cited here.</note>, who posed this in his physical inquiries and, if I am not mistaken, explained it in this sense. He says that all water contains a portion of very thin air, which makes it healthful; it also contains earthy dregs, which are heavy like the earth itself. When, therefore, it is forced to become warm by the cold and frost of the air, it is necessary that either through evaporation that very thin air is squeezed out of it, or that as it settles it turns into a curdled mass <note>original: "coagulum"</note>, with only the earthy nature remaining in it. This is apparent from the fact that when the same water has been melted by the heat of the sun, a smaller measure of it is found than there was before it froze. What is missing is that which evaporation consumed—the only healthy part of the water. Snow, therefore, which is nothing other than water loosened in the air, has lost its thinness when it is melted; and thus, from the drinking of this resolved liquid, various kinds of diseases are sown into the internal organs.

<margin>Why wines never, or rarely, freeze.</margin>
Having mentioned frost, I am reminded of an old question that used to trouble me: why do wines either never, or only rarely, freeze, while most other liquids are usually forced to solidify by an excess of cold? Is it because wine contains certain seeds of heat within itself, and for that reason **Homer** called it "sparkling wine" <note>original Greek: "αἶθοπα οἶνον" (*aithopa oinon*); often translated as ruddy, dark, or fiery-looking wine.</note>? Is it, as some think, because of heat, or is there some other cause? I desire to know, for I am ignorant of it. To this, **Disarius** replied: "Even if wines are protected by natural heat, is oil any less 'fiery,' or does it have less power to warm bodies? And yet it is gripped by frost. Certainly, if you think that those things which are warmer are harder to freeze, it would be consistent that oil should not solidify either, and that those things which are colder should be easily forced by frost. Vinegar, however, is the most cooling of all things; yet it is never gripped by frost. Is the cause of quicker curdling in oil perhaps that it is smoother and thicker? For those things which are smoother seem more prone to coming together among dense things. Wine, however, does not possess such softness, and is much more fluid than oil."

<margin>Why vinegar does not freeze.</margin>
Vinegar is indeed the most fluid among all other liquids, and so sharp that it is harsh in its acidity; and following the example of sea water—which is itself harsh because of its bitterness—it is never contracted by frost. For as to what 

<margin>How the sea freezes.</margin>
**Herodotus** <note>The "Father of History" (5th century BC); he wrote about the lands and customs surrounding the Black Sea.</note>, the writer of histories, wrote—contrary to the opinion of almost everyone who has experienced these things—that the **Bosporan** sea (which he also calls Cimmerian) and all that part of the sea called **Scythian** <note>The Scythian sea refers to the northern parts of the Black Sea near modern-day Ukraine/Russia.</note> is constricted and stands still with frost, it is otherwise than is thought. For it is not the sea water that is contracted; but because there are many rivers in those regions, and marshes flowing into those very seas, the surface of the sea (upon which the fresh waters float) freezes. Thus, the sea water is seen in the sea beneath the ice, unharmed, but the ice is formed from the arriving waves <note>i.e., the fresh river water on top.</note>. We see this happening also in the **Pontus** <note>The Black Sea.</note>, in which certain fragments and, as it were, frozen surfaces are carried along, contracted from the multitude of river or marsh waters; although these are solidified by the cold, they are nevertheless floating, being lighter than the sea water. Indeed, a great deal of such water flows into the Pontus, and its entire surface is covered by fresh liquor; because of this, **Sallust** <note>A Roman historian (86–35 BC) who wrote about the geography of the Black Sea region.</note> says the water of the Pontic sea is fresher than the rest. There is also this evidence: if you throw straw or wood or any other floating things into the Pontus with force, they are carried out of the Pontus into the **Propontis** <note>The Sea of Marmara.</note>, and so into the sea that washes the coast of Asia; though it is certain that sea water flows *into* the Pontus, not *out* of it. For the only passage <note>term: "Meatus" (a passage or channel)</note> which transmits waters received from the Ocean into our seas is in the **Strait of Gades** <note>The Strait of Gibraltar.</note>, which lies between Spain and Africa. And without doubt, that very inundation proceeds along the Spanish and Gallic shores into the Tyrrhenian Sea, then makes the Adriatic Sea, from which it goes right into the Parthenian, left into the Ionian, and straight into the Aegean. And thus it enters the Pontus.

<margin>Currents.</margin>
What reason, then, makes it so that waters flow out of the Pontus in streams, when the Pontus receives waters flowing in from outside? But both reasons are established. For the surface of the Pontus, because of the excessive fresh waters that flow in from the land, flows outward; but underneath, the inflow proceeds inward. From this it is proven that floating things which are thrown in (as I said above) are pushed out of the Pontus. But if a column <note>An ancient experimental proof; if a heavy object like a stone pillar is lowered, it is pulled inward by the deep current.</note> were lowered, it would go inward into the sea. And this has often been proven by experience: that any heavier things at the bottom of the Propontis are pushed toward the interior of the Pontus.

<margin>Why sweet things are sweeter when cold than when warm.</margin>
To these things I shall keep silent after one consultation: why does everything sweet seem more sweet when it is cold than if it is warm? Disarius answered: "Heat occupies the senses, and the fervor of the tongue interferes with the taste. Therefore, the sweetness that arrives is excluded by the irritation of the mouth. But if the injury of heat is absent, then at last the tongue—its pleasant sensation unharmed—can receive the sweetness according to its merit. Furthermore, sweet juice does not penetrate the veins through heat without consequence...

<margin>
Why those who fast are more thirsty than they are hungry.
</margin>
Horus then took up the conversation: "While **Avienus** <note>Avienus is a character in this dialogue, likely based on the Roman geographical poet Rufus Festus Avienus.</note> has asked many questions regarding drink and food," he said, "he has—whether by choice or forgetfulness, I do not know—overlooked one most necessary point: why those who fast are more thirsty than they are hungry. If you would be so kind, **Disarius** <note>Disarius is the learned physician character in the dialogue.</note>, please resolve this for us." 

And Disarius replied: "The matter you raise, Horus, is indeed worthy of discussion, but its reasoning is quite clear. Since a living creature consists of diverse elements, there is one among those that form the body which, alone or at least far more than the others, seeks out nourishment suitable for itself: I speak of **heat** <note>In ancient medicine, "natural heat" was considered the vital force of life that "cooked" or digested food.</note>, which always demands that liquid be provided to it. Certainly, among the four elements themselves in the external world, we see that neither water, nor air, nor earth requires anything to feed upon or consume; they do no harm to the things neighboring or placed near them. Fire alone, out of a desire for perpetual nourishment, consumes whatever it encounters. 

"Observe also the infancy of the earliest age: how much food it consumes because of its excessive heat. On the other hand, consider how elderly men easily tolerate fasting, as if the heat within them, which is usually refreshed by nutrients, has been nearly extinguished. Furthermore, if a person of middle age excites his natural heat through much exercise, he seeks food more eagerly. Let us also consider bloodless animals; they seek no food because of their lack of heat. Therefore, if heat is always in a state of desire, and liquid is the proper nourishment of heat, it is natural that when the body seeks nutrients during a fast, the heat especially demands its own share. Once this is received, the whole body is refreshed and waits more patiently for more solid food."

<margin>
Why the ring is worn on the finger closest to the smallest.
</margin>
After these words, Avienus picked up a ring from the table which had suddenly slipped off the smallest finger of his right hand. When those present asked why he would place it on a different hand and finger than those usually assigned for such wear, he showed that his left hand was somewhat swollen from a wound. 

This gave Horus an opportunity for a new question. "Tell us, Disarius," he said, "for the entire state of the body pertains to the physician’s knowledge—and you have attained learning even beyond what medicine requires—tell us why common consent has persuaded us that the ring should be worn on the finger neighboring the smallest (which they even call the 'medical finger' <note>original: "medicinalem"; this is the ring finger.</note>), and specifically on the left hand."

And Disarius said: "A certain report regarding this very question came to us from **Egypt**. I used to doubt whether I should call it a fable or a true explanation. But after later consulting the books of the anatomists, I found it to be true: that a certain nerve, originating from the heart <note>Ancient anatomy often incorrectly linked nerves directly to the heart as the center of the vascular and nervous system.</note>, travels directly to the finger of the left hand that is closest to the smallest, and ends there, entwined with the other nerves of that same finger. For this reason, it seemed right to the ancients that this finger should be surrounded by a ring as if by a crown."

And Horus replied: "Indeed, Disarius, it is so true that the Egyptians hold this opinion that I myself have seen their priests (whom they call **Prophets**) in the temple, standing around the altars of the gods, anointing this single finger on each hand with prepared perfumes. When I inquired into the reasons for this, I learned from their leader the story of the nerve which you just mentioned, and furthermore, about the number signified by that finger. For when that finger is folded, it demonstrates the **number six** <note>original: "senarium numerum"; in ancient finger-counting (digitalis computus), different positions of the fingers represented specific numbers.</note>, which is in every way full, perfect, and divine. He asserted many reasons why this number is 'full,' but I shall leave them aside now as they are less suited to our present conversation. These are the things I learned in Egypt—the possessor of all divine disciplines—as to why the ring is placed on this finger above others."

During this, **Cecinna Albinus** said: "If it pleases you, I shall bring into our midst what I remember reading on this same subject in the works of **Ateius Capito** <note>Ateius Capito (c. 30 BC – 22 AD) was a famous Roman jurist and expert in pontifical (religious) law.</note>, a man foremost among those skilled in pontifical law. While he decreed it a sin for the images of gods to be carved into rings, he went so far as to not remain silent about why the ring was worn on this finger or on this hand. 

'The ancients,' he said, 'carried a ring with them not for ornament, but for the purpose of **sealing** <note>original: "signandi causa"; rings were primarily functional signet tools used to stamp wax seals on documents.</note>.' Hence, it was not permitted to have more than one, nor was it allowed to any but a free man; for only to free men did the law grant the 'faith' <note>original: "fides"; here meaning legal reliability or trust.</note> which is contained in a seal. Therefore, slaves did not have the right to wear rings. The carving was impressed into the material of the ring, whether it was made of iron or gold; and each person wore it as he wished, on whichever hand or finger. Later," he said, "the custom of a more luxurious age began to engrave seals into precious gems; and everyone began to compete in this imitation, boasting of the increased price they paid for the stones to be carved. Thus it happened that the use..."

<margin>Why the fasting are more thirsty than they are hungry.</margin>
¶ Horus then took up the conversation: "Since Avienus has inquired much regarding drink and food, he has overlooked—whether by choice or forgetfulness, I do not know—one most necessary point: why those who are fasting are more thirsty than they are hungry. If it seems right to you, Disarius, you shall resolve this common question for us." And he replied: "The matter you ask about is indeed worthy of discussion, but its reasoning is quite accessible. Since a living creature consists of diverse elements, there is one among them which always demands that liquid be administered to it. Certainly, regarding the four elements <note>The four elements are Earth, Air, Fire, and Water—the fundamental building blocks of the universe in ancient science.</note> themselves, we see from the outside that neither water, nor air, nor earth requires anything to nourish it or anything to consume; they bring no harm to things near or placed against them. Fire alone, out of a desire for perpetual nourishment, consumes whatever it encounters. Look even at the infancy of the earliest age: how much food it consumes due to excessive heat; and by contrast, consider how old men easily tolerate fasting, as if the heat within them, which is usually restored by nutrients, has been extinguished. But even those in middle age, if they have stirred up their natural heat through much exercise, seek food more eagerly. Let us also consider animals that lack blood; they seek no food because of their lack of heat. Therefore, if heat is always in a state of craving, and liquid is the proper nourishment for heat, it follows that when nutrients for the body are sought during a fast, the heat especially makes its demand. Once this is received, the whole body is refreshed, and it waits more patiently for more solid food."

¶ Having said these things, Avienus retrieved a ring from the table, which had suddenly fallen from the shortest finger of his right hand. When those present asked why he would place it on a different hand and finger than those usually assigned for this wearing, he showed that his left hand was somewhat swollen from a wound. This gave Horus the opportunity for a question: "Tell us, Disarius," he said, "for every position of the body pertains to the physician’s knowledge—and you have attained learning even beyond what medicine requires—tell us why common consent has persuaded us that a ring should be worn on the finger next to the smallest, which they even call the 'medical finger' <note>This is the ring finger. In antiquity, it was believed to have a direct connection to the heart.</note>, and specifically on the left hand."

<margin>Why the ring is worn on the finger closest to the smallest. The views of the ancients.</margin>
And Disarius said: "Regarding this very question, a certain report came to us from Egypt, which I used to doubt—whether to call it a fable or a true reason. But having later consulted the books of the anatomists, I found it to be true: that a certain nerve, originating from the heart, proceeds as far as the finger of the left hand closest to the smallest, and there ends, entwined with the other nerves of that same finger. Therefore, it seemed to the ancients that this finger should be encircled by a ring as if by a crown."

And Horus said: "Indeed, Disarius, it is so true as you say the Egyptians believe, that when I was in the temple, I saw their priests—whom they call prophets—anointing this particular finger with prepared perfumes around the altars of the gods. When I inquired into the reasons for this, I learned from their leader what has already been said about the nerve, and furthermore about the number signified by it. For this finger, when folded, demonstrates the number six <note>original: "senarium numerum." In ancient finger-counting (dactylonomy), specific gestures represented numbers; the number 6 was considered "perfect" because its factors 1, 2, and 3 add up to 6.</note>, which is in every way full, perfect, and divine. He asserted many reasons why this number is full; I shall leave them aside for now as they are less suited to our present talk. These are the things I learned in Egypt, a land possessed of all divine disciplines, as to why the ring is inserted onto this finger rather than others."

Among these remarks, Cecinna Albinus said: "If it pleases you, I shall bring into our midst what I remember reading on this same cause in the works of Ateius Capito <note>Ateius Capito (c. 30 BC – 22 AD) was one of the most distinguished Roman jurists of the early Empire, specializing in pontifical and public law.</note>, a man most skilled in priestly law. While he decreed it a religious crime for the images of the gods to be engraved on rings, he went so far as to not remain silent on why the ring was worn on this finger or on this hand. The ancients, he says, did not carry a ring for the sake of ornament, but for the sake of sealing.

¶ Hence, it was not permitted to have more than one, nor for anyone except a free man—whom alone 'faith' <note>original: "fides." In this context, it refers to legal trust and the ability to witness or sign contracts.</note> would distinguish, which is maintained by a seal. Therefore, they did not have the right of rings for the household. Now, the sculpture was impressed into the material of the ring, whether it was made of iron or gold; and each man wore it as he wished, on whichever hand or whichever finger. Later, he says, the custom of a luxurious age began to engrave seals into precious gems, and everyone challenged each other in imitation, so that one might boast of the increase in price for which they had obtained stones to be engraved.
