...the rings were removed from the right hand, which performs much work, and relegated to the left, which is more idle, so that the precious stones would not be broken by the frequent movement and labor of the right hand. It is said that the finger next to the smallest was chosen on that left hand as being more suitable than the others to be entrusted with the value of the ring. For the thumb—which received its name from the fact that it is powerful <note>The Latin *pollex* (thumb) was traditionally thought to derive from *pollere* (to be powerful).</note>—is not idle even on the left hand, and is no less involved in work than the whole hand itself. Hence among the Greeks, it is called the <term>anticheir</term> <note>original: "ἀντίχειρ"; literally "instead of a hand" or "a second hand."</note>, as if it were another hand. The finger next to the thumb, however, appeared bare and without the protection of another placed next to it. For the thumb is so much lower that it scarcely reaches past the root of that finger. They avoided the middle and the smallest fingers, it is said, as being unsuitable: one because of its size and the other because of its shortness. Thus, the finger was chosen which is enclosed by both of the others and performs the least work, and is therefore better adapted for preserving a ring. These are the things contained in the priestly readings. Each person may follow whichever opinion he wishes, whether the Etruscan or the Egyptian.

<margin>Why fresh water is more suitable for washing away filth than salt water.</margin>
¶ Amidst these discussions, Horus, who was stern in seeking counsel, said: "You know, Disarius, that besides this cloak which covers me, I have nothing else to my name. Therefore, I have no servant, nor do I wish for one; instead, I provide for myself every necessity required for living. Recently, then, while I was staying in the town of Ostia, I washed my soiled cloak in the sea for a long time and dried it in the sun on the shore; nevertheless, after the washing, those same stains of filth were visible upon it. While I was marvelling at this, a sailor who happened to be standing by said, 'Why don't you rather wash your cloak in the river, if you want it cleaned?' I obeyed, to see if it were true, and I saw that after being washed in fresh water and dried, its brightness was restored. Since then, I have been searching for the reason why fresh water is more suitable than salt water for washing away filth." 

Disarius replied: "Some time ago, this question was both proposed and solved by Aristotle. For he says that sea water is much thicker than fresh water; indeed, that sea water is full of dregs, while fresh water is pure and refined. He says that for this reason, the sea more easily supports even those who do not know how to swim, whereas river water, being weak as it were and supported by no substance, soon gives way and sends any weight it receives to the bottom. Therefore, he said that fresh water, being naturally light, sinks more quickly into the things that must be washed, and while it dries, it draws out the stains of filth with it. Sea water, however, being thicker, does not easily penetrate for the purpose of cleaning because of its density, and since it hardly dries, it does not pull much filth away with it."

When Horus seemed to agree with these points, Eustachius <note>Eustachius is the host of the banquet and a high-ranking Roman official.</note> said: "I pray you, do not deceive this trusting man who has committed himself and his question to your good faith. For Aristotle, as in several other matters, argued these points with more cleverness than truth. Indeed, the density of water does not hinder washing to such an extent; in fact, those who want certain <margin>Materials.</margin> materials cleaned, lest they achieve this too slowly with fresh water alone, often mix in ash or (if that is lacking) earth dust, so that the water, having been made thicker, can wash more quickly. Therefore, the density of sea water is no hindrance. Nor is it because it is salty that it washes less. For saltiness usually splits and, as it were, opens <margin>Water is more fatty.</margin> the pores, and therefore it ought to have drawn out the filth even more. But this is the one reason why sea water is not fit for washing: because it is oily, just as Aristotle himself often testified; and salts teach us this, for no one is ignorant that there is a certain fattiness within them. There is also this evidence of the fattiness of sea water: that when it is sprinkled on a flame, it is not so much extinguished as it is ignited at the same time, because the oiliness of the water provides nourishment to the fire. Finally, let us read Homer, who alone was privy to the secrets of nature. For he depicts Nausicaa, the daughter of Alcinous, washing clothes when she was by the sea, not in the sea, but in a river. That same passage of Homer teaches us that there is a certain fatness mixed into sea water. For Ulysses <note>Known as Odysseus in Greek.</note>, when he had finally escaped the sea and was standing with his body dried, said to the handmaidens of Nausicaa:

> "Maidens, stand thus far away, so that I myself may wash the brine from my shoulders and rub myself with oil; for it has been long since ointment touched my skin." <note>original: "ἀμφίπολοι στῆθ' οὕτω ἀπόπροθεν ὄφρ' ἐγὼ αὐτὸς / ἅλμην ὤμοιιν ἀπολούσομαι ἀμφὶ δὲ λαίῳ / χρίσομαι. ἢ γὰρ δηρὸν ἀπὸ χροός ἐστὶν ἀλοιφή"; Odyssey 6.218-220.</note>

¶ After this, when he had gone down into the river, the divine poet—who followed nature in every matter—expressed what usually happens: that for those who come out of the sea, if they stand in the sun, the water is indeed quickly dried by the sun, but there remains on the surface of the body a kind of film <note>The Latin word *flos* (flower) is used here metaphorically to mean a residue or thin layer.</note> which is felt upon being touched. And this is the oiliness of sea water which alone prevents effective washing.

# THE SATURNALIA
## BOOK SEVEN
### CHAPTER XIV

<margin>Why images appear larger than they truly are in water.</margin>
"Since you have cleared up the other matters for the rest of the company," Disarius said, "indulge me for a little while. Indeed, our conversation has been about water; I ask, then, why do images appear larger than they truly are in water? We see this kind of thing at the taverns <note>original: "popinatores"; these were keepers of cook-shops or wine-shops where food was displayed in glass vessels.</note> where many glass vessels are set out, appearing fuller in appearance than in substance. For we see eggs in glass jars filled with water appearing as larger globes, small livers with more swollen fibers, sow’s wombs <note>original: "buluas" (vulvas); a Roman culinary delicacy often displayed in jars.</note> with huge coils, and indeed everything looks larger. By what reasoning is this established for us? For many are accustomed to hold views on this that are neither true nor even likely."

And Disarius continued, "Water is denser than the thinness of air; and therefore the force of sight penetrates it more slowly. Struck by this resistance, the keenness of our vision is split and recoils upon itself. While this split vision returns, no longer in a direct strike but spreading out from every side, it runs into the outlines of the object; and thus it happens that the image is seen as larger than its original model <term>archetype</term> <note>From the Greek *archetypon*, meaning the original pattern or actual object being reflected.</note>. For even the morning orb of the sun <margin>The sun's orb is larger in the sea.</margin> appears larger to us than usual because the air between us and it is still dewy from the night, and its image grows larger as if it were being viewed in a mirror of water. 

Epicurus looked into the nature of vision itself, and not <margin>Ignorantly.</margin> ignorantly; his opinion in this matter is not, in my estimation, to be rejected, especially as Democritus supports it, for they held similar views on this as in other matters. Therefore, Epicurus believes that from all bodies there flows a constant stream of certain images <term>simulacra</term> <note>Epicurus’s theory of "idols" or "films" (simulacra) suggested that objects constantly shed thin layers of atoms that fly through the air and enter our eyes.</note>; and that not even the slightest delay occurs, but rather these skins shed from bodies fly far and wide, held together in an empty form. The receptacles for these are in our eyes, and thus they return to the seat of their own sense assigned to them by nature. These are the things that great man records; if you disagree with them, I wait to hear what you might say in return."

<margin>Openly.</margin> At this, Eustachius said with a smile, "What deceived Epicurus is plainly visible. For he fell away from the truth by following the example of the other four senses. Because in hearing, tasting, smelling, and touching, we emit nothing from ourselves, but receive from the outside that which moves the sense. Indeed, the voice comes to the ears of its own accord, scents flow into the nostrils, what produces flavor is placed upon the palate, and things to be felt by touch are applied to our body. From this, he thought that nothing proceeds outward from the eyes either, but that the images of things travel into the eyes of their own accord. 

But his opinion is contradicted by the fact that in mirrors, the reflected image faces its own observer; whereas it ought—if indeed it originated from us and proceeded in a straight path—to show its back as it departs, just as a left hand raised would see a right hand facing it. For an actor, once the mask is pulled away from him, sees it from the side he wore it—that is, not from the face, but from the hollow back. 

Furthermore, I would like to ask this man: do these images fly away from things only when someone wishes to see, or do these images flash out from everywhere even when no one is looking? For if he holds to the first point I mentioned, how can the images be ready for anyone who looks upon them? And as often as someone chooses to turn his face, the images must also turn themselves. But if he clings to the second point—that images flow from all things in a perpetual stream—how do they remain held together for so long when they are joined by no bond to keep them lasting? Or if we grant that they last, how will they retain color? For while the nature of color is incorporeal, it can never exist without a body. 

Then, who can bring himself to believe that the moment you turn your eyes, the images of the sky, the sea, the shore, the meadow, ships, flocks, and countless other things rush in—all of which we see with a single glance of the eyes—when the pupil, which possesses the power of sight, is so very small? And in what way is a whole army seen? Do the images proceeding from each individual soldier heap themselves together, and so collected, do these many thousands penetrate the eyes of the beholder? 

But why do we labor to beat such a hollow opinion with words, when the very emptiness of the thing refutes itself? It is established, however, that sight reaches us by this reasoning: a kind of light flashes out from the pupil in a straight line, wherever you turn it. If this domestic overflow of the eyes finds light in the air surrounding us, it proceeds straight through it as long as it hits an object. And if I may use an old comparison: as you look around, the line of sight proceeds straight in both directions. The beam itself, which we said flashes from our eyes, begins from a thin root and becomes wider at the top, just as rays are depicted by a painter.

<margin>Three things are necessary for sight.</margin> By looking with the eyes through a very tiny hole, one sees the depth of the sky. Therefore, these three things are necessary for the effect of seeing: the light that we emit from ourselves; that the air lying between be bright; and a body which, when struck, causes the gaze to stop. If this gaze should proceed further, its straight intention being weary, it does not..."

# BOOK SEVEN

prevails: but it spreads out, split to the right and the left. This is why, wherever on earth you stand, you seem to see a certain boundary of the sky; and this is what the ancients called the horizon. Their diligent investigation discovered that the line of sight directed from the eyes across a flat plane toward those looking back does not proceed beyond one hundred and eighty stades <note>original: "stadia"; a Greek unit of distance roughly equal to 600 feet or 185 meters.</note>, and from there it begins to curve back into a circle. I added "across a flat plane" because we can see heights from a very great distance, since we can even see the sky. Therefore, in the whole circle of the horizon, the observer himself is the center. And since we have said how far the sight extends from the center to the edge of the circle, the <term>diameter</term> <note>original: "Διάμετροσ" (diametros)</note> of the horizon's circle is undoubtedly three hundred and sixty stades; and if the observer moves further forward or steps backward, he will see a similar circle around himself. 

As we have said, then, when the light that proceeds from us falls upon an object through the clarity of the air, the function of seeing is fulfilled. But so that the thing seen may be understood, the sense of the eyes reports the visible appearance to the reason, and memory, being called upon, recognizes it. Therefore, to see belongs to the eyes, to judge belongs to reason, and to remember belongs to memory; for the function that completes the visual process in order to distinguish a shape is threefold: sense, reason, and memory. Sense pours the seen object back to reason. Reason recalls what has been seen. Indeed, the function of reason is so necessary for observing that often, within the single sense of sight, reason—prompted by memory—detects even another sense. For if fire should appear, reason knows it is hot even before it is touched. If it is snow that is seen, reason understands the coldness of touch within that very sight. When reason is idle, sight is ineffective—so much so that an oar appears broken in water, or a tower seen from a distance is estimated to be round when it is actually angular. This is caused by the negligence of reason; for if reason applies itself, it recognizes the angles in the tower and the wholeness of the oar. 

Reason distinguishes all those things which gave the Academics <note>A school of philosopher-skeptics who argued that the senses are unreliable and certain knowledge is impossible.</note> the opportunity to condemn the senses, even though a single sense should be held among the most certain of things when accompanied by reason—though sometimes a single sense is not enough to distinguish a particular appearance. For if the shape of a fruit called an apple is seen from a distance, it is not necessarily an apple. For a likeness of an apple could have been fashioned out of some other material. Therefore, another sense must be called upon, such as smell. But it could have caught the aura of the scent itself by being placed among a pile of apples. Here, touch must be consulted, which can judge by the weight. But there is a fear that touch itself might be deceived if a deceptive craftsman chose a material that imitated the weight of an apple. We must, therefore, flee to taste; if taste agrees with the form, there is no doubt that it is an apple. Thus it is proved that the effectiveness of the senses depends upon reason. For this reason, God the Creator placed all the senses in the head: that is, around the seat of reason.

**WHEN THESE THINGS** had been said, a wave of approval arose from everyone, admiring the soundness of his words—so much so that they did not hesitate to attest even to the Gospel <note>original: "Euāgelū"; likely a reference to the truth of the statement rather than the Christian text, though Macrobius's circles were predominantly pagan.</note> itself. Disarius then added: "These are the rounds of applause that provoke philosophy to claim for itself treatises belonging to other arts. Because of this, it often falls into manifest errors—as when your Plato, while failing to abstain from anatomy (which is specific to medicine), handed down a laughingstock of himself to posterity. For he said that there were separate paths for swallowing food and drink: that food is drawn through the stomach, but drink flows down through the <term>artery</term> <note>original: "ἀρτηρίαν" (artērian); here referring to the windpipe or trachea.</note>, which is called <term>rough</term> <note>original: "τραχεία" (tracheia)</note>, into the lobes of the lungs. It is a wonder—or rather a tragedy—that such a man either believed this or recorded it in his books. On this point, Erasistratus <note>A famous Greek anatomist and royal physician (c. 304–250 BCE) known for his descriptions of the heart and nervous system.</note>, the most noble of ancient physicians, rightly attacked him, saying that Plato reported things far different from what reason discovers. 

For there are two tubes of these channels, and they proceed downward from the back of the mouth. Through one of them, all food and drink are introduced and glide down into the stomach, which in Greek is called <term>the belly cavity</term> <note>original: "ἡκοιλία" (hē koilia)</note>; and there they are worked upon and digested. Then, the drier remains from these gather in another place which in Greek is called <term>the colon</term> <note>original: "κόλον" (kolon)</note>; but the more liquid parts are drawn through the kidneys into the bladder. Through the other of the two upper tubes, which in Greek is called the <term>rough artery</term> <note>original: "τραχεία ἀρτηρία" (tracheia artēria)</note>, breath travels from the top of the mouth into the lungs, and from there back again into the mouth and nostrils; and the passage of the voice occurs through the same. And lest drink or food drier than it should be go into the stomach, or rather, fall out of the mouth into that tube through which the breath moves back and forth—and by that obstruction block the path of the soul—there was placed, by a certain art and work of nature, the <term>epiglottis</term> <note>original: "ἐπιγλωττίδα" (epiglottida)</note>. This is like a mutual barrier for each tube, which are joined together; and it..."

<meta>This page continues the medical and philosophical debate within Macrobius's Saturnalia. The previous page discussed the mechanics of vision and the role of reason. Here, the conversation shifts to anatomy and physiology, specifically the path of food and drink through the body, debating whether liquid enters the lungs or the stomach.</meta>

# SATURNALIA

...the <term>epiglottis</term> <note>original: "ἐπιγλωττίδα" (epiglottida)</note> to cover and protect the path of eating and drinking, namely the <term>trachea</term> <note>original: "τὴν τραχεῖαν" (tēn tracheian)</note>, so that nothing from the food or drink might fall into that path of the panting breath, as it were; and for this reason, no moisture flows into the lung, the mouth of the windpipe itself being protected. This is the view of Erasistratus <note>A famous Greek anatomist and royal physician (c. 303–250 BCE) who founded a school of anatomy in Alexandria.</note>, with whom (as I estimate) true reason agrees. For since food—not dry and rough, but softened by a temperate amount of moisture—must be brought into the belly, it was necessary that the same path lie open for both, so that the food, tempered by the drink, might be stored in the stomach and then the belly; nature would not have composed it otherwise, unless it were for the health of the living creature. Furthermore, since the lung is both solid and smooth, if anything thick were to fall into it, how could it penetrate or be transmitted to the place of digestion? For it is well known that if ever, by chance, something a little too dense falls into the lung while a violent breath is being drawn, a very harsh cough immediately arises, along with other shakings, even to the point of endangering one’s health. If, however, the natural path drew drink into the lung, what would the lung produce when thick things are drunk, or when a draught of drink is swallowed mixed with grains or some other denser substance? Therefore, the epiglottis was provided by nature so that when food is taken, it acts as a lid for the <term>windpipe</term> <note>original: "arteria," referring here to the "rough artery" or trachea.</note>, lest anything slip through it into the lung while the breath is being drawn in everywhere. Just as when speech is to be emitted, it is inclined to block the path of the stomach, so as to permit the <term>windpipe</term> <note>original: "ἀρτηρίαν" (artērian)</note> to be open for the voice. This is also known from experience: those who draw in their drink slowly have wetter bellies, as the moisture which is taken in little by little remains longer. But if anyone gulps it down more greedily, the moisture is drawn in with the same impetus and passes into the bladder, and slow digestion results for the drier food. This difference would not arise if the passages for food and drink were divided from the beginning. As for what the poet Alcaeus <note>A Greek lyric poet from Lesbos (c. 620–580 BCE). His poetry often praised the medicinal or social benefits of wine.</note> said, and which is commonly sung:

->Wet your lungs with wine, for the dog-star is rising.<-

This was said because the lung truly rejoices in moisture, but it draws only as much as it estimates is necessary for itself. Whence it would have been enough for the prince of all philosophers to abstain from the opinions of others, rather than to bring forward things that are less known.

¶ At this, Eustachius, being a little more moved, said: "Disarius, I used to count you no less among philosophers than among physicians; but now you seem to me to give over to oblivion a thing celebrated by the consensus of the human race and firmly believed: that philosophy is the art of arts and the discipline of disciplines. And now medicine attacks her with a parricidal daring, even though you hold philosophy to be at her narrowest when she disputes concerning the rational part—that is, concerning incorporeal things—and at her most inclined when she treats physics, which concerns divine bodies, the heavens, or the stars. Medicine, however, is the lowest dregs of the physical part, having its reasoning with earthen and worldly bodies. But why do I mention 'reasoning,' since conjecture reigns more among them than reason? How then does she, who conjectures about muddy flesh, dare to trample upon philosophy, which treats incorporeal and truly divine things with certain reason? But lest this general defense seem to avoid the treatment of the lung, hear the reasons which the Platonic majesty followed. The epiglottis which you mention is an invention of nature for ruling and uncovering the paths of food and drink with a certain alternation: so that it may transmit the former to the stomach, and the lung may receive the latter. For this reason, it is distinguished by so many passages and lies open with gaps—not so that the spirit may have exits, for which a hidden exhalation would suffice, but so that through them, if any food falls into the lung, its juice may soon migrate into the seat of digestion. Furthermore, if by some chance the <term>windpipe</term> <note>original: "ἀρτηρία" (artēria)</note> is cut, the drink is not swallowed, but as if the passage were cut, the fluid is thrown back outside, while the stomach remains unharmed; which would not happen unless the windpipe were the path for moisture. Moreover, this is evident because those whose lung is diseased are inflamed with the greatest thirst; but this would not happen unless the lung were the receptacle of drink. Consider this also: that animals which have no lung do not know drink. For nature made nothing superfluous, but made each individual member for some service of living; when the member is missing, the use of it is not required. Or consider this: if the stomach received both food and drink, the use of the bladder would be superfluous. For the stomach could have handed over the waste of both things to the intestine, to which it now hands over food alone. Nor would there be need for diverse passages through which each might be delivered; rather, one would suffice for both, transmitted from the same station. But now...

<meta>catchword: Modo autē (But now)</meta>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical banquet discussions in Macrobius's Saturnalia, Book VII. Following the previous discussion on whether drink passes through the lungs, the text concludes that physiological argument by citing classical poets and then pivots to a famous philosophical paradox: the priority of the egg or the chicken.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN

...the bladder is separate, and the intestine serves health separately; for the stomach delivers to the latter, while the lung delivers to the bladder. Nor should this be overlooked: that in urine, which is the waste product of drink, no trace of food is found, nor does it take on any quality of those food wastes, whether in color or odor. If they had been in the belly together, some quality of those impurities would have been infused. Finally, why do the stones <note>Referencing kidney or bladder stones.</note> that are produced from drink in the bladder never form in the belly, since they are only made from drink? They ought to have been born in the belly as well, if the belly were the receptacle for drink. Even noble poets are not ignorant that drink flows down into the lung. For one says:

->Eupolis in the play titled *The Flatterers*:<-
<note>original: "cœlaces" (from Greek 'Kolakes'). Eupolis was an Athenian poet of Old Comedy and a contemporary of Aristophanes.</note>

Euripides, indeed, is the most manifest supporter of this matter. Since, therefore, both the reasoning of the bodily structure and the noble authority of witnesses support Plato, does anyone who thinks otherwise not seem insane?

<margin>Whether the egg existed first, or the chicken.</margin>

Among these things, Evangelus, envying and mocking the glory of the Greeks, said, "Away with these matters which are debated among you for the sake of displaying loquacity! Rather, if your wisdom is at all clever, I wish to know from you: did the egg exist first, or the chicken?" Disarius replied, "You think you are mocking, and yet the question you have moved is worthy of both inquiry and knowledge. For you, comparing me to yourself in terms of the utility of the matter, have consulted me: whether the chicken first came from the egg, or the egg from the chicken. But this is to be introduced among serious matters in such a way that it ought to be disputed with great care. And I shall bring forward what occurs to me to be said on both sides, leaving it to you to decide which of them you prefer to seem more true. If we concede that all things which exist had a beginning at some time, then the egg will rightly be estimated to have been made first by nature. For that which begins is always as yet imperfect and unformed, and is shaped toward its own perfection by the additions of preceding art and time. Therefore, nature, fashioning the bird, began from an unformed beginning, and the egg existed—in which there is not yet a specific form—as the effect of maturity proceeded little by little. Then, whatever is provided by nature with various ornaments undoubtedly began from the simple, and was thus varied by the addition of complexity. Therefore, the egg is seen to be simple and created with a uniform appearance on all sides, and from that, the variety of ornaments by which the completed form of the bird consists is perfected. For just as the <term>elements</term> <note>The basic building blocks of matter: earth, air, fire, and water.</note> existed first, and thus the remaining bodies were created from their mixture, so the <term>seminal principles</term> <note>original: "rationes seminales" — the inherent generative powers within matter.</note> which are in the egg (if this transition is vital) must be believed to be, as it were, certain elements of the chicken. Nor would I inappropriately compare the egg to the elements from which all things come. For in every kind of living creature produced from mating, you will find that for some, the egg is the beginning, like an element. For living creatures either walk, or creep, or live by swimming or flying. Among those that walk, lizards and similar creatures are created from eggs. Those that creep are born from eggs. From the beginning, all flying things come forth from eggs, except for one which is of an uncertain nature. For the bat indeed flies with skin-covered wings, but it is not to be held among the flying things, as it walks on four feet and gives birth to formed young, and nourishes those it generates with milk. Almost all swimming things arise from eggs of their own kind; the crocodile even comes from shelled eggs like those of flying things. And lest I seem to have extolled the egg too much by the name of an 'element,' consult those initiated into the sacred rites of <term>Father Liber</term> <note>The Roman name for Bacchus/Dionysus; his mystery cults often used the egg as a symbol of cosmic creation.</note>, in which the egg is worshipped with such veneration that, because of its smooth and almost spherical form, closed on all sides and enclosing life within itself, it is called the image of the world. And by the consensus of all, it is established that the world is the beginning of the universe. 

Let the person who wants the chicken to be first come forward and attempt to assert what he defends in these words: An egg is neither the beginning nor the end of the thing to which it belongs. For the beginning is the seed, and the end is the formed bird itself. The egg, however, is the <term>concoction</term> <note>original: "digestio" — here meaning the metabolic processing or maturation of seed.</note> of the seed. Since, therefore, the seed is of the animal, and the egg is of the seed, the egg could not exist before the animal, just as the digestion of food cannot occur before there is one who eats. And it is the same to say the egg was made before the chicken as if someone were to say the womb was made before the woman. And he who asks how there could be a chicken without an egg is like one asking in what way men were made before the genitals by which men are procreated. Whence, just as no one would rightly say that a man belongs to the seed, but rather the seed belongs to the man, so neither does the chicken belong to the egg, but the egg belongs to the chicken. Then, if we concede—as has been said by the opposing side—that these things which exist took some beginning in time, nature first created individual animals in perfect form...

<meta>This page continues the discussion in Book VII of Macrobius's Saturnalia. Disarius is concluding his argument on the chicken-and-egg paradox, asserting that nature produces "perfect" beings first, before moving to Evangelus's new challenge regarding the strange effects of moonlight on meat and health.</meta>

# OF THE SATURNALIA

...Then he gave a perpetual law: that succession through procreation should continue. That it was possible for "perfected" beings <note>In this context, "perfect" means fully formed or adult, rather than a "seed" like an egg.</note> to be created at the very beginning is evidenced even now by many animals that are born fully formed from the earth and rain—such as mice in Egypt, and in other places frogs, snakes, and the like. Eggs, however, were never created from the earth, because there is no "perfection" in them. Nature, in truth, forms what is perfect first, and from those perfect things, these others proceed, just as parts come from the whole. For even if I grant that eggs are the nurseries of birds, let us see what the definition of the philosophers testifies regarding the seed itself, which is decreed thus:

<margin>What a seed is.</margin>
"Seed is a generation proceeding toward the likeness of that from which it comes." But it cannot proceed toward the likeness of a thing that does not yet exist, just as a seed cannot emanate from that which has not yet stood firm. Therefore, in the first origin of things, let us understand that—along with all other living creatures which are born from seed alone and about which there is no doubt they existed before their seed—birds also existed as perfect works of nature the craftswoman. And because the power of generating was inserted into each individual, from these there then proceeded the modes of being born, which nature varied according to the diversity of living things. You have it, Evangelus, on both sides, something to hold onto; and having put aside your mockery for a moment, deliberate with yourself which side you will follow.

And Evangelus said: "Because he makes serious things out of jokes through a violent way of speaking, I wish you would resolve this for me, the true consideration of which has occupied me for a long time. For recently, boars were delivered to me from my Tiburtine estate <note>Tibur is the modern city of Tivoli, near Rome, where many wealthy Romans held villas.</note>, which the woods offered to the hunters.

<margin>Why the flesh of cattle rots more at night than by day.</margin>
And because the hunt had been long-continued, some were carried during the day and others by night. Those which the daylight brought stayed firm with the integrity of their flesh unharmed; but those which were carried through the night, while the moon was at its full brightness, rotted. When this was discovered, those who brought them the following night carried the boars with their flesh intact by thrusting a sharp bronze object into any part of the body. I ask, therefore: why did the lunar light effect a harm that the rays of the sun did not give to the slaughtered cattle?"

"The answer is easy and simple," said Disarius. "For rot never occurs in any thing unless heat and moisture come together. The rotting of cattle is nothing else but when a certain hidden flowing dissolves the solidity of the flesh into liquid. Now, if heat is temperate and moderate, it nourishes moisture; if it is excessive, it dries it out and thins the consistency of the flesh. Therefore, from the slain bodies, the sun draws out the moisture by the force of its greater heat; but the lunar light, in which there is manifest heat but a hidden warmth, spreads the moisture more. And from this, with the addition of time and increased moisture, rot arises."

After these things were said, Evangelus, looking at Eustachius, said: "If you agree with the reason given, you ought to nod your head; or if there is something that moves you otherwise, do not be reluctant to bring it forward, for the force of your speech has ensured that I will not listen to you with a wandering ear."

Eustachius said: "Everything has been said by Disarius both elegantly and truthfully. But this must be looked at more closely: whether the measure of heat is the cause of rot, such that it is said not to happen from greater heat, but to proceed from lesser and temperate heat. For the heat of the sun, which burns excessively when the year is in summer and grows lukewarm in winter, rots meat in summer, not in winter. Therefore, the moon does not spread moisture simply because of its more submissive heat. Rather, there is a certain property which the Greeks call <term>idioma</term> <note>original: "ἰδίωμα" — a specific, unique characteristic or "peculiarity" of a substance.</note>, and a certain nature inherent in the light that flows from it, which moistens bodies and makes them wet as if with a hidden dew; the lunar heat itself, mixed with this, rots the flesh into which it has been infused for a long time. For not every heat is of one quality, such that it differs from another only by being greater or lesser. But it is proven by manifest facts that there are very different qualities in fire that have no fellowship with one another. Goldsmiths use no fire for forming gold except that from straw, because others seem unsuitable for bringing out this material. Physicians, in cooking their remedies, require fire from brushwood rather than from other wood. Those who care for melting and strengthening glass supply their fire with fuel from the tree whose name is the tamarisk <note>original: "myricæ"</note>. The heat from olive wood, while it is healthy for bodies, is ruinous to baths and effectively harmful for dissolving the joints of marble. Therefore, it is no wonder if, by reason of the property which is in each, the heat of the sun dries and the lunar heat moistens. Hence, nurses nourishing children also cover them with wrappings when they are exposed under the moon, lest the lunar light further moisten those who are already full of natural moisture due to their age; and just as wood that is damp with greenness is curved when it receives heat, so the addition of moisture may twist their limbs. Indeed, this is well known: that if anyone gives himself to sleep for a long time under the moon..."

<summary>The text concludes a debate on the chicken-and-egg paradox by arguing for the priority of "perfect" beings over seeds, then transitions into a scientific discussion on why moonlight causes meat to rot and how different types of heat possess unique physical properties.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Book VII of the *Saturnalia* by Macrobius. The dialogue has shifted from the origins of life (the chicken and the egg) to a scientific discussion on the physical properties of the moon and the medicinal qualities of bronze. The speaker, likely the physician Disarius, is answering Evangelus’s earlier questions about why moonlight rots meat and why bronze tools affect wounds differently than iron ones.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN

...it is: he is awakened with difficulty and becomes close to insane, weighed down by the pressure of the humor <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids believed to control health and temperament.</note> which has been diffused and dispersed throughout his entire body. This is due to the lunar property which, in order to flood the body, opens and loosens all its channels. Hence it is that Diana, who is the Moon, is called *Artemis* <note>original: $\alpha\rho\tau\epsilon\mu\iota\sigma$</note> as if she were *Aerotemis* <note>original: $\alpha\epsilon\rho\omicron\tau\epsilon\mu\iota\sigma$</note>, which is to say "cutting the air." She is also invoked by those in labor as Lucina <note>The Roman goddess of childbirth, often identified with Juno or Diana/the Moon.</note>, because it is her specific task to stretch the openings of the body and give way to the channels, which is life-saving for accelerating birth. And this is what the poet Timotheus elegantly expressed.

The property of the moon is shown no less regarding inanimate things. For wood that has been felled either when the moon is full or still waxing is unfit for building, because of its absorption of moisture. Farmers also take care to gather grain from the threshing floors only when the moon is waning, so that it remains dry. Conversely, whatever you wish to be moist, you should handle while the moon is waxing. In that time you will also plant trees more successfully, especially when the moon is above the earth, because the nourishment of moisture is necessary for the growth of stems. The air itself both experiences and reveals the property of lunar moisture. For when the moon is full, or when it is "born" (for even then the side that looks upward is full), the air is either dissolved into rain, or if it is calm, it emits a great deal of dew. This is why the lyric poet Alcman called dew the "son of the air and the moon." Thus it is proved on all sides: that there is a property in the light of the moon for moistening and dissolving flesh, which experience discovers more than logic. 

As for what you said, Evangelus, regarding the sharp bronze—if my conjecture does not fail me—it does not deviate from the truth. For there is in bronze a sharper power which the Greeks call *styptic* <note>original: "stipticam"; an astringent quality that contracts tissues.</note>. This is why they add its scales <note>Copper or bronze flakes produced during forging.</note> to remedies used against the destruction of rot. Furthermore, those who work in bronze mines always possess healthy eyes, and those whose eyelids were previously bare of hair are there reclothed. For the aura that proceeds from the bronze, falling upon the eyes, draws out and dries up the harmful fluids. Whence Homer also...

...calling upon these causes. Aristotle, indeed, is the authority that wounds made by a bronze point are less harmful than those made by iron, and are more easily cured, because, he says, there is in bronze a certain remedial and drying power which it leaves in the wound. By the same reasoning, therefore, a bronze object fixed in the body of a beast resists the lunar moisture.
